<note>This label identifies the book as part of the John Adams Library, a collection of roughly 3,500 volumes that Adams gave to his hometown of Quincy, Massachusetts, in 1822. The "Shelf Number" (Adams 134.11) is a unique <term>call number</term>—a standardized code used by librarians to organize books so they can be easily retrieved from the stacks. In 1894, the town of Quincy transferred the collection to the Boston Public Library to ensure these historically significant books were professionally preserved and accessible to researchers.</note>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page follows the title page of Henri Estienne’s 1570 edition of Diogenes Laertius. It begins the formal dedication to Johann Crato von Krafftheim, a highly influential physician and counselor to three Holy Roman Emperors. The transition from the title page to this personal address signals Estienne’s intent to frame this ancient work for a contemporary elite audience.</meta>

# TO JOHANN CRATO,
## Counselor to the Emperor, a most distinguished man. <note>Johann Crato von Krafftheim (1519–1585) was the personal physician to Emperors Ferdinand I, Maximilian II, and Rudolf II. He was a central figure in the intellectual and political life of the Imperial court.</note>

->HENRI ESTIENNE SENDS GREETINGS. <note>original Latin: "HENR. STEPH. S. D."; an abbreviation for "salutem dicit," the standard formal greeting in Latin correspondence.</note><-

I am sending you these "philosophical lives," most excellent man—or rather, the "lives of philosophers." For most of them (if we are willing to admit the truth) are anything but philosophical—that is, worthy of philosophers. Unless, perhaps, we should say that these lives were indeed worthy of those men, but that the men themselves were unworthy of the name of philosopher. Certainly, we shall find here certain lives of philosophers that are suitable for "courtly philosophy" (for I am pleased to speak with a man of the court about courtly matters). From these, we might first learn **to scrape the blush from one's face** <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐρυθριᾶν ἀποξύσαι τοῦ προσώπου; a Greek idiom for losing all sense of shame or modesty</note>—for what is more destructive to courtiers than modesty? Next, we might learn to be **inclined toward flattery, lying, greed, mockery, jesting, and pleasure.** <note>original Greek: κολακευτικῶς ἔχειν, φιλοψευδῶς, φιλοχρημάτως, φιλογελοίως, φιλοσκωμμόνως, φιληδόνως</note> I even add—so as to please your fellow courtiers—to be **fond of drinking.** <note>original Greek: φιλοπότως</note> Clearly, **this is the "sweet life," the thrice-longed-for, the thrice-blessed.** <note>original Greek: οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ ἡδὺς βίος, ὁ τριπόθητος, ὁ τρισμακάριστος</note> 

But what? You will say, "My dear Estienne, do you place me also in the number of such courtiers?" Certainly not. For not everyone who is a "courtier"—that is, who lives in the court—should be considered a courtier in his life and character. Since, therefore, for those I have mentioned, some kind of life is suitable...

<sig>a.ii. <note>This is a signature mark, used by early printers to help bookbinders assemble the pages in the correct order. "a.ii." indicates the second leaf of the first gathering.</note></sig>

<summary>In this dedication, Henri Estienne introduces his edition of Diogenes Laertius to Johann Crato, using sharp wit to contrast the supposed "wisdom" of ancient philosophers with the vices of 16th-century court life. He distinguishes his addressee, Crato, from the typical corrupt courtier, framing the book as both a scholarly gift and a social commentary.</summary>

<keywords>Johann Crato von Krafftheim, Henri Estienne, court life, satire, Greek philosophy, moral character, Renaissance humanism, dedication</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s dedicatory epistle to Johann Crato von Krafftheim. On the previous page, Estienne jokingly suggested that Diogenes Laertius’s "Lives of the Philosophers" provides a guide for the vices of court life—flattery, greed, and shamelessness. Here, he transitions to a more serious discussion on the distinction between being "learned" and being "good," citing classical authorities like Horace and Cicero.</meta>

I consider [this courtly philosophy] to be compounded from the lives of many philosophers, namely **Aristippus** <note>Aristippus of Cyrene (c. 435–356 BCE) was a pupil of Socrates but founded a school that prioritized pleasure; he was famous for his ability to adapt to the luxurious life of royal courts.</note> (who certainly was a truly courtly philosopher), **Diogenes**, **Crates**, and **Epicurus**; for you, on the contrary, and for those like you, I judge the **Socratic** <note>Socrates was often contrasted with the more "courtly" or "pleasurable" philosophers because of his unwavering commitment to truth and virtue, even unto death.</note> life to be a better fit. But let me have joked enough so far. For everyone knows that from this work of Diogenes, we should seek not what makes us *better*, but what makes us *more learned*. I would have said "wiser," had I not remembered that "wise" is coupled with "good" by Horace himself—just as when he writes in *Epistles, Book I*:

->*“Nor should you think anyone blessed other than the wise and good man.”* <note>original Latin: "Neve putes alium sapiente bonoque beatum." From Horace, Epistles 1.16.20.</note><-
->Also:<-
->*“Or [should he] roam silently among the healthful woods,*<-
->*caring for whatever is worthy of a wise and good man?”* <note>original Latin: "An tacitum sylvas inter reptare salubres, / Curantem quicquid dignum sapiente bonoque est?" From Horace, Epistles 1.4.4-5.</note><-
->Also:<-
->*“A good and wise man will dare to say, 'Pentheus...'”* <note>original Latin: "Vir bonus & sapiens audebit dicere, Pentheu." From Horace, Epistles 1.16.73. This refers to a scene in Euripides' Bacchae where a character remains defiant against a tyrant.</note><-
->Also:<-
->*“A good and wise man says he is ready for the worthy.”* <note>original Latin: "Vir bonus & sapiens dignis ait esse paratum." From Horace, Epistles 1.7.22.</note><-

And **Cicero** himself complains that the "wise" are separated from the "good," and says that this brings great ruin. "This then is that ruin," he says, "that they consider some to be good, and others to be wise." <note>Cicero often argued that true wisdom (sapientia) could not exist without moral goodness (bonitas).</note> And yet, when I say that from these books of Diogenes we should seek things that make us more learned rather than better, I would not want this to be taken as if nothing were read here that might teach us what the duty of a good man is (a good man, I say, judged not by a Christian but by a philosophical standard); but since others...

<summary>Estienne argues that while Diogenes Laertius provides intellectual learning, true wisdom requires a moral "goodness" that is often lacking in the figures he describes. He uses quotes from Horace and Cicero to emphasize that wisdom and virtue should never be separated.</summary>
<keywords>Aristippus, Socratic life, Horace, Cicero, wisdom vs. learning, courtly philosophy, moral standards</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s dedication to Johann Crato von Krafftheim. On the previous page, Estienne quoted Horace to argue that true happiness belongs only to the "wise and good" man, suggesting that while Diogenes Laertius's work makes one "learned," other texts are better for making one "good."</meta>

...there are the books of others from which those things <note>referring to becoming "good" rather than just "learned"</note> can be better learned by us. Indeed, even the one little book of **Epictetus** <note>The *Enchiridion* or "Handbook," a famous guide to Stoic ethics. Estienne notes with surprise that Diogenes Laertius omitted Epictetus from his *Lives*.</note> (whose life I wonder was omitted by our Diogenes) would be an excellent teacher for us in this matter. But just as readers of that golden little book are rare, so certainly rare are those who would prefer to be *better* than to be *more learned*. 

Moreover, the learning that can be sought by us from this work of **Diogenes** is varied and manifold. If I were to begin to speak about it point by point, I would fear that, wishing to teach such things to **Crato** (truly a second **Crates** <note>Estienne makes a play on words between his friend's name, Crato, and the Cynic philosopher Crates of Thebes.</note>), I might seem to want to "teach the sow to Minerva" <note>A classical proverb (*sus Minervam docet*) used when an ignorant person attempts to instruct an expert.</note>. Rather, therefore, it would be my duty at present to discourse briefly on this edition of mine of this work, and on its interpretation published at the same time. And I will do this all the more willingly, because in the meantime I shall excellently (like that character of **Terence** <note>Likely referring to the character Gnatho in Terence's play *The Eunuch*, who was known for using flattering and flowery language.</note>) "adorn with words" this gift of mine which I am sending to you. 

Therefore, **Diogenes Laertius** comes forth, collated with ancient manuscripts with the highest care and diligence by three **Henries** (but especially by **Henry Scrimgeour** <note>A Scottish humanist and scholar (1506–1572) who provided Estienne with valuable manuscript readings.</note>, whom I name for the sake of honor). From these manuscripts, he has obtained the emendation of many passages, and also many words that were missing, and in some places the addition of entire sentences. He is also augmented by the annotations of one of those Henries <note>Referring to Estienne himself.</note>, in which many variant readings that had not been received into the main text are brought forward, and certain passages are also emended by conjecture. There are also some passages in which the translator did not act in good faith...

<page-num>5</page-num>
<sig>a.iii.</sig>

<summary>Estienne transitions from discussing the moral value of the text to describing the scholarly labor behind this edition, specifically citing the contributions of Henry Scrimgeour and the use of ancient manuscripts to fix errors.</summary>
<keywords>Epictetus, Henry Scrimgeour, philology, textual criticism, Henricus Stephanus, Crato von Krafftheim, Terence</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page concludes Henri Estienne’s dedicatory epistle to Johann Crato von Krafftheim. Picking up from the previous page, Estienne is finishing his description of the technical improvements made to the Greek text of Diogenes Laertius before turning his attention to the Latin translation and the physical challenges of early printing.</meta>

...were faithfully rendered. These are the things provided in that Greek edition of **Diogenes**. 

But the Latin translation owes this especially to my edition: that it has been cleared of many (though not all) errors <term>menda; literally "blemishes," used here for typographical or scribal mistakes</term> which previous editions had committed. It is manifest that these occurred because those who printed the first edition—using the translator’s own original manuscript or at least a copy sent by him—were unable to read certain shorthand marks, and in some places even certain words written out in full and without abbreviation. (It is of such great importance to send manuscripts to printers that are **easy to read** <note>original Greek: *εὐανάγνωστα* (euanagnosta)</note>!) 

A single example could be the particle *Quanquam* <note>meaning "although"</note>, which was placed in some spots instead of *Quámque* <note>meaning "and how"</note>, in others instead of *Quomodo* <note>meaning "how"</note>, or in place of another particle. I remember also that in a certain place "Io" was used instead of *Ideo* <note>meaning "therefore"</note>; this happened because of the abbreviation by which some write that little word, namely with an *i* and an *o* carrying a tittle <note>A "tittle" or *titulus* was a small mark or stroke over a letter in a manuscript used to indicate that letters had been omitted to save space.</note>. 

Furthermore, although it was clear that such errors originated not from the translator but (as I said) from those who misread his manuscript, those who boasted that they had restored many things in this translation were so far from actually doing so that they did not even correct these obvious mistakes. 

These are the things, my dear **Crato**, which I wanted you to know concerning both editions of **Diogenes**—that is, the Greek as well as the Latin—which I have given and dedicated to you as a perpetual pledge of our friendship. Moreover, since my edition of **Herodotus** <note>Henri Estienne’s 1570 edition of Herodotus was another major achievement of his press; he frequently bundled his publications for important patrons.</note> was published by me at the same time as **Diogenes**, I have sent it to you along with him. Farewell.

<summary>Estienne explains how his edition of Diogenes Laertius corrects previous typographical errors caused by misreading manuscript abbreviations and concludes his dedication to Crato.</summary>
<keywords>textual criticism, printing history, Johann Crato von Krafftheim, Diogenes Laertius, Herodotus, Latin translation, Greek typography, scribal abbreviations</keywords>

<meta>This page begins the main text of Diogenes Laertius's "Lives and Opinions of Eminent Philosophers," following the alphabetical index of names provided in the previous section. This first page opens the "Prologue," where the author explores the origins of philosophical thought.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut headpiece (band) at the top of the page featuring symmetrical foliate scrolls and a central mask or grotesque face.</image-desc>

# DIOGENES LAER-
tius on the lives, doctrines, and apo-
phthegms of those who distinguished 
themselves in philosophy, BOOK 1 of 10.

elegaic couplet was inscribed upon his tomb:

> The soil of Phalerum holds Eumolpus's dear son,

It is from the father of Musaeus that the Eumolpidae 
<term>Eumolpidae: a prominent Athenian family who held the hereditary priesthood of the Eleusinian Mysteries</term> are 
named among the Athenians. As for Linus, they say he 
was the son of Hermes and the Muse Urania. He com-
posed a "Cosmogony" <term>Cosmogony: an account of the origin of the physical universe</term>, describing the paths 
of the sun and moon, and the origins of animals and 
fruits. The beginning of his poems is as follows:

> There was once a time when all things grew together.

From this source, Anaxagoras <note>A later pre-Socratic philosopher (c. 500–428 BC).</note> took his idea, 
stating that all things were together, and that Mind 
<note>original: "nous"</note> came and set them in order. Linus 
died in Euboea, shot by the arrows of Apollo; and 
his epitaph reads:

> Here the earth received the Theban Linus in death,
> the son of the well-crowned Muse Urania.

And thus philosophy began with the Greeks, whose 
very name shuns any barbarian designation. But those 
who attribute its discovery to foreigners also bring 
forward Orpheus the Thracian, saying he was a 
philosopher and the most ancient of all. For my part, 
I do not know if one should call a man a philosopher 
who has uttered such things about the gods. For what 
should we call one who unsparingly attributes every 
human passion to the gods, including those shameful 
deeds rarely committed by even the worst of men...

### THE PROLOGUE

...having lived <note>The OCR "ζαιῶν" is likely a fragment of "βιοῦν" (to live), referring to the lifespan of the previously mentioned poet.</note> for many years. Myth says that he [Orpheus] was destroyed by women; but the inscription at Dium in Macedonia says he was struck by lightning, reading as follows:

> Here the Muses buried the Thracian Orpheus of the golden lyre,
> Whom Zeus, ruling on high, slew with a smoking bolt.

Those who claim that philosophy began among the Barbarians also set forth the particular style it took among each people. They say that the **Gymnosophists** <term>Gymnosophists: literally "naked wise men," a term Greeks used for Indian ascetics and yogis</term> and the **Druids** <term>Druids: the high-ranking priestly class in ancient Celtic societies</term> expressed their philosophy in riddles. They taught men to honor the gods, to do no evil, and to practice courage. Clitarchus <note>A historian who accompanied Alexander the Great.</note> says in his twelfth book that the Gymnosophists even despise death. 

The **Chaldeans** <note>Ancient astronomers and astrologers of Babylon.</note> occupy themselves with astronomy and prediction. The **Magi** <term>Magi: the priestly caste of ancient Persia (modern Iran), followers of Zoroaster</term> spend their time in the service of the gods, performing sacrifices and prayers, believing that they alone are heard by the divine. They make pronouncements about the substance and origin of the gods, whom they believe to be fire, earth, and water. They condemn the use of images, especially those made by people who claim the gods are male and female. 

They discourse on justice and consider it unholy to burn the dead in fire <note>In Zoroastrianism, fire is a sacred element that must not be polluted by dead flesh.</note>; yet they think it lawful to consort with one’s mother or daughter, as Sotion says in his twenty-third book. They also practice divination and prediction, claiming that the gods appear to them in person. Furthermore, they say the air is full of **phantom-shapes** <term>phantom-shapes: "eidola," or subtle images that flow from objects</term>, which enter the eyes of those with keen sight through a kind of vaporous emission. 

They forbid personal ornaments and the wearing of gold. Their clothing is white, their bed is the ground, and their food consists of vegetables, cheese, and coarse bread. Their staff is a reed, with which they pierce the cheese—so they say—to lift it and eat. As for sorcerous magic <note>original: "goetike," referring to "low" magic or trickery as opposed to the "high" religious rites of the Magi.</note>, they were not even acquainted with it, according to Aristotle in his work *On Magic* and Dinon in the fifth book of his *History*. Dinon also says that the name **Zoroaster**, when translated, means "star-worshipper" <note>original: "astrothuten." This is an ancient folk etymology; modern scholars derive the name from Old Persian meaning "possessor of yellow camels."</note>. He says...

->ΔΙΟΓ. ΛΑΕΡΤ.<-

...which is also the view of Hermodorus. Aristotle, in the first book of his work *On Philosophy*, says that the **Magi** <term>Magi: the priestly caste of ancient Persia (modern Iran)</term> are even more ancient than the Egyptians. According to them, there are two first principles: a good spirit and an evil spirit. To the first, they give the names **Zeus** and **Oromasdes** <note>original: "Ὠρομάσδης" — the Greek form of Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of Zoroastrianism</note>; to the second, **Hades** and **Areimanius** <note>original: "Ἀρειμάνιος" — the Greek form of Angra Mainyu or Ahriman, the spirit of darkness and destruction</note>.

Hermippus also mentions this in his first book *On the Magi*, as does Eudoxus in his *Description of the Earth*, and Theopompus in the eighth book of his *Philippics*. Theopompus further states that, according to the Magi, humans will one day return to life and become immortal, and that the world will endure through their invocations. Eudemus of Rhodes records these same things.

Hecataeus, however, says that according to them [the Magi], the gods are "begotten" <note>Meaning they have a birth or origin, rather than existing eternally from the start.</note>. Clearchus of Soli, in his work *On Education*, claims that the **Gymnosophists** <term>Gymnosophists: literally "naked wise men," a term Greeks used for Indian ascetics and yogis</term> are actually descendants of the Magi. Some writers even suggest that the **Jews** are descended from them.

Furthermore, those who write about the Magi criticize **Herodotus** <note>The famous Greek historian, known as the "Father of History."</note>. They argue that **Xerxes** <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece.</note> would never have shot arrows at the sun or cast chains into the sea <note>Referring to stories in Herodotus where Xerxes "punished" the Hellespont and the sun for hindering his invasion.</note>, because the Magi taught that these were gods. However, it makes sense that he would destroy statues [of foreign gods], as the Magi do not recognize images of the divine.

The philosophy of the **Egyptians** is described as follows: it concerns the gods and justice. They claim that **matter** <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle)</note> was the first principle; from it, the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note> were separated, and eventually, living creatures were produced. They believe the Sun and Moon are gods, naming the former **Osiris** and the latter **Isis**. 

They represent these gods through riddles and symbols <note>original: "αἰνίττεσθαί" — to speak in riddles or allegories</note> such as the beetle, the serpent, and the hawk, as stated by **Manetho** <note>A famous Hellenistic Egyptian priest and historian who wrote about Egyptian history for a Greek audience.</note> in his *Epitome of Physical Doctrines*, and by Hecataeus in the first book of his *On the Philosophy of the Egyptians*.

They build statues and sacred precincts because they do not know the true form of God. They believe the universe had a beginning, is perishable, and is spherical in shape. The stars are made of fire, and their mixtures determine what happens on earth. The moon is eclipsed when it falls into the earth's shadow. They hold that the **soul** both survives after death and migrates into other bodies <note>original: "μετεμβαίνειν" — the doctrine of transmigration or reincarnation.</note>. Rain is produced by changes in the atmosphere. They provide physical explanations for other phenomena as well, as recorded by Hecataeus and...

### THE PROLOGUE

...and Aristagoras relate. They also established laws regarding justice, which they attributed to **Hermes** <note>original: "Ἑρμῆν" — the Greek messenger god, whom the Greeks often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, the bringer of laws and writing</note>, and they honored useful animals as being divine. They also claim that they themselves discovered **geometry**, **astrology**, and **arithmetic**. These are the various accounts regarding the discovery of these arts.

**Pythagoras** <note>original: "Πυθαγόρας"</note> was the first to use the term **philosophy** <term>Philosophy: literally "love of wisdom"</term> and to call himself a **philosopher** <term>Philosopher: "one who seeks or loves wisdom"</term>. This took place in Sicyon while he was conversing with **Leon**, the tyrant of the Sicyonians (or the Phliasians), according to **Heraclides Ponticus** <note>A student of Plato known for his historical and scientific dialogues</note> in his book *On the Woman Who Ceased to Breathe* <note>original: "περὶ τῆς ἄπνου"</note>. Pythagoras argued that no human is truly "wise," for that is a title for God alone. Previously, the discipline was called **wisdom** <note>original: "σοφία"</note> and the man who practiced it was called a "wise man" <note>original: "σοφὸς"</note>—implying he had reached the very peak of mental perfection—whereas a "philosopher" is simply one who embraces and seeks out wisdom.

In those early times, the "wise" were also called **Sophists** <term>Sophists: in this early context, the term meant "experts" or "learned men" rather than its later negative meaning of "deceptive reasoners"</term>. And not only they, but the poets were called sophists as well; for instance, **Cratinus**, in his play *Archilochus*, calls the followers of **Homer** and **Hesiod** by this name when he praises them.

The following men were specifically named as the "Wise Men": **Thales**, **Solon**, **Periander**, **Cleobulus**, **Chilon**, **Bias**, and **Pittacus**. To these, some writers add **Anacharsis the Scythian**, **Myson of Chen**, **Pherecydes of Syros**, and **Epimenides the Cretan**; some even include the tyrant **Pisistratus**. These, then, were the "Wise Men."

Furthermore, there were two original starting points for **philosophy**: one beginning with **Anaximander**, and the other with **Pythagoras**. Anaximander was a student of Thales, while Pherecydes was the teacher of Pythagoras. The first was called the **Ionian School**, because Thales, who was an **Ionian** <note>Ionia was the Greek-settled coast of modern-day Turkey</note> from **Miletus**, was the teacher of Anaximander. The second was called the **Italian School**, named after Pythagoras, because he spent most of his life in **Italy**.

The Ionian lineage ends with **Cleitomachus**, **Chrysippus**, and **Theophrastus**; the Italian school ends with **Epicurus**.

The succession of the Ionian school is as follows: **Thales** was followed by **Anaximander**, then **Anaximenes**, then **Anaxagoras**, then **Archelaus**, and then **Socrates**, who introduced the study of **ethics** <note>the branch of philosophy dealing with moral principles</note>. Socrates was followed by the other "Socratics" and by **Plato**, the founder of the **Ancient Academy**. Plato was followed by **Speusippus** and **Xenocrates**, then **Polemon**, then **Crantor** and **Crates**, then **Arcesilaus**, who established the **Middle Academy**...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...having founded only one [school]. Following him was **Lacydes**, who practiced philosophy in the **New Academy** <term>New Academy: a later phase of Plato's school that became famous for its skeptical approach, questioning whether absolute knowledge is possible</term>; after him came **Carneades**, and then **Clitomachus**. This is how the line reaches Clitomachus. The line ending with **Chrysippus** <note>The third and most prolific head of the Stoic school</note> follows this order: **Socrates**, then **Antisthenes**, then **Diogenes the Dog** <note>The most famous of the Cynics, known for his extreme poverty and social provocations</note>, then **Crates of Thebes**, then **Zeno of Citium** <note>Founder of the Stoic school</note>, then **Cleanthes**, and then **Chrysippus**.

The line ending with **Theophrastus** is: from **Plato** to **Aristotle**, and then **Theophrastus**. In this way, the **Ionian** <note>The branch of philosophy originating in the Greek colonies of Asia Minor</note> school concludes. The **Italian** school proceeds as follows: **Pherecydes**, then **Pythagoras**, then his son **Telauges**, then **Xenophanes**, then **Parmenides**, then **Zeno of Elea**, then **Leucippus**, then **Democritus**, then many others, specifically **Nausiphanes** and **Naucydes**, from whom came **Epicurus**.

Among the philosophers, some have been **Dogmatists**, and others have been **Skeptics** <note>original: "ἐφεκτικοί" (ephektikoi) — literally "those who suspend judgment"</note>. Dogmatists are those who make pronouncements about things as being "graspable" <note>original: "καταληπτών" — meaning they believe the truth can be clearly perceived and understood</note>; Skeptics are those who suspend judgment about things, viewing them as "ungraspable."

Some of them left behind written commentaries, while others did not write at all—such as, according to some, **Socrates**, **Stilpo**, **Philippus**, **Menedemus**, **Pyrrho**, **Theodorus**, **Carneades**, and **Bryson**. Others say **Pythagoras** wrote nothing, nor did **Aristo of Chios**, except for a few letters. Some wrote only a single book, like **Melissus**, **Parmenides**, and **Anaxagoras**. **Zeno** wrote many books, **Xenophanes** even more, **Democritus** more still, and **Aristotle**, **Epicurus**, and **Chrysippus** were even more prolific.

Philosophers have also been named in different ways. Some were named after their cities, such as the **Elians**, the **Megarians**, the **Eretrians**, and the **Cyrenaics**. Others were named after specific locations, such as the **Academics** <note>named after the Grove of Academus where Plato taught</note> and the **Stoics** <note>named after the "Stoa" or Painted Porch where they met</note>. Some were named after circumstances, such as the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "Περιπατητικοί" — meaning "those who walk about," because they often walked while discussing philosophy</note>; and some from insults, such as the **Cynics** <note>original: "κυνικοί" — literally "dog-like," a nickname given to them for their rejection of social norms</note>. Some were named for their dispositions, like the **Eudaemonists** <term>Eudaemonists: from "eudaemonia," the Greek word for happiness or human flourishing</term>. Some took names from their own pretensions, like the **Truth-lovers**, the **Eclectics** <note>those who selected the best doctrines from different schools</note>, and the **Analogists**. Others were named after their teachers, such as the **Socratics** and **Epicureans**, and so forth. Finally, some are called **Natural Philosophers** <note>original: "φυσικοί" (physici)</note> because of their study of nature, while others...

...of the school concerned with character, the **Ethicists**. **Dialecticians**, on the other hand, are those who occupy themselves with the intricacies <note>original: "τερθρείαν" (terthreian) — refers to the subtle or sometimes trivial hair-splitting involved in logical debate</note> of arguments. There are three parts of philosophy: **Physics**, **Ethics**, and **Dialectic**. **Physics** is the study of the universe and its contents; **Ethics** is the study of life and matters concerning us; and **Dialectic** is that which governs the reasoning of both. Until the time of **Archelaus** <note>A teacher of Socrates and the last of the major "Physical" philosophers of the Ionian school</note>, the physical branch was the primary form; from the time of **Socrates**, as previously mentioned, the ethical branch became dominant; and from **Zeno of Elea**, the dialectical branch began.

Of the **Ethical** branch, ten schools <term>school: original "αἵρεσις" (hairesis), meaning a "choice" or a system of principles that one chooses to follow</term> have arisen: the **Academic**, **Cyrenaic**, **Elian**, **Megarian**, **Cynic**, **Eretrian**, **Dialectical**, **Peripatetic**, **Stoic**, and **Epicurean**.

The leaders of these schools were as follows:
*   **Plato** founded the **Old Academy**.
*   **Arcesilaus** led the **Middle Academy**.
*   **Lacydes** led the **New Academy**.
*   **Aristippus of Cyrene** founded the **Cyrenaic** school.
*   **Phaedo of Elis** founded the **Elian** school.
*   **Euclides of Megara** founded the **Megarian** school.
*   **Antisthenes the Athenian** founded the **Cynic** school.
*   **Menedemus of Eretria** founded the **Eretrian** school.
*   **Clitomachus of Carthage** founded the **Dialectical** school.
*   **Aristotle of Stagira** founded the **Peripatetic** school.
*   **Zeno of Citium** founded the **Stoic** school.
*   The **Epicurean** school is named after **Epicurus** himself.

However, **Hippobotus** in his work *On Schools* says there are nine schools and systems: first, the **Megarian**; second, the **Eretrian**; third, the **Cyrenaic**; fourth, the **Epicurean**; fifth, the **Annicerean**; sixth, the **Theodorean**; seventh, the **Zenonian** (which is the same as the **Stoic**); eighth, the **Old Academic**; and ninth, the **Peripatetic**. He does not include the **Cynic**, **Elian**, or **Dialectical** schools. As for the **Pyrrhonian** <note>The school of extreme skepticism founded by Pyrrho of Elis</note> school, most do not include it because of its lack of clarity. Some say it is a school in certain respects, but in others it is not. It appears to be a school, for we define a "school" as one that follows—or seems to follow—a specific rational principle based on appearances. ...if they lack a consistent connection in their doctrines, it can no longer be called a school <term>school: original "αἵρεσις" (hairesis), meaning a "choice" or a system of principles that one chooses to follow</term>; for it would possess no settled teachings. These, then, are the origins and successions, the various parts, and the many schools of philosophy. Quite recently, an **Eclectic** school was also introduced by **Potamo of Alexandria**, who selected those doctrines that pleased him from each of the existing schools.

He holds (as he says in his *Elementary Instruction*) that there are two criteria of truth: first, that by which the judgment is made—namely, the "ruling faculty" <note>original: "ἡγεμονικόν" (hegemonikon) — the central, governing part of the soul or mind according to ancient psychology</note>; and second, that through which the judgment is made—such as the most accurate perception. He identifies the principles of the universe as matter, quality, the active power, and place (answering the questions: out of what, by what agent, of what kind, and in what location). The ultimate goal <term>goal: original "τέλος" (telos), the final end or purpose of human life</term> toward which everything is directed is a life made perfect by every virtue, which includes the natural needs of the body and external goods.

We must now speak of the men themselves, beginning first with **Thales**.

## T H A L E S

**Thales**, then—according to **Herodotus**, **Duris**, and **Democritus**—was the son of Examyas and Cleobuline, of the family of the Thelidae. These were Phoenicians, the most noble of the descendants of Cadmus and Agenor, as **Plato** also confirms. He was the first person to be called "Wise" during the year Damasias was archon <note>A high-ranking magistrate in Athens</note> at Athens, the same period when the group known as the Seven Sages was named, as **Demetrius of Phalerum** records in his *List of Archons*. He was enrolled as a citizen in **Miletus** <note>A powerful Greek city on the coast of modern-day Turkey</note> when he arrived there with Neleus, who had been expelled from Phoenicia. However, most writers claim he was a native-born Milesian of a distinguished family.

After his involvement in politics, he devoted himself to the study of nature. According to some authorities, he left no written work behind; for the *Nautical Astronomy* often attributed to him is said to be the work of **Phocus of Samos**. (**Callimachus**, however, recognizes him as the discoverer of the Little Bear <note>The constellation Ursa Minor, used for navigation</note>, writing in his *Iambics* as follows:

<meta>This page continues the biography of Thales of Miletus, transitioning from his ancestry to his scientific discoveries and personal anecdotes.</meta>

<page-num>9</page-num>
<header>T H A L E S. Book 1</header>

And he is said to have measured the small stars of the **Wain** <note>original: "ἁμάξης" (hamaxes) — referring here to the constellation Ursa Minor (the Little Dipper)</note>, by which the **Phoenicians** sail. According to some accounts, he wrote only two treatises: *On the Solstice* and *On the Equinox*, <margin>but some say</margin> considering everything else to be beyond comprehension. According to others, he was the first to study astronomy <term>astronomy: original "ἀστρολογῆσαι" (astrologēsai), which in antiquity referred to the scientific study of the stars</term>, and the first to predict solar eclipses and solstices, as **Eudemus** says in his *History of Astronomy*. For this reason, both **Xenophanes** and **Herodotus** express their admiration for him; **Heraclitus** and **Democritus** also bear witness to his fame.

Some also claim that he was the first to declare that souls are immortal; among these is **Choerilus** the poet. He was also the first to discover the sun's path from solstice to solstice, and the first to declare that the size of the sun is 1/720th part of the lunar circle <note>This likely refers to the angular diameter of the sun or moon as seen from earth—a remarkably accurate ancient measurement</note>. According to some, he was also the first to call the last day of the month the "thirtieth." He was also the first to discuss nature <note>original: "περὶ φύσεως" (peri physeōs) — the study of the physical world</note>, as some tell it. 

**Aristotle** and **Hippias** say that he even attributed a soul to inanimate things, using the **magnet** <note>original: "λίθου τῆς μαγνήτιδος" (lithou tēs magnētidos) — the lodestone</note> and **amber** <note>original: "ἠλέκτρου" (ēlektrou)</note> as evidence, because they have the power to move other objects. **Pamphila** says that, having learned geometry from the **Egyptians**, he was the first to inscribe a right-angled triangle in a circle, whereupon he sacrificed an ox. Others, however—among whom is **Apollodorus** the calculator—attribute this <margin>to</margin> **Pythagoras**. Thales further developed the discoveries that **Callimachus** says in his *Iambics* were found by **Euphorbus the Phrygian**, such as scalene triangles and other matters related to theoretical geometry. 

He also seems to have given excellent counsel in political matters. For instance, when **Croesus** <note>The wealthy King of Lydia</note> sent a proposal to the **Milesians** for a military alliance, Thales blocked it; this act saved the city when **Cyrus** <note>Cyrus the Great of Persia</note> later emerged victorious. **Heraclides** records that Thales himself said he lived a solitary life as a private individual. <margin>of the</margin> Some say he married and had a son named **Kibisthus**, while others say he remained unmarried but adopted his sister's son. When he was once asked why he did not have children of his own, he replied, "Because I love children." They also say that when his mother tried to force him to marry, he would say, "By Zeus, it is not yet the time!" Then, when he had passed his prime and she pressed him again, he said, "It is no longer the time."

...of memory, it is no longer the time to speak. Hieronymus of Rhodes also says, in the second book of his *Scattered Notes*, that Thales once wished to show how easy it is to grow rich. Foreseeing that there would be an abundant harvest of olives, he took an option on the lease of the oil presses <note>original: "ἐλαιουργεῖα" (elaiourgeia) — this is a famous anecdote intended to prove that philosophers could be wealthy if they chose, but their interests lie elsewhere</note> and collected a vast amount of money. He proposed that water was the first principle <term>first principle: original "ἀρχὴν" (archēn) — the fundamental substance or "stuff" from which everything else is made</term> of all things, and that the world is alive and full of spirits <note>original: "δαιμόνων" (daimonōn) — in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but divine guiding spirits or forces</note>. They say he also discovered the seasons of the year and divided it into three hundred and sixty-five days. No one was his teacher, except that he went to Egypt and lived among the priests. Hieronymus also says that he measured the pyramids by observing their shadow at the exact moment when our own shadow is equal to our height. He also lived with Thrasybulus, the tyrant of Miletus, as Minyes reports. The story of the tripod found by the fishermen is well known, which was sent to the wise men by the people of Miletus. For they say that certain Ionian youths bought a "catch" of the net in advance from Milesian fishermen; but when the tripod was hauled up, a dispute arose. Eventually, the Milesians sent to Delphi to consult the oracle, and the god gave this response:

> Offspring of Miletus, do you ask Phoebus about the tripod?
> Who is first of all in wisdom? To him I award the tripod.

Accordingly, they gave it to Thales. He gave it to another, and that one to another, until it came to **Solon**. He, however, declared that God was first in wisdom, and so he sent it to Delphi. But **Callimachus** <note>A celebrated scholar-poet of the Library of Alexandria</note> tells the story differently in his *Iambics*, having taken it from Leandrius of Miletus. He says that a certain Bathycles of Arcadia left a bowl <note>original: "φιάλην" (phialēn) — a shallow ceramic or metal bowl used for libations</note> at his death, with instructions that it be given to whichever of the wise men was the best. It was given to Thales, and after going the rounds, it came back to Thales again. He then dedicated it to Didymaean Apollo, with this inscription, according to Callimachus:

> Thales gives me to the ruler of the people of Neleus,
> Having received this prize twice for his excellence.

But the prose version of the inscription is as follows: **Thales, son of Examyas, a Milesian, to Delphinian Apollo.**

### THALES. Book 1.

...twice receiving the prize of the Greeks <note>original: "Ἑλλήνων ἀριστεῖον δὶς λαβών"</note>. The son of Bathycles who carried the bowl around was named Thueion, as stated by Hellousis in his work *On Achilles*, and by Alexon of Myndus in the ninth book of his *Legends*. Eudoxus of Cnidus and Euanthes of Miletus say that one of the friends of Croesus <note>the famously wealthy King of Lydia</note> received a golden cup from the king to give to the wisest of the Greeks. He gave it to Thales, and it passed from him to Chilon. Chilon then asked the Pythian <note>the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi</note> who was wiser than himself; the Oracle named Myson, whom we shall discuss later. Eudoxus places this Myson among the Seven Sages in place of Cleobulus, while Plato <note>the philosopher</note> places him there instead of Periander. Concerning Myson, the Pythian Oracle spoke as follows:

> I declare that Myson of Chen in Oeta is 
> better equipped with sharp wits than you.

The one who had asked the question was Anacharsis. Daidachus the Platonist and Clearchus say that a bowl <term>phiale</term> <note>a shallow ceremonial bowl used for pouring drink offerings to the gods</note> was sent by Croesus to Pittacus, and thus it began its circuit. But Andron, in his work *The Tripod*, says that the people of Argos offered a tripod <term>tripod</term> <note>a three-legged copper or bronze vessel, often given as a prestigious prize in ancient Greece</note> as a prize for excellence to the wisest of the Greeks; Aristodemus of Sparta was judged the winner, but he yielded the honor to Chilon. Alcaeus mentions Aristodemus in these lines:

> For they say that once Aristodemus spoke 
> no foolish word in Sparta: "Money is the man," 
> and "no poor man is ever noble."

Some say that a ship laden with goods was sent by Periander to Thrasybulus, the tyrant of Miletus, and when it was wrecked in the Sea of Cos, the tripod was later found by some fishermen. Phanodicus, however, says it was found in the Athenian sea and brought to the city; there, after a public assembly was held, it was sent to Bias. We will explain the reason for this in the section on Bias. Others claim it was crafted by Hephaestus <note>the god of fire and metalworking</note> and given by the god to Pelops on his wedding day. It later passed to Menelaus and was carried off by Helen...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

The tripod was said to have been thrown into the sea of Cos by Alexander <note>original: "Ἀλεξάνδρου" — this likely refers to the Trojan prince Paris, also known as Alexander</note> because of a Spartan woman who predicted it would be a cause of great strife. Much later, when certain men from Lebedus purchased a "cast" <term>bolon</term> <note>the total catch of a single throw of a fishing net</note> at that spot, the tripod was caught in the net. A fight broke out with the fishermen, and the dispute reached as far as the city of Cos. When they could achieve no resolution, they reported the matter to the Milesians, who were their mother city. After the Milesians' ambassadors were treated with contempt, Miletus went to war against the Coans. After many had fallen on both sides, an oracle was delivered declaring that the tripod must be given to the wisest man. Both sides agreed to give it to Thales. After he had completed his turn with the prize, he dedicated it to Apollo of Didyma <note>the site of a famous temple and oracle near Miletus</note>. The oracle given to the Coans was delivered in this manner:

> Strife shall not cease between the mortals of Ionia, 
> Until you send from your city that golden tripod, 
> Which Hephaestus <note>the god of fire and craftsmanship</note> cast into the sea; 
> Let it reach the house of the man 
> Who understands the things that are, that shall be, and that were before.

The oracle given to the Milesians was:

> Offspring of Miletus, do you ask Phoebus <note>a title for Apollo meaning "the Bright One"</note> about the tripod?

This is the account as it has been told. However, Hermippus <note>a biographer from the 3rd century BCE</note>, in his *Lives*, attributes to Thales the saying which some others attribute to Socrates. For he says that Thales used to say he was grateful to Fortune for three things: first, that I was born a human and not a beast; second, that I was born a man and not a woman; and third, that I was born a Greek and not a barbarian. 

It is also said that while he was being led out of his house by an old woman to observe the stars, he fell into a ditch. When he cried out in pain, the old woman said: "How, Thales, do you think you will know what is in the heavens when you are not even able to see what is right at your feet?" Timon <note>the Skeptic philosopher and satirist</note> also knew of his work in astronomy. In his *Silli* <note>a work of satirical poetry</note>, he praises him, saying:

> Such a one among the Seven Sages was Thales, wise in his astronomical study.

Lobon of Argos <note>an ancient author who wrote about poets</note> says that the writings of Thales reached two hundred verses. He also reports that the following was inscribed upon the philosopher's statue:

# THALES. Book 1

Ionian Miletus raised and brought forth this Thales,
-> The astronomer eldest of all in wisdom. <-
<note>original: "Ἀστρολόγον" — while we usually distinguish between astronomy and astrology today, in Thales' time, the term referred broadly to the study of the stars.</note>
Regarding his own compositions, some say he left nothing in writing, while others claim he wrote on the solstice and the equinox. He declared that many words are not proof of a wise opinion. "Seek one wise thing, choose one good thing, for you will loosen the tongues of chatterers who speak without end." The following sayings of his are widely reported:

The oldest of all things is God, for he is unbegotten. 
The most beautiful is the universe <term>kosmos</term> <note>meaning "orderly arrangement"</note>, for it is the handiwork of God. 
The greatest is space, for it contains all things. 
The fastest is the mind, for it runs through everything. 
The strongest is necessity, for it rules over all. 
The wisest is time, for it discovers everything. 

He said that death differs in no way from living. Someone then asked him, "Why then do you not die?" He replied, "Because it makes no difference." To one inquiring which was created first, night or day, he replied, "Night, by one day." Someone asked him if a man doing wrong can hide his actions from the gods. "No," he said, "not even his thoughts." To an adulterer who asked if he should swear an oath that he had not committed the act, he replied, "Perjury is no worse than adultery." <note>Thales implies that if you are willing to commit the first sin, the second—lying under oath—is just as likely.</note>

When asked what is difficult, he said: "To know oneself." 
What is easy? "To give advice to another." 
What is sweetest? "Success." 
What is the divine? "That which has neither beginning nor end." 
Asked what was the strangest thing he had ever seen, he replied: "An old tyrant." <note>Implying that tyrants usually died young by violence.</note>
How can one bear misfortune most easily? "By seeing one's enemies faring worse." 
How might we live most excellently and justly? "If we ourselves do not do the things we blame in others." 
Who is happy? "He who is healthy in body, resourceful in fortune, and uneducated in soul." <note>The OCR reads "ἀπαίδευτος" (uneducated), though most standard manuscripts read "εὐπαίδευτος" (well-educated). This may be a scribal error in the source text.</note>

He says to remember friends whether they are present or absent. Do not beautify your appearance, but be beautiful in your conduct. "Do not get rich through evil means," he says, "nor let slander turn you against those who have shared your trust." "Whatever support you provide to your parents," he says, "expect the same from your children." 

He said that the Nile rises because its flow is blocked by the Etesian winds <note>strong, seasonal Mediterranean winds</note> blowing from the opposite direction. Apollodorus, in his *Chronology*, says...

### DIOG. LAERT.

...he was born in the first year of the 35th Olympiad <note>640 BCE</note>. He died at the age of seventy-eight, or—as Sosicrates says—ninety. He is said to have passed away during the 58th Olympiad <note>548–545 BCE</note>, having lived in the time of Croesus, for whom he promised to make the river Halys passable without a bridge by diverting the stream.

According to Demetrius of Magnesia in his work *On People of the Same Name*, there were five other men named Thales: first, a rhetorician from Callantia who was known for a strained and affected style; second, a painter from Sicyon of great natural talent; third, a very ancient figure who lived in the time of Hesiod, Homer, and Lycophron; fourth, one mentioned by Duris in his treatise *On Painting*; and fifth, a more recent and obscure man mentioned by Dionysius in his *History of the Celts*.

The sage himself died while watching an athletic contest, overcome by heat, thirst, and the weakness of old age. Upon his tomb, the following is inscribed:

> Indeed, this monument is small, but its fame reaches the heavens; 
> Behold this, the tomb of the most thoughtful Thales.

We ourselves also wrote an epigram for him in our first book of *Epigrams in Various Meters*:

> Once, while watching an athletic contest, O Sun-God Zeus,
> You snatched the wise man Thales from the stadium.
> I praise you for leading him close to yourself, for the old man
> Could no longer see the stars from the earth.

To him is attributed the phrase <term>Know thyself</term> <note>original: "Γνῶθι σαυτόν" (Gnothi sauton)</note>; although Antisthenes in his *Successions of Philosophers* says it belongs to Phemonoe <note>a mythical Greek prophetess</note>, and that Chilon claimed it as his own.

Regarding the Seven Sages—for it is worthwhile to speak of them collectively here—the following accounts are given: Damon of Cyrene, who wrote *On the Philosophers*, criticizes them all, but especially the Seven. Anaximenes, however, says they all applied themselves to poetry. But Dicaearchus says they were neither sages nor philosophers, but were rather men of practical intelligence and legislators. Archetimus of Syracuse has written an account of their meeting...

# THALES. Book 1

...at the court of Cypselus <note>The tyrant of Corinth</note>, where he himself says he met them. Ephorus, however, says they met at the court of Croesus <note>The famously wealthy King of Lydia</note>, with the exception of Thales. Some say they gathered at the Panionion <note>A sanctuary and meeting place for the Ionian League</note>, in Corinth, and at Delphi. There is also disagreement regarding their famous maxims, as different sayings are attributed to different people, such as this one:

> Chilon was a wise Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> who said these things:
> "Nothing in excess; all beautiful things belong to the right moment." <note>original: "Μηδὲν ἄγαν, καιρῷ πάντα πρόσεστι καλά"</note>

There is also debate concerning their total number. Leandrius, for instance, omits Cleobulus and Myson, and instead approves of Leophantus son of Gorsiadas (either from Lebedus or Ephesus) and Epimenides the Cretan. Plato, in his dialogue *Protagoras*, includes Myson instead of Periander. Ephorus includes Anacharsis instead of Myson. Some even add Pythagoras to the list. Dicaearchus transmits four names that are universally agreed upon: Thales, Bias, Pittacus, and Solon. He mentions six others, from whom three are to be selected: Aristodemus, Pamphilus, Chilon the Lacedaemonian, Cleobulus, Anacharsis, and Periander. 

Some add Acusilaus, as well as Cabas (or Scabras), the Argive. Hermippus, in his book *On the Sages*, claims there are seventeen in total, from whom different authors choose different sets of seven; these are: Solon, Thales, Pittacus, Bias, Chilon, Cleobulus, Periander, Anacharsis, Acusilaus, Epimenides, Leophantus, Pherecydes, Aristodemus, Pythagoras, Lasus (son of Charmantides or Sisymbrinus, or, as Aristoxenus says, son of Chabeinus), the Hermionian <note>Lasus of Hermione, a lyric poet and music theorist</note>, and Anaxagoras. Hippobotus, in his *Catalogue of Philosophers*, lists: Orpheus, Linus, Solon, Periander, Anacharsis, Cleobulus, Myson, Thales, Bias, Pittacus, Epicharmus, and Pythagoras. The following letters of Thales are also in circulation:

->Thales to Pherecydes.<-

I hear that you are to be the first of the Ionians to reveal a discourse to the Greeks about divine matters. Perhaps your decision is a righteous one, to commit your writing to the public good...

### Thales to Solon.

If you should depart from Athens, it seems to me that you would most suitably establish a home in Miletus among your own colonists. For here, I assure you, there is nothing to fear. Even if you are distressed that we Milesians are ruled by a tyrant—for you hate all absolute rulers <note>original: "αἰσυμνήτας" (aisymnetas), referring to elective dictators or supreme magistrates</note>—you might still find pleasure living out your life with us, your companions. Bias <note>Bias of Priene, another of the Seven Sages</note> has also written to you, inviting you to come to Priene; if you prefer the city of the Prienians as a place to dwell, we ourselves will come to live there with you.

## SOLON.

Solon, the son of Execestides, a native of Salamis, was the first to introduce the <term>Seisachtheia</term> <note>Literally the "shaking off of burdens," a set of laws designed to alleviate debt</note> to the Athenians. This was a redemption of both persons and property. For previously, men borrowed money by putting up their own bodies as collateral, and many were forced into servitude because of poverty. Since seven talents were owed to him from his paternal inheritance, he was the first to waive the debt, and he encouraged the rest to do the same. This law was called the "shaking off of burdens," and the reason for the name is obvious. Afterward, he established the rest of his laws, which would be a long task to recount in detail, and inscribed them upon the <term>axones</term>... <note>original: "ἄξονας" (axones), revolving wooden tablets or pillars used for public display of the law</note>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>SOLON. Book I.</header>

...he set up the law-tablets <note>original: "ἄξονας" (axones). These were revolving wooden beams on which Solon's laws were inscribed for public view.</note>. But his greatest achievement occurred when his homeland of Salamis was being contested by both the Athenians and the Megarians. The Athenians had been defeated many times in these wars and had passed a decree that if anyone should ever again advise fighting for Salamis, they would be punished with death. Solon, pretending to be insane and wearing a garland on his head, rushed into the marketplace. There, he had a herald read to the Athenians the elegies he had composed concerning Salamis, and he stirred their spirits. They went to war against the Megarians once more and were victorious because of Solon. These were the elegiac verses that most deeply moved the Athenians:

->I would then rather be a man of Pholegandros or Sicinus<-
->Instead of an Athenian, having traded my homeland.<-
->For quickly would this rumor spread among men:<-
->'This is an Attic man from among those who abandoned Salamis.'<-

->And then,<-

->Let us go to Salamis to fight for the island<-
->So lovely, and to push away our bitter shame.<-

He also persuaded them to acquire the Chersonese in Thrace <note>The Thracian Chersonese is the modern Gallipoli Peninsula.</note>. So that it might not seem that he held Salamis by force alone but also by right, he dug up some graves and showed that the dead were turned toward the east, as was the Athenian custom of burial. Furthermore, the tombs themselves faced the east, and the registrations of the names were engraved according to their demes <note>A 'deme' was a local district of Athens; Solon was arguing that the ancient burials followed Athenian administrative patterns.</note>, which was characteristic of Athenians. Some also say that he inserted a line into the "Catalogue of Ships" in Homer’s *Iliad*, following the verse:

->Ajax led twelve ships from Salamis,<-
->And stationed them where the Athenian battalions stood.<-

From that time on, the common people looked up to him, and they would have gladly been ruled by him as a tyrant. But he did not choose this; instead, having sensed the intentions of his kinsman Peisistratus <note>Peisistratus eventually became the tyrant of Athens, despite Solon’s warnings.</note>, as Sosicrates says, he did everything in his power to prevent it. ...into the assembly with breastplate and shield <note>Solon appeared in full military gear to signal a state of emergency, a dramatic gesture intended to wake the citizens to the threat of tyranny.</note>, he foretold to them the coming attack of Peisistratus. Not only did he warn them, but he declared he was ready to help. He said: "Men of Athens, I am wiser than some of you, and braver than others. I am wiser than those who do not see through the deception of Peisistratus, and braver than those who understand it but remain silent out of fear." The Council, who were supporters of Peisistratus <note>original: "Πεισιιστρατίδαι" (Peisistratids). This refers to the political faction favoring the future tyrant.</note>, claimed he was mad. ->A short time will show my madness to the citizens,<-
->It will show when the truth comes into the open.<-

And regarding the tyranny of Peisistratus which he saw coming, he wrote these verses:

->From a cloud comes the force of snow and hail,<-
->And thunder is born from the bright lightning-flash.<-
->By great men a city is destroyed; through the ignorance<-
->Of the people, they fall into the slavery of a monarch.<-

When Peisistratus finally seized power, Solon could not persuade the people to resist. He then placed his weapons in front of the general’s office <note>original: "στρατηγίου" (strategion), the headquarters of the Athenian generals.</note> and said, "O my fatherland, I have helped you in both word and deed." After this, he sailed away to Egypt and to Cyprus. He eventually came to the court of Croesus <note>Croesus was the King of Lydia, famous for his immense wealth.</note>. When Croesus asked him, "Who seems happy to you?" Solon replied, "Tellus the Athenian, and Cleobis and Biton," mentioning these famous examples of virtuous lives. Some say that Croesus, having adorned himself in all sorts of finery and seating himself upon his throne, asked Solon if he had ever seen a more beautiful sight. Solon replied that cocks, pheasants, and peacocks were more beautiful, for they are adorned with a natural brilliance that is ten thousand times better.

Leaving there, he went to Cilicia and founded a city which he called Soloi after himself. He settled a few Athenians there, who, in the course of time, corrupted their pure Greek speech by mixing with the locals; they were then said to "solecize" <note>term: <term>solecize</term> (σολοικίζειν). This is the legendary origin of the word "solecism," referring to a grammatical error or a blunder in speech.</note>. Those from this city in Cilicia are called *Soleis*, while those from the city in Cyprus are called *Solioi*. ### Peisistratus to Solon.

I am not the only one of the Greeks to have seized a tyranny <note>In the ancient Greek context, a "tyranny" (tyrannis) referred to a ruler who took power through unconventional or unconstitutional means, not necessarily a cruel or "tyrannical" leader in the modern sense.</note>, nor do I do so as one without a claim, being of the lineage of the Codrids <note>The Codridae were the descendants of Codrus, the semi-mythical last King of Athens. Peisistratus claimed he was merely reclaiming his ancestral right to rule.</note>. For I have taken back what the Athenians once swore to provide to Codrus and his descendants, but which they later took away. In all other matters, I commit no sin against either gods or men; rather, I allow the citizens to manage their affairs according to the laws <note>original: "θεσμούς" (thesmous). This refers specifically to the legal code or "statutes" established by Solon himself.</note> that you laid down for them. Indeed, they live better now than they did under a democracy; for I permit no one to act with insolence. 

And though I am the tyrant, I receive nothing more than my due dignity and honor; I take only those defined rewards that belonged to the kings of old. Every Athenian pays a tenth <note>A 10% income or agricultural tax.</note> of his own plot, not for my personal profit, but to provide for public sacrifices and other communal expenses, and to be ready should war overtake us. 

I do not blame you for revealing my intentions; you did so out of goodwill for the city rather than out of hatred for me. Furthermore, you did so because you were ignorant of the kind of government I would establish. For had you known, you might perhaps have supported me as I established it, and you would not have fled. Return home, then, and trust my word—even without an oath—that Solon shall suffer nothing unpleasant at the hands of Peisistratus. Know that none of my other enemies have suffered either. If you choose to be one of my friends, you will be among the first; for I see nothing deceitful or untrustworthy in you. Whether you choose otherwise...

...to live in Athens, it shall be permitted to you. For our sake, do not be deprived of your fatherland.

These things Peisistratus wrote. But Solon says that the limit of a human life is seventy years. He also seems to have established most excellent laws: "If anyone does not support his parents, let him be disenfranchised" <note>original: "ἄτιμος" (atimos). In ancient Athens, *atimia* was a loss of civil rights, meaning the person could no longer vote, hold office, or speak in the assembly.</note>. Likewise, also for the one who has squandered his paternal inheritance; and the idle man <note>original: "ἀργός" (argos). Solon famously made idleness a punishable offense to ensure all citizens contributed to the city's economy.</note> shall be liable to prosecution by anyone who wishes to indict him. Lysias, however, in his speech against Nicias, says that Draco <note>Draco was Solon's predecessor, known for his extremely harsh "Draconian" laws where even minor offenses were punished by death.</note> wrote this law, but Solon enacted it. He also barred the one who had lived a life of debauchery from the speaker’s platform <note>original: "βήματος" (bēmatos). The Bema was the stone platform in the assembly where citizens stood to address the public.</note>.

He also reduced the rewards of the athletes in the games, fixing the prize for an Olympic victor at five hundred drachmas, and for an Isthmian victor at one hundred, and proportionally for the others. For he said it was in poor taste <note>original: "ἀπειρόκαλον" (apeirokalon). This implies a lack of refinement or a vulgar sense of proportion.</note> to inflate the honors of these men, but rather only for those who died in wars, whose sons should also be supported and educated at public expense. Because of this, men were eager to become noble and brave in war: men like Polyzelus, Cynegirus, Callimachus, and indeed all those who fought at Marathon. Furthermore, Harmodius and Aristogeiton, and Miltiades, and countless others. 

Athletes, on the other hand, even while practicing, are very expensive; when they win, they are a burden to the state; and they are crowned more against their own country than against their antagonists. And when they grow old, as Euripides says:

> Like old cloaks, they lose their threads and perish.

Solon, seeing this, treated them with only moderate favor. Most excellent was also this law: that a guardian should not live with the mother of the orphans, and that no one should be a guardian to whom the estate would fall if the orphans were to die. Also this: that a seal-engraver <note>original: "Δακτυλιογλύφῳ" (daktylioglyphō). A craftsman who carves the intricate designs on signet rings used to sign official documents.</note> is not permitted to keep an impression of a ring that has been sold. And if anyone knocks out the eye of a man who has only one eye, he shall have both of his own eyes knocked out in return. "What you did not set down, do not take up; otherwise, the penalty is death." If the Archon <note>The Archon was the chief magistrate of Athens.</note> is caught being drunk, the penalty shall be death. He also wrote that the poems of Homer should be recited by prompt <note>original: "ἐξ ὑποβολῆς" (ex hypobolēs). This refers to a regulated performance where rhapsodes followed a fixed sequence of the text, rather than performing random fragments.</note>, so that...

# SOLON. Book 1.
### b. iiii.

...that where the first reciter left off, from that point the next should begin. Thus, Solon did more to bring Homer to light than Peisistratus did, as Dieuchidas <note>Dieuchidas of Megara was a 4th-century BCE historian who wrote about the history of the region.</note> says in the fifth book of his *History of Megara*. The verses he particularly emphasized were those beginning: "And those who held Athens..." <note>original: "Οἳ δ' ἄρ' Ἀθήνας εἶχον." This refers to a passage in the Iliad (2.546) which established Athens' ancient prestige; Solon was accused of inserting lines here to bolster Athenian territorial claims.</note> and what follows. Solon was also the first to call the thirtieth day of the month "the old and the new" <note>original: "ἔνην καὶ νέαν" (enēn kai nean). Solon reformed the calendar so the last day of the lunar month accounted for the transition to the new moon.</note>. He was also the first to organize a joint meeting of the nine archons <term>Archons: the nine chief magistrates or executive officers of the Athenian state.</term> so they might deliberate together, as Apollodorus says in the second book of his *Treatise on Legislators*. Furthermore, when civil strife broke out, he refused to take sides with those from the City, nor with those from the Plain, nor even with those from the Coast <note>These three factions—the Pedieis (wealthy landowners of the plain), the Paralioi (merchants of the coast), and the Diakrioi (poorer hill-dwellers/city-folk)—represented the deep social and economic divisions in Athens.</note>.

He used to say that speech was the "image" or mirror of deeds; and that the King was the one most powerful in strength. He compared laws to spiderwebs: for just as a spider's web, if something light and weak falls into it, holds it fast, but if something larger falls in, it breaks through and escapes, so too do the laws treat the weak and the powerful. He also said that speech should be sealed with silence, and silence should be sealed by the "opportune moment" <note>original: "καιρῷ" (kairō). Kairos refers to the critical, right, or opportune moment for action or speech.</note>. 

He remarked that those who held power under tyrants were much like the pebbles used on a counting-board <note>original: "ψήφοις ταῖς ἐπὶ τῶν λογισμῶν." Ancient Greeks used an abacus-like board with pebbles (psephoi) for calculations. Depending on its position on the board, the same pebble could represent a very large or a very small number.</note>. For just as each pebble sometimes signifies more and sometimes less, so too do tyrants make each of their followers appear great and glorious at one moment, and at another, worthless. 

When asked why he had not established a law against parricide <note>The murder of one's father.</note>, he replied, "Because I did not expect it to happen." When asked how men might be least likely to commit injustice, he said, "If those who are not being wronged felt just as much resentment as those who are." He taught that "surfeit" or greed <note>original: "κόρον" (koron). A state of being over-filled or excessively wealthy.</note> is born of wealth, and that "insolence" <note>original: "ὕβριν" (hubrin). Hubris refers to the pride and violent overconfidence that leads to a person's downfall.</note> is born of greed.

He also required the Athenians to calculate their days according to the moon. He even forbade Thespis <note>Thespis is traditionally considered the first actor and the inventor of tragedy.</note> from performing and teaching tragedies, believing that such "false-telling" <note>The idea that actors "lying" or pretending to be someone else was morally dangerous.</note> was useless. Later, when Peisistratus wounded himself <note>Peisistratus famously wounded himself and his mules to trick the people into giving him a bodyguard, which he then used to seize the Acropolis and become tyrant.</note>, Solon said that his actions sprang from that very same theatrical impulse.

He gave the following advice to men (as Apollodorus records in his *On the Sects of Philosophers*):

*   Hold noble character <term>Kalokagathia: the ideal of "nobility and goodness," a combination of moral virtue and social grace.</term> to be more trustworthy than an oath.
*   Do not tell lies.
*   Devote yourself to serious matters.
*   Do not be quick to make friends; but once you have made them, do not cast them off.
*   Rule only after you have first learned to be ruled.
*   Give advice not based on what is most pleasant, but on what is best.
*   Let reason be your leader.
*   Do not...

...f deeds. <insert>Do not</insert> associate with the wicked. Honor the gods, respect your parents. They say that when Mimnermus <note>Mimnermus was an elegiac poet of the 7th century BCE known for his poems on the fleeting nature of youth.</note> wrote:

> Do not be annoyed that I have thought of something better.

> May the fate of death find me at eighty years.

Of his popular songs, the following are well known:

> Be on your guard against every man,
> Lest, hiding a secret sword within
> His heart, he speaks to you with a bright face,
> While a double-tongued voice
> Rings out from a black soul.

It is clear that he wrote his laws, public speeches, and advice to himself in elegiac verse, as well as five thousand lines concerning Salamis and the Athenian constitution, plus iambics and epodes <note>Iambics and epodes are specific meters of Greek poetry often used for sharper, more critical, or satirical commentary.</note>. On his statue is inscribed the following:

> This man, who stopped the Persians’ <note>original: "Μήδων" (Medes). The Greeks frequently used the term "Medes" to refer to the Persian Empire.</note> unjust insolence,
> The holy lawgiver Solon, was born here in Salamis.

He flourished <note>The "akme," or the peak of a person's life and career, usually considered to be around age forty.</note> around the forty-sixth Olympiad <note>Approximately 596–593 BCE.</note>, in the third year of which he was Archon at Athens, as Sosicrates says. It was then that he established his laws. He died in Cyprus, having lived eighty years. He gave instructions to his relatives that they should carry his bones to Salamis, and having cremated them, they should scatter the ashes over the land. Thus Cratinus <note>A famous Athenian comic playwright and contemporary of Aristophanes.</note> says in his play *The Chirons*, portraying Solon speaking:

> I dwell on an island, as men tell the tale,
> Scattered throughout the whole city of Ajax <note>Ajax was the legendary hero-king of Salamis who appears in the Iliad; Solon’s ashes were said to be scattered over his home island.</note>.

There is also an epigram of my own in the aforementioned *Pammetros*... <note>Diogenes Laertius frequently references his own collection of poems, the *Pammetros* or "Book of All Meters," which contained epigrams about the philosophers he discussed.</note>

### Solon to Periander.

You write to tell me that many people are plotting against you. If you intend to do away with all of them, you will not be fast enough. Even someone you do not suspect might plot against you—perhaps one fearing for his own safety, or another who despises you because he fears nothing you can do. Such a man would think he was doing the city a favor by finding a way to remove you while you are off your guard. The best course, then, is to step down from the tyranny to be rid of the blame. But if you are absolutely determined to remain a tyrant, see to it that you maintain a foreign mercenary force greater than the city’s own power; then no one will be a threat to you, and you will not have to execute anyone.

For divinity and lawgivers cannot, by themselves, benefit cities; only those who lead the masses can, according to the mindset they happen to have. So it is with the divine and the laws: when the leaders guide the people well, they are useful; but when they guide them badly, they provide no benefit at all. Since...

"...my laws are better, and so were the things I legislated. Truly in vain did I strive to free the poor among them from their servitude <term>theteia: a state of being a 'thete' or landless laborer, often bound by debt to the wealthy</term>, for now they all serve one man, Peisistratus."

## Solon to Peisistratus.

I believe that I shall suffer no evil at your hands. For even before the tyranny, I was your friend; and now I am no more of an enemy than any other Athenian who does not like tyranny. Whether it is better for them to be ruled by one man or to have a democracy <term>demokratia: rule by the people</term>, let each man be convinced as he judges for himself. I even say that you are the best of all tyrants. But I see that it is not honorable for me to return to Athens, lest someone should blame me: if—after establishing equal rights <term>isopoliteia: a system of equal political rights and social standing for all citizens</term> for the Athenians and having refused the tyranny for myself when it was possible—I should now return and be satisfied with what you are doing.

<header>CHILON. Book 1</header>

## Solon to Croesus.

I admire you for the kindness you have shown us. By Athena, if I did not value living in a democracy above all else, I would have preferred to live in your kingdom rather than in Athens, now that Peisistratus is ruling as a violent tyrant. However, life is more pleasant for us where there is justice and equality for all. Nevertheless, I shall come to visit you, for I am eager to be your guest. <note>Croesus was the King of Lydia, famous for his immense wealth; Solon’s visit to him is a legendary encounter in Greek history where they discussed the nature of happiness.</note>

## CHILON.

Chilon, son of Damagetas, was a Lacedaemonian <note>A Lacedaemonian is an inhabitant of the region around Sparta.</note>. He composed elegiac poems totaling about two hundred lines. He used to say that the excellence of a man consisted in perceiving the future through reasoning. 

When his brother was annoyed because Chilon had been made an Ephor <term>Ephor: one of five senior magistrates in Sparta who oversaw the kings</term> while he had not, Chilon said: "I know how to bear being wronged, but you do not." He became an Ephor during the fifty-sixth Olympiad <note>Approximately 556–553 BCE. The Olympiads were four-year periods used by the Greeks to track time.</note>. However, Pamphila <note>A female historian of the 1st century AD.</note> says it was during the sixth. Sosicrates says he was the first Ephor during the year Euthydemus held office. He was also the first to propose that Ephors should be joined as advisors to the kings, though Satyrus attributes this to Lycurgus <note>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta.</note>. 

Herodotus relates that when Hippocrates <note>The father of the future tyrant Peisistratus.</note> was sacrificing at Olympia and the cauldrons began to boil of their own accord, Chilon advised him either not to marry, or if he already had a wife, to divorce her and disown his children. It is also said that he once asked Aesop <note>The famous author of fables.</note> what Zeus was busy doing; Aesop replied: "He is humbling the high and exalting the low." 

When asked how the educated differ from the uneducated, Chilon replied: "By their good hopes." When asked what was difficult, he said: "To keep secrets, to make good use of leisure time, and to be able to bear an injustice." He also gave these instructions: To rule one’s tongue, especially at a banquet. Not to speak ill of neighbors; otherwise, you will hear things that will cause you pain. Not to threaten anyone...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Chilon of Sparta, one of the Seven Sages of Greece.
