This page details his famous ethical maxims, a legal anecdote, and a notable political prophecy regarding the island of Cythera.</meta>

<page-num>26</page-num>
<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

...for it is like a bell <note>The Greek text here is a fragment "κῶδες" (likely for κώδων, "bell"). In the full context of this biography, it refers to the tongue acting as a warning signal if not controlled.</note>. Go more quickly to the misfortunes of friends than to their successes. Hold a modest wedding. Do not speak ill of the dead. Honor old age. Keep watch over yourself. Choose loss rather than shameful profit; for the one brings pain once, but the other forever. Do not laugh at one in misfortune. When you are strong, be gentle, so that your neighbors respect you rather than fear you. Learn to manage your own home well. Let not the tongue outrun the mind. Master your anger. Do not despise the art of divination. Do not desire the impossible. Do not hurry while traveling. Do not gesticulate with your hand while speaking; for it is the mark of a madman. Obey the laws. Be calm. 

Of his sung verses, this one was most highly regarded:

->Gold is tested on whetstones, which provide a clear proof; but through gold, the mind of good and bad men reveals its true character.<-
<note>original: "Ἐν λιθίναις ἀκόναις ὁ χρυσὸς ἐξετάζεται... ἐν δὲ χρυσῷ ἀνδρῶν ἀγαθῶν τε κακῶν τε νοῦς ἔδωκ’ ἔλεγχον."</note>

They say that once, when he was already an old man, he said he was not conscious of any illegal act in his life. However, he was uncertain about one matter: when judging a case involving a friend, he himself voted according to the law, but he persuaded his fellow judge to acquit the man, so that he might uphold both the law and his friendship. 

He became especially famous among the Greeks for his prophecy regarding Cythera, an island off the coast of Laconia <note>Laconia is the region of the Peloponnese where Sparta was the dominant city.</note>. Having observed its nature, he said: "I wish it had never been born, or having been born, that it were sunk beneath the sea." And he foresaw this with good reason. For Demaratus, a Spartan exile, advised Xerxes <note>The Persian King who invaded Greece in 480 BCE.</note> to anchor his fleet at that island. Greece would have been conquered if Xerxes had followed this advice. Later, during the Peloponnesian War, Nicias <note>A prominent Athenian general and statesman.</note> captured the island and placed an Athenian garrison there, dealing the Spartans many terrible blows.

He was a man of few words <note>This "brief" style of speaking is the origin of the term "laconic," named after the Laconian region of Sparta.</note>; this is why Aristagoras of Miletus calls this style of speaking "Chilonian." He was also said to be the son of Branchus, the founder of the temple at Branchidae. He was an old man around the fifty-second Olympiad <note>Approximately 572–569 BCE.</note>, at the time when Aesop the storyteller was at his peak.

He died, as Hermippus says, in Pisa, just after he had embraced his son who had been crowned an Olympic victor in boxing. His death was caused by an excess of joy combined with the weakness of his many years. All those present at the festival escorted him in the most honorable funeral procession. There is also an epigram of our own dedicated to him:

->I give thanks to you, O light-bearing Polydeuces, <note>Polydeuces (Pollux) was one of the divine twins and a patron of boxing.</note> because the son<-
->of Chilon won the fresh wild-olive crown with his fists.<-
->And if the father, seeing his child crowned, breathed his last in his joy,<-
->it is not a matter for reproach; may such a death be mine. On the<-
->base of his statue this is inscribed:<-
->Spear-crowned Sparta brought forth this man, Chilon,<-
->Who was the first of the Seven Sages in wisdom.<-

He also uttered the famous saying: "Give a pledge, and ruin is at hand." <note>original: "Ἐγγύα, πάρα δ' ἄτα." This was a famous warning against acting as a financial guarantor for others.</note> There is also this short letter of his:

->Chilon to Periander.<-

You send word to me of an expedition against foreigners, as if you yourself would go abroad. But I think that even domestic affairs are precarious for a man who is a monarch; and I consider that tyrant most happy who dies at home by his own natural end.

## P I T T A C U S.

Pittacus, son of Hyrradius, was a man of Mitylene. Duris says that his father was a Thracian. He, along with the brothers of the poet Alcaeus, overthrew Melanchrus, the tyrant of Lesbos. Later, when the Athenians and Mitylenaeans were fighting over the territory of Achilleis, he served as general; the Athenian general was Phrynon, a champion in the *pancratium* <note>The pancratium was a grueling ancient Greek sport combining boxing and wrestling.</note> and an Olympic victor. Pittacus agreed to meet him in single combat. Having a net hidden under his shield, he secretly threw it over Phrynon, and by killing him, he recovered the territory for his city. However, Apollodorus says in his *Chronicles* that later the Athenians brought the matter to trial...

<page-num>28</page-num>
<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

...concerning the territory against the Mytileneans, while Periander heard the case; he <note>Periander was the tyrant of Corinth, also counted among the Seven Sages, who acted as an arbitrator in this territorial dispute.</note> awarded the land to the Athenians. At that time, the Mytileneans held Pittacus in the highest honor and entrusted him with the supreme power. Having held it for ten years and brought the government into order, he resigned his authority. He lived for ten more years after that. The Mytileneans assigned him a tract of land, but he dedicated it as sacred, and it is still called the "Pittacean" today. Sosicrates says that he took only a small portion of it for himself, declaring that "The half is more than the whole." <note>original: "Τὸ ἥμισυ τοῦ παντὸς πλεῖον εἶναι." This is a famous Greek paradox suggesting that a modest portion taken justly is better than a large portion taken through greed.</note> Furthermore, when Croesus <note>The fabulously wealthy King of Lydia.</note> offered him money, he did not accept it, saying he already had twice as much as he wished, for he had inherited the estate of his brother who had died childless.

Pamphile says in the second book of her *Commentaries* that his son Tyrrhæus <note>The OCR reads Πυρῥαῖον (Pyrrhæus), though other historical records often list him as Tyrrhæus.</note> was sitting in a barber's shop in Cyme when a certain blacksmith struck and killed him with an axe. When the people of Cyme sent the murderer to Pittacus, he learned the circumstances and released him, saying: "Forgiveness is better than repentance." <note>original: "Συγγνώμη μετανοίας κρείσσων."</note> However, Heraclitus says that it was the poet Alcaeus <note>Alcaeus was a famous lyric poet and a political rival of Pittacus who frequently attacked him in verse.</note> whom he had in his power and released, saying: "Forgiveness is better than punishment." <note>original: "Συγγνώμη τιμωρίας κρείσσων."</note>

He enacted a law that if a man committed an offense while drunk, the penalty should be double. This was to discourage drunkenness, as the island produced a great deal of wine. He also said: "It is a hard thing to be good." Simonides <note>A famous lyric poet.</note> mentions this when he says: "Truly to become a good man is hard." Plato also mentions this in the *Protagoras*. He also said: "Even the gods do not fight against necessity." <note>original: "Ἀνάγκᾳ δ' οὐ θεοὶ μάχονται."</note> And: "Power shows the man." <note>original: "Ἀρχὴ ἄνδρα δείκνυσι." This implies that one's true character is revealed only when they are given authority.</note>

When asked once what is best, he replied: "To do well what is currently at hand." And asked by Croesus what is the greatest power, he said: "That of the variegated wood," signifying the Law. <note>original: "Ἡ τοῦ ποικίλου ξύλου." The laws in ancient Greek cities were often inscribed on wooden tablets called "axones" which were sometimes painted or "variegated" for readability or distinction.</note> He also used to say that victories should be achieved without bloodshed. To a man from Phocaea who remarked that one must seek out a virtuous man, he replied: "If you search too diligently, you will not find one." When people asked what is ungrateful, he said: "Time." What is hidden? "The future." What is faithful? "The earth." What is unfaithful? "The sea." He also said it is the part of wise men, before troubles arise...

### CHILON. Book 1.

...is necessary to provide in advance so that they <note>Referring to misfortunes or troubles.</note> do not happen; but it belongs to the brave to deal well with them once they have occurred. Do not reproach anyone for their misfortune, out of respect for Nemesis. <note>Nemesis was the goddess of divine retribution who punished human arrogance.</note> If you have received a trust, restore it. > ->One should carry a bow and a quiver full of arrows,<-

He also composed six hundred elegiac verses, and a prose code of laws for his fellow citizens. He flourished, then, around the forty-second Olympiad; <note>The 42nd Olympiad corresponds to approximately 612–609 BC. And this was inscribed upon his tomb:

> ->With their own tears, holy Lesbos here buries<-
> ->Pittacus, washing his grave with spring water.<-

His motto was: "Know the right moment." <note>original: "Καιρὸν γνῶθι" (Kairon gnōthi). This refers to 'Kairos,' the opportune or "fated" moment, rather than chronological time.</note> There was also another Pittacus, a lawgiver (as Favorinus says in the first book of his *Memorabilia*, and Demetrius in his *Treatise on Namesakes*), who was called "the Small." It is said that when a young man once consulted our Sage <note>Pittacus of Mitylene.</note> about marriage, he gave the advice that Callimachus <note>A famous scholar-poet of the Library of Alexandria.</note> records in his epigrams:

> ->He spoke. The old man, raising his staff, his aged weapon, said:<-

It seems he spoke these things from his own disposition. For his wife, being the sister of Draco, the son of Penthilus, was quite a source of pain to him and treated him with great insolence. Alcaeus <note>The lyric poet Alcaeus was a political rival of Pittacus and frequently attacked him in verse.</note> calls him "splay-footed" <note>original: "σαράποδα" (sarapoda)</note> and "shuffling-footed" because he had broad feet and dragged them; "cracked-footed" <note>original: "χειροπόδην" (cheiropodēn)</note> because of the cracks in his feet, which they called "hand-sores"; "braggart" <note>original: "γαύρικα" (gaurika)</note> because he boasted without cause; "pot-bellied" <note>original: "φύσκωνα" (physkōna)</note> and "fat-gutted" <note>original: "γάστρωνα" (gastrona)</note> because he was stout; and also "dark-diner" <note>original: "ζοφοδορπίδαν" (zophodorpidan)</note> because he ate his supper without a lamp; and "slovenly" <note>original: "ἀγάσυρτον" (agasyrton)</note> because he was messy and filthy. His exercise was grinding grain, as Clearchus the philosopher says; <note>Manual grinding of grain was usually the work of slaves; Pittacus reportedly used it to maintain his physical strength.</note> and there is a short letter of his as follows:

### Pittacus to Croesus.

> You bid me to come to Lydia so that I might see your wealth; but even without seeing it, I am convinced that the son of Alyattes <note>King Croesus of Lydia, famous for his legendary wealth.</note> is the most golden of kings. There would be no advantage for me in coming to Sardis; for I do not need gold, but what I already possess is sufficient for me and my companions. Nevertheless, I will come, so that I may become an acquaintance to you as a guest.

# BIAS. Book I.

...it is said to have happened. Phanodicus <note>Phanodicus was a historian who wrote about the history of Ionia.</note> says that Bias ransomed some Messenian girls who had been taken captive, raised them as if they were his own daughters, gave them dowries, and sent them back to Messene to be reunited with their fathers. In time, in Athens (as was previously mentioned), when the tripod was found by the fishermen, which bore the bronze inscription: "To the Wise," Satyrus says that the girls came forward into the assembly (though others say their father did, as Phanodicus records) and declared Bias to be "The Wise One," after they had recounted all he had done for them.

And so the tripod was sent to him. But Bias, when he saw it, said that it was Apollo <note>The god of wisdom and prophecy; Bias modestly suggests that true wisdom belongs only to the divine.</note> who was truly Wise, and he would not accept the gift. Others say that he dedicated it to Hercules at Thebes, since he was a descendant of the Thebans who had established a colony in Priene; Phanodicus also supports this account.

It is also told that when Alyattes <note>Alyattes II, King of Lydia and father of Croesus, who reigned in the early 6th century BCE.</note> was besieging Priene, Bias fattened up two mules and drove them out into the enemy camp. The king, seeing them, was struck with amazement, thinking that the city’s abundance must extend even to their irrational beasts. Wanting to reach a truce, he sent a messenger into the city. Bias then heaped up piles of sand and covered the tops with a layer of grain, showing this to the messenger. When Alyattes learned of this, he finally made peace with the people of Priene, believing they had plenty of food to withstand a long siege.

Shortly after, when the king sent a message to Bias, ordering him to come to his presence, Bias replied: "I command Alyattes to eat onions," <note>original: "κρόμμυα ἐσθίειν" (krommya esthiein). This was a witty pun; eating raw onions makes one cry, so he was effectively telling the king to "go weep."</note> which is the same as telling him to mourn. It is also said that he was a most formidable speaker in legal trials. However, he always used the strength of his words for a good purpose. Hence Demodocus of Leros <note>A poet known for his sharp, gnomic verses.</note> alludes to this when he says:

"If you happen to be a judge, decide the case in the manner of Priene."

And Hipponax <note>An iambic poet famous for his biting satire.</note> says: "To plead a case even better than Bias of Priene."

He met his end in the following way: having pleaded a case on behalf of someone when he was already at a very great age, after he had finished 
<note>The syllable "πα" is repeated in error across the line break.</note>
speaking, he leaned his head back into the lap of his daughter's son. After the opposing counsel had also spoken,

He composed a poem of two thousand verses about Ionia <note>A region on the central coast of western Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey) inhabited by Ionian Greeks.</note> and the best way it might prosper. Of the songs for which he was famous, these are the most esteemed: "Seek to please all the citizens in whatever city you remain; for this brings the greatest favor. But a stubborn character often flashes forth into harmful ruin." 

He also said that being physically strong is a work of nature, but being able to speak what is beneficial to one's country is a unique quality of the soul and of wisdom. He noted that a lack of money <term>poverty</term> happens to many through mere chance. 

He used to say that the truly unfortunate man is the one who cannot bear misfortune. He called it a disease of the soul to long for the impossible and to be unmindful of the troubles of others. 

When asked what is difficult, he replied: "To bear a change for the worse with dignity." Once, while sailing with a group of impious men, a storm arose and they began to call upon the gods for help. Bias said, "Be silent, lest they <note>The gods.</note> notice that you are the ones sailing here!" 

When asked by a godless man what piety truly is, he remained silent. When the man asked the reason for his silence, Bias replied: "I am silent because you are asking about matters that are no concern of yours." 

When asked what is sweet to men, he answered: "Hope." 

He said he would rather judge between enemies than between friends; for in the case of friends, one of them will certainly become an enemy, but in the case of enemies, one of them will become a friend. 

When asked what activity brings a man the most delight, he said: "Profit." He also said that one should measure out their life as if...

<meta>catchword: ...they were going to live for a long time</meta>

<header>BIAS. Book 1.</header>

...both for those who expect to live a long time and those who expect to live a short time. He also advised people to love as if they might one day hate; for he believed that most people are wicked. He used to give counsel in this manner: "Be slow to undertake a task; but whatever you choose, persist in it firmly. Do not speak quickly, for it shows a state of madness <term>mania</term>. Love practical wisdom. Speak of the gods as being what they are. Do not praise an unworthy man because of his wealth. Gain your point by persuasion, not by force. Whatever good you may do, attribute it to the gods. Take wisdom as your provision <term>ephodion</term> for the journey from youth to old age; for this is more enduring than all other possessions." 

<note>The word "ephodion" refers to travel-money or supplies for a journey; Bias suggests that wisdom is the only currency that lasts into the "journey" of old age.</note>

Hipponax also mentions Bias, as has been said before. Even the hard-to-please Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus was a philosopher known for his weeping or "dark" disposition and his frequent criticism of others.</note> praised him above all, writing: "In Priene was born Bias, son of Teutamas, whose renown <note>original: "logos"</note> is greater than that of all others." And the people of Priene dedicated a sacred precinct to him called the Teutameion. His famous saying was: "Most men are bad."

## CLEOBULUS

Cleobulus was the son of Euagoras and a citizen of Lindos <note>A city on the island of Rhodes.</note>; though according to Duris, he was a Carian. Some say he traced his lineage back to Hercules. He was said to excel in strength and beauty, and to have taken part in the philosophy of Egypt. He had a daughter, Cleobulina, who was a composer of riddles in hexameter verse; she is mentioned by the playwright Cratinus in his play of the same name, though he uses the plural title. It is also said that Cleobulus restored the temple of Athena which had been founded by Danaus. 

He composed songs and riddles amounting to three thousand lines. Some say that he was the author of the epitaph inscribed for Midas:

> I am a maiden of bronze, and I lie upon the tomb of Midas.
> As long as water flows and tall trees bloom,
> And the rising sun shines, and the bright moon,
> And rivers run and the sea washes the shore,
> Abiding here upon this much-wept tomb,
> I shall tell those who pass by that Midas is buried here.
<note>original: "Χαλκῆ παρθένος εἰμὶ...". This famous epigram was also sometimes attributed to Homer, but Diogenes notes the tradition linking it to Cleobulus.</note>

As evidence of his work, there is a song by Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos was a famous lyric poet; here he is cited as a critic of Cleobulus’s poetic claims.</note>, where he says: "Who with a sound mind would praise Cleobulus, the inhabitant of Lindos, for setting the strength of a pillar against ever-flowing rivers, spring flowers, the flame of the sun, the golden moon, and the eddies of the sea? For all things are inferior to the gods; even mortal hands can break a stone. This is the thought of a foolish man." <note>Simonides argues that Cleobulus was foolish to suggest a man-made monument could outlast the eternal forces of nature.</note> Furthermore, the epitaph for Midas is not by Homer, for they say Homer lived many years before Midas. There is also a riddle of his recorded in the commentaries of Pamphila <note>Pamphila of Epidaurus was a female historian of the 1st century AD who compiled miscellaneous historical notes.</note>, which goes like this:

> The father is one, the children are twelve; and to each of these
> belong thirty children, twofold in their appearance;
> some are white to see, and the others in turn are black;
> though they are immortal, they all fade away.

The answer is "the year." <note>The father is the year, the twelve children are the months, and the thirty children are the days and nights (white and black).</note> Of his recorded sayings, these are the most highly regarded: Ignorance <term>amousia</term> <note>original: "amousia" — literally "a lack of the Muses," referring to a lack of culture, education, or refinement.</note> and a floor of words are common among mortals. But the right moment <note>original: "kairos"</note> is best. Think good thoughts. Do not become vain or ungrateful. He said that one should marry off daughters when they are maidens in age, but women in understanding; thereby indicating that girls, too, ought to be educated. He also said that one should do good to a friend to make him even more of a friend, and to make a friend out of an enemy. For we must guard against the blame of friends and the plots of enemies. Whenever someone leaves their house, they should first ask what they intend to do; and when they return again, they should ask what they have accomplished. 

He also advised people to exercise the body. To be a lover of hearing rather than a lover of talking. To be a lover of learning <term>philomathes</term> rather than ignorant. To keep a well-omened tongue. To be a friend to virtue and a stranger to vice. To flee injustice. To give the best advice to the city. To master pleasure. To do nothing by force. To educate children. To dissolve enmity. Do not be overly fond of your wife, nor quarrel with her, in the presence of strangers; for the former signifies folly, and the latter signifies madness <term>mania</term>.

Do not punish a drunken servant, for you will seem to be acting like a drunkard yourself. Marry from among your equals. For if you take a wife from those of higher status <note>original: "κρειττόνων" (kreittonon) — meaning those superior in wealth, rank, or power.</note>, you will acquire masters instead of kinsmen. Do not laugh at those being mocked, for you will become hated by them. When successful, do not be arrogant. When in need, do not be humble <note>Cleobulus advises maintaining dignity even in poverty, rather than becoming servile or "lowly."</note>. Know how to bear the changes of fortune nobly. He died at an old age, having lived seventy years; and upon him was inscribed:

-> This, his fatherland Lindos, which prides itself on the sea, <-
-> mourns for the wise man Cleobulus, who has perished. <-

His famous saying <term>apophthegm</term> was: "Moderation is best" <note>original: "Μέτρον ἄριστον" (Metron ariston) — one of the most famous maxims of ancient Greece.</note>. He also wrote to Solon in this manner:

-> Cleobulus to Solon. <-

There are many friends and a home everywhere. But I say that Lindos, being democratically governed, would be the most pleasant place for Solon to stay. The island is by the sea, and those living there have nothing to fear from Pisistratus <note>Pisistratus was the tyrant of Athens; Cleobulus is offering Solon a safe haven from political turmoil.</note>. And your friends from all sides will come to visit you there.

### PERIANDER.

Periander, the son of Cypselus, was a Corinthian from the race of the Heraclidae <note>The Heraclidae were the "descendants of Hercules," a prestigious lineage for Dorian Greeks.</note>. He married Lyside—whom he himself called Melissa—who was the daughter of Procles, the tyrant of Epidaurus, and Eristheneia, the daughter of Aristocrates and sister of Aristodemus. These men ruled almost all of Arcadia (as Heraclides Ponticus says in his work *On Rule*). He had two sons by her: Cypselus and Lycophron. The younger son was intelligent, but the elder was witless. In a later time, in a fit of rage, Periander killed his wife while she was pregnant by throwing a footstool at her or kicking her. He had been persuaded by the slanders of his concubines, whom he later burned alive. He also banished his son to Corcyra <note>Modern-day Corfu.</note> because the boy was grieving for his mother.

...his name was Lycophron. When Periander had already reached old age, he sent for his son so that he might take over the tyranny; but the people of Corcyra <note>Corcyra is modern-day Corfu; at the time, it was a colony of Corinth that often rebelled.</note>, getting ahead of him, put the young man to death. Enraged by this, Periander sent the sons of the Corcyreans to Alyattes <note>Alyattes was the King of Lydia and father of the famous Croesus.</note> to be castrated <note>original: "ἐπ' ἐκτομῇ" (ep' ektome) — Periander intended for them to be made eunuchs in the Lydian court.</note>. However, when the ship docked at Samos, the boys took sanctuary as suppliants in the temple of Hera and were saved by the Samians. Periander eventually died of despondency, having lived eighty years. Sosicrates says he died forty-one years before the time of Croesus, just before the forty-ninth <term>Olympiad</term> <note>The 49th Olympiad corresponds to approximately 584–581 BCE. An Olympiad was a four-year period used by Greeks to track time.</note>. Herodotus says in his first book that Periander was a guest-friend of Thrasybulus, the tyrant of Miletus. 

Aristippus, in the first book of his work *On Ancient Luxury*, tells this story about him: that his mother Crateia fell in love with him and shared his bed in secret. He was initially pleased by this, but when the affair became public, he became harsh and cruel to everyone out of the pain caused by the discovery. 

Ephorus also records that Periander made a vow: if he should win the four-horse chariot race at Olympia, he would dedicate a golden statue. Having won, but lacking the gold, he observed the women at a local festival dressed in their finery; he stripped them of all their ornaments and sent them as the offering. Some say that because he did not want his grave to be known, he devised the following plan: he ordered two young men to go out at night by a specific road he pointed out, to kill the first person they met and bury him. Then he ordered four others to follow them, kill those two, and bury them; and then even more to kill those four. In this way, he himself went out, met the first two, and was killed. The Corinthians, however, inscribed this epitaph for him on a <term>cenotaph</term> <note>A cenotaph is a "hidden" or "empty" tomb, a monument erected when the body is elsewhere or lost.</note>:

-> This fatherland Corinth, on its sea-beaten shores, <-
-> holds within its bosom Periander, the ruler of wealth and wisdom. <-

There is also a poem of my own:

-> Do not ever let the failure to obtain something grieve you; rather, <-
-> take joy in all things alike which God bestows. <-

τ.iii.

For the wise Periander died of despondency,
->Because he did not obtain the outcome he desired.<-

To him also belongs the saying: "Do nothing for the sake of money <gloss>original: χρημάτων (chrematon)</gloss>; for one should only seek to gain what is worthy of gain." He also composed a work of moral instructions in two thousand verses. He said that those who intend to rule as a tyrant <note>In ancient Greece, a 'tyrant' (tyrannos) was an absolute ruler who often seized power unconstitutionally, though not always viewed as "evil" in the modern sense.</note> securely should be guarded by the goodwill of the people, rather than by arms. 

When he was once asked why he continued to rule as a tyrant, he replied: "Because both voluntary resignation and forced removal carry great danger." He used to say the following: 
Rest is a beautiful thing. 
Haste is dangerous. 
Base gain is a disgrace. 
Democracy is better than tyranny. 
Pleasures are mortal, but honors are immortal. 
In good fortune, be moderate; in misfortune, be prudent. 
Be the same toward your friends whether they are successful or unsuccessful. 
Whatever you agree to, keep to it. 
Do not give utterance to secret words. 
Punish not only those who do wrong, but also those who intend to. 

He was the first to have a bodyguard and to change his governance into a strict tyranny; and he would not allow those who wished to do so to live in the city <note>He likely forced the aristocracy to live on their rural estates to prevent them from plotting against him in the city center.</note>, as Ephorus and Aristotle say. He flourished around the thirty-eighth <term>Olympiad</term> <note>Approximately 628–625 BCE.</note> and ruled as tyrant for forty years. 

However, Sotion, Heracleides, and Pamphila (in the fifth book of her *Commentaries*) say there were actually two men named Periander: one was the tyrant, and the other was the Wise Man and a native of Ambracia. Neanthes of Cyzicus also says this, adding that they were cousins to one another. Aristotle says the Corinthian was the wise one, but Plato disagrees <note>In the *Republic*, Plato excludes Periander from the list of the Seven Sages because of his reputation for cruelty.</note>. To him is attributed the famous motto: "Practice is everything" <note>original: "Μελέτη τὸ πᾶν" (Melete to pan). This remains one of the most famous Greek philosophical maxims.</note>. He also desired to dig a canal through the Isthmus <note>The Isthmus of Corinth. This was a massive engineering dream to link the two seas, not fully realized until the 19th century.</note>. A letter of his is also preserved:

->**Periander to the Wise Men**<-

"Great thanks are due to Pythian Apollo that you are coming together in one place. My letters will also come to you at Corinth. I will receive you, as you yourselves know, in a most democratic fashion. I hear that your first gathering was held with the Lydian King..."

You should do the same if you wish to enjoy the fruits of your absolute rule <term>aisymneteia: a term for an elective or absolute dictatorship</term>: remove the most eminent of the citizens, whether they seem to be your enemies or not. To a man in power, even his own companions are a source of suspicion.

## ANACHARSIS THE SCYTHIAN.

Anacharsis the Scythian was the son of Gnurus and the brother of Kadouidas, the King of the Scythians; his mother, however, was Greek. For this reason, he was bilingual. He composed eight hundred verses comparing the customs of the Scythians and the Greeks regarding simplicity of life and matters of war. Because of his directness in speech, he provided the origin for the proverb "Scythian speech" <note>This refers to blunt, unrefined, or brutally honest communication.</note>. Sosicrates says he came to Athens during the forty-seventh Olympiad <note>Roughly 592–589 BCE.</note>, when Eucrates was archon. Hermippus relates that when he arrived at the house of Solon, he told one of the servants to announce...

...to inform Solon that Anacharsis had arrived to see him and, if possible, to become his guest <note>original: ξένος (xenos); a term for a formal relationship of hospitality and friendship between people from different cities</note>. The servant delivered the message and was instructed by Solon to tell him that "people usually make guests for themselves in their own native lands." At this, Anacharsis stepped inside and said that he was now indeed in his own native land, and therefore it was Solon’s duty to make him a guest. Solon, struck by his readiness and wit, admitted him and made him one of his greatest friends. 

After some time, Anacharsis returned to Scythia. Because he was perceived to be undermining the traditional customs of his homeland by being so devoted to Greek ways, he was shot by an arrow while hunting by his own brother and died. His final words were: "I was saved in Greece because of my speech, but in my own home I am destroyed because of envy." Some others say he was executed while performing Greek religious rites <note>original: τελετὰς (teletas); referring to mystery rites or initiations</note>. We have also written an epigram about him:

->When Anacharsis returned to Scythia after much wandering,<-
->He tried to persuade all to live by Greek customs.<-
->But while the speech was still unfinished in his mouth,<-
->A winged arrow snatched him swiftly to the immortals.<-

He used to say that the vine bears three clusters of grapes: the first of pleasure, the second of intoxication, and the third of disgust <note>original: ἀηδίας (aëdias); also meaning unpleasantness or nausea</note>. He expressed wonder that among the Greeks, the experts <note>original: τεχνῖται (technitai); skilled craftsmen or professionals</note> compete in the games, while those who are not experts act as the judges. When asked how one might avoid becoming a lover of drink <term>philopotes: a person habitually fond of wine</term>, he replied, "By keeping before one's eyes the unseemly behaviors of the intoxicated." 

He also wondered how the Greeks, while passing laws against acts of violence <note>original: ὑβριζόντων (hybrizontōn); referring to hubris or physical assault</note>, honored their athletes for striking one another. Upon learning that the hull of a ship was only four fingers thick, he remarked that those on board were only that far from death. He called oil "the medicine of madness" because athletes, when anointed with it, seem to go mad against one another. He asked how it was that the Greeks, who forbid lying, openly tell lies in their taverns <note>original: καπηλείαις (kapēleiais); also referring to small retail shops where cheating on weights and measures was common</note>. He also expressed wonder at how the Greeks, when they begin drinking, use small cups...

When he was asked if there were flutes in Scythia, he replied, "There are not even vines" <note>Anacharsis links the music of the flute with the cult of Dionysus and wine-drinking, neither of which were traditional to the nomadic Scythians</note>. When asked what kind of ships were the safest, he said, "Those that have been hauled up onto dry land."

When asked which are more numerous, the living or the dead, he asked, "In which category, then, do you place those who are at sea?" <note>In antiquity, sailors were considered to be in a state between life and death due to the constant peril of the voyage</note>. Being reproached by an Athenian for being a Scythian, he said, "My homeland is a reproach to me, but you are a reproach to your homeland." 

When asked what is both good and bad among men, he said, "The tongue." He used to say it was better to have one friend of great worth than many who are worth nothing. He described the marketplace <note>original: ἀγορὰν (agoran)</note> as a place specifically set aside for people to deceive and cheat one another. Having been insulted by a youth while drinking, he said, "Young man, if you cannot carry your wine while you are young, you will be a water-carrier when you are old." According to some, he was the inventor of both the anchor and the potter's wheel.

He wrote a letter as follows:

->Anacharsis to Croesus.<-

"I, O King of the Lydians, have come to the land of the Greeks to be taught their customs and practices. I have no need for gold; rather, it is enough for me to return to the Scythians a better man. However, I am coming to Sardis, as I consider it a matter of great importance to become known to you."

They say that his father was even a tyrant. It is said that when a certain Anacharsis inquired of the oracle if anyone was wiser than...

<page-num>41</page-num>
# MYSON. Book 1

...[asked who] might be [wiser than he], the **Pythian priestess** <note>The oracle at Delphi</note> gave the response that was previously mentioned in the *Life of Thales* as having been given to Chilon:

->I declare that Myson of Chenae, born in Oeta,<-
->Is better equipped with a wise mind than you.<-
<note>original: "Οἰταῖόν τινα φημὶ Μύσων' ἐν Χηνὶ γενέσθαι / Σοῦ μᾶλλον πραπίδεσσιν ἀρηρότα πευκαλίμῃσι." This oracle famously humbled the questioner by naming an obscure peasant as the wisest of men.</note>

Having been very curious, [Anacharsis] went to the village and found Myson in the summer, fitting a handle to a plow. He said to him, "But Myson, it is not the season for the plow now." And Myson replied, "It is very much the season to repair it."

Others say the oracle was phrased this way: "I declare a certain man of Etea," and they inquire what "of Etea" means. **Parmenides** says it was a district of Laconia <note>The region around Sparta</note>, from which Myson came. **Sosicrates**, in his *Successions of Philosophers*, says he was an Etean on his father’s side and a Chenean on his mother’s. **Euthyphron**, the son of Heraclides of Pontus, says he was a Cretan, as Etea is a city in Crete. **Anaxilaus**, however, says he was an Arcadian.

**Hipponax** also mentions him, saying: "And Myson, whom Apollo declared to be the most prudent <note>original: σωφρονέστατον (sōphronestaton) — meaning most temperate or sound-minded</note> of all men." **Aristoxenus**, in his *Stray Notes*, says that his character was not far from that of **Timon** and **Apemantus** <note>Timon of Athens was the legendary misanthrope or "man-hater"</note>, for he was a misanthrope. At any rate, he was seen in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> laughing all by himself in a deserted place. When someone suddenly appeared and asked why he was laughing when no one was present, he replied, "For that very reason."

Aristoxenus says the reason he remained obscure was because he did not belong to a great city, but to a village, and an insignificant one at that. Because of his obscurity, some people attributed his sayings to **Peisistratus** the tyrant <note>The ruler of Athens in the 6th century BCE</note>, with the exception of **Plato** the philosopher. For Plato also mentions Myson in his *Protagoras*, including him in the list of Sages instead of Periander <note>Plato likely excluded Periander because he disapproved of tyrants being called "wise"</note>.

Myson used to say: "One should not seek to understand things from words, but words from things." For things are not brought to completion for the sake of words, but words are spoken for the sake of things. He died after having lived ninety-seven years.

## EPIMENIDES.

**Epimenides**, as Theopompus and many other writers state, was the son of Phaisias; however, some say his father was Dosiadas, and others Agesarchus. He was a Cretan by birth, from the city of Knossos, and was distinctive in the way he wore his hair <note>original: "θέσει τῆς κόμης τὸ εἶδος παραλλάσσων" — suggesting he may have worn his hair long or in a style associated with holy men or "Kouretes" of Crete.</note>. 

One day, having been sent by his father into the countryside to look for a sheep, he turned off the road at midday and fell asleep in a certain cave for fifty-seven years. When he finally woke up after this long time, he began searching for the sheep, believing he had only slept for a short while. When he could not find it, he reached the farm, but seeing the buildings changed and the property in the possession of another, he returned to the city in a state of total confusion. There, as he entered his own house, he encountered people who demanded to know who he was; finally, he found his younger brother—now an old man—and learned the whole truth from him. 

Once he became known to the Greeks, he was believed to be a man most dear to the gods. Because of this reputation, when the Athenians were once gripped by a plague, the **Pythian priestess** <note>The oracle at Delphi</note> gave a prophecy that they must purify the city. The Athenians then sent a ship and **Nicias**, the son of Niceratus, to Crete to summon Epimenides. 

He arrived during the forty-sixth **Olympiad** <note>Approximately 596–593 BCE</note> and purified their city, ending the plague in the following manner: he took sheep, both black and white, and led them to the **Areopagus** <note>Mars Hill, the seat of the high court in Athens</note>. From there, he allowed them to wander wherever they wished, instructing those following the sheep that wherever an animal lay down, they should sacrifice it to the "appropriate god" <note>original: "τῷ προσήκοντι θεῷ" — literally the 'fitting' or 'relevant' deity for that spot.</note>. In this way, the Great Evil was stopped. 

This is why, even to this day, one can find throughout the districts of the Athenians "anonymous altars" <note>Altars dedicated to "The Unknown God," famously mentioned later in the New Testament (Acts 17:23)</note>, which serve as a memorial of the atonement that took place then. 

Some writers, however, say that Epimenides identified the cause of the plague as the **Cylonian pollution** <note>original: "Κυλώνειον ἄγος" — a hereditary curse on the Alcmaeonid family for murdering supporters of the rebel Cylon who had taken sanctuary</note>, and that he showed them how to gain deliverance; they claim that two young men, Cratinus and Ctesibius, died to resolve the calamity. In gratitude, the Athenians voted to give Epimenides a talent <note>A very large sum of silver</note> and a ship to return to Crete...

<page-num>43</page-num>
<header>EPIMENIDES. Book 1</header>

...which were meant to honor him. However, he did not accept the money offered; instead, he established a bond of friendship and an alliance between the people of Knossos and the **Athenians**. After returning home, he passed away shortly thereafter—as **Phlegon** states in his work *On Long-Lived People* <note>original: "Περὶ μακροβίων"</note>—having lived for one hundred and fifty-seven years. The Cretans, however, claim he lived for three hundred years, lacking only one. But **Xenophanes of Colophon** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher known for criticizing Homeric mythology</note> says he has heard that Epimenides lived to be one hundred and fifty-four.

He composed a poem on the *Birth of the Curetes and Corybantes* <note>Minor deities associated with Zeus and Rhea, often depicted as armored dancers</note> and a *Theogony* <note>An account of the origins of the gods</note> consisting of five thousand verses. He also wrote a work on the *Building of the Argo and Jason’s Voyage to Colchis* in six thousand, five hundred verses. Furthermore, he wrote prose works concerning sacrifices and the **Cretan Constitution**, as well as a work on **Minos** and **Rhadamanthus** <note>The legendary kings and judges of Crete</note> in four thousand verses.

He also established the temple of the **Venerable Goddesses** <note>original: "σεμνῶν θεῶν" — referring to the Eumenides or Furies</note> among the Athenians, according to **Lobon of Argos** in his book *On Poets*. It is also said that he was the first to purify houses and fields, and the first to found shrines. There are some, however, who claim that he did not actually fall asleep in the cave, but rather spent that time wandering abroad, occupied with **root-cutting** <note>original: "ῥιζοτομίαν" — the study of medicinal plants and herbalism, often associated with shamanic figures</note>. 

There is also a letter of his addressed to **Solon** the lawgiver, which contains a description of the constitution that **Minos** established for the Cretans. However, **Demetrius of Magnesia**, in his work *On Poets and Writers of the Same Name*, attempts to prove the letter is a forgery <note>original: "νεαράν" — literally "new" or "recent," implying it is a late imitation</note> because it is written not in the **Cretan dialect** but in **Attic**, and a modern form of it at that. I have, however, found another letter from him which reads as follows:

## Epimenides to Solon.

"Take heart, my friend. For if **Peisistratus** <note>The tyrant of Athens</note> had set his sights on the Athenians while they were still in a state of servitude and not yet governed by good laws, he would have held his power forever by reducing the citizens to slaves. But as it stands, he is enslaving men who are not base; they remember **Solon’s** warnings and feel the pain of their situation, and they will not tolerate being ruled by a tyrant. Even if Peisistratus manages to hold the city today..."

<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

“...I do not truly expect that the sovereign power will pass to his children. For it is difficult to enslave men who have been liberated by the best laws. As for yourself, do not wander, but come to us in Crete. For the monarch here will not be at all fearsome to you. But I fear that if you should encounter him in any public place, my friends, you might suffer some lasting harm.” <note>This paragraph is the conclusion of a letter, likely attributed to Solon writing to Epimenides, regarding the threat of tyrants.</note>

And so much for that. **Demetrius** <note>Demetrius of Magnesia, a contemporary of Cicero who wrote about famous men</note> says that some record how he received a certain kind of food from the nymphs and kept it in a cow’s hoof. By taking small portions of this, he never required any bodily excretion, and he was never seen eating. **Timaeus** <note>A Greek historian from Sicily</note> also mentions him in his second book. Some say that the Cretans even offer sacrifices to him as if to a god, for they say he was possessed of extraordinary foresight. For instance, when he saw **Munychia** <note>A strategic hill in the port of Piraeus</note> at Athens, he is said to have remarked that the Athenians did not realize how much evil that place would cause them; otherwise, they would have torn it apart with their own teeth to get rid of it. He said this many years before it actually came to pass <note>Referring to the later occupation of the hill by foreign garrisons to control Athens</note>. 

It is also said that he was the first to claim he had once been **Aeacus** <note>A legendary king of Aegina and a judge in the Underworld</note>, and he foretold to the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans</note> their defeat and capture by the **Arcadians**. He also claimed to have lived several lives through reincarnation. **Theopompus** <note>A historian known for his interest in the supernatural</note> relates in his *Wondrous Tales* that while Epimenides was building a shrine to the nymphs, a voice rang out from heaven: “Epimenides, not a shrine for the nymphs, but for Zeus!” He also forewarned the Cretans about the Spartan defeat by the Arcadians, as mentioned before; and indeed, they were taken captive at **Orchomenus**. 

The story goes that he grew old in as many days as the years he had spent asleep; for Theopompus reports this as well. **Myronianus** says in his work on *Similarities* that the Cretans used to call him a "**Cures**" <note>A name linking him to the Curetes, the mythical guardians of the infant Zeus on Crete</note>. The Spartans still preserve his body among them, following the instruction of an oracle, as **Sosibius the Laconian** records. There have been two other men named **Epimenides**: one was a genealogist, and the third was a man who wrote about **Rhodes** in the Doric dialect.

<header>PHERECYDES. Book 1.</header>

## PHERECYDES.

**Pherecydes**, son of **Badys**, was a native of the island of **Syros** <note>One of the Cycladic islands in the Aegean Sea</note>. According to **Alexander** <note>Alexander Polyhistor, a scholar of the 1st century BCE</note> in his *Successions of Philosophers*, he was a pupil of **Pittacus** <note>One of the Seven Sages of Greece</note>. **Theopompus** <note>A famous 4th-century BCE historian</note> states that he was the first person to write for the Greeks on the subjects of nature and the gods. Many wonderful stories are told about him. For instance, while walking along the shore at the Sands in Syros, he saw a ship sailing along with a favorable wind and remarked that it would sink before long; and indeed, it sank before his very eyes. On another occasion, after drinking water drawn up from a well, he predicted that there would be an earthquake within three days; and it happened. Furthermore, while traveling from Olympia to **Messene**, he advised his host **Perilaus** to move away with all his household. Perilaus did not follow the advice, and subsequently Messene was captured. He is also said to have told the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans</note> to value neither gold nor silver, as Theopompus says in his *Book of Wonders*. He claimed that **Heracles** <note>The hero Hercules</note> had commanded him to say this in a dream, and that very same night, Heracles also appeared to the Spartan kings and ordered them to obey Pherecydes. Some writers, however, attribute these stories to **Pythagoras**.

**Hermippus** <note>A biographer known for collecting anecdotes about philosophers</note> relates that during a war between the **Ephesians** and the **Magnesians**, Pherecydes wanted the Ephesians to win. He asked a passerby where he was from, and when the man replied, "From Ephesus," Pherecydes said: "Drag me by the legs and place me in the territory of the Magnesians; then tell your fellow citizens that after they have won the victory, they are to bury me right there." Pherecydes gave these instructions as a dying command. The man delivered the message, and a day later the Ephesians attacked and defeated the Magnesians. Finding Pherecydes dead, they buried him on that spot and honored him with great magnificence. 

Other accounts say that he went to **Delphi** and threw himself down from **Mount Corycium**. However, **Aristoxenus** <note>A philosopher and music theorist who was a pupil of Aristotle</note>, in his work *On Pythagoras and His Acquaintances*, says that Pherecydes fell ill and was buried by Pythagoras on the island of **Delos**. Others still claim that he died of a <term>lice infestation</term> <note>original: φθειριάσαντα (phthiriasanta). This was a common legendary death in antiquity for significant figures, implying a wretched or "divine" end</note>. At which point...

When **Pythagoras** <note>The famous philosopher and mathematician, said to be Pherecydes' student</note> arrived and asked how he was doing, **Pherecydes** is said to have poked his finger through the doorway and replied: "My skin shows it clearly." <note>original: "Χρωπὶ δῆλα" (Chrōpi dēla). This refers to his "louse-disease" (phthiriasis), where his skin was visibly infested with parasites.</note> From that time on, scholars have used this phrase to describe a turn for the worse; however, those who use it to describe a turn for the better are mistaken. He also used to say that the gods call a table a "guardian of the incense." <note>original: "θυωρὸν" (thyōron). This suggests the table was viewed as a sacred object or altar-server.</note>

**Andron of Ephesus** <note>A writer on the Seven Sages</note> says that there were actually two men named **Pherecydes** from the island of **Syros**: one was an astronomer, and the other was a theologian, the son of **Badys**, who was the teacher of **Pythagoras**. **Eratosthenes** <note>The librarian of Alexandria and polymath</note>, however, claims there was only one Pherecydes from Syros, and that the other was an **Athenian** genealogist.

The book written by the Syrian philosopher has been preserved. It begins as follows:

"**Zeus** and **Time** <note>original: "Chronos"</note> and **Earth** <note>original: "Chthon"</note> existed always. But Chthon <note>The primordial, underworldly earth</note> received the name **Gaia** <note>The surface, habitable earth</note> because Zeus gave her the earth as a gift of honor."

A sundial <note>original: "heliotropion"</note> made by him is also preserved on the island of **Syros**. **Dotheis**, in the second book of his *Sacred Matters*, says that the following epigram was inscribed upon his tomb:

> All wisdom’s end is found in me; but if there be more,
> tell my **Pythagoras** this: that he is first of all
> throughout the land of **Greece**. I do not lie in saying this.

**Ion of Chios** <note>A poet and contemporary of Sophocles</note> says of him:

> Thus he, distinguished for his manly virtue and his modesty,
> even in death possesses a joyful life for his soul.
> If indeed the wise **Pythagoras** truly saw and learned
> the thoughts of all men beyond all others.

There is also a poem of my own <note>Diogenes Laertius often inserted his own verses into the biographies</note> written in the **Pherecratean meter**:

->The famous **Pherecydes**,<-
->Whom **Syros** once brought forth,<-
->The story goes that he exchanged<-
->His former form for lice.<-
<note>This refers to the legend that Pherecydes died of phthiriasis, a disease where the body is consumed by lice, often cited in antiquity as a "philosopher's death."</note>

### Pherecydes to Thales.

May you meet a good death when your fated time arrives. A disease has seized me, even as I received your letter. I am swarming all over with lice <note>original: "φθειρῶν" (phtheirōn). There is no absolute certainty in these matters, nor do I claim to know the truth. As I was pressed even harder by the disease, I did not admit any of the physicians or my companions. When they stood at the door and asked how I was doing, I would stick my finger through the keyhole and show them how I was being consumed by the evil. And I told them to come on the next day for the funeral of Pherecydes.

And these were the men called the Sages, to whom some also add Peisi- <note>This refers to Peisistratus, the tyrant of Athens, who was sometimes included in the list of the Seven Sages.</note>

# ANAXIMENES.

Anaximenes, son of Eurystratus, a Milesian, was a pupil of Anaximander. Some say he was also a pupil of Parmenides <note>Parmenides was a later philosopher from Elea; most chronologies suggest Anaximenes preceded him or was a contemporary.</note>. He declared that the first principle is air <note>original: "ἀέρα" (aera)</note>, and the infinite <note>original: "ἄπειρον" (apeiron)</note>. He also said that the stars move not under the earth, but around the earth. He used the Ionic dialect, simple and unadorned. He flourished, according to Apollodorus, in the 63rd Olympiad <note>Approximately 528–525 BCE.</note>, and died about the time of the capture of Sardis <note>The fall of the Lydian capital to the Persians, c. 546 BCE, though dates for Anaximenes' death vary in ancient sources.</note>. There were also two other men named Anaximenes, both from Lampsacus: one an orator, and the other a historian, who was the nephew of the orator who wrote the deeds of Alexander. Our philosopher wrote the following letters:

->Anaximenes to Pythagoras.<-

Thales has met an unfortunate end in his old age. One night, as was his custom, he went out of his courtyard with a maid-servant to gaze at the stars. Because he did not keep his mind on where he was walking, while looking up, he fell over a steep place. Thus the astronomer of Miletus came to his end. We, his pupils, should cherish the memory of the man, as should our children and students. Let us continue to discuss his teachings. Indeed, let every discourse begin with a reference to Thales. And again:

->Anaximenes to Pythagoras.<-

You were the most well-advised of us all when you moved from Samos to Croton <note>A Greek colony in Southern Italy where Pythagoras established his famous school.</note>; there you live in peace. But the sons of Aeacus <note>A reference to the family of Polycrates, the tyrant of Samos.</note> continue to commit outrages, and Miletus is never without tyrants. The King of the Medes <note>The Persians, who were expanding their empire into Ionia at this time.</note> is also a constant terror to us, unless we are willing to pay tribute. For the Ionians are on the verge of going to war with the Medes for the sake of the liberty of all...

->### ANAXAGORAS.<-

Anaxagoras, the son of Hegesibulus or Eubulus, was a native of Clazomenae <note>An ancient Greek city on the coast of Ionia, in modern-day Turkey.</note>. He was a pupil of Anaximenes. He was the first to place Mind <term>Mind: "νοῦς" (nous) in Greek, signifying a cosmic intelligence that organizes the universe</term> over matter, beginning his treatise—which is written in a pleasing and grand style—in this way: “All things were together; then Mind came and set them in order.” For this reason, he himself was nicknamed "Mind." Timon <note>Timon of Phlius, a satirical poet and philosopher.</note> speaks of him in his *Satires* as follows:

> And they say Anaxagoras was a valiant hero,
> Called Mind, because he truly had a mind; he suddenly gathered
> All things together and bound them in order, though they were confused before.

He was distinguished by his noble birth and wealth, but even more so by his greatness of soul, for he surrendered his ancestral property to his relatives. When they accused him of neglecting his estate, he replied, “Why then do you not take care of it yourselves?” At last, he withdrew from such affairs entirely. He devoted himself to the study of nature <note>original: "φυσικῶν θεωρίαν" (physikon theorian), the investigation of the physical world.</note>, ignoring politics. Thus, when someone asked him, "Do you have no concern for your fatherland?" he replied, "Be silent, for I care very much for my fatherland," while pointing his finger toward the heavens. 

He is said to have been twenty years old at the time of Xerxes' crossing <note>The Persian invasion of Greece in 480 BCE.</note>, and to have lived for seventy-two years. Apollodorus says in his *Chronicles* that he was born in the 70th Olympiad <note>Approximately 500–497 BCE.</note> and died in the first year of the 78th Olympiad <note>Approximately 468 BCE, though other historical records suggest he lived until the 420s BCE.</note>. He began to practice philosophy in Athens during the archonship of Callias, being twenty years old, as Demetrius of Phalerum states in his *Register of Archons*; they say he stayed there for thirty years. This man used to say that the sun was a red-hot mass <note>original: "μύδρον" (mydron), meaning a white-hot mass of metal or stone; this was a controversial scientific claim that challenged the divinity of the celestial bodies.</note>...

<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

...a mass of glowing metal and larger than the Peloponnese <note>The large peninsula forming the southern part of mainland Greece.</note>. Others say that the sun is Tantalus <note>original: "Τάνταλον" (Tantalon). This likely refers to a mythological allegory or a play on the name of the king punished by Zeus.</note>. He held that the moon contains dwellings, as well as hills and ravines. He taught that the first principles of all things are the "homoeomeries" <term>Homoeomeries: "ὁμοιομέρειαι" (homoiomereiai), meaning "similar parts." This is Anaxagoras's unique theory that matter is composed of infinitely divisible particles that contain a portion of everything else.</term>. For just as gold is said to be composed of what are called gold-dust filings, so the entire universe is a composition of small, similar bodies.

He held that Mind <note>original: "νοῦν" (noun)</note> is the principle of motion. Of the different bodies, the heavy ones—such as the earth—occupy the lower region, while the light ones—such as fire—occupy the upper region; water and air hold the middle position. In this way, the sea settled upon the earth, which is flat, after its moisture was evaporated by the sun. He claimed that the stars originally moved in a dome-like fashion <note>original: "θολοειδῶς" (tholoeidōs), like a vaulted roof.</note>, so that the pole which is always visible was directly over the summit of the earth, but that later they took on a tilted inclination. 

The Milky Way, he said, is a reflection of the light of the sun from stars that are not themselves illuminated. Comets are a conjunction of planets that emit flames; and "shooting stars" are like sparks that are thrown off by the air. Winds occur when the air is thinned by the sun. Thunder is a collision of clouds; lightning is the friction of clouds. An earthquake is the sinking of air into the earth. 

He believed that living creatures were first produced from moisture, heat, and earth-like matter; but later, they were produced from one another. Males, he said, come from the right side and females from the left. 

It is said that he predicted the fall of the stone <note>A famous meteorite that fell in 467 BCE.</note> that occurred at Aegospotami, which he said would fall from the sun. For this reason Euripides, who was his pupil, called the sun a "golden mass" in his play *Phaethon*. Furthermore, it is said that when he went to Olympia, he sat down wearing a leather cloak <note>original: "δερματίνῳ" (dermatinō), a cloak made of skins, usually worn for protection against rain.</note> as if it were about to rain; and it did rain. 

To someone who asked him if the mountains of Lampsacus <note>A Greek city on the Hellespont.</note> would ever become sea, he is said to have replied: "Yes, if time does not fail." When he was once asked why he had been born, he said, "For the contemplation <note>original: "θεωρίαν" (theōrian), the source of our word 'theory.'</note> of the sun, the moon, and the heavens." To a man who said, "You have been deprived of the Athenians," he replied, "Not at all, but they have been deprived of me." On seeing the tomb of Mausolus <note>The Monumental tomb of the Carian ruler, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>, he said, "A costly tomb is the image of wealth turned to stone..."

-># ANAXAGORAS. Book 2<-
<sig>d.iii.</sig>

...is a shadow of reality <note>original: "οὐσίας εἴδωλον" (ousias eidōlon). This concludes a thought from the previous page regarding the nature of light or the moon's reflection.</note>. To a man who was grieving because he was dying in a foreign land, he said, "The descent to the underworld <note>original: "ᾅδου κατάβασις" (hadou katabasis)</note> is the same from everywhere." He is also thought to be the first—as Favorinus <note>A Roman-era author of a diverse encyclopedia of history and philosophy.</note> says in his *Miscellaneous History*—to declare that Homer’s poetry is about virtue and justice. This line of reasoning was further developed by his acquaintance, Metrodorus of Lampsacus, who was the first to study the poet’s work from a physical perspective. Anaxagoras was also the first to publish a book with a written composition.

Silenus <note>An ancient historian whose works are mostly lost.</note> says in the first book of his *Histories* that during the archonship <note>The term of a chief magistrate in Athens.</note> of Dimylus, a stone fell from the sky. Anaxagoras is said to have declared that the whole heaven is composed of stones; it is held together by its rapid rotation, and if this rotation were relaxed, it would fall. 

Regarding his trial, various accounts are given. Sotion, in his *Succession of Philosophers*, says he was prosecuted for impiety <note>original: "ἀσεβείας" (asebeias)</note> by Cleon, because he claimed the sun was a red-hot mass of metal <note>original: "μύδρον... διάπυρον" (mydron diapyron). In traditional Greek religion, the sun was a god (Helios); calling it a physical object was a crime against the state religion.</note>. After his pupil Pericles defended him, he was fined five talents <note>A massive unit of currency, roughly equivalent to 6,000 drachmas or the weight of a person in silver.</note> and exiled. 

However, Satyrus says in his *Lives* that the case was brought by Thucydides <note>Likely Thucydides son of Melesias, a political rival of Pericles, rather than the historian.</note>, who was a political opponent of Pericles. He was charged not only with impiety but also with Medism <note>The crime of treasonous sympathy for the Persians (Medes).</note>, and was condemned to death in his absence. It is reported that when he received two pieces of news at once—his death sentence and the death of his sons—he said of the sentence: "Nature long ago passed that sentence on both my judges and me." Of his children, he said: "I knew I had fathered mortals." Some attribute this saying to Solon, others to Xenophon. 

Demetrius of Phalerum <note>An Athenian statesman and philosopher.</note> says in his work *On Old Age* that Anaxagoras buried his sons with his own hands. But Hermippus says in his *Lives* that he was imprisoned to await execution. Pericles then came forward and asked the people if they had any complaint against his life. When they said they had none, Pericles replied, "And yet I am his pupil; do not be carried away by slanders..."

"...you should not kill this man, but rather be persuaded by me and release him." And so he was released. However, because he could not bear the insult <note>original: "ὕβριν" (hybrin) — referring to the public shame of the trial.</note> of the proceedings, he took his own life <note>original: "ἑαυτὸν ἐξήγαγεν" (heauton exagagen) — literally 'he led himself out,' a common Greek euphemism for suicide.</note>. But Hieronymus <note>A Peripatetic philosopher and historian.</note> says in the second book of his *Miscellaneous Notes* that Pericles brought him into the courtroom so weakened and thinned by disease that he was released more out of pity than by a formal judgment. So much for the stories regarding his trial. 

It is also thought that he held some hostility toward Democritus <note>The famous proponent of the atomic theory.</note>, having failed to gain access to him for conversation. Eventually, he withdrew to Lampsacus <note>An ancient Greek city on the Hellespont in modern-day Turkey.</note>, where he ended his life. It is said that when the rulers of the city asked what he wished to have done for him, he requested that the children be allowed to play every year during the month in which he died. This custom is still observed even now. When he died, the people of Lampsacus buried him with great honor and inscribed the following:

->Here lies Anaxagoras, who, having traveled<-
->to the furthest boundary of truth regarding the celestial world.<-

->I have also written an epigram for him:<-

> Anaxagoras once claimed the Sun was a mass of red-hot metal,
> And for this reason, he was sentenced to die;
> But his friend Pericles rescued him, yet he still
> Departed from life, through the gentle weakness of his wisdom. <note>The author, Diogenes Laertius, frequently includes his own amateur poetry (the *Pammetros*) in these biographies.</note>

There have been three other men named Anaxagoras, though none possessed all the qualities of the first: one was a rhetorician of the school of Isocrates; another was a sculptor mentioned by Antigonus; and another was a grammarian of the school of Zenodotus.

### ARCHELAUS.

Archelaus was either an Athenian or a Milesian; his father was Apollodorus, or according to some, Mydon. He was a student of Anaxagoras and the teacher of Socrates. He was the first to bring physical philosophy <note>The study of nature and the cosmos, as opposed to ethics or logic.</note> from Ionia to Athens, and for this, he was nicknamed "The Physicist." Indeed, physical philosophy ended with him, as Socrates introduced the study of ethics. It also seems...

# ARCHELAUS. Book II.

<margin>it is</margin> <note>original: "ἐστὶ" (esti)</note> possible to say he touched upon ethics. Indeed, he also philosophized about laws, and things beautiful and just. Socrates took these subjects from him, and by increasing them to the point of discovery, he was credited with founding the field. Archelaus said there were two causes <margin>to be</margin> <note>original: "εἶ)" (einai) — likely a shorthand for "to be," indicating the causes of existence.</note> of generation: the hot and the cold. He also claimed that animals were born from slime <note>original: "ἰλύος" (ilyos) — the primordial mud or silt from which early Greeks believed life spontaneously emerged.</note>. He held that the just and the shameful exist not by nature <note>original: "φύσει" (physei)</note>, but by law <note>original: "νόμῳ" (nomō) — or convention.</note>. His reasoning is as follows: he says that water is melted by heat; in the part where it settles into a fire-like state, it creates earth, but where it flows around, it generates air. Consequently, the earth is held in place by the air, and the air by the circulation of the fire. He says animals are generated from the warmth of the earth, which sends up a slime similar to milk to serve as nourishment; in this same way, he says, the earth produced humans. He was the first to say that the nature of the voice is the striking of the air. He believed the sea was formed by water being filtered through the hollows in the earth. The sun is the greatest of the stars, and the universe is infinite. There have been three other men named Archelaus: the geographer <note>original: "χωρογράφος" (chōrographos)</note> of the lands traversed by Alexander the Great, a poet who wrote on the unique properties of things, and another who was a teacher of rhetoric.

## SOCRATES.
---

Socrates was the son of Sophroniscus, a stonemason, and Phaenarete, a midwife (as Plato also says in his dialogue *Theaetetus*). He was an Athenian, from the district <note>original: "δήμων" (demōn) — the 'demes' or administrative districts of ancient Athens.</note> of Alopece. It was thought that he helped Euripides <note>The famous tragic playwright.</note> compose his plays; for this reason, the comic poet Mnesilochus says:

> The *Phrygians* is a new play by Euripides,
> For which Socrates provides the firewood. <note>original: "φρύγανα" (phrygana) — a pun on the play's title 'Phrygians,' suggesting Socrates provides the basic material or 'kindling' for the work.</note>

And again, he calls Euripides' plays "Socrates-bolted." And Callias, in his play *The Prisoners*, writes:

> Are you so solemn now and think so highly of yourself?
> I have every right; for Socrates is the cause.

And Aristophanes, in his play *The Clouds*, says:

> Euripides, the one who writes those tragedies,
> Those talkative, overly-clever things.

According to some, Socrates was a pupil of Anaxagoras, but according to Alexander <note>Likely Alexander Polyhistor, a scholar of the 1st century BCE.</note>, he also studied under Damon.

### Book II

In the *Successions* <note>original: "διαδοχαῖς" (diadochais) — a genre of ancient literature tracing the "genealogy" of philosophical schools.</note>, it is said that after the former’s condemnation, he [Socrates] was a student of Archelaus the physicist. Aristoxenus says that he was also Archelaus's beloved <note>original: "παιδικὰ" (paidika) — referring to the socially structured pederastic relationships common in ancient Greek education.</note>. It is also thought that he was a slave and worked with stones. Some even say that the statues of the Graces on the Acropolis, which are clothed, are his work. Because of this, Timon says in his *Silli* <note>original: "Σίλλοις" — lampoons or satirical poems.</note>:

> ->From these then turned away the stone-cutter, the talker on laws,<-
> ->The charmer of the Greeks, the one who revealed precise arguments,<-
> ->The sneerer, half-rhetorician, quintessential Athenian, the ironist.<-

For he was also skilled in rhetoric, as Idomeneus says. Furthermore, the Thirty <note>The Thirty Tyrants, a pro-Spartan oligarchy that ruled Athens after the Peloponnesian War.</note> forbade him from teaching the art of words, as Xenophon tells us. Aristophanes also mocks him in his comedies for making the "weaker argument the stronger" <note>A common accusation against Sophists; Aristophanes famously parodied Socrates in his play, *The Clouds*.</note>. For he was the first (as Favorinus also says in his *Miscellaneous History*) who, along with his pupil Aeschines, taught how to speak rhetorically. Idomeneus also mentions this in his work *On the Socratics*. He was also the first to discuss the conduct of life <note>original: "περὶ βίου" (peri biou) — ethics.</note>, and the first of the philosophers to be condemned to death and executed. Aristoxenus, the son of Spintharus, says that he even made money; he would at least collect the coins tossed to him, gather them up, and after spending them, start collecting again. But Demetrius of Byzantium says that Crito raised him up from his workshop and educated him, having fallen in love with the grace of his soul. Socrates, realizing that the study of nature <note>original: "φυσικὴν θεωρίαν" (physiken theorian)</note> had nothing to do with us, began to philosophize about ethics <note>original: "τὰ ἤθη" (ta ethe)</note> both in the workshops and in the marketplace. He used to say that he sought after:

> ->Whatever of evil or good has occurred in your halls.<-
<note>A quote from Homer’s *Odyssey*, book 4, line 392.</note>

Often, when he was being too forceful in his investigations during a discussion, people would punch him or pull out his hair; for the most part, he was laughed at and treated with contempt, but he bore all this with patience. Thus, when he was once kicked and bore it calmly, someone marveled at him, to which he replied, "If a donkey had kicked me, would I have brought a lawsuit against it?" These things are related by Demetrius. He felt no need for travel, and—

# SOCRATES. Book II

...most people saw him, except when there was a need to go on military campaign. For the rest of the time, remaining there in Athens, he would engage in discussion with those he met quite contentiously, not so much to take away their opinions, but to try and learn the truth. They say that Euripides <note>The famous Athenian playwright, known for his intellectual and often skeptical tragedies.</note> gave him the writing of Heraclitus <note>Heraclitus was known as "The Obscure" because his philosophical aphorisms were notoriously difficult to understand.</note> and asked, "What do you think of it?" Socrates replied, "What I understood was noble; and I believe what I did not understand was noble as well; but it requires a Delian diver <note>original: "Δηλίου... κολυμβητοῦ" — Delian divers were famous for their skill in reaching great depths; Socrates suggests one needs an expert to reach the bottom of Heraclitus's deep meaning.</note>." He also took care of his physical exercise and was in excellent condition. At any rate, he served on campaign at Amphipolis; and when Xenophon <note>Socrates's student and a famous historian.</note> fell from his horse in the battle at Delium, Socrates stepped in and saved him. Moreover, when all the other Athenians were fleeing, he retreated calmly, turning around every so often and keeping watch to defend himself if anyone should attack him. He also campaigned at Potidaea by sea; for it was not possible to go by land while the war was obstructing the way. It was there they say he remained standing in one posture for an entire night; and having distinguished himself there, he yielded the prize of valor <note>original: "ἀριστείου" (aristeiou) — the award for the bravest soldier in a battle.</note> to Alcibiades. Aristippus says in the fourth book of his work *On Ancient Luxury* that Socrates was also in love with Alcibiades. Ion of Chios <note>A contemporary of Socrates and a tragic poet.</note> says that while he was still young, he traveled to Samos with Archelaus; and Aristotle says he also went to Pytho <note>Delphi, the site of the famous Oracle.</note>. Furthermore, he went to the Isthmus, as Favorinus says in the first book of his *Memoirs*<gloss>Memorabilia</gloss>. He was also strong-willed and a supporter of democracy, as is clear from his refusal to yield to Critias <note>The leader of the "Thirty Tyrants" who ruled Athens through terror after the war.</note> and his followers when they ordered him to bring Leon of Salamis, a wealthy man, to them so that he might be put to death. Moreover, he was the only one to vote against the conviction of the ten generals <note>Refers to the illegal collective trial of the generals after the Battle of Arginusae; Socrates was the only presiding officer who refused to break the law by voting on them as a group.</note>; and though it was possible for him to escape from prison, he was unwilling to do so. He rebuked those who wept for him, and while bound in chains, he delivered those most beautiful discourses. He was self-sufficient and dignified. Once, when Alcibiades (as Pamphila <note>A rare and important female historian from the 1st century AD.</note> says in the seventh book of her *Commentaries*<gloss>Notes</gloss>) offered him a large plot of land so that he might build a house, he said: "If I needed shoes and you gave me a whole hide of leather so that I could make shoes for myself, would I not be a laughingstock for taking it?"
