### SOCRATES. Book 2

"Nor do you feel the cold too much, nor do you crave breakfast; you abstain from wine and gluttony, and from senseless delicacies." <note>original: "Οὔτ' αὖ ῥιγοῦν ἄχθῃ λίαν..." — This quote from Aristophanes' play *The Clouds* mocks Socrates’ asceticism, which the philosopher's followers viewed as a virtue.</note> And the comic poet Ameipsias, bringing him onto the stage wearing a coarse cloak, says: "Socrates, best among a few men, but most vain among many, you too have come to us; you are a man of endurance. But where could you get a proper cloak? <note>term: *tríbon* — A cheap, threadbare cloak that became the "uniform" of the ascetic philosopher.</note> This misfortune of the shoemakers happened just to spite you." Yet even though he was so hungry, he never stooped to flattery. Aristophanes also reveals this haughty and high-minded character of his when he says:

->You strut through the streets, and cast your eyes sideways,<-
->And you go barefoot, enduring many hardships, and among us you maintain<-
->a solemn face.<-

Yet sometimes he adapted to the occasion and dressed in fine clothes, such as when he was going to Agathon’s house in Plato’s *Symposium*. He was capable of both: of encouraging and of discouraging people. Just as he sent Theaetetus away filled with divine inspiration after discussing knowledge, as Plato says. And Euthyphro, who had brought a lawsuit against his father for the death of a stranger, he turned away from his purpose after a discussion on what is holy. <note>This refers to the *Euthyphro*, a dialogue where Socrates questions the definition of "piety."</note> He also made Lysis a most moral person through his encouragement. For he was skilled at finding the right arguments based on the facts of a situation.

He also dissuaded his son Lamprocles when he was behaving fiercely toward his mother, as Xenophon has recorded. And Glaucon, the brother of Plato, who wanted to enter politics, he turned away because he was inexperienced, as Xenophon says; but Charmides, on the other hand, he encouraged to enter public life, as he was naturally suited for it.

He also inspired pride in the general Iphicrates, by showing him how the fighting cocks belonging to Midas the barber would beat those of the wealthy Callias. And Glauconides thought it worth keeping Socrates for the city’s benefit, just like a rare pheasant or a peacock. He used to say it was a wonder that while anyone could easily say how many possessions they had, they could not name how many friends they possessed—so little did they care about them. Seeing...

### DIOG. LAERT.
<page-num>60</page-num>

To Euclid, who was devoted to contentious arguments, <note>original: "ἐριστικοὺς λόγους" (*eristikous logous*). Eristic was a style of debate focused on winning through clever linguistic tricks rather than seeking truth.</note> Socrates said: "Euclid, you will be able to deal with sophists, but with men, not at all." For he thought that quibbling over such matters was useless, as Plato also says in the *Euthydemus*. When Charmides offered him slaves so that he might derive an income from them, he did not accept them; and according to some, he even looked down upon the beauty of Alcibiades. <note>Alcibiades was a famously handsome and charismatic Athenian general; Socrates' refusal to be swayed by his looks was seen as a sign of his self-control.</note> He also praised leisure as the most beautiful possession, as Xenophon says in the *Symposium*. 

He used to say that there was only one good—knowledge—and only one evil—ignorance. He held that wealth and low birth possessed no inherent dignity, but were, on the contrary, evils. At any rate, when someone told him that Antisthenes was born of a Thracian mother, he replied: "Did you think that such a noble man could only be born of two Athenians?" 

When Phaedo was taken captive and forced to live in a brothel, <note>Phaedo of Elis was a noble youth captured in war; Socrates recognized his potential despite his circumstances.</note> Socrates ordered Crito to ransom him, and thus made him a philosopher. He even learned to play the lyre whenever he had the time, saying that there was nothing strange about a man learning what he does not know. Furthermore, he danced constantly, believing that such exercise contributed to the body's well-being, <note>term: *euexia* — a state of physical fitness and health.</note> as Xenophon also states in the *Symposium*. 

He also said that his divine sign <note>term: *daimonion* — Socrates' famous "inner voice" or "divine sign" that warned him against certain actions.</note> forewarned him of things to come. He said that starting well was no small thing, but that it was close to it. <note>This is a play on a Greek proverb: "the beginning is half of the whole." Socrates suggests that while the start is small, its importance is nearly the entire matter.</note> He also claimed to know nothing, except for the very fact that he knew nothing. He remarked that those who bought produce out of season at high prices were despairing of ever reaching the proper season. 

Once, when asked "What is the virtue of a young man?", he replied: "Nothing in excess." <note>original: "Μηδὲν ἄγαν" (*Mēden agan*). This was one of the famous maxims carved on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note> He claimed that one should study geometry only as far as a person needs to be able to measure land for receiving or handing it over. When Euripides, in his play *Auge*, said of virtue: "It is best to let these things go at random," Socrates stood up and left the theater. He remarked that it was ridiculous that if a slave went missing, one would think it right to search for him, yet one would let virtue perish in such a way. 

Asked whether it was better to marry or not, he replied: "Whichever one you do, you will regret it." He also said he wondered at those who made stone statues—that they... <note>The text breaks off here; the full anecdote usually concludes that sculptors take pains to make the stone look like a man, but take no pains to keep themselves from being like stones.</note>

<summary>This page captures Socrates' rejection of Sophistry, his emphasis on knowledge over wealth, and several of his most famous paradoxes, including his "divine sign" and his claim to "know nothing."</summary>

[He said that sculptors] take care that the stone is made as similar as possible to the subject, but they neglect themselves, so that they do not appear to be like the stone. He also thought that young people should look in the mirror frequently, so that if they were handsome, they might become worthy of their beauty; but if they were ugly, they might hide their lack of looks through education. <note>Socrates emphasizes that "beauty" is a matter of character and learning (paideia), not just physical appearance.</note> 

When he had invited some wealthy men to dinner and his wife Xanthippe was embarrassed by their meager resources, he said: "Be of good cheer. For if they are moderate men, they will be content; but if they are worthless, we will not care about them at all." He used to say that while other men lived to eat, he himself ate to live. 

Regarding the worthless crowd, he said it was as if someone rejected a single four-drachma coin <note>original: "τετράδραχμον" (*tetradrachmon*). A silver coin of high value in ancient Athens.</note> as counterfeit, yet accepted a whole pile of the same coins as genuine. 

When Aeschines said, "I am poor and have nothing else, but I give myself to you," Socrates replied: "Do you not realize, then, that you are giving me the greatest of gifts?" To a man who was complaining about being overlooked when the Thirty <note>The "Thirty Tyrants," a pro-Spartan oligarchy that ruled Athens after the Peloponnesian War (404–403 BCE).</note> rose to power, he said: "You don't regret it, do you?" 

To the person who said, "The Athenians have condemned you to death," he replied: "And nature has condemned them." (Though some attribute this saying to Anaxagoras). <note>Anaxagoras was an earlier philosopher also prosecuted in Athens; this highlights the overlapping oral traditions of philosophical "zingers."</note> When his wife said, "You are dying unjustly," he replied: "Would you have preferred that I die justly?" 

Having dreamed that someone said to him: 

> On the third day you will reach fertile Phthia, <note>original: "Ἤματί κεν τριτάτῳ Φθίην ἐρίβωλον ἵκοιο." A quote from Homer's *Iliad* (9.363), where Achilles speaks of returning home. In the dream, "Phthia" (home) represents the afterlife.</note>

he told Aeschines: "I shall die on the third day." When he was about to drink the hemlock, Apollodorus offered him a beautiful cloak so that he might die in it. But Socrates said: "What? Is my own cloak fit to live in, but not to die in?" 

To someone who said, "So-and-so is speaking ill of you," he replied: "That is because he has not learned to speak well." When Antisthenes turned the torn part of his philosopher's cloak <note>original: "τρίβων" (*tribon*). A simple, coarse cloak worn by philosophers to show their rejection of luxury.</note> outward for all to see, Socrates remarked: "I can see your vanity through the hole in your cloak." <note>Socrates was wary of "performative" poverty, where the display of humility is actually a form of pride.</note> 

To someone who asked, "Is so-and-so not insulting you?" he replied: "No, for those insults do not apply to me." He also said that one ought to offer oneself up to the comic poets; for if they said anything true of our faults, they would correct us, and if not, it was nothing to us. When Xanthippe was first scolding him...

[...scolding] him, and later she even poured water over him. "Did I not say," he remarked, "that when Xanthippe thunders, she will also bring rain?" When Alcibiades said that Xanthippe’s scolding was unbearable, Socrates replied, "But I have grown accustomed to it, just as one gets used to the constant noise of a pulley." <note>original: "τροχλέας" (*trochleas*). A mechanical device like a windlass or block and tackle that makes a rhythmic, grinding noise.</note> "And you," he added, "put up with the noise of geese cackling." When Alcibiades replied, "But they provide me with eggs and goslings," Socrates said, "And Xanthippe bears me children." 

Once, when she even tore off his cloak in the marketplace, his acquaintances urged him to defend himself with his hands. "By Zeus," he said, "so that while we are boxing, each of you can shout, 'Well done, Socrates! Well done, Xanthippe!'" He used to say that he lived with a difficult woman just as horsemen deal with high-spirited horses. "Just as they," he said, "once they have mastered such horses, easily manage all others, so I, through my habit of dealing with Xanthippe, will be able to get along with all other people."

Because of these and similar words and deeds, he was testified to by the Pythian priestess <note>The priestess of the Oracle at Delphi who delivered the prophecies of Apollo.</note> when she gave that famous response to Chaerephon:

-> Of all men, Socrates is the wisest. <-

From this he gained the greatest envy, especially because he exposed those who thought highly of themselves as being foolish—certainly including Anytus, as is seen in Plato's *Meno*. For Anytus, unable to bear Socrates' mockery, first stirred up Aristophanes and his circle <note>A reference to the comic playwright Aristophanes, who parodied Socrates in the play *The Clouds*.</note> against him, and then persuaded Meletus to bring a formal charge <note>original: "γραφή" (*graphē*). A public indictment in the Athenian legal system.</note> of impiety and of corrupting the youth. 

Meletus, then, brought the indictment, but Polyeuctus delivered the speech, as Favorinus says in his *Miscellaneous History*. The speech itself was composed by Polycrates the Sophist, according to Hermippus, or by Anytus, as some say. Lycon the demagogue <note>original: "δημαγωγός" (*dēmagōgos*). A popular leader or political orator.</note> prepared everything beforehand. Antisthenes, in his *Successions of the Philosophers*, and Plato in the *Apology*, state that his accusers were three...

<page-num>63</page-num>

...as they say, Anytus, Lycon, and Meletus. Anytus was motivated by his anger on behalf of the craftsmen and the politicians; Lycon on behalf of the orators; and Meletus on behalf of the poets—all of whom Socrates used to ridicule. Favorinus, however, states in the first book of his *Memorabilia* that the speech written by Polycrates <note>A sophist who wrote a "Prosecution of Socrates" as a rhetorical exercise after the actual trial.</note> against Socrates is not authentic; for in it, he says, mention is made of the walls rebuilt by Conon, which occurred six years after Socrates’s death. And this is indeed the case. 

The sworn indictment <note>original: "ἀντωμοσία" (*antomosia*). A legal term for a formal, sworn statement of a claim or defense.</note> of the trial was in this manner; for it is still preserved even now, as Favorinus says, in the Metroon: <note>The temple of the Mother of the Gods in Athens, which served as the official state archives.</note> 

"This indictment was sworn and delivered by Meletus, son of Meletus of the deme of Pitthos, against Socrates, son of Sophroniscus of the deme of Alopece: <note>A "deme" was a local administrative district or suburb of Athens.</note> Socrates is guilty of not acknowledging the gods whom the city acknowledges, but introducing other new divinities; he is also guilty of corrupting the youth. The proposed penalty <note>original: "τίμημα" (*timema*). In Athenian law, if a defendant was found guilty, both the prosecutor and the defendant would propose a punishment.</note> is death." 

When the philosopher had read the defense speech that Lysias <note>A famous Athenian speechwriter (*logographos*) known for his clear and persuasive style.</note> had written for him, he said, "It is a fine speech, Lysias, but it is not suited to me." For it was clearly more forensic <note>Designed for a law court rather than a philosophical discussion.</note> than philosophical. When Lysias asked, "How can a speech be fine and yet not suit you?" Socrates replied, "Might not fine clothes and shoes also be unsuited to me?" 

During the trial, Justus of Tiberias says in his book *The Wreath* that Plato ascended the platform and began to say, "Men of Athens, though I am the youngest of all those who have ascended the platform..." but the judges shouted out, "Step down!" <note>original: "Καταβαίνον" (*Katabainon*), meaning "the one stepping down." The text explains this meant "Κατάβηθι" (*Katabethi*), the direct command "Get down!"</note> 

So, when he was convicted by 281 votes more than those for acquittal, <note>This high number is debated by historians, as it differs from the account in Plato's *Apology* which suggests a much closer vote.</note> and the judges were assessing what he should suffer or what fine he should pay, he said he would pay twenty-five drachmae. <note>A drachma was a silver coin; twenty-five was a very small, almost insulting, amount for a capital trial.</note> Eubulides, however, says he agreed to pay one hundred. But when the judges raised an uproar, he said, "On account of my deeds, I assess my penalty as maintenance in the Prytaneum." <note>The *Prytaneum* was the city's town hall where distinguished citizens and Olympic victors were given free meals at public expense for life. This was considered a great honor.</note> At this, they condemned him to death.

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
<page-num>64</page-num>

...adding another eighty votes against him <note>In the second stage of an Athenian trial, the jury voted on the penalty. Socrates's defiant speech—suggesting he be honored with free meals rather than punished—angered the jurors, leading eighty more people to vote for the death penalty than had previously voted him guilty.</note>. After being imprisoned, not many days later he drank the hemlock, having engaged in many noble and beautiful discussions, which Plato records in the *Phaedo*. According to some, he even composed a paean <note>A song of praise or thanksgiving, usually dedicated to Apollo.</note>, which began: "Hail, Delian Apollo, and Artemis, you famous children." However, Dionysodorus denies that the paean was his work. He also composed an Aesopic fable, though not very successfully; it began:

->Aesop once spoke to those who dwell in the city of Corinth,<-
->Not to judge virtue by the wisdom of the common folk.<-

So he passed away from among men. But the Athenians immediately felt such regret that they closed the wrestling schools and the gymnasia. They sent the accusers into exile and condemned Meletus to death. They honored Socrates with a bronze statue, the work of Lysippus <note>One of the greatest sculptors of the Classical period, famous for his statues of Alexander the Great.</note>, which they placed in the Pompeion <note>A public building in Athens used for organizing religious processions.</note>. When Anytus visited Heraclea, the inhabitants immediately banished him by public proclamation. Nor was it only in the case of Socrates that the Athenians acted this way; they did so with many others. For they fined Homer fifty drachmae as if he were a madman (according to Heraclides) and said that Tyrtæus was out of his mind. They also honored Astydamas <note>A prolific tragic poet.</note> with a bronze statue before any of the circle of Aeschylus. Euripides even reproaches them in his play *Palamedes*, saying: 

"You have slain, you have slain the all-wise nightingale of the Muses, who caused no grief." <note>original: "Ἐκάνετ' ἐκάνετε τὰν πάνσοφον τὰν οὐδὲν ἀλγύνουσαν ἀηδόνα μουσᾶν." Euripides used the character Palamedes—a hero unjustly executed—to criticize the Athenians for their treatment of wise men like Socrates.</note> 

And so much for that. Philochorus, however, says that Euripides died before Socrates. Socrates was born (as Apollodorus says in his *Chronicles*) in the archonship of Apsephion <note>An archon was a chief magistrate of Athens; their names were used to date the years.</note>, in the fourth year of the 77th Olympiad <note>Approx. 469/468 BCE.</note>, on the sixth day of the month Thargelion, when the Athenians purify the city <note>This was the festival of the Thargelia, a time of ritual cleansing.</note>, and the day the Delians say Artemis was born. He died in the first year of the 95th Olympiad <note>399 BCE.</note> at the age of seventy. Demetrius of Phalerum also agrees with this, though some say he was sixty when he died. Both of them <note>The text likely refers to Socrates and another figure, or perhaps his teachers, continuing on the next page.</note> were students of Anaxagoras...

<margin>and</margin> and also Euripides, who was born in the first year of the seventy-fifth Olympiad <note>480 BCE, the year of the Battle of Salamis.</note> during the archonship of Calliades. It seems to me that Socrates also discussed natural philosophy <term>natural philosophy: the study of the physical world and nature, the precursor to modern science</term>, seeing that he held discussions on providence, as Xenophon states, even though Xenophon also says that Socrates only conducted discourses on ethics. But Plato, too, in the *Apology* <note>Plato’s account of Socrates’s defense speech at his trial.</note>, mentions Anaxagoras and other natural philosophers <margin>which</margin> whom Socrates himself denies, even though Plato attributes all his own teachings to Socrates. Aristotle says that a certain magus <term>magus: a priest or wise man, often associated with Eastern traditions like those of Persia or Syria</term> came from Syria to Athens and, among other criticisms of Socrates, even predicted that he would meet a violent end. I myself have written an epigram for him as follows:

->Drink now, being in the house of Zeus, O Socrates. For truly<-
->The god called you wise, and wisdom itself is a god.<-
->For from the Athenians you received the hemlock, simply put,<-
->But they themselves drank it through your mouth.<-
<note>This poem by Diogenes Laertius suggests that by killing Socrates, the Athenians poisoned their own reputation and collective soul.</note>

According to Aristotle in the third book of his *On Poetics* <note>original: "περὶ ποιητικῆς"</note>, a certain Antilochus of Lemnos was a rival to him, as was Antiphon the interpreter of omens, just as Cylon and Onatas were rivals to Pythagoras; and Sagaris to Homer while he was alive, and Xenophanes of Colophon after his death; and Cercops to Hesiod while alive, and the aforementioned Xenophanes after his death; and Amphimenes of Cos to Pindar; and Pherecydes to Thales, and Salarus of Priene to Bias; Antimenidas and Alcaeus to Pittacus, Sosibius to Anaxagoras, and Timocreon to Simonides. Of those who succeeded him—the so-called "Socratics"—the most prominent leaders were Plato, Xenophon, and Antisthenes; and of the ten commonly cited names, the four most famous were Aeschines, Phaedo, Euclid, and Aristippus. We must speak first about Xenophon, then about Antisthenes among the Cynics, then about the Socratics, and then about Plato; for he was the leader of the ten schools and established the First Academy himself—

There were also other men named Socrates: one a historian who wrote a description of Argos; another a Peripatetic <term>Peripatetic: a follower of Aristotle's school of philosophy, known for walking while teaching</term> from Bithynia; another a poet of epigrams; and one from Cos who wrote on the titles of the gods.

# XENOPHON

Xenophon, the son of Gryllus, was an Athenian from the deme <term>deme: a local district or subdivision of Attica, the region surrounding Athens</term> of Erchia. He was modest in character and exceptionally handsome in appearance. They say that Socrates met him in a narrow lane and, stretching out his staff, blocked his way, asking where various kinds of goods were sold. When Xenophon answered him, Socrates asked again, "And where do men become good and honorable?" <note>original: "καλοὶ κἀγαθοὶ" (kaloi kagathoi)—a Greek aristocratic ideal signifying a person of perfect moral and physical character.</note> Since Xenophon was at a loss for an answer, Socrates said, "Follow me then, and learn." From that time on, he was a student of Socrates. 

He was the first to take notes of what was said and bring them to the public by writing the *Memorabilia* <note>original: "ἀπομνημονεύματα"—literally "recollections." This was the first attempt to record Socrates's actual conversations.</note>. He was also the first to write a history of philosophers. Aristippus, in the fourth book of his work *On Ancient Luxury*, says that Xenophon was in love with Clinias, and that he even spoke these words regarding him: "For I now gaze upon Clinias more gladly than upon all the other beautiful things among men. I would choose to be blind to everything else rather than not see Clinias. I am vexed by both night and sleep because I cannot see him then; but to the day and the sun I owe the greatest thanks, because they reveal Clinias to me."

He became a friend to Cyrus <note>Cyrus the Younger, a Persian prince who attempted to seize the throne from his brother Artaxerxes II.</note> in this way: he had an acquaintance named Proxenus, a Boeotian by birth and a student of Gorgias of Leontini, who was a friend of Cyrus. While living in Sardis with Cyrus, Proxenus sent a letter to Athens for Xenophon, inviting him to come and become a friend to Cyrus. Xenophon showed the letter to Socrates and asked for his advice. Socrates sent him to Delphi to consult the god <note>Referring to the famous Oracle of Apollo at Delphi, where the Pythia gave divinely inspired advice.</note>. Xenophon obeyed and went to the god.

### XENOPHON

...he inquired <note>original: "πυνθάνεται" (punthanetai). This refers to Xenophon's visit to the Oracle at Delphi.</note> not whether he should go to Cyrus, but how he should go. For this, Socrates blamed him, yet nevertheless advised him to go. And so he joined Cyrus and became no less a friend to Proxenus <note>Proxenus was a general and a friend of Xenophon who invited him to join the expedition.</note> than Proxenus was to Cyrus. The other events that occurred during the march up-country <term>Anabasis: literally the "ascent," referring to the expedition from the coast into the heart of the Persian Empire</term> and the return journey to the sea, he himself has sufficiently narrated for us. However, he was hostile toward Menon of Pharsalus, the mercenary leader, during the time of the march; indeed, in his writings, he insults him by saying that Menon associated with favorites who were older than himself. He also reproached a certain Apollonides because his ears were pierced. 

After the march and the disasters in the Black Sea region, as well as the betrayals of Seuthes, the King of the Odrysians, he went to Asia to see Agesilaus, the King of the Spartans, providing him with Cyrus's soldiers for pay; and he became a friend to him in the extreme. At this time, he was condemned to exile by the Athenians for his pro-Spartan sympathies <term>Laconism: the act of favoring Spartan customs or politics over those of Athens</term>. While in Ephesus, having a sum of gold, he gave half to Megabyzus, the priest of Artemis, to keep until his return; but if he did not return, Megabyzus was to have a statue made and dedicate it to the goddess. The other half he sent to Delphi as offerings. 

From there, he went with Agesilaus to Greece, as the king had been summoned for the war against the Thiebians; and the Spartans granted him the status of a state guest <term>proxenia: a social and political arrangement where a citizen of one city looks after the interests of another city's citizens</term>. Leaving Agesilaus, he then went to Scillus, a place in Elis, a short distance from the city. He was accompanied by a little wife named Philesia, as Demetrius of Magnesia says; and two sons, Gryllus and Diodorus, as Deinarchus says in his speech *Against Xenophon on a Case of Desertion*; these sons were also nicknamed the Dioscuri <note>The Dioscuri were the "Heavenly Twins," Castor and Pollux; the nickname implies the boys were inseparable or perhaps physically striking.</note>. When Megabyzus arrived on the pretext of attending the festival, Xenophon recovered his money, bought a plot of land, and dedicated it to the goddess. Through this land flowed the river Selinus, which shared the same name as the river in Ephesus. From then on, he spent his time hunting, entertaining his friends, and—

...writing in his histories. Deinarchus states that the Spartans <note>original: "Λακεδαιμόνιοι" (Lakedaimonioi). The inhabitants of the city-state of Sparta.</note> gave him both a house and a field. During this time, when the Athenians voted to come to the aid of the Spartans, he sent his sons to Athens to fight on behalf of the Spartans. For they had been educated there in Sparta, as Diocles says in his *Lives of the Philosophers*. Now, Diodorus did not perform any notable deed, but survived the battle and had a son named after his brother. But Gryllus, who was stationed with the cavalry—the battle was at Mantinea <note>The Battle of Mantinea (362 BCE) was a major conflict where the Thebans fought the Spartans and Athenians.</note>—died after fighting valiantly, as Ephorus says in his twenty-fifth book; Cephisodorus was the cavalry commander and Hegesileus was the general. In this same battle, Epaminondas <note>The famous Theban general and statesman.</note> also fell. At that very time, they say Xenophon was performing a sacrifice, wearing a garland. When the death of his son was announced to him, he removed the garland; but then, having learned that he died nobly, he placed the garland back upon his head. Some say he did not even weep, but said:

"I knew I had begotten a mortal." <note>A famous expression of Greek stoicism; Xenophon prioritizes his son's honor and the natural order of life over personal grief.</note> 

Aristotle says that countless people wrote eulogies and funeral orations for Gryllus, partly to pay tribute to his father. Moreover, Hermippus in his work *On Theophrastus* says that even Socrates <note>original: "Σωκράτη". This is likely a manuscript error or variant for the orator Isocrates, who was famous for writing such praises.</note> wrote a eulogy for Gryllus. However, Timon mocks Xenophon in these lines:

### AESCHINES.

Aeschines was the son of Charinus the sausage-seller <note>original: "ἀλλαντοποιοῦ" (allantopoiou). Sausage-selling was considered a low-status trade in ancient Athens.</note>—though some say he was the son of Lysanias. He was an Athenian, and from his youth he was very industrious. For this reason, he never left Socrates’ side; and so Socrates used to say, "Only the sausage-seller’s son knows how to honor us." Idomeneus says that it was this Aeschines, and not Crito, who advised Socrates in prison regarding his escape; but he claims that Plato—because Aeschines was more a friend to Aristippus than to him—attributed those words to Crito. Aeschines was much slandered, especially by Menedemus of Eretria, who claimed that most of his dialogues were actually written by Socrates and that Aeschines had obtained them secretly from Xanthippe <note>Socrates' wife</note>. Among these, the so-called "Headless" <note>original: "Ἀκέφαλοι" (Akephaloi). This refers to dialogues that seem to start abruptly without a proper introduction.</note> dialogues are very weak and do not show the characteristic Socratic vigor; Pisistratus of Ephesus even said they were not by Aeschines. ...son of Lysanias <note>Continuing from the previous page's sentence</note>. Some claim his dialogues are actually by Pasiphon of Eretria <note>A philosopher from the Eretrian school often accused of literary forgery</note>, and that Aeschines merely published them under his own name. It is also said that he plagiarized works from Antisthenes, specifically the *Little Cyrus*, the *Lesser Heracles*, and *Alcibiades*, as well as dialogues regarding various districts.

However, the dialogues of Aeschines that truly capture the Socratic spirit <note>original: "ἦθος" (ēthos). This refers to the distinct character and method of Socrates as depicted in literature.</note> are seven in number: first, *Miltiades* (which is considered somewhat weak in style), *Callias*, *Axiochus*, *Aspasia*, *Alcibiades*, *Telauges*, and *Rinon*.

It is reported that due to his extreme poverty, he traveled to Sicily to visit Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Elder or Younger, the tyrants of Syracuse known for hosting philosophers</note>. There, he was reportedly overlooked by Plato but was introduced to the court by Aristippus. After presenting some of his dialogues, he received gifts. Later, upon returning to Athens, he did not dare to set himself up as a <term>Sophist</term> <note>A professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy; at this time, the term often implied someone who taught for high fees</note>, because Plato and Aristippus were already so famous. Instead, he gave private, paid lectures. Eventually, he took to writing legal speeches for those who had been wronged. Because of this, Timon <note>Timon of Phlius, a satirical poet and philosopher</note> said of him:

->“The unpersuasive writings of Aeschines.”<-

They say that Socrates once told him, when he was hard-pressed by poverty, to “borrow from himself” <note>original: "παρ' ἑαυτοῦ δανείζεσθαι" (par' heautou daneizesthai)</note> by reducing his daily food rations. Aristippus was also suspicious of the authenticity of Aeschines' dialogues. It is said that while Aeschines was reading them aloud in Megara, Aristippus mocked him, asking, “Where did you get these, you thief?”

Polycritus of Mende says in the first book of his history *On Dionysius* that Aeschines lived with the tyrant until Dionysius was overthrown and remained until Dion’s return to Syracuse. He also mentions that Carcinus the comic poet was there with him. There is also a letter extant from Aeschines to Dionysius.

Aeschines was also quite well-trained in the art of rhetoric. This is evident from his defense of his father’s friend, the general Phaiax, and from those works in which he closely imitates Gorgias of Leontini <note>A famous orator known for his highly ornamental and rhythmic style</note>. Furthermore, the orator Lysias wrote a speech against him titled *On Sycophancy* <note>original: "συκοφαντίας" (sykophantias). In Athens, this referred to malicious prosecution or legal "shakedowns."</note>. From all this, it is clear that he was quite skilled in oratory. <header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

Panaetius <note>A prominent Stoic philosopher of the 2nd century BC</note> believed that the only authentic Socratic dialogues <note>original: "Σωκρατικῶν διαλόγων" (Sokratikōn dialogōn) — philosophical works written as conversations featuring Socrates</note> were those of Plato, Xenophon, Antisthenes, and Aeschines. He was doubtful regarding the dialogues of Phaedo and Euclides, but he rejected all the others as genuine. 

There have been eight men named Aeschines. The first was this man [the Socratic]. The second was the author of manuals on the art of <term>Rhetoric</term> <note>The study and practice of persuasive speech</note>. The third was the famous orator who was the rival of Demosthenes. The fourth was an Arcadian, a student of Isocrates. The fifth was from Mitylene, whom they called the "Scourge of Orators." The sixth was a Neapolitan and an Academic philosopher, who was the student and favorite of Melanthius of Rhodes. The seventh was a Milesian, a writer on political matters. The eighth was a sculptor.

### ARISTIPPUS

Aristippus was by birth a Cyrenaic <note>From Cyrene, a Greek city in modern-day Libya</note>, but he came to Athens, as Aeschines says, because of the fame of Socrates. Having become a <term>Sophist</term> <note>original: "σοφιστεύσας" (sophisteusas); here meaning a professional teacher who charges for his services</note>—as Phanias of Eresus, the Peripatetic philosopher, claims—he was the first of the Socratic circle to demand fees, and he even sent money to his teacher. It is said that on one occasion, after he sent Socrates twenty <term>minae</term> <note>An ancient unit of currency; 20 minae was a very large sum, roughly equivalent to several years' wages for a laborer</note>, Socrates sent the money back, saying that his <term>daimonion</term> <note>original: "δαιμόνιον" (daimonion); the divine "inner voice" or sign that Socrates claimed guided his actions</note> would not allow it; for Socrates was displeased by this behavior. 

Xenophon also felt ill-will toward him; for this reason, Xenophon attributed a discourse against pleasure to Socrates that was actually directed against Aristippus. Furthermore, Theodorus, in his work *On Sects*, spoke poorly of him, as did Plato in his dialogue *On the Soul* <note>The *Phaedo*, where Plato notes Aristippus's absence during Socrates' death</note>, as we have mentioned elsewhere. 

Aristippus was a man capable of adapting himself to every place, time, and person, and he could play his part in any circumstance with perfect harmony. For this reason, he was held in higher favor by Dionysius <note>The tyrant of Syracuse</note> than all the others, as he always made the best of whatever situation arose. He enjoyed the pleasure of what was currently available to him, but he did not labor to hunt for the enjoyment of things that were not present. Because of this, Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic, who famously lived in poverty</note> used to call him the "royal dog" <note>Implying he was a pampered pet of the court</note>. Timon also mocked him for his luxury and indulgence, saying something like this:

They say that he once ordered a partridge to be bought for fifty <term>drachmas</term> <note>original: "δραχμῶν" (drachmōn) — a silver coin roughly equal to a day's wage for a skilled worker; fifty was an extravagant price</note>. When someone criticized him, he asked, "Would you not have bought this for an <term>obol</term>?" <note>original: "ὀβολοῦ" (obolou) — a small coin, one-sixth of a drachma</note>. When the man agreed, Aristippus replied, "Well, fifty drachmas mean just as little to me." 

On another occasion, when Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Elder or Younger, the "Tyrant" or absolute ruler of Syracuse in Sicily</note> offered him the choice of one of three courtesans, he took all three away with him, saying, "Even Paris did not benefit from preferring one over the others." <note>A reference to the Judgment of Paris in Greek mythology, which sparked the Trojan War</note> However, they say that after leading them as far as the porch, he let them go. He was a man of such character that he could both indulge in luxury and despise it.

Because of this, Strato—or some say Plato—once said to him, "You are the only one given the gift to wear both a fine cloak and a rag." When Dionysius once spat on him, he put up with it. When someone blamed him for this, he said, "If fishermen endure being sprayed by the sea just to catch a tiny <term>goby</term> <note>original: "κωβιόν" (kōbion) — a small, common fish</note>, should I not endure being sprayed with spit to catch a <term>blenny</term>?" <note>original: "βλέννον" (blennon) — a slime-covered fish; the word was also a slang term for a fool or simpleton, implying Dionysius was the "catch"</note>.

As he was once passing by, Diogenes <note>The famous Cynic philosopher who lived in poverty</note>, who was washing vegetables, mocked him and said, "If you had learned to eat these, you would not be a servant in the courts of tyrants." But Aristippus replied, "And you, if you knew how to associate with men, would not be washing vegetables." 

When asked what he had gained from philosophy, he said, "The ability to speak with confidence to everyone." When he was once reproached for his expensive lifestyle, he said, "If this were a bad thing, it would not take place during the festivals of the gods." 

When asked what advantage philosophers have over others, he replied, "If all the laws were abolished, we would still live in the same way." When Dionysius asked him why philosophers visit the doors of the rich, but the rich no longer visit the doors of philosophers, he said, "Because the philosophers know what they need, but the rich do not." 

When asked how the educated differ from the uneducated, he replied, "In the same way that tamed horses differ from the untamed." Once, when he was entering the house of a courtesan and one of the youths with him blushed, he said, "It is not the enter-"

To enter <note>original: "ελθεῖν" (elthein). Aristippus is famously referring to entering a brothel or a house of pleasure</note>, he said, is not the difficult thing; it is being unable to leave.

When someone presented him with a riddle and said, "Solve it!" he replied, "Why, you fool, do you wish to untie that which causes us trouble even while it is tied up?"

He said it was better to be a beggar than to be uneducated; for the former lacks money, but the latter lacks humanity.

Once, when he was being insulted, he began to walk away. When his pursuer asked, "Why are you fleeing?" he replied, "Because while you have the authority to speak evil, I have the authority not to listen."

When someone remarked that he always saw philosophers at the doors of the rich, he replied, "So too are doctors always at the doors of the sick; but no one would choose to be the patient rather than the doctor for that reason."

Once, while he was sailing to Corinth and caught in a storm, he was visibly shaken. To a man who said, "We common people are not afraid, so why do you philosophers behave like cowards?" he replied, "Because we are not each fearing for the loss of the same kind of life." <note>Aristippus suggests his highly cultivated life is more valuable than that of an unrefined person, and thus more "costly" to lose</note>

When a man boasted of his vast learning, he said, "Just as those who eat the most and exercise the most are not healthier than those who consume only what is necessary, so too the truly excellent are not those who read many things, but those who read useful things."

To a speechwriter who had pleaded a case for him and won, and later asked him, "What good did Socrates do you?" he replied, "This: that the words you spoke on my behalf were true." <note>Aristippus credits Socrates with his personal integrity rather than his rhetorical skill</note>

He gave the best advice to his daughter Arete <note>Arete of Cyrene, who succeeded her father as head of the Cyrenaic school</note>, training her to be disdainful of excess.

When asked by a father what his son would gain by being educated, he replied, "If nothing else, at least in the theater he will not sit as one stone upon another." <note>A pun on the stone seats of the Greek theater; an uneducated person is as unfeeling and unmoving as the bench they sit on</note>

When someone presented a son to him for instruction, he asked for a fee of five hundred <term>drachmas</term> <note>original: "δραχμάς" (drachmas). A significant sum, roughly 500 days' wages for a laborer</note>. When the father said, "For that much money I could buy a slave!" Aristippus replied, "Buy one then, and you will have two." <note>Implying the uneducated son is no better than a slave</note>

He said he took money from his acquaintances not for his own use, but so that they might learn how money ought to be spent.

### ARISTIPPUS. Book 2

He said, "Whenever I host a dinner, I hire a cook." <note>Aristippus was often criticized for his luxurious lifestyle; here he argues that he simply pays for professional services when needed.</note> Once, when he was being forced by Dionysius <note>Dionysius I or II, the famously temperamental tyrants of Syracuse who hosted many philosophers at their court.</note> to speak on a matter of philosophy, he replied, "It is ridiculous that you ask me to speak, yet you are the one trying to teach me *when* I ought to speak." At this, Dionysius became annoyed and ordered him to take the very last seat at the table. Aristippus simply said, "You must have wanted to make this spot more honorable."

To a man who was boasting of his skill in swimming, he asked: "Are you not ashamed to brag about doing the work of a dolphin?"

Once asked how the wise man differs from the fool, he replied: "Send them both naked to a place where they are unknown, and you will see."

When someone was boasting about being able to drink a great deal without getting drunk, he remarked: "A mule can do the same."

To a man who was blaming him for living with a mistress <note>original: "ἑταίρᾳ" (hetaira), a high-class companion or courtesan in Ancient Greece.</note>, he asked, "Does it make any difference whether one takes a house where many people have lived before, or one where no one has lived?" When the man answered "No," Aristippus continued, "And does it matter whether you sail in a ship that has carried ten thousand passengers, or one that has carried none?" "Not at all," the man replied. "Then," said Aristippus, "it makes no difference whether the woman you are with has been used by many, or by none."

To someone who criticized him for taking money from students even though he was a disciple of Socrates, he said: "Certainly! For when people sent Socrates grain and wine, he would accept only a little and send the rest back; that was because he had the leading men of Athens as his stewards, but I have only Eutychides, a slave I bought with silver."

He also consorted with Lais the mistress, as Sotion says in the second book of his *Successions*. In response to those who found fault with him, he famously said: "I possess Lais, but I am not possessed by her." <note>original: "Ἔχω Λαΐδα, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἔχομαι" (Echo Laida, all' ouk echomai). This quote encapsulates the Cyrenaic philosophy: it is not the enjoyment of pleasure that is wrong, but being enslaved by it.</note> For he believed that the best thing is to master pleasures and not be defeated by them, rather than merely abstaining from their use.

To a man who reproached him for the high price he paid for his food, he asked: "Would you not have bought these items yourself if they cost only three obols?" <note>An obol was a small denomination of Greek currency; three obols was a very low price.</note> When the man agreed that he would, Aristippus replied: "Then it seems I am not a lover of pleasure, but you are a lover of money."

Once, when Simus—the treasurer of Dionysius—was showing off his magnificent house with its expensive paved floors (Simus was a Phrygian and a person of low character), Aristippus cleared his throat and spat right in the man's face. When Simus became enraged, Aristippus said: "I could not find a more suitable place to spit." <note>A classic philosophical "insult" meant to suggest that in a house where every object is treated with more care than the people in it, the owner's face is the only thing "dirty" enough to serve as a spittoon.</note>

To Charondas...

...having said this (others say he was speaking to Phaedo <note>Phaedo of Elis, a fellow student of Socrates and the namesake of Plato's famous dialogue on the soul.</note>), someone asked: "Who is this person smelling of perfume?" Aristippus replied, "It is I, wretch that I am, and even more wretched is the King of the Persians. <note>The Persian Kings were legendary in the Ancient Greek world for their extreme luxury and use of expensive scents.</note> But consider that just as no other animal is any worse for having a scent, neither is a man. May those foul men perish foully—those 'kinaidoi' <note>original: "κίναιδοι" (kinaidoi). This term refers to men considered effeminate or passive, often used as a slur. Aristippus is arguing that their poor reputation shouldn't ruin the use of good ointment for everyone else.</note>—who bring a good ointment into disrepute."

When he was once reproached by Plato <note>The famous philosopher and founder of the Academy, who generally favored a more ascetic and disciplined lifestyle than Aristippus.</note> for his expensive way of life, he asked, "Does Dionysius <note>The tyrant of Syracuse, whom both philosophers visited.</note> seem like a good man to you?" When Plato agreed that he was, Aristippus said, "And yet he lives even more expensively than I do. Therefore, nothing prevents one from living both expensively and well."

When asked how Socrates died, he replied, "In the way that I would pray to die." <note>Socrates died with great dignity and calm, accepting his execution by hemlock as a matter of principle.</note>

Once, when Polyxenus the sophist <note>A "sophist" was a professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy, often viewed as more concerned with winning arguments than finding truth.</note> came to visit him and saw women and expensive food being prepared, he began to criticize him. After a short silence, Aristippus asked, "Can you also join us today?" When the sophist agreed, Aristippus said, "Why then did you find fault? It seems you are not blaming the food, but the expense."

While his servant was carrying money on a journey and found it too heavy (as Bion <note>Bion of Borysthenes, a later philosopher known for his biting and witty social critiques.</note> relates in his discourses), Aristippus said, "Pour away the excess, and carry only as much as you can."

Once, while sailing, when he realized the ship belonged to pirates, he took out his gold and began to count it. Then, as if by accident, he let it drop into the sea and wailed aloud. Some say he added: "It is better for this money to be lost for the sake of Aristippus than for Aristippus to be lost because of the money." <note>Aristippus likely threw the money away to make himself an unprofitable target for the pirates, prioritizing his life over his wealth.</note>

When Dionysius once asked him why he had come, he replied that it was to share what he had and to receive what he did not have. Others say his answer was: "When I needed wisdom, I went to Socrates; now that I need money, I come to you."

He used to criticize people for examining the utensils they bought in the market with great care, while they judged their own lives haphazardly; however, some attribute this saying to Diogenes. <note>Diogenes the Cynic, who lived in extreme poverty and was famous for his public critiques of social norms.</note>

Once at a drinking party, Dionysius ordered everyone to put on a purple robe <note>Purple was the color of royalty and high luxury.</note> and dance. Plato refused to accept it, saying:

<page-num>77</page-num>
<header>ARISTIPPUS. Book II</header>

"I could not put on a woman’s robe." <note>original: "Οὐκ ἂν δυναίμην θῆλυν ἐνδῦναι στολήν." This is a line from Euripides' play *The Bacchae*. Dionysius, the tyrant of Syracuse, once asked his guests to dress in purple robes and dance; the philosopher Plato refused, citing this line.</note>
But Aristippus took the robe and, as he was about to dance, replied wittily with another line:
"—For even in the Bacchic revels,
She who is chaste will not be corrupted." <note>original: "καὶ γὰρ ἐν βακχεύμασιν / Οὖσ' ἥγε σώφρων οὐ διαφθαρήσεται." Also from Euripides' *Bacchae*. Aristippus argues that outward behavior or dress does not ruin a person's inner character.</note>

Once, when making a request to Dionysius on behalf of a friend and failing to succeed, he fell at the tyrant's feet. When someone mocked him for this, he said: "It is not my fault, but Dionysius’s, who has his ears in his feet." <note>A sharp commentary on the ego of the tyrant, suggesting one must grovel just to be heard.</note>

While staying in Asia, he was captured by Artaphernes the satrap. <note>A satrap was a provincial governor in the Persian Empire.</note> To someone who asked, "Are you confident even here?" he replied, "You fool, when would I be more confident than now, when I am about to converse with Artaphernes?"

He used to say that those who pursued the common studies <term>liberal arts (enkyklia paideumata)</term> but neglected philosophy were like Penelope's suitors. For the suitors were able to win over Melantho and Polydora and the other handmaidens, but were never able to marry the mistress herself. <note>In Homer's *Odyssey*, the suitors pursued Penelope but settled for sleeping with her servants. Aristippus uses this to show that philosophy is the "mistress" of knowledge, while other subjects are merely servants.</note>

Ariston said something similar: that when Odysseus descended into Hades, he saw and met with almost all the dead, but did not catch a glimpse of the queen herself. <note>Referring to Persephone, the queen of the underworld.</note>

When Aristippus was asked what things noble boys should learn, he replied: "The things they will use when they become men."

To someone who reproached him for leaving Socrates to go to Dionysius, he replied: "I went to Socrates seeking education <term>paideia (training/culture)</term>; but I went to Dionysius seeking recreation <term>paidia (play/amusement)</term>." <note>This is a clever pun in Greek between *paideia* and *paidia*, which sound very similar.</note>

When he had made a sum of money from his teaching, Socrates asked him, "Where did you get so much?" to which he replied, "From the same place you got your little bit." <note>Aristippus was the first of Socrates' students to charge fees for teaching, a practice Socrates famously avoided or kept to a minimum.</note>

When a courtesan <term>hetaira (high-status female companion)</term> said to him, "I am pregnant by you," he replied, "You can no more know that than if you were walking through a thicket of reeds and claimed to know which specific thorn pricked you."

Someone once criticized him for casting off his son, as if the boy were not his own offspring. He replied, "We know that even phlegm and lice are produced from our own bodies, yet because they are useless, we cast them as far away from us as possible."

Aristippus once took money from Dionysius. When Plato had taken a book instead, and someone criticized Aristippus for this, he replied: "I am in need of money, but Plato is in need of books." <note>original: "Ἐγὼ μὲν γὰρ (εἶπεν) ἀργυρίου, Πλάτων δὲ βιβλίων ἐστὶν ἐνδεής." Aristippus was famous for his practical—some said greedy—nature, while Plato was seen as the more intellectual scholar.</note> To a man who asked why he was being rebuked by Dionysius, he said: "For the same reason that everyone else rebukes me." He once asked Dionysius for money, and the tyrant replied: "But did you not say that the wise man is never in want?" Aristippus countered by saying: "Give it to me first, and then let us discuss the matter." Once the money was given, he said: "Do you see now that I am not in want?" When Dionysius quoted these lines to him:

> For whoever travels to a tyrant’s court,
> Is that man’s slave, though he comes as a free man; <note>original: "Ὅστις γὰρ ὡς τύραννον ἐμπορεύεται, / Κείνου ᾽στὶ δοῦλος, κἂν ἐλεύθερος μόλῃ." This is a famous tragic fragment often attributed to Sophocles.</note>

Aristippus replied: "He is no slave, if he comes as a free man." This is recorded by Diocles in his *Lives of the Philosophers*, though others attribute the exchange to Plato. Having become angry with Aeschines <note>Aeschines of Sphettus, another follower of Socrates known for his dialogues.</note> a short time later, Aristippus said: "Shall we not be reconciled? Shall we not stop talking nonsense? Or will you wait until some fool reconciles us over a cup of wine?" Aeschines replied: "Gladly." Aristippus then said: "Remember then, that although I am older than you, I was the one who approached you first." And Aeschines replied: "By Hera, you speak truly and reasonably; for you are much better than I. I was the one who began the enmity, but you began the friendship." These stories are attributed to him.

There have been four men named Aristippus: first, the subject of this account; second, the man who wrote a history of Arcadia; third, the "mother-taught" <term>Metrodidaktos (one instructed by his mother)</term>, who was the grandson of the first Aristippus; and fourth, a member of the New Academy. <note>The New Academy was a later phase of Plato's school characterized by skepticism.</note>

Of the Cyrenaic philosopher, the following books are in circulation: three volumes of a history of Libya, which he sent to Dionysius; and one volume containing twenty-five dialogues, written some in the Attic and some in the Doric dialect. <note>Attic was the dialect of Athens, while Doric was spoken in parts of the Peloponnese and in Cyrene, Aristippus's home.</note> These are the titles: *Artabazus*; *To the Shipwrecked*; *To the Exiles*; *To a Poor Man*; *To Lais*; *To Porus*; *To Lais concerning the Mirror*; *Hermeias*; *The Dream*; *To the Man at the Wine-Cup*; *Philomelus*; *To his Kin*; *To those who Censure*...

...those who rebuke him for possessing old wine and mistresses; *To those who rebuke him for buying food at great expense*; *A Letter to his daughter Arete*; *To the man training himself for the Olympic Games*; *A Question*; *Another Question*; *A Maxim addressed to Dionysius*; *Another regarding the Statue*; *Another regarding the daughter of Dionysius*; *To the man who thinks himself dishonored*; and *To the man attempting to give advice*. 

Some say that he also wrote six books of *Discourses* <term>diatribai: philosophical lectures or informal dialogues</term>. Others, however, claim he wrote nothing at all; among these is Sosicrates of Rhodes. But according to Sotion in his second book, and Panaetius, these are his writings: *On Education*, *On Virtue*, *An Exhortation to Philosophy*, *Artabazus*, *The Shipwrecked*, *The Exiles*, six books of *Discourses*, three books of *Maxims* <term>chreiai: brief, pithy anecdotes or "useful" sayings</term>, *To Lais*, *To Porus*, *To Socrates*, and *On Fortune*. He defined the ultimate goal <note>original: "τέλος" (telos)</note> of life as the smooth motion transmitted to sensation.

Now that we have recorded his life, let us go through the Cyrenaic <note>The Cyrenaics were a school of philosophy founded by Aristippus, named after his home city of Cyrene in North Africa.</note> philosophers who descended from him; some called themselves Hegesiacs, others Annicereans, and others Theodorians. We shall also touch upon the followers of Phaedo, the most prominent of whom were the Eretrians. 

The succession is as follows: Aristippus was heard by his daughter Arete, as well as Ethiops of Ptolemais and Antipater of Cyrene. Arete taught Aristippus, who was nicknamed "the Mother-taught" <note>original: "μητροδίδακτος" (metrodidaktos). He received this name because his mother, Arete, was his primary teacher—a rarity in the male-dominated world of Greek philosophy.</note>; he in turn taught Theodorus, who was called "the Atheist" and later "God." Antipater was the teacher of Epitimides of Cyrene, who taught Paraebates, who in turn taught Hegesias, known as "the Death-persuader" <note>original: "Πεισιθάνατος" (Peisithanatos). Hegesias was so pessimistic about the possibility of pleasure in life that his lectures reportedly led his students to commit suicide.</note>, and Anniceris, the man who ransomed Plato <note>Anniceris is famously said to have paid the ransom to free Plato from slavery after the philosopher was captured on his return from Syracuse.</note>.

Those who remained faithful to the school of Aristippus and were called Cyrenaics held the following doctrines: They maintained that there are two states <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe), referring to feelings or internal experiences.</note>, pain and pleasure. Pleasure they called "smooth motion," while pain they called "rough motion." They held that one pleasure does not differ from another pleasure, and that nothing is inherently "pleasant" except the experience itself. Pleasure is sought by all living creatures, while pain is avoided. Furthermore, they held that bodily pleasure is the final goal, just as Panaetius also records...

<margin>On the Sects</margin>
In his work *On the Sects* <note>original: "περὶ αἱρέσεων" (peri haireseōn)</note>, Hippobotus says that they [the Cyrenaics] do not believe that "static" pleasure <term>katastematic: pleasure derived from a stable state or the absence of pain</term>—which consists in the removal of pains and the "freedom from annoyance" <term>aochlēsia</term> accepted by Epicurus—is the ultimate goal. They also believe 
<margin>Goal</margin>
that the "ultimate goal" <term>telos: the highest good or end-purpose of life</term> differs from "happiness." For the ultimate goal is particular 
<margin>Happiness</margin>
pleasure, whereas happiness is the system composed of these particular pleasures, in which are counted both those that have passed and those yet to come. Furthermore, particular pleasure is choice-worthy for its own sake; but happiness is not chosen for its own sake, but for the sake of the particular 
<margin>Proof</margin>
pleasures. The proof <note>original: "πίστιν" (pistin)</note> that pleasure is the goal is the fact that from childhood we are instinctively attached to it without any deliberate choice, and once we have obtained it, we seek nothing else; likewise, we flee nothing so much 
<margin>Pleasure</margin>
as its opposite, which is pain. They hold that pleasure is a good even if it arises from the most unseemly things, as Hippobotus says in *On the Sects*. For even if the action itself is out of place, the pleasure remains choice-worthy for its own sake and is a good. However, the "removal of pain" (as stated by Epicurus) does not seem to them to be a pleasure; nor is the "lack of pleasure" <term>ahēdonia</term> the same as pain. For both pleasure and pain consist in motion, whereas 
<margin>Absence of pain</margin>
<margin>Lack of pleasure</margin>
freedom from pain <term>aponia</term> or the lack of pleasure are not motions. Indeed, freedom from pain is like the state of someone sleeping. They say it is possible for some people not to choose pleasure because of a perversion of mind. 
<margin>Mental</margin>
<margin>Bodily</margin>
Moreover, they do not believe that all mental pleasures and pains arise from bodily ones. For joy can arise from the simple prosperity of one's country, just as it does from one's own. But they also deny that pleasure is produced through the memory of past goods or the expectation of future ones (which was a view held by Epicurus); for they argue that the movement of the soul is weakened by the passage of time. They also say that pleasures are not produced by simple sight or hearing alone. For instance, we listen to those imitating laments with pleasure, but we listen to those truly lamenting with displeasure. They called the middle states "lack of pleasure" and "freedom from pain." However, they maintained that bodily pleasures are much better than mental ones, and bodily annoyances are much worse. This is why criminals are punished with these [bodily pains]...

It highlights their belief that bodily pleasures are superior to mental ones and that happiness is merely the sum of individual pleasant moments.</summary>

...[more so than] those who do wrong. For they held that suffering pain is more difficult, while feeling pleasure is more akin <note>original: "οἰκειότερον" (oikeioteron) meaning something naturally suited or familiar to one’s being</note> to our nature. Hence, they also paid more attention to the management of the latter [pleasure]. Therefore, even though pleasure is choice-worthy in itself, they held that the things which produce certain pleasures are often troublesome; so that to them, the accumulation of pleasures—which does not [necessarily] create happiness—appeared to be a most difficult task. 

It is also their view that neither does the wise man always live pleasantly, nor the foolish man always live in pain; rather, it is true only for the most part. It is sufficient if one can live pleasantly by following each particular pleasure as it occurs. They say that prudence <term>phronēsis: practical wisdom or the ability to navigate life’s choices</term> is a good, but it is not choice-worthy for its own sake; rather, it is chosen for the things that result from it. 

A friend is valued for the sake of utility <note>The Cyrenaics were known for a "utilitarian" view of friendship, believing we love others for the benefits they provide us</note>. For indeed, we cherish a part of our own body only as long as it is present. They also believe that some of the virtues can even be found among the foolish. Physical training, they say, contributes to the acquisition of virtue. 

The wise man will neither feel envy, nor be in love, nor be superstitious <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονήσειν" (deisidaimonēsein), literally "fearing the spirits"</note>. For they believe these things arise from "empty opinion." He will, however, feel grief and fear, for these occur naturally. Wealth, too, is a producer of pleasure, but is not choice-worthy for its own sake. 

They held that the "feelings" <term>pathē: internal experiences or affections</term> are graspable <note>original: "καταληπτά" (katalēpta), meaning things we can know with certainty</note>; they said they could know the feelings themselves, but not the external things from which they arise. They avoided the study of nature <term>physics: the study of the physical world</term> because of its apparent incomprehensibility <term>akatalēpsia: the state of things being unknowable</term>. However, they applied themselves to logic <note>original: "λογικῶν" (logikōn)</note> because of its utility. 

Meleager, in the second book of *On Opinions*, and Clitomachus in the first book of *On the Sects*, say they consider both the natural part [physics] and the dialectic part [logic] to be useless. For they argue that one can speak well, be free from superstition, and escape the fear of death by having thoroughly learned the discourse on good and evil. 

They also believe that nothing is just, or honorable, or shameful by nature, but only by law and custom <note>This is a radical moral relativism: morality is a social contract, not a natural law</note>. Nevertheless, the good man will do nothing out of place because of the penalties imposed and the public opinion. They allow that the wise man can make progress both in philosophy and in other areas. They say that one person feels grief more than another, and that the senses are not alwa- <note>The text cuts off mid-word "πάν-" (pan-), likely "always" or "entirely"</note>

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the various sects derived from the Cyrenaic school. <page-num>82</page-num>
<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

...[nor does he] always speak the truth. Those called the Hegesiacs <note>Followers of Hegesias of Cyrene, who was so pessimistic about the possibility of happiness that he was nicknamed the "Advocate of Death" (Peisithanatos)</note> held the same goals: pleasure and pain. They believed that there is neither such a thing as gratitude, nor friendship, nor beneficence; because we do not choose these things for their own sake, but because of the utility they provide us, without which these things do not even exist. 

They held that happiness <term>eudaimonia: the state of flourishing or overall life-satisfaction</term> is completely impossible; for the body is filled with many sufferings, and the soul suffers along with the body and is disturbed, and fortune prevents many of the things we hope for. Thus, for these reasons, they believed that happiness has no real existence. 

Both life and death are matters of choice. They supposed that nothing is inherently pleasant or unpleasant by nature; rather, because of rarity, novelty, or satiety, some are pleased by things and others are displeased. 

Poverty and wealth, in the calculation of pleasure, are of no account; for the rich are not more significantly pleased than the poor. Slavery is likewise indifferent to freedom regarding the magnitude of pleasure, as is noble birth versus low birth, and fame versus obscurity. 

To the fool, living is profitable; but to the wise man <term>phronimos: one possessing practical wisdom</term>, it is a matter of indifference. The wise man will do everything for his own sake; for he considers no one else equally worthy as himself. Even if he seems to reap the greatest benefits from another, they are not equal to what he himself has provided. 

They also rejected the senses, as they do not provide accurate knowledge, but they would do everything according to what appears reasonable. They said that mistakes should meet with forgiveness; for a person does not sin willingly, but because they are oppressed by some passion. One should not hate such a person, but rather re-teach them. 

The wise man will not so much excel in the choice of goods as in the avoidance of evils, setting his goal as living without toil and without pain—a state which comes to those who have become indifferent toward the things that produce pleasure. 

The Annicereans <note>Followers of Anniceris, who moderated the extreme egoism of the Hegesiacs by reintroducing social virtues</note>, while agreeing with the others in most respects, did allow for friendship in life, as well as gratitude, honor toward parents, and acting on behalf of one's country. Hence, because of these things, even if the wise man undergoes troubles, he will be no less happy, even if only a few [pleasures]...

<page-num>83</page-num>
<header>ARISTIPPUS. Book II</header>

...[nor does] force overcome him. They <note>The Annicereans, a branch of the Cyrenaic school</note> also held that a friend’s happiness is not desirable for its own sake; for it is not something that can be perceived by one’s neighbor. They believed that reason <term>logos: rational argument or discourse</term> is not sufficient on its own to provide confidence or to rise above the opinions of the masses; rather, one must be habituated through practice, because of the poor disposition that has been "dyed" into us over a long period of time. 

They taught that a friend should not be accepted solely for the sake of utility—where, if the utility failed, one would no longer pay attention—but also because of the goodwill that has grown between them. For the sake of this goodwill, one should even endure hardships, even though pleasure is the established goal. Even if one is pained by being deprived of a friend’s company, one still willingly endures it out of affection for the friend.

The group called the Theodoreans took their name from the previously mentioned Theodorus and followed his doctrines. This Theodorus was a man who completely abolished the prevailing opinions regarding the gods. We have come across a book of his entitled *On the Gods* <note>original: "Περὶ θεῶν" (Peri theon)</note>, which is not to be looked down upon; indeed, they say that Epicurus took most of what he wrote from this book. 

Theodorus was a student of Anniceris and of Dionysius the Dialectician, as Antisthenes says in his *Successions of Philosophers*. He supposed the "End" <term>telos: the ultimate goal or purpose of life</term> to be joy and grief—the former based on wisdom, and the latter on folly. He categorized wisdom and justice as "goods," and their opposite habits as "evils." Intermediate things <note>Things that are neither inherently good nor evil</note> included pleasure and pain.

He also did away with friendship, claiming it exists neither among the foolish nor the wise. Among the foolish, friendship vanishes once the utility is removed; whereas the wise, being self-sufficient, have no need of friends. 

He further argued that it is reasonable for a virtuous man not to sacrifice himself for his fatherland; for he should not cast away his wisdom for the benefit of the foolish. He claimed that the world <term>kosmos: the universe or world-city</term> is one's fatherland. He also taught that a person might steal, commit adultery, or commit sacrilege at the right opportunity. For none of these things, he argued, is shameful by nature, if the common opinion regarding them is removed—an opinion which was merely put together for the sake of the...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Theodorus "the Atheist," a philosopher of the Cyrenaic school. The previous page ended mid-sentence describing the Theodoreans' view on the "End" or goal of life: that joy comes from wisdom, while grief comes from the company of fools.</meta>

<page-num>84</page-num>
<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

...of a gathering of fools. He openly maintained that a person should indulge in their passions with their loved ones without any restraint. To this end, he would pose such arguments as these: 

"Is a woman who is literate <note>original: γραμματικὴ (grammatikē) - meaning skilled in letters or grammar</note> useful insofar as she is literate?" 
"Yes," was the reply. 
"And is a boy or a young man who is literate useful insofar as he is literate?" 
"Yes." 
"Therefore, is not a beautiful woman also useful insofar as she is beautiful? And is not a beautiful boy or young man useful insofar as he is beautiful?" 
"Yes." 
"And is not a beautiful boy or young man useful for that very purpose for which he is beautiful?" 
"Yes." 
"Now, the purpose for which he is beautiful is for intimacy <term>plēsiazōn: sexual approaching or intimacy</term>." 
Having gained these admissions, he would conclude: "Therefore, if someone makes use of intimacy insofar as it is useful, he does not commit an error; nor, then, will he be doing wrong if he makes use of beauty insofar as it is useful." By asking such questions, he sought to prevail through logic. 

He is said to have been called "God" <note>This is a pun on his name, Theo-dorus, which means "Gift of God"</note> after Stilpo questioned him in the following way: 
"Theodorus, is what you say you are, what you actually are?" 
When Theodorus nodded in agreement, Stilpo asked: "And do you say that you are a god?" 
When he admitted this, Stilpo concluded: "Then you are a god." 
Theodorus accepted this gladly, but Stilpo said with a laugh: "You rascal! By this same logic, if you agreed to it, you would have to admit you were a jackdaw, or a thousand other things!"

On another occasion, Theodorus sat down beside Euryclides the Hierophant <term>hierophant: the chief priest who "shows the sacred things" during the Athenian Mysteries</term> and said: 
"Tell me, Euryclides, who are those who commit impiety regarding the mysteries?" 
When the priest replied, "Those who disclose them to the uninitiated," Theodorus retorted: "Then you yourself are impious, for you explain them to those who have not been initiated."

Indeed, he narrowly escaped being brought before the Areopagus <note>The high court of Athens, which handled cases of homicide and religious impiety</note>, and would have been, had not Demetrius of Phalerum rescued him. However, Amphicrates, in his work *On Famous Men*, says that he was eventually condemned to drink hemlock. 

While staying at the court of Ptolemy, the son of Lagus, he was once sent as an ambassador to Lysimachus. During this embassy, his speech was so bold that Lysimachus said to him: "Tell me, Theodorus, are you not the one who was expelled from Athens?" 
To which he replied: "You have heard correctly. For the city of the Athenians, unable to bear me—just as Semele was unable to bear Dionysus—cast me out." <note>In Greek myth, Semele died because she could not withstand the divine presence of Dionysus's father, Zeus; Dionysus was then "cast out" from her womb.</note> 
When Lysimachus then said, "See to it that you do not come to us again," Theodorus replied, "I would not,"

# ARISTIPPUS. Book 2.

...he said, "unless Ptolemy should send me away." When Mithras <note>original: Μίθρου (Mithrou) - Mithras was the high steward or treasurer of King Lysimachus</note>, the steward of Lysimachus <note>One of Alexander the Great’s generals who became King of Thrace</note>, stood by and said, "You seem to be ignorant not only of the gods, but also of kings," Theodorus replied: "How can I be ignorant of them, when I consider you yourself to be an enemy of the gods?" 

It is said that once in Corinth, while he was walking about with a great number of students following him, Metrocles the Cynic <note>A philosopher who gave up his wealth to live in poverty</note>, who was washing wild chervil <note>original: σκανδικας (skandikas) - a common, cheap vegetable</note>, said to him: "You, the great 'Sophist' <note>here used as a slight, implying a teacher who sells wisdom for money</note>, would not have needed so many students if you would just wash vegetables." But Theodorus retorted: "And you, if you knew how to associate with men, would have no use for these vegetables." 

A similar story is also told (as mentioned previously) regarding Diogenes and Aristippus. This, then, is the character of Theodorus in broad strokes. Finally, having departed for Cyrene, he lived with Magias and continued to be held in every honor. When he was eventually expelled from there, he is reported to have said quite wittily: "You do a poor thing, men of Cyrene, in exiling me from Libya to Greece."

There have been twenty men named Theodorus: 
1. The first was from Samos, the son of Rhoikos. He was the one who advised placing charcoal <note>original: ἄνθρακας (anthrakas)</note> beneath the foundations of the Temple at Ephesus. (For as the ground was very damp, he said the charcoal, having lost its woody quality, would remain solid and be unaffected by water.) 
2. The second was from Cyrene, a mathematician, whom Plato studied under. 
3. The third was the philosopher described above. 
4. The fourth was the author of a very fine book on voice training. 
5. The fifth was one who wrote a treatise on lawgivers, beginning with Terpander <note>A famous poet and musician from Lesbos</note>. 
6. The sixth was a Stoic. 
7. The seventh was one who wrote a history of the Romans. 
8. The eighth was from Syracuse, who wrote on military tactics. 
9. The ninth was from Byzantium, known for political speeches. 
10. The tenth was also a Byzantine, whom Aristotle mentions in his *Epitome of Rhetoricians*. 
11. The eleventh was from Thebes, a sculptor. 
12. The twelfth was a painter mentioned by Polemon. 
13. The thirteenth was a painter from Athens, whom Menodotus writes about. 
14. The fourteenth was a painter from Ephesus, whom Theophanes mentions...

...the fifteenth was a poet of epigrams; the sixteenth wrote about poets; the seventeenth was a physician, a student of Athenaeus; the eighteenth was a Stoic philosopher from Chios; the nineteenth was from Miletus, also a Stoic philosopher; and the twentieth was a tragic poet.

## PHAEDO.

<margin><unclear>On [...]</unclear></margin>
Phaedo of Elis <note>original: Ἠλεῖος (Eleios) - Elis was a city-state in the Peloponnese, famous as the site of the ancient Olympic Games</note> was of noble birth. However, when his city was captured, he was taken as a prisoner of war and forced to work in a house of ill repute <note>original: ἐπ’ οἰκήματος (ep’ oikēmatos) - a euphemism for a brothel</note>. Even there, he would close his door and manage to attend the teachings of Socrates, until Socrates persuaded Alcibiades or Crito and their circle to ransom him. From that time on, he pursued philosophy as a free man. Hieronymus, however, in his work *On Holding Back*, attacks him and claims he remained a slave. 

He wrote several genuine dialogues: *Zopyrus*, *Simon*, and the *Nicias* (though its authenticity is debated); also *Medius* (which some attribute to Aeschines and others to Polyhaenus), *Antimachus* or *The Elders* (this too is doubted), and the *Scythian Discourses* (which some also attribute to Aeschines). His successor was Pleistanus of Elis. The third generation of his school included the followers of Menedemus of Eretria and Asclepiades of Phlius, who moved toward the views of Stilpo. Up until their time, they were called the "Elian school," but from the time of Menedemus they were known as the "Eretrian school." We shall speak of them later, as Menedemus also founded a school of thought.

## EUCLID.

<margin><unclear>On [...]</unclear></margin>
Euclid was from Megara <note>A city on the Isthmus between Corinth and Athens</note>, or from Gela according to some, as Alexander says in his *Successions of Philosophers*. He devoted himself to the teachings of Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who taught that reality is a single, unchanging "Being"</note>. His followers were called the Megarians, then later the "Eristics" <note>original: ἐριστικοί (eristikoi) - from 'eris', meaning strife or wrangling; these were thinkers famous for using logical puzzles to win debates</note>, and eventually the "Dialecticians." Dionysius of Carthage was the first to give them this latter name because they arranged their arguments in a question-and-answer format—
