<page-num>87</page-num>
### EUCLID. Book 2.

...to him <note>Referring to Euclid of Megara, mentioned on the previous page</note>, Hermodorus <note>A student of Plato who was said to have published Plato's lectures without permission</note> says that Plato and the rest of the philosophers traveled after the death of Socrates, fearing the cruelty of the tyrants. This Euclid declared that the Good is one, though it is called by many names: sometimes Wisdom <note>original: φρόνησιν (phronēsin)</note>, sometimes God, and at other times Mind <note>original: νοῦν (nous)</note>, and so forth. But things contrary to the Good he did away with, claiming they do not exist. In his method of demonstration, he did not rely on premises <note>original: λήμματα (lēmmata) — the steps of an argument</note>, but rather attacked the conclusion <note>original: ἐπιφοράν (epiphoran)</note>. He also rejected the use of arguments by analogy, saying they were based either on similar or dissimilar things. If based on similar things, it was better to deal with the things themselves rather than their likenesses; if based on dissimilar things, the comparison was irrelevant. Because of this, Timon <note>Timon of Phlius, a satirical poet and philosopher</note> says of him, while also lashing out at the other followers of Socrates:

> But I care nothing for these triflers, nor for any
> Other, neither for Phaedo, whoever he may be, nor for the
> Contentious Euclid, who cast upon the Megarians a frenzy of dispute.

He wrote six dialogues: *Lamprias*, *Aeschines*, *Phoenix*, *Crito*, *Alcibiades*, and the *Eroticus*. Among the successors of Euclid was Eubulides of Miletus, who devised many famous arguments in the field of dialectic <term>Dialectic: the art of investigating the truth through logical discussion and the use of paradoxes</term>, such as "The Liar," "The Disguised," "The Electra," "The Masked Man," "The Sorites" <term>Sorites: Also known as the 'Heap' paradox; it asks how many grains of sand must be removed before a heap ceases to be a heap</term>, "The Horned One" <term>The Horned One: A trap logic argument: 'If you haven't lost something, you still have it. You haven't lost horns, therefore you have horns'</term>, and "The Bald Man." Concerning him, one of the comic poets says:

> The insolent Eubulides, who asked his 'horned' questions,
> And with his false, boastful words confounded the orators,
> Has departed, taking with him the petty chatter of Demosthenes.

For it seems that Demosthenes was his pupil and managed to cure his speech impediment <note>original: ῥωβικώτερος (rhōbikōteros) — referring to a physical defect or shuffling speech</note> under him. Eubulides was also at odds with Aristotle and spoke much ill of him. Among the others in the succession of Euclid was Alexinus of Elis, a man very fond of controversy, for which reason he was nicknamed "The Refuter" <note>original: Ἐλεγξῖνος (Elegxinos), a pun on his name and the word for logical refutation, *elenchos*</note>. He was particularly opposed to Zeno. Hermippus says of him that he left Elis for Olympia and lived there...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...[they might] philosophize. When his students asked why he lived in that place, he said he wished to establish a sect that would be called the "Olympic." However, the students, burdened by the cost of travel and provisions and judging the place to be unhealthy, departed. For the rest of his life, Alexinus lived there in solitude with only a single servant. Later, while swimming in the Alpheius <note>The Alpheius is the longest river in the Peloponnese, flowing through Olympia</note>, he was pierced by a reed and thus met his end. We have written an epigram about him as follows:

<margin>fittingly</margin>
> It was then no idle tale, 
> That a certain unlucky man, while swimming, met his fate
> By a nail. For even that solemn man, before he could step 
> Out of the Alpheius, Alexinus, died pierced by a reed.
<note>The poem mocks the philosopher's death by comparing the trivial reed that killed him to a nail or a spike.</note>

He wrote not only against Zeno <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism</note> but also other books, including one against the historian Ephorus. Among the students of Eubulides was Euphantus of Olynthus, who wrote a history of his own times. He also composed several tragedies, for which he was well-regarded in the dramatic competitions. He became the teacher of King Antigonus <note>Antigonus II Gonatas, King of Macedon</note>, for whom he wrote a discourse *On Kingship*, which was highly esteemed. He died in old age. There were others who attended the lectures of Eubulides, including Apollonius Cronus <note>Apollonius was nicknamed "Cronus," which can mean "Old Fool" or "The Ancient One," a name later passed to his student Diodorus</note>.

### DIODORUS.

Diodorus of Iasus, son of Ameinias, was himself also nicknamed "Cronus." Concerning him, Callimachus says in his *Epigrams*:
> Momus <note>The Greek god of mockery and unfair criticism</note> himself wrote on the walls: "Cronus is wise."
He was also a dialectician <term>Dialectician: a philosopher specializing in the logic of arguments and the art of debate</term>, and according to some, he was the first to have discovered the "Veiled Man" and the "Horned Man" arguments <note>These are logical paradoxes: The "Veiled Man" asks if you know your father if he is standing right there but veiled; the "Horned Man" argues that since you haven't lost your horns, you still have them</note>. While he was staying with Ptolemy Soter <note>Ptolemy I, the Macedonian ruler of Egypt and founder of the Library of Alexandria</note>, certain dialectical puzzles were put to him by Stilpo. Being unable to solve them on the spot, he was rebuked by the king in various ways, and in particular, he was called "Cronus" by way of a joke.

# DIODORUS. Book II

...having left the banquet and written a treatise on the problem <note>referring to a logical puzzle or "paradox" posed to him</note>, he ended his life in despondency. We have written an epigram about him as follows:

> O Diodorus Cronus, what evil spirit of 
> Despair dragged you down,
> So that you threw yourself into Tartarus <note>the deepest pit of the underworld</note>,
> Because you could not solve the riddling words 
> Of Stilpo? Thus you were found to be a "Cronus"
> Once the "rho" and "kappa" were removed.
<note>original: "Ἔξωθεν τοῦ ρῶ κάππα τε." This is a clever and biting pun. If you take the Greek letters R (rho) and K (kappa) out of the name Kronos (Κρόνος), you are left with "onos" (ὄνος), the Greek word for "ass" or "donkey."</note>

Among the followers of Euclid was Ichthyas the Metallite <note>originally from the city of Metallus in Crete</note>, a noble man, with whom Diogenes the Cynic held a dialogue. There was also Clinomachus of Thurii, who was the first to write on propositions <term>axiomata: the basic premises of a logical argument</term> and predicates <term>kategorēmata: what is stated or "predicated" about a subject</term>, and other such logical matters. Finally, there was Stilpo of Megara, a most illustrious philosopher, about whom we must now speak.

## STILPO

Stilpo, a native of Megara in Greece, was a student of some of the followers of Euclid. However, some say he studied under Euclid himself, and also under Thrasymachus of Corinth, who was an associate of Ichthyas, according to Heraclides. He so far surpassed all others in his inventiveness of speech <note>original: "heuresilogia"</note> and his skill in sophistry that almost the whole of Greece, with its eyes fixed upon him, began to "Megarize." <note>To "Megarize" usually meant to act like a Megarian, but here it suggests that all of Greece was adopting Stilpo’s specific brand of Megarian philosophy.</note> Regarding him, Philip of Megara writes exactly as follows: "From Theophrastus <note>The successor of Aristotle</note> he drew away Metrodorus the theorist and Timagoras of Gela; from Aristotle the Cyrenaic <note>A philosopher of the Hedonist school</note> he took Cleitarchus and Simmias. And from the dialecticians, he drew Paeonius from the circle of Aristides, and Diphilus of Bosporus from the circle of Euphantus, as well as Myrmex the son of Exaenetus; though these last two had come specifically to refute him, they both became his devoted followers." In addition to these, he brought over Phrasidemus the Peripatetic, who was an expert in natural philosophy, and the rhetorician Alcimus, who was the foremost of all those in Greece...

<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

...illustrious orators, Crates, and many others whom he "hunted down" <note>Diogenes uses the verb *ethērase* (hunted), suggesting Stilpo won them over from other schools through his persuasive arguments</note>. Indeed, he even carried off Zeno the Phoenician <note>Zeno of Citium, who would later found the Stoic school of philosophy</note> from among them. He was also very involved in public affairs; he married a wife, but also lived with the courtesan Nicarete, as Onetor mentions somewhere. He had a daughter of loose character, who was married to a certain Simmias of Syracuse, one of his acquaintances. When someone told Stilpo that she was bringing shame upon him by her behavior, he replied, "She does not bring shame to me any more than I bring honor to her."

It is said that Ptolemy Soter <note>Ptolemy I, the Macedonian general of Alexander the Great who became the ruler of Egypt</note> also held him in high esteem. When Ptolemy became master of Megara, he offered Stilpo money and invited him to sail back to Egypt with him. But Stilpo accepted only a very modest amount of the money; declining the journey, he moved to Aegina until Ptolemy had set sail. Furthermore, Demetrius, the son of Antigonus <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes, known as "the Besieger," a powerful king and rival to Ptolemy</note>, when he captured Megara, saw to it that Stilpo's house was guarded and all his plundered goods were returned to him. When the king wished to receive a list of the things Stilpo had lost so they could be restored, Stilpo replied that he had lost nothing of his own—for no one had carried off his education, and he still possessed his reason and his knowledge <term>epistēmē: systematic, scientific knowledge</term>. After speaking with the king about doing good to mankind, Demetrius was so moved that he became his attentive listener.

They say that Stilpo asked a question of this sort regarding the statue of Athena made by Phidias <note>The colossal gold and ivory statue of Athena Parthenos in the Parthenon</note>: "Is it not true that Athena, the daughter of Zeus, is a god?" When someone replied, "Yes," he said: "But this statue is not the child of Zeus; it is the child of Phidias." When this was admitted, he concluded: "Therefore, this is not a god." For this argument, he was summoned before the Areopagus <note>The ancient and prestigious high court of Athens</note>. He did not deny the charge but argued that his reasoning was correct: for she was not a "god" <term>theos: in Greek, this is a masculine noun</term>, but a "goddess" <term>thea: the feminine form</term>; and that "gods" <note>original: "theous"</note> are specifically male. Nevertheless, the judges of the Areopagus immediately ordered him to leave the city. At this, Theodorus, who was nicknamed "the God" <note>This is a sarcastic reference to Theodorus the Atheist; his nickname "the God" was a joke on his denial of the divine</note>, mockingly asked: "How did Stilpo know that? Did he lift up her garment and look at her 'garden'?" <note>A euphemism for the goddess's private parts, highlighting the absurdity of treating the statue as a physical being</note>. Truly, Theodorus was most bold in speech, while Stilpo was most refined. At any rate, when Crates asked...

# STILPO. Book II

...[someone asked] him if the gods delight in our prostrations and prayers. It is said he replied, "You fool, do not ask about such things in the street, but only when we are alone." They say Bion <note>Bion of Borysthenes, a philosopher known for his wit and stinging social commentary</note> gave a similar reply when asked if the gods exist:

> Will you not scatter the crowd from me, much-enduring old man? <note>original: "Οὐκ ἀπ' ἐμοῦ σκεδάσεις ὄχλον ταλαπείριε πρέσβυ;" — This is a parody of a line from Homer's Iliad, used here to avoid a dangerous public theological debate.</note>

Stilpo was also simple and unaffected in his manners, and could easily adapt himself to the common man. For instance, when Crates the Cynic <note>Crates of Thebes, a famous wandering philosopher who gave away his wealth</note> once failed to answer a question and instead let out a loud fart, Stilpo said, "I knew you would utter anything rather than what you ought." On another occasion, Crates held out a dried fig to him along with a logical puzzle; Stilpo took the fig and ate it. When Crates cried out, "By Heracles! I have lost my fig!" Stilpo replied, "Not only that, but you have lost the question too, for which the fig was the deposit." <note>original: "arrhabōn" — a legal term for a down-payment or earnest money</note> Later, seeing Crates shriveled up with cold in the winter, Stilpo said, "Crates, you seem to me to be in need of a new <term>himation</term> <note>A Greek mantle or cloak; here Stilpo makes a pun on "himation" and "nous" (mind/sense), suggesting he needs both a coat and some sense</note>." Feeling ashamed, Crates composed this parody about him:

> And indeed I saw Stilpo, suffering hard pains,
> In Megara, where they say the bed of Typhon lies.
> There he would dispute, and many companions were about him,
> Wasting their time while pursuing virtue by a single letter. <note>original: "para gramma" — This suggests the Megarians were obsessed with hair-splitting linguistic and logical distinctions.</note>

It is said that Stilpo so turned the heads of the people in Athens that they would run out from their workshops just to catch a glimpse of him. When someone said, "Stilpo, they admire you as if you were a god," he replied, "No, not as a god, but as a true human being." He was exceedingly clever at <term>eristic</term> <note>A style of philosophy focused on logical puzzles and winning arguments</note> discourse, and even sought to do away with the "Forms." <note>The Platonic theory that universal concepts like "Man" or "Beauty" have a real existence beyond individual examples</note> He used to argue that if a person says "man" exists, he is speaking of no one. For he is speaking neither of this man nor that man. Why should he mean this one rather than that one? Therefore, he means no one at all. Again, he argued: "The vegetable is not that which is shown to us here. For 'vegetable' existed ten thousand years ago. Therefore, this item here is not a vegetable." 

They say that once while he was talking with Crates, he walked off in the middle of the conversation to buy some fish. When Crates tried to pull him back and asked, "Are you leaving the <term>logos</term>?" <note>logos: meaning both "the argument" and "reasoned speech"</note> Stilpo replied, "I am not leaving the argument; I still have the argument, but I am leaving you. For the argument will wait, but the fish are being sold."

DIOG. LAERT.

...will try with the eye. Nine dialogues are attributed to him which are considered "cold" <note>original: "psychroi" — in ancient literary criticism, this term described a style that was frigid, lifeless, or lacked rhetorical fire</note>: *Mochus*, *Aristippus* or *Callias*, *Ptolemy*, *Chaerecrates*, *Metrocles*, *Anaximenes*, *Epigenes*, *To His Own Daughter*, and *Aristotle*. Heraclides says that Zeno, the founder of the Stoa <note>The Stoic school of philosophy</note>, was one of his students. Hermippus states that he died at a great age, having intentionally drunk wine so that he might die more quickly. We have also written a poem about him:

> The Megarian Stilpo (whom you likely know)
> Old age then disease laid low—a double-fighting yoke; <note>original: "dimachon zygon" — an image of two different burdens or opponents working together to pull someone down</note>
> But he found wine a better charioteer
> Than that wretched pair. For drinking, he drove away.

He was also mocked by the comic poet Sophilus in his play *The Marriage*:

-> Charinus’s speech is a plug for Stilpo’s mouth. <- <note>A joke implying that someone's talk is so dull or heavy it acts as a "stopper" (bysma) to Stilpo's own philosophical discourse.</note>

---

### CRITO.

Crito was an Athenian. He was most affectionately disposed toward Socrates, and he took such care of him that he never allowed him to lack anything for his needs. His sons were also students of Socrates: Critobulus, Hermogenes, Epigenes, and Ctesippus. Crito wrote seventeen dialogues which are contained in a single volume, under the following titles: *That the Good are Not Made So by Learning*, *On Having More*, *What is Fitting* (or *The Statesman*), *On the Beautiful*, *On Doing Evil*, *On Lack of Public Spirit*, *On Law*, *On the Divine*, *On the Arts*, *On Social Intercourse*, *On Wisdom*, *Protagoras* (or *The Statesman*), *On Letters*, *On Poetry*, *On the Beautiful*, *On Learning*, *On Knowing* (or *On Science*), and *What it is to Know*.

<header>SIMON. Book II</header>

->SIMON.<-

Simon was an Athenian and a shoemaker <term>shoemaker: Greek *skytotomos*</term>. It is said that whenever Socrates came to his workshop and held a discussion, Simon would make notes of what he could remember. Because of this, his dialogues are known as the "Leather Dialogues" <note>original: "Skytikous" — a play on his profession as a worker of leather (skytos).</note>. There are thirty-three of these dialogues contained in a single volume:

*On the Gods*, *On the Good*, *On the Beautiful*, *What is the Beautiful?*, *On the Just* (Books I and II), *On Virtue: That it Cannot be Taught*, *On Courage* (Books I, II, and III), *On Law*, *On Demagoguery*, *On Honor*, *On Poetry*, *On Freedom from Passion*, *On Love*, *On Philosophy*, *On Knowledge*, *On Music*, *On Poetry* <note>The original Greek repeats "On Poetry" and "What is the Beautiful" in this list.</note>, *What is the Beautiful?*, *On Teaching*, *On the Art of Conversation*, *On Judgment*, *On Being*, *On Number*, *On Diligence*, *On Working*, *On Greed*, *On Arrogance*, and *On the Beautiful*.

Some also attribute to him: *On Deliberation*, *On Reason* (or *On Fitness*), and *On Malice*.

Simon is said to have been the first to compose Socratic dialogues <note>original: "dielechthe" — referring here to the literary format of a dialogue imitating Socrates' style of questioning.</note>. When the statesman Pericles promised to provide for him and invited Simon to come live with him, Simon replied that he would not sell his "freedom of speech" <note>original: "parrhesia" — the prized Greek right to speak one's mind frankly, regardless of the listener's status.</note>.

There were others named Simon: a rhetorician who wrote on the technical arts; a physician who lived during the time of Seleucus Nicator; and a sculptor.

---

->GLAUCON.<-

Glaucon was an Athenian. There are nine dialogues of his circulating in a single volume: *Phaedylus*, *Euripides*, *Amyocus*, *Euthias*, *Lysithides*, *Aristophanes*, *Cephalus*, *Anaxiphemus*, and *Menexenus*. There are also another thirty-two dialogues attributed to him which are considered counterfeit <note>original: "notheuontai" — works that circulated under his name but were judged by ancient scholars to be spurious.</note>.

# SIMMIAS.

Simmias was a Theban. There are twenty-three dialogues of his circulating in a single volume: *On Wisdom*, *On Reason*, *On Music*, *On Verses*, *On Courage*, *On Philosophy*, *On Truth*, *On Letters*, *On Teaching*, *On Art*, *On Knowledge*, *On Propriety* <note>original: "prepontos" — referring to what is appropriate or fitting in behavior and speech.</note>, *On Choice and Avoidance*, *On a Friend*, *On Knowing*, *On the Soul*, *On Living Well*, *On the Possible*, *On Wealth*, *On Life*, *What is the Beautiful?*, *On Diligence*, and *On Love*.

# CEBES.

Cebes was a Theban. Three dialogues of his are in circulation: *The Tablet* <note>original: "Pinax" — a famous allegorical work describing the path of human life; though its authorship is debated by modern scholars, Diogenes attributes it to Cebes here.</note>, *The Seventh*, and *Phrynichus*.

# MENEDEMUS.

Menedemus belonged to the school of Phaedo <note>Phaedo of Elis was a student of Socrates whose name titles one of Plato's most famous dialogues.</note>. He was the son of Cleisthenes, a member of the family known as the Theopropidae. Though he was of noble descent, his father was a builder and a poor man. Some say Menedemus himself was a scene-painter <term>scene-painter: Greek *skenographos* — someone who painted the backdrops for theatrical performances</term>, and that he learned both crafts. For this reason, when he later drafted a certain public decree, a follower of the philosopher Alexinus attacked him, saying that it was fitting for a wise man to write neither a theatrical scene nor a decree.

When Menedemus was sent by the Eretrians to Megara as a member of a garrison, he went up to the Academy to visit Plato. Having been "captured" <note>original: "theratheis" — literally "hunted" or "caught," a common metaphor for being won over by a philosopher's charisma.</note> by philosophy, he abandoned his military service. However, after Asclepiades of Phlius drew him away, he went to Megara to study under Stilpo. They both attended the lectures of both teachers. From there, they sailed to Elis and joined Anchipylus and Moschus, who belonged to the school of Phaedo. Until this time, as was mentioned previously in the section on Phaedo, they were called the "Elian School." They were later renamed the "Eretrian School" after the homeland of the man who—

...the account. It appears that Menedemus was a man of considerable dignity. Because of this, Crates <note>Crates of Thebes, a famous Cynic philosopher known for his poverty and wisdom.</note> says in a parody:

-> The Phliasian Asclepiades, and the Bull of Eretria. <-

And Timon <note>Timon of Phlius, a skeptic poet who wrote the 'Silli', satirical poems mocking other philosophers.</note> describes him thus:

-> Setting up his discourse with arched eyebrows, a boaster of pompous nonsense. <-
<note>original: "aphrosebombax" — a comic compound word meaning one who makes a loud, buzzing noise out of folly or froth.</note>

He was so dignified that when Eurylochus of Cassandrea and a youth named Cleippides of Cyzicus were invited by King Antigonus <note>Antigonus II Gonatas, King of Macedonia and a patron of philosophers.</note>, Eurylochus declined. He said he was afraid that Menedemus would find out.

He was also a man who delighted in verbal rebukes and was extremely plain-spoken. For instance, when a young man behaved with excessive boldness, Menedemus said nothing; instead, he took a twig and drew a shameful figure <note>This likely refers to a graphic or suggestive drawing in the dirt intended to mock the youth's behavior or reputation.</note> on the ground until the youth, realizing the insult in front of everyone, left. When Hierocles, the governor of the Piraeus, was walking with him near the temple of Amphiaraus and spoke at length about the recent capture of Eretria, Menedemus said nothing else, but simply asked him: "Why then does Antigonus treat you like a dog?" <note>original: "aphainei" — literally "makes you bark" or "shows you off," suggesting Hierocles was merely a subservient mouthpiece for the King.</note>

To a bold adulterer, he said, "Do you not know that not only cabbage has a good flavor, but radishes too?" <note>original: "rhaphanides" — radishes. In Ancient Greece, "rhaphanidosis" was a humiliating punishment for caught adulterers involving the insertion of a large radish into the rectum.</note> To a younger man who was shouting, he said, "See to it that you do not realize too late that you have something behind you." <note>A biting double entendre implying either that the youth was being followed by trouble or making a crude joke about sexual passivity.</note>

When Antigonus consulted him on whether he should go to a revel, Menedemus remained silent about everything else, but told the messenger to simply report back that "He is the son of a king." To an ignorant man who was relating something to him at random, he asked if he owned a farm; when the man replied that he had many estates, Menedemus said, "Go then and look after them, lest it happens that you ruin those as well, and lose the status of a refined private citizen." <term>private citizen: Greek *idiotes* — referring to a person not involved in public office or professional philosophy.</term>

To someone who asked if a wise and good man should marry, he replied, "Do I seem to you to be a good man or not?" When the person said he was, Menedemus replied, "Well then, I am married." To a man who claimed there were many "good things," he asked how many exactly, and if he thought there were more than a hundred. Once, when he was invited to a dinner and was unable to curb the host's extravagance, he said nothing; however, by his silence, he rebuked the man...

...eating only olives. Indeed, because of this same bluntness of speech, he nearly fell into grave danger in Cyprus, at the court of Nicocreon <note>Nicocreon was the King of Salamis in Cyprus during the late 4th century BCE.</note>, together with his friend Asclepiades. For when the king was celebrating a monthly festival and had invited them as he had the other philosophers, Menedemus reportedly said that if the gathering of such men was a good thing, the festival should be held every day; but if it was not, then it was superfluous even now. When the tyrant replied to this, saying that he had this day free to listen to philosophers, Menedemus pressed him even more sternly, arguing during the sacrifice that one ought to listen to philosophers at every possible opportunity. They would have perished had not a certain flute-player helped them escape. Later, when they were being tossed by a storm in their boat, they say Asclepiades remarked that while the flute-player’s lack of musical skill <note>original: "amousia" — literally a lack of cultivation or art; here it implies his playing was a distraction that allowed their escape.</note> had saved them, Menedemus’s bluntness had nearly destroyed them.

They say he was also relaxed and indifferent regarding the formal organization of his school. At any rate, no fixed order could be seen there, nor were benches placed in a circle; instead, each person would listen while walking or sitting wherever he happened to be, and Menedemus himself followed this same informal manner.

However, they say he was otherwise quite anxious for fame and concerned with his reputation. Consequently, when he and Asclepiades were working together as builders in their youth, Asclepiades was seen naked on the roof carrying mortar; but Menedemus, if he saw anyone coming, would hide himself. Later, when he entered political life, he was so nervous that even when placing incense on the altar, he missed the incense-burner. Once, when Crates <note>Crates of Thebes, the famous Cynic philosopher known for his lifestyle of voluntary poverty.</note> stood around him and attacked him for being involved in politics, Menedemus ordered the "dogs" <note>original: "kusin" — This likely refers to the public guards or prison attendants, though it is a play on Crates being a "Cynic" (literally "dog-like").</note> to throw him into prison. But Crates nonetheless kept watch for him as he passed by, peering out and calling him "A Little Agamemnon" and "Leader of the City" <note>original: "Agamemnoneion" and "Hegesipolis" — satirical nicknames mocking Menedemus's perceived self-importance and political ambitions.</note> to mock him.

He was also, in a way, slightly inclined toward superstition. For instance, once while he was at an inn with Asclepiades, and some meat was being thrown out through ignorance...

# MENEDEMUS: Book 2

...and while he was alive, whenever he learned [that he had eaten meat], he would become distressed and turn pale. This continued until Asclepiades rebuked him, saying that it was not the meat that bothered him, but the mere thought of it. In all other respects, he was a magnanimous and free-spirited man. Regarding his physical appearance, even when he had reached old age, he remained as firm as an athlete and had a sun-drenched complexion <note>original: "epikekaumenos" — literally "burnt by the sun," suggesting he spent much time outdoors or in the gymnasium.</note>; he was well-built and physically fit. In stature, he was well-proportioned, as is evident from the small statue of him in Eretria in the ancient stadium. For that statue is—purposely, it seems—undraped, revealing most parts of his body.

He was also very fond of hosting guests, and because the climate of Eretria was considered unhealthy <note>Eretria was known for its marshy environment, which contemporary Greeks believed caused illness.</note>, he organized frequent banquets. These gatherings included both poets and musicians. He warmly welcomed Aratus, Lycophron the tragic poet, and Antagoras of Rhodes. Most of all, he devoted himself to Homer, then to the lyric poets, and then to Sophocles. He also had a high regard for Achaius, whom he ranked second in the writing of Satyr-plays, while he awarded the first place to Aeschylus. Because of this preference, he used to quote these lines against his political opponents:

->So the swift is caught even by the weak,<-
->And the eagle by the tortoise in a short time.<-

These lines are by Achaius, from his Satyr-play *Omphale*. Thus, those who claim he had read nothing except the *Medea* of Euripides—which some say is actually by Neophron of Sicyon—are mistaken. He held the teachers of the schools of Plato and Xenocrates in contempt, as well as Paraebates of Cyrene. However, he greatly admired Stilpo; and once, when asked about him, he said nothing other than that Stilpo was a "free man."

Menedemus was also difficult to understand, and in the heat of an argument, he was a formidable opponent. He could turn his mind to any subject, was inventive with language, and was extremely ironic <note>original: "eironikotatos" — in the Socratic sense of feigning ignorance to expose the errors of others.</note>, as Antisthenes says in his *Successions of Philosophers*. He was also in the habit of posing questions like this: "Is one thing 'other' than another thing?" "Yes," the person would reply. "And is 'being beneficial' something 'other' than 'the Good'?" "Yes." "Then it is not the case..."

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

“Do good, for it is beneficial.” It is said that he also did away with negative propositions, replacing them with affirmative ones. Furthermore, among these, he only accepted simple propositions, rejecting those that were not simple—by which I mean conditional and complex statements <note>original: "syneimmena kai sympeplegmena" — technical terms in Stoic and Megarian logic referring to "if-then" statements and "both-and" conjunctions.</note>. Heraclides states that while Menedemus was a Platonist in his core doctrines, he nonetheless mocked the study of dialectics <note>Dialectics: the formal logic and argumentative methods popularized by the Megarian school.</note>.

For instance, when Alexinus once asked him in a pointed logical trap whether he had stopped beating his father, Menedemus replied, “I neither was beating him, nor have I stopped.” When Alexinus insisted that he ought to resolve the ambiguity by answering either a simple “yes” or “no,” Menedemus retorted, “It is ridiculous to follow your rules when one can resist at the very gates.” 

On another occasion, when Bion was diligently attacking the credit of diviners, Menedemus told him that he was “merely slaughtering the dead” <note>A metaphor suggesting Bion was attacking a target that was already discredited or lacked the life to fight back.</note>. When he heard someone remark that the greatest good was to obtain everything one desires, he replied: “It is a much greater good to desire only what is proper.”

Antigonus of Carystus reports that Menedemus wrote nothing and composed no treatises; consequently, he held no fixed, rigid dogmas. In his philosophical inquiries, he was so combative that he would often walk away with black eyes. Yet, despite being so fierce in speech, he was the gentlest of men in his actions. For example, although he often mocked Alexinus and teased him harshly, he performed a great kindness for him by escorting Alexinus’s wife all the way from Delphi to Chalcis, as she was terrified of the thieves and highway robberies common on that route.

He was a most devoted friend, as is evident from his harmony with Asclepiades—a bond that was in no way inferior to the famous brotherly love of Pylades <note>Pylades was the legendary companion of Orestes, known in Greek mythology as the ultimate symbol of faithful friendship.</note>. However, Asclepiades was the elder of the two, leading people to say that Asclepiades was the “poet” while Menedemus was the “actor” <note>This suggests Asclepiades provided the intellectual substance or "script," while Menedemus was the public face and orator.</note>. It is said that once, when Archipolis offered them three thousand pieces of silver, they fell into a dispute over who should take the smaller portion, and in the end, neither would accept the money. 

It is also told that they both took wives; Asclepiades married the daughter, and Menedemus the mother. When Asclepiades’ wife passed away, he eventually took Menedemus’ wife to live with him <note>The text implies a shared household where the distinctions of marriage were secondary to their philosophical brotherhood.</note>. And when Menedemus...

### MENEDEMUS. Book II.

When he advanced in public life, he married a wealthy woman. Nevertheless, even though there was only a single household, Menedemus entrusted its entire management to his first wife <note>Menedemus appears to have maintained a complex household where his former and current wives lived together, showing his unconventional approach to social norms.</note>. Asclepiades, however, passed away first in Eretria at an advanced age, having lived with Menedemus in extreme simplicity despite their great means. 

Consequently, when some time later a former favorite of Asclepiades arrived for a revel <note>original: "komon" — a traditional Greek procession of revelers, often involving music and drinking.</note> and the young men of the house were barring him entry, Menedemus ordered them to let him in, saying that Asclepiades, even though he was beneath the earth, was still opening the doors for him. 

Those who provided them with financial support were Hipponicus the Macedonian and Agetor of Lamia; the latter gave thirty minae <term>mina: a unit of currency equivalent to 100 drachmae, roughly representing several months' wages for a skilled laborer</term> to each of them, while Hipponicus gave Menedemus two thousand drachmae for the dowries of his daughters. He had three daughters (as Heraclides states) born to him by a woman from Oropus. 

His banquets were conducted in this manner: he would eat a midday meal with two or three companions until late in the day. Then someone would invite the guests who had arrived, who had already finished their own dinner; thus, if anyone arrived early, they would walk back and ask those leaving what was being served and what time it was. If the report was merely of a bit of vegetable or salt-fish, they would depart; but if it was a bit of meat, they would enter. 

In the summer, there was a rush mat upon the couches, and in the winter, a sheepskin fleece. Each guest was required to bring his own pillow. The cup that was passed around was no larger than a half-pint <term>cotyliaion: a measure of roughly 0.27 liters, emphasizing the moderation of the drinking</term>. For dessert, there were lupin-seeds or beans; sometimes seasonal fruits like a pear, a pomegranate, peas, or—by Zeus—dried figs. 

All these details are mentioned by Lycophron in the Satyr plays <note>Satyr play: a lighthearted, often ribald ancient Greek drama featuring a chorus of satyrs, usually performed after a trilogy of tragedies.</note> he composed for him, which he entitled *Menedemus*, turning the drama into a tribute to the philosopher. Some of the lines are as follows:

->How from a meager feast a tiny cup<-
->Goes round in measured turns; the dessert<-
->Is sobering discourse for those who love to listen.<-

In the beginning, he was held in contempt, called a "dog" and a "babbler" by...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...listening to the Eretrians; later he was held in such high esteem that he was even entrusted with the government of the city. He served as an ambassador to Ptolemy <note>Ptolemy I Soter, the ruler of Egypt</note> and Lysimachus <note>A general of Alexander the Great who became King of Thrace</note>, being honored everywhere he went. He also went as an envoy to Demetrius <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes, "the Besieger," King of Macedon</note>. When the city was paying Demetrius a yearly tribute of two hundred talents <term>talent: a massive unit of weight/currency, roughly 6,000 drachmae, often representing the weight of a person in silver</term>, Menedemus succeeded in having fifty talents removed from the total. Having been slandered to Demetrius on the grounds that he was planning to hand the city over to Ptolemy, he defended himself in a letter, which began: "Menedemus to King Demetrius, greetings. I hear that reports have been brought to you concerning us." 

There is a story that a certain Aeschylus, one of his political opponents, was the one slandering him. He is also thought to have conducted an embassy to Demetrius with great dignity on behalf of Oropus <note>A strategic border town between Athens and Boeotia</note>, as Euphantus mentions in his *Histories*. Antigonus <note>Antigonus II Gonatas, King of Macedon and a patron of philosophers</note> also held him in high affection and used to proclaim himself Menedemus's pupil. When Antigonus defeated the barbarians <note>original: "barbarous" — here referring to the Gauls whom Antigonus defeated in 277 BCE</note> near Lysimachia, Menedemus drafted a decree for him that was simple and free from flattery. It began: "The generals and the counselors have stated: Since King Antigonus, having conquered the barbarians in battle, has returned to his own kingdom and is conducting all other affairs according to his purpose, it has seemed good to the Council and the People." 

Because of these dealings and his general friendship with the King, he was suspected of intending to betray the city to him. After being further slandered by Aristodemus, he withdrew from the city and stayed in Oropus, in the temple of Amphiaraus <note>A sanctuary dedicated to a local hero and seer, known for its oracular dreams</note>. When some golden cups went missing there, he was ordered to leave by a common decree of the Boeotians (as Hermippus tells us). Despondent at this, he secretly slipped back into his homeland, took his wife and daughters with him, and went to Antigonus, where he ended his life in despair. 

However, Heraclides says quite the opposite: that while serving as the chief magistrate of the Eretrians, Menedemus frequently liberated the city from tyrants by bringing in Demetrius. According to this account, he would never have betrayed the city to Antigonus, but was instead the victim of false slander; he supposedly went to Antigonus specifically to seek the liberation of his homeland. When Antigonus did not comply, Menedemus was so overcome by despair that he fasted for seven days and died.

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
## MENEDEMUS. Book II

...days, he departed from this life. Antigonus of Carystus <note>A 3rd-century BCE biographer and bronze-worker who wrote about philosophers he knew personally</note> relates similar details about him. He maintained a fierce and constant war of words with Persaeus <note>Persaeus of Citium, a Stoic philosopher and a favorite of King Antigonus Gonatas</note> alone. For it seemed that when Antigonus <note>Antigonus II Gonatas</note> wished to restore democracy to the Eretrians as a favor to Menedemus, Persaeus prevented it. Because of this, once at a drinking party, Menedemus refuted him in argument and said, among other things: "Such a philosopher he may be, but as a man, he is the worst of all who are or ever shall be."

He died (according to Heraclides <note>Heraclides Lembus, a historian known for abridging biographies</note>) having lived seventy-four years. We have also written an epigram for him as follows:

->I heard of your fate, Menedemus, how<-
->Of your own will you quenched your life, in seven days<-
->Eating nothing. You performed a deed worthy of an Eretrian,<-
->But yet a mindless one; for despair <note>original: "ἀψυχίη" (apsychia) — literally "soullessness" or "faint-heartedness"</note> was the guide that drove you.<-

And these were the Socratic philosophers and those who descended from them. Now we must move on to Plato, the founder of the Academy, and those who came after him, as many as have become famous.

g.iii.

-> PLATO. Book 3 <-
g.iiii.

[Antileon] says that he [Plato] died at eighty-four years of age. He was therefore six years younger than Isocrates <note>A famous Athenian orator and contemporary of Plato</note>. For Isocrates was born during the archonship <note>The term of office for an archon, a chief magistrate of Athens</note> of Lysimachus, while Plato was born during that of Ameinias, the year in which Pericles died <note>429 BCE; Pericles was the most prominent statesman of Athens' Golden Age</note>. He belonged to the deme <note>A local district or township of Athens</note> of Collytus, as Antileon says in the second book of his work *On Chronology* <note>original: "Περὶ χρόνων" (Peri chronon)</note>. Some say he was born in Aegina, in the house of Phidiades, the son of Thales (as Favorinus says in his *Miscellaneous History*), his father having been sent there as a <term>cleruch</term> <note>A citizen-colonist (κληροῦχος) who received a plot of land in conquered territory while retaining Athenian citizenship</note> with others, and returning to Athens when they were expelled by the Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> who were aiding the Aeginetans. He also served as a <term>choregos</term> <note>A wealthy citizen (χορηγός) who financed and organized the chorus for theatrical performances</note> at Athens, with Dion paying the expenses, as Athenodorus says in the eighth book of his *Walks* <note>original: "περιπάτων" (peripaton)</note>. He had brothers named Adeimantus and Glaucon, and a sister named Potone, who was the mother of Speusippus <note>Who would later succeed Plato as the head of the Academy</note>.

He was educated in letters by Dionysius, whom he mentions in the *Rival Lovers*; and he practiced gymnastics under Ariston the Argive wrestler. It was from him that he was renamed "Plato" because of his robust physique <note>The name "Plato" is derived from the Greek word "platys," meaning broad or wide</note>, having previously been called Aristocles after his grandfather, as Alexander says in his *Successions of Philosophers* <note>original: "Διαδοχαῖς" (Diadochais)</note>. Some say, however, that he was so named because of the breadth of his eloquence; or because he was broad across the forehead, as Neanthes says. There are those who say he also wrestled at the Isthmian Games <note>A major Panhellenic athletic festival held every two years</note>, as Dicaearchus says in the first book of his *Lives*; and that he applied himself to painting and wrote poems—first dithyrambs <note>Choral hymns sung in honor of the god Dionysus</note>, then lyric songs and tragedies.

He had a thin voice, they say, as Timotheus the Athenian says in his work *On Lives*. It is said that Socrates saw in a dream a cygnet <note>a young swan</note> sitting on his knees, which suddenly grew feathers and flew away, uttering a sweet cry; and the next day Plato was introduced to him, whereupon Socrates said that he [Plato] was the bird. At first he studied philosophy in the Academy, and then in the garden near Colonus, as Alexander says in his *Successions* following Heraclitus. Then, however, when he was about to compete...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

<margin>Regarding the Theater of Dionysus</margin>
...when he was about to compete with a tragedy at the Theater of Dionysus, having heard Socrates, he burned his poems, saying:
> “Hephaestus, come hither; Plato now has need of thee.” <note>original: "῞Ηφαιστε πρόμολ' ὧδε, Πλάτων νύ τι σεῖο χατίζει." A parody of a line from Homer's Iliad, where Thetis calls upon Hephaestus, the god of fire and craftsmanship. Plato is calling for fire to consume his writings.</note>

<margin>Regarding the Socratic circle</margin>
From then on, being (they say) twenty years old, he became a pupil of Socrates. When Socrates had passed away, he attached himself to Cratylus the Heraclitean <note>A follower of Heraclitus, who famously believed that "all things flow" (change is constant)</note>, and to Hermogenes, who followed the philosophy of Parmenides <note>Who argued that change is an illusion and reality is single and unchanging</note>. Then, at twenty-eight years of age (as Hermodorus says), he withdrew to Megara to stay with Euclid, along with certain other Socratics. Afterwards, he went to Cyrene to study with Theodorus the mathematician; and from there to Italy to visit the Pythagoreans, Philolaus and Eurytus. From there he went to Egypt to visit the prophets <note>The priestly class or oracles</note>; they say that Euripides <note>The famous tragedian</note> accompanied him there, and that Plato fell ill and was cured by the priests by means of sea-water treatment. This led him to say:
> “The sea washes away all the ills of men.” <note>original: "Θάλασσα κλύζει πάντα τἀνθρώπων κακά." A quote from Euripides' play *Iphigenia in Tauris*.</note>

Moreover, following Homer, he said that all Egyptians were physicians. Plato also intended to meet with the Magi <note>Persian priests and astrologers</note>, but he was prevented by the wars in Asia.

<margin>Regarding the Academy</margin>
Returning to Athens, he settled in the Academy. This is a gymnasium <note>A public place for physical and intellectual exercise</note> in a wooded suburb, named after a certain hero, Academus, as Eupolis says in his play *The Exempt from Service*:
> “In the well-shaded walks of the god Academus.”

Indeed, Timon also says, referring to Plato:
> “The broadest of all led them, but a sweet-speaking orator,
> like the cicadas that, perched on the trees of Hecademus,
> send forth a lily-like voice.” <note>Timon of Phlius uses "broadest" (*platy-statos*) as a pun on Plato’s name. In Greek literature, the "lily-like" voice of cicadas was a metaphor for a clear, sweet sound.</note>

For formerly, the place was called Hecademia with an 'e'. Now, the philosopher was also a friend of Isocrates. And Praxiphanes recorded a certain conversation of theirs concerning poets, which took place when Isocrates was a guest of Plato at his country estate.

<meta>This page continues the biography of Plato, specifically detailing his military service and the various philosophical influences that shaped his unique system of thought, following his return from his travels in Egypt and Italy.</meta>

### PLATO. Book III

Aristoxenus <note>A philosopher and music theorist who was a pupil of Aristotle</note> states that Plato served in the army three times: first at Tanagra, second at Corinth, and third at Delium, where he is said to have distinguished himself for his bravery. 

He created a synthesis of the doctrines of Heraclitus, the Pythagoreans, and Socrates. Regarding the world of the senses <term>sensibles: physical objects we perceive through sight, touch, etc.</term>, he followed the teachings of Heraclitus; regarding the world of the mind <term>intelligibles: abstract concepts or "Forms" that are constant</term>, he followed Pythagoras; and in matters of social and moral life, he followed the example of Socrates. 

Some writers, including Satyrus <note>A 3rd-century BCE biographer</note>, claim that Plato wrote to Dion in Sicily asking him to purchase three Pythagorean books from Philolaus <note>A famous Pythagorean who first committed their secret oral teachings to writing</note> for the price of one hundred minas. It is said he was able to do this because, although he was otherwise in financial need, he had received more than eighty talents from Dionysius <note>The ruler of Syracuse</note>, a detail also mentioned by Onetor in his work titled *Whether the Wise Man should Make Money*. 

Plato also benefited greatly from the comic poet Epicharmus, transcribing many of his ideas, as Alcimus says in his four books dedicated *To Amyntas*. In the first of these, Alcimus writes: "It is evident that Plato says many things belonging to Epicharmus; this is worth examining." 

Plato defines a "sensible" thing <note>original: αἰσθητὸν</note> as that which never remains the same in its quality or quantity, but is in a state of constant flux and change—meaning that if you were to take away number from these things, they would no longer be equal, nor specific types of things, nor have quantity or quality. These are things that are always "becoming" <note>in a process of change</note> but never truly "are" <note>possessing a fixed essence</note>. 

On the other hand, an "intelligible" thing <note>original: νοητὸν</note> is that from which nothing is ever lost and to which nothing is added. This represents the nature of eternal things, which are always characterized by being similar and the same as themselves. Indeed, the poet Epicharmus spoke clearly about these sensible and intelligible things:

> "But the gods were always present, and they never failed; these things are always present in the same way, and through the same things always. But it is said that Chaos was the first among the gods to be born. Yet how could that be? It is impossible for anything to come from nothing; how could anything come first? Therefore nothing came first; nor, by Zeus, second; but regarding these things of which we now speak, it is about to be. If someone adds a number to a number—or if you wish, add a pebble to a man who lacks sense, or take one away from those already there—do you think the person remains the same? Not to me, I think. Nor indeed, he who..."

<summary>This page outlines Plato's military career and his philosophical origins as a blend of Heraclitean, Pythagorean, and Socratic thought, while also suggesting he borrowed significantly from the poet Epicharmus.</summary>
<keywords>Aristoxenus, military service, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Socrates, Epicharmus, Philolaus, sensibles, intelligibles, metaphysics</keywords>

--- Page 120 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Plato's philosophical influences, specifically the claim by the writer Alcimus that Plato’s central "Theory of Forms" was actually derived from the earlier comedic poet Epicharmus. It bridges the gap between the concept of constant physical change and the existence of eternal, unchanging truths.</meta>

<page-num>106</page-num>
->### DIOGENES LAERTIUS<-

...if a measure were thick and one chose to add another length to it, or to cut away from what was already there, would that same measure still exist? <note>original: "μέτρον παχὺ ἐὸν..." This is a famous philosophical puzzle known as the "Growing Argument," suggesting that if you change any part of a thing, it becomes a new thing entirely.</note> No, it would not. Do you not see that humans are the same way? For one grows, while another surely wastes away; all are in a state of change <note>original: μεταλλαγᾷ</note> all the time. That which changes according to its nature, and never stays the same within itself, must be something different from what it just was. By this logic, you and I are different people yesterday than we are now, and we will be different again in the future, never remaining the same person according to this reasoning.

Alcimus also says this: "The wise say that the soul perceives some things through the body, such as when it is hearing or seeing; but other things it considers by itself, without using the body at all." Therefore, of all things that exist, some are **sensible** <term>perceived by the senses: things we can see, touch, or hear</term> and others are **intelligible** <term>perceived by the mind: abstract concepts like math or justice</term>. 

For this reason, Plato said that those who desire to understand the principles of the universe must first distinguish the **Ideas** <note>original: ἰδέας — often called "Forms," these are the perfect, unchanging patterns of things in the physical world</note> in and of themselves, such as Likeness, Unity, Plurality, Magnitude, Rest, and Motion. 

Secondly, one must assume the existence of the Beautiful, the Good, and the Just, each in and of itself. 

Thirdly, one must understand how many of the Ideas relate to one another, such as Knowledge, or Magnitude, or Mastery; keeping in mind that the things in our world are called by the same names as those Ideas because they **participate** in them. I mean, for example, that things are called "just" because they partake in Justice, and things are called "beautiful" because they partake in Beauty. 

Each of these **Forms** <note>original: εἰδῶν</note> is eternal; it is a thought, and it is "impassive" <note>original: ἀπαθές — meaning it cannot be changed or affected by the physical world</note>. This is why he says that the Ideas stand in nature like **paradigms** <note>original: παραδείγματα — perfect models or blueprints</note>, while all other things resemble them, existing only as likenesses of them. 

Now, Epicharmus <note>A 5th-century BCE comic playwright from Sicily whom Alcimus claims Plato plagiarized</note> speaks about the Good and about the Ideas in this way: 

"Is flute-playing a real thing?" 
"Most certainly." 
"Is a human being, then, 'flute-playing'?" 
"Not at all." 
"Well then, let me see: what is a flute-player? Who do you think he is? A man, is he not?" 
"Most certainly." 
"Do you not think the same holds true regarding the Good? The Good is the thing itself; but as for the person who has learned it and knows it... <note>The text cuts off here, but the argument suggests that "The Good" is a perfect concept while the "good person" is merely a human participating in that concept.</note>

<summary>This page records the argument that Plato's Theory of Forms was influenced by the poet Epicharmus, using the "Growing Argument" to show that while physical things change, the abstract "Ideas" or "Forms" remain eternal and unchanging.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Epicharmus, Theory of Forms, Ideas, sensible vs intelligible, Justice, Beauty, The Good, Growing Argument, Alcimus</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the argument by the writer Alcimus, who claimed that Plato’s most famous philosophical concepts were actually borrowed from the Sicilian comic poet and philosopher Epicharmus. The text continues a musical analogy and transitions into the relationship between memory, the "Ideas," and the natural instincts of animals.</meta>

<page-num>107</page-num>
->## PLATO. Book 3.<-

...more of these things, he already becomes good. For just as if someone learned flute-playing from flute-players, or dancing from dancers, or weaving from weavers, or any similar thing you like, he himself would not be the art itself, but he would certainly be skilled in that art. 

Plato, in his conception of the **Ideas** <note>original: ἰδέων — often translated as "Forms," these are the perfect, unchanging patterns of things in the physical world</note>, says: "If memory exists, then the Ideas must exist within things, because memory is of something that is at rest and remains still; and nothing remains still except the Ideas." For in what way (he asks) could living creatures be preserved if they did not grasp the Idea and receive a natural intellect for this? But as it is, they remember likeness and nourishment, whatever kind they have, showing that in all living creatures the observation of **likeness** <note>original: ὁμοιότητος</note> is innate. This is why they recognize those of their own kind. 

How then does Epicharmus put it? "Eumaeus, wisdom <note>original: τὸ φρονεῖν</note> is not found in just one thing alone, but all things that live also have intelligence. For even the female race of hens—if you care to observe closely—does not give birth to living young, but hatches eggs and makes them have a soul. Nature alone knows how this wisdom is; for she has been taught by these very things." 

And again: "It is no wonder that I say these things, and that they [the animals] please themselves and think they are well-made. For a dog seems most beautiful to a dog, an ox to an ox, a donkey to a donkey, and a pig to a pig." 

Alcimus inserts these and similar points through his four books, indicating the benefit Plato derived from Epicharmus. That Epicharmus himself was not unaware of his own wisdom can be learned from these lines, in which he predicts the one who will emulate him: "As I think—for I think this is clear—that there will yet be a memory of these words of mine. Someone will take them, strip away the meter they now have <note>Epicharmus wrote in verse; Plato wrote in prose</note>, give them a new garment, and embroider them with beautiful words; being a **difficult wrestler** <term>a metaphor for a formidable debater or philosopher</term>, he will make all others look like poor wrestlers." 

It also seems that Plato imitated the mimes of Sophron <note>Sophron of Syracuse wrote "mimes," which were rhythmic prose dialogues depicting everyday life</note>, which had been neglected...

<summary>Alcimus argues that Plato's "Theory of Forms" and his views on natural instinct were inspired by the poet Epicharmus, even quoting a "prophecy" where Epicharmus predicts his work will be turned into prose by a great thinker.</summary>
<keywords>Plato, Epicharmus, Alcimus, Theory of Forms, memory, animal intelligence, Sophron, mimicry, philosophical influence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Plato, specifically discussing his literary influences and his first voyage to Sicily. The previous page ended with a discussion of how animals possess a natural instinct or "likeness" to wisdom, quoting the poet Epicharmus. This page transitions into Plato's personal history and his dangerous encounters with political power.</meta>

<page-num>108</page-num>
->### DIOGENES LAERTIUS<-

...before bringing these works to Athens, he had already prepared the way for them. It is said that these books <note>The text likely refers to the mimes of Sophron or the works of Epicharmus, which Plato was famously fond of</note> were even found under his head <note>original: ὑπὸ τῇ κεφαλῇ — referring to his pillow or deathbed</note> after he died. 

He sailed to Sicily three times. The first time was to see the island and its volcanic craters <note>specifically Mount Etna</note>. It was then that Dionysius I, the son of Hermocrates and tyrant of Syracuse, forced Plato to meet with him. During their conversation, they spoke about **tyranny**. Plato argued that the mere "interest of the stronger" is not enough unless it is also joined with **virtue** <note>original: ἀρετῇ — excellence or moral character</note>. This offended the tyrant. In a fit of anger, Dionysius said, "Your words smell of dotage" <note>original: γεροντιῶσι — "acting like an old man"</note>. To which Plato replied, "And yours smell of tyranny." 

Infuriated by this, the tyrant first intended to have him executed. However, having been persuaded otherwise by Dion and Aristomenes, he spared Plato’s life but handed him over to Polis the Lacedaemonian <note>a Spartan envoy</note>, who happened to be there on an embassy, with orders to sell him into slavery. Polis took him to **Aegina** and put him up for sale. 

At that time, a man named Charmandrus, the son of Charmandrides, brought a capital charge against Plato. He invoked a local law which stated that the first Athenian to set foot on the island should be put to death without a trial. This law had actually been proposed by the very man who brought the charge, according to Favorinus in his *Miscellaneous History*. However, when someone pointed out (perhaps as a "philosopher’s joke") that the man who had landed was a philosopher, the people of Aegina set him free. 

Others say he was brought before the public assembly and, though closely watched, he did not say a single word, prepared to accept whatever happened. The assembly decided not to kill him, but instead decreed he should be sold in the manner of a prisoner of war. By chance, **Anniceris of Cyrene** was present; he ransomed Plato for twenty minas <note>original: μνῶν — some sources say thirty</note> and sent him back to Athens to his companions. 

When his friends immediately tried to pay Anniceris back, he refused the money, saying that they were not the only ones worthy of caring for Plato. Some say that Dion actually sent the money and Anniceris would not take it, but instead used it to buy the small garden in the **Academy** <note>The famous school Plato founded, named after the hero Academus</note> for him. As for Polis, the story goes that he was later defeated by the general Chabrias and then drowned at sea at Helice—a fate seen as a sign of divine wrath <note>original: τοῦ δαιμονίου μηνίσαντος — the anger of the divinity</note>.

# PLATO. Book III

...him because of the philosopher <note>referring to Aristomenes or perhaps Dion, mentioned on the previous page</note>; this is also what Favorinus says in the first book of his *Memorabilia* <note>original: ἀπομνημονευμάτων — a collection of historical anecdotes and recollections</note>. However, Dionysius did not remain quiet; having learned of Plato's safety, he wrote to him, warning him not to speak ill of him. Plato replied that he did not have so much leisure time as to even remember Dionysius.

He came a second time to the court of the younger Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the son and successor of the first tyrant</note>, requesting land and people who would live according to his ideal **Republic** <note>original: πολιτείαν — his blueprint for a perfect society</note>. Dionysius, although he had promised this, did not follow through. Some say that Plato was again in danger, as he was suspected of encouraging Dion and Theotas to liberate the island. At that time, Archytas the Pythagorean <note>a famous mathematician and statesman from Tarentum</note> wrote a letter to Dionysius, interceding for Plato and securing his safe return to Athens. The letter is as follows:

->Archytas to Dionysius, greetings.<-

> All of us, the friends of Plato, have sent Lamiscus and Photidas to bring the man back, in accordance with the agreement you made. You would do well to remember us with all sincerity, just as you did when you invited us all to support Plato's arrival, requesting that he come and promising to provide for his safety, his stay, and his departure. Remember this too: that you valued his arrival highly and loved him at that time more than anyone else. If some friction <note>original: τραχύτας — "roughness" or "harshness"</note> has arisen between you, you must act with humanity and return the man to us unharmed. By doing this, you will act justly and do us a favor.

He went a third time to reconcile Dion with Dionysius. Failing in this, he returned to his homeland without having achieved his goal. There, he did not involve himself in politics, although he was a "political" man in the sense of his writings <note>the *Republic* and the *Laws*</note>. The reason for this was that the people were already accustomed to a different system of government. Pamphila <note>a female historian of the 1st century AD</note> says in the twenty-fifth book of her *Commentaries* that when the Arcadians and the Thebans were founding a "Great City" <note>Megalopolis, founded around 371 BCE</note>, they invited him to be their lawgiver; but when he learned, perhaps...

<meta>Catchword: perhaps</meta>

<meta>This page continues the biography of Plato, following the account of his safe return to Athens from Syracuse with the help of Archytas the Pythagorean.</meta>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...willingly for those who were unwilling, he departed. There is a story that he even accompanied Chabrias the general when he was facing a capital trial, though none of the other citizens were willing to do so. It is said that as he was going up to the Acropolis with Chabrias, Crobylus the sycophant <note>original: συκοφάντης — in ancient Athens, this referred to a professional informer or malicious accuser who brought lawsuits for profit</note> met him and said: "Are you here to advocate for another, unaware that the hemlock of Socrates is waiting for you too?" To which Plato replied: "When I served as a soldier for my fatherland, I endured dangers; and now for the sake of duty to a friend, I will endure them still."

He was the first to introduce the method of argument through questioning, as Favorinus says in the eighth book of his *Miscellaneous History*. He was also the first to explain the method of mathematical analysis <note>original: ἀνάλυσιν — a method of solving problems by tracing them back to established principles</note> to Leodamas of Thasos. Furthermore, he was the first in philosophy to use the terms **antipodes** <note>literally "those with feet opposite," referring to people on the other side of the globe</note>, **element** <note>original: στοιχεῖον (stoicheion) — the fundamental building blocks of matter</note>, **dialectic**, **poems**, and **oblong number** <note>a number that is the product of two non-equal factors</note>, as well as the **plane surface** of limits and **divine providence**. 

He was also the first philosopher to argue against the speech of Lysias, son of Cephalus, by setting it out word-for-word in his dialogue, the *Phaedrus*. He was the first to examine the power of grammar. Because he argued against almost everyone who came before him, the question is often asked why he never mentioned Democritus <note>Democritus was the famous proponent of the atomic theory; Plato's silence regarding him is a noted historical mystery</note>.

Neanthes of Cyzicus says that when Plato went up to the Olympic Games, all the Greeks turned their gaze toward him. It was there that he met Dion, who was planning an expedition against Dionysius. In the first book of the *Memorabilia* of Favorinus, it is recorded that Mithridates the Persian dedicated a statue of Plato in the Academy and inscribed upon it: "Mithridates, son of Rodobates, a Persian, dedicated this image of Plato to the Muses, which Silanion fashioned."

Heraclides says that when he was young, he was so modest and orderly that he was never seen laughing excessively. Despite being such a man, he was nevertheless mocked by the comic poets. Theopompus, for instance, in his play *Autochares*, says the following:

# 214 DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...to contradict. When Antisthenes asked, “How then can you write about this very subject?” and demonstrated that the argument was circular, Plato wrote a dialogue against him, giving it the title *Sathon* <note>original: Σάθωνα (Sathona) — a vulgar nickname derived from the word for the male organ, used by Plato to mock Antisthenes' name and character</note>. From that point on, the two men remained estranged from one another. They also say that when Socrates heard Plato reading the *Lysis*, he exclaimed, “By Heracles, what a lot of lies this young man is telling about me!” For the man wrote down a great many things that Socrates never actually said. 

Plato was also ill-disposed toward Aristippus <note>Founder of the Cyrenaic school, who believed pleasure was the highest good</note>. At any rate, in his dialogue *On the Soul* <note>The *Phaedo*</note>, he disparages him by saying that he was not present when Socrates died, even though he was nearby in Aegina. He also felt a certain professional jealousy toward Aeschines. The story goes that Aeschines was held in high regard by Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse</note>, but when he arrived in Sicily in a state of poverty, he was snubbed by Plato and only gained an introduction through the help of Aristippus. 

Furthermore, Idomeneus <note>An author who wrote about the famous men of Athens</note> claims that the arguments which Plato assigned to Crito—who, in the prison, advises Socrates to flee—actually belonged to Aeschines. He says Plato attributed them to Crito because of his personal enmity toward Aeschines. Plato makes no mention of Aeschines anywhere in his own writings, except in the dialogue *On the Soul* and in the *Apology*. 

Aristotle says that the style of Plato’s dialogues lies somewhere between poetry and prose. Favorinus <note>A Roman-era scholar and friend of Plutarch</note> mentions somewhere that when Plato was reading his work *On the Soul*, only Aristotle remained until the end, while all the other listeners got up and left. 

Some claim that Philip of Opus <note>A student of Plato and an astronomer</note> transcribed Plato's *Laws*, which were originally written on wax tablets. They also say that the *Epinomis* <note>A sequel to the Laws concerning mathematics and astronomy</note> was written by Philip. Euphorion and Panaetius have noted that the opening of the *Republic* was found to have been rearranged and rewritten many times. Aristoxenus <note>A philosopher and music theorist who studied under Aristotle</note> claims that almost the entire *Republic* was already written in the *Controversies* of Protagoras. 

It is said that the *Phaedrus* was the first dialogue he wrote; indeed, the subject matter has a somewhat youthful character. Dicaearchus <note>A Greek philosopher and geographer</note> even criticizes the entire style of the writing as being overly ornate or vulgar. It is said that Plato, having seen...

PLATO. Book 3.
h.ii.

...[seeing] someone <note>original: τινὰ (tina) — the beginning of the word is lost from the previous page</note> playing dice, he rebuked him. When the man replied that he was only playing for small stakes, Plato said, "But the habit itself is no small matter." When asked if there would be any memoirs written about him as there had been for those before him, he replied, "I must first win a name for myself, and then there will be many." 

Once, when Xenocrates <note>Plato’s student and eventual successor as head of the Academy</note> came into the room, Plato asked him to flog his slave for him. He explained that he could not do it himself because he was too angry. Similarly, he said to one of his slaves, "I would have given you a flogging if I were not in a temper." After mounting a horse, he immediately got down again, saying he was afraid he might be seized by "horse-conceit" <note>original: ἱπποτυφίᾳ (hippotyphia) — a pun on the word *typhos*, meaning smoke, delusion, or vanity; here referring to the arrogance associated with being a horseman</note>. 

He advised those who were drunk to look at themselves in a mirror, for they would surely turn away from such an unsightly appearance. He maintained that drinking to the point of intoxication was never appropriate anywhere, except during the festivals of the god who gave us wine <note>Dionysus</note>. He also strongly disliked sleeping too much. In his work, the *Laws*, he states:
> "No one who is asleep is worth anything." <note>Laws, 808b</note>

He also held that truth was the most pleasant of all things to hear—though others say he meant "telling the truth." Regarding truth, he writes in the *Laws* as follows:
> "Truth is a beautiful thing, stranger, and lasting; yet it seems no easy thing to persuade men of it." <note>Laws, 663e</note>

Furthermore, he deemed it worthy to leave behind a memorial of himself, whether in his friends or in his books. He even surpassed most men [in fame], as some say. He died in this manner: in the thirteenth year of the reign of King Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great; the year was roughly 348/347 BCE</note>, as Favorinus states in the third book of his *Memorabilia*. Theopompus adds that he was criticized by the king. 

Myronianus, in his *Book of Similarities*, says that Philon mentions a proverb about "Plato's lice," suggesting that he died from a lice infestation <note>original: φθειρῶν (phtheirōn) — the "disease of lice" or phthiriasis was a common, often legendary, cause of death attributed to famous figures in antiquity to suggest a humble or even shameful end</note>. He was buried in the Academy, where he had spent the greatest part of his time practicing philosophy. It is for this reason that the school of thought following him was called the "Academic" sect. He was escorted to his grave by the entire population of the city, having first made his will in the following manner:

# These things Plato left and disposed of by will:
The estate in Hephaestiadae <note>A district or "deme" in ancient Attica</note>, bounded on the north by the road coming from the temple at Kephisia, and on the south by the sanctuary of Herakles in Hephaestiadae; on the east by the property of Archestratus of Phrearrhii, and on the west...

> But his earth-born body is held by the Attic land.

### PLATO. Book III

There is also an epigram of our own, which runs as follows:

->And how, if Phoebus <note>original: Φοῖβος (Phoibos) — an epithet for Apollo, god of healing and prophecy</note> had not brought forth Plato throughout Greece,<-
->Could he have healed the souls of men with his writings?<-
->For as Asclepius <note>The god of medicine and son of Apollo</note> became the healer<-
->Of the body, so is Plato the healer of the immortal soul.<-

And another, concerning the manner of his death:

->Phoebus fathered for mortals both Asclepius and Plato,<-
->The one to save the soul, the other to save the body.<-
->And having celebrated a wedding feast, he departed to the city which he once<-
->Founded for himself, and settled in the soil of Zeus.<-

These then are the epigrams. His disciples were Speusippus of Athens, Xenocrates of Chalcedon, Aristotle of Stagira, Philip of Opus, Hestiaeus of Perinthus, Dion of Syracuse, Amyklas of Heraclea, Erastus and Coriscus of Skepsis, Timolaus of Cyzicus, Evaion of Lampsacus, Pithon and Heracleides of Aenos, Hippothales and Callippus of Athens, Demetrius of Amphipolis, Heracleides of Pontus, and many others. Among them were also two women, Lastheneia of Mantinea and Axiothea of Phlius, who—as Dicaearchus says—even wore men’s clothing. Some say that Theophrastus also attended his lectures; Chamaeleon says the same of Hyperides the orator and Lycurgus; Polemon likewise records this of Demosthenes. Sabinus, in the fourth book of his *Materials for Declamation*, mentions Mnesistratus of Thasos, and this is indeed probable.

Now, since you are a devoted "lover of Plato" <note>original: φιλοπλάτωνι (philoplatoni) — Diogenes is addressing an unidentified woman of high status who studied philosophy</note>, as is only right, and since you zealously seek out the philosopher's doctrines <term>doctrines</term> <note>original: δόγματα (dogmata) — the core principles or "tenets" of a philosophical school</note> more than anyone else, I have thought it necessary to outline the nature of his discourses, the arrangement of his dialogues, and the method of his <term>induction</term> <note>original: ἐπαγωγῆς (epagoges) — the logical process of reasoning from specific instances to a general conclusion</note>. I shall do so as elementally and summarily as possible, so that your collection of facts about his life may not be lacking in his teachings. For it would be "carrying owls to Athens" <note>A Greek proverb similar to "carrying coals to Newcastle," meaning to bring something to a place that already has it in abundance</note> if I were to describe his specific teachings to you in exhaustive detail. There-
