# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

<margin><unclear>Zeno</unclear></margin> Now, they say that Zeno of Elea was the first to write <term>dialogues</term> <note>Literally "written discourses" or "arguments" in the form of a conversation.</note>. 
<margin><unclear>Aristotle</unclear></margin> However, Aristotle, in the first book of his work *On Poets*, says it was Alexamenus 
<margin><unclear>Plato</unclear></margin> of Styra or Teos, as does Favorinus in his *Memorabilia*. But it seems to me that Plato, having perfected this literary form, should rightly carry off the first prize for its invention as well as for its beauty. A **dialogue** is a discourse consisting of <margin><unclear>dialogue</unclear></margin> question and answer on some philosophical or political subject, combined with the appropriate characterization of the individuals introduced and the careful arrangement of the language. **Dialectic** is the art of discourse by which we either refute <margin><unclear>dialectic</unclear></margin> or establish a point through the question and answer of the participants.

There are two primary styles of Platonic discourse: the **expository** <note>original: ὑφηγητικός (uphēgētikos) — intended for instruction or guidance</note> and the **exploratory** <note>original: ζητητικός (zētētikos) — intended for inquiry or searching for truth</note>. The expository style is further divided into two types: the **theoretical** and the **practical**. The theoretical is divided into **physics** and **logic**; the practical is divided into **ethics** and **politics**. 

The exploratory style also has two primary divisions: the **training** style and the **competitive** style. The training style is divided into the **obstetric** <note>original: μαιευτικός (maieutikos) — referring to Socrates' "midwifery," helping others give birth to their own ideas</note> and the **testing** styles. The competitive style is divided into the **demonstrative** and the **subversive**. 

We are not unaware that some scholars distinguish the dialogues in other ways. They say some are **dramatic**, some **narrative**, and others **mixed**. However, those scholars have named these differences in a manner more suited to the theater <note>original: τραγικῶς (tragikōs) — literally "tragically" or "theatrically"</note> than to philosophy. 

To the **physical** category belongs, for example, the *Timaeus*. To the **logical** belong the *Statesman*, *Cratylus*, *Parmenides*, and the *Sophist*. To the **ethical** belong the *Apology*, *Crito*, *Phaedo*, *Phaedrus*, *Symposium*, *Menexenus*, *Cleitophon*, the *Letters*, *Philebus*, *Hipparchus*, and the *Lovers*. To the **political** belong the *Republic*, the *Laws*, *Minos*, *Epinomis*, and the *Atlantic* <note>The *Critias*, which deals with the story of Atlantis.</note>. To the **obstetric** belong the *Alcibiades*, *Theages*, *Lysis*, and *Laches*. To the **testing** belong...

<summary>This page discusses the origins of the dialogue form, attributing its perfection to Plato, and provides a detailed taxonomic classification of Plato’s works into categories such as theoretical, practical, and exploratory.</summary>
<keywords>Zeno of Elea, Alexamenus, Plato, dialogue, dialectic, physics, logic, ethics, politics, Socratic midwifery, classification of Platonic works</keywords>

### PLATO. Book 3

...*Euthyphro, Meno, Ion, Charmides,* and *Theaetetus*. To the **midwifery** style <note>original: μαιευτικῷ (maieutikō) — refers to the "obstetric" method mentioned on the previous page</note> belong these; while to the **refutative** style belong the *Protagoras*, and to the **subversive** <note>original: ἀνατρεπτικοῦ (anatreptikou)</note> style belong the *Euthydemus*, the two *Hippias* dialogues, and the *Gorgias*. Regarding what a dialogue is and how its varieties differ, enough has been said. 

Since there is a great deal of debate—with some saying that Plato **dogmatizes** <term>original: δογματίζειν — to state certain principles as established truths</term> and others saying he does not—let us distinguish between these views as well. To **dogmatize** is to lay down a **dogma** <note>original: δόγμα — a decree or tenet</note>, just as to legislate is to lay down laws. The term "dogma" is used in two ways: it is both the thing one thinks, and the thought itself. Of these, the thing thought is a **proposition**, while the thought itself is a **conception**. 

Now, concerning things he has fully grasped, Plato expresses his own views; he refutes things that are false; and on matters that are unclear, he **suspends judgment** <note>original: ἐπέχει (epechei) — a technical term in skepticism for withholding a final decision when evidence is balanced</note>. He expresses his own opinions through the mouths of four characters: Socrates, Timaeus, the Athenian Stranger, and the Eleatic Stranger. These "Strangers" are not, as some have supposed, Plato and Parmenides; rather, they are anonymous fictional characters. When Plato records the words of Socrates or Timaeus, he is dogmatizing <note>i.e., presenting his own philosophical system</note>. 

However, when he wishes to refute falsehoods, he introduces characters such as Thrasymachus, Callicles, Polus, Gorgias, Protagoras, Hippias, Euthydemus, and others like them. 

In constructing his proofs, he most frequently makes use of **induction** <term>original: ἐπαγωγή (epagōgē) — a method of reasoning that moves from specific instances to a general rule</term>. He does not use a single form of it, but rather two kinds. Induction is an argument that, through certain truths, appropriately infers a truth similar to itself. One form of induction works through **contradiction**, and the other through **consequence**. 

The form that works through **contradiction** is one where, whatever answer the person being questioned gives, the opposite of their claim will follow. For example: "My father is either different from your father, or he is the same. If your father is different from my father, then by being 'different from a father,' he would not be a father. But if he is the same as my father, then by being 'the same as my father,' he would be my father." 

And again: "If man is not an animal, he would be stone or wood. But he is not stone or wood (for he has a soul and moves of his own accord); therefore, he is an animal. But if he is an animal, then an animal..."

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...or if both a dog and an ox were the same, then a human would also be an animal, a dog, and an ox. This is the method of **induction** <term>original: ἐπαγωγῆς (epagōgēs) — a way of reaching a general conclusion by looking at specific examples</term> through opposition and conflict; he used this method not to establish doctrine, but for **refutation** <note>original: διελέγχειν — the Socratic method of cross-examining a person to reveal their inconsistencies</note>.

The method of logical consequence is twofold: one type demonstrates a specific point by using another specific point; the other establishes a universal truth by using specific points. The first is **rhetorical**, while the second is **dialectical**. 

For example, in the rhetorical type, one might ask if a specific man committed a murder. The proof offered is that he was found at that time covered in blood. This is a rhetorical form of induction because rhetoric deals with specific cases rather than universal principles. It does not ask about the nature of "Justice" itself, but about specific just or unjust acts. 

The other type is dialectical, where a universal truth is proven through specific examples. For instance, the question is asked whether the soul is immortal, and whether the living come from the dead. This is demonstrated in the treatise *On the Soul* <note>This refers to Plato's dialogue, the *Phaedo*</note> through a universal principle: that opposites arise from opposites. This universal principle itself is constructed from certain specific facts: such as sleep follows wakefulness and vice versa, or that the greater comes from the smaller and vice versa. Plato used this method to establish the doctrines he believed in.

Just as in ancient times with **tragedy** <note>original: τραγῳδίᾳ</note>, at first the chorus performed the entire drama alone. Later, **Thespis** invented a single actor to give the chorus a rest; **Aeschylus** added a second actor, and **Sophocles** a third, which completed the form of tragedy. In the same way, the study of philosophy was originally of one type—**natural philosophy** <note>original: φυσικός — the study of the physical world and its origins</note>. Secondly, **Socrates** added **ethics** <note>original: ἠθικόν — the study of character and conduct</note>. Thirdly, **Plato** added **dialectics** <note>original: διαλεκτικόν — the art of logical investigation</note>, and thus brought philosophy to its finished perfection.

**Thrasyllus** <note>A 1st-century scholar and astrologer who organized Plato's works</note> says that Plato even published his dialogues in the form of tragic **tetralogies** <term>original: τετραλογία — a set of four plays performed together</term>. He compares them to the way poets competed with four plays at the festivals of the **Dionysia**, the **Lenaea**, the **Panathenaia**, and the **Chytroi** <note>original: Χύτροις — "The Pots," a day of the Anthesteria festival held in honor of Dionysus and the dead</note>, where the fourth play in the set was a **Satyr play** <note>original: Σατυρικόν — a ribald, comic play featuring mythical satyrs</note>. These four...

There are nine Tetralogies, with the *Republic* occupying the space of one volume and the *Laws* another.

He places the **First Tetralogy** as having a common theme; for he wishes to demonstrate what kind of life the philosopher’s would be. He uses double titles for each of the books: one from the name [of the main character] and the other from the subject matter.

4. ***Statesman***, or *On Kingship*, which is **logical**. 

The **Third Tetralogy** is led by: 
1. ***Parmenides***, or *On Ideas*, which is **logical**. 
2. ***Philebus***, or *On Pleasure*, which is **ethical**. 
3. ***Symposium***, or *On the Good*, which is **ethical**. 
4. ***Phaedrus***, or *On Love*, which is **ethical**. 

The **Fourth Tetralogy** is led by: 
1. ***Alcibiades***, or *On the Nature of Man*, which is **maieutic** <term>original: μαιευτικός (maieutikos) — the "midwife" method where Socrates helps others "give birth" to their own latent ideas</term>. 
2. ***Second Alcibiades***, or *On Prayer*, which is **maieutic**. 
3. ***Hipparchus***, or *The Profiteer*, which is **ethical**. 
4. ***The Rivals***, or *On Philosophy*, which is **ethical**. 

The **Fifth Tetralogy** is led by: 
1. ***Theages***, or *On Philosophy*, which is **maieutic**. 
2. ***Charmides***, or *On Temperance*, which is **probative**. 
3. ***Laches***, or *On Courage*, which is **maieutic**. 
4. ***Lysis***, or *On Friendship*, which is **maieutic**. 

The **Sixth Tetralogy** is led by: 
1. ***Euthydemus***, or *The Contentious*, which is **refutative** <term>original: ἀνατρεπτικός (anatreptikos) — aimed at overturning or knocking down an opponent's argument</term>. 
2. ***Protagoras***, or *The Sophists*, which is **demonstrative**. 
3. ***Gorgias***, or *On Rhetoric*, which is **refutative**. 
4. ***Meno***, or *On Virtue*, which is **probative**.

The **Eighth Tetralogy** is led by ***Clitophon***, or *The Exhortation*, which is **ethical**; the ***Republic***, or *On Justice*, which is **political**; ***Timaeus***, or *On Nature*, which is **physical** <note>referring to "physics" in the ancient sense of the study of the natural world and the cosmos</note>; and ***Critias***, or *The Atlantic*, which is **ethical**.

The **Ninth Tetralogy** is led by ***Minos***, or *On Law*, which is **political**; the ***Laws***, or *On Legislation*, which is **political**; ***Epinomis***, or *The Nocturnal Council*, or *The Philosopher*, which is **political**; and the thirteen ***Letters***, which are **ethical**. In these letters, Plato used the greeting "To do well" <note>original: Εὖ πράττειν (Eu prattein) — a phrase that implies both moral rectitude and general prosperity</note>, whereas **Epicurus** used "To live well" and **Cleon** used "Greetings." These are the divisions made by some authorities. However, others (including **Aristophanes the Grammarian** <note>a famous scholar and head of the Library of Alexandria who lived in the 3rd–2nd century BCE</note>) group the dialogues into **trilogies**. 

They arrange the **First Trilogy** as: the ***Republic***, ***Timaeus***, and ***Critias***. 
The **Second Trilogy**: the ***Sophist***, the ***Statesman***, and ***Cratylus***. 
The **Third Trilogy**: the ***Laws***, ***Minos***, and ***Epinomis***. 
The **Fourth Trilogy**: ***Theaetetus***, ***Euthyphro***, and the ***Apology***. 
The **Fifth Trilogy**: ***Crito***, ***Phaedo***, and the ***Letters***. 

The remaining works they arrange individually and without a fixed order. 

As for the starting point of his works, some (as mentioned before) begin with the ***Republic***; some with the ***Greater Alcibiades***; some with ***Theages***; others with ***Euthyphro***; others with ***Clitophon***; some with ***Timaeus***; others with ***Phaedrus***; and others with ***Theaetetus***. Many, however, make the ***Apology*** the beginning.

The following dialogues are universally acknowledged as **spurious** <term>original: νοθεύονται (notheuontai) — recognized as forgeries or works falsely attributed to Plato</term>: ***Midon*** (or *The Horse-Breeder*), ***Eryxias*** (or *Erasistratus*), ***Alcyon***, ***Acephalos*** (or *Sisyphus*), ***Axiochus***, ***Phaeacians***, ***Demodocus***, ***Chelidon***, ***The Seventh***, and ***Epimenides***. Of these, the ***Alcyon*** is thought to be the work of a certain Leon, as **Favorinus** <note>a Roman-era historian</note> says in the fifth book of his *Memorabilia*.

# PLATO. Book 3. 123

He [Plato] considers **wisdom** <term>original: σοφία (sophia)</term> to be the knowledge of things that are intelligible and truly exist, which he says concerns God and the soul when it is separated from the body. In a specific sense, he also calls **philosophy** "wisdom," as it is a desire for this divine wisdom. In a more general sense, however, he uses "wisdom" to refer to any kind of skill or practical experience—for instance, when he calls a craftsman a "wise man" <note>original: σοφὸν... τὸν δημιουργόν (sophron... ton dēmiourgon). In ancient Greek, "sophos" could mean "clever" or "skilled in a craft" as well as "spiritually wise."</note>.

He also uses the same words to refer to things with different meanings. For example, the word **paltry** <term>original: φαῦλος (phaulos) — usually meaning "cheap," "bad," or "common"</term> is used by him to mean "simple" or "plain," just as **Euripides** uses it in his play *Licymnius* when speaking of **Heracles**:

->Simple, unrefined, but in the greatest things good,<-
->cutting away all "wisdom" in deed,<-
->unpracticed in idle talk.<-
<note>This fragment of Euripides describes the hero Heracles as a man of action rather than a sophisticated speaker, using "phaulos" to mean a "plain" man of integrity.</note>

Plato sometimes uses this same word to mean "beautiful," and at other times "small." Conversely, he often uses different names for the same meaning. For instance, he calls the **Idea** by many names: **Form** <term>original: εἶδος (eidos)</term>, **Genus**, **Model**, **Principle**, and **Cause**.

He even uses opposite terms for the same thing. For example, he calls a "sensible thing" <note>an object perceived by the senses rather than the mind</note> both "being" and "non-being"—"being" because it has come into existence, but "non-being" because it is in a state of constant change. He says the Idea is neither "moving" nor "at rest," and that it is "the same," "one," and "many."

He is accustomed to doing this with several other concepts as well. There is a **threefold method** for explaining his writings:
1. First, one must explain exactly what each term means.
2. Second, why it was said—whether as a primary argument or as an illustration, and whether it was meant to establish a doctrine or to refute a falsehood.
3. Third, whether the statement is actually correct.

Since certain **signs** <note>these are marginal symbols (sigla) used by ancient librarians in Alexandria to mark specific types of passages</note> are placed alongside the text in his books, let us speak of these as well:

The **X** <term>the Greek letter Chi</term> is used to mark noteworthy phrases, figures of speech, and generally for characteristic Platonic usage.

The **diple** ( **>** ) is used for Plato’s own doctrines and favored opinions.

The **dotted X** is used for selections of particularly beautiful writing.

The **dotted diple** ( **>·** ) is used for passages where editors have made corrections to the text.

The **dotted obelos** ( **—·** ) is used for passages that have been rejected as suspect or out of place without strong evidence.

The **dotted antisigma** <term>an inverted C shape with dots</term> is used for places where a passage has a double meaning or where the text has been transposed.

The **keraunion** <note>literally "thunderbolt"; a marker used for a group of related passages or to signal a break</note>...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...regarding the presentation of his philosophy; the **asterisk** <note>original: ἀστερίσκος (asteriskos)</note> indicates the agreement of his doctrines; the **obelus** <note>original: ὀβολός (obolos) — a horizontal line mark</note> indicates the rejection of a passage as spurious. 

These are the signs used, and his books are as numerous as previously stated. Antigonus of Carystus says in his work *On Zeno* that when these books were first published, anyone who wished to read them had to pay a fee to the owners. 

Plato's favorite doctrines were as follows: He stated that the **soul is immortal** and that it wears many bodies in succession, like changing garments. He believed its origin is mathematical <note>based on numbers</note>, while the body’s origin is geometrical <note>based on shapes and dimensions</note>. He defined the soul as the "Idea of an all-pervading spirit." It is self-moving and consists of three parts:

*   The **rational** part is seated in the head.
*   The **spirited** part <term>original: θυμοειδές (thymoeides) — the seat of courage, anger, and will</term> is located around the heart.
*   The **appetitive** part <term>original: ἐπιθυμητικόν (epithymētikon) — the seat of physical desire and hunger</term> is situated around the navel and the liver.

The soul encompasses the whole body in a circle, extending from the center, and is composed of the elements. When it was divided according to harmonic intervals, it formed two joined circles. The inner circle was divided six times to create a total of seven circles. This inner circle is placed along the diameter toward the left on the inside, while the other is placed along the side toward the right. Because of this, the outer circle remains a single, dominant unity, while the inner one is divided. He called the one the circle of the **Same** and the others the circles of the **Different**, stating that the former represents the movement of the individual soul, while the latter represents the motion of the universe and the orbits of the planets.

Because this central division is fitted to the extremities of the body, the soul is able to perceive existing things and bring them into harmony, for it contains the elements within itself in a state of harmony. **Opinion** arises when the circle of the "Different" moves correctly, whereas **knowledge** <term>original: ἐπιστήμη (epistēmē)</term> arises when the circle of the "Same" does. 

He declared that there are two primary principles of all things: **God** and **Matter**. He also refers to God as **Mind** <term>original: νοῦς (nous)</term> and **Cause**. He taught that matter is formless and infinite, and from it all compound objects are created. He says that while matter was once moving in a disordered fashion, it was brought together into a single place by God, who judged that order was superior to disorder. This substance was then transformed into the four elements: fire, water, air, and earth; out of which...

### PLATO. Book 3.

...the world itself and everything within it are created. He says that **only the earth is unchangeable** <note>original: ἀμετάβολον (ametabolon)</note>, believing the cause to be the difference in the shapes from which it is composed.
<margin>x</margin> For he says the shapes of the other elements are of the same kind; all of them are composed of a single type of **right-angled triangle**, whereas the shape of the earth is unique. The element of **fire** is a **pyramid**; **air** is an **octahedron** <note>an eight-sided solid</note>; **water** is an **icosahedron** <note>a twenty-sided solid</note>; and **earth** is a **cube**. For this reason, earth does not change into these other elements, nor do they change into earth. 

He also argues that each element is not strictly separated into its own proper place, because the rotation <note>of the universe</note> exerts a squeezing force and, by drawing everything toward the center, it fuses the small particles together and separates the large ones. Thus, as the forms change, their locations change as well.

The **universe is one** and was created, since it is also perceptible to the senses, having been fashioned by God. It is **endowed with a soul** <note>living</note>, because that which has life is superior to that which does not. This entire work is subject to the most excellent Cause. It was fashioned as one and not infinite, because the **model** <note>the archetype or "Idea"</note> after which it was created was also one. 

It is **spherical** <note>original: σφαιροειδῆ (sphairoeidē)</note> because its creator possesses such a shape. For while the creator contains the other living beings, the world contains all their shapes. It is **smooth**, possessing no organs around its exterior, because there is no use for them. Furthermore, the world remains imperishable, because it does not dissolve back into God.

God is the cause of the entire process of generation, for it is the nature of the Good to do good. The best cause produced the generation of the heavens. For the best of the objects of thought is the cause of the most beautiful of created things. Therefore, since God is such a being, and the heavens—being most beautiful—are like that which is best, the heavens would be like nothing among created things except **God himself**.

The world is composed of **fire, water, air, and earth**. It contains fire so that it may be visible, and earth so that it may be solid. It contains water and air so that it may be proportionate; for the properties of solids are harmonized by two intermediate means <term>original: μεσότησιν (mesotēsin) — mathematical means used in geometric ratios to link two extremes</term>, so that the whole might become a unity. It is made of all these elements so that it may be perfect and imperishable. Finally, **time** was created as an **image of eternity** <note>original: εἰκόνα τοῦ ἀϊδίου (eikona tou aidiou)</note>. And while eternity remains forever...

<meta>This page continues the summary of Plato’s physical philosophy and cosmology, specifically focusing on the structure of the elements (Platonic solids) and the creation of the world as described in the "Timaeus."</meta>

<page-num>126</page-num>
->DIOG. LAERT.<-

He [Plato] says that the **rotation of the heavens is time**. For night and day, months, and all such things, are parts of time. Therefore, **without the nature of the universe, time does not exist**; for time exists simultaneously with the universe itself. The **sun, the moon, and the planets** <note>original: πλανώμενα (planōmena), literally "the wanderers"</note> were created for the generation of time. To ensure that the number of the seasons <note>or "hours," original: ὡρῶν (hōrōn)</note> was clear, and so that living creatures could participate in the knowledge of number, **God lit the light of the sun**. 

The moon is located in the circle closest to the earth, the sun in the next, and the planets in the regions above. The universe is **entirely alive** <note>original: ἔμψυχον (empsychon), "ensouled"</note>, because it is bound within a living motion. In order that the world might be perfected by becoming like the **Intelligible Living Being** <note>the divine archetype or "Idea" of a living thing</note>, the nature of other living beings was created. Since that archetype contained them, the heavens too must contain them. Thus, he holds that the **gods are mostly made of fire**; the other three kinds of beings are winged <note>birds</note>, aquatic <note>fish</note>, and those that walk on land. 

**Earth** is the most ancient of the gods within the heavens. It was fashioned to create night and day. Being situated at the center, it **revolves around the center** <note>This phrase, "κινεῖσθαι περὶ τὸ μέσον," is a famous point of scholarly debate: did Plato mean the earth rotates on its axis or is stationary at the center?</note>.

Since there are two types of causes, he says we must speak of those that provide stability and those that arise from **necessity** <note>original: ἐξ ἀνάγκης (ex anangkēs)</note>. These necessary components are air, fire, earth, and water. These are not actually "elements" in the strict sense, but rather **receptacles** <note>original: δεκτικά (dektika)</note>. They are composed of **triangles** joined together, and they can be dissolved back into them. Their basic components are the **scalene triangle** <note>literally "the prolonged triangle," original: προμήκες (promēkes)</note> and the **isosceles triangle**.

The principles and causes, then, are the two mentioned: **God** as the model and **Matter**. Matter must necessarily be formless, just like other things that receive impressions. He says that this matter is a necessary cause. By receiving the **Ideas** <note>the Forms</note> in some way, it gives birth to substances; it is moved because of its imbalance of power, and in its movement, it in turn moves the things that arise from it. Before the world began, these things moved **irrationally and without order**; but when God began to organize the universe, he made them as **symmetrical and ordered** as possible...

# PLATO. BOOK 3 #

...to be produced. For he says there are two causes, and a third is generation <note>the process of coming-into-being</note>, regarding the creation of the heavens; but these were not clear, being only traces and disordered. But once the world was created, these also took on order. Out of all existing elements, the whole universe and the heavens were created. He believes that **God**, like the **soul**, is **incorporeal** <note>original: ἀσώματον (asōmaton), "without a body"</note>. For in this way, He is most especially free from decay and suffering. He posits the **Ideas** <note>the eternal "Forms" or archetypes of all things</note> as has been said: they are certain causes and principles by which things that exist by nature are the kind of things they are.

Regarding **goods and evils**, he spoke in this way: the **end** <note>the ultimate goal or "telos"</note> is **assimilation to God**. He taught that **virtue** is sufficient for **happiness** <note>original: εὐδαιμονία (eudaimonia)</note>, but that it requires instrumental bodily advantages—such as strength, health, soundness of the senses, and the like—as well as external advantages, such as wealth, noble birth, and reputation. Nonetheless, the **wise man** will be happy even if these things are not present. Furthermore, he will take part in public life, he will marry, and he will not violate the established laws. As far as circumstances permit, he will even legislate for his own country, unless he sees that the state of affairs has fallen into a completely hopeless condition due to the extreme corruption of the people. 

He also believes that the **gods watch over human affairs** and that there are **spirits** <note>original: δαίμονας (daimonas), intermediary beings between gods and humans</note>. He was the first to declare that the concept of the **Beautiful** <note>original: καλοῦ (kalou)</note> is that which is linked to what is praiseworthy, rational, useful, fitting, and harmonious; all of which are linked to what follows nature and is in agreement with it. 

He also discussed the **correctness of names**; thus, he was the first to establish the science of correctly asking and answering questions <note>Dialectics</note>, having used it to the fullest extent. In his dialogues, he also understood **justice** to be a **divine law**, so as to more strongly encourage people to do what is right, so that criminals might not suffer punishments <note>or "pay the penalty"</note> even after death. Hence he was thought by some to be rather fond of myths, because he mixed such narratives into his writings, so that through the uncertainty of the manner [of telling]...

...after death, so that they might abstain from wrongdoings. These, then, were his preferred views. He also used to divide things in the following manner (as **Aristotle** says). Of **goods**, some exist in the **soul**, some in the **body**, and some are **external**. For example, justice, wisdom, courage, temperance, and similar virtues exist in the soul; beauty, physical fitness, health, and strength exist in the body; while friends, the prosperity of one's homeland, and wealth are among the external goods. There are, therefore, three types of goods: those in the soul, those in the body, and those that are external.

Of **friendship**, there are three types: one is **natural**, another is **social** <note>original: ἑταιρική (hetairikē), referring to the bond between companions or comrades</note>, and the third is **hospitable** <note>original: ξενική (xenikē), the bond between a host and a guest</note>. We call that friendship **natural** which parents have toward their offspring and relatives toward one another; this form is also granted to other living creatures. We call that friendship **social** which arises from long-standing familiarity and has nothing to do with family ties—such as the friendship of **Pylades and Orestes** <note>In Greek mythology, these two were the ultimate symbols of loyal friendship</note>. **Hospitable friendship** is that which arises from a formal introduction or through letters of recommendation to strangers. Thus, of friendship, one kind is natural, one is social, and one is between guests and hosts. Some people also add a fourth type: **romantic love** <note>original: ἐρωτική (erōtikē)</note>.

Of **government** <note>original: πολιτείας (politeias), referring to the constitution or way a city is organized</note>, there are five types. One is **democratic**, another **aristocratic**, a third **oligarchic**, a fourth **monarchical**, and a fifth **tyrannical**. 

The **democratic** form is found in those cities where the multitude <note>the common people</note> is in control and chooses the magistrates and the laws by itself. 

**Aristocracy** exists where neither the rich, nor the poor, nor the famous rule, but the **best** men <note>original: ἄριστοι (aristoi)</note> preside over the city. 

**Oligarchy** exists whenever the magistrates are chosen based on property qualifications <note>original: ἀπὸ τιμημάτων (apo timēmatōn), a census of wealth</note>, for the rich are always fewer in number than the poor. 

Of **monarchy** <note>original: βασιλείας (basileias), literally "kingship"</note>, one kind is according to **law** and another is according to **lineage**. The form in **Carthage** is according to law (for it is a civil office), while the forms in **Lacedaemon** <note>Sparta</note> and **Macedonia** are according to lineage (for they establish the kingship from a specific family line). 

**Tyranny** is that form in which the people are ruled by someone who has either deceived them or used force against them. Of...

<header>PLATO. Book 3</header>

...of **government**, one kind is **democracy**, another **aristocracy**, another **oligarchy**, another **monarchy**, and another **tyranny**. 

Of **justice**, there are three types. One part is concerned with the **gods**; another with **humans**; and another with the **departed** <note>original: ἀποιχομένους (apoichomenous), a euphemism for the dead, literally "those who have gone away"</note>. For those who offer sacrifices according to the laws and look after sacred sites are clearly acting piously toward the gods. Those who return loans and deposits are acting justly toward humans. Those who look after tombs and monuments are clearly acting justly toward the departed. Thus, of justice, one part is toward the gods, one toward humans, and one toward the departed.

Of **knowledge** <note>original: ἐπιστήμη (epistēmē), often translated as science or organized body of knowledge</note>, there are three types: the **practical**, the **productive**, and the **theoretical**. Architecture and shipbuilding are **productive** <note>original: ποιητικόν (poiētikon), meaning "to make" or "create"</note>; for one can see a finished work that has been produced by them. Politics, flute-playing, lyre-playing, and similar skills are **practical** <note>original: πρακτικόν (praktikon), meaning "to act" or "do"</note>; for there is no tangible object to see that has been made by them, but they perform an action. For the one plays the flute or the lyre, while the other conducts affairs of state. Geometry, harmony, and astronomy are **theoretical**; for they neither act nor produce anything. Instead, the geometer contemplates how lines relate to one another; the musician <note>original: ἁρμονικός (harmonikos), a student of musical intervals</note> contemplates sounds; and the astronomer contemplates the stars and the universe. Thus, of the sciences, some are theoretical, some are practical, and some are productive.

Of **medicine**, there are five types: **pharmacology**, **surgery**, **dietetics**, **diagnostics** <note>original: νοσογνωμονική (nosognomonikē), literally "knowledge of disease"</note>, and **emergency care** <note>original: βοηθητική (boēthētikē), literally "helpful" or "palliative" care</note>. Pharmacology treats illnesses through drugs; surgery heals through cutting and cauterizing; dietetics removes illnesses through the regulation of lifestyle; diagnostics works by identifying the nature of the illness; and emergency care, by providing immediate aid, brings relief from pain. Thus, of medicine, one part is pharmaceutical, one surgical, one dietetic, one emergency care, and one diagnostic.

There are two divisions of **law**: for one part of it is **written**, [and the other is unwritten...]

...the other is **unwritten**. The kind by which we conduct ourselves in cities is the **written** law; however, that which arises from custom is called **unwritten**. For example, not walking through the marketplace naked, or not wearing women’s clothing; for no written law forbids these things, yet we still do not do them because they are forbidden by an **unwritten law**. **Discourse** <note>original: λόγος (logos), which can mean speech, reason, or account</note> is divided into five parts. One is that which public figures speak in assemblies, which is called **political**. A second division of discourse is that which orators write and present for display, such as for eulogies, criticisms, and accusations; this kind is **rhetorical**. A third division of discourse is that which private individuals use when conversing with one another; this style is called **private** <note>original: ἰδιωτικός (idiōtikos), referring to a layperson or someone not in public office</note>. A fourth division of discourse is that used by those who converse through brief questions and answers with their interlocutors; this is called **dialectical** discourse. The fifth division of discourse is that which craftsmen use when discussing their own craft, which is called **technical**. Thus, of discourse, one type is political, another rhetorical, another private, another dialectical, and another technical.

**Music** <note>original: μουσική (mousikē), which for the Greeks included poetry and various arts governed by the Muses</note> is divided into three parts. For one is performed by the mouth alone, such as singing; the second is by the mouth and the hands together, such as singing to the lyre <note>original: κιθαρῳδία (kitharōdia)</note>; the third is from the hands alone, such as lyre-playing <note>original: κιθαριστική (kitharistikē)</note>. Thus, of music, one part is from the mouth alone, another from the mouth and hands, and another from the hands.

**Nobility** <note>original: εὐγένεια (eugeneia), literally "good birth"</note> is divided into four kinds. First, if the ancestors were honorable, good, and just, then those born from them are said to be **noble**. Another kind is if the ancestors were rulers and men in power, those born from them are called **noble**. Another is if the ancestors were famous, for instance, for military leadership or for winning crowned games; for those born from them we also call **noble**. Another kind is if [a person themselves...] <note>The text cuts off mid-definition; usually, the fourth category refers to one's own personal excellence or character.</note>

### P L A T O. Book 3. 133

...if someone is noble in spirit and great-souled <note>original: μεγαλόψυχος (megalopsychos), referring to the "magnanimous" person who is worthy of great things</note>, they say he too is well-born. And of **nobility** <note>original: εὐγενείας (eugeneias)</note>, this is the most excellent kind. Thus, of nobility, one kind is derived from excellent ancestors, another from powerful rulers, another from famous ones, and a final kind from one's own personal excellence of character <note>original: καλοκαγαθίας (kalokagathias), the Greek ideal of being both "beautiful and good" in a moral sense</note>.

**Beauty** is divided into three parts. One kind of beauty is praiseworthy, such as the visual attractiveness of form; another is functional, such as a tool or a house, which are beautiful for our use. A third kind relates to laws and social practices, which are beautiful for their benefit. Thus, of beauty, one kind is for pleasure <note>original: παίγνιον (paignion), literally a "plaything" or for sport</note>, another is for use, and another is for benefit.

**The Soul** is divided into three parts. One part of it is **rational**; another is **appetitive**; and the third is **spirited**. Of these, the rational part is the cause of deliberating, calculating, thinking, and all such activities. The appetitive part of the soul is the cause of the desire to eat, of sexual intimacy <note>original: πλησιάσαι (plēsiasai), literally "to draw near," often a euphemism for intercourse</note>, and of all such things. The spirited part is the cause of courage, and of feeling pleasure, pain, and anger. Thus, of the soul, one part is rational, another appetitive, and another spirited.

There are four types of **perfect virtue**: one is **prudence**; one is **justice**; a third is **courage**; and the fourth is **temperance**. Of these, **prudence** <note>original: φρόνησις (phronēsis), or practical wisdom</note> is the cause of doing things correctly; **justice** <note>original: δικαιοσύνη (dikaiosynē)</note> is the cause of acting rightly in social interactions and business transactions; **courage** <note>original: ἀνδρεία (andreia)</note> is the cause of not abandoning one's post in dangers and fears, but rather standing firm; and **temperance** <note>original: σωφροσύνη (sōphrosynē), or self-control</note> is the cause of mastering one's desires and not being enslaved by any pleasure, but rather living in an orderly way. Thus, of virtue, one kind is prudence, another justice, a third courage, and a fourth temperance.

**Rule** <note>original: ἀρχὴ (archē), meaning power, office, or beginning</note> is divided into five parts: one by **law**; one by **nature**; one by **custom**; a fourth by **birth**; and a fifth by **force**. When rulers in cities are chosen by the citizens, they rule according to law.

Others [rule] according to nature, as males do; this is evident <margin>315</margin> not only among humans but also among the other animals (for generally, everywhere the males rule over the females). There is also a kind of rule based on custom <note>original: ἔθος (ethos), meaning habit or social usage</note>, such as that which tutors <note>original: παιδαγωγοὶ (paidagōgoi), referring to the household guardians who supervised children</note> exercise over children and teachers over their pupils. Rule according to birth <note>original: γένος (genos), or lineage</note> is described as the kind of rule the Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> kings exercise; for the kingship is derived from a specific lineage. In Macedonia, they rule in the same manner, for there too the kingship is established by birth. Finally, there are those who rule by force or by deception, ruling over citizens against their will; such a rule is said to be based on violence. Thus, of **Rule**, one kind is according to law, another according to nature, another according to custom, another according to birth, and another according to violence.

There are six species of **rhetoric** <note>the art of persuasive public speaking</note>. When men urge for war or for making an alliance with someone, such a species is called **exhortation** <note>original: προτροπή (protrope)</note>. When they demand that there be no war and no alliance, but rather that peace be kept, such a species is **dissuasion** <note>original: ἀποτροπή (apotrope)</note>. The third species of rhetoric is when someone claims to have been wronged by another and points to them as the cause of many evils; this species is named **accusation** <note>original: κατηγορία (kategoria)</note>. The fourth species of rhetoric is called **defense** <note>original: ἀπολογία (apologia)</note>, when one demonstrates that they have done no wrong, nor performed any other out-of-place action; this is what they call a defense. The fifth species of rhetoric is when someone speaks well of another and demonstrates them to be noble and good <note>original: καλὸν κἀγαθόν (kalon kagathon), the classic Greek ideal of a gentleman</note>; such a species is called **praise** <note>original: ἐγκώμιον (enkomion)</note>. The sixth species is when someone demonstrates that another is base; such a species is called **censure** <note>original: ψόγος (psogos)</note>. Thus, of rhetoric, one kind is praise, another is censure, another is exhortation, another is dissuasion, another is accusation, and another is defense.

**Correct speaking** <note>original: τὸ ὀρθῶς λέγειν (to orthōs legein)</note> is divided into four parts: first, what must be said; second, how much must be said; third, to whom one must speak; and fourth, when one must speak. "What must be said" refers to things that are going to be beneficial to both the speaker and the listener. "How much must be said" means saying neither more nor less than what is sufficient. "To whom one must speak" refers to [addressing the audience appropriately], such as toward elders...

...when speaking to those who err, one should use words that are fitting for elders; if addressing younger people, the words should be fitting for the youth. Thus, of beneficence, one kind is through money, the second through physical action, the third through knowledge, and the fourth through speech.

The **end** <note>original: τέλος (telos), meaning the goal, completion, or final outcome of a process</note> of matters is divided into four kinds. One kind of "end" is achieved according to law, such as when a decree is passed and the law brings it to completion. An "end" according to nature is found in things like the day, the year, and the seasons. An "end" according to art <note>original: τέχνη (technē), referring to a craft or specialized skill</note> is seen in matters such as architecture—for it completes a house—and shipbuilding—for it completes ships. Finally, an "end" happens to matters by chance when a result turns out differently than one expected. Thus, of the final outcome of matters, one is according to law, another according to nature, another according to art, and another according to chance.

**Power** <note>original: δύναμις (dynamis), which can mean physical strength, political power, or the latent capacity to do something</note> is divided into four species. One is what we are able to calculate and conceive with our intellect. The second is that of the body, such as the ability to walk, to give, to receive, and the like. The third is the power we possess through a multitude of soldiers and wealth; this is why a king is said to have "great power." The fourth division of power is the capacity to be affected <note>original: πάσχειν (paschein), the "passive" side of power—the capacity to undergo a change or experience something</note>, as well as to do well or to do poorly; for example, we have the "power" to fall ill, to be educated, to become healthy, and all such things. Of **power** <note>original: δύναμις (dynamis), meaning capacity or potential</note>, one kind exists in the mind, another in the body, another in armies and wealth, and another in the capacity to act and to be acted upon. 

There are three kinds of **philanthropy** <note>original: φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpia), literally "love of humanity"</note>. One occurs through greetings, such as when people address everyone they meet and greet them by shaking hands. Another kind is when someone is helpful to everyone who is in misfortune. A third kind of philanthropy is when people are "lovers of dining together" <note>original: φιλοδειπνισταί (philodeipnistai)</note>. Thus, of philanthropy, one part is through greeting, another through doing good, and another through hosting and social gathering.

**Happiness** <note>original: εὐδαιμονία (eudaimonia), often understood as human flourishing</note> is divided into five parts. One part of it is **good counsel**; the second is **sound perception** and health of the body; third is **good fortune** in one’s actions; fourth is **good reputation** among men; and fifth is an **abundance of wealth** and the things useful for life. 

**Good counsel** <note>original: εὐβουλία (euboulia)</note> arises from education and from becoming experienced in many things. **Sound perception** <note>original: εὐαισθησία (euaisthēsia)</note> arises from the parts of the body. For example, if one sees with the eyes, hears with the ears, and perceives with the nose and the mouth those things which one ought to perceive; such a condition is sound perception. **Good fortune** <note>original: εὐτυχία (eutychia)</note> is when someone achieves what they aim for by correctly doing what a person of excellence <note>original: σπουδαῖος (spoudaios), a serious or virtuous person</note> ought to do. **Good reputation** <note>original: εὐδοξία (eudoxia)</note> is when one is "well spoken of" <note>original: εὖ ἀκούῃ (eu akouē), literally "hears well of oneself"</note>. **Abundance of wealth** <note>original: εὐπορία (euporia)</note> is when someone is so situated regarding the uses of life that they can both do good to friends and perform public duties <note>original: ἀπολειτουργῆσαι (apoleitourgēsai), referring to "liturgies," the public services funded by wealthy citizens in Greece</note> with generosity and without lack. The person to whom all these things belong is perfectly happy. Thus, of happiness, one part is good counsel, another sound perception and bodily health, another good fortune, another good reputation, and another abundance of wealth.

The **arts** <note>original: τέχναι (technai), encompassing crafts, skills, and sciences</note> are divided into three kinds: the first, the second, and the third. The first are the **extractive** and **wood-cutting** arts; for these are "preparatory" <note>original: παρασκευαστικαί (paraskeuastikai)</note>. The second are **metal-working** and **carpentry**, which are "transformative" <note>original: μετασκευαστικαί (metaskeuastikai)</note>. For from iron, the metal-working art makes weapons, and from wood, carpentry makes flutes and lyres.

...the **utilitarian** <note>original: χρηστική (chrēstikē)</note> kind, such as horsemanship, uses bridles; the art of war uses weapons; music uses flutes and the lyre. Of **art** <note>original: τέχνη (technē), meaning a craft, skill, or system of knowledge</note>, there are therefore three kinds: the first, the second, and the third. 

The **good** <note>original: ἀγαθόν (agathon)</note> is divided into four classes: one we call the individual good of the person who possesses virtue; another we say is virtue itself and **justice** <note>original: δικαιοσύνη (dikaiosynē)</note>; third is that such as food and suitable exercise and medicines; fourth, we say things like the art of flute-playing, acting, and such things are good. There are, then, four kinds of good: one is the possession of virtue; another is virtue itself; third, beneficial food and exercise; fourth, we call flute-playing, acting, and poetry good. 

Of **existing things**, some are bad, some are good, and some are neutral. Of these, we call bad those things which are always capable of doing harm, such as **excess** <note>original: ἀκρασία (akrasia), a lack of self-control or moderation</note>, folly, and injustice, and such things; the opposites of these are good. Those things which sometimes benefit and sometimes harm—such as walking, sitting, and eating—or which generally neither benefit nor are capable of harming; these are neither good nor bad. Therefore, of existing things, some are good, some are bad, and some are neutral between these. 

**Good governance** <note>original: εὐνομία (eunomia), meaning "good order" or being well-governed by laws</note> is divided into three: one, if the laws are excellent, we say it is good governance; another, if the citizens abide by the established laws, we say this also is good governance; third, if there are no laws, but the people conduct their affairs well according to customs and practices, we also call this good governance. Of good governance, then, one part is for the laws to be excellent; another, if they abide by the existing laws; third, if they conduct their affairs well by custom and practice. 

**Lawlessness** <note>original: ἀνομία (anomia)</note> is divided into three: of which one is if the laws are wretched, both toward foreigners and toward citi-

<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

...laws; a second is when people do not obey those that exist; and another is when there is no law at all. **Lawlessness** <note>original: ἀνομία (anomia)</note> therefore consists of one of these: the laws being corrupt; or, if people do not obey the existing ones; or thirdly, if there is no law. 

**Opposites** <note>original: ἐναντία (enantia)</note> are divided into three types. For example, we say good things are the opposites of bad things, such as **justice** <note>original: δικαιοσύνη (dikaiosynē)</note> being the opposite of injustice, and **wisdom** <note>original: φρόνησις (phronēsis)</note> the opposite of folly, and so on. 

Bad things can also be the opposites of other bad things, such as **prodigality** <note>original: ἀσωτία (asōtia), or wasteful extravagance</note> and **illiberality** <note>original: ἀνελευθερία (aneleutheria), or stinginess</note>; also, being tortured unjustly is the opposite of being tortured justly. Such things are bad things as opposites of other bad things. 

Finally, there are neutral things which are the opposites of other neutrals, such as being poor and being wealthy. For each of these, in itself, is neither good nor bad, yet they are still opposites. Similarly, the heavy is opposite to the light, the fast to the slow, and black to white; these are neutral things acting as opposites to other neutrals. Of opposites, then, some are good things opposed to bad, some are bad opposed to bad, and some are neutrals opposed to neutrals.

There are three kinds of **good things** <note>original: ἀγαθῶν (agathōn)</note>. Some are "possessible," some are "participable," and some are "subsistent" <note>These terms describe how a person relates to a virtue or an ideal: whether they can own it, share in it, or simply embody it.</note>. 

Those that are **possessible** <note>original: ἑκτά (hekta)</note> are whatever one can possess, such as justice and health. Those that are **participable** <note>original: μεθεκτά (methekta)</note> are those which one cannot possess as a personal object, but one can participate in them; for instance, one cannot "possess" the Absolute Good, but it is possible to participate in it. Those that are **subsistent** <note>original: ὑπαρκτά (hyparkta)</note> are those which one can neither share nor possess, but which simply must be present as a state of being; for example, being virtuous and being just is a good; these qualities are not for possessing or sharing, but must simply exist—to be virtuous and to be just. Thus, of good things, some are possessible, some are participable, and some are subsistent.

**Counsel** <note>original: συμβουλία (symboulia), referring to political or personal deliberation and advice</note> is divided into three parts. One part is drawn from past times, one from the future, and one from the present. The part from the past uses examples, such as what the **Spartans** <note>original: Λακεδαιμόνιοι (Lakedaimonioi)</note> suffered because they trusted [others]... the part from the present...

...of those, for example, to point out that walls were weak, or to show people that there was little grain <note>This refers to using past events or current states to inform a decision</note>. Deliberation regarding the future includes, for example, the warning not to wrong embassies based on suspicions, so that Greece does not fall into ill repute. Thus, of **deliberation** <note>original: συμβουλίας (symboulias)</note>, some concerns the past, some the present, and some the future.

**Voice** <note>original: φωνή (phōnē)</note> is divided into two types. One part of it is **animate** <note>original: ἔμψυχον (empsychon), meaning "living" or "ensouled"</note>, and the other is **inanimate** <note>original: ἄψυχον (apsychon)</note>. Animate voice is that of living creatures; inanimate voice refers to sounds and echoes. Of animate voice, one kind is **articulate** <note>original: ἐγγράμματος (engrammatos), literally "capable of being written"</note>, and the other is **inarticulate** <note>original: ἀγράμματος (agrammatos)</note>. Articulate voice belongs to human beings, whereas inarticulate belongs to animals. Therefore, of voice, there is the animate and the inanimate.

Of things that exist, some are **divisible** <note>original: μεριστά (merista)</note> and others are **indivisible** <note>original: ἀμέριστα (amerista)</note>. Among these divisible things, some are **homogeneous** <note>original: ὁμοιομερῆ (homoiomerē), meaning having parts that are the same as the whole</note> and others are **heterogeneous** <note>original: ἀνομοιομερῆ (anomoiomerē)</note>. **Indivisible** things are those that cannot be split, nor are they composed of other things—such as the **unit** <note>original: μονὰς (monas), the number one in its simplest form</note>, the **point** <note>original: στιγμὴ (stigmē)</note> in geometry, and a single **musical tone** <note>original: φθόγγος (phthongos)</note>. **Divisible** things are those composed of something else, such as syllables, musical harmonies, animals, water, and gold. **Homogeneous** things are those where the whole is made of similar parts, and the whole does not differ from the part except in quantity; for example, water, gold, and everything of that kind. **Heterogeneous** things are those composed of dissimilar parts, like a house and such things. Therefore, of existing things, some are divisible and some are indivisible; and of the divisible, some are homogeneous and some are heterogeneous.

Of things that exist, some are **absolute** <note>original: καθ' ἑαυτὰ (kath’ heauta), or "in themselves"</note> and others are called **relative** <note>original: πρός τι (pros ti), literally "toward something"</note>. Those called **absolute** are whatever require no further explanation in their definition; these would include "man," "horse," and other animals. For none of these are understood through a relationship to something else. Of those called **relative**, these are whatever require a further definition, such as the "greater" than something, the "faster" than something, the "more beautiful," and so on. For the greater is greater than a lesser thing, and the faster is faster than some other thing. Therefore, of existing things, some are absolute...

## SPEUSIPPUS.

These were the facts concerning Plato <note>This refers to the extensive biography and catalog of Plato's works provided in the previous book</note> that we were able to collect, having industriously gathered the accounts told about the man. He was succeeded by **Speusippus**, the son of Eurymedon and an Athenian. He belonged to the deme <note>A 'deme' was a local district or suburb of ancient Athens</note> of Myrrhinus, and was the son of Plato’s sister, Potone. He served as the head of the school for eight years, beginning his leadership in the 108th Olympiad <note>Approximately 348–347 BC</note>. He dedicated statues of the **Graces** <note>original: Χαρίτων (Charitōn). These were the goddesses of charm, beauty, and creativity</note> in the shrine of the Muses <note>The *Mouseion*, from which we get the word "museum"</note> which had been established by Plato in the Academy. While he adhered to the same doctrines as Plato, he did not remain like him in character; for he was quick-tempered and a slave to his pleasures. It is said, for instance, that in a fit of anger he threw his little dog into a well, and that for the sake of pleasure he traveled to Macedonia to attend the wedding of Cassander <note>A powerful Greek statesman and later King of Macedon</note>. 

It was also said that the same female students who had studied under Plato now listened to him: **Lastheneia** of Mantinea and **Axiothea** of Phlius. At that time, Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the former tyrant of Syracuse</note>, writing to him in a mocking tone, said: "One can even learn your brand of philosophy from your Arcadian student" <note>This is a jab at Lastheneia, who was from Arcadia; Dionysius is implying Speusippus's teaching is only fit for women or provincial outsiders</note>. He also wrote: "And while Plato made his students exempt from fees, you collect tribute from them, taking it from both those who give it willingly and those who do not." He was the first, as Diodorus says in his *Memoirs* <note>Text breaks for catchword: ἀπομνημονεύμασι (apomnēmoneumasin)</note>

## XENOCRATES

Xenocrates, the son of Agathenor, was a native of Chalcedon <note>The Greek text here reads "Carthaginian" (Καρχηδόνιος), but historical records generally agree he was from Chalcedon, a Greek city in what is now Turkey</note>. From his youth, he was a student of Plato and even accompanied him on his travels to Sicily. He was naturally sluggish in his disposition, so much so that they say Plato used to say of him—comparing him to Aristotle—that while the one required a spur, the other required a bridle. Plato would also say, "I am grooming a horse against an ass." In other respects, Xenocrates was solemn and always had a somber expression, which led Plato to say to him constantly, "Xenocrates, sacrifice to the Graces" <note>original: θύε ταῖς Χάρισι (thye tais Charisi) — The Graces were goddesses of charm, beauty, and social grace; Plato was gently suggesting that Xenocrates needed to be more approachable and less stern</note>. 

He spent most of his time in the Academy. Whenever he was about to go into the city of Athens, it is said that all the rowdy and lustful people would shrink back and make way for him as he passed. On one occasion, the famous courtesan Phryne <note>A celebrated and wealthy woman known for her beauty</note> wished to test him. Pretending she was being chased by some men, she took refuge in his small house. Because of his sense of human kindness, he took her in. As there was only one small bed, he shared the couch with her at her request. Finally, despite her many persistent entreaties, she rose and left without having achieved her goal. To those who questioned her afterward, she said that she had risen from the bed not of a man, but of a statue. 

Some say it was Lais <note>Another famous courtesan of the era</note> whom his students placed in bed with him; however, he was so self-controlled that he frequently endured medical cuttings and cauterizations <note>term: cauterization (burning) — a common ancient medical treatment used to seal wounds or treat infections</note> around his private parts. He was also remarkably trustworthy; so much so that, although it was not legal to give testimony without an oath, the Athenians granted this privilege to him alone. Furthermore, he was extremely self-sufficient. For instance, when Alexander the Great sent him a large sum of money...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...to him, but Xenocrates set aside only three thousand Attic drachmae <note>The Attic drachma was a standard silver coin; three thousand was a significant sum, but far less than the fifty talents Alexander the Great is said to have originally sent him</note> and sent the rest back, saying that Alexander needed more money since he had more people to feed. Myronianos also states in his *Similar Passages* that Xenocrates refused a gift sent by Antipater. Furthermore, when he was honored with a gold crown for winning a drinking contest at the court of Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse</note>, he took the crown as he was leaving and placed it at the base of a statue of Hermes, in the same spot where he was accustomed to leaving his floral wreaths.

There is also a story that he was sent as an ambassador to Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great</note> along with several others. While the other ambassadors were softened by Philip's gifts and accepted his invitations to banquets and private conversations, Xenocrates did neither. For this reason, Philip would not grant him an audience. When the ambassadors returned to Athens, they claimed that Xenocrates had accompanied them to no purpose, and the people were ready to fine him. 

However, after they learned from him that they now needed to care for the city’s interests more than ever—for, as he said, "Philip has already bribed the others, but he could not win me over by any means"—they say the city honored him with double the usual respect. Philip himself later remarked that Xenocrates was the only man among those who had come to him who was immune to bribes.

Later, during the Lamian War <note>A conflict (323–322 BCE) between Athens and Macedon following the death of Alexander the Great</note>, he went as an ambassador to Antipater to negotiate for Athenian prisoners. When he was invited to dinner by Antipater, he responded by quoting these lines:

> "O Circe, what man who is right-minded
> could endure to taste food and drink
> before he has ransomed his comrades and seen them before his eyes?"
> <note>original: Ὦ Κίρκη, τίς γάρ κεν ἀνὴρ... — These lines are from Homer's *Odyssey*, spoken by Odysseus when he refuses to eat until Circe restores his men to human form</note>

Antipater was so struck by the appropriateness of the quote that he immediately released the prisoners.

On another occasion, when a sparrow being chased by a hawk flew into his lap, he stroked it and let it go, declaring that one should never betray a suppliant <note>In the ancient world, a "suppliant" was someone seeking protection or mercy; betraying one was considered a grave moral and religious offense</note>. When he was mocked by Bion <note>Bion of Borysthenes, a cynical and witty philosopher known for his sharp tongue</note>, Xenocrates refused to answer him, saying that Tragedy does not deign to answer when it is mocked by Comedy. 

To a man who had studied neither music, nor geometry, nor astronomy, but who nevertheless wished to attend his lectures, Xenocrates said, "Go your way..."

*   **Theory of Numbers**, one book
*   **On Intervals**, one book
*   **On Astrology**, six books
*   **Elements addressed to Alexander**
*   **On Kingship**, six books
*   **To Arybas**
*   **To Hephaestion**
*   **On Geometry**, two books

The total number of lines in his writings is 224,239.

Despite his great character, the Athenians once put him up for sale because he was unable to pay the <term>metoikion: a tax imposed on resident aliens living in Athens</term>. Demetrius of Phalerum bought him, thereby paying the debt to the Athenians and restoring Xenocrates to his freedom. This story is told by Myronianus of Amastris in the first book of his *Historical Parallels*.

He succeeded Speusippus as the head of the school <note>The Platonic Academy</note> and led it for twenty-five years during the time of Lysimachus, beginning in the second year of the 110th Olympiad <note>approximately 339 BCE</note>. He died during the night after tripping over a bronze basin, at the age of eighty-two. We have written an epigram about him as follows:

> Having once tripped over a bronze basin,
> And striking his forehead, he cried out as he fell silent, and then died—
> Xenocrates, a man who was all things in every way.

There have been six other men named Xenocrates:
1.  A military tactician of very ancient times.
2.  A relative and fellow-citizen of the philosopher mentioned above.
3.  An author of a discourse on Arsinoe <note>original: "Ἀρσινοητικός" (Arsinoetikos)</note>, written upon the death of Queen Arsinoe.
4.  A philosopher who wrote unsuccessful elegiac poetry. (This is a curious thing: poets who attempt prose often succeed, but prose writers who take up poetry usually stumble. This clearly shows that the former is a gift of nature, while the latter is a matter of technical skill).
5.  A sculptor.
6.  A songwriter, as mentioned by the music theorist Aristoxenus.

<note>original: "ΠΟ." — likely a scribal or printer mark</note>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
### Page 145
### POLEMON. Book 4.

->POLEMON.<-

Polemon was the son of Philostratus, an Athenian from the deme <note>A 'deme' was a local district or suburb of Athens, similar to a parish.</note> of Oea. In his youth, he was so unrestrained and dissolute that he used to carry money with him for the immediate satisfaction of his desires. He would even hide coins in narrow alleyways for quick access. In the Academy <note>The school founded by Plato</note>, a three-obol coin <note>A small silver coin worth half a drachma</note> was once found plastered to a pillar, hidden by him for the same reason mentioned before. One day, having made an agreement with his young companions, he burst into the school of Xenocrates while drunk and wearing a festive garland. Xenocrates, not at all disturbed by the intrusion, continued his lecture just as before (the topic happened to be temperance). As the young man listened, he was gradually "captured" by the discourse. He became so industrious that he surpassed all the other students and eventually succeeded to the leadership of the school himself, beginning in the 116th Olympiad <note>approximately 314 BCE</note>.

Antigonus of Carystus says in his *Lives* that Polemon’s father was among the leading citizens and kept horses for chariot racing. He also notes that Polemon was once sued by his wife for "ill-treatment" <term>kakosis: a legal charge in Athens for the neglect or abuse of family obligations</term> because of his associations with young men. However, from the moment he began to study philosophy, he intensified his self-discipline to such an extent that he always maintained the same facial expression. Even his voice remained unchanging; it was this steady character that "captured" the admiration of Crantor. For instance, when a rabid dog once bit him and tore the back of his leg, he did not even turn pale; and when a riot broke out in the city, upon hearing what had happened, he remained completely unperturbed.

In the theaters, he was equally impassive. For example, once when Nicostratus (who was nicknamed "Clytemnestra") was reading a poetic work to him and Crates, Crates was deeply moved by the performance, but Polemon acted as if he had not even heard it. In general, he was the kind of person described by the painter Melanthius in his work *On Painting*. Melanthius says that a certain "stubbornness" and "hardness" should be present in works of art, and likewise in human character. Polemon used to say that one should exercise oneself in practical affairs, and not merely in dialectical <note>original: "διαλεκτικοῖς" (dialektikois) — referring to logical or verbal arguments</note> exercises...

theorems; for having absorbed and practiced a certain harmonic skill, he was admired for his manner of questioning, but in his general disposition, his critics found themselves at odds. He was a refined and noble man, avoiding those qualities which Aristophanes ascribes to Euripides, calling them "vinegary and stained." <note>original: "Oxotas kai Spilota." These are metaphors for a harsh or unpolished style of writing.</note> These things, as Polemon himself said, are "shamelessness compared to a great body of meat." <note>This likely means that petty stylistic criticisms are insignificant compared to the substance of a great work.</note> Furthermore, they say he did not sit down when delivering his discourses to the audience, but used to lecture while walking about.

Because of his love for physical exercise, he was honored in the city. However, he also lived a secluded life, spending his time in the Garden. His students built small huts nearby and lived close to the shrine of the Muses <note>The 'mouseion' was a place dedicated to the Muses, often serving as a center for music and learning.</note> and the lecture hall. It seems that Polemon sought to emulate Xenocrates in everything. Aristippus, in the fourth book of *On Ancient Luxury*, even says that Polemon was in love with him. At any rate, Polemon was always mindful of him, adopting the man's guilelessness, his austere appearance, and his gravity—much like a Dorian musical arrangement. <note>The Dorian mode was considered the most solemn and dignified of the Greek musical scales.</note>

He was also a lover of Sophocles, especially in those passages where, compared to the comic poets, he seemed like a Molossian hound. <note>A famous breed of large, fierce dog from Epirus, known for its strength and used for guarding.</note> And in those places he was (according to the poet Phrynichus) "neither arrogant nor dilute, but like Pramnian wine." <note>Pramnian wine was a famous, strong, and long-lasting wine; the metaphor suggests Sophocles' poetry was potent and unwatered-down.</note> He used to say that Homer was "an epic Sophocles," and that Sophocles was "a Bacchic Homer." He died at an old age from consumption <term>phthisis: a wasting disease, usually referring to tuberculosis</term>, leaving behind a significant number of writings. And there is an epigram of ours dedicated to him:

->Do you not hear? We have hidden Polemon, whom sickness,<-
->The terrible affliction of men, placed here.<-
->Or rather, not Polemon, but only his body. For he himself,<-
->About to cross to the stars, left that upon the ground.<-

Hence it is said that Arcesilaus, <note>Arcesilaus would later become the head of the Academy and shift it toward Skepticism.</note> after leaving the school of Theophrastus to join them, remarked that they were like gods or remnants of the Golden Race. <note>original: "χρυσοῦ γένους" (chrysou genous). He boasted that no one had ever heard any of his melodies either on a trireme <note>A standard Greek warship where flutists often kept time for the rowers.</note> or at a public fountain, unlike the music of Ismenias. Arcesilaus shared a residence with Crantor, while Polemon lived with Crates at the house of a certain citizen named Lysicles. Crates was (as has been said before) the beloved <term>eromenos<note>In ancient Greek social customs, an 'eromenos' was the younger partner in a pedagogical and often romantic relationship with an older mentor ('erastes').</note></term> of Polemon, while Arcesilaus was the beloved of Crantor. 

When Crates died (as Apollodorus says in the third book of his *Chronicles*), he left behind books—some on philosophy, others on comedy, and still others being public speeches and ambassadorial addresses. He also left behind distinguished disciples, among whom was Arcesilaus (whom we shall discuss, for he was a student of Crates) and Bion the Borysthenite <note>Bion came from the Greek colony of Olbia near the Borysthenes (modern Dnieper) river.</note>, and later Theodorus, who was nicknamed "the Atheist" because of his sect; we will discuss him immediately after Arcesilaus.

### CRANTOR.

Crantor of Soli, <note>Soli was an ancient city in Cilicia, modern-day Turkey.</note> having been greatly admired in his own homeland, traveled to Athens and became a student of Xenocrates, while also attending the school of Polemon. He left behind commentaries consisting of thirty thousand lines; some of these works are attributed by certain people to Arcesilaus. <note>Arcesilaus was Crantor's student and friend who later founded the "Middle Academy."</note> They say that when he was asked what it was about Polemon that captivated him, he replied that it was because he had never heard Polemon's voice sound too sharp or too deep. <note>original: "μήτε ὀξύτερον μήτε βαρύτερον" (mete oxyteron mete baryteron). This refers to Polemon's famously steady and composed temperament.</note> 

When he fell ill, he retired to the temple of Asclepius <note>Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine; his temples, or "Asclepieia," served as centers for healing and sanctuary.</note> and spent his time walking there. People flocked to him from all directions, believing he was there not because of illness, but because he intended to establish a school in that place. Among those who visited was Arcesilaus, who wished to be introduced by him to Polemon, even as Crantor was regaining his strength—as we shall mention in the section on Arcesilaus. Nevertheless, even after he recovered, Crantor continued to attend Polemon’s lectures, a fact for which he was greatly admired. 

It is also said that he left his estate to Arcesilaus, a fortune amounting to twelve talents. <note>A talent was a massive unit of currency; twelve talents represented a very large sum for a philosopher.</note> When Arcesilaus asked him where he wished to be buried, he replied:

> It is a beautiful thing to be hidden in the friendly depths of the earth.

It is said that he also wrote poetry, and that he sealed his poems and deposited them in the temple of Athena in his homeland. The poet Theaetetus writes of him in this way:

> Crantor was pleasing to men, but even more pleasing to the Muses,
> and he did not travel far into the years of old age. 
> O Earth, you shall receive this holy man now that he is dead,

Crantor admired Homer and Euripides above all others, saying that it was a difficult task to write in a way that was simultaneously tragic and compassionate. He would frequently quote this line from the *Bellerophon*: <note>Bellerophon is a lost tragedy by Euripides.</note>

> Alas! But why "alas"? We have suffered only what mortals must. <note>original: "Οἴμοι. τί δ' οἴμοι; θνητά τοι πεπόνθαμεν." This line suggests a stoic acceptance of human suffering as an inescapable part of the human condition.</note>

It is also said that the poet Antagoras composed these verses regarding Crantor's love affairs:

-> My heart is in doubt, oh famous name, <-
-> Should I call you Love, the first of the eternal gods, <-
-> Of those children whom ancient Erebus and Queen Night <-
-> Bore long ago beneath the waves of the sounding Ocean; <-
-> Or are you the son of wise Aphrodite, or of Earth, <-
-> Or of the Winds? For such a spirit do you wander, bringing <-
-> Both evil and good to men; thus is your body dual-natured. <-
<note>Antagoras of Rhodes was a court poet. These lines reflect on the mysterious, dual nature of Eros (Love)—both a primordial cosmic force and a fickle bringer of joy or pain.</note>

He was also quite clever at coining descriptive terms. For instance, he described a tragic actor with a rough, unrefined voice as "unhewn" and "full of bark." <note>original: "ἀπελέκυτον" (unhewn/unpolished) and "φλοιού μεστήν" (full of bark). These metaphors suggest a voice that lacks the smooth finish of a trained performer.</note> He remarked that the verses of a certain poet were "full of moths," and that the *Theses* of Theophrastus were "written with an oyster." <note>original: "ὀστρέῳ γεγράφθαι" (ostreo gegraphthai). This obscure phrase might imply that the work was either written with bitterness (like the sharp edge of a shell) or was as difficult to "open" as an oyster.</note> His most admired work is his book *On Grief*. <note>The treatise "On Grief" (De Luctu) was considered a masterpiece of ancient consolation literature; Cicero later called it a "golden book."</note> He passed away before Polemon and Crates, having succumbed to a condition of dropsy. <note>Dropsy, or edema, is a swelling of the body tissues, often associated with heart or kidney failure in antiquity.</note> I have written an epigram for him:

-> Even you, Crantor, were flooded by that worst of diseases, <-
-> And thus you descended into the black abyss of Pluto. <-
-> And while you are happy there now, the Academy stands <-
