...suspension of judgment <note>original: "ἀποφάσεις" (apophaseis), here referring to the Skeptical practice of withholding final judgment</note> because of the contradictions between opposing arguments. He was the first to argue both sides of a question, and the first to alter the traditional discourse handed down from Plato, making it more contentious through the use of question and answer. He was compared to Crantor in this style. He was the fourth of several brothers, having two by the same father and two by the same mother. Of those by the same mother, the elder was Pylades; of those by the same father, the elder was Moireas, who also served as his guardian. In his early years, before departing for Athens, he studied under the mathematician Autolycus, who was his fellow countryman; he even traveled to Sardis with him. Later, he studied under Xanthus the Athenian musician, and after him, he attended the lectures of Theophrastus. Eventually, he moved to the Academy to study with Crantor. For while his brother Moireas, whom I mentioned before, tried to lead him toward the study of rhetoric, Arcesilaus was in love with philosophy. Crantor, being quite fond of him, persuaded him to stay by quoting these lines from Euripides' *Andromeda*:

> O maiden, if I should save you, will you show me gratitude? <note>This is a line spoken by the hero Perseus to Andromeda, whom he is about to rescue from a sea monster.</note>

->And Arcesilaus replied with the following lines:<-

> Take me, O stranger, whether you wish me as a servant or a wife. <note>original: "Ἄγου με (ὦ ξένε) εἴτε δμωΐτ᾽ ἐθέλεις, εἴτ᾽ ἄλοχον." Arcesilaus playfully casts himself in the role of the rescued maiden to express his devotion to his teacher.</note>

From then on, they lived together. Because of this, they say Theophrastus was annoyed and remarked that a talented and bold young man had left his school. For indeed, Arcesilaus became very serious in his discourse and quite well-read, even trying his hand at poetry. Some epigrams of his addressed to Attalus are preserved, which go like this:

> Pergamum is famous not only for arms, but also for horses, 
> as is often proclaimed throughout holy Pisa. <note>Pisa was a region near Olympia; the "horses" refer to victories in the chariot races at the Olympic Games.</note>
> And if it is permitted for a mortal to speak the mind of Zeus, 
> it shall be much more celebrated in songs to come.

He also wrote for Mionodorus, the son of Eudamus and the beloved of one of his fellow students:

> Phrygia is far away, and holy Thyatira...

# ARCESILAUS. Book 4, 151

O Menodorus, your fatherland was Cadyanda. <note>original: "Καδαυάδη" (Kadauade). Cadyanda was a city in ancient Lycia.</note>
But to Acheron, that river of which no one speaks, the paths are equal,
Since they are measured the same from all sides by the countless numbers of men.
Eudamus built this clearly visible tomb for you, to whom you
Were the most beloved of many poor men.

He [Arcesilaus] admired Homer above all others, and whenever he was going to sleep, he would always read something of his. Even at dawn, he would say he was going to visit his "beloved" whenever he wanted to read Homer. He used to say that Pindar was powerful at filling the voice with resonance and providing an abundance of names and words. When he was young, he also used to imitate the style of Ion. <note>Ion of Chios, a versatile writer of tragedies, lyrics, and philosophy.</note> He also attended the lectures of Hipponicus the geometer, whom he used to mock; for while Hipponicus was sluggish and prone to yawning in other matters, he was highly skilled in his craft. Arcesilaus used to say that geometry fell into Hipponicus' mouth while he was yawning. When Hipponicus lost his mind, Arcesilaus took him into his own home and cared for him until he was fully restored.

When Crates died, Arcesilaus took charge of the school <note>The Academy in Athens.</note>, as a certain Socratides stepped aside in his favor. Because he practiced the suspension of judgment <note>original: "ἐπέχειν" (epechein), the central Skeptical practice of withholding assent to any non-evident proposition.</note> on all things, it is said that he never wrote a book. Others, however, say he was caught correcting certain works, which some claim he published and others claim he burned. He clearly admired Plato and possessed copies of his books. But according to some, he also emulated Pyrrho <note>The founder of the Skeptical school.</note>; he applied himself to dialectics and the arguments of the Eretrian school. <note>A school founded by Menedemus of Eretria, known for its interest in logic and ethics.</note> For this reason, Ariston said of him:

->Plato in front, Pyrrho behind, Diodorus in the middle.<-
<note>This is a parody of a line from Homer's *Iliad* describing the Chimera: "Lion in front, snake behind, and goat in the middle." It suggests Arcesilaus' philosophy was a hybrid of Platonism, Pyrrhonian skepticism, and the dialectics of Diodorus Cronus.</note>

And Timon says of him:

> Having Menedemus beneath his breast, he will place lead, or Pyrrho all the flesh, or Diodorus.

And after a pause, Timon makes him say:

> I shall swim toward Pyrrho and toward crooked Diodorus.

He was highly dignified and concise, and in his speech...

...and his name was "The Reprover." <note>original: "διαστατικός" (diastatikos). This suggests someone who is distinguishing or critical in his speech.</note> He was quite a mocker and spoke his mind with great freedom. Because of this, Timon <note>Timon of Phlius, the Skeptic poet and satirist.</note> spoke of him in this way:

*And you will not fail to mix reproofs even with the young.*

For this reason, when a rather bold young man was speaking, Arcesilaus asked, "Will no one take this fellow away with a knucklebone?" <note>original: "ἀστραγάλῳ" (astragalo). Knucklebones were used as dice or children's toys; Arcesilaus is suggesting the youth is a child who needs to be distracted or disciplined.</note> To a man who was accused of looking effeminate but claimed that one thing does not seem to be greater than another <note>A reference to the Skeptical doctrine of "indifference" or "non-preference" between appearances.</note>, Arcesilaus asked if a ten-finger length did not seem greater than a six-finger one.

There was a man named Hemon from Chios who was quite ugly, but he imagined himself to be handsome and always walked about in a fine woolen cloak. <note>original: "χλανίην" (chlanien), a luxury garment associated with wealth or effeminacy.</note> When Hemon asked if Arcesilaus thought a wise man would ever fall in love with him, Arcesilaus replied: "What, even if someone is not as 'handsome' as you, and even if they do not wear such 'handsome' clothes?"

When a certain man of questionable character spoke harshly to Arcesilaus, quoting a line from a play:

-> "Is it permitted to ask a question, my lady, or must I keep silence?" <-

Arcesilaus took him up and replied:

-> "Woman, <-
-> why do you speak so harshly to me, and not in your usual way?" <-

When a clever but talkative fellow was giving him trouble, Arcesilaus said:

-> "The children of slaves grow up to talk without restraint." <-

To a chatterbox who was babbling a great deal, he said that the man must have been "treated with harsh pitch." <note>This is a pun on a painful method of hair removal, suggesting the man's "smooth" but irritating tongue.</note> He then refused to answer him further. To a certain dialectician <term>dialectician: a philosopher specializing in logic and formal debate</term> and scholar who claimed to be ignorant of something, Arcesilaus replied:

-> "For even the passages of the winds remain hidden <-
-> From the female bird, until her offspring is present." <-

These lines are from the *Oenomaus* of Sophocles. <note>A lost play by the famous tragedian.</note> To a certain dialectician named Alexinus, who was unable to properly explain one of Alexinus's own theories, Arcesilaus recounted the story of what Philoxenus <note>A famous dithyrambic poet known for his wit.</note> did to the brick-makers. <note>original: "πλινθιακούς" (plinthiakous).</note> Philoxenus once found some brick-makers singing his songs badly; he immediately began trampling on their bricks, saying: "Just as you are ruining my work, I am ruining yours."

He was also annoyed with those who took up their studies at the wrong time. In his discussions, he had a natural way of using his voice...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
### Page 153

...I say"; and, "So-and-so will not assent to mental impressions." <note>original: "Οὐ συγκαταθήσεται τύποις" (Ou synkatathesesetai typois). This reflects Arcesilaus's Skeptical stance, where he argued that a wise person should withhold "assent" or belief from sensory impressions because they can be deceptive.</note> He was also nicknamed "The Reprover," a name which many of his students sought to imitate, along with his style of speaking and his whole manner. He was also most skillful in meeting objections unexpectedly, bringing the flow of the argument back to the subject at hand, and adapting himself to every occasion. He was more biting in his criticism than anyone else; for this reason, many people flocked to his school, even though they were stung by his sharp tongue. But they bore it gladly, for he was a truly good man and filled his listeners with hope. <margin>en-</margin> <note>The syllable "en" is printed at the margin, indicating the start of the next word "en" (in) on the following line.</note> In his private life, he was most companionable; he was eager to do favors and most humble in receiving gratitude. 

Once, when he visited **Ctesibius** while he was ill and saw him oppressed by poverty, he secretly placed a purse of money under his pillow. When Ctesibius found it, he said, "This is Arcesilaus's little joke." <note>original: "παίγνιον" (paignion). A "plaything" or "joke," suggesting Arcesilaus treated his significant charity as a mere trifle to avoid embarrassing his friend.</note> But he also sent him two thousand drachmas. Furthermore, by introducing **Archias the Arcadian** to **Eumenes**, he helped him attain great dignity.

Being a liberal man and most indifferent to money, he was the first to attend public displays of wealth; and at the festivals of **Archecrates** and **Callicrates**, he was more eager than anyone else to contribute to the feasts. He assisted many people and contributed to their funds. Once, when someone borrowed his silver plate to entertain friends and then refused to return it, Arcesilaus did not demand it back nor did he act as if he had been robbed. Others say he lent it on purpose, and when they tried to return it, he gave it as a gift because the man was poor. 

He also had property in **Italy**, from which his brother **Pylades** sent him supplies. Moreover, **Eumenes**, the son of **Philetaerus**, provided him with many things; for this reason, Arcesilaus addressed his writings only to him among all the kings. Although many people fawned over **Antigonus** <note>Antigonus II Gonatas, King of Macedonia.</note> and went out to meet him whenever he arrived, Arcesilaus remained quiet, not wishing to force himself upon the king's acquaintance. He was a very close friend to **Hierocles**, the governor of **Munichia** and the **Piraeus** <note>The primary port of Athens and its nearby fortified hill.</note>, and he visited him regularly during festivals. Even though Hierocles tried many times to persuade him to go and greet Antigonus, he was not convinced.

...but having gone as far as the gates, he turned back. After the naval battle of **Antigonus**, when many people approached him and wrote encouraging letters, he himself remained silent. <note>Antigonus II Gonatas was the King of Macedon and a patron of several philosophers. Arcesilaus’s silence here may reflect his Skeptical caution or political neutrality.</note> Nevertheless, he was sent as an ambassador by his home city to Demetrias to see Antigonus, but he was unsuccessful in his mission. He spent nearly all his time in the **Academy**, avoiding political involvement. 

Once at Athens, in the **Piraeus**, he spent a long time discussing philosophical theses, as he was on intimate terms with **Hierocles**. For this, he was slandered to **Zeno**. <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism. Arcesilaus and Zeno were contemporary rivals, representing the Skeptical and Dogmatic traditions respectively.</note> Being very fond of luxury—for what was he, indeed, but another **Aristippus**? <note>Aristippus of Cyrene was a student of Socrates who famously embraced pleasure and luxury, arguing that a wise man should control his circumstances rather than be controlled by them.</note>—he would go out to dinners with those who shared his habits. He lived openly with **Theodote** and **Philaine**, courtesans from Elis; and when people mocked him for this, he would quote the witty maxims of Aristippus to defend himself. <note>original: "χρείας" (chreias). These were a specific genre of philosophical anecdotes or "pithy sayings" used to teach a lesson or win an argument.</note> 

He was also fond of young men and prone to desire. Because of this, **Ariston of Chios** and his followers among the Stoics attacked him, calling him a "corrupter of youth," a "speaker of obscenities," and "shameless." For it is said he was especially enamored with **Demetrius**, who sailed to Cyrene, and with **Leochares of Myrlea**. Regarding Leochares, it is told that when some revelers came to his door, Arcesilaus said that he himself wished to open it, but Leochares prevented him. **Demochares** (the son of Laches) and **Pythocles** (the son of Bugelus) were also in love with him. When he caught them there, he said with characteristic forbearance that he would step aside for them. 

For these reasons, the aforementioned critics would bite at him and mock him as a "crowd-pleaser" and as one "fond of glory." They attacked him most especially at the house of **Hieronymus the Peripatetic**, whenever he gathered his friends for the birthday celebration of **Alcyoneus** (the son of Antigonus). For this occasion, Antigonus had sent a large sum of money for the festivities. There, Arcesilaus would avoid giving lengthy philosophical lectures over the wine cups; he did not propose any eternal theorem, and when asked why, he replied: 

"The very hallmark of philosophy is knowing the right season for everything." <note>original: "τὸ καιρὸν ἑκάστων ἐπίστασθαι" (to kairon hekastōn epistasthai). This highlights the Greek concept of *Kairos*—the opportune or "right" moment. Arcesilaus argues that a true philosopher knows when it is time for serious study and when it is time for social enjoyment.</note>

*Then, having spoken, he plunged into the surrounding crowd;*

*“Why, you poor wretch, do you puff yourself up so, being such a fool?”*
<note>This satirical verse is by Timon of Phlius, a Skeptic poet who famously mocked almost every philosopher of his time in his work called the *Silloi*.</note>

Nevertheless, he was so free from vanity that he would advise his students to listen to other teachers as well. When a young man from Chios was not satisfied with his lectures but preferred those of **Hieronymus** the Peripatetic, Arcesilaus personally took him and introduced him to that philosopher, after first asking the youth to behave himself. 

Another witty saying of his is often repeated. To someone who asked why it was that students from all the other schools would defect to the **Epicurean** school, but no one ever left the Epicureans to join the others, he replied: 
“Because men can become eunuchs, but eunuchs can never become men.” 
<note>original: "γάλλοι" (galli). The *Galli* were the castrated priests of the goddess Cybele. Arcesilaus is using a sharp, somewhat crude metaphor: once a person "gives up" their intellectual rigor for the easy pleasures of Epicureanism, they lose the "manhood" required for difficult philosophy and can never return.</note>

When he drew near his end, he left all his property to his brother **Pylades**, whom he had secretly brought from Pitane to Athens. Arcesilaus never married and had no children. He made three copies of his will and deposited them in different places: one in **Eretria** with Amphicritus, another in Athens with some of his friends, and the third he sent to his home in Pitane to **Thaumasias**, one of his relatives, asking him to keep it safe. To this Thaumasias he wrote the following letter:

->Arcesilaus to Thaumasias, greetings.<-

> I have given Diogenes my will to bring to you. Because I am frequently ill and my body is in a weak state, I decided to settle my affairs; I do this so that if anything should happen to me, I may not depart having done any wrong to you, who have shown such great devotion and affection toward me. You are the person I trust most of all those back home to keep these documents, both because of your age and our close kinship. Try, therefore, to remember that I am placing in your hands a most vital trust. Act justly toward me, so that as far as it depends on you, my affairs may be administered with dignity. The other copies are deposited in Athens...

# BION

**Bion** was by birth a **Borysthenite** <note>From the region of the Borysthenes river, modern-day Dnieper in Ukraine.</note>. He himself explained to King **Antigonus** who his parents were and from what circumstances he turned to philosophy. For when the King asked him:

> “Who are you? From what men? Where is your city and your parents?”
<note>original: This is a famous line from Homer's *Odyssey* (Book 10, line 325), often used as a formal greeting or challenge in antiquity.</note>

Bion, sensing that he had already been slandered to the King, replied: “My father was a freedman who used to wipe his nose on his elbow” (by which he meant he was a seller of salted fish). “He was a Borysthenite by birth, having not a face, but a brand upon his face—a symbol of his master’s cruelty. My mother was the kind of woman a man like that would marry...”
<note>original: "τῷ ἀγκῶνι ἀπομυσσόμενος" (wiping his nose on his elbow). This was a derogatory idiom for a common laborer or fishmonger who didn't even have a cloth to clean himself. The "brand" refers to the practice of tattooing or branding slaves as punishment.</note>

# BION
### Book 4

...born in a brothel. Later, my father, having committed some fraud in his tax-collecting, was sold into slavery with his whole household, including us. A certain rhetorician bought me when I was still young and graceful; when he died, he left everything to me. I then burned all his writings, cleared everything out, and went to Athens to study philosophy.

->Of this race and blood I boast myself to be.<-
<note>original: "Ταύτης τοι γενεῆς τε καὶ αἵματος εὔχομαι εἶν." Bion is humorously quoting Homer’s *Iliad* (6.211), where a hero proudly declares his noble lineage. Bion uses it to mock his own low birth.</note>

These are the facts of my life. So, let **Persaeus** and **Philonides** stop recounting them; look at them with me as I am. 

In truth, **Bion** was in other respects a man of many parts, a versatile sophist, and one who gave many opportunities to those wishing to trample upon philosophy. In some matters he was also ostentatious and capable of indulging in vanity. He left behind many memoirs, but also pithy sayings that have practical value. 

For instance, when he was reproached for failing to win over a certain youth, he said: "One cannot pull up soft cheese with a fish-hook." 

Once, when asked who suffers the most anxiety, he replied: "The man who wishes for the greatest success." 

Asked if he should marry (for this saying is also attributed to him), he said: "If you marry an ugly woman, you will have a punishment; if you marry a beautiful one, you will have her in common." 
<note>This is a famous Greek pun: "punishment" is *poinē* and "in common" (meaning unfaithful or shared by others) is *koinē*.</note>

He used to say that old age was the harbor of all evils; for at least all things take refuge in it. He said that reputation was the mother of years <note>The Greek text here reads "ἐτῶν" (years), though some scholars suggest it should be "ἀρετῶν" (virtues). Bion likely means that fame is what makes one's years significant.</note>; beauty was a good that belongs to another; and wealth was the sinews of affairs. 

To a man who had squandered his estates, he said: "The earth swallowed **Amphiaraus**, but you have swallowed the earth." 
<note>Amphiaraus was a mythological seer who was swallowed by the earth during the war of the Seven Against Thebes.</note>

He said it was a great evil not to be able to bear evil. He also condemned those who cremated people as if they were without feeling, yet burned offerings alongside them as if they could feel. 

He said repeatedly that it was more desirable to grant one's own prime of life to another than to harvest it from another; for in the latter case, one is harmed in both body and soul. 

He even attacked **Socrates**, saying that if **Socrates** had a need for **Alcibiades** and yet abstained from him, he was a fool; but if...

...[if] he didn’t have it, he was doing nothing strange. He used to say that the road to the underworld was easy; at least people go there with their eyes closed. 

He criticized **Alcibiades**, saying that when he was a boy, he drew husbands away from their wives, and when he became a young man, he drew wives away from their husbands. 

In Rhodes, while the Athenians were teaching rhetoric, he taught philosophy. To one who found fault with this, he said: "I brought wheat, and I am selling barley." 
<note>original: "Πυροὺς ἐκόμισα, καὶ κριθὰς πωλῶ." Wheat (rhetoric) was considered more "noble" and expensive, while barley (philosophy) was the staple of the poor. Bion suggests he is providing what is necessary, even if it is less "prestigious."</note>

He said that those in the underworld would be punished even more if they carried water in sound jars rather than leaky ones. 
<note>This is a cynical take on the myth of the Danaids, who were condemned to carry water in sieves. Bion suggests that a task that can actually be completed might be a worse "eternal" labor than one that is obviously futile.</note>

To a chatterbox who begged him for help, he said: "I will do enough for you if you send messengers and do not come yourself." 

While sailing with some wicked men, they fell among pirates. When the men said, "We are lost if we are recognized!" Bion replied: "And I am lost if I am *not* recognized." 

He called conceit the "hindrance to progress." 

To a stingy rich man, he said: "This man does not possess his wealth; his wealth possesses him." 

He used to say that stingy people take care of their property as if it were their own, but get no benefit from it, as if it belonged to others. 

He said that men should use courage while young, but their <term>wisdom (phronēsis)</term> <note>The Greek term *phronēsis* implies practical wisdom or "common sense" applied to living well.</note> reaches its peak as they grow old. He said that wisdom differs from the other virtues as much as sight differs from the other senses. 

He said one should not reproach old age, "into which," he said, "we all pray to arrive." 

To an envious man who was looking gloomy, he said: "I do not know whether some evil has happened to you, or some good has happened to someone else." 

He said that impiety was a wicked companion to <term>freedom of speech (parrhēsia)</term>: 

->For it reveals the man, even if he be bold-tongued.<- 
<note>original: "Δηλοῖ γὰρ ἄνδρα, κἂν θρασύστομός τις ᾖ." This is a quote from Euripides' play *Hippolytus* (line 422). Bion suggests that even a brave talker is betrayed by a guilty conscience.</note>

He said one should keep friends, whatever they may be like, so that we do not seem to have associated with wicked men or to have rejected good ones. 

At the beginning of his studies, he was a student of the **Academic** school, during the time he was a pupil of **Crates**. Then he took up the **Cynic** way of life, taking the characteristic cloak and the leather pouch. 
<note>The "cloak and pouch" were the standard uniform of the Cynics, philosophers who lived in intentional poverty to show their independence from social norms.</note>

And indeed, what else transformed him toward a state of <term>impassivity (apatheia)</term>? <note>In Greek philosophy, *apatheia* is not "apathy" in the modern sense, but a state of mind where one is not disturbed by emotions or external misfortunes.</note> He then moved on to the teachings of **Theodorus**...

# BION. Book 4

[Bion] listened to **Theodorus the Atheist**, who practiced sophistry <note>Sophistry here refers to the art of clever, sometimes deceptive, argumentation.</note> in every kind of discourse. Along with these teachers, he also attended the lectures of **Theophrastus the Peripatetic**. He possessed a theatrical flair and was very skilled at dispersing jests, often using coarse language to describe things. Because he employed such a mixture of every style of speech, they say that **Eratosthenes** remarked of him that Bion was the first to "dress philosophy in flowery robes." 
<note>original: "τὴν φιλοσοφίαν ἀνθινὰ ἐνέδυσεν." This suggests that Bion replaced the sober, plain language of traditional philosophy with colorful, poetic, and entertaining rhetoric.</note>

He was naturally gifted at parody; for instance, he wrote these lines:

> O dear **Archytas**, born of the lute, swollen with vanity, 
> Most skilled of all men at the highest pitch of strife.
<note>Bion is parodying epic poetry to mock Archytas, a famous Pythagorean mathematician and statesman. The phrase "highest pitch of strife" plays on the double meaning of musical tuning and intellectual argument.</note>

In general, he made fun of both music and geometry. He lived a lavish lifestyle, and for this reason, he moved from city to city, sometimes employing artifice to create a grand impression. In **Rhodes**, for example, he persuaded the sailors to put on students' robes and follow him. When he entered the gymnasium <note>The gymnasium in Ancient Greece was a center for both physical training and intellectual education.</note> with them, he became the center of everyone’s attention. 

He was also in the habit of "adopting" certain young men, both to use them for his own pleasures and so that he might be guarded by their loyalty. Furthermore, he was intensely self-loving and frequently insisted on the maxim: "Friends' goods are common property." 
<term>Common property (Koinā ta philōn)</term>: A traditional Greek proverb often associated with Pythagoras, suggesting that true friends share everything. Bion, however, was accused of using this philosophy as an excuse to live off the wealth of others.

Because of this attitude, not a single pupil is recorded as his official follower, despite the many who studied with him. Indeed, he led some of them into shamelessness. **Betion**, one of his associates, is said to have once remarked to **Menedemus**: "I tell you, Menedemus, I spend my nights with Bion, and I don't feel I have suffered anything improper." 

Bion behaved bitterly and quite godlessly toward his companions—a trait he inherited from his time with Theodorus. Yet later, when he fell into a sickness (as those in **Chalcis** say, for he died there), he was persuaded to wear amulets <note>Magical charms or "periapta" used to ward off evil or disease.</note> and to repent for his offenses against the divine. When he fell into poverty and lacked people to nurse him in his illness, he suffered terribly, until King **Antigonus** sent two servants to him. Indeed, Antigonus even followed him in a litter <note>A portable couch or bed carried by servants.</note>, as **Favorinus** records in his *Universal History*. But regarding how he died, we ourselves...

->“Farewell,” he said, “Farewell, Pluto!”<-
<note>original: "Χαῖρε Πλουτεῦ" (Hail, Pluto). Pluto is the god of the Underworld. Diogenes Laertius mocks Bion for greeting the god of death after a lifetime of atheism.</note>

There have been ten men named Bion: first, a contemporary of Pherecydes of Syros, who is credited with two books (he was from Proconnesus); second, a man from Syracuse, who wrote works on the art of rhetoric; third, the same person as the second; fourth, a follower of Democritus and a mathematician from Abdera, who wrote in both the Attic and Ionic dialects (he was the first to claim that there are certain regions where there is a six-month night and a six-month day); fifth, a man from Soli, who wrote a history of Ethiopia; sixth, a rhetorician, of whom nine books titled *The Muses* are circulated; seventh, a lyric poet; eighth, a sculptor from Miletus, mentioned by Polemon; ninth, a tragic poet of the so-called Tarsic style; and tenth, a sculptor from Clazomenae or Chios, who is also mentioned by Hipponax.

## LACYDES.

Lacydes, the son of Alexander, was a native of Cyrene. He was the founder of the New Academy, having succeeded Arcesilaus.
<note>The "New Academy" refers to a skeptical phase of Plato's famous school in Athens, where philosophers argued that certainty in knowledge is impossible.</note>
He was a man of great dignity and had no small number of followers. From a young age, he was industrious; although he was poor, he was otherwise graceful and refined in his manners. It is said that he managed his household affairs in a most peculiar manner. Whenever he took anything out of his storehouse, he would seal the door with his signet ring, and then throw the ring back inside through a small hole, so that he could be certain his stored goods could never be stolen or carried away while the seal was intact. However, his servants, having learned of this habit, would break the seal, take whatever they pleased, and then throw the ring back through the hole into the gallery. Even though they did this constantly, he never...

...was discovered. At any rate, Lacydes used to hold his school in the Academy, in the garden that had been constructed by King Attalus; for this reason, it was called the "Lacydion" after him. He was the only person who, while still living, handed over the leadership of his school to others—specifically to Telecles and Evander, both from Phocis—after having held it since the beginning of his career. Evander was succeeded by Hegesinus of Pergamum, who was in turn followed by Carneades. 

A witty remark is attributed to Lacydes. When King Attalus <note>Attalus I of Pergamum, a patron of the arts and philosophy.</note> sent for him, they say he replied that "images should be viewed from a distance." 

Late in his life, while he was studying geometry, someone asked him, "Is it really the right time for this now?" To which he replied, "If not now, when?" 

He died after having served as the head of the school for twenty-six years. His death occurred in the fourth year of the 134th Olympiad <note>Approximately 241–240 BCE.</note>. The cause of his death was paralysis brought on by excessive drinking. We ourselves composed a playful poem about him, which goes like this:

> I heard the story of you too, Lacydes, how you
> Were seized by Bacchus <note>original: "Βάκχον" (Bacchus), the god of wine.</note> and dragged to Hades by your very toes.
> It was surely clear: Dionysus, when he enters the body in Great quantity,
> Will loosen the limbs; which is exactly why he is called the "Loosener."
> <note>original: "Λυαῖος" (Lyaios). This is a pun on a title for Dionysus meaning "The Deliverer" or "The Loosener." The poet jokes that the god "loosened" Lacydes' body into a state of paralysis.</note>

## CARNEADES

**C**arneades was the son of Epicomus (or Philocomus, according to Alexander in his *Successions*), and was a native of Cyrene. Having read the books of the Stoics—especially those of Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoic school and its most prolific writer.</note>—with great care, he argued against them with such success and moderation that he used to say: "If Chrysippus had not existed, I would not be." 

He was a man of immense industry <note>original: "Φιλόπονος" (Philoponos), meaning "lover of labor" or "hard-working."</note>, if ever there was one. While he was less focused on natural philosophy, he excelled in ethics. Because of his total devotion to his studies, he even let his hair and his nails grow long. He possessed such great influence in philosophy that even the students of rhetoric would leave their own schools and go to him to hear his lectures. 

He also had a very powerful voice, so much so that the gymnasarch <note>The official in charge of the gymnasium where the school was located.</note> once sent a message to him asking him not to shout so loudly. To this, Carneades replied...

# CARNEADES. BOOK IV

...to say, "Give me a measure for my voice." <note>Carneades was famous for his powerful, booming voice which often drowned out other teachers in the same facility.</note> Whereupon it is said that the person he asked <note>Likely a slave or assistant who tried to regulate his volume.</note> replied inappropriately, "You have your audience as your measure." He was terrifying when administering a rebuke and a formidable opponent in formal investigations. Eventually, he declined dinner invitations for the reasons mentioned previously. <note>Earlier sections of his biography suggest he was so absorbed in his thoughts that he forgot to eat or groom himself.</note> 

Once, when Mentor the Bithynian—who had been his student—came to the school after attempting to seduce Carneades' mistress (as Favorinus says in his *Miscellaneous History*), Carneades mocked him by parodying verses from Homer while lecturing:

-> "A certain old man of the sea comes this way, unerring," <-
-> "Resembling Mentor in both body and voice." <-
<note>Carneades is playing on the name of his student, Mentor. In Homer's Odyssey, the goddess Athena often takes the form of the wise elder Mentor to guide Telemachus. Here, the "unerring old man" refers to the student's deceitful character rather than wisdom.</note>

He also remarked that Mentor had not been "purged of his gall." <note>original: "χολῆς" (choles). This is a medical metaphor suggesting Mentor still possessed a bitter or corrupt temperament.</note>

-> To which Mentor stood up and replied: <-
-> "The heralds made the proclamation, and the people gathered quickly." <-
<note>Mentor responds with another Homeric parody, implying that despite the insult, Carneades' school is still crowded with listeners.</note>

He seems to have behaved somewhat remarkably regarding his end, as he would constantly say, "Nature, which put me together, will also dissolve me." Hearing that Antipater <note>Antipater of Tarsus, a Stoic philosopher and a long-time rival of Carneades.</note> had died by drinking poison, he was spurred toward a courageous departure and said: "Give some to me then." When people asked, "What?" he replied, "Honey-wine." <note>original: "Οἰνόμελι" (Oinomeli). This is a final bit of wit; while the Stoic died by poison, Carneades asks for a sweet drink to meet his end.</note> 

They say that at the moment of his death there was an eclipse of the moon, suggesting (as one might say) the sympathy <term>sympatheia: the ancient belief in a physical or spiritual interconnection between the heavens and the earth</term> of the most beautiful of the stars after the sun. Apollodorus says in his *Chronicles* that he departed from among men in the fourth year of the 162nd Olympiad <note>Approximately 129–128 BCE.</note>, having lived eighty-five years. 

Letters of his addressed to Ariarathes, the King of Cappadocia, are in circulation, but his disciples wrote down the rest of his teachings. He himself left nothing in writing. There is also an epigram of ours for him, in the Logadic and Archebulian meters:

-> "Why, O Muse, do you wish to reproach me regarding Carneades?" <-
-> "He is ignorant who knows nothing of how he feared" <-
-> "To die; when even while suffering from a most wretched" <-
-> "Wasting disease, he did not wish for a release; but hearing..." <-

-> Is it because Antipater died by drinking poison? <-
-> "Give me, then," he said, "something to drink as well." "Or nothing?" <-

-> "Nature, which holds me together, will also surely dissolve me." <-

<note>This is an epigram by Diogenes Laertius himself, mocking or memorializing the philosopher. It references the Stoic Antipater of Tarsus, who committed suicide by poison. Carneades, not wanting to be outdone even in death, asks for his own "poison" in the form of sweetened wine.</note>

It is also said that his vision failed at night and he became blind. He ordered his boy to light a lamp. When the boy brought it in and said, "I have brought it," Carneades replied, "Then you read." <note>This anecdote highlights the philosopher's loss of sight in his old age and his continued dependence on his students and assistants for his intellectual work.</note> This man had many other students, but the most distinguished was Clitomachus, of whom we must now speak. There was, however, another Carneades, who was a dull writer of elegiac poetry.

## CLITOMACHUS

Clitomachus was a Carthaginian. He was originally called Hasdrubal <note>original: "Ἀσδρουβας" (Asdroubas). Clitomachus is the Greek name he adopted later.</note>, and he used to practice philosophy in his own native language in his homeland. But when he came to Athens at the age of forty, he became a student of Carneades. Carneades, welcoming his industrious nature, saw to it that he learned Greek literature and trained the man himself. Clitomachus reached such a degree of diligence that he wrote more than four hundred books. He succeeded Carneades as head of the school <note>The <term>Academy</term>, the school founded by Plato which had moved into a Skeptical phase under Carneades.</note> and brought light to his master's doctrines primarily through his own writings. He was a man who spent time studying in the three <term>sects</term> <note>original: "αἱρέσεσι" (haireseis), meaning schools of thought or philosophical choices.</note>: the Academic, the Peripatetic, and the Stoic. On the whole, Timon <note>Timon of Phlius, a skeptical satirist known for mocking almost all philosophers.</note> ridicules the Academics in this way:

> Nor the un-watered, wide-mouthed talk of the Academics.
<note>Timon is mocking the Academics for what he perceived as their verbose and endless debates that lacked substance or "refreshment."</note>

Having now completed our account of the Academics who descended from Plato, let us move on to the Peripatetics who also descended from Plato, a line which began with Aristotle.

## ARISTOTLE.

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'A' depicting a scholar or philosopher seated at a desk within a room.</image-desc>

ARISTOTLE, son of Nicomachus and Phaestis, was a native of Stageira. His father, Nicomachus, traced his descent back to Nicomachus, the son of Machaon, the son of Asclepius <note>Asclepius was the Greek god of medicine; this lineage emphasizes the family's deep roots in the medical profession.</note>, as Hermippus states in his work *On Aristotle*. He lived with Amyntas, King of the Macedonians, serving as both physician and friend. Aristotle was the most distinguished of Plato’s students. He had a lisping voice <note>original: "τραυλὸς τὴν φωνήν" (traulos tēn phōnēn)</note>, as Timotheus the Athenian mentions in his *On Lives*. It is also said that he had slender legs and small eyes, and he was known for wearing striking clothing and rings, as well as for his particular way of cutting his hair. He had a son named Nicomachus by his concubine Herpyllis, according to Timotheus. He broke away from Plato while the master was still alive; because of this, they say Plato remarked, "Aristotle has kicked us, just as colts do to their mother when they are born." <note>This famous anecdote suggests a perceived lack of gratitude or a sharp intellectual departure from his teacher.</note> Hermippus says in his *Lives* that while Aristotle was serving as an ambassador to Philip [of Macedon] on behalf of the Athenians, Xenocrates became the head of the school in the Academy. When Aristotle returned and saw the school under someone else’s leadership, he chose a place for walking <term>peripatos</term> <note>original: "περίπατον" (peripaton). A covered walkway or garden path.</note> in the Lyceum. There, walking back and forth until it was time for the athletes to be anointed for exercise <note>The "anointing" refers to the time of day when gymnasium users would oil themselves, marking the end of the morning's intellectual discourse.</note>, he would discuss philosophy with his students, which is why he was called the Peripate-

...sacrifice. Others say that while Alexander was recovering from an illness and taking walks, Aristotle accompanied him and discussed various matters; but when the group grew larger and Aristotle sat down, he remarked:

->It is a shame to keep silent and let Xenocrates speak.<-
<note>Xenocrates was a fellow student of Plato and later the head of the Academy; Aristotle likely felt his own philosophical style or the school's direction was superior or more pressing at that moment.</note>

He also trained his students in the discussion of a <term>thesis</term> <note>A "thesis" in this context refers to a formal proposition or philosophical question set for debate.</note>, while simultaneously practicing the art of rhetoric. Afterward, however, he departed to join Hermias the eunuch, who was the tyrant of Atarneus. Some say that Hermias was his favorite <note>original: "παιδικά" (paidika); a term often used for a beloved youth in a relationship.</note>; others say they became related by marriage when Hermias gave Aristotle his daughter or niece, as Demetrius of Magnesia states in his work *On Poets and Writers of the Same Name*. Demetrius also claims that Hermias was originally a slave of Eubulus and a Bithynian by birth, and that he eventually killed his master. Aristippus, in the first book of his *On Ancient Luxury*, claims that Aristotle fell in love with Hermias’s concubine. With Hermias’s permission, he married her and, in his overwhelming joy, offered sacrifices to the woman just as the Athenians do to Eleusinian Demeter <note>Demeter was the goddess of the harvest; comparing a mortal woman to her in worship was considered scandalous or even blasphemous to contemporaries.</note>. He even wrote a <term>Paean</term> <note>A song of praise or triumph, usually dedicated to a god.</note> for Hermias, which is transcribed further on.

From there, he went to Macedonia to the court of Philip and received Philip's son, Alexander, as a pupil. He requested that Philip rebuild his hometown <note>Stageira</note>, which had been razed by the king, and his request was granted; he even established laws for the city. He also acted as a legislator within his own school, imitating Xenocrates’ practice of appointing a leader every ten days. When he felt he had spent a sufficient amount of time with Alexander, he departed for Athens, having recommended his relative Callisthenes of Olynthus to the king. When Callisthenes spoke too boldly to the king and refused to obey him, they say Aristotle rebuked him by quoting:

->Short-lived, then, my child, will you be, from what you say.<-
<note>original: "Ὠκύμορος δή μοι τέκος ἔσσεαι, οἷ' ἀγορεύεις" — a quote from Homer’s *Iliad*, where Thetis warns Achilles of his impending death.</note>

And indeed, it happened just so. For having been thought to participate with Hermolaus in the conspiracy against Alexander, Callisthenes was carried about in an iron cage, infested with lice and neglected; finally, he was thrown to a lion and thus met his end. Aristotle, meanwhile, arrived in Athens...

### ARISTOTLE. Book 5.

...and after leading the school for thirteen years, he withdrew to Chalcis. This was because Eurymedon the <term>Hierophant</term> <note>A Hierophant was a high priest, specifically the one who interpreted the sacred mysteries at Eleusis.</note>—or Demophilus, according to Favorinus in his *Miscellaneous History*—brought an indictment for impiety against him. The charge was based on the fact that Aristotle had composed a hymn to the aforementioned Hermias, as well as an epigram for his statue at Delphi, which read as follows:

->In violation of the holy law of the blessed gods,<-
->the king of the bow-bearing Persians once impiously slew this man;<-
->not by conquering him openly with a spear in bloody combat,<-
->but by relying on the treacherous faith of a man.<-

In Chalcis, he died by drinking <term>aconite</term> <note>A poisonous plant, often called monkshood or wolfsbane; here used as a method of suicide to avoid execution.</note>, as Eumolpus says in the fifth book of his *Histories*, having lived seventy years. The same author states that he was thirty years old when he joined Plato, but this is an error. In truth, he lived to be sixty-three, and joined Plato at the age of seventeen. The hymn he wrote is of the following sort:

Virtue, won by much toil for the human race, the fairest prize in life! For your sake, O Virgin, even to die is an envied fate in Greece, and to endure fierce, unwearied labors. Such is the immortal fruit you cast upon the mind—better than gold, better than noble birth or soft-eyed sleep. For your sake the son of Zeus, Heracles, and the sons of Leda endured much, heralding your power through their deeds. Out of longing for you, Achilles and Ajax went to the house of Hades. And for the sake of your beloved form, the foster-child of Atarneus <note>Refers to Hermias, the ruler of the city of Atarneus.</note> left the rays of the sun. Therefore, his deeds shall be celebrated in song, and the Muses, the daughters of Memory, shall make him immortal, exalting the majesty of Zeus the God of Hospitality and the reward of constant friendship. 

There is also a poem of our own regarding him, which goes like this:

->Eurymedon once intended to indict Aristotle for impiety,<-
->being a minister of Demeter of the Mysteries.<-
->But by drinking aconite, he escaped this without a struggle;<-
->it was thus he defeated unjust slanders.<-

<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

Favorinus says in his *Miscellaneous History* that Aristotle was the first to write a forensic speech in his own defense for this very trial, and that he told the Athenians:

> Pear grows old upon pear, and fig upon fig. <note>original: "Ὄγχνη ἐπ' ὄγχνῃ γηράσκει, σῦκον δ' ἐπὶ σύκῳ." A quote from Homer's *Odyssey* (7.120), here used to mock the "crop" of informers or sycophants in Athens who were constantly bringing new accusations.</note>

Apollodorus states in his *Chronology* that Aristotle was born in the first year of the 99th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>The 99th Olympiad began in 384 BCE. The Greeks measured time in four-year cycles between Olympic Games.</note>. He joined Plato and remained with him for twenty years, having been seventeen when he was first introduced to him. He went to Mitylene during the <term>archonship</term> <note>The term of office for an "archon," a chief magistrate in Athens used as a calendar marker.</note> of Eubulus, in the fourth year of the 108th Olympiad [345/4 BCE]. When Plato died in the first year of the 109th Olympiad [348/7 BCE], during the archonship of Theophilus, Aristotle departed to join Hermias and remained there for three years. In the archonship of Pythodotus, he went to the court of Philip [of Macedon], in the second year of the 109th Olympiad [343/2 BCE], when Alexander was already fifteen years old. 

He arrived back in Athens in the second year of the 111th Olympiad [335/4 BCE] and taught in the <term>Lyceum</term> <note>A gymnasium and public meeting place in Athens where Aristotle established his philosophical school, the Peripatetic school.</note> for thirteen years. Afterward, he withdrew to Chalcis in the third year of the 114th Olympiad [322/1 BCE] and died of a disease at about sixty-three years of age—the same time that Demosthenes is said to have ended his life at Calauria, during the archonship of Philocles.

It is said that he offended King Alexander because of his recommendation of Callisthenes. To spite Aristotle, the king promoted Anaximenes and sent gifts to Xenocrates. Theocritus of Chios also mocked him in an epigram, written as follows (according to Ambryon in his work *On Theocritus*):

> To the eunuch Hermias and Eubulus the slave, 
> a hollow tomb was built by hollow-minded Aristotle. <note>Theocritus is mocking Aristotle for honoring Hermias, whom he considers unworthy, and for the "hollow" nature of his philosophy or his loyalty.</note>

Furthermore, Timon attacked him, saying:

> Nor did Aristotle escape the pains of mindless vanity.

And such was the life of the philosopher. We have also come across his will, which is arranged roughly as follows: "All shall be well; but should anything happen, Aristotle has made these dispositions..."

<meta>This page continues from the account of Aristotle’s final years in Chalcis, moving into the formal legal text of his last will and testament as preserved by Diogenes Laertius.</meta>

<page-num>169</page-num>
<header>ARISTOTLE. Book 5</header>

In the event that anything should happen <note>A common legal euphemism for "in the event of my death."</note>, Aristotle has made the following dispositions: 

Antipater <note>A powerful Macedonian general and regent, a lifelong friend of Aristotle.</note> is to be the general and permanent executor of all matters. Until Nicanor <note>Aristotle’s nephew and adopted son.</note> can take charge, the executors shall be Aristomenes, Timarchus, Dioteles, and—if he is willing and it is possible for him—Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor as head of the Peripatetic school.</note>. These men shall take care of the children, Herpyllis, and all the property left behind. When the girl <note>His daughter, Pythias.</note> is of age, she is to be given in marriage to Nicanor. 

If anything should happen to the girl—which may it not happen, and it shall not!—before she is married, or after she is married but before there are children, Nicanor shall have the authority to manage both the child <note>Referring to the young son, Nicomachus.</note> and all other affairs in a manner worthy of himself and of us. Nicanor shall take care of both the girl and the boy Nicomachus, acting as he sees fit for their interests, as both a father and a brother. 

If anything should happen to Nicanor—which may it not happen!—either before he receives the girl in marriage or after he has received her but before there are children, any arrangements he may have made shall be valid. If, in such a case, Theophrastus should wish to live with the girl, the same provisions shall apply as for Nicanor. Otherwise, the executors, consulting with Antipater, shall manage the affairs of both the girl and the boy as they see best. 

The executors and Nicanor shall also take care of Herpyllis <note>Aristotle’s companion after the death of his wife.</note>, remembering me and how devoted she has been to me. If she should wish to take a husband, they must ensure she is not given to someone unworthy of us. In addition to what has already been given to her, they shall give her a <term>talent</term> <note>A massive sum of money, roughly equivalent to 6,000 drachmas or the weight of about 26kg of silver.</note> of silver from the estate, and three handmaids if she wants them, plus the young maid she already has and the slave boy Pyrraeus. 

If she chooses to live in Chalcis, she shall have the guest-house by the garden; if she chooses to live in Stagira <note>Aristotle’s birthplace.</note>, she shall have the ancestral house. Whichever of these she chooses, the executors shall furnish the house with such equipment as they and Herpyllis deem appropriate and sufficient. Nicanor shall also take care of the boy Myrmex, ensuring he is returned to his own people in a manner worthy of us, along with the property he brought with him.

Ambracis <note>A female servant in Aristotle's household.</note> is to be set free, and when the girl <note>Aristotle's daughter, Pythias.</note> is given in marriage, the executors are to give Ambracis five hundred drachmae <term>drachma: a standard silver coin; 500 was a substantial sum for a dowry or pension</term> and the young maidservant she currently has. Care must also be taken regarding the statues commissioned from Gryllion <note>A known sculptor of the 4th century BCE.</note>, to ensure they are completed and dedicated: these include the statue of Nicanor, the one of Proxenus <note>Aristotle’s guardian after his father died.</note> which I intended to have commissioned, and the statue of Nicanor’s mother. Furthermore, as a thank-offering for Nicanor’s safe return, for which I made a vow on his behalf, stone figures of animals four cubits <note>A cubit is roughly the length of a forearm, about 18 inches.</note> high are to be dedicated to Zeus the Savior and Athena the Savior at Stagira <note>Aristotle's birthplace in Macedonia.</note>.

Such is the nature of his will. It is also said that a great many gourmet dishes were found among his possessions. Lycon <note>A later head of Aristotle's school, often critical of his predecessors.</note> claims that Aristotle used to bathe in a tub of warm oil and then sell the oil afterward. Some say he would even place a skin of warm oil against his stomach; and whenever he went to sleep, a bronze sphere was placed in his hand with a basin underneath it, so that when the sphere fell into the basin, he would be woken up by the noise.

There are also some very fine sayings attributed to him. When asked what profit liars gain from their habit, he replied, "That when they do speak the truth, they are not believed." Being reproached—

# ARISTOTLE Book V

<page-num>171</page-num>

->ARISTOTLE Book V<-

When he was once reproached for giving alms to a wicked man, he said, "I did not pity his character, but the man." <note>original: "Οὐ τὸν τρόπον... ἀλλὰ τὸν ἄνθρωπον" — Aristotle distinguishes between the moral quality of a person and their shared humanity.</note> He was accustomed to say constantly to his friends and those who attended his lectures, wherever and whenever he happened to be staying, that just as sight receives light from the surrounding air, so the soul receives light from the subjects of study. Often, speaking at length, he would claim that the Athenians had discovered both wheat and laws; but while they used the wheat, they did not use the laws. He said that the roots of education are bitter, but the fruits are sweet. When asked what grows old quickly, he replied, "Gratitude." When asked what hope is, he said, "A waking dream." When Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic, known for his public stunts intended to humble famous philosophers.</note> offered him a dried fig, Aristotle realized that if he did not take it, Diogenes had prepared a witty jest <term>chreia: a brief, useful anecdote or sharp saying</term> to use against him; so he took it and said, "Diogenes, you have lost both your joke and your fig." On another occasion when Diogenes offered him one, Aristotle took it and held it up high (as children do), and saying, "Great is Diogenes!" he gave it back to him. 

He said three things were necessary for education: nature, learning, and practice. Hearing that he was being slandered by someone, he said, "Let him even scourge me, provided it is in my absence!" He used to say that beauty was more persuasive than any letter of introduction. Others say it was Diogenes who defined beauty this way; while they claim Aristotle called it "a gift for the plain-featured" <note>original: "δῶρον ἀμορφίας" — meaning beauty is a gift that compensates for other lack of form or status.</note>; Socrates called it "a short-lived tyranny"; Plato called it "a privilege of nature"; Theophrastus "a silent deception"; Theocritus "an ivory mischief"; and Carneades "a kingdom without a bodyguard." 

When asked how much the educated differ from the uneducated, he said, "As much as the living from the dead." He used to say that education is an ornament in prosperity, and a refuge in adversity. He held that teachers who educate children are more to be honored than the parents who merely gave them birth; for the latter provided only life, while the former provided the art of living well. To a man boasting that he came from a great city, he said that was not the point to consider, but rather who is worthy of a great fatherland. When asked what a friend is, he replied, "A single soul dwelling in two bodies." He used to say of mankind...

### ARISTOTLE. Book 5

->ARISTOTLE. Book 5<-

He divided philosophy into the **ethical** and the **political**; the latter of which outlines matters concerning the city and matters concerning the household. Within the **theoretical** branch, he included the **physical** and the **logical**. Logic, however, he treated not as a standalone part of the whole, but as a precisely crafted tool <term>organon: literally 'instrument'; the name traditionally given to Aristotle's logical treatises because logic was seen as the tool used by all other sciences</term>. For this logical branch, he established two distinct goals: the **plausible** and the **true**.

He employed two powers for each of these goals: **dialectic** and **rhetoric** for the plausible, and **analytics** and **philosophy** for the true. He left nothing overlooked, addressing the means for **discovery**, for **judgment**, and for **application**.

For discovery, he provided a wealth of propositions through his *Topics* and *Methodics*, from which one can draw plausible arguments for problems. For judgment, he provided the *Prior* and *Posterior Analytics*. Through the *Prior Analytics*, the premises are judged; through the *Posterior Analytics*, the resulting conclusion is examined. For application, he provided his works on debate, on the art of questioning, on eristics <note>original: "eristika" — a type of argumentative dialogue focused on winning the debate rather than finding truth</note>, on sophistical refutations, on syllogisms, and similar subjects.

As for the **criterion of truth**, he declared that **sensation** is the judge for those activities involving mental impressions <note>original: "phantasia" — the process by which a sensory object is presented to the mind</note>. However, for ethical matters—those concerning the city, the household, and the laws—he declared **mind** <note>original: "noun" — intellect or intuitive reason</note> to be the criterion.

He established one single end <note>original: "telos" — the ultimate goal or purpose of human life</note>: the **use of virtue in a complete life**. He also stated that **happiness** <note>original: "eudaimonia" — often translated as 'flourishing' or 'living well'</note> is a fulfillment derived from three kinds of goods:
1.  **Goods of the soul**, which he calls "first" in terms of their power.
2.  **Goods of the body**, such as health, strength, beauty, and similar qualities.
3.  **External goods**, such as wealth, noble birth, reputation, and the like.

He maintained that **virtue** is not self-sufficient for happiness, for it also requires the goods of the body and external goods; thus, the wise man will be unhappy if he is in pain, in poverty, or in similar circumstances. However, he held that **vice** *is* self-sufficient for misery, even if...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

[Happiness is complete when] external goods and bodily goods are also present. He stated that the **virtues** <term>aretai: excellence or moral virtues</term> do not necessarily follow from one another. For it is possible for someone who is **prudent** <term>phronimos: a person possessing practical wisdom</term>, and equally just, to be unrestrained and lacking in self-control. 

He also said that the **wise man** <term>sophos: the idealized philosophical sage</term> is not **without passion** <term>apathe: the state of being 'apathetic' or free from all emotion, a goal for Stoics but not Aristotelians</term>, but rather **moderate in passion** <term>metriopathe: the state of 'metriopatheia,' or having balanced, appropriate emotions</term>. He defined **friendship** <term>philia: a broad term covering everything from family bonds to business partnerships and deep affection</term> as a reciprocal equality of goodwill. One type of friendship is based on kinship, another on erotic love, and another on hospitality toward guests. He held that love is not merely for physical union, but also for **philosophy**. Furthermore, the wise man will fall in love, will participate in politics, will marry, and will even live at the court of a king.

Of the three types of lives—the **contemplative**, the **practical**, and the **pleasure-seeking** <term>theoretikos, praktikos, and hedonikos</term>—he gave preference to the contemplative. He also considered the **general education** <term>enkyklia mathemata: literally 'circular studies,' the precursor to the liberal arts</term> to be useful for the attainment of virtue. 

In the realm of physics, he was the most concerned with finding causes, so much so that he provided the causes even for the smallest things. For this reason, he composed many books of **physical memoirs** <term>physikon apomnematon: records or commentaries on natural phenomena</term>. He declared God to be incorporeal, just as Plato did. God's **providence** <term>pronoia: divine foresight or care</term> extends as far as the heavenly bodies, and he himself is unmoved; however, earthly affairs are governed by their sympathy <note>original: "sympatheian" — here meaning a natural resonance or connection between the celestial and terrestrial realms</note> with these heavenly bodies. He taught that besides the four **elements** <term>stoicheia: earth, air, fire, and water</term> there is a fifth element, out of which the ethereal bodies are composed. Its motion is different from the others because it moves in a circle. 

He also defined the **soul** <term>psyche: the animating principle of a living thing</term> as incorporeal, being the first **entelechy** <term>entelecheia: the state of completion or actualization of a potential</term>. For the soul is the entelechy of a natural, organic body that has the potential for life. According to him, this entelechy is twofold. He defines entelechy as having an incorporeal form. One type exists in potentiality, like the figure of Hermes in the wax, having the fitness to receive the stamped features, or the statue within the bronze. But the entelechy is said to be "according to habit" <note>original: "kath' hexin" — meaning a settled state or realized capacity</note> when it is the completed Hermes or the finished statue. 

Since some bodies are man-made (produced by art, such as a tower or a ship) and others are produced by nature (such as plants and animals), he called the body "organic," meaning it is constructed for a specific purpose—just as sight is for seeing and hearing is for

# ARISTOTLE. Book 5

...to hear. He defines the soul as the first actuality of a physical body **potentially possessing life** <note>original: "δυνάμει δὲ ζωὴν ἔχοντος" (dynamei de zoen echontos). This refers to Aristotle’s famous definition of the soul in his treatise "On the Soul" (De Anima).</note>, where the potential exists within the body itself, either potentially or in actuality. By **actuality** <term>energeia: the state of being in active operation or "at work"</term>, he means in the same sense that a person who is awake is said to possess a soul; by **disposition** <term>hexis: a stable state or habit</term>, he means as a sleeper does. To ensure that this latter case was included, he added the word "potentially."

He also made many other pronouncements on many subjects, which would be a long task to list. In general, he was the most industrious and inventive of men, as is clear from the catalog of his writings provided earlier, which number close to four hundred—at least those that are undisputed. For many other works are also attributed to him, as well as spoken sayings and clever remarks captured from his unwritten voice.

There have been eight men named Aristotle:
1. First, the man himself.
2. Second, the statesman at Athens, whose elegant legal speeches are still in circulation.
3. Third, a man who wrote a scholarly study on the *Iliad*.
4. Fourth, a Sicilian rhetorician, who wrote a reply to Isocrates’ *Panegyric*.
5. Fifth, the man nicknamed "The Myth," a companion of Aeschines the Socratic.
6. Sixth, a man of Cyrene, who wrote on the art of poetry.
7. Seventh, a trainer of athletes, mentioned by Aristoxenus in his *Life of Plato*.
8. Eighth, an obscure grammarian, whose treatise *On Pleonasm* is still in circulation.

The **Stagirite** <note>Aristotle was born in Stagira, hence this common epithet.</note> had many disciples, but the most distinguished was **Theophrastus**, whom we must now discuss.

## THEOPHRASTUS.

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'Theta' (Θ) containing foliate motifs within a circular frame.</image-desc>
Theophrastus of Eresus was the son of Melaitas, a **fuller** <note>A fuller was a worker who cleaned, shrunk, and thickened cloth.</note>, as Athenodorus says in the eighth book of his *Walks* <note>original: "Peripatoi," likely referring to a work about the Peripatetic school of philosophers.</note>. He first studied under Leucippus, his fellow countryman, in his home city; then, after hearing Plato, he moved to study with Aristotle. When Aristotle withdrew to Chalcis, Theophrastus himself took over the leadership of the school in the hundred and fourteenth **Olympiad** <note>Approximately 322–321 BCE. The Greeks measured time in four-year cycles based on the Olympic Games.</note>. A slave of his named Pompylus is also recorded as having been a philosopher.

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
## Page 178

...as Myronianus of Amastris says in the first book of his *Historical Chapters on Similarities*. **Theophrastus** was a man of the greatest intelligence and was most industrious. As Pamphila says in the thirty-second book of her *Commentaries*, he was the teacher of **Menander** the comic poet. He was also a man of a beneficent nature and a lover of learning <note>original: "φιλόλογος" (philologos). This term implies someone who loves literature, reason, and scholarly pursuits.</note>. For instance, **Cassander** <note>King of Macedonia (r. 305–297 BCE) and a former student of Aristotle.</note> held him in high regard, and **Ptolemy** sent for him.

He was held in such high esteem by the Athenians that when **Agnonides** dared to indict him for **impiety** <term>asebeia: a legal charge of "lack of reverence" for the gods of the city, the same charge brought against Socrates</term>, Agnonides himself narrowly escaped being fined. As many as two thousand students would attend his lectures. Among other matters, he discusses the nature of the law courts in a letter to **Phanias** the Peripatetic, saying:

->“It is not only difficult to find a public festival, but even a council such as one would wish for. Public readings lead to improvements, but our advanced age no longer permits us to postpone and neglect everything.”<-

In this letter, he used the term "scholarly" <note>original: "σχολαστικὸν" (scholastikon). In this context, it refers to the leisure required for study or a person dedicated to the schools.</note>. Despite his great reputation, he—along with all the other philosophers—was forced to go abroad for a short time when **Sophocles**, the son of Amphiclides, introduced a law decreeing that no philosopher should lead a school unless it was approved by the Council and the People; the penalty for doing otherwise was death.

However, the philosophers returned the following year after **Philion** indicted Sophocles for passing an illegal law. On that occasion, the Athenians declared the law invalid, fined Sophocles five talents, and voted for the return of the philosophers, so that Theophrastus might also return and continue in his previous position.

His original name was **Tyrtamus**, but **Aristotle** renamed him **Theophrastus** <note>Meaning "Divine Speaker."</note> because of his divinely inspired style of expression. **Aristippus**, in the fourth book of his work *On Ancient Luxury*, claims that Aristotle was romantically devoted to Theophrastus's son, **Nicomachus**, even though Aristotle was his teacher. It is said that Aristotle spoke of Theophrastus and **Callisthenes** in the same way that people say **Plato** (as mentioned previously) spoke of **Xenocrates** and Aristotle himself.

...describing their characters; for he said that while **Theophrastus**, because of his excessive sharpness of mind, could explain everything he conceived, the other <note>Aristotle was famously comparing Theophrastus to his fellow student, Callisthenes.</note> was slow by nature. Thus, he said the one needed a bridle, while the other needed a spur.

It is said that he also acquired a garden of his own after **Aristotle's** death, with the help of **Demetrius of Phalerum** <note>A student of Theophrastus who became the ruler of Athens (317–307 BCE) and later helped found the Library of Alexandria.</note>, who was an acquaintance of his. The following useful sayings of his are reported: He said that one should trust an unbridled horse sooner than a disorganized speech. To a man who remained silent throughout an entire banquet, he said: "If you are ignorant, you are acting wisely; but if you are educated, you are acting foolishly." He also used to say constantly that "time is a costly expenditure." 

He died at a great age, having lived eighty-five years, shortly after he had relaxed from his labors. We have written these verses for him:

> Not in vain, then, was this word spoken by some mortal,
> That the bow of wisdom breaks when it is unstrung.
> For indeed, while **Theophrastus** labored, he was sound of limb;
> But once he relaxed, he died with withered frame. <note>original: "πυρομελής" (pyromeles), likely a corruption or rare term implying limbs wasted by age or "fire-limbed" in a metaphorical sense of being consumed.</note>

They say that when he was asked by his students if he had any final instructions, he replied: "I have no instructions, except that life, for the sake of reputation, makes a great boast of many pleasures. For just as we begin to live, we die. Therefore, nothing is more unprofitable than the **love of glory** <term>philodoxia: the pursuit of fame or public opinion rather than truth</term>. But may you be happy; either give up the pursuit of learning (for the labor is great) or stand by it nobly (for the glory is great). The vanity of life is greater than its profit. But for me, it is no longer possible to decide what must be done; you must consider what you should do." Having said this, it is said he breathed his last.

The story goes that the **Athenians** escorted him to his grave on foot, the whole city coming together to honor the man. **Favorinus** <note>A philosopher and historian of the 2nd century CE.</note> says that in his old age he was carried about in a litter. He says **Hermippus** reports this, citing **Arcesilaus of Pitane** <note>Founder of the Second or Middle Academy.</note> in the remarks he made to **Lacydes of Cyrene**. Theophrastus himself left behind a very great number of books, which...

Such, then, are the books of this man. I have also found his will, which follows this form:

"All shall be well. But should anything happen, I make these dispositions. Everything I have at home I give to Melantes and Pancreon, the sons of Leon. Regarding the property contributed by Hipparchus, I wish the following to be done: First, the matters regarding the Museum <note>The "shrine of the Muses," which served as the physical heart of the Peripatetic school.</note> and the Goddesses [the Muses] are to be completed, and if anything else can be added to them for their further beautification. Then, the image of Aristotle is to be placed in the shrine, along with the other offerings that were previously in the shrine. Then, the small portico <note>original: "στωΐδιον" (stoïdion).</note> near the Museum is to be rebuilt no worse than it was before. Also, the maps <note>original: "πίνακας" (pinakas), literally "tablets" or "panels." Theophrastus is referring to geographical charts or "circuits of the earth."</note> on which the circuits of the earth are drawn are to be set up in the lower portico. The altar is also to be repaired so that it possesses perfection and decency. I also wish that the image of Nicomachus <note>Aristotle’s son, for whom the "Nicomachean Ethics" was likely named.</note> be completed to the same size. Praxiteles <note>The famous Athenian sculptor; this suggests the high status of the school's patrons.</note> has the model for the casting; let the remaining expense be paid from this estate. It is to be placed wherever those in charge of the other matters written in the will see fit. And let the matters concerning the shrine and the offerings be handled in this manner. The estate belonging to us in Stagira <note>The hometown of Aristotle.</note> I give to Callinus. And all the books, I give to Neleus." <note>Neleus of Scepsis, whose family famously hid these books in a cellar for generations to protect them from book-collecting kings.</note>

The garden, and the walkway <note>original: "περίπατον" (peripaton); the covered walking-place from which the "Peripatetic" school of philosophy derived its name.</note>, and all the houses adjacent to the garden, I give to those of my listed friends who wish to spend their time in study and practice philosophy together there—since it is not possible for all men to be in permanent residence—provided that they neither alienate the property nor claim it as their own private possession. Rather, they shall hold it in common as a sacred space, living in a familiar and friendly manner with one another as is fitting and right. 

Let the members of this community be: **Hipparchus**, **Neleus**, **Strato**, **Callinus**, **Demotimus**, **Demaratus**, **Callisthenes**, **Melantas**, **Pancreon**, and **Nicippus**. 

**Aristotle**, the son of Midias and Pythias, shall also have the right to study philosophy and share in these facilities if he so desires. The elders of the group must take every care for him, so that he may be advanced as far as possible in philosophy. 

As for myself, let me be buried in whatever part of the garden seems most suitable, without any excessive expense regarding the funeral or the monument. 

As has been stated before, after the arrangements for my burial are settled, the shrine, the monument, the garden, and the walkway must all be maintained. **Pompylus**, who lives on the grounds and takes care of everything as he did before, shall continue his supervision. The expenses for this upkeep shall be provided by those who hold these properties. 

Regarding **Pompylus** and **Threpta**, who have long been free <note>original: "ἐλευθέροις" (eleutherois); they were former slaves previously manumitted.</note> and have provided me with great service: I believe they should securely hold whatever I previously gave them, whatever they have acquired for themselves, and the two thousand drachmas I have now instructed **Hipparchus** to give them. I have spoken of this many times with **Melantas** and **Pancreon**, and they have fully agreed with me. I also give to them the slave **Somatale** and the young girl. 

Of my other house-slaves, I hereby grant immediate freedom to **Molon**, **Cimon**, and **Parmeno**. As for **Mania** and **Callias**, they shall be granted their freedom after they have remained working in the garden for four more years, provided they work together and remain blameless in their conduct.

### THEOPHRASTUS. Book 5. 185

As for the household furniture, let the executors give to **Pompylus** <note>Theophrastus’s trusted steward, mentioned on the previous page as a former slave who was granted his freedom.</note> whatever items they deem appropriate; the remainder shall be sold. I give the slave **Carion** to **Demotimus**, and **Donax** to **Neleus**; as for **Eubius**, let him be sold. 

Let **Hipparchus** pay to **Callinus** three thousand <term>drachmae</term> <note>A drachma was a standard silver coin; 3,000 was a significant sum, roughly equivalent to several years' wages for a skilled laborer.</note>. Regarding **Melantas** and **Pancreon**, if I did not see that **Hipparchus** had previously been of service to us and is now in a state of financial ruin <note>original: "νεναυαγηκότα" (nenauagēkota); literally "shipwrecked," a common metaphor for total financial or personal disaster.</note> in his private affairs, I would have ordered that he manage the estate alongside **Melantas** and **Pancreon**. However, since I see it is not easy for them to manage these affairs together, and I believe it is more advantageous for them to receive a fixed sum from **Hipparchus**, let **Hipparchus** give to **Melantas** and to **Pancreon** one <term>talent</term> <note>A talent was the largest unit of currency, equal to 6,000 drachmae.</note> each. 

**Hipparchus** shall also provide the executors with funds for the expenses specified in this will, as the various occasions for spending arise. Once these matters have been settled, **Hipparchus** shall be released from all contracts and obligations made toward me. Furthermore, if **Hipparchus** has conducted any business in **Chalcis** <note>A city on the island of Euboea, where both Aristotle and Theophrastus had property interests.</note> in my name, that property shall belong to **Hipparchus**.

The executors of the provisions written in this will shall be: **Hipparchus**, **Neleus**, **Strato**, **Callinus**, **Demotimus**, **Callisthenes**, and **Ctesarchus**.

The copies of this will, sealed with the signet ring of **Theophrastus**, are deposited as follows:
*   One copy is held by **Hegesias**, son of **Hipparchus**; the witnesses are **Callippus of Pelana**, **Philomelus of Euonymus**, **Lysander of Hyba**, and **Philion of Alopece**. 
*   A second copy is held by **Olympiodorus**; the witnesses are the same. 
*   A third copy was taken by **Adeimantus**, and delivered by his son **Androsthenes**; the witnesses are **Aeimnestus** son of **Cleobulus**, **Lysistratus** son of **Phidon of Thasos**, **Strato** son of **Arcesilaus of Lampsacus**, **Thesippus** son of **Thesippus of Ceramicus**, and **Dioscourides** son of **Dionysius of Epicephisia**.

Such are the contents of his will. There are those who say that **Erasistratus** the physician was also a pupil of his; and this is quite probable.
