DIOGENES LAERTIUS. Book 5. 186

# STRATO.

**Strato**, the son of Arcesilaus and a native of **Lampsacus** <note>A Greek city in Asia Minor on the eastern side of the Hellespont.</note>, succeeded to the school of Theophrastus; he is the same man mentioned in the previously recorded will. He was a man of the highest reputation, and was nicknamed **"the Physicist"** <note>original: "φυσικὸς" (physikos); this title was given to him because he focused his philosophy on the study of nature and the physical world more than on ethics or logic.</note> because he devoted himself to this branch of study with greater diligence than anyone else. He also served as the tutor to **Ptolemy Philadelphus** <note>The second Pharaoh of the Ptolemaic Kingdom of Egypt, famous for his patronage of the Great Library of Alexandria.</note> and it is said that he received eighty talents from him. 

According to **Apollodorus** <note>A famous Athenian historian and grammarian who wrote a chronological history of philosophers.</note> in his *Chronicles*, Strato began to lead the school in the 123rd Olympiad <note>Approximately 288–285 BCE.</note>, and he presided over the school for eighteen years.

The following books are attributed to him: 
*On Kingship* (three books); *On Justice* (three books); *On the Good* (three books); *On the Gods* (three books); *On First Principles* (three books); *On Lives*; *On Happiness*; *On Philosophy*; *On Courage*; *On the Void*; *On the Heavens*; *On the Spirit* <note>original: "πνεύματος" (pneumatos); in this context, it refers to the physical "breath" or vital force believed to move through the body.</note>; *On Human Nature*; *On the Generation of Animals*; *On Mixture*; *On Sleep*; *On Dreams*; *On Sight*; *On Sensation*; *On Pleasure*; *On Colors*; *On Diseases*; *On Crises*; *On Powers*; *On Mining Machinery*; *On Hunger and Vertigo*; *On Lightness and Heaviness*; *On Inspiration*; *On Time*; *On Nutrition and Growth*; *On Animals whose existence is doubted*; *On Animals in Mythology*; *On Causes*; *Solutions to Problems*; *Introductions to Commonplaces*; *On Accidents*; *On the Definition*; *On the More and the Less*; *On Injustice*; *On the Prior Genus*; *On the Specific Characteristic*; *On the Future*; and two books of *Refutations of Discoveries*. 

The authenticity of his *Commentaries* is doubted. His *Letters* begin with the greeting: "**Strato** to **Arsinoe** <note>Arsinoe II, the sister and wife of Ptolemy Philadelphus.</note>, prosperity." It is said that he became so thin that he passed away without even feeling it. My own epigram regarding him is as follows:

->A man thin of body he was, unless he had made use of the oracles,<-

STRATO. Book 5. 187

->I say this is that Strato of Lampsacus;<-
->Whom Lampsacus once produced; always struggling with diseases,<-
->He died unobserved, nor did he perceive death.<-

There have been eight men named Strato: the first was a pupil of **Isocrates** <note>A famous Athenian orator and teacher of rhetoric.</note>; the second was this man himself; the third was a physician, a disciple of **Erasistratus** <note>A famous ancient Greek physician often called the father of physiology.</note>, though some say he was called **Trophimus**; the fourth was a historian who wrote about the deeds of **Philip and Perseus** <note>The last kings of Macedon who fought against the expanding Roman Republic.</note> during their wars with the Romans; the sixth <note>The fifth Strato is omitted in this transcription.</note> was a poet of epigrams; the seventh was another man of ancient times, as **Aristotle** mentions; and the eighth was a **Peripatetic** <note>A member of the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle.</note> who lived in Alexandria.

Of this "Physicist" then, his will <note>original: "διαθῆκαι" (diathekai)</note> is also circulated, having this form: "I make these arrangements in case anything should happen to me <note>A common legal euphemism for death.</note>. All my property at home I leave to **Lampyeion** and **Arcesilaus**. Regarding the money belonging to me in Athens, first, let the **executors** <note>original: "ἐπιμεληταὶ" (epimeletai); these were the men appointed to carry out the terms of a will.</note> take care of the funeral arrangements and whatever is customary after the funeral, doing nothing excessive or stingy. Let these be the executors of the terms of the will: **Olympicous, Aristides, Mnesigenes, Hippocrates, Epicrates, Gorgylus, Diocles, Lyco,** and **Athanes**.

I leave the **school** <note>original: "διατριβήν" (diatriben); literally a place of study or a lecture-hall, here referring to the leadership and physical premises of the Peripatetic school.</note> to **Lyco**, since of the others, some are older and others are too busy. It would be well if the rest of them would also assist him in maintaining it. I also leave to him all the books—except those we have written ourselves—and all the furniture in the dining-hall, the coverlets, and the drinking cups. 

Let the executors give to **Epicrates** five hundred drachmae <note>A standard unit of silver currency in ancient Greece.</note> and one of the servants <note>original: "παίδων" (paidon); literally 'boys' or 'children,' but used here to refer to domestic slaves.</note>, whomever they see fit. As for Arcesilaus, first let Lampyeion and Arcesilaus cancel the contracts which **Daippus** made on behalf of **Iraeus**; and let him owe nothing to Lampyeion or Lampyeion's heirs, but let him be released from every legal bond. Let the executors also give him five hundred drachmae of silver and one of the servants, whomever he selects..."

Strato himself was a man (as has been shown above) worthy of great approval, having excelled in every branch of learning, and most especially in what is called **Physics** <note>In the ancient world, "Physics" or "Natural Philosophy" encompassed the study of nature, the soul, and the physical universe.</note>, a branch which is both older and more serious.

## L Y C O.

**Lyco**, son of **Astyanax**, a native of **Troas** <note>The region in northwest Asia Minor surrounding the ancient city of Troy.</note>, succeeded him. He was a man of eloquent speech and was extremely dedicated to the education of children. For he used to say that modesty and ambition should be yoked to children, just as the spur and the bit are to horses. His expressive and polished style of interpretation is also evident here; for he speaks in this manner regarding a poor maiden: "For a daughter is a heavy burden to a father when, for lack of a **dowry** <note>In ancient Greek society, a dowry was essential for a woman to secure a respectable marriage; without one, she might remain unmarried, becoming a financial burden on her family.</note>, she passes the prime of her life." Because of this, they say that **Antigonus** <note>Likely Antigonus II Gonatas, King of Macedonia, a patron of philosophers.</note> said of him...

->### LYCO. Book 5.<-

...it was not possible to transfer his fragrance and grace to another, any more than one can do so with an apple; rather, in the man himself, as if upon a tree, each of his qualities had to be observed. It was said of him that while he was incredibly sweet in his speaking—so much so that some people even added a "G" to his name, calling him **Glyco** <note>original: "Γλύκων" (Glykon). A pun on the Greek word "glykys," meaning "sweet."</note>—he was quite unlike himself when it came to writing. Certainly, regarding those who regretted not learning when they had the chance and who let the opportunity pass, he would say that when they tried to speak elegantly, they were merely exposing their own failures; he accused them of clumsily imitating a "repentance for laziness" at the very start, which was a fault that could no longer be corrected.

He also used to say that those who intended to deliberate correctly often failed in their reasoning because they were examining **divine nature** <note>original: "θείαν φύσιν" (theian physin)</note> with a crooked rule, as if looking at a face in storm-tossed water or a distorted mirror. He remarked that while many would go to win a crown in the marketplace, only a few, or even none, would go to the **Olympic Games** to compete for one. 

He frequently gave advice to the **Athenians** and was of great service to them in matters of the highest importance. He was also exceptionally neat in his dress, wearing garments of unsurpassed softness, as **Olympis** reports. Yet, he was also highly skilled in gymnastics and possessed a healthy physique, displaying the full bearing of an athlete, with the flattened ears and the scarred skin of a wrestler, according to **Antigonus of Carystus**. Because of this, it is said that he wrestled in the **Ilieia** <note>Games held in Ilium (Troy) in honor of Athena.</note> in his homeland and was a skilled ball player. 

Furthermore, he was a friend like no other to **Eumenes** and **Attalus** <note>Eumenes I and Attalus I, rulers of the Kingdom of Pergamum, who were major patrons of philosophy.</note>, who provided him with most of his resources. **Antiochus** <note>Likely Antiochus II or III of the Seleucid Empire.</note> also tried to win his favor, but did not succeed. He was such a bitter enemy of **Hieronymus the Peripatetic** that he made it a point never to meet him, except on the annual anniversary day which we discussed in the *Life of Arcesilaus*. 

He led the school for forty-four years, after **Strato** left it to him in his will during the 127th **Olympiad** <note>Approximately 272–268 BCE.</note>. Moreover, he was a student of **Panthoides** the **dialectician** <note>A specialist in logic and formal argument.</note>. He died at the age of seventy-four, having been worn down by a bout of **gout** <note>original: "ποδαγρικῇ" (podagrike), a common affliction in antiquity often associated with wealthy lifestyles.</note>.

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...and there is also an epigram of our own written for him:

> No, by Zeus, we shall not pass over Lyco, who died
> Of the gout. This is what I wonder at most:
> That long road to Hades, which he previously walked
> Upon others' feet, he ran in a single night.
> <note>original: "ποδαγρὴς" (podagres). Lyco suffered from gout, a painful swelling of the joints that often made walking impossible without assistance. The poet jokes that while Lyco needed others to carry him in life, he reached the underworld remarkably fast.</note>

There have been other men named Lyco: first, a follower of **Pythagoras**; second, this man himself; third, an epic poet; fourth, a poet of epigrams. We have also come across the will of this philosopher, which is as follows:

I make these dispositions regarding my affairs, in case I am unable to survive this current illness. All the property in my house I give to my brothers, **Astyanax** and **Lyco**. I believe it is right that from these assets there should be paid back whatever I have borrowed from anyone in **Athens**, whether I still have the items or have used them; likewise, whatever is spent on my funeral and other customary rites. 

The property I own in the city and in **Aegina** <note>An island in the Saronic Gulf near Athens.</note> I give to Lyco, because he bears our name and has spent a great deal of time living with me, behaving quite rightly, as was appropriate for one who held the place of a son. I leave the **walkway** <term>Peripatos</term> <note>The "Peripatos" refers to the shaded walkway and school grounds where the philosophers met. Lyco is leaving the physical infrastructure of the school to his community of students.</note> to those of my acquaintances who wish to use it: **Bulon, Callinus, Ariston, Amphion, Lyco, Python, Aristomachus, Heracleius, Lycomedes**, and **Lyco my nephew**. They should place in charge of it whichever person they believe will persevere in the work and will be best able to keep the school together. 

The rest of my acquaintances should also assist in the upkeep, both for my sake and for the sake of the place. As for the matters of my funeral and cremation, let Bulon and Callinus take care of them along with my close friends, ensuring that it is neither stingy nor extravagant. After my passing, let Lyco distribute the shares I own in Aegina to the young men for the **provision of oil** <note>original: "ἐλαιοχρηστίαν" (elaiochrestian). In ancient Greece, providing oil for athletes to rub on their bodies in the gymnasium was a prestigious form of public charity.</note>, so that through this useful gift, a fitting memory of myself and of the one who honored me may be preserved. Let him also erect a statue of me. As for the location of the statue, let him see that it is appropriate...

### LYCO. Book 5

...and let **Diophantus** and **Heracleides**, the son of **Demetrius**, assist in these matters. Regarding my property in the city, let **Lyco** <note>This refers to Lyco’s nephew, mentioned on the previous page, who shares his name.</note> be present and pay back to all those things I received after his journey abroad. Let **Bulon** and **Callinus** oversee this, as well as the expenses for my funeral and the other customary rites. Let him take these funds from the household assets I have left to both of them in common. Let him also honor the physicians **Pasithemis** and **Midias**, for they are worthy—both because of their care for me and because of their skill—of even greater honor.

I give to the child of **Callinus** a pair of **Thericlean cups** <term>Thericleia</term> <note>original: "θηρικλείων" (therikleion). These were a famous style of expensive, finely crafted Athenian drinking vessels, traditionally named after the potter Thericles.</note>, and to his wife I give a pair of pomegranate-patterned cups, a smooth rug, a shaggy rug, a coverlet, and two pillows—the best of those remaining—so that, in proportion to her kindness toward us, we may show that we are not unmindful of these things.

Regarding those who have served me, I make the following arrangements: To **Demetrius**, who has long been a free man, I remit the price of his ransom <note>Under Greek law, a slave could be freed but still owe a "ransom" or debt to their former master; Lyco is cancelling this debt.</note>, and I give him five **minae** <term>mna</term> <note>A mina was a unit of currency worth 100 drachmae; five minae was a substantial sum, roughly equivalent to several hundred days' wages for a laborer.</note>, as well as a cloak and a tunic, so that after having labored much with me, he may [not] have an unseemly life <note>The Greek text here reads "βίον ἀσχήμονα ἔχῃ" (that he may have an unseemly life), but this is likely a scribal error for "μὴ ἀσχήμονα" (that he may NOT have an unseemly life), given the generous context.</note>. To **Criton of Carthage**, I also remit the ransom price and give him four minae.

I also set **Micrus** free; and let **Lyco** support and educate him for six years from this time. I also set **Chares** free; let **Lyco** support him, and I give him two minae and those of my books that have already been published. However, the unpublished books are to be given to **Callinus**, so that he may edit and publish them with care. 

I give to **Syrus**, who is already free, four minae and also **Menodora** <note>It was common in antiquity to bequeath the service or ownership of one person to another within a will.</note>; and if he owes me anything, I remit the debt. I give to **Hilara** five minae, a shaggy rug, two pillows, a coverlet, and whichever bed she chooses. I also set free the mother of **Micrus**, as well as **Noemon**, **Dion**, **Theon**, **Euphranor**, and **Hermeion**. **Agathon** is to be set free after he has remained in service for two more years. I also set free the litter-bearers **Ophelion** and **Poseidonius**...

Thus, just as he conducted all his affairs with wisdom—both in matters of education and in all his discourse—so too did he manage the arrangements of his will in a highly organized and careful manner, so that in this respect also he is worthy of emulation.

## DEMETRIUS.

**Demetrius**, the son of **Phanostratus**, a man of **Phalerum** <note>original: "Φαληρεύς" (Phalereus). A resident of Phalerum, a coastal district of Athens. This Demetrius was a student of Aristotle's successor, Theophrastus.</note>; he was a student of **Theophrastus**. While addressing the Athenian people, he led the city for ten years and was honored with three hundred and sixty bronze statues. Most of these depicted him on horseback, in chariots, and driving pairs of horses, and they were all completed in fewer than three hundred days. Such was the great zeal shown for him.

**Demetrius of Magnesia** says in his *Men of the Same Name* that he began his political career at the time when **Harpalus** <note>Alexander the Great's treasurer who fled to Athens after embezzling a massive fortune; his arrival caused a major political scandal.</note> arrived in **Athens** having fled from **Alexander**. He performed many excellent services for his homeland; for he increased the city's revenues and its infrastructure, although he was not of noble birth. For he was of the house of **Conon** <note>A famous Athenian general from the late 5th century BCE; the author is likely defending Demetrius's pedigree against critics.</note>, as **Favorinus** states in the first book of his *Memorabilia*. However, he also lived with the low-born **Lamia**, his mistress, as the same author says in his first book. He also records in his second book that he suffered at the hands of **Cleon**. **Didymus** in his *Table Talk* says he was nicknamed "Fair-Eyelids" and "Radiant" <note>original: "χαριτοβλέφαρον" (charitoblepharon) and "λάμπετω" (lampeto). These nicknames likely referred to his striking physical appearance or his use of cosmetics.</note>...

->### DEMETRIUS. Book 5<-

...says he was born from a certain courtesan. It is said that after he lost his sight in **Alexandria**, he recovered it again through the grace of **Sarapis** <note>original: "Σαράπιδος". A Graeco-Egyptian deity whose cult was promoted by the Ptolemaic kings; he was associated with healing and the afterlife.</note>; for this reason, he composed the paeans <note>hymns of praise or thanksgiving</note> that are sung to this day. However, although he was exceedingly illustrious among the **Athenians**, he was eventually overshadowed by the envy that runs through all things. For, after being plotted against by certain enemies on a capital charge, he was condemned to death in his absence.

His enemies did not get hold of his physical body, but they spat their venom onto the bronze instead, pulling down his statues; some they sold, some they sank in the sea, and others they cut up into chamber pots <note>A particularly insulting way to destroy a monument, turning a symbol of honor into a vessel for waste.</note>; for this also is told. Only one statue is preserved on the **Acropolis**. **Favorinus** says in his *Universal History* that the **Athenians** did this at the command of **King Demetrius** <note>Demetrius Poliorcetes, the "Besieger," who ousted Demetrius of Phalerum from power in 307 BCE.</note>. They even inscribed the term "lawlessness" over his period of rule, according to **Favorinus**. 

**Hermippus** says that after the death of **Cassander**, fearing **Antigonus**, he went to **Ptolemy Soter** <note>Ptolemy I, the founder of the Ptolemaic Kingdom in Egypt.</note>; and while spending a considerable time there, he advised **Ptolemy**, among other things, to settle the kingdom on the children of **Eurydice** <note>Ptolemy's first wife.</note>. But **Ptolemy** did not listen, and instead gave the diadem to his son by **Berenice** <note>Ptolemy II Philadelphus.</note>. After the elder **Ptolemy's** death, **Demetrius** was ordered by the new king to be kept under guard in the countryside until a final decision was made about him. 

There he lived in low spirits; and somehow, while he was sleeping, he was bitten on the hand by an asp <note>original: "ἀσπίδος". A venomous snake, famously used as a method of suicide or execution in Egypt.</note> and departed this life. He is buried in the **Busirite** district, near **Diospolis**. And we ourselves have written an inscription for him:

> Among us, an asp killed the wise **Demetrius**,
> Possessing much unyielding venom,
> Not shining light from its eyes, but the darkness of **Hades**.

**Heraclides**, in his *Abridgement of the Successions by Sotion*, says that **Ptolemy** [Soter] wanted to yield the kingdom to **Philadelphus**, but **Demetrius** tried to dissuade him, saying, "If you give it to another..."

# HERACLIDES

**Heraclides**, the son of **Euthyphron**, was a native of **Heraclea** in **Pontus** and a man of great wealth. Upon arriving in **Athens**, he first associated himself with **Speusippus**; <note>Speusippus was the nephew of Plato and his successor as head of the Academy.</note> however, he also attended the lectures of the **Pythagoreans** and was an admirer of **Plato's** teachings. Later, he became a student of **Aristotle**, as **Sotion** records in his *Successions of Philosophers*. He was known to wear soft, delicate clothing and was of such massive physical stature that the **Athenians** did not call him "the man from **Pontus**" <note>original: "Ποντικόν" (Pontikon)</note> but rather "the Pompous" <note>original: "Πομπικὸν" (Pompikon). This is a pun on his place of origin; "Pompikos" suggests one who belongs in a solemn procession or someone who is grand and stately.</note> because of his girth. He walked with a gentle and dignified gait. 

He is credited with writings that are considered most beautiful and excellent. These are written in the form of **Dialogues**, <note>A literary format, made famous by Plato, where philosophical ideas are debated by characters.</note> of which the following are on **Ethics**: *On Justice* (three books); one book *On Temperance*; *On Impiety* (one book); *On Courage* (one book); generally *On Virtue* (one book); *On Happiness* (one book); *On Government* (one book); *On Laws* (one book), and other works related to these; *On Names* (one book); *Covenants* (one book); *The Involuntary Lover*; and *Cleinias* (one book). 

His works on **Physics** <note>In the ancient sense, "Physics" referred to the study of the natural world and the soul.</note> include: *On the Intellect*; *On the Soul*; a separate work *On the Soul*; *On Nature*; *On Images*; *Against Democritus*; *On Celestial Phenomena* (one book); *On Things in Hades*; *On Lives* (two books); *Causes of Diseases* (one book); *On the Good* (one book); *Against the Doctrines of Zeno* (one book); and *Against the Doctrines of Metron* (one book).

His works on **Grammar** include: *On the Age of Homer and Hesiod* (two books); and *On Archilochus and Homer* (two books). He also wrote on **Music**...

### HERACLIDES. Book 5

6. *On those in **Euripides** and **Sophocles***, three books; *On Music*, two books; *Homeric Solutions*, two books; *Theoretical*, one book; *On the Three Tragic Poets*, one book; *Characters*, one book; *On Poetics and the Poets*, one book; *On Conjecture*, one book; *Perspective*, one book; *Explanations of **Heraclitus***, six books; *Explanations against **Democritus***, one book; *Eristic Solutions*, <note>Eristic refers to a type of philosophical argument focused on winning a debate rather than finding truth.</note> two books; *Axioms*, one book; *On Species*, one book; *Solution*, one book; *Instructions*, one book; *To **Dionysius***, one book. 

**Rhetorical works**, eight books. *On the Art of Oratory, or Protagoras*. 

**Historical works**, *On the **Pythagoreans***, and *On Discoveries*. 

Some of these he composed in a comic style, such as the treatises *On Pleasure* and *On Temperance*; others in a tragic style, such as *On those in the Underworld*, *On Impiety*, and *On Power*. He also employed a certain "middle" conversational style <note>original: "μεσότης τις ὁμιλητικὴ" (mesotēs tis homilētikē)</note> featuring dialogues between philosophers, generals, and politicians. Furthermore, there are works by him on geometry and dialectics. In all these, he is clearly versatile and distinct in his expression, possessing a great ability to captivate the soul. <note>original: "ψυχαγωγεῖν" (psychagōgein). This term implies a persuasive power that literally "leads the soul" of the listener.</note>

It is also believed that he liberated his homeland from tyranny by killing the monarch, as **Demetrius of Magnesia** records in his *Men of the Same Name*. **Demetrius** also tells this story about him: that he raised a serpent <note>original: "δράκοντα" (drakonta) - while often translated as "dragon," in this context it refers to a large snake used in religious or theatrical displays.</note> from its youth, and when it was fully grown and he himself was about to die, he commanded one of his trusted friends to hide his body, but to place the serpent upon his funeral bier so that he might appear to have departed to the gods. All of this was carried out. However, while the citizens were escorting the funeral procession of **Heraclides** and offering shouts of praise, the serpent, hearing the commotion, slipped out from the burial shrouds and threw the majority of the crowd into a state of panic. Later, the whole trick was uncovered, and **Heraclides** was seen not as he wished to be thought of, but as he truly was.

And there is an epigram of ours concerning him, which goes like this:

> You wished to leave a legend among men, **Heraclides**,
> That when you died, you became a living serpent for all to see.
> But you were deceived, you clever schemer; for the beast indeed
> Was a serpent, but you—a beast who was not wise—were caught.

<note>original Greek epigram: Ἤθελες ἀνθρώποισι λιπεῖν φάτιν, Ἡρακλείδη... This poem is a satirical jab at the philosopher's vanity, suggesting he was less "wise" than the animal he tried to use.</note>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

**Hippobotus** also provides this account. But **Hermippus** says that when a famine gripped the region, the people of **Heracleia** <note>Heracleia Pontica, the philosopher's birthplace on the Black Sea.</note> asked the **Pythian priestess** at **Delphi** for a solution. **Heraclides** allegedly bribed the sacred envoys and the prophetess herself so that she would declare the following: they would be released from their misfortunes if, while he lived, **Heraclides** (son of Euthyphron) was crowned by them with a golden crown, and after his death, was honored as a hero. <note>In ancient Greece, a "hero" was a person who received religious veneration and sacrifices after death, occupying a status between mortals and gods.</note>

This so-called oracle was brought back, but those who forged it gained nothing from their scheme. For immediately, while being crowned in the theater, **Heraclides** suffered a stroke; at the same time, the envoys were trampled and killed by the crowd. Furthermore, at that very hour, the **Pythian priestess**, as she was descending into the inner shrine and standing there, was bitten by one of the sacred serpents and died instantly. These are the stories told concerning his death.

**Aristoxenus the Musician** says that **Heraclides** also composed tragedies and published them under the name of **Thespis**. <note>Thespis is traditionally considered the first actor and inventor of tragedy.</note> **Chamaeleon** claims that **Heraclides** stole his own research on **Hesiod** and **Homer** to write his own books. Even **Autodorus the Epicurean** censures him, writing in opposition to his works on justice.

There is also the story of **Dionysius the Renegade**—or **Spintharus**, as some say—who wrote a play titled *Parthenopaeus* and attributed it to **Sophocles**. **Heraclides**, believing it to be authentic, used it in one of his own writings as evidence of **Sophocles’** style. When **Dionysius** realized this, he revealed the truth to him. When **Heraclides** denied it and refused to believe he had been fooled, **Dionysius** sent him a letter telling him to look at the acrostic <note>original: "παραστιχίδα" (parastichis). An acrostic is a hidden message where the first letters of each line form a word or sentence.</note>, and it was perfectly arranged.

It contained the name of **Dionysius's** favorite youth. When **Heraclides** still doubted, saying it could have happened by mere chance, **Dionysius** wrote back again, saying that he would also find these lines:

> An old ape is not caught in a trap;
> He is caught indeed, but it takes time to catch him.
> And in addition to these: **Heraclides** is ignorant of letters.

At this, **Heraclides** was thoroughly shamed. 

There have been fourteen men named **Heraclides**: first, this man himself; second, a fellow citizen of his who composed pyrrhic dances and light entertainments; third, a man of **Cyme**, who wrote...

### ANTISTHENES.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>
**ANTISTHENES**, the son of Antisthenes, was an **Athenian**. It was said, however, that he was not a "pure-born" citizen <note>original: "ἰθαγενής" — referring to the legal status of having two Athenian parents.</note>; hence, to a man who was reproaching him on this point, he replied, "Even the Mother of the Gods is Phrygian." For he was thought to have been born of a **Thracian** mother. This was also why, after he had distinguished himself in the battle at **Tanagra**, he gave **Socrates** cause to say that a son born of two Athenians could never have been so noble. And Antisthenes himself, when mocking the Athenians for being proud of being "born from the earth" <note>original: "γηγενεῖς" — the myth of autochthony, where Athenians claimed their ancestors literally sprang from the soil of Attica.</note>, would say they were no more noble than snails or wingless locusts. 

In his early years, he was a student of **Gorgias** the rhetorician <note>Gorgias was a famous Sophist known for his highly ornamental and persuasive style of speech.</note>. From this education, he brought a rhetorical style into his dialogues, especially in his work titled *The Truth* and in his *Exhortations*. **Hermippus** states that Antisthenes originally intended, during the general assembly of the **Isthmian Games**, to deliver a speech both praising and criticizing the Athenians, Thebans, and Spartans; however, he ultimately declined to do so when he saw how many people had arrived from those various cities. 

Later on, he associated himself with **Socrates**, and he benefited so greatly from him that he even advised his own students to become his fellow-pupils under Socrates. Since he lived in the **Piraeus** <note>The port city of Athens, about 4-5 miles from the city center.</note>, he would walk up the forty stadia <note>Approximately 4.6 miles.</note> every day just to hear Socrates speak. It was from Socrates that he acquired his famous quality of endurance <note>original: "τὸ καρτερικόν" — the ability to withstand hardship, which became a core tenet of the Cynic and later Stoic schools.</note>...

### ANTISTHENES. Book 6

Having adopted the <unclear>ethical</unclear> <note>original: "ηθικόν" — ethikon</note> side of philosophy and emulating a state of detachment <note>original: "ἀπαθὲς" — *apathes*, a state of being undisturbed by emotions or external circumstances</note>, he was the first to found the way of the <unclear>C</unclear>ynic <note>Cynicism, from the Greek word *kyon* (dog), emphasized living simply and in accordance with nature.</note>. He established that toil <note>original: "πόνος" — *ponos*, meaning hard work, struggle, or physical labor</note> is a good thing, proving it by the examples of the <unclear>m</unclear>ighty **Hercules** and of **Cyrus**; he drew the former from the **Greeks** and the latter from the <unclear>n</unclear>on-Greeks <note>original: "βαρβάρων" — *barbaroi*, referring to foreigners, specifically the Persians in Cyrus's case.</note>. <unclear>He</unclear>aring once that **Plato** was speaking ill of him, he remarked: "It is the lot of <unclear>ro</unclear>yalty to do good and yet be spoken of poorly." <meta>This page continues the collection of sayings and anecdotes of Antisthenes, the founder of the Cynic school. It follows from the previous page's discussion of his interactions with students and his emphasis on mental discipline over physical tools.</meta>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

He used to say that cities are destroyed when they are no longer able to distinguish the wicked from the virtuous. Once, when he was being praised by wicked men, he remarked, "I am dreadfully afraid that I have done something wrong." He stated that the harmony of brothers living together is stronger than any defensive wall. He said that a person should provide themselves with such travel provisions <note>original: "ἐφόδια" — *ephodia*, literally things for the journey; here referring to internal resources or knowledge</note> as would swim ashore with them even in a shipwreck. 

When he was once reproached for associating with wicked men, he replied: "Physicians also associate with the sick, but they do not catch the fever themselves." He called it absurd that we weed out the tares from the corn and exclude the unfit from service in war, but in the administration of the state we do not reject those who are driven by envy. When asked what he had gained from philosophy, he replied: "The ability to converse with myself." When someone said to him during a drinking party, "Sing to us," he replied, "Then you play the flute for me." To **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes of Sinope, the most famous of the Cynics, who became Antisthenes’ most renowned pupil.</note> who was asking him for a tunic, he directed him to fold his cloak in two <note>Antisthenes is credited with being the first to double his cloak, a practice that became the standard "uniform" of the Cynic philosophers to endure all weather.</note>. 

Asked what subject was most necessary to learn, he replied: "To unlearn what is evil." He used to advise that those who are spoken of ill should endure it more patiently than if they were being pelted with stones. He used to mock **Plato** for being conceited <note>original: "τετυφωμένον" — *tetyphomenon*, a key Cynic term meaning "puffed up with smoke/vanity."</note>. Thus, during a procession, seeing a spirited horse, he said to **Plato**, "It seems to me that you, too, would have made just such a showy horse." He said this because **Plato** was constantly praising horses. And once, visiting **Plato** when he was ill and seeing a basin into which **Plato** had vomited, he remarked: "I see the bile in there, but I do not see the conceit." 

He advised the **Athenians** to pass a vote that donkeys are horses. When they thought this irrational, he said: "And yet, you have men who become generals without having learned anything, simply by a show of hands." To the person who said, "Many people are praising you," he replied, "Why, what evil have I done?" Once, when he turned the torn part of his coarse cloak <note>original: "τρίβωνος" — *tribon*, the simple, rough garment worn by Cynics.</note> so that it was visible, **Socrates** saw it and said, "I see your vanity through the holes in your cloak." When asked by someone (as **Phanias** says in his work *On the Socratics*) what he should do to become a man of character <note>original: "καλὸς κἀγαθὸς" — *kalos kagathos*, the Greek ideal of being "noble and good."</note>, he replied: "If you learn from those who know that the evils you possess are things to be avoided." To someone praising luxury, he said: "May the children of my enemies live in luxury!"

### ANTISTHENES. Book 6

...they might live luxuriously. To a young man posing for a sculptor <gloss>with a posture</gloss>, he said, "Tell me, if the bronze could speak, what would it pride itself on?" When the boy replied, "On its beauty," Antisthenes said, "Are you not ashamed, then, to rejoice in the same qualities as an inanimate object?"

When a young man from Pontus promised to take great care of him if only his ship of salt-fish <note>original: "ταρίχων" — *tarichon*, refers to preserved or dried fish, a staple commodity in the ancient world</note> should arrive, Antisthenes took him and an empty sack to a woman who sold flour and, having filled it, started to leave. When she asked for the price, he said, "This young man will pay, once his ship of salt-fish arrives."

He is also thought to have been the cause of **Anytus's** exile and **Meletus's** death <note>Anytus and Meletus were the primary accusers responsible for the trial and execution of Socrates.</note>. For when he met some young men from Pontus who had come to Athens because of the fame of Socrates, he led them away to Anytus, telling them that in some respects Anytus was wiser than Socrates. At this, those standing by were so indignant that they drove Anytus out. 

Whenever he saw a woman elaborately adorned, he would go to her house and command her husband to bring out his horse and weapons; then, if the husband possessed these things, he would let the woman continue her luxury (for he would have the means to defend himself), but if not, he told him to strip off her finery. 

The following doctrines also pleased him: He maintained that virtue <note>original: "ἀρετή" — *arete*, often translated as virtue or moral excellence; for Antisthenes, it was the only true goal of life.</note> can be taught, and that those who are well-born are the same as those who are virtuous. For he held that virtue is sufficient for happiness <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία" — *eudaimonia*, the state of human flourishing or a life well-lived</note>, needing nothing further except the strength of a Socrates. He taught that virtue consists in deeds and requires neither a great abundance of words nor many lessons. He maintained that the wise man is self-sufficient, for all the goods of others belong to him. He claimed that ill-repute is a good thing and equal to hard labor. He also held that the wise man should not govern himself according to the established laws of the state, but according to the law of virtue. 

He said he would marry for the sake of having children, joining with the most gifted women. He would also fall in love, for the wise man alone knows who is worthy of being loved. **Diocles** <note>Diocles of Magnesia, an ancient biographer and source for the lives of philosophers.</note> also records these sayings of his: To the wise man, nothing is foreign or impossible. The good man is worthy of love. The virtuous are friends. One should make allies of those who are both brave and just. Virtue is a weapon that cannot be taken away.

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
## Book 6: Antisthenes

...virtue. <note>original: "ἀρετή" — *arete*, meaning moral excellence or functional perfection</note>. He said it is better to fight with a few good men against all the wicked, than with many wicked men against a few. One should pay attention to enemies, for they are the first to notice one's mistakes. He held that a just man should be valued more than a relative. He believed that the virtue of a man and a woman is the same. Good things are beautiful, and bad things are ugly; everything that is evil you should consider foreign. He called wisdom <note>original: "φρόνησις" — *phronesis*, practical wisdom or prudence</note> the safest wall, for it neither collapses nor is ever betrayed. He said we must build walls within our own unconquerable reasoning.

He used to lecture in the gymnasium of **Cynosarges** <note>The Cynosarges was a public gymnasium outside the walls of Athens, traditionally used by those who were not full Athenian citizens.</note> a short distance from the city gates. From this, some believe the <term>Cynic</term> <note>The name likely derives from the gymnasium name or the Greek word for dog (*kyon*), reflecting the school's "back to basics" and sometimes biting social critiques.</note> school got its name. He himself was nicknamed the "Simple Dog" <note>original: "Ἁπλοκύων" — *Haplokuon*</note>. He was the first to double his cloak <note>The *tribon*, a coarse, cheap garment that became the standard uniform of the Cynic philosophers.</note>—as **Diocles** says—and it was the only garment he used. He also took up a staff and a beggar’s bag. **Neanthes** says he was the first to wear the cloak single-layered; however, **Sosicrates**, in the third book of his *Successions*, says it was **Diodorus of Aspendus** who first did this, and also let his beard grow and used the staff and bag.

**Theopompus** praises him alone out of all the followers of Socrates, saying he was clever and could win over anyone through pleasant conversation. This is clear from his writings and from **Xenophon's** *Symposium*. He also seems to have founded the most "manly" branch of the Stoic school. Therefore, **Athenaeus** the epigram-writer says of them:

->O you who know the Stoic tales, O best of men,<-
->Who placed the holiest doctrines in your sacred pages:<-
->That the virtue of the soul is the only good. For this alone<-
->Rescues the lives of men and their cities.<-
->But the pleasure of the flesh, the goal so dear to withered men,<-
->Only one of the daughters of Memory <note>Referring to the Muses; the poem implies that carnal pleasure is a mere mental distraction compared to virtue.</note> provided.<-

<margin>of him</margin> He led the way for the indifference <note>original: "ἀπάθεια" — *apatheia*, meaning freedom from disturbing passions</note> of **Diogenes**, the self-control <note>original: "ἐγκράτεια" — *enkrateia*</note> of **Crates**, and the fortitude <note>original: "καρτερία" — *karteria*</note> of **Zeno**, having himself laid the foundations for the state. **Xenophon** says he was most pleasant in conversation, and most self-controlled in all other matters.

## DIOGENES

Diogenes was the son of Hicesias, a banker from Sinope. Diocles <note>Diocles of Magnesia, a source frequently cited for the lives of philosophers.</note> says that he went into exile because his father, who was in charge of the public exchange, had defaced the currency <note>original: "παραχαράξαντος τὸ νόμισμα" (paracharaxantos to nomisma) — this is a pivotal pun in Cynic history; it means both debasing the coins and "altering the political values" or social customs.</note>. Eubulus, in his work *On Diogenes*, says that Diogenes himself did this and then wandered in exile with his father. 

Indeed, Diogenes himself says in his work *Pordalus* <note>original: "Ποδάλῳ" (Podalo) — likely a corruption of "Pordalus," meaning "The Leopard."</note> that he defaced the coinage. Others say that when he was appointed overseer, he was persuaded by the mint-workers to do it. He then went to Delphi (or to the Delium, in the birthplace of Apollo) and asked the god if he should do what he was being urged to do. When the god gave him permission to "alter the political currency," he misunderstood the meaning; he debased the coins, was caught...

# DIOGENES. Book 6.

According to some, he was exiled; according to others, he withdrew voluntarily, fearing the consequences of his actions. Some say that having received the authority over the coinage from his father, he defaced it. <note>original: "παραχαράξαι" (paracharaxai) — this term can mean both to physically deface or counterfeit coins and to "change the political currency," i.e., to subvert social norms.</note> They say his father died in prison, while Diogenes fled and came to Delphi. When he asked the oracle not whether he should deface the currency, but what he should do to become most famous, he received the instruction to do just that.

When he arrived in Athens, he attached himself to Antisthenes. Although Antisthenes tried to drive him away—since he would admit no pupils—Diogenes forced his way in through sheer persistence. Once, when Antisthenes raised his staff <note>A traveler's walking stick, which became a symbol of the Cynic philosophers.</note> against him, Diogenes offered his head and said: "Strike, for you will not find wood so hard that it can keep me away from you, as long as you seem to be saying something worth hearing." From that time on, he became his pupil, and being an exile, he set out upon a life of simple means. 

Watching a mouse running about (as Theophrastus <note>A student of Aristotle and a noted naturalist/philosopher.</note> says in his *Megarian Dialogue*), and seeing that it neither sought a soft bed, nor feared the dark, nor yearned for any of the things considered luxuries, he discovered a way to adapt to his own circumstances. According to some, he was the first to double his cloak <note>original: "τρίβωνα" (tribōna) — a coarse, cheap garment worn by the poor and adopted by the Cynics as a "uniform" of self-sufficiency.</note> because he was forced to sleep in it. He also carried a pouch where he kept his food. He used every place for every purpose: for eating, for sleeping, or for conversation. He used to point to the Portico of Zeus and the Hall of Processions and say that the Athenians had built these for him to live in.

He leaned on a staff when he grew weak, but eventually he carried it all the time—not in the city, but when walking along the roads, along with his pouch, as stated by Olympiodorus, the leader of the Athenians, Polyeuctus the orator, and Lysanias, son of Aeschrion. Having written to someone to provide him a small hut, and that person delaying, he took up the large storage jar <term>pithos: a massive ceramic jar used for grain or oil, often large enough for a person to crawl inside</term> in the temple of the Mother of the Gods as his home, as he himself explains in his letters. 

In the summer, he would roll in the hot sand, and in winter, he would embrace statues covered in snow, training himself in every way to endure hardship. He was also skilled at mocking others: he used to call the school <note>original: "σχολήν" (scholēn)</note> of Euclides "gall" <note>original: "χολήν" (cholēn) — a pun on the similarity between the Greek words for school and bile/bitterness.</note>, and Plato’s...

...a pastime into a waste of time. <note>original: "διατριβὴν, κατατριβήν" — a pun on *diatribē* (a school or lecture) and *katatribē* (a wearing down or wasting).</note> He used to say that the Dionysian festivals <note>Annual dramatic competitions in Athens honoring Dionysus.</note> were great wonders for fools, and that demagogues were the servants of the mob. He also said that when he saw pilots, doctors, and philosophers in the course of life, he thought man was the most intelligent of animals; but when, on the other hand, he saw interpreters of dreams, soothsayers, and those who paid attention to them, or those puffed up by fame and wealth, he considered nothing to be more vain than man.

He used to say repeatedly that for life one should prepare either reason or a rope. <note>original: "λόγον ἢ βρόχον" (logon ē brochon) — meaning one must live by the light of reason or, failing that, end one's life.</note> Once, noticing Plato at a costly banquet eating only olives, he asked: "Why did you, the 'wise man,' sail to Sicily for the sake of these tables, and yet now that they are set before you, you do not enjoy them?" <note>Referring to Plato's famous, and often criticized, visits to the court of the tyrant Dionysius in Syracuse.</note> And Plato replied, "But by the gods, Diogenes, even there I mostly ate olives and the like." Diogenes retorted, "Then why was there a need to sail to Syracuse? Did Attica not bear olives at that time?"

Favorinus, however, says in his *Universal History* that it was Aristippus who said this. <note>Aristippus was another student of Socrates who lived luxuriously at court.</note> And once, while Diogenes was eating dried figs, he met Aristippus and said, "You may share in these." When Aristippus took some and ate them, Diogenes said, "I said you may share in them, not devour them."

Once, while trampling on Plato's carpets when the latter had invited friends from Dionysius's court, Diogenes said, "I trample upon Plato's vanity." <note>original: "κενοδοξίαν" (kenodoxian) — literally 'empty glory' or conceit.</note> To which Plato replied, "How much pride you show, Diogenes, by appearing not to be proud!" Others say Diogenes said, "I trample on Plato's pride," <note>original: "τύφον" (typhon) — a central Cynic term for the 'smoke' or 'fog' of social delusion and intellectual arrogance.</note> and Plato answered, "With pride of a different sort, Diogenes." Sotion, in his fourth book, says that Plato said this to "the Dog" <note>A common nickname for Diogenes, from which the word 'Cynic' (dog-like) is derived.</note> himself.

Diogenes once asked Plato for some wine and also some dried figs. Plato sent him a whole jar of wine. Diogenes remarked: "If you are asked how much two and two make, will you answer twenty? Thus you neither give according to what is asked, nor do you answer according to the question." He mocked him for being a "word-waster." <note>original: "ἀδραντολόγον" (adrantologon) — one who talks much but achieves little.</note>

### DIOGENES. Book 6
-> 209 <-

...finding no success <note>original: "εὐστόχει" — the text likely began with "when he did not succeed [in speaking seriously]"</note>, he began to whistle a tune <note>original: "τερετίζειν" — to chirp or whistle like a bird, often used for humming nonsense songs</note>. When a crowd gathered, he reproached them, saying that they came in haste for nonsense, but for serious matters, they were slow and indifferent. He used to say that men competed against each other in digging and kicking <note>References to athletic training or physical toil</note>; but as for nobility of character <note>original: "καλοκἀγαθία" (kalokagathia) — the Greek ideal of being both "beautiful" in conduct and "good" in soul</note>, no one competed for that.

He expressed wonder at the grammarians <note>Literary scholars</note>, who searched out the misfortunes of Odysseus but remained ignorant of their own. And likewise, he marveled that musicians would tune the strings of their lyres, yet allow the habits of their own souls to remain out of harmony. He wondered at the mathematicians who gazed at the sun and the moon, but overlooked the things right at their feet. He noted that the orators were eager to speak about what is just, but would not do it in practice. Furthermore, he criticized the miserly for finding fault with money, while loving it above all else. He also condemned those who praised the righteous for being above the love of wealth, yet envied those who were very rich. 

He was disturbed by the fact that people would sacrifice to the gods for the sake of health, yet during the sacrifice itself, they would feast in a way that ruined their health. He marveled at the slaves who, seeing their masters eating greedily, did not snatch away any of the food. 

He used to praise those who were about to marry, and yet did not marry; those about to go on a voyage, and yet did not sail; those about to enter politics, and yet did not do so; those about to raise children <note>original: "παιδοτροφεῖν" (paidotrophēin)</note>, and yet did not raise them; and those who prepared to live with powerful rulers, but then never approached them <note>Diogenes valued the freedom found in avoiding social and political obligations</note>. He said that one ought to stretch out one's hands to friends without the fingers being clenched <note>Signifying open-handed generosity</note>. 

Menippus says in his book, *The Sale of Diogenes* <note>original: "Διογένους πράσει" (Diogenous prasei)</note>, that when Diogenes was captured and put up for sale, he was asked what he knew how to do. He replied, "To rule men." And to the auctioneer, he said, "Cry out: 'If anyone wants to buy a master for himself!'" When he was forbidden to sit down, he said, "It makes no difference; for even fish are sold regardless of how they lie." He said he was amazed that when people buy a pot or a dish, they examine it closely, but when buying a human being, they are satisfied with a mere glance. He said...

### DIOGENES. Book 6
-> 210 <-

[He told] Xeniades, or whoever it was that bought him, that he ought to be obeyed, even if he were a slave. For if a doctor or a pilot were a slave, he said, people would still obey him. Eubulus says in the work entitled *The Sale of Diogenes* <note>original: "Διογένους πρᾶσις" (Diogenous prasis) — a lost work depicting the philosopher’s time in slavery</note> that he brought up Xeniades' sons in this way: after their other studies, he taught them to ride, to shoot with the bow, to use the sling, and to throw the javelin. Then, in the wrestling school, he did not allow the trainer <note>original: "παιδοτρίβῃ" (paidotribē) — a physical education instructor</note> to drill them like professional athletes, but only enough to give them a healthy color and physical fitness. 

The boys also learned many passages from poets and prose writers, as well as from the works of Diogenes himself. He practiced every possible shortcut to learning to make things easy for them to remember. In the house, he taught them to serve themselves, being content with simple food and drinking only water. He made them wear their hair cropped close <note>original: "ἐν χρῷ κουρείας" — cut right to the skin</note> and remain unadorned; they went without tunics <note>original: "ἀχίτωνας" — a sign of extreme austerity, wearing only a cloak or nothing at all</note> and without shoes, remaining silent and looking down at themselves as they walked in the streets. He also took them out hunting. They, in turn, took care of Diogenes and made requests to their parents on his behalf. 

The same author says that Diogenes grew old in Xeniades' house, and when he died, he was buried by Xeniades' sons. At that time, when Xeniades asked how he should bury him, he replied, "On my face." When asked "Why?", he said, "Because in a little while, what is down is going to be turned up." <note>Diogenes likely refers to the "turning of the world upside down" by the rising power of the north.</note> This was because the Macedonians <note>The kingdom of Philip II and Alexander the Great</note> were already becoming powerful, rising from low status to high. When someone led him into a luxurious house and forbade him from spitting, he cleared his throat and spat in the man's face, saying he could find no worse place. Others, however, say this story belongs to Aristippus. 

Once, shouting out, "Ho, men!", and when a crowd gathered, he fell upon them with his staff, saying, "I called for men, not for dregs" <note>original: "καθάρματα" (katharmata) — literally 'off-scourings' or 'trash,' often used for criminals or the lowest social class</note>, as Hecato says in the first book of his *Anecdotes*. They say that Alexander the Great even said that if he had not been Alexander, he would have wanted to be Diogenes. He used to say that "cripples" were not the deaf and the blind, but those who did not have a beggar's wallet <note>original: "πήραν" (pēran) — the characteristic leather scrip or bag of the Cynic philosopher, symbolizing self-sufficiency</note>. ### DIOGENES. Book 6
-> 211 <-

Metrocles <note>A Cynic philosopher and student of Crates of Thebes</note> says in his *Anecdotes* <note>original: "χρείαις" (chreiais) — short, pithy stories or sayings of a famous person</note> that Diogenes once received a beating. Afterwards, having written the names of those who struck him on a white tablet, he walked around with it hung upon him; in this way, he brought shame upon them, as they were condemned and rebuked by everyone who saw them. He used to say that he was a dog of the kind that is praised, but that none of those who praised him dared to go out with him to the hunt <note>A metaphor for how people admired his philosophy from a distance but feared to live his ascetic lifestyle</note>.

To a man who said, "I conquer men at the Pythian games," he replied, "I am the one who conquers men; you only conquer slaves." To those who said, "You are an old man; for what remains of your life, relax," he replied: "What? If I were running the long race <note>original: "δολιχὸν" (dolichon) — a long-distance race in the ancient Olympics</note>, should I relax when I am near the finish line, and not rather strain myself even more?" 

When invited to a dinner, he said he would not attend, for the day before he had not even been thanked for his company. He used to walk on snow with bare feet, and practiced the other hardships mentioned previously. He even attempted to eat raw meat, but he was unable to digest it.

He once caught Demosthenes the orator <note>The famous Athenian statesman known for his professional eloquence, which the Cynics often found artificial</note> breakfasting in a tavern. When Demosthenes tried to retreat further inside to hide, Diogenes said, "The more you retreat, the more you will be inside the tavern." Once, when some strangers wanted to see Demosthenes, Diogenes stretched out his middle finger and said, "This is our Athenian demagogue" <note>In antiquity, as today, extending the middle finger was an insulting and obscene gesture</note>. 

When someone dropped a loaf of bread and was ashamed to pick it up, Diogenes, wishing to give him a lesson, tied a string to the neck of an earthenware jar and dragged it through the Ceramicus <note>The "Potter's Quarter" of Athens, a busy public area</note>. He said he imitated the choir-masters, for they also set the note slightly higher than the proper pitch <note>original: "ὑπὲρ τόνον" (hyper tonon)</note> so that the rest of the choir might hit the correct tone. 

He used to say that most people were within a finger's breadth of being mad. For if a man walks extending his middle finger, he will be thought mad, but if he extends his forefinger, he will not. He said that things of great value were sold for nothing, and vice versa. For instance, a statue might be sold for three thousand drachmae, while a measure of flour <note>original: "χοίνικα" (choinika) — about a quart</note> sells for only two coppers <note>original: "χαλκῶν" (chalkōn) — low-value bronze coins</note>. 

To Xeniades, who had purchased him as a slave, he said: "Come, see that you do what you are ordered." When Xeniades replied with the proverb, "The sources of the rivers flow upward" <note>A common Greek saying meaning that the natural order of the world is being overturned—in this case, a slave commanding a master</note>, Diogenes asked: "If you were sick and had purchased a doctor, would you not obey him? Or would you tell him that the sources of the rivers flow upward?"

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
-> 272 <-

...wanted him to practice philosophy. Diogenes gave him a salted fish <note>original: "σαπέρδην" (saperden) — a type of salted or pickled fish, often considered cheap food</note> to carry and told him to follow. When the man threw it away out of shame and departed, Diogenes met him some time later, laughed, and said, "A salted fish has dissolved our friendship." Diocles <note>An early historian of philosophy</note> records the story this way: when someone said to him, "Give us orders, Diogenes," he led the man away and gave him a half-obol's worth of cheese to carry. When the man refused, he said, "A tiny half-obol cheese has dissolved our friendship."

Having once observed a child drinking from his hands, he threw the cup <note>original: "κοτύλην" (kotylen) — a small vessel or deep cup</note> out of his wallet, saying, "A child has beaten me in simplicity." He also threw away his bowl <note>original: "τρυβλίον" (tryblion)</note> when he similarly saw a child, after breaking his vessel, take up his lentil soup in the hollowed-out part of a piece of bread. He used to reason as follows: "All things belong to the gods; the wise are friends of the gods; and among friends, all things are held in common; therefore, all things belong to the wise." 

Seeing a woman prostrating herself before the gods in an unseemly <note>The Greek implies she was crouching or bending in a way that exposed her immodestly</note> manner, and wishing to rid her of her superstition <note>original: "δεισιδαιμονίαν" (deisidaimonian) — literally 'fear of spirits,' often used to describe excessive or irrational religious practice</note> (as Zoïlus of Perga says), he approached her and said, "Are you not afraid, woman, that since a god may be standing behind you—for all things are full of his presence—you might be behaving in an unseemly way?" He dedicated to Asclepius <note>The god of healing</note> a "striker" <note>original: "πλήκτην" (plekten) — a boxer or a fist-shaped votive</note> who would run up and strike those who fell on their faces <note>A joke at the expense of those who prostrated themselves excessively in temples</note>. 

He was in the habit of saying that the tragic curses had come upon him; at any rate, he was: "Cityless, homeless, deprived of a fatherland, a beggar, a wanderer, having a life lived from day to day" <note>These lines are likely quoted from a lost tragedy, used by Diogenes to describe the Cynic's lifestyle as a badge of honor rather than a misfortune</note>. He claimed that he set courage against fortune, nature against law, and reason against passion. 

While he was sunning himself in the Craneion <note>A gymnasium and cypress grove in Corinth</note>, Alexander <note>Alexander the Great</note> stood over him and said, "Ask of me whatever you wish." Diogenes replied, "Stand out of my light." When someone was reading a long work and pointed to a blank space at the end of the book, Diogenes cried out, "Take heart, men! I see land." To someone who had proven by a syllogism that Diogenes had horns <note>A famous logic puzzle: 'What you have not lost, you have; you have not lost horns; therefore you have horns'</note>, he touched his forehead and said, "Well, I certainly do not see them." In the same way, when someone claimed that motion does not exist, he got up and walked about. To a man who was speaking about celestial phenomena <note>original: "μετεώρων" (meteoron)</note>, he asked, "How many days has it been since you arrived from heaven?"

### DIOGENES. Book 6
-> 213 <-

When a wicked eunuch had inscribed over the door of his house, "Let no evil enter here," Diogenes asked: "Then where is the master of the house to enter?" Having rubbed his feet with perfume <note>original: "μύρῳ" (myro) — scented oil or ointment, usually reserved for the head</note>, he remarked that when perfume is put on the head, it vanishes into the air, but when put on the feet, the scent rises up to the nose. When the Athenians urged him to be initiated into the Mysteries <note>The Eleusinian Mysteries, which promised a better afterlife</note>, telling him that those who have been initiated obtain the front seats <note>original: "προεδρίας" (proedrias) — the right to the best seats at public events</note> in the underworld, he replied: "It is ridiculous if Agesilaus and Epaminondas <note>Famous virtuous generals who were not initiated</note> are to live in the mire of Hades, while some worthless people, just because they have been initiated, will dwell in the Isles of the Blessed." 

To the mice that scurried toward his table, he said: "Behold, even Diogenes feeds parasites <note>original: "παρασίτους" (parasitous) — literally 'those who eat at another’s table,' referring to social leeches</note>." When Plato called him a dog <note>A reference to the nickname 'Cynic,' derived from the word for dog</note>, he replied: "True, for I have returned to those who sold me <note>A reference to his earlier capture and sale into slavery</note>." 

Leaving the bathhouse, he was asked by one man if many humans were bathing, and he said "No." But when another asked if there was a large crowd <note>original: "ὄχλος" (ochlos) — implying a mindless mob</note>, he admitted there was. When Plato defined man as "a featherless, two-footed animal" and the definition was well-received, Diogenes plucked a rooster and brought it into Plato's school, saying: "This is Plato's man." Because of this incident, "with broad nails" was added to the official definition. 

To a man who asked at what hour one ought to dine <note>original: "ἀριστᾶν" (aristan) — the first or midday meal</note>, he replied: "If you are a rich man, whenever you wish; if you are a poor man, whenever you have food." In Megara, seeing that the sheep were protected by leather coverings <note>To keep their wool clean and soft</note> while the Megarians' own children went naked, he remarked: "It is more profitable to be a Megarian’s ram than his son." 

To a man who struck him with a staff and then shouted, "Watch out!", Diogenes replied: "Why? Are you going to hit me again?" He used to say that demagogues were the servants of the mob, and that the crowns <note>Wreaths of leaves awarded for public achievement</note> given to them were the blisters <note>original: "ἐξανθήματα" (exanthemata) — literally 'skin eruptions' or pustules</note> of glory. 

Having lit a lamp in the broad daylight, he walked about saying, "I am looking for a human being <note>original: "Ἄνθρωπον" (Anthropon) — famously translated as 'an honest man,' though the Greek emphasizes the search for someone truly human among the 'mob'</note>." He once stood under a fountain during a downpour; when the bystanders took pity on him, Plato, who was passing by, said: "If you truly wish to pity him, move away," pointing out Diogenes' vanity <note>original: "φιλοδοξίαν" (philodoxian) — love of fame or reputation</note> in making a display of his endurance. When someone gave him a punch to the head, he exclaimed: "By Heracles! What a thing to have overlooked—that I should walk about wearing a helmet." And when Meidias punched him...

### DIOG. LAERT.

him <note>The context suggests a man who had mocked Diogenes with a promise of money</note>, and when the man said, "Four thousand [drachmas] are lying on the table for you," Diogenes took boxing thongs the next day and, after giving him a thorough beating, said: "Four thousand are lying on the table for you." When Lysias the pharmacist asked him if he believed in the gods, he replied: "How could I not believe in them, when I consider even you to be an enemy of the gods?" <note>original: "θεοῖς ἐχθρὸν" (theois echthron) — someone hated by the gods; a common insult for the wicked</note> Others, however, say that it was Theodorus who said this. Seeing someone being sprinkled for purification, he remarked: "Wretched man, do you not know that just as you cannot be rid of errors in grammar by being sprinkled, so you cannot be rid of the errors of your life?" He reproached people regarding fortune, saying that they pray for what *seems* good to them, rather than what is good in truth. To those who were obsessed with dreams, he said that they pay no attention to what they do while awake, but make a great fuss over what they imagine while they are sleeping. When a herald at the Olympic games announced, "Dioxippus <note>A famous Athenian pankratiast (a combat athlete)</note> conquers men!", Diogenes replied: "He only conquers slaves; I am the one who conquers men."

He was also beloved by the Athenians. For instance, when a youth broke his jar <note>original: "πίθον" (pithon) — the large ceramic storage jar Diogenes lived in</note>, they gave the boy a beating and provided Diogenes with another one. Dionysius the Stoic says that after the Battle of Chaeronea <note>The 338 BCE battle where Philip II of Macedon defeated the Greeks</note>, Diogenes was captured and brought before Philip. When asked who he was, he replied: "A scout <note>original: "Κατάσκοπος" (Kataskopos)</note> of your insatiable greed." He was so admired for this that he was released. 

Once, when Alexander sent a letter to Antipater <note>Alexander's regent in Macedonia</note> in Athens by a man named Athlias, Diogenes, who was present, remarked: "Miserable from the miserable, by means of the miserable, to the miserable." <note>A pun on the name Athlias, which sounds like the Greek word "athlios" (ἄθλιος), meaning wretched or miserable</note> When Perdiccas <note>One of Alexander’s generals</note> threatened to kill him if he did not come to him, Diogenes replied: "That is nothing great; even a beetle or a venomous spider could do that." He suggested it would be a more worthy threat to say: "Even without me, you would live a happy life." <note>Diogenes is mocking the idea that a ruler's power to kill is impressive, suggesting instead that the ability to live happily without him would be a true feat</note> He would often cry out, saying that the gods have granted a simple life to mankind, but it has been hidden from those who seek out honey-cakes, perfumes, and such things. Thus, to a man who was having his shoes put on by a servant, he said: "You are not truly happy yet, unless he also blows your nose for you."

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
-> 216 <-

...performing his toilet in the marketplace, people gathered round, and he said: "You wonder that I behave like this, yet you do not wonder at a man of such talent as this musician playing for money and not stealing." <note>original: "τηλικοῦτος ὢν κιθαρωδεῖ, καὶ οὐ λῃστεύει" — Diogenes is likely making a dark joke that it is more surprising for a poor, talented man to remain honest than for a philosopher to ignore social taboos.</note>

To a musician who was constantly being abandoned by his audience, he gave a greeting: "Hail, Cock!" <note>original: "ἀλέκτωρ" (alektor)</note> When the man asked why he called him that, Diogenes replied, "Because by your singing, you wake everyone up."

When a youth was putting on a display of vanity, Diogenes filled his own lap with lupines <note>term: lupines (thérmoi) — a common, cheap legume, often referred to as "Cynic food" to signify a life of poverty and simplicity</note> and began eating them right in front of him. When the crowd began to stare at Diogenes instead of the boy, he said he wondered how they could ignore the youth and look at him instead.

To a man who was intensely superstitious and said to him, "I will split your head open with a single blow!" Diogenes replied, "And I, by simply standing on your left, will make you tremble." <note>In ancient Greek culture, an omen appearing from the left was considered an unlucky or frightening sign; Diogenes mocks the man's superstition by claiming he himself will become a bad omen.</note>

When Hegesias <note>A philosopher of the Cyrenaic school, known for his pessimistic views</note> asked him to read some of his writings, Diogenes replied: "You are a foolish man, Hegesias. You would not choose painted figs over real ones, yet you ignore real training <note>term: training (askēsis) — the core Cynic practice of physical and mental discipline intended to harden the body and soul</note> to pursue mere written words."

To a man who reproached him for his exile, he said: "But it was because of that exile, you wretch, that I became a philosopher." And again, when someone told him, "The people of Sinope have condemned you to banishment," he replied, "And I have condemned them to stay at home."

Once, seeing an Olympic victor tending sheep, he said: "My good fellow, how quickly you have moved from the Olympics to the Nemean games!" <note>This is a clever pun: the Nemean games were a famous athletic festival, but the Greek word "nemos" also means a wooded pasture.</note>

When asked why athletes are so dull-witted, he said: "Because they are built out of nothing but pig's meat and beef."

Once he was seen begging for alms from a statue. When asked why he did this, he replied: "I am practicing being rejected." <note>Cynics often engaged in "shameless" acts to build emotional resilience against the opinions of others.</note>

When asking for something from a man (which he first began to do out of sheer poverty), he said: "If you have given to others, give to me also; if you have given to no one, start with me."

Being asked by the tyrant what kind of bronze was best for a statue, he replied: "The kind from which Harmodius and Aristogeiton <note>Harmodius and Aristogeiton were the celebrated "Tyrannicides" who assassinated the Athenian tyrant Hipparchus, becoming symbols of democracy.</note> were cast."

When asked how Dionysius <note>The tyrant of Syracuse, known for his volatile nature</note> treats his friends, he said: "Like bags; he hangs up the full ones and throws away the empty ones."

A newly-married man had inscribed upon his house: "The son of Zeus, Hercules the Victor, dwells here; let no evil enter." Diogenes added to the wall: "After the war, the alliance." <note>Diogenes quips that marriage is essentially a state of war, and any "alliance" or peace only comes after the initial conflict.</note>

He used to say that greed was the "mother-city" <note>original: "metropolis"</note> of all evils.

### DIOGENES. Book 6
-> 219 <-

...and of all evils. Seeing a spendthrift in an inn eating nothing but olives, he said: "If you had breakfasted like this, you would not be dining like this." <note>Diogenes suggests that if the man had been frugal earlier in his life, he wouldn't be reduced to eating such cheap fare now.</note> He used to say that good men were images of the gods; and that love was the occupation of the idle. When asked what was the most wretched thing in life, he replied: "A poor old man." When asked which of the beasts gave the most dangerous bite, he said: "Of the wild beasts, the sycophant; <note>term: sycophant (sykophantēs) — in ancient Athens, this referred to a professional informer or malicious accuser who brought lawsuits for profit.</note> and of the tame ones, the flatterer."

Seeing once two Centaurs very poorly painted, he said: "Which of these is Chiron?" <note>original: "Πότερος τούτων χείρων ἐστί;" — This is a pun. "Cheiron" was the name of the wise Centaur, but the word "cheirōn" in Greek also means "worse." Diogenes is asking which of the two paintings is the worse one.</note> He used to say that speech meant only to please was a "honeyed noose," and he called the belly the "Charybdis of life." <note>term: Charybdis — a mythical, ship-devouring whirlpool; Diogenes implies the appetite is a bottomless pit that destroys a person's life.</note> Hearing once that an adulterer named Didymus had been caught, he said: "He deserves to be hanged by his name." <note>original: "Ἄξιος... ἐκ τοῦ ὀνόματος κρέμασθαι" — A double pun: Didymus means "twin," but the plural form "didymoi" was also a common Greek euphemism for the testicles.</note>

When asked why gold has a pale color, he said: "Because it has so many people plotting against it." Seeing a woman in a litter, <note>term: litter (phoreion) — a portable couch or chair used by the wealthy to be carried through the streets.</note> he said: "The cage is not suited to the beast." Seeing a runaway slave sitting on the edge of a well, he said: "Young man, take care you don't fall in." Seeing a clothes-thief in the baths, he asked: "Are you here for a little oil, or for another cloak?" <note>Bathers would rub themselves with oil; Diogenes mocks the thief by asking if he's there for the meager supplies or a more substantial theft.</note> Seeing once some women who had been hanged from an olive tree, he remarked: "Would that all trees bore such fruit." <note>A characteristic example of the "Cynic" bite; Diogenes frequently used harsh, misogynistic humor to shock his audience and express his disdain for conventional society.</note> Seeing a footpad, <note>term: footpad (lōpodytēs) — a thief who robs people of their clothes, especially at night.</note> he said:

> "Why are you here, O best of men?
> Is it to strip some of the dead corpses?"
> <note>Diogenes is parodying a line from Homer’s "Iliad" (10.387), where a spy is questioned. Diogenes treats the thief as if he were a character in an epic poem.</note>

When asked if he had a maid-servant or a boy-servant, he said: "No." When the questioner followed up with, "Then if you die, who will carry you out for burial?" he replied: "Whoever needs the house." Seeing a handsome youth sleeping unguarded, he nudged him and said:

> "Wake up, lest someone plant a spear in your back while you sleep."
> <note>Another Homeric parody, this time from the "Iliad" (10.99), used here to mockingly warn the boy of unwanted sexual advances.</note>

To a man who was buying very expensive delicacies, he said:

> "Short-lived indeed will you be, my child, by what you buy."
> <note>A parody of a line spoken by Thetis to Achilles in the "Iliad" (1.416). While the original warned of a hero's fate, Diogenes warns that the man's extravagant spending will lead to his ruin.</note>

...When Plato was discussing his theory of ideas and using terms like "tableness" and "cupness," Diogenes said, "I see a table and a cup, for I have eyes; but that by which 'tableness' and 'cupness' are perceived, you do not seem to have." <note>Diogenes is mocking Plato’s Theory of Forms. He argues that while anyone can see a physical object, Plato’s abstract "Forms" (the perfect essence of a table or cup) are invisible and, to Diogenes, nonexistent.</note> When asked by someone, "What sort of man does Socrates seem to you, Diogenes?" he replied, "A madman." <note>original: "Μαινόμενος" (Mainomenos). Asked if wise men eat honey-cake, he said, "They eat everything, just like the rest of mankind." Asked why people give money to beggars but not to philosophers, he replied, "Because they expect they might one day become lame or blind themselves, but they never expect to become philosophers."
