"And I went away," someone said, "and I was not made any worse [Cheiron]." Diogenes replied, "Not worse, perhaps, but certainly Eurytion." <note>original: "Χείρων... Εὐρυτίων." This is a pun on the names of two famous Centaurs. "Cheiron" sounds like the Greek word for "worse" (cheiron), while Eurytion suggests someone broad or wide-ranging—likely a jab at the man's character or physical stature.</note> He was asking for something difficult. When the man said, "If you can persuade me," Diogenes replied, "If I could persuade you of anything, I would have persuaded you to hang yourself." He was once returning from Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note> to Athens; to someone who asked, "From where and to where?" he replied, "From the men's quarters to the women's quarters." <note>Diogenes frequently praised the Spartans for their rugged masculinity and criticized the Athenians as being "soft" or "effeminate."</note>

Upon returning from the Olympic Games, when someone asked if there was a great crowd, he said, "A great crowd, yes, but very few human beings." He used to say that profligate people were like fig trees growing on a precipice: their fruit is never tasted by any man, but only by crows and vultures. When Phryne <note>A famously wealthy and beautiful courtesan (hetaira) of the 4th century BCE.</note> dedicated a golden statue of Aphrodite at Delphi, he suggested it should bear the inscription: "From the lack of self-control of the Greeks."

Once, when Alexander the Great stood over him and said, "I am Alexander, the great king," he replied, "And I am Diogenes, the dog." When asked what he did to be called a "dog," he said, "I fawn on those who give me something, I bark at those who refuse, and I sink my teeth into rascals."

He was once gathering fruit from a fig tree; when the guard told him, "A man hanged himself from that tree just the other day," he replied, "Then I shall be the one to purify it." Seeing an Olympic victor staring quite frequently at a courtesan, he remarked, "Look at this warlike ram, how he is led by the neck by a common slip of a girl."

He used to say that beautiful courtesans were like a lethal mixture of honey and wine. While he was eating his breakfast in the marketplace, the people standing around kept calling him "Dog." He retorted, "It is you who are the dogs, for you stand around watching a man eat." When two effeminate men were trying to hide from him, he said, "Do not be afraid; a dog does not eat beets." <note>original: "τεῦτλα" (teutla). In ancient slang, "beets" were associated with lack of vigor or effeminacy; Diogenes is mocking their character by saying he has no appetite for such things.</note>

Asked where a boy who had prostituted himself came from, he replied, "He is a Tegeate." <note>original: "Τεγεάτης." A pun on Tegea (a city) and the word "tegeos," meaning "under a roof," often referring to a brothel.</note> Seeing an unskillful wrestler who had turned to practicing medicine, he asked, "What is this? Is it so that you can finally throw down those who once defeated you?" Seeing the son of a courtesan throwing a stone into a crowd, he called out, "Watch out, boy, lest you hit your father!" When a young boy showed him a dagger he had received from a lover, Diogenes said, "The dagger is beautiful, but the handle is..." <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "ἡ δὲ" (but the...). The full joke usually concludes "the handle is shameful," referring to the way the boy acquired the gift.</note>

## Book 6

...if he should receive them, they are shameful. When some people were praising a man who had given him a gift, he said, "And do you not praise me, who was worthy to receive it?" When someone demanded back a <term>tribon</term> <note>A coarse, double-folded cloak typically worn by Cynic philosophers to signify their poverty and rugged lifestyle.</note>, he said, "If it was a gift, I own it; if it was a loan, I am still using it." When a certain person suggested that he had gold hidden in his cloak, he replied, "Indeed, and that is why I sleep with it folded under me." 

When asked what he had gained from philosophy, he replied, "If nothing else, at least to be prepared for every turn of fortune." When asked where he was from, he said, "I am a **Cosmopolitan**." <note>original: "Κοσμοπολίτης." This is one of the earliest recorded uses of the term, meaning "a citizen of the world," expressing his rejection of local or nationalistic ties in favor of a universal human identity.</note> When certain people were sacrificing to the gods because a son had been born to them, he said, "And do you not offer a sacrifice for what kind of man he will turn out to be?" 

Once, when asking for a contribution from a collector of funds, he said:
> "To the others do destruction, but from Hector hold back your hands." 
<note>original: "Τοῖς ἄλλοις ἐνάριζ’, ἀπὸ δ’ Ἕκτορος ἴσχεο χεῖρας." This is a parody of a line from Homer’s *Iliad*. Diogenes identifies himself with the hero Hector to humorously warn the collector to stay away from him while taking from others.</note>

He used to say that courtesans were the "queens of kings," for kings would do whatever they desired. When the Athenians voted to declare Alexander the Great to be the god Dionysus, he said, "Then you should make me **Serapis** too." <note>Serapis was a Greco-Egyptian god whose cult was popular at the time. Diogenes is mocking the absurdity of humans granting divinity to rulers through political decrees.</note> 

To a man who reproached him for entering "unclean places" (such as latrines or brothels), he replied, "The sun also enters the latrines, yet it is not defiled." While dining in a temple, when some dirty loaves of bread were set before him, he picked them up and threw them away, saying that nothing "unclean" should enter a holy place. To someone who said, "You practice philosophy though you know nothing," he replied, "Even if I only pretend to wisdom, that too is to practice philosophy." To a man who had sold a slave boy and was claiming the boy was "of poor natural talent but of excellent character," Diogenes asked, "Then what need does he have of me?" 

He used to say that those who speak of serious things but do not act upon them are no different from a lyre; for a lyre, too, has no hearing or feeling despite the music it makes. He once entered a theater by walking in the opposite direction to those who were leaving; when asked why, he said, "This is what I have practiced doing my whole life." <note>A metaphor for the Cynic practice of deliberately acting contrary to social expectations and the "crowd."</note> 

Seeing a young man who was dressed in an effeminate manner, he said, "Are you not ashamed to be planning a nature for yourself that is worse than the one you were given? For nature made you a man, but you force yourself to be a woman." Seeing a fool tuning a psaltery <note>A stringed instrument similar to a harp or lyre.</note>, he said, "Are you not ashamed to be harmonizing the sounds of a piece of wood, while leaving your own soul out of tune?"

# DIOGENES. Book 6
### Page 223

...[to provide] self-control to the young, consolation to the elderly, wealth to the poor, and an ornament to the rich. 

To Didymon, an adulterer who was once treating a girl’s eye, he said: "See to it that while you are healing the 'pupil' of the maiden, you do not ruin the maiden herself." <note>original: "Ὅρα μὴ τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν τῆς παρθένου ἰατρεύων, τὴν κόρην φθείρῃς." Diogenes uses a pun on the Greek word *kore*, which means both the "pupil" of the eye and a "young girl" or "maiden."</note> When someone mentioned that he was being plotted against by his friends, Diogenes remarked: "And what is there left to do, if one must treat friends and enemies in the same way?" Asked what is the most beautiful thing among men, he replied: "Freedom of speech." <note>original: "Παρρησία" (Parrhesia). This was a core Cynic value: the right and duty to speak the blunt truth to anyone, regardless of their status.</note> Entering a schoolroom where he saw many statues of the Muses but very few students, he said: "With the help of the gods, teacher, you have many 'students' indeed." 

He was accustomed to doing everything in public, whether it pertained to <term>Demeter</term> <note>A reference to eating, as Demeter was the goddess of the harvest and grain.</note> or to <term>Aphrodite</term>. <note>A reference to sexual acts, as Aphrodite was the goddess of love.</note> He would use such arguments as this: "If eating breakfast is not out of place in itself, then it is not out of place in the marketplace. But eating breakfast is not out of place; therefore, it is not out of place in the marketplace." **X**eirourgōn <note>The original Greek implies masturbation ("working with the hand"). Diogenes practiced this in public to demonstrate that natural urges are not shameful.</note> constantly in public, he would say: "I wish it were possible to banish hunger as well just by rubbing one's belly." Many other sayings are attributed to him, which would be a long task to list, as they are so numerous.

**D**iogenes used to say that there are two kinds of <term>askesis</term> <note>Training or exercise; the root of the modern word "asceticism."</note>: one of the soul, and the other of the body. He claimed that the latter—whereby constant practice in the gymnasium creates mental impressions—provides an ease for the performance of virtuous deeds. He held that one form of training is incomplete without the other, for health and strength are no less necessary for the soul than for the body in the pursuit of what is fitting. 

He offered evidence that virtue can be easily attained through such training. He noted that in the manual arts and other crafts, one can see that craftsmen acquire an extraordinary dexterity through practice. One can also see flute-players and athletes, and how much they excel because of their own specific and constant toil. If these men had transferred this same training to the soul, they would not have labored so unprofitably or so incompletely. Nor indeed did he say at all...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
### Page 224

...nothing in life can be achieved without training <note>original: "askesis." This refers to the rigorous physical and mental discipline the Cynics practiced to achieve self-sufficiency.</note>, and with it, everything can be overcome. It is necessary, therefore, that instead of useless labors, we choose those in accordance with nature so that we might live happily; but instead, men suffer through their own folly. For the very contempt of pleasure becomes most pleasant when one has practiced it. Just as those who are accustomed to living luxuriously find it unpleasant to move toward the opposite, so those who have trained in the opposite way find more pleasure in the very act of despising pleasure. 

This was the nature of his talk, and he clearly acted upon it, truly **re-stamping the currency** <note>original: "nomisma paracharatton." This is the most famous pun in Cynic history. "Nomisma" means both "legal currency" and "social custom." Diogenes was literally exiled for defacing coins, but philosophically he sought to "devalue" false social conventions in favor of natural truth.</note>, giving nothing to legal custom that he did not first give to nature. He claimed to lead the same kind of life as **Heracles** <note>Heracles was the patron hero of the Cynics because of his legendary endurance, his labors, and his preference for strength of character over material comfort.</note>, valuing nothing above freedom. 

He said that all things belong to the wise, using arguments such as those we mentioned earlier: "All things belong to the gods; the gods are friends to the wise; friends hold all things in common; therefore, all things belong to the wise." 

Concerning the law, he said that it is impossible for a state to exist without it. For he says: "Without a city, there is no use for a civilized thing; the city is a civilized thing; without law, there is no use for a city; therefore, the law is a civilized thing." 

He made fun of noble birth, fame, and all such things, calling them the "ornaments of vice," and said that the only correct government is that which exists in the universe <note>The concept of "Cosmopolitanism," or being a "citizen of the world."</note>. He also said that wives should be held in common, recognizing no marriage other than the union of a man who persuades with a woman who is persuaded. Because of this, he held that sons should also be common to all. 

He saw nothing wrong in taking something from a temple or tasting the flesh of any animal. Nor did he consider it unholy to touch even human flesh, as is clear from the customs of other nations. He supported this with the rational argument that "all things exist in all things and through all things." For instance, there is meat in bread, and bread in vegetables, and in the body <gloss>x</gloss> <note>The letter 'x' appears as a mark in the original manuscript, likely indicating a cross-reference or a point of emphasis regarding the physical composition of matter.</note> of all other things, particles enter through certain unseen pores and passages and are evaporated together, as he makes clear in the *Thyestes*—if indeed the tragedies are his and not by Philiscus of Aegina, his acquaintance, or by Pasiphon the son of Lucianus, who Favorinus says in his *Universal History*...

# DIOGENES. Book 6
<sig>p. i.</sig>

...to write after his death. He believed that music, geometry, astrology, and similar subjects should be neglected, as they were useless and unnecessary. He was exceptionally witty in his verbal retorts, as is evident from what we have already mentioned. He also bore being sold into slavery with the greatest nobility. For while sailing to Aegina, he was captured by pirates under the command of Scirpalus, taken to Crete, and put up for sale. When the herald asked what he knew how to do, he replied, "**To rule men.**" Then, pointing to a certain Corinthian in a fine robe—the aforementioned Xeniades—he said, "Sell me to this man; he is in need of a master." 

Xeniades did indeed buy him and, after bringing him to Corinth, set him over his own children and entrusted him with the entire household. Diogenes managed everything so well that Xeniades used to go about saying, "A **good spirit** <note>original: "agathos daimon." In Greek belief, a daimon was a guiding spirit or a divine power that influenced a person's luck or character; Xeniades is suggesting Diogenes brought divine good fortune to his home.</note> has entered my house." 

Cleomenes says in his work entitled *The Pedagogue* that Diogenes’ friends wished to ransom him, but he mockingly <note>original: "eiros." This implies a dry, ironic wit characteristic of the Cynics.</note> told them they were fools; for lions, he said, are not the slaves of those who feed them, but rather those who feed them are the servants of the lions. For it is the mark of a slave to be afraid, but wild beasts are things that men fear. 

There was a certain wonderful power of persuasion about the man, so that he could easily win over anyone at all with his words. It is said, for instance, that a certain Onesicritus of Aegina sent one of his two sons, Androsthenes, to Athens; but after hearing Diogenes, the boy stayed there. Then the father sent the other son, the elder Philiscus mentioned earlier, to fetch him. But Philiscus was likewise captivated. Finally, the father himself went a third time, and he ended up staying no less than his sons, joining them in the study of philosophy. Such was the "**magic charm**" <note>original: "iynx." This refers to the wryneck bird, used in ancient Greek love-magic to draw a person toward the caster. Here, it signifies Diogenes’ irresistible verbal charisma.</note> that Diogenes possessed in his speech. Phocion, nicknamed "**the Good**," also studied under him, as did Stilpo of Megara and many other political figures. It is said that he lived to be nearly ninety years old before he died. Regarding his death, various accounts are told. Some say that after eating an ox’s foot...

It also highlights his immense persuasive power, which led entire families to abandon their former lives to follow his philosophy.</summary>

# DIOGENES. Book 6

...after eating it raw, he was seized by a fit of cholera <note>The Greek term *cholerikos* refers to a violent digestive ailment, often attributed in antiquity to eating raw or tainted seafood.</note> and so met his end. Others say he died by holding his breath. Among those who hold this view is Cercidas of Megalopolis (or perhaps the Cretan), who writes in his *Meliambics* <note>A style of satirical or philosophical poetry.</note> as follows:

> The Sinopian wanderer of old was no ordinary man,
> The staff-bearer, wearer of the **double-cloak**, who lived on the open air,
> But he ascended by pressing his lip against his teeth,
> And biting back his breath. For truly,
> Diogenes was a son of Zeus, and a dog from heaven.

Others say that while he was attempting to divide an octopus among some dogs, he was bitten on the tendon of his foot and died as a result. However, his personal friends (as Antisthenes says in his *Successions of Philosophers*) guessed it was the deliberate holding of his breath. He happened to be living in the **Craneum**, the gymnasium <note>A public space for exercise and intellectual gathering.</note> just outside of Corinth. 

Following their usual custom, his friends arrived and found him completely wrapped up in his cloak. At first, they did not even suspect he was sleeping, for he was never a man given to much slumber or late hours. Therefore, when they pulled back his **rough cloak** <note>original: "tribon." This was the signature garment of the Cynic—a single, coarse piece of wool folded over to serve as both clothing and bedding.</note>, they found him already dead. They assumed he had done this because he wished to depart from life at last.

There then arose a dispute (so they say) among his disciples as to who should bury him; the argument even grew so heated that it came to blows. But when their fathers and the leading citizens arrived, the man was buried by them near the gate leading to the Isthmus. They placed a column over his grave, and upon it, a dog carved from Parian marble. Later, even his fellow citizens honored him with bronze statues and inscribed the following:

> Even bronze grows old with time; but your
> Glory, Diogenes, all eternity shall never destroy;
> Since you alone showed to mortals **self-sufficiency** <note>original: "autarkeia." This is a core Cynic value: the ability to be happy and virtuous regardless of external circumstances.</note> in life,
> And the easiest path through existence.

I have also written an epigram for him in the proceleusmatic meter...

# DIOGENES. Book 6

->Come Diogenes, tell us, what fate took you?<-
->To the underworld! A wild dog’s bite took hold of me.<-

Some say that as he was dying, he gave orders to be left **unburied**, cast out so that every wild beast might have a share of him. Others say he wished to be pushed into a pit and covered with just a little dust. Still others say he wished to be thrown into the **Ilissus** <note>A river in Athens; Diogenes often spoke of his "kinship" with all creatures, even in death.</note> so that he might be useful to his brothers. Demetrius says that Alexander the Great died in **Babylon** on the very same day that Diogenes died in **Corinth**. He was an old man during the **113th Olympiad** <note>This period corresponds to approximately 324–321 BCE.</note>.

The following books are attributed to him: *Dialogues on Major Topics*, *The Fish*, *The Jackdaw*, *The Leopard*, *The Athenian People*, *The Republic* <note>original: "Politeia." This work was notorious in antiquity for its radical Cynic proposals, such as the abolition of marriage and traditional property.</note>, *The Art of Ethics*, *On Wealth*, *On Love*, *Theodorus*, *Hypsias*, *Aristarchus*, *On Death*, and his *Letters*. He is also credited with seven tragedies: *Helen*, *Thyestes*, *Hercules*, *Achilles*, *Medea*, *Chrysippus*, and *Oedipus*.

However, **Socrates** <note>This likely refers to the historian Sosicrates of Rhodes, though the transcription reads Socrates.</note> in the first book of his *Successions*, and **Satyrus** in the fourth book of his *Lives*, claim that Diogenes wrote nothing at all. Satyrus further asserts that the short tragedies were actually written by **Philiscus of Aegina**, an associate of Diogenes. **Sosion** <note>OCR reads "Sopion."</note> in his seventh book claims only these works belong to Diogenes: *On Virtue*, *On the Good*, *On Love*, *The Beggar*, *Tolmaeus*, *The Leopard*, *Cassander*, *Cephalion*, *Philiscus*, *Aristarchus*, *Sisyphus*, *Ganymede*, *Anecdotes* <note>original: "Chreiai." These were short, pithy moral stories or "useful sayings" for which the Cynics were famous.</note>, and *Letters*.

There have been five men named **Diogenes**:
First, the man from **Apollonia**, a natural philosopher <note>original: "physikos." He was known for his theory that air is the primary substance of the universe.</note>; the beginning of his treatise is as follows: *"At the start of every discourse, it seems to me necessary to provide an indisputable starting point."* 
Second, a man from **Sicyon**, who wrote about the Peloponnese. 
Third, this man himself <note>The famous Cynic.</note>. 
Fourth, a **Stoic** born in Seleucia, but called **The Babylonian** because of his neighboring region. 
Fifth, a man from **Tarsus**, who wrote on poetic problems and attempted to solve them. 

Regarding our philosopher, **Athenodorus** says in the eighth book of his *Walks* that he always appeared to be **shining** <note>original: "stilpnon." This suggests a healthy, polished, or radiant appearance.</note> because he rubbed himself with oil.

# MONIMUS.

Monimus of Syracuse was a student of Diogenes and, as Sosicrates <note>The Greek text reads Socrates, but historical context suggests the biographer Sosicrates of Rhodes is intended.</note> says, a servant to a Corinthian money-changer <term>trapezitēs</term> <note>Literally a "table-man," a banker who dealt in currency exchange and loans.</note>. Xeniades, the man who had purchased Diogenes as a slave, frequently visited this banker; by recounting Diogenes’ virtue and describing his deeds and words, he inspired in Monimus a passionate love for the philosopher. 

To gain his freedom, Monimus immediately began to feign madness; he started scattering the small change <note>original: "kerma," referring to small-denomination coins.</note> and all the money on the banking table until his master finally dismissed him. Once free, he immediately joined Diogenes. He also frequently followed Crates the Cynic and adopted a similar way of life. Seeing this, his former master was even more convinced that Monimus was truly insane. 

He became a distinguished man, such that even the comic poet Menander mentions him. In one of his plays, *The Groom* <note>original: "Hippokomos."</note>, he wrote as follows:

> There was a certain man named Monimus, Philon, a wise man;
> Rather obscure, yet he carried a small leather scrip <note>original: "pēra," the characteristic traveler's bag or wallet used by Cynic philosophers to hold their meager possessions.</note>.
> Not just one, but three scrips! And yet, by Zeus,
> He never uttered a single word resembling
> "Know Thyself," nor any of those famous, shouted slogans.
> Far beyond those, he was a beggar and filthy.
> For he declared that every human assumption is but smoke <term>typhos</term> <note>A central Cynic term referring to the "fog" of vanity, intellectual pride, or social delusion that obscures the truth.</note>.

Monimus became a very grave and serious man, such that he looked down on reputation but urged others toward the truth. He wrote "diversions" <note>original: "paignia," light-hearted or satirical works.</note> mixed with a hidden seriousness, as well as two books *On Impulses* and an *Exhortation* <note>original: "Protreptikon."</note>.

# CRATES.

Crates, the son of Ascondus, was a Theban and also one of the Dog’s <note>Referring to Diogenes of Sinope, the "Dog" philosopher from whom the term "Cynic" is derived.</note> most famous students. However, Hippobotus claims that he was not a student of Diogenes, but rather of Bryson the Achaean. The following "playful verses" <note>original: "paignia," light-hearted or parodic poems used to teach serious philosophical lessons.</note> of his are widely circulated:

> There is a city called Scrip <note>original: "Pēra," the leather bag carried by Cynic beggars. Here, Crates parodies Homer’s description of Crete to describe the ideal Cynic life.</note> in the midst of the wine-dark smoke <term>typhos</term> <note>A central Cynic concept meaning vanity, illusion, or social pretension.</note>,
> Fair and fertile, surrounded by filth, possessing nothing.
> Into this city no foolish parasite ever sails,
> Nor any lecher who delights in the backside of a prostitute,
> But it yields thyme and garlic, figs and bread.
> For these things the citizens do not wage war against each other,
> Nor do they possess weapons for the sake of small change or glory.

There is also his famous "Day-book" or journal, which goes as follows: 
"Set down for the cook: ten minae. For the doctor: one drachma. For the flatterer: ten talents. For the counselor: smoke. For the prostitute: a talent. For the philosopher: three obols." <note>This list satirizes social priorities by showing how people pay huge sums for luxury and vice (talents and minae), but almost nothing for health or wisdom (drachmas and obols).</note> 

He was also called the "Door-opener" <note>original: "Thyrepanoiktes."</note> because he would enter into every house to give advice and rebuke the inhabitants. There is also this verse of his:

> All that I have learned and thought is mine, and with the Muses 
> I have studied noble things; but all else—my vast wealth—has been snatched away by smoke <term>typhos</term>.

He also said that what he gained from philosophy was...

After converting his property into silver (for he was one of the distinguished men of the city), he collected around two hundred talents <note>An enormous sum of money in antiquity; one talent was roughly 6,000 denarii or 57 lbs of silver.</note> and distributed it to the citizens. ->In the summer, he wore a thick cloak<-

It is said that Crates’ house was destroyed by Alexander <note>Alexander the Great, during his destruction of Thebes in 335 BCE.</note>, and that of Hipparchia <note>His wife and a fellow Cynic philosopher.</note> by Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon.</note>. Often, when some of his relatives would approach him and try to turn him from his path, he would chase them away with his staff. He was a man of great resolve. Demetrius of Magnesia says that he entrusted his money to a certain banker with the agreement that if his children turned out to be ordinary people <note>original: "idiōtai," meaning non-philosophers or private citizens.</note>, he should return the money to them; but if they became philosophers, he should distribute it to the people, for if they were practicing philosophy, they would need nothing. Eratosthenes says that by Hipparchia (about whom we shall speak later), he had a son named Pasicles. When the boy reached adulthood, Crates took him to a brothel and told him that this was his "ancestral marriage." <note>This anecdote illustrates the Cynic rejection of traditional marriage rituals and their view of sex as a simple physical necessity.</note> He remarked that those who commit adultery are the subjects of tragedies, with exile and murder as their rewards, while those who visit courtesans are the subjects of comedies—for madness is the result of luxury and intoxication. This man had a brother, Pasicles, who was a student of Euclid <note>Euclid of Megara, founder of the Megarian school of philosophy.</note>. For the sake of...

<header>CRATES. Book 6</header>

Favorinus <note>A Roman-era historian and philosopher who wrote a multi-volume *Memorabilia* or collection of anecdotes.</note> mentions him in the second book of his *Memorabilia*. He says that once, when someone was petitioning the gymnasiarch <note>term: "gymnasiarch" — an official in charge of the gymnasium and the education of youths.</note>, the man touched the official’s private parts. When the official grew indignant, Crates said, "Why do you mind? Are these not yours just as much as your knees?"

He used to say that it was impossible to find a person who was entirely without a flaw, but rather that, just as in a pomegranate, there is always at least one rotten seed. 

Having provoked Nicodromus the cithara-player <note>A professional musician who played the cithara, a type of ancient lyre.</note>, Crates received a black eye. He then placed a small label on his forehead and wrote upon it: *Nicodromus did this* <note>original: "Nikodromos epoiei." This is a witty parody of how famous sculptors would sign their statues—as if his bruised face were a "work" created by the musician.</note>. 

He would deliberately insult prostitutes to train himself against being affected by verbal abuse. When Demetrius of Phalerum <note>A powerful Athenian statesman and philosopher who was eventually exiled.</note> sent him loaves of bread and wine, Crates reproached him, saying, "I wish the barley would produce loaves of bread as well" <note>This suggests Crates found the processed bread too luxurious compared to simple grain, or was mocking the gift's extravagance.</note>. It was clear from this that he drank only water. 

When he was reprimanded by the Athenian city officials <note>term: "astynomoi" — magistrates responsible for public order and decency in the streets.</note> for wearing fine linen, he said, "I will show you Theophrastus <note>The successor of Aristotle as head of the Peripatetic school.</note> wearing fine linen as well." When they didn’t believe him, he led them to a barber shop and showed them Theophrastus being shaved <note>Theophrastus was wearing the standard linen cloth used by barbers to catch hair.</note>. 

While in Thebes, he was whipped by the gymnasiarch (though others say it was in Corinth, by a man named Euthycrates). As he was being dragged away by his foot, he quoted a line from Homer <note>A parody of *Iliad* 1.591, where Hephaestus describes being thrown from heaven by Zeus.</note> with total unconcern:

> He seized me by the foot and hurled me from the celestial threshold.

Diocles, however, says he was dragged by Menedemus of Eretria. Because Crates was physically unattractive and seemed to be helping Asclepiades of Phlius <note>A philosopher and friend of Menedemus.</note>, Crates touched Menedemus’ thighs and remarked, "Asclepiades is inside." Menedemus, taking offense at the implication, dragged him away, while Crates repeated the same Homeric line.

Zeno of Citium <note>The founder of the Stoic school, who began as a student of Crates.</note> says in his *Anecdotes* that Crates once sewed a sheepskin <note>term: "kōdion" — a rough, unrefined animal skin.</note> to his philosopher's cloak <note>term: "tribōn" — the coarse, double-folded cloak that was the "uniform" of the Cynics.</note> without giving a thought to appearances. He was physically ugly to look at, and when he exercised, people would laugh at him. He was accustomed to say, raising his hands, "Take courage, Crates, for the sake of your eyes and the rest of your body! For soon you will see those who are now laughing at you being doubled over by disease, and they will call you happy while they blame themselves for their own laziness." 

He used to say that one should study philosophy until...

### METROCLES

**M**etrocles was a student of Crates and the brother of Hipparchia. He had previously been a student of Theophrastus the Peripatetic <note>term: "Peripatetic" — a member of the school of philosophy founded by Aristotle, which met in the Lyceum walk-ways (peripatoi).</note>, and had been so thoroughly corrupted by vanity that once, while practicing a speech, he accidentally broke wind <note>original: "apopardon"</note>. Out of despondency, he shut himself up at home, intending to starve himself to death. 

When Crates learned of this, he was invited to visit him. Having intentionally eaten a meal of lupins <note>term: "lupins" — a type of legume (thermos) known in antiquity for causing flatulence.</note>, he came to him. He tried to persuade Metrocles through reasoning that he had done nothing wrong, for it would be a miracle if a man did not discharge his natural gases according to nature. Finally, Crates even broke wind himself to encourage him, comforting him by matching his own actions to the "offense." From that time on, Metrocles became his student and began...

<page-num>233</page-num>
<header>METROCLES. Book 6</header>

...f Metrocles. He was a man well-versed in philosophy. This man burned his own writings (as Hecaton <note>Hecaton of Rhodes, a Stoic philosopher whose works are now lost.</note> says in the first book of his *Apophthegms*), remarking:
> These are the phantoms of netherworld dreams,
or simply "nonsense." Others say that as he was burning his notes from the lectures of Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was the successor of Aristotle. Metrocles originally studied with him before a social mishap led him to feel such shame that he turned to the Cynics for a more "natural" way of life.</note>, he recited:
> Come hither, Hephaestus; Thetis has need of you.
<note>original: "Ἥφαιστε πρόμολ' ὧδε, Θέτις νύ τι σεῖο χατίζει." This is a playful parody of a line from Homer’s *Iliad*, where the goddess Thetis calls upon the god of fire, Hephaestus. Here, Metrocles calls upon the fire to consume his old academic papers.</note>

He used to say that some things can be bought with money, like a house; but other things require time and diligence, such as education. Wealth, he said, was a harmful thing unless one used it worthily. In the end, he took his own life in old age by holding his breath. <note>The text says "strangled himself," which was a common literary trope for the death of a philosopher who felt his life was complete.</note> His students were Theombrotus and Cleomedes. Theombrotus taught Demetrius of Alexandria; Cleomedes taught Timarchus of Alexandria and Echecles of Ephesus. However, Echecles also listened to Theombrotus, and Echecles taught Menedemus, whom we shall discuss later. Menippus of Sinope <note>A famous Cynic satirist after whom "Menippean Satire" is named.</note> was also distinguished among them.

---

## HIPPARCHIA

**H**ipparchia, the sister of Metrocles, was also captured by these teachings. Both siblings were from Maroneia. She fell in love with Crates—both his words and his way of life—and paid no mind to any of her other suitors, regardless of their wealth, noble birth, or beauty. For her, Crates was everything. Indeed, she even threatened her parents that she would kill herself if she were not given to him in marriage.

Crates, having been asked by her parents to discourage the girl, did everything he could. Finally, failing to persuade her, he stood up and stripped off his gear <note>original: "σκεύην" (skeuēn). This refers to his characteristic Cynic attire: the rough cloak, the beggar's bag, and the staff.</note> right in front of her, saying: "Here is the bridegroom; this is all he owns. Decide based on this." He told her she could not be his partner unless she adopted the very same habits. The girl chose his path. Adopting the same dress as him, she went about with her husband, even appearing in public...

These and countless other stories are told of this female philosopher. There is also a book of *Letters* by Crates <note>Hipparchia’s husband and teacher.</note> in circulation, in which he philosophizes excellently; his style is at times very similar to Plato’s. He also wrote tragedies which possess a very high philosophical character. For example, he wrote:

> My fatherland is not a single tower, nor one roof;
> But every land is a city and a home
> Ready for us to dwell in.
<note>This reflects the Cynic ideal of "Cosmopolitanism"—being a citizen of the world rather than a single city-state.</note>

He died at a great age and was buried in Boeotia <note>A region in central Greece.</note>.

As he became quite a persistent beggar due to his love of money, he managed to become a citizen of Thebes. # MENIPPUS. Book 6

Hermippus states that Menippus was a "day-lender" <note>Greek: *hemerodaneistes*; a money-lender who collected interest daily, often seen as a predatory or lowly profession.</note> and was called by that name. He used to lend money at <term>maritime interest</term> <note>original: "nautikō tokō"; high-interest loans for sea voyages that were only repaid if the ship arrived safely.</note> and took property as collateral, with the result that he amassed a vast amount of wealth. > A Phoenician by race, but a Cretan hound—a daily money-lender,
> (For this was the nickname he was called), you likely know Menippus.
> When his home at Thebes was once broken into and he lost everything,
> Had he truly understood the nature of a "Dog," <note>The word "Cynic" comes from the Greek word for "Dog" (*kyon*). The joke here is that a true Cynic philosopher shouldn't care about losing money.</note> he would never have hanged himself.

Some say that his books are not actually his own, but were written by Dionysius and Zopyrus of Colophon. These men, writing for the sake of a joke, supposedly gave the works to Menippus because he was well-suited to arrange and distribute them.

There have been six men named Menippus: first, the one who wrote about the Lydians and made an abridgment of Xanthus; second, this man himself; third, Stratonikus the <term>sophist</term>, who was originally from Caria; fourth, a sculptor; fifth and sixth, both painters, both of whom are mentioned by Apollodorus. The books of the Cynic philosopher number thirteen: *The Descent to the Underworld*, *Wills*, *Polished Letters* written from the perspective of the gods, *Against the Physicists, Mathematicians, and Grammarians*, *The Birth of Epicurus*, *The Religious Festivals of the Twentieth Day* <note>The "Twentieth" (*Eikas*) was a monthly celebration held by Epicureans to honor Epicurus and Metrodorus.</note> as observed by them, and several others.

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...reaching to his feet, and around him was a crimson belt. He wore an Arcadian cap <note>original: *pilos Arkadikos*; a felt cap often associated with travelers or hunters, here part of a costume representing a Fury or a messenger from the underworld.</note> on his head, which had the twelve signs of the zodiac woven into it. He wore tragic buskins <note>original: *embatai tragikoi*; high-soled boots used by actors in Greek tragedies.</note>, a beard of great length, and carried an ash-wood staff in his hand.

These, then, are the lives of the individual Cynics. Let us now provide a sketch of their common doctrines, for we maintain that this philosophy is a distinct <term>sect</term> <note>original: *hairesin*; literally a "choice" or school of thought, from which we get the word "heresy."</note> and not, as some claim, merely a specific lifestyle. It is their view, then, that the fields of logic and physics should be discarded—much like the views of Aristo of Chios—and that one should attend only to ethics. What some record concerning Socrates, Diocles records concerning Diogenes, claiming he used to say that one must seek:

> Whatever of evil and good has been wrought in your halls. <note>A famous line from Homer’s *Odyssey* (4.392), used by philosophers to argue that practical morality at home is more important than theoretical science.</note>

They also reject the standard curriculum <note>original: *egkyklia mathemata*; the "circle of learning" or general education involving music, geometry, and rhetoric.</note>. Antisthenes, for instance, used to say that those who had become wise should not even learn to read, so that they might not be corrupted by the opinions of others. They discard geometry, music, and all such subjects. Diogenes, for example, once said to a man showing him a sundial <note>original: *hōroskopion*; literally an "hour-watcher."</note>, "This is a useful tool for ensuring one is not late for dinner." To a man showing him a musical performance, he said:

> For by the wisdom of men are cities well governed,
> And the household likewise, not by songs and trills.

They also hold that the end of life is to live according to virtue—as Antisthenes says in his *Heracles*—just as the Stoics do; for there is a certain fellowship between these two schools. Hence, they have called Cynicism the "shortcut to virtue." Indeed, Zeno of Citium <note>The founder of Stoicism, who began his studies under the Cynic Crates.</note> lived in this manner. They also advocate for living simply, using only enough food to be <term>self-sufficient</term> <note>original: *autarkeia*; the Cynic ideal of needing nothing from the outside world.</note>, and wearing only the <term>coarse cloak</term> <note>original: *tribōn*; the single, rough garment that became the standard uniform of the philosopher.</note>, while looking down upon wealth, fame, and noble birth. Some of them even subsist on nothing but herbs and cold water, making use of whatever shelters they happen upon or...

### MENEDEMUS. Book 6

...ometry, music, and all such subjects, attending instead to virtuous **habits** <note>original: *ēthesi*; the OCR fragment "θοις" likely completes the word *ēthesi*, meaning customs, characters, or habits.</note>. Just as Diogenes used to say, it is the unique property of the gods to need nothing at all, and the property of those who resemble the gods to need but very little.

It is also their conviction that virtue can be taught—as Antisthenes asserts in his work titled *Heracles* <note>Heracles was the patron hero of the Cynics, representing the strength to endure "labors" and live according to nature rather than social convention.</note>—and that once virtue is acquired, it can never be lost. They believe that the wise person is worthy of love, is free from error, and is a friend to those like themselves; they also leave nothing to the whims of chance.

As for the things that lie between virtue and vice, they call these **indifferent** <term>indifferent</term> <note>original: *adiaphora*; things that have no inherent moral value, such as wealth, health, or reputation, which do not contribute to true happiness.</note>, in the same manner as Aristo of Chios. These, then, are the Cynics. 

We must now move on to the **Stoics**, whose school was founded by Zeno, who had been a pupil of Crates.

### ZENO.

ZENO, the son of Mnaseas (or Demeas), was a native of Citium in Cyprus, a small Greek town which had received Phoenician settlers. He had his neck tilted to one side, as Timotheus the Athenian says in his work *On Lives*. Apollonius of Tyre also says that he was thin, quite tall, and dark-skinned; for which reason someone called him an "Egyptian vine-shoot" <note>original: Αἰγυπτίαν κληματίδα; a reference to his slender frame and dark complexion</note>, as Chrysippus relates in the first book of his *Proverbs*. He had thick legs, and was flabby and weak. For this reason, Persaeus says in his *Sympotic Memoirs* that he declined most invitations to dinner. It is said he took great pleasure in green figs and those dried in the sun. 

He was a student of Crates (as mentioned before). Furthermore, they say he studied under Stilpo and under Xenocrates for ten years, as Timocrates says in his *Dion*, and also under Polemon. Hecaton and Apollonius of Tyre say in the first book of their works *On Zeno* that when he consulted the oracle to ask how he might live the best life, the god replied that he should **take on the complexion of the dead** <note>original: συγχρωτίζοιτο τοῖς νεκροῖς; a pun meaning both to look pale like a corpse from intense study and to "consort" with the authors of the past</note>. Understanding this to mean he should read the works of the ancients, he acted accordingly. He came across Crates in the following way: having been engaged in the trade of **purple dye** <term>purple dye</term> <note>A highly valuable luxury commodity in the ancient world, extracted from murex sea snails</note> from Phoenicia, he was shipwrecked near...

->### ZENO. Book 7<-

...at Piraeus <note>The primary port of Athens</note> he was shipwrecked. Having come up to Athens, already thirty years old, he sat down at a bookseller's shop. While the bookseller was reading the second book of Xenophon's *Memorabilia*, Zeno was so pleased by the description of Socrates that he asked where such men were to be found in his own day. Just then, Crates the Cynic happened to pass by; the bookseller pointed to him and said, "Follow this man." From then on, Zeno became a student of Crates. He was otherwise very vigorous in his pursuit of philosophy, but he was too modest for the "shamelessness" characteristic of the Cynic school.

Therefore, Crates, wanting to cure him of this embarrassment, gave him a pot of lentil soup to carry through the Kerameikos <note>The "Potters' Quarter," a busy public area in Athens</note>. When Crates saw that Zeno was ashamed and was trying to hide the pot under his cloak, he struck the pot with his staff and broke it. As Zeno ran away with the lentil soup running down his legs, Crates called out, "Why do you run, my little Phoenician? <note>original: φοινικίδιον; a diminutive nickname referencing Zeno's heritage</note> Nothing terrible has happened to you!"

For a while, Zeno remained a student of Crates. During this time, he wrote his *Republic*, which some jokingly said he wrote "on the tail of the dog" <note>A pun on "Cynic," which is derived from the Greek word for "dog-like."</note>. In addition to the *Republic*, he also wrote the following works: *On the <gloss>according to</gloss> Nature Life*, *On Impulse (or On the Nature of Man)*, *On Passions*, *On Duty*, *On Law*, *On Greek Education*, *On Sight*, *On the Universe*, *On Signs*, *Pythagorean Matters*, *General Matters*, *On Styles of Speech*, *Five Homeric Problems*, and *On Poetic Hearing*. There are also works of his titled *Technical Solutions*, two books of *Refutations*, *Memorabilia*, and the *Ethics of Crates*.

These are his books. Eventually, however, he left Crates and studied under the teachers mentioned previously <note>Stilpo, Xenocrates, and Polemon</note> for twenty years. This led him to say, as they report: "I made a prosperous voyage when I suffered a shipwreck." Others say he said this specifically in reference to his time with Crates. Others claim that while he was staying in Athens, he heard the news of his shipwreck and said, "Fortune does well to drive us toward philosophy." Some, however, say he stayed in Athens to sell his cargo and only then turned to philosophy. He used to walk to and fro in the "Painted Stoa," which is also called the "Stoa of Peisianax"...

<summary>Zeno begins his philosophical education in Athens under the Cynic Crates after a shipwreck, eventually transitioning to other teachers and writing many of the foundational texts of Stoicism.</summary>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
**Page 240**

...decorated by Polygnotus <note>A famous 5th-century BCE Greek painter</note>, known as the **Painted Stoa** <note>original: ποικίλη (Poikile); a public colonnade in the Athenian marketplace</note>, he held his discourses, wishing to make the place a peaceful sanctuary. For under the Thirty <note>The "Thirty Tyrants," a pro-Spartan oligarchy that ruled Athens in 404 BCE after the Peloponnesian War</note>, fourteen hundred citizens had been put to death there. From then on, people came to hear him and were called **Stoics**, and his followers were named likewise, though they were previously called **Zenonians**, as Epicurus also mentions in his letters. Earlier, the poets who spent their time there were called "Stoics," according to Eratosthenes in his eighth book *On the Ancient Comedy*; these poets had further increased the fame of the place. 

The Athenians held Zeno in such high regard that they even entrusted him with the keys to the city walls, and they honored him with a golden crown and a bronze statue. His own fellow citizens in Citium <note>Zeno’s birthplace on Cyprus</note> did the same, considering the man’s statue to be an ornament to their city. The Citians living in Sidon <note>A Phoenician port city in modern Lebanon</note> also laid claim to him. Antigonus <note>Antigonus II Gonatas, King of Macedonia</note> also admired him, and whenever he came to Athens, he would listen to him; he frequently invited Zeno to come and visit him in Macedonia. 

Zeno declined this invitation, but he sent Persaeus, one of his acquaintances, who was the son of Demetrius and a native of Citium. Persaeus was in his prime around the hundred and thirtieth Olympiad <note>Approximately 260–256 BCE</note>, when Zeno was already an old man. The letter from Antigonus was written in this manner, as Apollonius of Tyre says in his works *On Zeno*:

-> King Antigonus to Zeno the philosopher, greetings. <-

> I consider myself superior to you in fortune and glory, but I believe I fall behind you in reason and education, and in that perfect happiness which you possess. Therefore, I have decided to invite you to come to me, being persuaded that you will not refuse my request. Try, then, by all means to meet with me, understanding this: that you will not be the teacher of me alone, but of all the Macedonians together. For he who educates and leads the ruler of Macedonia toward virtue clearly prepares all his subjects to be virtuous as well.

->King Antigonus, Zeno sends greetings.<-

I welcome your love of learning <note>original: φιλομάθειαν (philomatheian)</note>, in so far as you hold fast to that education which is true and tends toward utility, rather than that which is common and leads to the corruption of morals, as one who yearns for philosophy. <margin>5.</margin> By turning away from the much-talked-about pleasure <note>A reference to the rival Epicurean school, which prioritized pleasure (hedoné) as the highest good</note>, which weakens the souls of some young men, you show yourself to be inclined toward nobility not only by nature but also by choice. But I am confined by a body weakened by old age (for I am eighty years old <note>The Greek text here literally says "twenty and eighty," though Zeno’s age at this time is traditionally cited as eighty or older</note>); therefore I cannot meet with you. I am, however, sending you some of my own fellow students <note>original: σχολαστῶν (scholastōn)</note> who are not behind me in the qualities of the soul, and who surpass me in those of the body; by living with them, you will fall behind no one in those things that lead to perfect <margin>15.</margin> happiness.

### ZENO. Book VII

...led him away. It is said that he was somewhat difficult to associate with <note>original: ἀσυμφέροφορος (asympherophoros); suggesting he was austere or didn't care for social niceties</note>. At any rate, they say that King Antigonus often came to carouse with him, and once even brought Aristocles the cithara-player with him to a revel, but Zeno eventually slipped away. He also avoided crowds, it is said, so much so that he would sit at the very end of a bench, thereby saving himself from half the annoyance of being squeezed by others. 

Moreover, he never walked with more than two or three companions. Sometimes he would even demand a small copper coin <note>original: χαλκόν (chalkon)</note> from those who stood around him, so that they would not trouble him, as Cleanthes says in his work *On Bronze*. Once, when many people were crowding around him, he pointed to a wooden railing around an altar at the end of the Stoa <note>The "Stoa Poikile" or Painted Porch, where Zeno taught and from which "Stoicism" takes its name</note> and said, "This once stood in the middle, but because it was in the way, it was placed to the side. If you would likewise take yourselves out of the middle, you would trouble us less."

When Demochares, the son of Laches, greeted him and told him to speak or write to him regarding anything he might need from Antigonus—promising that the King would provide everything—Zeno heard this and never associated with him again. It is said that after Zeno’s death, Antigonus remarked, "What a theater I have lost!" <note>The King likely meant that Zeno’s life was a public spectacle of virtue worth watching</note>. For this reason, he used Thrason as an envoy to request from the Athenians that Zeno be buried in the Ceramicus <note>The state cemetery of Athens</note>. When asked why he admired Zeno so much, the King replied, "Because, though I gave him many great gifts, he was never puffed up, nor was he ever seen to be humble."

He was also a man of great inquiry, and was precise about all matters. This is why Timon, in his *Silloi* <note>original: Σίλλοις (Sillois); Satires written by Timon of Phlius to mock various philosophers</note>, says:

> And I saw a Phoenician woman, a greedy old crone in shadowy pride,
> Longing for all things; her little basket was perishing,
> Being small, and she had a mind smaller than a skindapsos.
> <note>Timon mocks Zeno’s Phoenician roots and his perceived vanity. A "skindapsos" was a term for a four-stringed instrument or a word used by grammarians to signify something meaningless or of no value.</note>

He used to dispute quite diligently with Philo the Dialectician and would study with him. Because of this, he was admired by the younger Zeno, no less than by his own teacher, Diodorus <note>Diodorus Cronus, a famous dialectician of the Megarian school</note>. There were also certain "naked-and-dirty" followers <note>original: γυμνορρύπαροί (gymnorryparoi); a reference to the Cynics or those who adopted extreme poverty as a lifestyle</note> who gathered around him...

He himself was gloomy and bitter, with a face that was always pinched. He was also extremely cheap, possessing a "barbaric stinginess" <note>original: βαρβαρικῆς μικρολογίας (barbarikēs mikrologias); a common contemporary jab at Zeno’s non-Greek, Phoenician origins</note> which he disguised under the pretense of "financial management." If he were to rebuke someone, he did so indirectly and with restraint, keeping his distance rather than being blunt. 

For instance, he spoke thus regarding a man who was behaving like a dandy. As the man was hesitantly stepping over a gutter, Zeno said, "You are right to look down at the mud, for you certainly cannot see your reflection in it." <note>A witty insult suggesting the man was so vain he only looked at the ground to find a mirror</note> 

When a certain Cynic philosopher claimed he had no oil in his flask and asked Zeno for some, Zeno refused to give him any. However, after the man had left, Zeno told his students to "flip a finger" <note>original: σκιμαλίσαι (skimalisai); an obscene or mocking gesture, likely the middle finger</note> at him to see which of the two was truly more shameless.

Being romantically attracted to Chremonides, he once sat down while both Chremonides and Cleanthes were sitting nearby, but then he immediately stood up and moved away. When Cleanthes wondered why, Zeno said, "I hear from the best physicians that the most effective remedy for inflammations <note>referring here to the 'heat' of passion or desire</note> is quiet and rest." 

Once, when two men were reclining together at a drinking party, and the one positioned above was kicking the one below him with his foot, Zeno himself gave the kicker a nudge with his knee. When the man turned around to complain, Zeno asked, "What do you think the person below you suffers at your hands?"

To a man who was overly fond of boys, he remarked that neither the teachers—who spend all their time among children—nor the boys themselves possessed any real sense. 

He used to say that the speech of unrefined people, even if unpolished, was like Alexandrian silver coinage: it is pleasing to the eye and well-struck, but it is no better for its appearance. Conversely, he compared the speech of the wise to the Attic tetradrachms <note>The "Owl" coins of Athens, famous for their high silver purity but often crudely manufactured</note>; though they were struck at random and were "unpolished" <note>original: σολοίκοις (soloikois); a play on words meaning both 'grammatical errors' and 'roughly made'</note>, they often outweighed the most elegantly phrased words.

When his disciple Ariston was discoursing at length—not without talent, but sometimes recklessly and boldly—Zeno remarked, "It is impossible to say that your father did not conceive you while he was drunk." Because of this, he called Ariston a "chatterbox," since Zeno himself was a man of few words <note>original: βραχυλόγος (brachylogos)</note>. To a glutton, who...

### ->ZENO. Book 7<-

...leaving nothing for his companions. Once, when a large fish was served, he picked it up as if he intended to eat the whole thing himself. When his companion stared at him, Zeno said, "What do you think your companions suffer every day, if you cannot bear my gluttony <note>original: ὀψοφαγίαν (opsophagian); specifically referring to the love of rich side-dishes or delicacies like fish</note> for even one day?" 

When a youth was asking a question that was more meddlesome than was appropriate for his age, Zeno led him to a mirror and told him to look into it. Then he asked the boy if such questions seemed to suit a face like that. 

To a man who claimed that he did not like Antisthenes <note>A student of Socrates and a precursor to the Cynics</note> for the most part, Zeno brought up an anecdote <term>chreia: a brief, useful anecdote about a famous person</term> regarding Sophocles, and asked if he thought Sophocles also had some beautiful qualities. When the man said he didn't know, Zeno replied, "Are you not ashamed then, that if something bad was said by Antisthenes, you pick it out and remember it; but if something is good, you do not even attempt to grasp it?" 

When someone remarked that the little arguments of philosophers seemed very small to him, Zeno said, "You speak the truth; however, even their syllables ought to be short, if possible." 

When someone told him that Polemo <note>Head of the Platonic Academy and one of Zeno’s teachers</note> proposed one topic but spoke on another, Zeno frowned and said, "At what price then did he value the things being given to him?"

He used to say that a speaker, much like stage actors, should have a great voice and great power; however, they should not pull the mouth too wide—which is a habit of those who talk a lot but have no real ability. 

He said that when something is well-said, there should be no "room" left for the audience to look around, just as one does not look away from the work of good craftsmen. On the contrary, the listener should be so intent on what is being said that they do not even have time to take notes <note>original: ἐπισημείωσιν (episēmeiōsin); refers to marking or noting down points during a lecture</note>. 

To a youth who was talking far too much, he said, "Your ears have run down into your tongue." 

To a handsome man who remarked that it did not seem to him that a wise man would ever fall in love, Zeno replied, "Then nothing will be more miserable than you handsome people!" <note>Zeno implies that if wise men—the only ones capable of true love—stayed away from the beautiful, the beautiful would be deprived of the most worthy companionship</note>.

He also used to say that most philosophers were unwise in many major things, and in small or accidental matters, they were simply ignorant. He would cite the case of Kaphesias <note>A famous flute-player known for his teaching methods</note>. When one of Kaphesias' students was striving to blow the flute with a great, puffed-up sound, Kaphesias struck him...

Zeno used to say that pride <note>original: τῦφος (typhos); literally "smoke" or "mist," used by philosophers to describe vanity, delusion, or intellectual arrogance</note> was the most unseemly of all things, especially in the young. He taught that one should not merely memorize sounds and words, but occupy the mind with the intended meaning and application <term>chreia: a brief, useful anecdote or maxim with a moral purpose</term> of the lesson, rather than receiving information like a stew or a culinary preparation. He also said that the young should practice every kind of orderliness in their gait, their bearing, and their dress. He said that nothing was more foreign to the grasping of the sciences than poetry; and that there is nothing we are so much in need of as time. When asked "What is a friend?", he replied, "Another self." It is said that once he was flogging a slave for theft. When the slave said, "It was my fate to steal," Zeno replied, "And to be beaten as well." He said that beauty is the flower of the voice; others say he called the voice the flower of beauty. Seeing one of his acquaintances' young slaves covered in bruises, he said to the man, "I see the tracks of your anger." To a man anointed with perfume, he said, "Who is this who smells like a woman?"

To a chatterbox of a youth, he said, "The reason we have two ears and only one mouth is so that we may hear more and speak less." ### ZENO. Book VII.

...invited him to report back to the King that there was someone present who knew how to be silent. Those who had asked him this were ambassadors who had arrived from Ptolemy, and they wished to learn what they should say about him to the King. When Zeno was asked how he felt about being insulted, he said, "The same as if an envoy were sent back without an answer."

Apollonius of Tyre says that when Crates <note>Crates of Thebes was a famous Cynic philosopher and Zeno's first teacher.</note> tried to drag him by his cloak away from Stilpo <note>Stilpo was a philosopher of the Megarian school; Zeno was known for "shopping around" different schools of thought.</note>, Zeno said, "O Crates, the proper handle for philosophers is the one by the ears; so persuade me and lead me that way. But if you use force, my body will be with you, but my soul will remain with Stilpo." 

He also studied with Diodorus, according to Hippobotus, under whom he worked hard at dialectics <term>dialectic: the formal logic and art of debating used by ancient philosophers</term>. As he progressed, he also attended the lectures of Polemo out of a lack of vanity <note>original: ἀτυφίας (atyphias); literally "freedom from smoke," referring to Zeno’s lack of intellectual arrogance despite his own growing fame</note>. Consequently, they say Polemo remarked, "You do not escape my notice, Zeno, slipping in through the garden doors and stealing my doctrines, only to dress them up in Phoenician style." <note>Polemo, head of the Academy, is joking that Zeno—who was from the Phoenician colony of Citium—was simply rebranding the Academy's old ideas as his own new Stoic system.</note> 

When a dialectician showed him seven dialectical forms in "The Reaper" argument <term>The Reaper: a famous logical paradox used to challenge notions of time and possibility</term> and asked what fee he charged, Zeno, hearing it was a hundred drachmas, gave him two hundred. So great was his devotion to learning. They say he was also the first to name "duty" <term>kathekon: a technical Stoic term meaning 'appropriate action' or 'moral obligation'</term> and wrote a treatise on it. He used to rewrite Hesiod’s verses in this way:

<margin>»</margin>
> He is best of all who obeys one who speaks well.
> Good, in turn, is he who himself understands all things.

<note>Zeno famously reversed Hesiod's original order. Hesiod claimed the self-thinker was best; Zeno argued the one who listens to good advice is better because they combine understanding with the action of being persuaded.</note>

For he argued that the one capable of listening well to what is said and making use of it is superior to the one who has understood everything by himself. For the latter has only understanding; but the one who is well-persuaded adds action to it. 

<margin>κ</margin>
When asked (they say) why he was so cheerful when drinking despite being so naturally austere, he replied, "Lupines <note>original: θέρμοι (thermoi); a common, bitter bean</note> are bitter, but when soaked they become sweet." Hecato also says in the second book of his *Anecdotes* that he would let himself go in such social gatherings. He used to say it was better to slip with the feet than with the tongue. He also taught that "well-being" is achieved by small steps, but it is no small thing. Others...

### ZENO. Book VII.

**Socrates.** <note>The author likely starts here by comparing Zeno's character to that of Socrates, the ultimate model of philosophical endurance.</note> In this regard, Zeno was most enduring and most frugal, subsisting on uncooked food <note>original: ἀπύρῳ τροφῇ (apyro trophe); referring to a diet of raw vegetables, fruits, and bread that required no cooking fire</note> and wearing a thin, cheap cloak. > Neither icy winter, nor the endless rain,
> Nor the sun’s flame subdues him, nor dreadful disease,
> Not like one who counts for nothing among the people, but he, tireless,
> Devotes himself night and day to teaching.

The comic poets, indeed, were unknowingly praising him through their jokes; thus Philemon says as follows in his play *The Philosophers*:

> For bread, a bit of relish, a dried fig, and water to wash it down.
> For he practices a new kind of philosophy:
> He teaches how to be hungry, and yet he finds students!

Others attribute these lines to Posidippus. Indeed, his reputation almost passed into a proverb; at any rate, it was a common saying about him: "More self-controlled than the philosopher Zeno." Even Posidippus says in his play *The Transferred*:

> So that in ten days he seemed to be more self-controlled than Zeno.

For in truth, he surpassed everyone in this quality, and in dignity, and—by Zeus—even in happiness. For he ended his life having lived ninety-eight years, remaining free from disease and healthy throughout. But Persaeus says in his *Ethical Lectures* that he died at seventy-two, and that he came to Athens at twenty-two. Apollonius, however, says that he presided over the school <term>schole: the Stoic school of philosophy, which met in the Painted Stoa (Stoa Poikile) in Athens</term> for fifty-eight years <note>original: ἔτη δυοῖν δέοντα ἑξήκοντα (ete dyoin deonta hexekonta); literally "years wanting two of sixty"</note>. 

He died in the following way: as he was leaving the school, he tripped and broke a toe. Striking the ground with his hand, he quoted the line from the play *Niobe*: 

-> "I am coming; why do you call me?" <- 
<note>This quote comes from a lost tragedy about Niobe. Zeno interprets his accidental injury as a signal from the gods or nature that it is time for him to depart life.</note>

And he died on the spot, having strangled himself <note>original: ἀποπνίξας ἑαυτόν (apopnixas heauton); ancient sources often claim Zeno died by voluntarily holding his breath, a feat of the will consistent with Stoic mastery over the body.</note>. The Athenians buried him in the Kerameikos <note>The Kerameikos was the city's most prestigious public cemetery.</note> and honored him with the aforementioned decrees, bearing witness to his virtue. The author composed these lines:

For some say he ended his life in this way. So much for his death. # DIOGENES LAERTIUS
## BOOK VII.

Upon arriving in Athens, Zeno is said to have associated with Crates <note>Crates of Thebes, a famous teacher of the Cynic school, which emphasized living simply and according to nature.</note>. <margin>...ι-</margin> It is also said that he himself feared the ultimate end (φασὶ) of those who wander <margin>...ε-</margin> regarding their judgments <note>This likely refers to the confusion of those who lack a firm philosophical foundation.</note>. They say he used to swear by the "caper-bush," <margin>...σε-</margin> just as Socrates used to swear by "the dog." However, some people <margin>...πε-</margin> (among whom are the followers of Cassius the Skeptic), bringing many charges <margin>...χρη-</margin> against Zeno, first claim that he declares <term>general education</term> <note>original: "ἐγκύκλιον παιδείαν" (enkyklion paideian); the standard curriculum of the time, including grammar, logic, and rhetoric</note> to be <margin>...στου</margin> useless at the beginning of his *Republic*. Second, they say <margin>...του</margin> that he describes all those who are not virtuous as being <margin>...στου</margin> enemies, foes, slaves, and aliens to one another—even parents <margin>...τη</margin> to their children, brothers to brothers, and relatives to relatives. Again, <margin>...ου</margin> in his *Republic*, he introduces only the virtuous as citizens, friends, <margin>...του</margin> family, and free men. Consequently, for the Stoics, parents <margin>...σε</margin> and children are enemies if they are not wise. He also lays down the <margin>...ου</margin> doctrine that wives should be held in common, likewise in his *Republic*. <margin>...πε</margin> And according to the two hundred <note>Likely referring to the number of lines or a specific section of the text</note>, he states that neither <margin>...με</margin> temples, nor law-courts, nor gymnasia should be built <margin>...σε</margin> in cities. Regarding currency, he writes that <margin>...πε</margin> one should not think it necessary to produce coinage for the sake of <margin>...με</margin> exchange or for travel abroad. He also commands men and <margin>...σε</margin> women to wear the same clothing and that no part <margin>...πε</margin> of the body should be hidden. That the *Republic* <margin>...με</margin> is indeed Zeno’s work is confirmed by Chrysippus in his own work *On the Republic*. <margin>...σε</margin> He also discusses erotic matters at the beginning of the work titled *The Art of Love*. Furthermore, he writes similar things in his *Discourses*.

Reports of this nature are found in the writings of Cassius, and also in the works of Isidorus the rhetorician of Pergamum. Isidorus says that these "shameful" passages written by the Stoics were actually cut out of the books by Athenodorus the Stoic, who was entrusted with the library at Pergamum. However, the passages were later restored when Athenodorus was caught and put in danger. So much for the works of his that are disputed.

-># ZENO. Book VII.<-

...the third <gloss>is</gloss> from Rhodes, who wrote a specific history of his own country; the fourth is an historian, who wrote the history of Pyrrhus's campaigns in Italy and Sicily, as well as an epitome of the deeds of both the Romans and the Carthaginians; the fifth was a disciple of Chrysippus, who wrote few books but left behind a great many students; the sixth was a physician of the school of Herophilus <note>Herophilus was a famous Alexandrian physician known for early anatomical studies; Zeno the physician was capable of understanding medicine but, as the text says, "lacked the energy to write."</note>, capable in understanding but weak in writing; the seventh was a grammarian, whose epigrams, among other works, are still circulated; the eighth was Sidonian by birth, an Epicurean philosopher, who was clear both in his thinking and his expression.

The disciples of Zeno were many, and many were famous. There was Persaeus, the son of Demetrius, of Citium, whom some call a close friend, while others claim he was a household servant—one of those sent to Zeno by King Antigonus <note>Antigonus II Gonatas, the King of Macedonia and a patron of Zeno.</note> to serve as a copyist. Persaeus also acted as a tutor to the King’s son, Halcyoneus. On one occasion, Antigonus, wishing to put Persaeus to the test, had a false message brought to him claiming that his estates had been seized by the enemy. When Persaeus's face fell and he became gloomy, the King remarked:

> "Do you see," he said, "that wealth is not an <term>indifferent</term>?" <note>original: "ἀδιάφορον" (adiaphoron). A core Stoic doctrine was that external things like wealth or health are "indifferent"—neither good nor bad for one’s moral character. Persaeus's distress proved he still valued wealth as a "good."</note>

The following books are attributed to Persaeus: *On Kingship*, *The Spartan Constitution*, *On Marriage*, *On Impiety*, *Thyestes*, *On Loves*, *Exhortations*, eight books of *Discourses*, *Moral Anecdotes*, and seven books of *Notes on Plato’s Laws*.

Other pupils included Ariston, the son of Miltiades, of Chios, who introduced the doctrine of absolute indifference; Herillus of Carthage, who claimed that knowledge was the <term>end</term> <note>original: "τέλος" (telos); the ultimate goal or "chief good" of life.</note> of all things; and Dionysius, known as "the Renegade" because he converted to the school of Pleasure <note>The Epicurean school.</note>. Due to a severe affliction of the eyes, he could no longer bring himself to say that pain was "indifferent." This Dionysius was from Heraclea. There was also Sphaerus of Bosporus, and Cleanthes, the son of Phanias, of Assos, who succeeded Zeno as head of the school. Zeno used to compare Cleanthes to hard wax tablets, which are difficult to write upon but preserve what is written once it is inscribed. Sphaerus also studied under Cleanthes after Zeno's death; we shall speak of him in the section on Cleanthes. According to Hippobotus, Athenodorus of Soli and Philonides were also students of Zeno...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Zeno of Citium, shifting from a list of men who shared his name and his immediate disciples to a systematic overview of the Stoic school of philosophy. -># DIOG. LAERT.<-

...the Theban; Colotes of Corinth; Posidonius of Alexandria; and Zeno of Sidon. I have decided to discuss the Stoic doctrines in general within this life of Zeno, because he was the founder <note>original: "κτίστην" (ktisten) — literally a "builder" or "colonizer," used here to mean the architect of the school's ideology.</note> of the sect. He wrote many books, and in them he spoke with an eloquence unmatched by any other Stoic. Their doctrines, in general, are as follows. I shall present them in summary, just as I am accustomed to doing for the other schools.

They say that philosophical discourse <note>original: "λόγον" (logon) — here meaning the structured study or reasoning of philosophy.</note> is divided into three parts: one part is **Physical**, another is **Ethical**, and another is **Logical**. Zeno of Citium was the first to divide it in this way in his work *On Reason*, as did Chrysippus in the first book of his *On Reason* and the first book of his *Physics*; as well as Apollodorus the son of Ephillus in the first book of his *Introduction to Doctrines*, Eudromus in his *Elements of Ethics*, Diogenes the Babylonian, and Posidonius. 

Apollodorus calls these parts "topics" <note>original: "τόπους" (topous) — specific areas of inquiry.</note>, while Chrysippus and Eudromus call them "species," and others call them "genera." They compare philosophy to a living creature: **Logic** they liken to the bones and sinews; **Ethics** to the fleshier parts; and **Physics** to the soul. 

They also compare it to an egg: the outermost part is **Logic** <note>The shell.</note>; the next part is **Ethics** <note>The white.</note>; and the innermost part is **Physics** <note>The yolk.</note>. Or to a fertile field: the surrounding fence is **Logic**; the fruit produced is **Ethics**; and the earth or the trees are **Physics**. Or again, to a well-walled city, governed according to reason.

Some of them say that no part is to be preferred over another, but that they are all intermingled; for this reason, they delivered their teachings as a mixture. Others, however, place **Logic** first, **Physics** second, and **Ethics** third; among these are Zeno in his work *On Reason*, Chrysippus, Archedemus, and Eudemus. Diogenes of Ptolemais begins with **Ethics**; Apollodorus places **Ethics** second; while Panaetius and Posidonius begin with **Physics**, as stated by Phanias, a student of Posidonius, in the first book of his...
