-># ZENO. Book 7.<-

...of the Stoic schools. But <term>Cleanthes</term> <note>Cleanthes of Assos (c. 330–230 BCE) was the second head of the Stoic school, succeeding Zeno of Citium.</note> says there are six parts: the **Dialectical**, the **Rhetorical**, the **Ethical**, the **Political**, the **Physical**, and the **Theological**. Others, however, say these are not parts of the discourse itself, but of philosophy as a whole—this is the view held by Zeno of Tarsus. 

Some say the **Logical** part is divided into two sciences: **Rhetoric** and **Dialectic**. Certain others add a third "definitive" part <note>original: "ὁρικὸν" (horikon)</note> which deals with rules and criteria <note>original: "κανόνων καὶ κριτηρίων" (kanonōn kai kritēriōn) — the standards used to judge truth.</note>. Some, however, exclude this definitive part. Those who include the study of rules and criteria do so as a means to discover the truth; for it is in this study that they refine the differences between our mental impressions. Similarly, they include the definitive part for the recognition of truth, because things are understood through concepts <note>original: "ἐννοιῶν" (ennoiōn).</note>.

They define **Rhetoric** as the science of speaking well in continuous <note>long-form or oratorical</note> discourse, and **Dialectic** as the science of conversing correctly in discourse consisting of questions and answers. Because of this, they also define Dialectic as the "science of things true, false, and neither."

They say that **Rhetoric** itself has three parts:
1. **Advisory** <note>original: "συμβουλευτικόν" — also known as deliberative rhetoric, used in politics.</note>
2. **Forensic** <note>original: "δικανικόν" — used in legal settings.</note>
3. **Encomiastic** <note>original: "ἐγκωμιαστικόν" — used for praise or ceremonial speeches.</note>

They further divide Rhetoric into invention, style, arrangement, and delivery. A rhetorical speech is divided into the introduction, the narrative, the replies to opponents, and the epilogue.

**Dialectic**, they say, is divided into the topic of "things signified" <note>original: "σημαινομένων" (sēmainomenōn) — the meanings or concepts behind words.</note> and the topic of "utterance" <note>original: "φωνῆς" (phōnēs) — the actual sounds or speech.</note>. The part concerning things signified is divided into the study of mental impressions and the resulting "sayables" <note>original: "λεκτῶν" (lekta) — a technical Stoic term for the underlying meaning of a statement that can be expressed in language.</note>. This includes propositions, complete expressions, predicates <note>original: "κατηγορημάτων" (katēgorēmatōn)</note>, and similar direct and indirect forms, as well as genera and species. 

In the same way, they study arguments, moods, and syllogisms, and the various fallacies <note>original: "σοφισμάτων" (sophismatōn)</note> that arise from language or from the things themselves. These include:
* The **"Liar"** argument <note>A paradox such as: "If I say I am lying, am I telling the truth?"</note>
* The **"True-Teller"** and **"Negator"** arguments
* The **"Sorites"** <note>original: "σωρείτας" (sōreitas) — also called the "Heap" paradox: at what point does a collection of grains become a "heap"?</note> and similar types
* Arguments that are incomplete, unsolvable, or concluding
* The **"Veiled"** argument <note>also known as the "Electra" paradox.</note>
* The **"Horned"** argument <note>A trap such as: "Have you lost your horns? If you say yes, you had them; if no, you still have them."</note>
* The **"Nobody"** argument <note>original: "οὔτιδας" (outidas).</note>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...are divided. They say that a specific area of **Dialectic** is the aforementioned topic concerning the **voice** itself. In this area, the "articulated voice" <note>original: "ἐγγράμματος φωνή" (engrammatos phōnē) — literally "voice that can be written," referring to human speech as opposed to animal sounds.</note> is demonstrated, as well as the various parts of speech. It also covers **solecism** <note>A grammatical mistake or absurdity.</note>, **barbarism** <note>The use of non-standard or foreign words.</note>, poems, ambiguities, melodic voice, and music. According to some, it also includes the study of **definitions** <term>horōn — boundaries or formal descriptions of things</term>, divisions, and vocabulary.

They claim that the theory of **syllogisms** <note>The source text here reads "most useless" (achrestotatēn), but given the context that follows—describing its great contribution to logic—most scholars believe this is an error for "most useful" (chrēsimōtatēn).</note> is most useful. For it reveals the nature of proof, which contributes greatly to the correction of doctrines; it also provides order and aids the memory by revealing the "authoritative grasp" <note>original: "ἐπιστατικὸν κατάλημμα" (epistatikon katalēmma) — a firm, scientific comprehension.</note> of a subject. An **argument** itself is a structure composed of premises and a conclusion; a **syllogism** is a logical argument formed from these. Furthermore, they define **proof** as an argument that, by using things more clearly grasped, concludes something previously less grasped.

A **mental impression** <term>phantasia</term> is defined as an "imprinting" in the soul. The name is appropriately borrowed from the impressions made in wax by a signet ring. Of these impressions, some are **apprehensive** <note>original: "καταληπτική" (katalēptikē) — an impression so clear it "seizes" the mind with its truth.</note> and others are **non-apprehensive**. The **apprehensive** impression—which they say is the true "criterion" or standard for judging reality—is that which comes from a real object, is in accordance with that object itself, and has been stamped and impressed upon the mind. The **non-apprehensive** impression is one that does not come from a real object; or, if it does come from a real object, it does not correspond to it—it is an impression that is neither clear nor distinct.

**Dialectic** itself is considered a necessary tool and a **virtue** <note>The Stoics famously argued that logic and dialectic were not just tools, but moral virtues, because they prevent the mind from falling into error.</note> that encompasses several specific virtues:
1. **Freedom from Precipitancy** <term>apropsotōsia</term>: the knowledge of when one ought to give assent to an idea and when one should not.
2. **Freedom from Heedlessness** <term>aneikaiotēta</term>: a strong reason that resists the merely "probable," so as not to give in to it easily.
3. **Irrefutability** <term>anelexia</term>: strength in argument so as not to be led by it into a contradiction.
4. **Freedom from Vanity** <term>amataiotēta</term>: a mental habit that refers all impressions back to "right reason."

They define **knowledge** itself as either a "secure apprehension" or a mental habit in the acceptance of impressions that is unchangeable by...

# ZENO. Book 7

...of reason. They hold that without **dialectical theory**, the wise man will not be **infallible** in argument. For by this study, truth and falsehood are distinguished, and the persuasive and the **ambiguous** <note>original: "ἀμφιβόλως λεγόμενον" (amphibolōs legomenon) — speech that can be interpreted in two ways.</note> are discerned. Without it, it is not possible to ask and answer questions properly. 

They also claim that **precipitancy** <term>propeteian — the habit of giving assent to a perception before it has been fully grasped</term> in making assertions extends even to our actions; therefore, those with untrained **impressions** <term>phantasias — the mental images or "appearances" we receive from the world</term> fall into disorder and randomness. In no other way can the wise man appear sharp, quick-witted, and generally skilled in reason; for it belongs to the same person to converse and reason correctly, to discuss the topics at hand, and to answer what is asked—all of which are considered by logicians to be the hallmarks of a man experienced in dialectic. 

These are their views in summary. To speak in more detail, we may add those things which pertain to their introductory art, as **Diocles of Magnes** sets them down in his *Survey of Philosophers*, saying the following:

> The **Stoics** prefer to put the discourse on **mental impressions** and **sensation** first, because the **criterion** <term>kritērion — the "test" or "standard" by which we judge truth</term> by which the truth of things is known is, in its genus, an impression; and because the discourse on **assent** <note>original: "συγκατάθεσις" (synkatathesis) — the mental act of accepting an impression as true.</note>, **grasping** <term>katalēpsis — a firm mental hold on a fact</term>, and **thought** cannot be established without an impression. For the impression comes first, and then **thought**, being capable of expression, brings out in speech what it experiences from the impression.

An **impression** <term>phantasia</term> differs from a **phantom** <term>phantasma</term>. For a phantom is a "seeming" of the mind such as occurs in sleep; but an impression is an **imprinting** <term>typōsis</term> in the soul—that is, an **alteration**—as **Chrysippus** <note>The third head of the Stoic school and its most prolific logician.</note> maintains in the twelfth book of his work *On the Soul*. For we should not take "imprinting" to mean something like the mark of a signet ring; since it is impossible for many imprints to exist at the same time in the same place. Rather, an impression is understood to be that which is molded by a real object in accordance with that object...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...**grasping** <note>The previous page ended mid-word; the Greek term here is "katalepsis," meaning a firm mental hold on an object.</note> and is imprinted and sealed, such as could not come from that which does not exist. Of **impressions** <term>phantasiōn — mental images or presentations of the world</term> (according to them), some are sensory and others are not. Sensory impressions are those received through a sense or the sense organs; non-sensory are those received through the mind, such as the impressions of **incorporeal things** <note>Things that lack a physical body, such as time or empty space.</note> and other things grasped by reason. Of the sensory impressions, those that arise from existing objects occur with yielding and **assent** <note>original: "συγκατάθεσις" (synkatathesis) — the mental act of agreeing that a perception is true.</note>. Among impressions, there are also "presentations" as long as they arise from existing objects. 

Of impressions, some are rational and others are irrational. Rational impressions are those belonging to rational animals; irrational are those of irrational animals. These rational impressions are called **thoughts**; the irrational ones have not received a specific name. Furthermore, some are **professional** <note>original: "τεχνικαί" (technikai) — skilled or artistic.</note> and others are **unskilled**. For an image is viewed in one way by an artist, and in another way by a person without that skill.

**Sensation** <term>aisthēsis — perception through the senses</term> is defined by the **Stoics** as the **spirit** <term>pneuma — a physical "breath" or tension that transmits information</term> that extends from the **ruling part** <term>hēgemonikon — the commanding part of the soul, located in the heart</term> to the senses. It also refers to the grasping that occurs through these senses, as well as the physical structure of the sense organs (by which some people may become impaired). The actual activity itself is also called sensation.

**Grasping** <term>katalēpsis — a clear and certain comprehension</term> occurs, according to them, by sensation in the case of white and black things, or rough and smooth ones. However, it occurs by reason in the case of conclusions drawn through demonstration, such as the fact that the gods exist and that they exercise **providence** <note>The Stoic belief that a rational divine power governs the universe for the best.</note>. Among the things we think of, some are conceived by **direct encounter**; some by **similarity**; some by **analogy**; some by **transposition**; some by **composition**; and some by **opposition**.

By **direct encounter**, we conceive of sensory objects. By **similarity**, we conceive of things from something nearby, as we recognize **Socrates** from his picture. By **analogy**, we conceive of things through increase—like the giant **Tityos** or the **Cyclops**—or through decrease, like the **Pygmy**. The center of the earth is also conceived by analogy from smaller spheres. By **transposition**, we imagine things like eyes on the chest. By **composition**, the **Hippocentaur** <note>A mythological creature, half-man and half-horse.</note> is conceived; and by **opposition**, we conceive of **death**. Concepts are also formed through a certain **transition**, such as **sayables** <term>lekta — the underlying meaning or "expressed" content of language</term> and space. Naturally, we conceive of things like the "just" and the "good." Finally, concepts can be formed by **privation**...

### ZENO. Book VII.

...to reach. <note>The text begins with a fragment of a word continued from the previous page.</note> They hold such doctrines concerning **impression**, **sensation**, and **thought**. They say that the **criterion of truth** is the **cataleptic impression** <term>katalēptikēn phantasian — a "grasping" mental image so clear and distinct that it could only come from a real object and commands the mind's assent</term>, that is, one which comes from a real object, as Chrysippus says in the twelfth book of his *Physics*, and also Antipater and Apollodorus. For Boethus admits several criteria: mind, sensation, desire, and knowledge; but Chrysippus, disagreeing with himself in the first book of his work *On Reason*, says the criteria are sensation and **preconception** <term>prolēpsin — an innate, natural concept of universal things formed over time</term>. Others among the older Stoics admit **right reason** <note>original: "orthon logon" — the rational principle that governs the universe and human logic.</note> as the criterion, as Poseidonius says in his treatise *On the Criterion*.

Most Stoics agree that the study of **dialectic** <note>For the Stoics, dialectic included both formal logic and the study of language, grammar, and meaning.</note> should begin with the topic of **voice**. Voice is "air that has been struck," or the specific object of the sense of hearing, as Diogenes of Babylon says in his *Art of Voice*. The voice of an animal is air struck by an impulse; but the voice of a human is articulate and sent forth from the mind, as Diogenes says—which becomes fully developed at the age of fourteen. According to the Stoics, the voice is also a **body** <note>The Stoics were materialists who believed that anything that acts or is acted upon must be a physical substance.</note>, as Archedemus says in his *On Voice*, as well as Diogenes, Antipater, and Chrysippus in the second book of his *Physics*. For everything that acts is a body; and the voice acts as it reaches listeners from those who are speaking.

**Diction** <note>original: "lexis" — speech as a physical sound made of letters.</note> is, according to the Stoics as Diogenes says, articulate voice represented by letters. For example: "It is day." **Discourse** <note>original: "logos" — speech that carries rational meaning.</note> is significant voice sent forth from the mind. **Dialect** is diction characterized by national or Greek usage; or diction of a certain kind according to a specific region. For example, in the Attic dialect, they say *thalatta* <note>original: "θάλαττα" — "sea" in the dialect of Athens.</note>, but in the Ionic, *hemere* <note>original: "ἡμέρη" — "day" in the dialect of Ionia.</note>. The elements of diction are the twenty-four letters. The term "letter" is used in three ways: the character of the element, its name (such as Alpha), and the element of the sound...

<meta>This page continues the Stoic discussion on linguistics and grammar, following the physical definition of "voice" as "struck air." It transitions from the physical properties of sound to the formal structures of language and the rules of proper expression.</meta>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...seven vowels: alpha, epsilon, eta, iota, omicron, upsilon, and omega <note>original: α, ε, η, ι, ο, υ, ω</note>; and six mutes: beta, gamma, delta, kappa, pi, and tau <note>original: β, γ, δ, κ, p, τ</note>. There is a difference between **voice** and **speech**, because while voice includes even a mere noise, speech is only that which is articulate. Speech, in turn, differs from **discourse** <term>logos — a coherent string of words</term> because discourse is always meaningful, whereas speech may be meaningless—such as the sound "blitiri" <note>A classic nonsense word used by ancient grammarians, similar to "gibberish."</note>—whereas discourse never is.

There is also a difference between **to speak** <term>legein</term> and **to utter** <term>propheresthai</term>. For sounds are uttered, but only actual things are spoken—which are then called **expressibles** <term>lekta — the underlying meaning or "truth-bearer" behind a spoken phrase</term>. There are five parts of discourse, as Diogenes [of Babylon] says in his work *On Voice* and as Chrysippus also states: **Proper Name**, **Common Noun**, **Verb**, **Conjunction**, and **Article**. (Antipater also adds the "Mean" <note>likely referring to the adverb</note> in his works *On Speech and things spoken*).

According to Diogenes, a **common noun** <term>prosēgoria</term> is a part of discourse signifying a common quality, such as "Man" or "Horse." A **proper name** <term>onoma</term> is a part of discourse indicating a quality unique to an individual, such as "Diogenes" or "Socrates." A **verb** <term>rhēma</term> is a part of discourse signifying an uncompounded predicate, as Diogenes says, or (as some define it) an element of discourse that is indeclinable <note>meaning it does not have "cases" like a noun</note>, signifying something that can be attached to one or more subjects, such as "I write" or "I speak."

A **conjunction** <term>syndesmos</term> is an indeclinable part of speech that binds the parts of the discourse together. An **article** <term>arthron</term> is a declinable element of discourse which distinguishes the genders and numbers of nouns, such as "the" [in its various masculine, feminine, and neuter forms] <note>original: ὁ, ἡ, τό, οἱ, αἱ, τά</note>.

There are five **virtues of speech**: **Hellenism**, **Clarity**, **Conciseness**, **Appropriateness**, and **Distinction**. **Hellenism** <term>Hellēnismos — correct Greek usage</term> is a style of phrasing that is correct according to technical rules and not based on random habit. **Clarity** is a way of speaking that presents the thought in a way that is easily recognized. **Conciseness** is a style of speaking that employs only those words absolutely necessary for explaining the matter at hand. **Appropriateness** is a style of speaking that is well-suited to the subject. **Distinction** <term>kataskeuē — also translated as "ornamentation" or "elaboration"</term> is a style of speaking that has escaped the level of the common person or the vulgar.

Among the **vices** of speech is **Barbarism**, which is a way of speaking that goes against the custom of cultivated Greeks. **Solecism** is discourse that is put together in a grammatically inconsistent way. A **poem** is (as Poseidonius says in his *Introduction to Speech*) speech that is in meter or rhythm, which, through its artistic arrangement, goes beyond the simple style of prose.

<summary>This page outlines the Stoic foundations of linguistics, defining the parts of speech, the differences between sound and meaning, and the five "virtues" of excellent communication.</summary>

### ZENO. Book 7

...the infinite number, or it is "Greatest Earth, and Zeus’s Aether" <note>This is a quotation from a lost play of Euripides, used here likely to illustrate a point about poetic infinity or cosmological elements.</note>. **Poetry** is a meaningful poem, containing an imitation of things both divine and human. A **definition** <term>horos</term> is (as Antipater says in his first book *On Definitions*) a discourse expressed with analytical completeness; or (as Chrysippus says in his work *On Definitions*) it is "the rendering" <note>original: apodosis; meaning the giving back of the essence of a thing</note>. A **description** <term>hypographē</term> is a discourse that introduces things in a general outline, or a definition that is simpler or contains the essential power of a definition.

A **genus** <term>genos</term> is the grouping together of many inseparable concepts, such as "Animal"; for this encompasses all individual animals. A **concept** <term>ennōēma</term> is a phantom of the mind, being neither a "something" nor "qualified," but appearing as if it were a "something" and as if it were "qualified"—just as an image of a horse arises in the mind even when no horse is present. A **species** <term>eidos</term> is that which is contained under a genus, as "Man" is contained under the genus "Animal." The **most generic** <term>genikōtaton</term> is that which, being a genus, has no higher genus above it; the **most specific** <term>eidikōtaton</term> is that which, being a species, has no further species below it, such as "Socrates."

**Division** <term>diairesis</term> is the cutting of a genus into its immediate species; for example: "Of animals, some are rational, while others are irrational." **Counter-division** <term>antidiairesis</term> is the cutting of a genus into species by way of contradiction, as if by negation; for example: "Of beings, some are good, others are not good." **Sub-division** <term>hypodiairesis</term> is a division following a previous division; for example: "Of beings, some are good, others are not good; and of those that are not good, some are bad, while others are indifferent." **Partition** <term>merismos</term> is the classification of a genus into specific categories (as Crinis says); for example: "Of goods, some pertain to the soul, while others pertain to the body."

**Ambiguity** <term>amphibolia</term> occurs when a phrase signifies two or more different things literally and properly, and according to the same custom, so that several meanings are understood simultaneously by the same phrase. For example: "The flute-girl has fallen" <note>original: Auletris peptōke. This is a famous Greek pun. It can mean "The flute-girl (Aulētris) has fallen" or "The courtyard (aulē) has fallen three times (tris)."</note>. For this phrase signifies both "The house has fallen three times" and "The flute-player has fallen."

**Dialectic** is (as Posidonius says) the science of things true, false, and neither. As Chrysippus states, it deals with signifiers <note>the words themselves</note> and things signi...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...concept. <note>original: υόμημα; likely the conclusion of the word "concept" or "notion" from the previous page.</note> Such, then, is the theory regarding the **voice** as it is discussed by the Stoics. However, in the section concerning **matters of fact** and **things signified**, they have organized the study of **sayables** <term>lekton; the meaning or "stuff" that is expressed by speech</term>, including those that are complete in themselves, propositions, and syllogisms. It also covers incomplete sayables, predicates, and both direct and passive expressions.

They define a **sayable** as that which subsists according to a rational presentation. The Stoics say that of these sayables, some are **complete** and others are **incomplete**. Incomplete sayables are those whose expression is unfinished, such as: "Writes." For in this case, we immediately ask: "Who?" Complete sayables are those whose expression is finished and entire, such as: "Socrates writes."

Therefore, among the incomplete sayables are classified the **predicates** <term>katēgorēmata</term>, while among the complete sayables are the **propositions** <term>axiōmata</term>, **syllogisms**, **interrogations**, and **inquiries**. 

A **predicate** is that which is said of something, or it is a thing that can be attached to one or more subjects (as the followers of Apollodorus say); or it is an incomplete sayable that must be joined with a nominative case <note>original: orthē ptōsis; literally "straight case"</note> to produce a proposition. 

Among predicates, some are **incidents** <term>symbamata</term>, such as "to sail through a rock." <note>This refers to an impersonal verb or a specific type of predicate where the action is an event happening to the subject.</note> Furthermore, some predicates are **direct** (active), some are **passive**, and some are **neuter**.

*   **Direct predicates** are those that are joined with one of the oblique cases to form a predicate, such as: "Hears," "Sees," or "Converses." 
*   **Passive predicates** are those joined with the passive marker, such as: "I am heard" or "I am seen." 
*   **Neuter predicates** are those that belong to neither of the above, such as: "To think" or "To walk." 
*   **Reflexive predicates** <note>original: antipaponthota; literally "reciprocal"</note> are found among the passive forms; these are passive in their grammatical shape but represent an active energy, such as: "He gets his hair cut" <note>original: Keiretai</note>, because the person getting their hair cut includes himself in the action.

The **oblique cases** are the genitive, the dative, and the accusative.

A **proposition** <term>axiōma</term> is that which is either true or false, or it is a complete thing that can be asserted by itself, as Chrysippus says in his *Dialectic Definitions*: "A proposition is that which can be asserted or denied by itself," for example: "It is day," or "Dion is walking." The proposition is named *axiōma* from the word "to be accepted" or "rejected" <note>original: axiousthai; the term suggests something that is "claimed" or "deemed worthy" of being true or false</note>; for the person who says "It is day"...

### ZENO. Book VII

...is, it seems to assert that "it is day." When it is indeed day, the proposed **proposition** <term>axiōma; in Stoic logic, a statement that is either true or false</term> becomes true; but when it is not day, it becomes false.

There is a difference between a proposition and an **interrogation**, an **inquiry**, an **imperative**, an **oath**, a **prayer**, a **hypothesis**, an **address**, and things that merely resemble a proposition. For a proposition is that which, in being spoken, expresses a judgment that is either true or false.

An **interrogation** <term>erōtēma</term> is a complete thing, just like a proposition, but it asks for an answer; for example: "Is it day?" This is neither true nor false. Thus, "It is day" is a proposition, while "Is it day?" is an interrogation.

An **inquiry** <term>pythma</term> is a matter to which one cannot respond with a simple sign (as with an interrogation where one might say "yes"), but instead one must state, for example: "He lives in this place." <note>The Stoics distinguished between yes/no questions (interrogations) and open-ended questions (inquiries).</note>

An **imperative** <term>prostaktikon</term> is a matter which we use to give a command; for example:

->Go yourself to the streams of Inachus.<- <note>original: "Σὺ μὲν βάδιζε τὰς ἐπ᾽ Ἰνάχου ῥοάς"; a line from a Greek tragedy used as a grammatical example.</note>

An **address** <term>prosagoreutikon</term> is a matter which, if one were to speak it, would be used to hail someone; for example:

->Most glorious son of Atreus, king of men, Agamemnon.<- <note>original: "Ἀτρείδη κύδιστε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγάμεμνον"; the famous opening address from Homer’s Iliad.</note>

A **quasi-proposition** <note>original: ὅμοιον ἀξιώματι; literally "similar to a proposition"</note> is something that, while having the structural form of a proposition, falls outside that category because of the addition of a particle or an emotional tone. For example:

->How beautiful the Parthenon is!<-
->How much the cowherd resembles the sons of Priam!<- <note>These are exclamations; they look like statements but express emotion rather than a logical truth-claim.</note>

There is also the **dubitative** <term>epaporētikon</term> type of speech, which differs from a proposition in that the speaker expresses doubt or hesitation: "Are sorrow and life somehow related?" Interrogations, inquiries, and similar forms are neither true nor false, whereas propositions must be one or the other.

Among propositions, some are **simple** and others are **non-simple**, as stated by the followers of **Chrysippus**, **Archedemus**, **Athenodorus**, **Antipater**, and **Crinis**. <note>These were prominent Stoic logicians who refined the school's teachings.</note> Simple propositions are those consisting of a single proposition that is not repeated, or from a single subject and predicate; for example: "It is day." **Simple propositions** <term>apla axiōmata</term> are those that consist of a single proposition that is not repeated, or of a repeated proposition. A repeated one would be: "If it is day, [it is day]." <note>The text here discusses the Stoic view that even a conditional can be "simple" in structure if it repeats the same statement, though they usually categorize conditionals as non-simple.</note> An example of a proposition consisting of different parts is: "If it is day, it is light."

Among the **simple propositions** are the **negative**, the **denying**, the **privative**, the **categorical**, the **definite**, and the **indefinite**.

Among the **non-simple propositions** <term>ouch apla</term> are the **conditional**, the **sub-conditional**, the **conjunction**, the **disjunction**, the **causal**, the **comparative** (indicating "more"), and the **comparative** (indicating "less").

A **negative proposition** <term>apophatikon</term> is one such as: "Not: it is day." <note>original: "Οὐχὶ ἡμέρα ἐστίν"</note>. A species of this is the **double-negative** <term>hyperapophatikon</term>. The double-negative is the negation of a negation, such as: "Not: not it is day." This actually posits the statement: "It is day."

A **denying proposition** <term>arnētikon</term> consists of a negative particle and a predicate, such as: "No one walks." <note>original: "Οὐδεὶς περιπατεῖ"</note>

A **privative proposition** <term>sterētikon</term> consists of a privative particle <note>In Greek, this is the "alpha privative," similar to the English prefix "un-" or "in-".</note> and a potential proposition, such as: "This man is **unkind**." <note>original: "Ἀϕιλάνθρωπός" (aphilanthrōpos); literally "un-philanthropic" or "not loving humans."</note>

A **categorical proposition** <term>katēgorikon</term> consists of a noun in the nominative case and a predicate, such as: "**Dion walks**."

A **definite proposition** <term>katagoreutikon</term> consists of a demonstrative pronoun in the nominative case and a predicate, such as: "**This man walks**."

An **indefinite proposition** <term>aoriston</term> consists of an indefinite particle or particles, such as: "**Someone walks**" or "**That one moves**."

Regarding **non-simple propositions**, a **conditional** <term>synēmmenon</term>—as **Chrysippus** <note>The third head of the Stoic school and its most prolific logician.</note> says in his *Dialectic* and **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes of Babylon, a later Stoic teacher.</note> says in his *Art of Dialectic*—is that which is formed by the connecting conjunction "if." This conjunction promises that the second part follows from the first, such as: "If it is day, it is light."

A **sub-conditional** <term>parasynēmmenon</term>—as **Crinis** <note>A Stoic logician known for refining technical definitions.</note> says in his *Art of Dialectic*—is a proposition connected by the conjunction "since" <term>epei</term>, beginning with one proposition and ending in another, such as: "Since it is day, it is light." This conjunction promises both that the second follows from the first and that the first is already an established fact.

### ZENO. Book VII
#### Page 263

...[a **conjunction**] <note>The Greek text begins mid-sentence, completing the definition of a conjunction or "symplektikon."</note> is that which is joined by certain copulative conjunctions; for example: "Both it is day, and it is light." 

A **disjunction** <term>diezeugmenon</term> is that which is separated by the disjunctive conjunction "Either... or"; for example: "Either it is day, or it is night." This conjunction promises that one of the propositions is false <note>The Stoics practiced "exclusive disjunction," meaning that in a pair of opposites, one must be true and the other must be false; they cannot both be true at once.</note>. 

A **causal proposition** <term>aitiōdes</term> is a proposition constructed by means of the word "Because"; for example: "Because it is day, it is light." For the first part is, as it were, the cause of the second. 

A **comparative proposition** indicating **more** <term>diasaphoun to mallon</term> is one constructed by the conjunction indicating "more" <note>original: "μᾶλλον" (mallon)</note> and the word "than" placed between the two parts of the proposition; for example: "It is more day than it is night." 

A **comparative proposition** indicating **less** <term>diasaphoun to hētton</term> is the opposite of the one just mentioned; for example: "It is less night than it is day." 

Furthermore, among propositions, those are **contradictories** <term>antikeimena</term> to one another in terms of truth and falsehood when one is the negative of the other; for example: "It is day" and "It is not day." 

A **conditional proposition** <term>synēmmenon</term> is true when the contradictory of its **consequent** <term>lēgon</term> <note>The "consequent" is the "then" part of an "if... then" statement.</note> conflicts with its **antecedent** <term>hēgoumenon</term> <note>The "antecedent" is the "if" part of the statement.</note>; for example: "If it is day, it is light." This is true, because "It is not light" (the contradictory of the consequent) conflicts with the statement "It is day." 

A **conditional proposition** is false when the contradictory of its consequent does not conflict with its antecedent; for example: "If it is day, Dion is walking." <note>Dion was a common name used by Greek philosophers as a placeholder, much like "John Doe."</note> For the statement "Dion is not walking" does not conflict with the statement "It is day." 

A **sub-conditional** <term>parasynēmmenon</term> is true when it begins with a truth and ends with a logical consequence; for example: "Since it is day, the sun is above the earth." It is false if it either begins with a falsehood or does not end with a consequence; for example: "Since it is night, Dion is walking," if this is said when it is actually daytime. 

A **causal proposition** <term>aitiōdes</term> is true when it begins with a truth and ends with a logical consequence, but the beginning does not follow conversely from the end; for example: "Because it is day, it is light." For while "It is light" follows from "It is day," the statement "It is day" does not necessarily follow from "It is light" <note>In Stoic logic, light could come from a source other than the sun, such as a lamp, so "light" does not always prove it is "day."</note>. A causal proposition is false if it either begins with a falsehood...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
#### Page 284

...or it ends in something inconsistent; or it has a beginning that is inconsistent with the conclusion; for example: "Because it is night, **Dion** is walking." <note>This completes a definition from the previous page regarding faulty causal propositions, where the cause given does not logically necessitate the result.</note>

A **probable proposition** <term>pithanon axioma</term> is one that leads us to give our internal agreement; for example: "If someone gave birth to a child, she is that child’s mother." However, this specific statement is actually false, for a bird is not the "mother" of an egg. <note>The Stoics used this example to show that "probability" is a psychological state of being convinced, which is different from absolute logical truth.</note>

Furthermore, some propositions are **possible**, others **impossible**; and some are **necessary**, while others are **not necessary**.

A **possible** proposition is one that is capable of being true, provided that external circumstances do not prevent it from being true; for example: "**Diocles** lives." <note>original: "Ζῇ Διοκλῆς" (Zē Dioklēs). Diocles of Magnesia was a contemporary and source for the author.</note>

An **impossible** proposition is one that is not capable of being true; for example: "The earth flies."

A **necessary** proposition is one which, being true, is not capable of being false. Alternatively, it is a proposition that might be capable of being false, but external circumstances prevent it from being so; for example: "**Virtue** is beneficial."

A **not necessary** proposition is one that is true, but is also capable of being false where external circumstances do not prevent it; for example: "**Dion** is walking."

A **reasonable proposition** <term>eulogon</term> is one that has more points in its favor for being true than false; for example: "I shall be alive tomorrow."

There are also other differences between propositions, and ways they transform from one to another into falsehoods or opposites, which we discuss at length in other writings.

An **argument** <term>logos</term> (as **Crinis** <note>A Stoic philosopher who specialized in formalizing logical definitions.</note> and his followers say) is a structure composed of a **premise** <term>lēmma</term> (or premises), an **additional premise** <term>proslēpsis</term>, and a **conclusion** <term>epiphora</term>. 

For example, an argument like this: "If it is day, it is light. But it is day; therefore it is light." 
In this case, the **premise** is: "If it is day, it is light." 
The **additional premise** is: "But it is day." 
The **conclusion** is: "Therefore it is light."

A **mood** <term>tropos</term> is a sort of "outline" or schema of an argument. For example: "If the 1st, then the 2nd; but the 1st is true; therefore the 2nd follows." <note>The Stoics used ordinal numbers as variables, similar to how modern logicians use P and Q.</note>

A **mixed form** <term>logotropos</term> is a combination of the two; for example: "If **Plato** lives, **Plato** breathes; but the 1st is true; therefore the 2nd follows." This "mixed form" was introduced for use in longer, more complex arguments so that one does not have to repeat a long additional premise or conclusion, but can instead say concisely: "but the 1st, therefore the 2nd."

Among arguments, some are **inconclusive** <term>aperantoi</term> and others are **conclusive** <term>perantikoi</term>. Inconclusive arguments are those in which the contradiction...

<meta>This page continues the Stoic classification of arguments (logoi), moving from invalid arguments to the distinction between "conclusive" and "syllogistic" forms. It then introduces Chrysippus's influential list of the five "indemonstrable" argument patterns, which form the bedrock of Stoic logic.</meta>

<page-num>265</page-num>
-> ## ZENO. Book 7 ## <-

...where the opposite of the conclusion conflicts with the combination of the premises; such as: "**If it is day, it is light; it is day; therefore, Dion is walking.**" <note>In this invalid argument, the conclusion "Dion is walking" is logically unrelated to the truth of the premises.</note>

Among **conclusive** <term>περαντικοί (perantikoi)</term> arguments, some are called "conclusive" in a general sense, while others are specifically called **syllogistic** <term>συλλογιστικοί (syllogistikoi)</term>. 

Syllogistic arguments are those which are either **indemonstrable** <term>ἀναπόδεικτοι (anapodeiktoi)</term> or can be reduced to the indemonstrable ones by means of one or more logical "rules" <term>θέματα (themata)</term>; for example: "**If Dion walks, then Dion moves.**" 

Those called "conclusive" in the specific sense are arguments that reach a valid conclusion but not through a strictly syllogistic form; for example: "**It is false that 'it is day and it is night'; it is day; therefore, it is not night.**" 

**Non-syllogistic** <term>ἀσυλλόγιστοι (asyllogistoi)</term> arguments are those which plausibly resemble syllogistic ones but do not actually reach a valid conclusion; for example: "**If Dion is a horse, Dion is an animal; but Dion is not a horse; therefore, Dion is not an animal.**" <note>This is a logical fallacy: just because Dion is not a horse does not mean he is not an animal (he could be a human).</note>

Of arguments, some are true and others are false. True arguments are those that reach a conclusion through true premises; for example: "**If virtue is beneficial, vice is harmful.**" 

False arguments are those which contain some falsehood in their premises or are **inconclusive** <term>ἀπέραντοι (aperantoi)</term>; for example: "**If it is day, it is light; it is day; therefore, Dion is alive.**" <note>Even if the conclusion is true in reality, the argument is "false" or "inconclusive" because the conclusion does not follow from the premises provided.</note> 

There are also possible and impossible arguments, as well as necessary and non-necessary ones. 

There are also certain **indemonstrable** <term>ἀναπόδεικτοι (anapodeiktoi)</term> arguments, so called because they are so self-evidently valid that they do not need proof. Different authorities list different numbers of these, but **Chrysippus** <note>The third head of the Stoic school and its most prolific logician.</note> identifies five, from which every argument is woven. These are used in conclusive arguments, syllogisms, and even in complex "hypothetical" arguments. 

The **first indemonstrable** is that in which the whole argument is composed of a **conditional** <term>συνημμένον (synēmmenon)</term> and its **antecedent** <term>ἡγούμενον (hēgoumenon)</term>—the part from which the conditional begins—and it results in the **consequent** <term>λῆγον (lēgon)</term>. 
For example: 
"**If the first, then the second; 
but the first is the case; 
therefore, the second is the case.**" <note>This is known in modern logic as Modus Ponens.</note>

The **second indemonstrable** is that which, through a conditional and the opposite of its consequent, has as its **conclusion** <term>συμπέρασμα (symperasma)</term> the opposite of the antecedent. 
For example: 
"**If it is day, it is light; 
but it is night; 
therefore, it is not day.**" <note>original: "νύξ ἐστιν" (it is night), which here functions as the opposite of "it is light." This pattern is known as Modus Tollens.</note> 
For the **additional assumption** <term>πρόσληψις (proslēpsis)</term> is formed from the opposite of the consequent, and the **result** <term>ἐπιφορά (epiphora)</term> from the opposite of the antecedent.

<keywords>syllogism, conclusive argument, indemonstrables, Chrysippus, antecedent, consequent, Modus Ponens, Modus Tollens, logic, fallacy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the list of Chrysippus’s five "indemonstrable" argument forms (syllogisms) from the previous page, specifically detailing the third, fourth, and fifth types. It then discusses the Stoic rules for logical consequence (what follows from truth versus falsehood) and concludes by listing famous logical paradoxes and explaining why the Stoics considered mastery of logic essential for the "Wise Man."</meta>

<page-num>266</page-num>
-> ### DIOGENES LAERTIUS ### <-

The **third indemonstrable** <term>ἀναπόδεικτος (anapodeiktos)</term> is that which, through a **negative conjunction** <term>ἀποφατικὴ συμπλοκή (apophatikē symplokē)</term> and one of the parts within that conjunction, concludes with the opposite of the remaining part. 
For example: 
"**It is not the case both that Plato is dead and Plato lives; 
but Plato is dead; 
therefore, Plato does not live.**" <note>This pattern (Not both A and B; A; therefore not B) is used to show that two states cannot exist simultaneously.</note>

The **fourth indemonstrable** is that which, through a **disjunction** <term>διεζευγμένος (diezeugmenos)</term> and one of the parts within that disjunction, has the opposite of the remaining part as its conclusion. 
For example: 
"**Either the first or the second is true; 
but the first is true; 
therefore, the second is not true.**" <note>This assumes an "exclusive" or (one or the other, but not both).</note>

The **fifth indemonstrable** is that in which the entire argument is composed of a disjunction and the opposite of one of its parts, and it results in the remaining part. 
For example: 
"**Either it is day or it is night; 
but it is not night; 
therefore, it is day.**"

According to the **Stoics** <term>Στωϊκοί (Stōïkoi)</term>, truth follows from truth, such as "**If it is day, there is light.**" 
Also, falsehood follows from falsehood, such as the false statement "**It is night**" leading to the false conclusion "**It is dark**" <note>original: "τὸ σκότος ἐστί" (it is dark/obscure). In logic, if the premise is false, the conclusion can also be false.</note>. 
A truth can also follow from a falsehood, such as the statement "**The earth flies**" leading to the conclusion "**The earth exists.**" <note>This is a fundamental rule of logic: a false premise can still lead to a true conclusion by accident or broader implication, but a true premise can *never* lead to a false conclusion.</note> 
For falsehood does not follow from truth: the statement "**The earth exists**" does not lead to the conclusion "**The earth flies.**"

There are also certain **puzzling arguments** <term>ἄποροι λόγοι (aporoi logoi)</term> that are "veiled" or "unnoticed," such as the **Soreites** <term>σωρεῖται (sōreitai)</term>, the **Horned One** <term>κερατίδες (keratides)</term>, and the **Nobody** <term>οὔτιδες (outides)</term>. 

The **Veiled** <term>ἐγκεκαλυμμένος (engekalymmenos)</term> argument is of this sort: 
"**It is not the case that two is 'a few' but three is not; it is not the case that three is 'a few' but four is not, and so on up to ten; but two is 'a few'; therefore, ten is also 'a few'.**" <note>This is a variation of the Sorites or "Heap" paradox: at what point does adding a single unit change a category like "few" or "a heap"?</note>

The **Nobody** <term>οὔτις (outis)</term> is an argument constructed from an indefinite and a definite term, having an additional assumption and a result. For example: "**If someone is here, he is not in Rhodes.**" <note>This plays on the ambiguity of "someone" (indefinite) versus a specific person (definite).</note>

The Stoics focus on these topics in their logic specifically to strengthen their position that the **Wise Man** <term>σοφός (sophos)</term> must always be a **dialectician** <term>διαλεκτικός (dialektikos)</term>. For they believe that all things are perceived through the study of arguments—including matters that belong to the study of **Physics** <term>φυσικός (physikos)</term> and, likewise, those belonging to **Ethics** <term>ἠθικός (ēthikos)</term>. 

Regarding the logical part: what need is there to speak of the **correctness of names** <term>ὀνομάτων ὀρθότης (onomatōn orthotēs)</term>? For they have shown how the laws are arranged for practical actions... <note>The text breaks off discussing how logic provides the necessary precision for both scientific understanding and moral law.</note>

<summary>This page concludes the definition of Chrysippus's five indemonstrable syllogisms and explains the Stoic rules for logical consequence. It also introduces several famous paradoxes (like the Sorites) used to train the Stoic Sage in dialectic.</summary>

<keywords>Indemonstrables, Disjunction, Logical Consequence, Sorites, Paradoxes, Dialectic, Stoic Sage, Chrysippus, Physics, Ethics</keywords>

-> ### ZENO. Book 7 ### <-

...virtue; one part considers what each thing is, and the other considers what it is called. This is how they handle the **logical** <term>λογικόν (logikon)</term> part of their system. 

They divide the **ethical part of philosophy** <term>ἠθικὸν μέρος τῆς φιλοσοφίας (ēthikon meros tēs philosophias)</term> into several topics:
1.  **Impulse** <term>ὁρμή (hormē)</term>
2.  **Good and evil** <term>ἀγαθά καὶ κακά (agatha kai kaka)</term>
3.  **Passions** <term>πάθη (pathē)</term>
4.  **Virtue** <term>ἀρετή (aretē)</term>
5.  **The End** <term>τέλος (telos)</term> <note>This refers to the "chief good" or the ultimate goal of life.</note>
6.  **Primary value** <term>πρώτη ἀξία (prōtē axia)</term>
7.  **Actions and duties** <term>πράξεις καὶ καθήκοντα (praxeis kai kathēkonta)</term>
8.  **Exhortations and dissuasions** <term>προτροπαί καὶ ἀποτροπαί (protropai kai apotropai)</term>

This is the sub-division used by the followers of **Chrysippus**, **Archedemus**, **Zeno of Tarsus**, **Apollodorus**, **Diogenes**, **Antipater**, and **Posidonius**. **Zeno of Citium** <note>The founder of Stoicism.</note> and **Cleanthes**, being the older thinkers, treated these matters more simply. However, they also divided Logic and Physics.

They say that the **primary impulse** <term>πρώτη ὁρμή (prōtē hormē)</term> of a living being is toward **self-preservation** <note>original: "τηρεῖν ἑαυτό" (to keep or guard oneself)</note>, because Nature from the beginning has made the creature "at home" with itself. This is stated by **Chrysippus** in the first book of his work **On Ends** <term>Περὶ τελῶν (Peri telōn)</term>: he says that the first thing "belonging" to every animal is its own constitution and the consciousness of it. <note>This concept, known as *oikeiosis*, is the foundation of Stoic ethics; it suggests that our first instinct is not pleasure, but an awareness and care for our own existence.</note> 

It is not likely that Nature would alienate a creature from itself, nor that she would create it and then leave it neither "at home" with itself nor alienated. Therefore, we must conclude that Nature, in constituting the creature, made it dear to itself. In this way, the creature repels what is harmful and accepts what belongs to its own nature.

The claim made by some <note>This is a critique of the Epicureans.</note> that the primary impulse of animals is toward **pleasure** <term>ἡδονή (hēdonē)</term> is shown to be false. For they say that pleasure, if it exists at all, is a **byproduct** <term>ἐπιγέννημα (epigennēma)</term> that occurs only after Nature has sought out and secured the things that harmonize with the creature’s constitution. It is similar to the way animals appear satisfied and plants bloom. 

Nature, they say, makes no difference between plants and animals in this regard, except that plants are governed without impulse or sensation, and even in us humans, certain processes occur in a plant-like manner. But since animals have the additional gift of **impulse**, which they use to go after what belongs to them, for them "following nature" means being governed by impulse. Since **reason** <term>λόγος (logos)</term> has been given to rational beings as a more perfect leadership, for them, the life according to reason... <note>The text continues on the next page to define the "life according to reason" as the ultimate goal for humanity.</note>

<summary>This page outlines the sub-divisions of Stoic Ethics and introduces the core doctrine of "oikeiosis," arguing that the primary instinct of all living things is self-preservation, not pleasure.</summary>

...becomes the correct guide for those things that happen according to nature. For reason supervenes as the **craftsman** <term>τεχνίτης (technitēs)</term> of impulse. Therefore, **Zeno** was the first to state, in his work *On the Nature of Man*, that the **End** <term>τέλος (telos)</term> <note>The ultimate goal or purpose of life.</note> is "to live in agreement with nature," which is the same as living according to **virtue** <term>ἀρετή (aretē)</term>. For nature leads us toward virtue. **Cleanthes** says the same in his work *On Pleasure*, as do **Posidonius** and **Hecaton** in their books *On Ends*.

Again, living according to virtue is equivalent to living according to one's experience of the things which happen by nature, as **Chrysippus** says in the first book of his work *On Ends*; for our individual natures are parts of the nature of the whole universe. Therefore, the End becomes a life lived according to nature—that is, according to one's own nature and the nature of the universe—where we do nothing that the **common law** is wont to forbid. This law is the **right reason** <term>ὀρθὸς λόγος (orthos logos)</term> <note>The Stoic belief that the universe is governed by a rational principle that humans can access through their own minds.</note> which pervades all things and is the same as **Zeus**, the lord and administrator of all that exists.

This very thing constitutes the virtue of the happy man and a **smooth flow of life** <term>εὔροια βίου (euroia biou)</term>, when all actions are performed in accordance with the harmony of the **inner spirit** <term>δαίμων (daimōn)</term> <note>In this context, the "daimon" refers to an individual's personal rational soul or "spark" of the divine.</note> in each person with the will of the administrator of the universe. 

**Diogenes** <note>Referring to Diogenes of Babylon, a later Stoic leader.</note> explicitly says the End is "to reason well in the selection of things according to nature." **Archedemus** defines it as "to live performing all one's duties." 

**Chrysippus** understands "nature" (in accordance with which we must live) to mean both universal nature and, specifically, human nature. **Cleanthes**, however, accepts only universal nature as the guide to follow, and not the particular nature of the individual. 

They also hold that virtue is a **harmonious disposition** <term>διάθεσις ὁμολογουμένη (diathesis homologoumenē)</term>, desirable for its own sake and not because of some fear, hope, or any external motive. Happiness lies in virtue itself, for virtue is a soul so fashioned as to produce harmony throughout the whole of life. 

The rational being is sometimes perverted—occasionally by the persuasiveness of external affairs, and sometimes by the influence of associates. This is notable because Nature herself provides us with **unperverted starting points** <term>ἀφορμὰς ἀδιαστρόφους (aphormas adiastrophous)</term>. 

Virtue is, in one sense, a general perfection for anything (as for a statue); there is also **non-theoretical** virtue, such as health; and **theoretical** virtue, such as **prudence** <term>φρόνησις (phronēsis)</term>. As **Hecaton** says...

...in the first book of his work *On Virtues*, he states that some virtues are **scientific** <term>ἐπιστημονικάς (epistēmonikas)</term> and theoretical—that is, those that have their structure based on established principles, such as **prudence** <term>φρόνησις (phronēsis)</term> and **justice** <term>δικαιοσύνη (dikaiosynē)</term>. Others are **non-theoretical** <term>ἀθεωρήτους (atheōrētous)</term>, which are understood by their extension to those virtues consisting of principles, such as health and strength. For instance, just as strength follows upon the structural integrity of an arch <note>original: ψαλίδος (psalidos). The author uses the physical stability of a stone vault or arch as an analogy for how certain physical "virtues" like strength depend on the underlying structure of the body.</note>, it happens that health follows alongside the subsidence of folly. 

These are called "non-theoretical" because they do not require acts of rational **assent** <term>συγκαταθέσεις (sygkatatheseis)</term> <note>In Stoicism, 'assent' is the mental agreement to a perception; non-theoretical virtues like health are considered more like physical states that supervene on the person.</note>; rather, they simply emerge, and they can even be found in base men, such as health or bravery. 

**Posidonius** says in the first book of his *Ethical Discourse* that the reality of virtue is proven by the fact that the followers of **Socrates**, **Diogenes**, and **Antisthenes** made actual progress toward it. He also argues that **vice** <term>κακία (kakia)</term> exists as a reality because it stands as the direct opposite of virtue. 

Furthermore, virtue can be taught. This is stated by **Chrysippus** in the first book of his work *On the End*, as well as by **Cleanthes**, **Posidonius** in his *Exhortations*, and **Hecaton** <note>The manuscript contains a likely error here, writing "Katon" for the philosopher Hecaton of Rhodes.</note>. That virtue is teachable is evident from the fact that people actually become good after having been base. 

On the division of virtues: **Panaetius** says there are two virtues, the theoretical and the practical. Others divide them into three: logical, physical, and ethical. The school of **Posidonius** counts four virtues, while the followers of **Cleanthes**, **Chrysippus**, and **Antipater** count even more. **Apollophanes**, however, claims there is only one: **prudence**.

Of the virtues, some are considered "primary" and others are "subordinate" to these. The primary virtues are: 
1. **Prudence**
2. **Courage** <term>ἀνδρεία (andreia)</term>
3. **Justice**
4. **Temperance** <term>σωφροσύνη (sōphrosynē)</term>

The subordinate species of these include **magnanimity** <term>μεγαλοψυχία (megalopsychia)</term>, **continence** <term>ἐγκράτεια (egkrateia)</term>, **endurance** <term>καρτερία (karteria)</term>, **shrewdness** <term>ἀγχίνοια (agchinoia)</term>, and **good counsel** <note>The Greek text likely contains a typo here, reading 'aboulia' (bad counsel), which contradicts the context of virtues; it should be 'euboulia' (good counsel).</note>.

Specifically:
**Prudence** is the knowledge of what is good, what is evil, and what is neither. 
**Justice** is the knowledge of what must be chosen, what must be avoided, and what is neither. 
**Magnanimity** is the knowledge or disposition that raises one above the common accidents of life, whether they be perceived as bad or good. 
**Continence** is a disposition that never oversteps **right reason**, or a habit that is unconquered by pleasures. 
**Endurance** is the knowledge...

...or a habit <note>The Stoics often defined virtues as both "knowledge" (epistēmē) and "dispositional habits" (hexis).</note> of what should be maintained, what should not, and what is neither. 

**Shrewdness** <term>ἀγχίνοια (agchinoia)</term> is a habit that finds what is appropriate <note>original: kathēkontos. This refers to "proper functions" or duties in Stoic ethics.</note> on the spur of the moment. 

**Good counsel** <term>εὐβουλία (euboulia)</term> is the knowledge of considering what things we should do and how we should do them in order to act advantageously. 

Analogously, among the **vices** <term>κακίαι (kakiai)</term>, some are primary and others are subordinate to these. **Folly** <term>ἀφροσύνη (aphrosynē)</term>, **cowardice** <term>δειλία (deilia)</term>, **injustice** <term>ἀδικία (adikia)</term>, and **intemperance** <term>ἀκολασία (akolasia)</term> are among the primary vices. **Lack of self-control** <term>ἀκρασία (akrasia)</term>, **slowness of wit** <term>βραδυνοία (bradynoia)</term>, and **bad counsel** <term>κακοβουλία (kakoboulia)</term> are among those subordinate to them. Vices are essentially forms of ignorance regarding the very things that virtues are the knowledge of.

The **Good** <term>ἀγαθόν (agathon)</term> is defined generally as that which is entirely beneficial, and specifically as either identical to or not different from utility. Consequently, virtue itself and that which participates in virtue are called "good" in three ways: 
1. As that from which a benefit results, such as an action performed in accordance with virtue. 
2. As that by which a benefit is brought about, such as the virtuous man who participates in virtue. 
3. In a more specific sense, they define the Good as that which is perfect according to the nature of a rational being. 

Virtue is this kind of perfection; while the actions performed in accordance with virtue and the virtuous people themselves are "good" by way of participating in it. 

The **offshoots** <term>ἐπιγεννήματα (epigennēmata)</term> <note>Literally "things born after." These are "by-products" or secondary results—positive mental states that naturally follow a state of virtue but are not the virtue itself.</note> of virtue include joy, cheerfulness, and similar feelings. 

In the same way, among the vices, there is **folly**, **cowardice**, **injustice**, and the like. The actions performed according to vice and base people are those that participate in vice. Their offshoots include despondency, gloominess, and similar states.

Furthermore, among goods, some pertain to the **soul**, some are **external**, and some are neither of the soul nor external. Those pertaining to the soul are the virtues and the actions that follow them. External goods include having a virtuous homeland and a virtuous friend, as well as the happiness of these. Those that are neither external nor of the soul include the state of being virtuous and happy within oneself. 

Conversely, among the vices, some pertain to the soul (the vices themselves and their corresponding actions). External vices include having an ignorant homeland or an ignorant friend, and their unhappiness. Those that are neither external nor of the soul include being oneself base and...

...unhappy. Regarding **goods** <term>ἀγαθά (agatha)</term>, some are **final** <term>τελικά (telika)</term> <note>These are "ends" in themselves—things valued for their own sake and not as a means to something else.</note> and others are **productive** <term>ποιητικά (poiētika)</term> <note>These are "means" or instrumental goods—things that produce or bring about a good result.</note>; while others are both final and productive. 

A friend, and the benefits resulting from him, are productive goods. **Courage** <term>θάρρος (tharros)</term>, **high-mindedness** <term>φρόνημα (phronēma)</term>, **liberty**, **delight**, **cheerfulness**, **freedom from pain**, and every action performed in accordance with virtue are final goods. 

Goods that are both productive and final include the virtues: insofar as they bring about **happiness** <term>εὐδαιμονία (eudaimonia)</term>, they are productive goods; but insofar as they complete happiness, so as to become actual parts of it, they are final. 

Similarly, among **evils** <term>κακά (kaka)</term>, some are final, others are productive, and some are both. An enemy and the harms resulting from him are productive. **Panic** <term>κατάπληξιν (kataplēxin)</term>, **meanness** <note>original: tapeinotēta. In a Stoic context, this refers to a "lowliness" or "smallness of soul," the opposite of high-mindedness.</note>, **slavery**, **joylessness**, **despondency**, **excessive grief**, and every action performed in accordance with vice are final. 

Evils that are both [productive and final]: insofar as they bring about **unhappiness** <term>κακοδαιμονία (kakodaimonia)</term>, they are productive; but insofar as they complete it, so as to become parts of it, they are final.

Regarding goods of the **soul**, some are **dispositions** <term>διαθέσεις (diatheseis)</term> <note>A 'disposition' for the Stoics is a permanent, fixed, and unchangeable state of character.</note>, some are **habits** <term>ἕξεις (hexeis)</term> <note>A 'habit' here refers to a state or condition that is not as fixed as a disposition and could potentially be lost.</note>, and some are neither habits nor dispositions. 

Dispositions are the virtues; habits are **practices** <term>ἐπιτηδεύματα (epitēdeumata)</term> <note>These are inclinations or pursuits that lead toward virtue but haven't reached the level of a fixed disposition.</note>; while those that are neither habits nor dispositions are the **activities** <term>ἐνέργειαι (energeiai)</term> <note>The actual "doing" of a virtuous act is an activity, which is fleeting, unlike the character state that produces it.</note>. 

In general, among goods, **mixed** ones include having good children and a good old age; while a **simple** good is **knowledge** <term>ἐπιστήμη (epistēmē)</term>. Some goods are always present, such as the virtues; others are not always present, such as **joy** or **walking**. 

Every good is **advantageous**, **requisite**, **profitable**, **useful**, **serviceable**, **beautiful**, **beneficial**, **desirable**, and **just**. 

It is **advantageous** <term>συμφέρον (sympheron)</term> because it "brings along" <note>The Greek term sympheron literally means "bringing together" or "conducing to."</note> things that result in our benefit. It is **requisite** <term>δέον (deon)</term> because it "holds us together" <note>original: synechei</note> in what is necessary. It is **profitable** <term>λυσιτελές (lysitelēs)</term> because it "pays for itself" <note>The Greek term is a pun on "loosening the cost" (lyein ta telē); the Stoics define it as something where the benefit exceeds the expenditure.</note>, so that the return from its use exceeds the cost in benefit. 

It is **useful** <term>χρήσιμον (chrēsimon)</term> because it provides a "use" of benefit. It is **serviceable** <term>εὔχρηστον (euchrēston)</term> because it makes that use praiseworthy. It is **beautiful** <term>καλόν (kalon)</term> because it is perfectly proportioned to its own use. It is **beneficial** <term>ὠφέλιμον (ōphelimon)</term> because...

There are four forms of the Beautiful: **justice**, **courage**, **orderliness**, and **knowledge**; for it is in these that beautiful actions are completed. Analogously, there are four forms of the **Base** <term>αἰσχροῦ (aischrou)</term>: **injustice**, **cowardice**, **disorderliness**, and **folly**. 

The "Beautiful" is spoken of in several ways: 
1. That which makes those who possess it worthy of praise (a good deserving of honor). 
2. That which is well-disposed toward its own specific function. 
3. That which adds ornament or grace—as when we say that only the wise man is "good and beautiful." 

They also claim that only the Beautiful is good, as Hecato says in the third book of his treatise *On Goods*, and Chrysippus in his works *On the Beautiful*. This is virtue and that which participates in virtue; which is equivalent to saying that every good is beautiful, and that "the good" and "the beautiful" have the same power. This is demonstrated as follows: since a thing is good, it is beautiful; and it is beautiful, therefore it is good. 

It is their view that all goods are equal, and that every good is desirable to the highest degree, admitting of neither decrease nor increase. 

Among existing things, they say some are **goods** <term>ἀγαθά (agatha)</term>, some are **evils** <term>κακά (kaka)</term>, and some are **neither** <term>οὐδέτερα (oudetera)</term>. 

**Goods** include the virtues: **prudence** <term>φρόνησιν (phronēsin)</term>, **justice**, **courage**, **temperance** <term>σωφροσύνην (sōphrosynēn)</term>, and the rest. 

**Evils** are their opposites: **folly** <term>ἀφροσύνην (aphrosynēn)</term>, **injustice**, and the rest. 

**Neither** (Neutral) are all those things which neither benefit nor harm, such as: life, health, pleasure, beauty, strength, wealth, reputation, and noble birth. Likewise, their opposites are also neutral: death, disease, pain, ugliness, weakness, poverty, low reputation, humble birth, and similar things. This is the view of Hecato in the seventh book of *On the End*, and Apollodorus in his *Ethics*, and Chrysippus. 

For these things are not goods, but **indifferents** <term>ἀδιάφορα (adiaphora)</term> that are "preferred" <term>προηγμένα (proēgmena)</term> in their kind. For just as the specific property of heat is to...

<meta>This page continues the Stoic argument regarding the nature of "the Good," specifically contrasting it with external things like wealth and health. It introduces the classification of "Indifferents" and the Stoic concept of "Value" (axia), which allows for certain neutral things to be "preferred" over others without being morally "good" in themselves.</meta>

<page-num>273</page-num>
-> ### DIOGENES LAERTIUS ### <-

-> ## ZENO. Book 7 ## <-

...to warm, not to chill, so it is the property of the **Good** to benefit, and not to harm. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, completing a comparison: just as the essential nature of fire is to heat, the essential nature of the "Good" is to provide benefit.</note> But wealth and health do not benefit a person any more than they might harm them; therefore, neither wealth nor health is a **Good**. Furthermore, they say that anything which can be used both well and badly is not a **Good**; since wealth and health can be used both well and badly, it follows that wealth and health are not **Goods**. 

Posidonius, <note>A later Stoic philosopher who often tried to reconcile Stoicism with the views of Plato and Aristotle.</note> however, claims that even these things are among the **Goods**. 

But the mainstream Stoics say that even **pleasure** is not a good, as Hecato says in the nineteenth book of his treatise *On Goods*, and Chrysippus in his works *On Pleasure*. Their reason is that there are such things as "shameful pleasures," and nothing that is shameful can ever be a **Good**. 

To **benefit** <term>ὠφελεῖν (ōphelein)</term> is defined as to move or to sustain something in accordance with **virtue**; whereas to **harm** <term>βλάπτειν (blaptein)</term> is to move or to sustain something in accordance with **vice**.

The term **Indifferents** <term>ἀδιάφορα (adiaphora)</term> <note>Literally "things which make no difference."</note> is used in two ways: 

1. First, it refers to things that contribute neither to **happiness** <term>εὐδαιμονίαν (eudaimonian)</term> nor to misery, such as wealth, reputation, health, strength, and the like. This is because it is possible to be happy even without these things; it is the specific *use* one makes of them that results in either happiness or misery. 

2. In another sense, "Indifferents" refers to things that trigger neither an impulse toward them nor an aversion away from them. For example, whether one has an even or an odd number of hairs on one's head, or whether one happens to extend or contract a finger. 

The things in the first category (like wealth) are not called "indifferent" in this second sense, because they *do* trigger impulses and aversions. Therefore, some of these are **selected** <term>ἐκλέγεται (eklegetai)</term>, whereas the second kind (like the number of hairs) are entirely neutral when it comes to choice or avoidance.

Of the **Indifferents**, they say some are **Preferred** <term>προηγμένα (proēgmena)</term> and some are **Rejected** <term>ἀποπροηγμένα (apoproēgmena)</term>. 

**Preferred** things are those that possess **Value** <term>ἀξίαν (axian)</term>, while **Rejected** things are those that possess "disvalue" or lack of value. 

They define **Value** in three ways: 
1. A contribution to the "harmonious life," which applies to every **Good**. 
2. A certain intermediate power or utility that contributes to the "life according to nature"—much like the contribution that wealth or health makes to a natural life. 
3. The "exchange-value" determined by an appraiser, which an expert in a particular field might assign—for example, the rate at which one might exchange wheat for barley along with a mule. 

The **Preferred** things, then, are those which possess value. For instance, in the case of...

<meta>catchword: psychological (of the things...)</meta>

<summary>This page explains the Stoic logic that external assets like wealth and health are "indifferent" because they can be used for both good and evil. It introduces the hierarchy of Indifferents, distinguishing between "preferred" things that have natural value and purely neutral things like the number of hairs on one's head.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Stoic classification of "Indifferents" (adiaphora) from the previous page. Having established that things like health and wealth are not "Goods" but are "Preferred," the text now categorizes specific examples into mental, physical, and external types, and transitions into the Stoic theory of "Duty" or "Appropriate Action" (kathēkon).</meta>

<page-num>274</page-num>

-> ### DIOGENES LAERTIUS ### <-

...of the mental [qualities], natural ability, skill, moral progress, and the like; among the bodily [qualities], life, health, strength, good physical condition, soundness of limbs, and beauty; and among the external [advantages], wealth, reputation, noble birth, and the like. 

Among the bodily [disadvantages] <note>These are the "Rejected Indifferents"—things to be avoided if possible, but which do not make a person "evil" or "unhappy" in the Stoic sense.</note> are death, disease, weakness, poor physical condition, mutilation, ugliness, and the like; and among the external [disadvantages], poverty, low reputation, humble birth, and similar things. 

Those things which are neither preferred nor rejected are those which are entirely neutral. 

Furthermore, among the **Preferred** things, some are preferred for their own sake, some for the sake of other things, and some both for their own sake and for the sake of others. 

*   **For their own sake:** natural ability, moral progress, and the like. 
*   **For the sake of other things:** wealth, noble birth, and the like. 
*   **For both:** strength, keenness of senses, and soundness of limbs. 

They are preferred for their own sake because they are in accordance with nature; they are preferred for the sake of other things because they provide a significant number of utilities. The same logic applies to **Rejected** things, following the opposite reasoning.

Furthermore, they say that **Duty** <term>καθῆκον (kathēkon)</term> <note>Often translated as "appropriate action." It refers to the "proper function" of a living being.</note> is an action that possesses a reasonable justification, such as that which is consistent in life; this concept extends even to plants and animals, for "duties" are observed in them as well. 

They say that the term **Duty** was first coined by Zeno, derived from the phrase "reaching to certain things" <note>original: "κατά τινας ἥκειν" (kata tinas hēkein)</note>, a name taken from its application. It is defined as an activity appropriate to a nature’s specific constitution. 

Of the actions performed through impulse, some are **Duties**, while others are **Contrary to Duty**. 

*   **Duties** are those things which reason chooses for us to do, such as honoring parents, siblings, and one's country, and socializing with friends. 
*   **Contrary to Duty** are those things which reason does not choose, such as neglecting parents, being unconcerned for siblings, failing to get along with friends, and disregarding one's country. 

Neither "duties" nor "contrary to duty" are those actions which reason neither chooses to do nor forbids, such as picking up a twig, holding a stylus, or a **strigil** <term>στλεγγίς (stlengis)</term> <note>A curved blade used by ancient Greeks to scrape oil and dirt from the skin after exercise.</note>, and similar examples. 

Furthermore, some duties are performed "regardless of circumstances," while others are "circumstantial." Those performed regardless of circumstances include taking care of one's health and one's sense-organs...

<summary>This page catalogs the specific types of Stoic "Indifferents" (mental, physical, and external) and introduces the concept of Kathēkon (Duty). It defines Duty as an action with a reasonable justification that is consistent with nature, applying to both humans and the wider natural world.</summary>
