### CHRYSIPPUS. Book 7

However, he did not keep still during his drinking bouts, even though his legs would wander; as a result, his female servant used to say, "Only Chrysippus’s legs are drunk." He was so full of self-confidence that when someone asked him, "To whom shall I entrust the education of my son?" he replied, "To me; for if I suspected there were anyone better than myself, I would be studying philosophy under him." Hence they say it was said of him:

->“He alone has understanding; the rest are but flitting shadows.”<-
<note>original: Οἷος πέπνυται, τοὶ δὲ σκιαὶ ἀΐσσουσι. This is a play on a line from Homer’s *Odyssey* describing the blind prophet Teiresias.</note>

->and also,<-

->“If there were no Chrysippus, there would be no Stoa.”<-
<note>The "Stoa" refers to the Painted Porch in Athens where the Stoic school met; the saying implies that Chrysippus was so vital that the school would not have survived or succeeded without his systematization of its doctrines.</note>

Later, according to Sotion in his eighth book, he studied philosophy at the Academy <note>The Academy was the school founded by Plato, which in Chrysippus's time had turned toward "Skepticism."</note> alongside Arcesilaus and Lacydes. For this reason, he took up arguments both against common custom and in favor of it, and he employed the style of the Academics when discussing magnitudes and quantities. Hermippus relates that while he was teaching in the Odeum <note>A public building used for musical performances and lectures.</note>, he was invited to a sacrifice by his students. There, after drinking some sweet, unmixed wine <note>Ancient Greeks typically diluted their wine with water; drinking "neat" or unmixed wine was considered risky to one's health and a sign of overindulgence.</note> and becoming dizzy, he departed from among men on the fifth day, having lived seventy-three years, during the 143rd Olympiad, as Apollodorus says in his *Chronicles*. We have written an epigram about him:

> Chrysippus grew dizzy after drinking Bacchus greedily,
> He spared neither the Stoa, nor his country,
> Nor his own life, but traveled instead
> To the house of Hades.

But some say that he died from a fit of laughter. For when a donkey had eaten his figs, he told the old woman to give the donkey a drink of unmixed wine to wash them down; then, laughing excessively, he died. However, it seems he actually died of a fever. Despite having written so many books, he never dedicated any of them to a king. He was content with the company of only one old woman, as Demetrius says in his *Namesakes*. When Ptolemy wrote to Cleanthes <note>Cleanthes was Chrysippus’s predecessor as head of the Stoic school.</note> asking him either to come to Egypt himself or to send someone, Sphaerus went, but Chrysippus...

# BIOGRAPHIES BY LAERTIUS

Chrysippus <note>The first part of the name "sippus" completes the name "Chrysippus" from the previous page.</note> took care of his relatives. Having sent for the sons of his sister, Aristocreon and Philocrates, he supported and trained them. He was also the first who had the courage to hold school in the open air in the Lyceum <note>The Lyceum was a famous gymnasium in Athens, traditionally associated with Aristotle and the Peripatetic school.</note>, as the aforementioned Demetrius <note>Demetrius of Magnesia, a scholar often cited by Diogenes Laertius.</note> records.

There was also another Chrysippus, a man of Cnidus, a physician, from whom Erasistratus <note>A famous ancient Greek anatomist and royal physician.</note> says he gained the most benefit. And there was another, the son of this man, who was a physician to Ptolemy <note>Likely Ptolemy II Philadelphus.</note>; having been falsely accused, he was led around and punished by scourging. Another was a disciple of Erasistratus, and one more wrote on the subject of agriculture.

The philosopher also used to propose logical puzzles <term>sophisms; clever but often fallacious arguments used to test the limits of logic</term> such as these:

->“He who reveals the mysteries to the uninitiated commits sacrilege; the high priest <note>original: ἱεροφάντης (hierophantes), the priest who revealed the sacred mysteries at Eleusis.</note> reveals them to the uninitiated; therefore, the high priest commits sacrilege.”<-

Another: “If something is not in the city, it is not in the house either; but there is no well in the city; therefore, there is no well in the house.”

Another: “There is a certain 'head.' But you do not have that [specific] head. Therefore, you do not have a head.” <note>This is a play on words regarding general categories versus specific instances.</note>

Another: “If someone is in Megara, he is not in Athens; but there is a man in Megara; therefore, there is no man in Athens.”

And again: “If you say something, that thing passes through your mouth; you say 'wagon'; therefore, a wagon passes through your mouth.”

And: “If you have not lost something, you have it; you have not lost horns; therefore, you have horns.” <note>This is the famous 'Horned One' paradox, designed to show flaws in syllogistic reasoning.</note> Some, however, attribute this last one to Eubulides.

There are some who attack Chrysippus on the grounds that he wrote many things in a shameful and unspeakable manner. In his treatise *On the Ancient Natural Philosophers*, he portrays the story of Hera and Zeus in a shameful way, devoting about six hundred lines to things that no one—even if they were most unfortunate—would soil their mouth by repeating. For they say he composed this story in a most disgusting fashion (even if he praises it as a physical allegory), one more suited to street-walkers than to gods.

Furthermore, these stories are not found recorded among those who wrote about paintings; for they are neither in Polemon, nor in Hypsicrates, nor even in Antigonus, but were invented by Chrysippus himself. In his work *On the Republic* <note>original: Περὶ πολιτείας (Peri politeias)</note>, he even says that it is permissible to have relations with mothers, daughters, and sons. He says the same things...

### CHRYSIPPUS. Book 7

...he says <note>The subject is Chrysippus, being cited for his own controversial statements.</note> also in his work *On Things Not Desirable for Their Own Sake*, right at the beginning. And in the third book of *On Justice*, at about the thousandth line, he even commands that the dead be eaten <note>original: "τοὺς ἀποθανόντας κατεσθίειν" (tous apothanontas katesthiein); this refers to the notorious Stoic "cynic" argument that once the soul has left the body, the remains are merely matter and cannibalism is not inherently immoral, though socially shocking.</note>. In the second book of *On Lives and Means of Livelihood*, he discusses how the wise man must provide for his needs. 

And yet, for what reason should he provide for himself? For if it is for the sake of living, life is an "indifferent" <term>adiaphoron; in Stoic philosophy, things like wealth, health, or life itself that are neither good nor evil in themselves</term>; if it is for pleasure, that too is indifferent; if for virtue, virtue is itself self-sufficient for happiness. The methods of earning he suggests are also ridiculous: for instance, earning from a king—but he would then have to yield to the king's whims. Or earning from friendship—but then friendship will be for sale for profit. Or earning from wisdom—but then wisdom becomes mercenary. 

These are the charges brought against him. However, since his books are held in the highest esteem, it seemed right to me to record them here, arranged by category. They are as follows:

# CHRYSIPPUS. Book 7

u. i.

# P Y T H A G O R A S.

**E**PINCE we have already gone through the Ionian philosophy, which began with Thales, and the noteworthy men who lived within that tradition, come now and let us also discuss the Italian philosophy. This school was founded by Pythagoras, the son of Mnesarchus, a **gem-engraver** <term>gem-engraver <note>original: "δακτυλιογλύφου"; a craftsman who carves intricate designs and seals into precious stones for signet rings</note></term>, as Hermippus says. Others, such as Aristoxenus, say he was a Tyrrhenian from one of the islands which the Athenians occupied after they drove out the Tyrrhenians. 

Some say, however, that he was the son of Marmacus, who was the son of Hippasus, the son of Euthyphron, the son of Cleonymus, an exile from Phlius. They claim that Marmacus lived in Samos, which is why Pythagoras is called a Samian. It is said that he traveled to Lesbos and was introduced to Pherecydes by his uncle Zoïlus. After having three silver cups made, he brought them as a gift to each of the priests in Egypt. 

He had brothers: the eldest was Eunostus, and the middle one was Tyrrhenus. He also had a slave named Zamolxis, to whom the Getae <note>A Thracian tribe living near the Lower Danube</note> offer sacrifices, believing him to be Cronus <note>The father of Zeus in Greek mythology; the Getae identified their own deity with him</note>, as Herodotus tells us. 

As previously mentioned, Pythagoras was a pupil of Pherecydes of Syros. After the death of Pherecydes, he returned to Samos and became a student of Hermodamas (the descendant of Creophylus), who was already quite old at the time. While still young and **fond of learning** <note>original: "φιλομαθὴς"; a common Greek term for someone with a voracious appetite for knowledge</note>, he departed from his homeland and was initiated into all the mysteries, both Greek and **barbarian** <note>original: "βαρβαρικὰς"; in this context, the term simply refers to non-Greek cultures, such as the Egyptians, Chaldeans, or Persians</note>...

...disciples. He then went to Egypt, at the time when Polycrates introduced him to Amasis <note>Amasis II, a Pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty known for his alliances with Greeks</note> by a letter of recommendation. He learned the Egyptian language, as Antiphon says in his book *On Those Who Excelled in Virtue*. He also spent time among the <term>Chaldeans <note>original: "Χαλδαίοις"; Babylonian astronomers and scholars renowned in antiquity for their mathematical and astrological knowledge</note></term> and the <term>Magi <note>original: "Μάγοις"; Persian priests and practitioners of sacred wisdom</note></term>. 

Afterward, in Crete, he went down into the Idaean cave <note>A cave on Mount Ida where, according to myth, Zeus was raised; it was a site of ancient initiation rituals</note> with Epimenides. He also entered the inner sanctuaries <note>original: "ἄδυτα"; the most sacred parts of a temple, restricted to priests</note> in Egypt and learned the secret lore concerning the gods. 

He then returned to Samos, but finding his homeland under the tyranny of Polycrates, he departed for Croton in Italy. There, having established laws for the people of Magna Graecia <note>The Greek-settled areas of Southern Italy</note>, he was held in high honor along with his disciples. These followers, numbering about three hundred, governed the state so excellently that the constitution was nearly an aristocracy <note>original: "ἀριστοκρατίαν"; literally "rule of the best"</note>.

Heraclides Ponticus says that Pythagoras told the following story about himself: that he had once been Aethalides, and was believed to be the son of Hermes. He claimed that Hermes told him he could choose whatever gift he wished, except for immortality. He therefore asked that, whether living or dead, he might retain the memory of everything that happened to him. Thus, during his life, he remembered all things, and when he died, he kept the same memory. 

Later on, his soul entered into Euphorbus, and he was wounded by Menelaus <note>A hero of the Trojan War; Euphorbus was the Trojan who first wounded Patroclus</note>. Euphorbus used to say that he had once been Aethalides, and that he had received this gift from Hermes: the <term>wandering of the soul <note>original: "περιπόλησιν"; a reference to the doctrine of metempsychosis or reincarnation</note></term>. He described how his soul had wandered, into what plants and animals it had entered, what the soul suffered in <term>Hades <note>The Greek underworld</note></term>, and what other souls must endure. 

When Euphorbus died, his soul migrated into Hermotimus. Hermotimus, wishing to provide proof of this, went to the <term>Branchidae <note>original: "Βραγχίδας"; a major temple and oracle of Apollo located near Miletus</note></term>. Entering the temple of Apollo, he pointed out a shield which Menelaus had dedicated there. He claimed that when Menelaus sailed back from Troy, he had dedicated the shield to Apollo; by Hermotimus's time, the shield had already rotted away, and only the ivory face remained. 

When Hermotimus died, he became Pyrrhus, a fisherman from Delos. He again remembered everything: how he had first been Aethalides, then Euphorbus, then Hermotimus, and finally Pyrrhus. When...

### PYTHAGORAS. Book 8
->u.iiii.<-

...after Pyrrhus died, he was destined to become Pythagoras and remember all the things that had been mentioned. Now, some say that Pythagoras left not a single written work, but they speak in jest. Certainly, Heraclitus the natural philosopher <note>Heraclitus of Ephesus, a pre-Socratic philosopher known for his doctrine of universal change</note> practically screams it when he says: "Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, practiced inquiry <note>original: "ἱστορίην"; meaning systematic research or "history" in the ancient sense</note> more than all other men. And having selected these writings, he fashioned a wisdom for himself—a much-learning <note>original: "πολυμαθίην"; often used by Heraclitus as a criticism of knowing many facts without true understanding</note> and a charlatanry <note>original: "κακοτεχνίην"; literally "evil-arts" or "crafty trickery"</note>." He said this because Pythagoras, at the beginning of his treatise *On Nature*, writes as follows: "By the air I breathe, by the water I drink, I will suffer no blame for this discourse." 

There are three works attributed to Pythagoras: *On Education*, *On Statesmanship*, and *On Nature*. The work currently circulating under Pythagoras's name, however, is actually by Lysis of Tarentum, a Pythagorean who fled to Thebes and became the teacher of Epaminondas <note>A famous Theban general and statesman</note>. Heraclides, the son of Sarapion, says in his *Epitome of Sotion* that Pythagoras also wrote a work *On the Universe* in verse; second, a *Sacred Discourse* which begins:

-> "O youths, come honor all these things in silence." <-

Third, he wrote *On the Soul*; fourth, *On Impiety*; fifth, *Helothales*, named after the father of Epicharmus of Cos; sixth, *Croton*, and others besides. The *Mystic Discourse*, they say, is actually by Hippasus, written to discredit Pythagoras. Many other works written by Aston of Croton were also attributed to Pythagoras. Aristoxenus <note>A Greek philosopher and music theorist</note> further claims that Pythagoras received most of his ethical doctrines from Themistoclea, the priestess at Delphi.

Ion of Chios, in his work *The Triads*, says that Pythagoras composed certain poems and attributed them to Orpheus <note>The legendary musician and prophet; this suggests Pythagoras used the prestige of Orpheus to spread his own teachings</note>. They also attribute to him *The Lookouts*, which begins: "Show no insolence to anyone." Sotion, in his *Successions of Philosophers*, says that when Leon, the tyrant of Phlius, asked him who he was, Pythagoras replied: "A Philosopher" <note>original: "Φιλόσοφος"; Pythagoras is credited with coining this term, meaning "lover of wisdom," to express humility before the gods who alone are truly "wise"</note>. 

He also compared life to a great festival <note>specifically the Great Games, like the Olympics</note>. Just as some people come there to compete for glory, and others come for trade and profit, the best people come as spectators. So it is in life: some, he said, are born with a slave-like nature, hunting for...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...hunters of glory and greed; but philosophers are hunters of truth. <margin>Pythagoras in his writings</margin> And these things are thus. In the three previously mentioned writings of Pythagoras, the following general principles are presented: he does not permit people to pray for themselves, because they do not know what is truly beneficial. 

He calls drunkenness a "singular harm" <note>original: "ἓν ἀνθ’ ἑνὸς βλάβην"; likely meaning a total harm or a harm that replaces all good</note>. He rejects all excess, saying that one should not exceed the proper measure <term>symmetry: "συμμετρίαν"; the Pythagorean ideal of proportion and balance</term> in either labor or diet. 

Regarding sexual matters, he speaks as follows: sexual activity should be practiced in winter, not in summer; in autumn and spring, it is less burdensome. <margin>When one should have sex</margin> It is heavy in every season, however, and not good for health. Indeed, when he was once asked when a man should approach a woman for sex, he replied, "Whenever you wish to become weaker than yourself." 

<margin>Four stages of life</margin> He divides human life into four parts: a child for twenty years; a youth for twenty; a young man for twenty; and an old man for twenty. These ages correspond to the seasons: the child is spring; the youth is summer; the young man is autumn; and the old man is winter. By his terminology, the "youth" is a lad <note>original: "μειράκιον"</note> and the "young man" is a man <note>original: "ἀνήρ"</note>.

<margin>Friends' goods are common</margin> He was the first to say (as Timaeus <note>Timaeus of Tauromenium, a historian of the 4th-3rd century BCE</note> claims) that "the goods of friends are common property," and that "friendship is equality." His disciples used to deposit their property into a single common fund. 

<margin>Five years of silence</margin> They also kept silence for five years, merely listening to his discourse without yet seeing Pythagoras, until they had been fully tested. From then on, they became part of his household and were permitted to see him in person. They avoided the use of cypress-wood coffins because the scepter of Zeus was made from that wood, as Hermippus <note>A biographer of the 3rd century BCE</note> says in his second book *On Pythagoras*. 

Indeed, he is said to have possessed a most majestic appearance. His disciples held the opinion that he was the god Apollo arrived from the Land of the Hyperboreans <note>A mythical, blessed land in the far north</note>. It is said that when he once stripped, his thigh was seen to be made of gold; and many people asserted that the river Nessos spoke to him as he was crossing it. 

Timaeus says in the tenth book of his *Histories* that Pythagoras told the women who lived with their husbands—addressing them with the names of goddesses—that they were "Maidens," then "Brides," <note>The text likely continued to "Mothers" and "Widows," associating each stage with a specific deity</note>...

### PYTHAGORAS: BOOK 8

...then those called mothers. He was the first to bring geometry to perfection, after Moeris first discovered the principles of its elements, as Anticleides says in the second book of his work *On Alexander*. Pythagoras especially devoted himself to the <term>arithmetical: "arithmetikon"; the study of number theory as the foundation of all things</term> aspect of geometry; he also discovered the <term>monochord: "kanona"; a single-stringed instrument used to measure the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</term>. Nor did he neglect the study of medicine. Apollodorus the Calculator says that Pythagoras sacrificed a hecatomb <note>a massive sacrifice of one hundred oxen</note> when he discovered that in a right-angled triangle, the square of the side subtending the right angle <note>the hypotenuse</note> is equal to the squares of the sides containing the right angle. There is an epigram about this, which runs:

->When Pythagoras found the famous figure,<-
->For which he offered a glorious sacrifice of oxen.<-

It is also said that he was the first to train athletes on a diet of meat; specifically Eurymenes (according to Favorinus in the third book of his *Memorabilia*). Previously, athletes had trained their bodies using dried figs, soft cheese, and even wheat, as the same Favorinus says in the eighth book of his *Miscellaneous History*. However, some say it was a different Pythagoras—a physical trainer—who established this meat diet, and not the philosopher. For the philosopher forbade the killing of animals, much less eating them, on the grounds that they share with us the right to a soul. 

This was his stated reason; but in truth, he forbade the eating of living things to train and accustom people to a simple life, so that their food might be easily obtained—eating uncooked foods and drinking plain water. He believed that from this diet, health of body and sharpness of soul would result. Indeed, at Delos, he would only worship at the altar of Apollo the Procreator <note>original: "Genetor"</note>, which is located behind the Altar of Horns, because only wheat, barley, and cakes were placed upon it without the use of sacrificial fire; no animal victim was ever slaughtered there, as Aristotle says in his *Constitution of Delos*. They also say he was the first to declare that the soul, passing through the <term>circle of necessity: "kyklon anankēs"; the inevitable cycle of reincarnation or transmigration</term>, is bound at different times in various living creatures. He was also the first to introduce weights and measures to the Greeks...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

### BOOK 8: PYTHAGORAS (Continued)

He also introduced measures and weights among the Greeks, according to Aristoxenus the musician. He was the first to identify the Evening Star and the Morning Star <note>original: "Hesperus and Phosphorus"</note> as the same celestial body <note>the planet Venus</note>, as Parmenides reports. He was held in such high admiration that his followers used to say his words were like the voices of a god. Indeed, he himself claimed in his writings that after two hundred and seven years he had returned from the underworld <note>original: "Hades"</note> to the world of men. 

For this reason, many sought his company and came to hear his teachings, including the Lucanians, the Peucetians, the Messapians, and the Romans <note>these were various tribes and peoples living in ancient Italy</note>. Until the time of Philolaus, it was impossible to know the true Pythagorean doctrines; Philolaus was the first to publish those three famous books, which Plato reportedly sent for and purchased for one hundred <term>minae: a unit of ancient Greek currency; 100 minae was an enormous sum, roughly equivalent to several years' wages for a skilled laborer</term>. No fewer than six hundred people would gather to attend his nightly lectures; and if any were deemed worthy to see him in person, they would write home to their families as though they had been granted a great privilege. 

The people of Metapontum even called his house the Temple of Demeter <note>the goddess of agriculture and grain</note>, and they called the narrow street where he lived the "Museum" <note>original: "mouseion," a place sacred to the Muses; this reflects the high intellectual and spiritual status he held</note>, according to Favorinus in his *Miscellaneous History*. Other Pythagoreans maintained that not everything should be revealed to everyone, as Aristoxenus records in the tenth book of his *Educational Laws*. In that work, it is mentioned that when Xenophilus the Pythagorean was asked how a man might best educate his son, he replied, "By having him born in a city that is well-governed" <note>the OCR text reads "lawless" (ἀνομουμένης), likely a scribal error for "well-ordered" (εὐνομουμένης)</note>. 

Pythagoras also turned many others throughout Italy into noble and virtuous men <note>original: "kaloi kai agathoi," the Greek ideal of a gentleman of character</note>, including the famous lawmakers Zaleucus and Charondas. For he was exceptionally gifted at fostering friendship; if he learned that someone shared his <term>symbols: "symbola"; secret passwords or metaphorical maxims used by the Pythagorean community to recognize and instruct one another</term>, he would immediately take that person as a companion and make them a friend. 

His symbols were as follows: 
* Do not stir the fire with a sword. <note>Metaphorically: do not provoke an angry person.</note>
* Do not step over the balance. <note>Metaphorically: do not overstep the bounds of justice and equality.</note>
* Do not sit upon a quart-measure <note>original: "choenix"</note>. <note>Metaphorically: do not live only for the present day or remain idle.</note>
* Do not eat your heart. <note>Metaphorically: do not waste away with grief or anxiety.</note>
* Help men take down a burden, but do not help them put one on. <note>Encouraging others toward virtue/effort rather than idleness.</note>
* Always keep your bedclothes bound together. <note>Likely referring to being ready for action or maintaining order.</note>
* Do not wear the image of a god on a ring. <note>Avoid treating sacred things with common familiarity.</note>
* Smooth over the mark of a pot in the ashes. <note>Forget past quarrels; do not leave traces of anger.</note>
* With oil in...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

### BOOK 8: PYTHAGORAS (Continued)

...not to wipe out a seat <note>original: "thakon me omorgnusthai"; this likely meant one should not occupy a place and then leave no trace of oneself, or perhaps a warning against sloth</note>, not to urinate while turned toward the sun, not to walk off the main highway, not to offer the right hand lightly <note>original: "me radiōs dexian emballein"; an admonition against making hasty oaths or friendships</note>, not to have swallows under one’s roof, not to keep birds with hooked claws, not to trample or sit upon nail parings or hair clippings, to turn away a sharp blade, and when traveling abroad, not to turn back at the borders.

By these things, he meant the following: by "Do not stir the fire with a knife," he meant not to provoke the anger and swelling pride of those in power. By "Do not overstep the balance," he meant not to overstep that which is equal and just. By "Do not sit upon a <term>choenix: an ancient Greek dry measure, roughly equivalent to a person's daily ration of grain</term>," he meant to care for the future as much as the present, for the choenix represents a single day's food. By "Do not eat the heart," he signaled that one should not consume the soul with anxieties and griefs. By "Do not turn back when departing on a journey," he was advising those who are departing from this life not to cling longingly to living, nor to be led astray by the pleasures of this world. Other symbols may be interpreted in a similar fashion, so that we do not dwell too long on them.

Above all else, he forbade the eating of the red-mullet <note>original: "erythinos"</note> and the black-tail <note>original: "melanouros"</note>; he also commanded his followers to abstain from the heart and from beans. Aristotle says he also occasionally forbade the womb and the red-mullet <note>original: "triglē"</note>. Some say that he himself was satisfied with only honey, or a bit of honeycomb or bread; he would not taste wine during the daylight hours. For a side dish, he mostly ate boiled or raw vegetables, and only rarely seafood.

His robe was white and clean, and his bed-coverings were white and made of wool; for linen had not yet reached those regions. He was never known to have relieved himself in public, nor to have engaged in sexual intercourse, nor to have been seen drunk. He avoided laughter and all forms of sycophancy, such as coarse jokes and vulgar stories. Even when he was angry, he would punish neither a slave nor a free man. He called the act of giving a warning "storking" <note>original: "pelargan," derived from the word for stork, "pelargos," perhaps referencing the stork's reputation for duty and care</note>. He made use of divination through omens and the flight of birds, but very rarely through the use of fire <note>original: "empyrōn"</note>, except for that which involved frankincense. He performed sacrifices...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...[eating only] inanimate things. Others say that he sacrificed only cocks and kids and suckling pigs—the so-called "tender ones"—but never lambs. Aristoxenus <note>Aristoxenus of Tarentum was a Greek philosopher and music theorist who studied under Aristotle; he is a primary source for details on the Pythagorean way of life</note>, however, says that Pythagoras allowed the eating of all other living things, and only abstained from the plough-ox and the ram. The same author says (as mentioned before) that he received his moral dogmas from Themistoclea at Delphi.

Hieronymus says that when Pythagoras descended into the underworld, he saw the soul of Hesiod bound to a bronze pillar and shrieking, and the soul of Homer hanging from a tree with snakes around it, as punishment for the things they said about the gods. He also reported that those who refuse to live with their own wives are punished in Hades; indeed, it was for this teaching that he was greatly honored by the people of Croton. Aristippus of Cyrene, in his work *On Physics*, says that he was named Pythagoras because he spoke the truth no less than the Pythian <note>Pythian is a title for the god Apollo at Delphi; Aristippus suggests a wordplay between "Pythios" (Apollo) and "Pythagoras"</note>. It is said that he used to advise his disciples to say these words to themselves whenever they returned to their homes:

> Where did I go wrong? What did I do? What duty did I leave unfulfilled?

He forbade the offering of blood sacrifices to the gods, commanding his followers to worship only at the bloodless altar. He taught that one should not swear by the gods, for a person should strive to make themselves worthy of belief without an oath. He taught that honor must be given to elders, as they considered that which precedes in time to be more honorable: just as in the universe, the east <note>literally "the rising"</note> is more honorable than the west <note>literally "the setting"</note>; in life, the beginning is more honorable than the end; and in living existence, birth is more honorable than decay. 

He taught that the gods should be preferred over spirits <term>daimones: divine beings or guardian spirits that rank between the immortal gods and mortal humans</term>; heroes over men; and of men, parents above all. He also taught that people should associate with one another in such a way as not to make enemies of friends, but to make friends of enemies. He held that nothing should be considered private property <note>This reflects the famous Pythagorean maxim: "Friends' goods are common property"</note>. One should assist the law and wage war against lawlessness. One should neither destroy nor <gloss>harm</gloss> a cultivated plant, nor even an animal that does not harm humans. 

Modesty and caution should be observed; one should neither be possessed by uncontrollable laughter nor wear a gloomy face. One should avoid an excess of flesh <note>meaning excess body fat or physical bulk</note>, and alternate between relaxation and intensity while walking. One should exercise the memory, and never speak or [act] while in a state of anger...

### PYTHAGORAS. Book 8

...<unclear>to ded</unclear>icate oneself, to honor every form of divination, to use songs accompanied by the lyre, and to render due thanks to gods and good men through hymns. He forbade the eating of beans because they are flatulent <note>original: πνευματώδεις (pneumatodeis), meaning "full of wind" or "spirit"</note> and therefore participate more in the nature of the soul. Furthermore, he argued that abstaining from them makes the stomach more orderly and, for this reason, renders the visions seen in sleep smooth and undisturbed. 

Alexander <note>Alexander Polyhistor was a 1st-century BCE scholar whose "Successions of Philosophers" is a major source for this account</note> also says in his *Successions of Philosophers* that he found these following doctrines in the Pythagorean memoirs: 

The principle of all things is the **Monad** <note>The Monad represents Unity or the number One</note>. From the Monad arises the **Indefinite Dyad** <note>The Indefinite Dyad represents duality or the principle of "otherness" and multiplicity</note>, which serves as a material substrate for the Monad, which is the cause. From the Monad and the Indefinite Dyad come numbers; from numbers, points; from these, lines; from which come plane figures; and from these, solid bodies. 

From these come the solid bodies whose elements are four: **fire, water, earth, and air**. These elements change and turn through the whole of existence, and from them is produced a world <note>original: κόσμον (kosmon), implying an ordered, beautiful universe</note> that is animate, intelligent, and spherical, containing the earth at its center—the earth itself being spherical and inhabited all around. He says there are even **Antipodes** <note>literally "those with feet opposite ours"</note>, and what is "down" for us is "up" for them.

In the world, light and darkness, heat and cold, and dryness and moisture are distributed in equal measure. When heat prevails, it becomes summer; when cold prevails, it becomes winter. When they are equal, the seasons are at their best: the blooming period is a healthy spring, while the fading period is a sickly autumn. In the same way, the morning is the "bloom" of the day, while the evening is its "fade," which is why evening is more prone to illness. 

The air surrounding the earth is stagnant and sickly, and everything within it is mortal. However, the air at the very top <note>the upper atmosphere or ether</note> is in constant motion, pure and healthy; everything within it is immortal and therefore divine. The sun, the moon, and the other stars are gods, for heat—which is the cause of life—prevails in them. The moon is illuminated by the sun. There is also a kinship between humans and the gods, because...

## DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...that humanity participates in heat. For this reason, God also exercises providence <note>original: προνοεῖσθαι (pronoeisthai). This suggests a divine care or "forethought" for human affairs</note> over us. There is a Destiny <note>original: εἱμαρμένην (heimarmenen), often translated as Fate</note> governing the whole universe, while the individual parts are the causes of its administration. He taught that a ray from the sun extends through the aether <note>The aether was considered by Greeks to be the "fifth element," a pure, fiery substance filling the upper heavens</note>, passing through both the "cold" and the "thick" regions. They call the air "cold aether," and they call the sea and moisture "thick aether." 

This solar ray reaches even into the depths, and through this, it gives life to all things. Everything that shares in this heat is alive; for this reason, even plants are considered living beings. However, not all things possess a soul. The soul is a "fragment" <note>original: ἀπόσπασμα (apospasma), literally something torn or detached from a larger whole</note> of the aether—both the hot and the cold varieties—since it shares in the cold aether as well. 

The soul is distinct from "life." Furthermore, the soul is immortal, because that from which it has been detached is itself immortal. Living creatures are born from one another through seed; birth from the earth is an impossibility. The seed is a drop from the brain <note>This "encephalocentric" theory of reproduction was common among some early Greek thinkers who believed the marrow and brain were the source of life-force</note> containing within it a warm vapor. 

When this seed is brought into the womb, "ichor" <note>A term often used for the watery fluid in the veins of the gods, here used for vital bodily fluids</note>, moisture, and blood are released from the brain. From these, the flesh, nerves, bones, hair, and the entire body are composed. From the vapor within the seed, the soul and the senses are formed. 

The first "thick" mass is shaped within forty days. Then, according to the **ratios of harmony**, the infant is brought to completion and born in seven, nine, or at most ten months. The infant contains within itself all the "ratios" or "logics" of life <note>original: λόγους (logous). In Pythagorean thought, these are the mathematical proportions that define a living being</note>; these are linked together and held in place by the laws of harmony, each part appearing at its ordained time. 

Sensation in general—and the sense of sight specifically—is a very hot vapor. This is why we are said to see through air and water, for the internal heat is resisted by the external cold. If the vapor in the eyes were cold, it would simply pass through and merge with the similar air. In some passages, he calls the eyes the **"gates of the sun."** He holds similar doctrines regarding hearing and the rest of the senses. The human...

### PYTHAGORAS. Book VIII

The soul is divided into three parts: intelligence, reason, and passion <note>original: νοῦν (noun), φρένα (phrena), and θυμόν (thymon). In Pythagorean thought, these represent the distinct faculties of the mind, from basic drive to high-order logic</note>. Now, intelligence and passion are found in other animals as well, but reason is found in humans alone. The seat of the soul extends from the heart to the brain. The part of it located in the heart is passion; whereas reason and intelligence are located in the brain. The senses are "drops" from these centers. The rational part is immortal, while the rest are mortal. The soul is nourished by the blood. The reasons <note>original: λόγους (logous). Here, Pythagoras likely refers to the rational principles or "discourses" that shape our identity</note> are the "winds" of the soul. Both the soul and these reasons are invisible, just as the aether itself is invisible. The veins, arteries, and nerves are the bonds of the soul; but when the soul is strong and rests within itself, its bonds become its words and deeds. When it is cast out upon the earth, it wanders in the air, appearing in a form similar to the body. Hermes is the steward of souls, and for this reason he is called the Escort <note>original: πομπαῖον (pompaios)</note>, the Gatekeeper <note>original: πυλαῖον (pylaios)</note>, and the Underworlder <note>original: χθόνιον (chthonion)</note>, since <margin>this one</margin> <note>The marginal note "τος" is a fragment, likely completing the word "οὗτος" (this one)</note> it is he who brings the souls out of their bodies, from both land and sea. Pure souls are led to the highest realm, while the impure are not allowed to approach them nor each other, but are bound in unbreakable chains by the Furies <note>original: ἐριννύων (Erinnyon), the female deities of vengeance who punish wrongdoing</note>. The whole air is full of souls, which are regarded as "daemons" <note>In the ancient world, *daimones* were not "demons" in a modern sense, but spirits or tutelary deities that mediated between the human and divine</note> and heroes; by these, dreams and signs of disease or health are sent to humans—and not only to humans, but to sheep and other cattle. Purifications, rituals to ward off evil, all forms of divination, omens, and the like are directed toward these spirits. He says the greatest thing for humans is to persuade the soul toward good or toward evil. A person is happy when a good soul is present; yet such a soul never remains still, nor does it keep the same flow. Justice is a sacred oath, and for this reason Zeus is called the God of Oaths <note>original: Δία ὅρκιον (Dia Horkion)</note>. Virtue is a harmony, and...

...health, and every good, and God; for this reason, the universe is also composed according to harmony <note>original: ἁρμονίαν (harmonían). Pythagoras believed the cosmos was structured on musical and mathematical ratios</note>. Friendship, too, is a harmonious equality. He held that one must believe in honors for the gods and for heroes, though not equal honors: for the gods, one should always offer praise while wearing white garments and remaining pure; for the heroes, honors should begin only from midday. Purity is achieved through cleansings, washings, and ritual sprinklings. For these reasons, he maintained purity from funerals, from the birthing-bed, and from every kind of pollution. animals, as well as beans and the other things forbidden by those who perform the initiations in the temples.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Aristotle says, in his work *On Beans*, that Pythagoras commanded his followers to abstain from beans either because they resemble the private parts, or because they are like the gates of Hades (for they are the only plant without joints), or because they cause decay, or because they resemble the nature of the universe, or because they are "oligarchic," since they are used for casting lots in elections <note>In ancient Greek democracy, officials were often chosen by drawing colored beans from a container; the Pythagoreans generally mistrusted this democratic randomness</note>. He also taught that one should not pick up what has fallen from the table, in order to train oneself not to eat immoderately, or perhaps because it signifies the death of someone.

<margin>Aristophanes</margin>
Aristophanes says that things which fall belong to the heroes, saying in his play *The Heroes*:
> Do not taste whatever may fall 
> inside the table’s edge.

<margin>Mên (The Month)</margin>
He taught not to touch a white rooster, because it is sacred to Mên <note>original: Μηνὸς (Mênos). Mên was a lunar deity worshipped in parts of the Greek world, often associated with months and the moon</note> and is a suppliant. Now, the rooster was considered a good thing, and was sacred to Mên because it signals the hours. One should not touch such fish as are sacred; for the same things should not be assigned to gods and to men, just as they are not shared between free men and slaves. White is of the nature of the Good, while black is of the nature of Evil. One should not break bread, because in ancient times friends used to gather around a single loaf, as barbarians still do today; nor should one divide that which brings them together. Others say this refers to the judgment in Hades; others that it creates cowardice in war; others that it is because the universe begins from a whole. Of solid shapes, he considered the sphere to be the most beautiful; and of plane figures, the circle. Old age and everything that diminishes are similar; and growth and youth are the same. Health is the [preservation] of form... <note>The text cuts off here at "δια-" (dia-); the catchword for the next page is "μονίαν" (monían), completing the word "διαμονίαν," meaning permanence or preservation</note>

Pythagoras met his end in the following manner: while he was meeting with his associates in the house of Milo the wrestler, it happened that the house was set on fire out of envy by one of those who had been deemed unworthy of admission into the inner circle. Some say, however, that the citizens of Croton <note>A Greek city in southern Italy where Pythagoras founded his school.</note> did this themselves, fearing that he was attempting to establish a tyranny. 

<margin>The Bean Field</margin>
Pythagoras was caught as he was fleeing; and when he came to a certain place full of beans, he stood there, saying that it was better to be captured than to trample them, and better to be killed than to speak <note>The Pythagoreans held a famous, though mysterious, taboo against beans, and were sworn to a vow of silence regarding their most sacred doctrines.</note>. Thus, he was slaughtered by his pursuers. In this same way, most of his companions were also destroyed, numbering about forty. A very few escaped, among whom were Archytas of Tarentum and Lysis, who was mentioned previously. 

Dicaearchus <note>A student of Aristotle and a respected historian.</note>, however, says that Pythagoras died after taking refuge in the Temple of the Muses at Metapontum, having fasted for forty days. Heraclides says in his *Abridgment of the Lives by Satyrus* that after burying Pherecydes <note>Pythagoras' teacher, who famously died of a skin disease at Delos.</note> in Delos, he returned to Italy, and finding a great feast being held by Milo of Croton, he departed for Metapontum, and there ended his life by starvation, not wishing to live any longer. 

Hermippus says that when the Agrigentines and the Syracusans were at war, Pythagoras went out with his associates and took his stand with the Agrigentines. When a rout occurred, he was attempting to go around the [field] of beans

...necessity, he was killed by the Syracusans. The others, numbering about thirty-five, were burned to death in Tarentum for attempting to oppose the ruling magistrates. Hermippus gives another account regarding Pythagoras. He says that when Pythagoras arrived in Italy, he made a small underground dwelling and instructed his mother to write down everything that happened on a writing tablet, noting the time of each event, and then to lower it down to him until he should ascend again. His mother did this. After some time, Pythagoras came back up, looking thin and like a skeleton. Entering the assembly, he claimed he had returned from Hades <note>The Greek underworld or realm of the dead.</note>; he even read aloud to them the events that had occurred in the world above during his absence. The people, deeply moved by his words, wept and lamented, and they believed Pythagoras was a divine being. They even went so far as to entrust their wives to him, so that they might learn some of his doctrines; these women were called the "Pythagoreans." This is the account given by Hermippus.

Pythagoras also had a wife named Theano, the daughter of Brontinus of Croton. Others, however, say she was the wife of Brontinus but a student of Pythagoras. He also had a daughter named Damo, as Lysis mentions in his letter to Hipparchus, writing about Pythagoras as follows: "Many say that you and Damasias are studying philosophy; this Pythagoras deemed unworthy, for he, having entrusted his commentaries <note>original: ὑπομνήματα (hypomnemata) — these were private notes or memoirs containing the core of his teachings.</note> to his own daughter Damo, commanded her to hand them over to no one outside of the house. And she, though she could have sold these discourses for much <term>wealth</term><gloss>money</gloss>, refused to do so. For she considered poverty and her father's injunctions more precious than gold, and this she did even though she was a woman."

He also had a son, Telauges, who succeeded his father and (according to some) was the teacher of Empedocles. Hippobotus, at least, says that Empedocles addressed Telauges as follows: "Illustrious youth, son of Theano and Pythagoras." No written work is attributed to Telauges, though there are a few extant works by his mother, Theano. It is said that when she was asked how many days after being with a man a woman is pure...

# PYTHAGORAS. Book 8.

...[he] saw, as did Xenophilus of Chalcis, from Thrace, and Phanton of Phlius, along with Echecrates, Diocles, and Polymnastus, who were also from Phlius. These men were students of Philolaus and Eurytus of Tarentum. There were, in fact, four men named Pythagoras around the same time, living not very far apart from one another. One was from Croton, a man of tyrannical character. Another was from Phlius, a physical trainer and an anointer <note>A trainer who rubbed athletes with oil</note>, as some say. A third was from Zacynthus, to whom they attribute the secret doctrines of the philosophy, acting as a teacher of them; it was because of him that the proverb <term>He himself said it</term> <note>original: "Autos epha," famously translated into Latin as "Ipse dixit." This phrase was used by students to signify that the master's word was the final, unarguable authority.</note> entered into common use. Others say there was yet another Pythagoras, a sculptor from Rhegium, who is thought to have been the first to aim for rhythm and symmetry in his work. There was also another who was a sculptor from Samos; another who was a mediocre orator; another a physician who wrote on hernias and composed a work on Homer; and still another who wrote a history of Dorian affairs, as Dionysius records.

Eratosthenes says (as Favorinus also notes in his *Universal History*) that this Pythagoras was the first to box with technical skill in the forty-eighth Olympiad <note>Approximately 588 BCE</note>. He wore his hair long and was dressed in a purple robe. Having been excluded from the boys' contest and mocked for it, he immediately entered the men's contest and emerged victorious. There is a simple epigram concerning him, written by Theaetetus:

> If you have heard of a certain Pythagoras, O stranger, 
> A long-haired, famous boxer from Samos,
> I am that Pythagoras. If you were to ask any 
> Of the people of Elis about my deeds, you would say they speak of things beyond belief.

Favorinus says that he employed definitions based on mathematical subject matter, though Socrates and those close to him did so even more extensively, and after them, Aristotle and the Stoics. Furthermore, he was the first to call the heavens the <term>Cosmos</term> <note>original: "kosmos." This word implies a beautiful, harmonious, and orderly arrangement.</note> and to say that the earth is spherical. However, Theophrastus attributes the idea of the spherical earth to Parmenides, and Zeno attributes it to Hesiod. It is said that he was opposed by...

## Pythagoras to Anaximenes.

<margin>On migration</margin>
Even you, most excellent friend, if you were in no way better than Pythagoras in spirit and reputation, would have departed from Miletus and moved elsewhere. But now the glory of your fathers keeps you there; and it would have kept me too, had I been like Anaximenes. But if you noble men abandon your cities, the order of the world <note>original: "kosmos"</note> will be lost, and the danger from the Medes <note>The Persians</note> will become even greater. It is not always 
<margin>On the Fatherland</margin>
noble to be gazing at the heavens <note>A term for studying astronomy or philosophy, sometimes used dismissively of those who ignore earthly affairs</note>, for it is more noble to be concerned for one's fatherland. And I myself am not entirely occupied with my own teachings, but also with the wars in which the <term>Italiotes</term> <note>Greeks living in Southern Italy</note> are engaged against one another.

<margin>Pythagoreans</margin>
Since we have completed our account of Pythagoras, we must now speak of the illustrious Pythagoreans; after them, we shall discuss those who are mentioned scattered here and there; then we shall connect the succession of those worthy of mention down to Epicurus, as we said before. We have already discussed Theano and Telauges. Now, we must first speak of Empedocles; for according to some, he was a student of Pythagoras.

# EMPEDOCLES.

<margin>Empedocles</margin>
Empedocles (as Hippobotus says) was the son of Meton, the son of Empedocles, and was a citizen of Acragas <note>Modern Agrigento in Sicily</note>. Timaeus says the same in the fifteenth book of his *Histories*, noting that Empedocles—the grandfather of the poet—was a distinguished man. Hermippus also says the same as Timaeus. Likewise, Heraclides, in his work *On Diseases*, says that he came from a splendid house, his grandfather having kept horses for racing. Eratosthenes also says...

<meta>Continuity Note: This page marks the beginning of the biography of Empedocles of Akragas. It follows the transition from Pythagoras to his followers and students, examining the contradictory accounts of Empedocles' ancestry and his early life.</meta>

<page-num>327</page-num>
-># EMPEDOCLES. Book 8<-

In the *List of Olympic Victors*, it is recorded that the father of Meton was victorious in the seventy-first Olympiad <note>The 71st Olympiad occurred around 496 BCE</note>; for this, [the author] cites Aristotle as a witness. Apollodorus the grammarian says in his *Chronicles* <note>original: "Chronica"</note> that Empedocles was the son of Meton. However, Glaucus says that he went to Thurii <note>A Greek colony in Southern Italy</note> when it had been only recently founded. Then, proceeding further, he says: "Those who record that he fled his home for Syracuse and fought with them against the Athenians seem to me to be entirely ignorant. For either he was no longer alive, or he was extremely aged; which does not appear to be the case." For Aristotle, as well as Heraclides, says that he died at sixty years of age. The man who won the horse race in the seventy-first Olympiad was certainly a namesake of his, so that the dates are correctly indicated by Apollodorus. 

Satyrus says in his *Lives* that Empedocles was the son of Exainetos, and that he himself also left behind a son named Exainetos. In that same Olympiad, the father won the horse race, while the son won in wrestling—or, as Heraclides says in his *Abridgment*, in the foot-race. But I found in the *Commentaries* of Favorinus that Empedocles sacrificed an ox to the sacred delegates <note>original: "theorois" - ambassadors sent to festivals</note> made of honey and barley-meal <note>Empedocles followed the Pythagorean prohibition against killing animals, so he crafted a "bloodless" sacrifice of dough</note>; he also had a brother named Callicratides. Telauges, the son of Pythagoras, says in his letter to Philolaus that Empedocles was the son of Archinomos. 

That he was from Acragas <note>Modern Agrigento</note> in Sicily, he himself says at the beginning of his *Purifications* <note>original: "Katharmoi", a famous philosophical poem on the soul and reincarnation</note>:

> O friends, who dwell in the great city of golden Acragas,
> High on the city's heights;

And such are the accounts concerning his lineage. Timaeus, in his ninth book, records that he was a student of Pythagoras, saying that he was convicted at that time of "word-theft" <note>original: "logoklopeia" — essentially plagiarism or revealing secret teachings</note> and, just like Plato, was then forbidden from participating in the discussions. He himself mentions Pythagoras, saying:

> And there was among them a man of extraordinary knowledge,

->x.iiii.<-

--- Page 342 ---
<meta>Continuity Note: This page continues the discussion of Empedocles’ education and influences, moving from the letter to Telauges mentioned on the previous page to the various historical accounts of who his teachers actually were.</meta>

<page-num>328</page-num>
<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

"He who indeed possessed the greatest wealth of understanding." <note>original: "Ὃς δὴ μήκιστον πραπίδων ἐκτήσατο πλοῦτον" — This is a line from Empedocles’ own poetry (Fragment 129), usually thought to praise Pythagoras for his vast knowledge, though here Diogenes notes a different attribution.</note>

Some scholars apply this line to Parmenides himself. Neanthes states that until the time of Philolaus and Empedocles, the Pythagoreans shared their secret teachings <note>original: "logon" — the oral or written doctrines of the school</note> among themselves. However, once Empedocles made these doctrines public through his poetry, they established a law that they would no longer share their knowledge with any epic poet. They say Plato suffered the same exclusion, for he too was barred from their group. Neanthes does not, however, say from whom Empedocles heard these teachings. Regarding the letter circulating as being addressed to Telauges <note>The son of Pythagoras</note>, which claims Empedocles associated with Hippasus and Brontinus, it is not considered reliable.

Theophrastus <note>The successor of Aristotle and a great classifier of philosophy</note> says that Empedocles became a devotee of Parmenides and an imitator of his style in his poems; for Parmenides had also published his discourse *On Nature* <note>original: "Peri physeos"</note> in epic verse. 

Hermippus, however, says he was not a follower of Parmenides, but rather of Xenophanes <note>An early philosopher known for his critiques of Greek mythology</note>, with whom he lived and whose epic style he imitated; it was only later that he encountered the Pythagoreans. 

Alcidamas says in his *Natural Philosophy* <note>original: "Physikos"</note> that Zeno and Empedocles studied under Parmenides at the same time, but later departed. He claims Zeno practiced philosophy in his own private way, while Empedocles studied under Anaxagoras and Pythagoras. From Pythagoras, he emulated the dignity of his life and his outward appearance, and from Anaxagoras, he took his study of the physical world <note>original: "physiologia"</note>.

Aristotle says in his work *The Sophist* that Empedocles was the first to discover <term>Rhetoric</term> <note>the art of effective or persuasive speaking</note>, just as Zeno discovered <term>Dialectic</term> <note>the art of investigating the truth of opinions through logical discussion</note>. In his work *On Poets*, Aristotle also remarks that Empedocles was "Homeric" and powerful in his phrasing, being fond of metaphors and employing other poetic techniques successfully. 

He also notes that although Empedocles wrote other poems—including one on the crossing of the Hellespont by Xerxes and a prelude to Apollo—these were later burned by either a sister or a daughter (according to Hieronymus). The prelude was burned accidentally, but the "Persian" poem was destroyed intentionally because it was unfinished. Generally speaking, he says Empedocles also wrote tragedies and political works. However, Heraclides, the son of Sarapion, says those tragedies belong to a different man of the same name.

<page-num>329</page-num>
<header>EMPEDOCLES. Book 8</header>

Hieronymus <note>A Peripatetic philosopher known for historical anecdotes</note> says that he came across forty-three of Empedocles’ tragedies. Neanthes, however, claims that Empedocles wrote these tragedies while he was still young, and that he himself had seen them. Satyrus, in his *Lives*, states that Empedocles was both a physician and an excellent orator. Indeed, Gorgias of Leontini <note>One of the most famous Greek Sophists and masters of rhetoric</note> became his student—a man who surpassed everyone in the art of rhetoric and who left behind a manual on the subject. Apollodorus says in his *Chronology* that this Gorgias lived to be one hundred and nine years old. Satyrus further reports that Gorgias claimed he was personally present when Empedocles was performing magic <note>original: "goēteuonti" — implying sorcery or supernatural wonder-working</note>. Moreover, Empedocles himself makes promises of this kind and more throughout his poems, where he says:

> You shall learn all the medicines that exist for ills, and a defense against old age;
> Since for you alone I shall accomplish all these things.
> You shall stay the force of tireless winds, which, rushing over the earth
> With their blasts, destroy the fields and crops.
> And again, if you wish, you shall bring back the winds in return.
> You shall bring a timely drought for men after dark rain,
> And after summer drought you shall bring tree-nourishing streams,
> Which flow through the summer air.
> And you shall lead from the underworld the spirit of a dead man.

Timaeus <note>A historian from Sicily</note> also says in his eighteenth book that the man was marveled at in many ways. For example, once when the Etesian winds <note>Strong, annual Mediterranean winds</note> blew so violently that they ruined the harvests, he ordered donkeys to be flayed and their skins made into bags. He then stretched these bags out on the hills and mountain peaks to catch the wind. When the wind ceased, he was given the name "Wind-Stayer" <note>original: "Kolysanemas"</note>. Heraclides, in his work *On Diseases*, says that Empedocles even gave instructions to Pausanias regarding the "woman without breath" <note>original: "apnoun" — a famous case where Empedocles reportedly kept a woman alive in a death-like trance for thirty days</note>. This Pausanias, according to Aristippus and Satyrus, was his beloved, to whom he dedicated his poem *On Nature* with these words:

> Pausanias, you listen, son of wise Anchitus.

Furthermore, he even composed an epigram for him:

He says he called Akragas <note>Modern Agrigento in Sicily</note> "great" because eight hundred thousand people lived there. It is said that Cleomenes the rhapsode <note>A professional singer of epic poetry</note> recited these very *Purifications* <note>original: "Katharmoi", Empedocles’ poem on the soul’s journey and ritual purity</note> at the Olympic Games, as Favorinus also mentions in his *Memoirs*. ### EMPEDOCLES. Book 8

...was being brought out <note>This text continues an anecdote from the previous page regarding a banquet where the host was acting like a tyrant</note>, while the others remained silent. Empedocles, being of a disposition that hated wickedness, ordered the wine to be served, but the host who had invited him said they must wait for the servant of the council. When the servant arrived, he was appointed master of the revels <term>symposiarch: the guest chosen to dictate the drinking pace and the mixture of wine and water</term>—the host clearly having appointed him as a preliminary step toward establishing a tyranny. For the master of the revels ordered the guests either to drink or have the wine poured over their heads. At that time, Empedocles remained quiet, but on the following day, he brought them both before the court and, having secured their conviction, had them executed—both the host who invited him and the master of the revels. This was the beginning of his political career.

Again, when Akron the physician asked the council for a site to build a family monument because of his own preeminence <term>akrotēs: a pun on the doctor's name, meaning "top-most excellence" or "pinnacle"</term> among doctors, Empedocles came forward and blocked the request. He spoke at length about the principle of equality, and even asked this witty question: "What elegiac couplet shall we engrave? Shall it be this?"

->Akron the doctor, Akron of Akragas, son of an eminent father,<-
->Is covered by the eminent cliff of his most eminent fatherland.<-
<note>The original Greek is a famous tongue-twister and play on words, repeating the "Ak-" sound to mock the doctor's name and ambition. original: "Ἄκρον ἰητρὸν Ἄκρων' Ἀκραγαντῖνον πατρὸς ἄκρου / Κρύπτει κρημνὸς ἄκρος πατρίδος ἀκροτάτης."</note>

Some, however, report the second line this way:

->The summit of a tomb on the most eminent peak holds him.<-

Some say this verse is by Simonides <note>A celebrated Greek lyric poet known for his clever epitaphs</note>. Later, Empedocles also dissolved the Assembly of the Thousand <note>An oligarchic body of the wealthiest citizens</note>, having held his influence for three years; thus, he was not only a man of the wealthy but also of those who held democratic sentiments. Indeed, Timaeus says in his first and second books (for he mentions him often) that Empedocles held views contrary to the established government. Yet one can see how boastful and self-loving he appears in his poetry. He says, for instance:

> Greetings! I walk among you as an immortal god, no longer mortal,
> I go about...

and so forth. At the time when he visited the Olympic Games, he was deemed worthy of so much attention that no other person was mentioned in conversation as much as Empedocles. Later, however, when the citizens of Akragas were being resettled, they opposed his return...

...the descendants of his enemies. For this reason, he departed for the Peloponnese and there he died. Even he did not escape the notice of Timon <note>Timon of Phlius (c. 320–230 BCE), a Skeptic philosopher known for writing "Silloi" (Satires) that mocked other philosophers</note>, who attacks him by saying:

> -> — And Empedocles, the charmer of marketplace speeches; <-
> -> however much strength he had, so much did he seize <-
> -> as a Magistrate, establishing offices that were dependent on others. <-

Regarding his death, there are various accounts. Heraclides <note>Heraclides Ponticus, a student of Plato known for blending philosophy with fantastic stories</note>, after relating the story of the woman without breath <term>apnous: a famous case where Empedocles reportedly kept a woman in a death-like trance alive for thirty days without a pulse or breath before reviving her</term>—and how Empedocles gained great fame by sending a dead woman away alive—says that he was performing a sacrifice at the farm of Peisianax.

Some of his friends had been invited, among whom was Pausanias <note>Empedocles’ close friend and student, to whom he addressed his poem "On Nature"</note>. Then, after the feast, the others departed and went to rest—some under the trees, as the farm was nearby, and others wherever they wished—but Empedocles himself remained on the spot where he had reclined. When they rose at daybreak, he alone was not found. When he was sought and the servants were questioned, they claimed they did not know where he was. However, one person said that at midnight he heard a voice of tremendous volume calling "Empedocles!" and then, starting up, he saw a heavenly light and the glow of torches, but nothing else.

While the others were amazed at what had happened, Pausanias went down and sent people to search for him. Later, however, he forbade them from prying further, saying that things worthy of prayer had occurred and that they should sacrifice to Empedocles as if to one who had become a god.

Hermippus <note>A biographer known for collecting diverse traditions, often focusing on the deaths of famous men</note> says that a certain Pantheia <note>original: "Gyntheia," likely a scribal error for Pantheia</note> of Akragas, who had been given up by the physicians, was cured by him, and for this reason he performed the sacrifice. Those invited to the feast numbered about eighty.

Hippobotus, however, says that when Empedocles rose up, he made his way toward Mount Etna. Then, having arrived at the craters of fire, he leaped in and disappeared, wishing to confirm the report about himself—that he had truly become a god. But later the truth was discovered when one of his sandals was blown back up by the flames; for he was accustomed to wearing sandals made of bronze. Regarding this...

### EMPEDOCLES. Book 8
<page-num>333</page-num>

...Pausanias <note>original: "Παυσανίας" (the first letter is missing in the OCR). Pausanias was Empedocles' student and friend.</note> objected. Diodorus of Ephesus, writing about Anaxander, says that Empedocles emulated him, adopting the "tragic vanity" <note>original: "τῦφον" (typhos) – a sense of delusion or pompous pride</note> and the solemn, dignified clothing of tragic actors. 

When a plague fell upon the people of Selinus <note>Selinus was a wealthy Greek colony in Sicily</note> because of the foul odors from the surrounding river, such that the people were perishing and the women suffered difficult childbirths, Empedocles conceived a plan. At his own expense, he diverted two of the nearby rivers into the stagnant waters; by mixing them, he "sweetened" the streams <note>This is an early historical account of an engineering project used to combat malaria by draining marshes</note>. When the plague had ceased in this way, and while the Selinuntines were once feasting by the river, Empedocles appeared. They stood up, offered him homage, and prayed to him as if to a god. It was this reputation that he wished to confirm, according to some, when he leapt into the fire <note>referring to the craters of Mount Etna</note>.

Timaeus <note>Timaeus of Tauromenium (c. 350–260 BCE), a Sicilian historian known for his critical approach</note> opposes these stories, explicitly stating that Empedocles departed for the Peloponnese and never returned at all; for this reason, the manner of his death remains unknown. In the fourth book of his history, Timaeus makes a rebuttal against Heraclides by name. He argues that Peisianax was a citizen of Syracuse and did not own a farm in Akragas. Furthermore, he claims that Pausanias erected a memorial for his friend—once the legend of his disappearance had spread—either a small statue or a shrine <term>sekos: a sacred enclosure or small chapel</term> as if for a god, for Pausanias was a wealthy man. 

"How then," Timaeus asks, "could he have jumped into the craters, when, though they were nearby, he never once made mention of them?" He concludes that he died in the Peloponnese. It is not at all strange that his tomb is not visible, for the same is true of many other famous men. After saying these things, Timaeus adds: "But Heraclides is always such a teller of marvels <note>original: "παραδοξολόγος" (paradoxologos) – one who tells incredible or 'paradoxical' stories</note>, even claiming that a man once fell from the moon."

Hippobotus says that a veiled statue of Empedocles used to stand in Akragas, but was later placed in front of the Roman Senate House <term>bouleuterion: here referring to the Roman Curia</term>, unveiled, evidently because the Romans had moved it there. There are also some painted portraits of him which are still in circulation today. Neanthes of Cyzicus, who also wrote about the Pythagoreans, says that upon the death of Meton...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
<page-num>534</page-num>

<margin><unclear>Regarding (?)...</unclear></margin>...prevented the seeds of a tyranny from taking root. Later, Empedocles persuaded the citizens of Akragas <note>A powerful Greek city in Sicily, now known as Agrigento</note> to put an end to their civil strife and to practice political equality. Furthermore, he provided dowries for many of the daughters of the citizens who were without means, using his own vast wealth. Because of this, he took to wearing a purple robe and placed a golden headband on his head, as Favorinus <note>A 2nd-century scholar known for his wide-ranging historical anecdotes</note> records in his *Memorabilia*.

<margin>Favorinus</margin> He also wore bronze sandals and a Delphic wreath <note>A laurel crown, usually associated with victory or divine favor from Apollo</note>. His hair was long, and he was followed by attendants; he himself was always somber with a consistent, dignified manner. He would go about in such a way that when the citizens encountered him, they regarded his appearance as a badge of a kind of kingship.

Later, while traveling in a carriage to Messene for a festival, he fell and broke his thigh. Having fallen ill from this accident, he died at the age of seventy-seven. It is said that his tomb is in Megara. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin> Regarding his age, Aristotle differs, for he says that Empedocles died at sixty; but others claim he lived to be one hundred and nine. He reached his prime during the 84th Olympiad <note>roughly 444–441 BCE</note>.

<margin>Demetrius</margin> Demetrius of Troezen, in his book *Against the Sophists* <note>original: "κατ’ Ὀφισῶν" — the title is likely a corruption of "Against the Sophists" (κατὰ σοφιστῶν)</note>, says that, in the style of Homer:

> Binding a steep noose from a high cornel tree,
> He hung his neck, and his soul went down to Hades. <note>original: "Ἁψάμενον βρόχον αἰπὺν ἀφ’ ὑψηλοῖο κρανείης / Αὐχέν’ ἀποκρεμάσαι, ψυχὴν δ’ ἄϊδόσδε κατελθεῖν."</note>

However, in the previously mentioned letter of Telauges <note>Empedocles’ alleged son or successor</note>, it is said that he slipped into the sea due to old age and died. These are the various accounts concerning his death. I have also written a satirical epigram about him in my *Collection of All Meters*, which goes like this:

> And you, Empedocles, once cleansing your body with searching flame,
> Drank fire from the immortal craters;
> I will not say that you threw yourself willingly into Etna’s stream,
> But wishing to hide, you fell in against your will. <note>original: "Καὶ σὺ ποτ’ Ἐμπεδόκλεις διφῇ φλογὶ σῶμα καθήρας..." Diogenes is mocking the legend that Empedocles jumped into the volcano to prove he was a god, suggesting he actually just tripped while trying to disappear.</note>

> Indeed, the story goes that Empedocles died when once from a carriage...

### EMPEDOCLES, BOOK VIII

> He fell and broke his right thigh.
> But if he had leaped into the craters of fire to "drink of life," 
> how could his tomb still be shown in Megara? 
<note>original: "Ἔκπεσε, καὶ μηρὸν κλάσατο δεξιτερόν..." — These verses argue against the famous legend that Empedocles committed suicide by jumping into the volcano Mount Etna to prove his divinity, pointing out that his physical tomb exists elsewhere.</note>

His doctrines were as follows: there are four elements—fire, water, earth, and air <note>original: "αἰθέρα" (aether); in Empedocles’ system, this refers to the element of air</note>; and there are two forces: Love, by which things are joined, and Strife, by which they are separated. He expresses it in this way:

> Bright Zeus, life-bringing Hera, and Aidoneus,
> and Nestis, who wets the mortal spring with her tears.
<note>Empedocles used the names of gods to represent the physical elements.</note>

By "Zeus" he means fire; by "Hera" he means earth; by "Aidoneus" he means air; and by "Nestis" he means water. And these things, he says, never cease their continuous exchange, as such a cosmic arrangement is eternal. He further adds:

> At one time all things come together into unity through Love,
> At another, each is carried apart by the hatred of Strife.

He says that the sun is a vast collection of fire and is larger than the moon; the moon is disk-shaped; and the heavens themselves are crystal-like. He also taught that the soul inhabits every kind of animal and plant form. Indeed, he says:

> For I have already been, in my time, a boy and a girl,
> a bush and a bird, and a scaly fish from the sea.
<note>original: "ἔμπυρος ἰχθύς" — literally "fiery fish," likely referring to the shimmering scales of a fish jumping from the water. This reflects his belief in the transmigration of souls.</note>

His works *On Nature* and his *Purifications* extend to five thousand verses, while his *Medical Discourse* reaches six hundred verses. Regarding his tragedies, we have spoken previously.

When he was only three months old, he was taken to Megara in Sicily, and from there to Syracuse, as he himself says in his own writings. Upon his statue, the following is inscribed:

> As much as the great shining sun surpasses the stars,

# ARCHYTAS

Archytas, the son of Mnesagoras (or according to Aristoxenus, the son of Hestiaeus), was a citizen of Tarentum <note>a Greek colony in Southern Italy</note> and was himself a Pythagorean. It was he who saved Plato by means of a letter when Plato was on the verge of being put to death by Dionysius <note>Dionysius II, the tyrant of Syracuse</note>. He was greatly admired by the common people for every kind of virtue. Indeed, he served as the general <note>term: "strategos"; the highest military and political office</note> of his fellow citizens seven times, whereas others were forbidden by law to serve as general for more than a year. Regarding him, Plato wrote two letters, since Archytas had first written to him in this manner:

->Archytas to Plato, greetings.<- <note>original: "ὑγιαίνειν" (hygiainein), literally "to be in good health," the standard Greek greeting for a letter</note>

You do well to have recovered from your illness. You have informed us of this yourself, and Damiscos also reported it to us. Regarding the commentaries, we have taken care of them; we went up into Lucania <note>a region in Southern Italy</note> and met with the descendants of Ocellus <note>referring to Ocellus Lucanus, an earlier Pythagorean philosopher</note>. Those works concerning laws, kingship, holiness, and the origin of the universe, we have in our possession and have sent some to you; the rest, however, cannot be found at this time. Should they be found, they will be sent to you. Thus wrote Archytas; and Plato replied to him in this manner:

<page-num>337</page-num>
<header>ARCHYTAS. Book 8</header>
<sig>y. i.</sig>

## ->Plato to Archytas, greetings.<- <note>original: "εὖ πράττειν" (eu prattein); a standard greeting meaning "to do well" or "fare well"</note>

The commentaries <note>original: "hypomnemata"; these were likely records of Pythagorean teachings</note> that came from you we received with wonderful pleasure, and we admired the one who wrote them as much as possible; he seemed to us a man worthy of those ancient ancestors of yours. For indeed, these men are said to be Myraeans <note>a group of people associated with the city of Myra, or perhaps a specific Trojan lineage</note>. They were among the Trojans who were displaced during the time of Laomedon <note>the father of King Priam of Troy</note>, noble men as the handed-down legend makes clear. As for my own commentaries, about which you wrote, they are not yet in a sufficient state; but however they happen to be at present, I have sent them to you. Regarding the guarding <note>likely referring to the Pythagorean practice of keeping their philosophical doctrines secret from the uninitiated</note> of them, we are both in agreement, so there is no need for further encouragement. Farewell.

And such were the letters they wrote to one another.

There have been four men named Archytas: first, this man himself; second, a musician from Mitylene; third, one who wrote on agriculture; and fourth, a writer of epigrams. Some also mention a fifth, an architect, of whom a book on mechanics is circulated, which begins as follows: "These things I learned from Teucer the Carthaginian." Regarding the musician, it is told that when he was reproached for not being heard by his audience, he said, "For it is the instrument, being played by me, that speaks."

Aristoxenus <note>a Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who wrote on music and biography</note> says that this Pythagorean Archytas was never defeated while serving as general; but once, when he was envied and gave up his command, his army was immediately captured. He was the first to give a systematic method to mechanics by applying mechanical principles, and the first to apply instrumental motion to a geometric diagram, seeking to find two mean proportionals <note>a complex mathematical procedure</note> by means of the section of a half-cylinder, in order to solve the doubling of the cube <note>known as the "Delian Problem," this involves finding the edge of a cube with twice the volume of a given cube</note>. And he was the first to find the cube through geometry, as Plato says in the *Republic*.
