### ALCMAEON.

Alcmaeon of Croton was a student of <term>Pythagoras</term> <note>the influential 6th-century BC philosopher and mathematician whose followers lived in communal, ascetic societies</note>, and most of what he says concerns medicine. Nevertheless, he occasionally discusses <term>natural philosophy</term> <note>original: "physiologei"; the study of the physical world and its laws</note>, saying, "Most human things come in pairs." He is thought to have been the first to write a treatise on nature (according to what <term>Favorinus</term> <note>a Roman historian and sophist known for his "Miscellaneous History"</note> says in his *Various History*) and that the moon possesses an entirely eternal nature. He was the son of <term>Pirithous</term>, as he himself says at the beginning of his book: 
"Alcmaeon of Croton, son of Pirithous, said these things to Brotinus, Leon, and Bathyllus. Concerning things unseen and concerning mortal matters, the gods possess clarity; but as far as men may judge by signs," and so forth. He also said that the soul is immortal, and that it moves continuously in the same manner as the sun.

---

### HIPPASUS.

Hippasus of Metapontum was also a <term>Pythagorean</term>. He said that there is a defined time for the change of the world, and that the universe is finite and eternally in motion. <term>Demetrius</term> <note>likely Demetrius of Magnesia, a biographer of philosophers</note> says in his *Men of the Same Name* that he left no written work behind. There have been two men named Hippasus: this man, and another who wrote a work in five books on the <term>Constitution of the Lacedaemonians</term> <note>original: "Lakōnōn politeian"; a study of the laws and governance of Sparta</note>. That man was himself a Spartan.

---

### PHILOLAUS.

Philolaus of Croton was a <term>Pythagorean</term>. It was from him that <term>Plato</term> <note>the famous Athenian philosopher and student of Socrates</note> wrote to <term>Dion</term> <note>Dion of Syracuse, Plato's friend and political ally</note> to purchase the <term>Pythagorean books</term> <note>these books were highly guarded and expensive; Plato supposedly used them to help compose his dialogue "Timaeus"</note>. He died under the suspicion that he was attempting to establish a <term>tyranny</term> <note>in ancient Greece, this referred to seizing absolute power outside of the traditional legal framework</note>. We have also written an epigram about him:

->I say to everyone: cure suspicion above all.<-
->For even if you do not act, but only seem to, you are unfortunate.<-

> Thus did Croton, his native land, one day slay Philolaus,
> Because he seemed to desire to hold a tyrant's house.
<note>original: "Ὡς μιν ἔδοξε θέλειν δῶμα τύραννον ἔχειν" — This refers to a tradition that Philolaus was killed during a political uprising against the Pythagoreans in Croton due to suspicions of his monarchical ambitions.</note>

He believes that all things are brought about by <term>necessity</term> <note>the idea that the universe follows unavoidable laws</note> and <term>harmony</term>. He was the first to state that the earth moves in a circle; though others say it was <term>Hicetas of Syracuse</term> <note>a philosopher who, like Philolaus, proposed that the Earth was not stationary</note>. He wrote a single book, which <term>Hermippus</term> <note>a Greek biographer from the 3rd century BC</note> says—citing some other author—that <term>Plato</term> the philosopher bought from Philolaus' relatives for forty Alexandrian silver <term>minas</term> <note>a very large sum of money, roughly equivalent to several years of wages for a skilled worker</note> when he visited <term>Dionysius</term> in Sicily. From this book, it is said, he transcribed the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s famous dialogue on the origin of the physical world</note>. Others say that Plato received these books from Dionysius after requesting the release from prison of a young man who had been arrested from among Philolaus' students. <term>Demetrius</term> says in his *Men of the Same Name* that he was the first of the <term>Pythagoreans</term> to publish a work "On Nature," the beginning of which is as follows: "Nature in the world was harmonized from both infinite and limiting elements, as was the whole universe and everything within it."

### EUDOXUS.

<margin>
Pros-
per-
ity
</margin>
Eudoxus, son of Aeschines, was a man of Cnidus, an <term>astrologer</term> <note>in the ancient world, this included the mathematical study of stars we now call astronomy</note>, a geometer, a physician, and a legislator. He learned his geometry from <term>Archytas</term> and his medicine from <term>Philistion the Sicilian</term>, as <term>Callimachus</term> <note>the famous scholar and librarian of Alexandria</note> says in his *Tables*. <term>Sotion</term> says in his *Successions* that he also heard Plato. For when he was about twenty-three years old and in a state of poverty, he traveled to Athens attracted by the fame of the <term>Socratics</term> <note>the circle of students and followers of Socrates</note>, accompanied by <term>Theomedon</term> the physician, who supported him. Some say he was even a favorite of his. Having arrived at the <term>Piraeus</term> <note>the port city serving Athens</note>, he would go up to Athens every day, and after listening to the <term>sophists</term> <note>professional teachers of wisdom and rhetoric</note> there, he would return. After spending two months there, he went back home, and having collected money from his friends, he set out for Egypt with <term>Chrysippus</term> the physician, carrying letters of introduction from <term>Agesilaus</term> to <term>Nectanebo</term> <note>Nectanebo I, an Egyptian Pharaoh of the 30th Dynasty</note>.

He lived there with the priests. Having spent a year and four months there, shaving his body and his eyebrows, he is said by some to have composed his <term>Eight-Year Cycle</term> <note>original: "ὀκταετηρίδα" — a period used in ancient Greek calendars to synchronize the lunar month with the solar year</note>. From there, he went to <term>Cyzicus</term> <note>an ancient Greek city in modern-day Turkey</note> and the <term>Propontis</term> <note>the Sea of Marmara</note>, teaching as a <term>sophist</term> <note>a professional teacher of rhetoric and philosophy</note>. It is said he also visited the court of <term>Mausolus</term> <note>the famous ruler of Caria whose tomb became one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World</note>. 

Afterward, he returned to Athens with a great many students. Some say he did this specifically to annoy <term>Plato</term>, because Plato had initially kept him at a distance. Others claim that when Plato gave a banquet, Eudoxus—owing to the large number of guests—introduced the innovation of <term>semicircular seating</term>. <term>Nicomachus</term>, the son of Aristotle, states that Eudoxus held <term>pleasure</term> to be the "Good" <note>the supreme goal of life</note>. 

He was received with great magnificence in his own country, as is demonstrated by the official decree passed in his honor. He also became most famous throughout the Greek world, writing laws for his fellow citizens—as <term>Hermippus</term> records in the fourth book of his work *On the Seven Sages*—and composing works on astronomy, geometry, and other noteworthy subjects. 

He had three daughters: Actis, Philtis, and Delphis. <term>Eratosthenes</term> says in his work *To Baton* that Eudoxus also composed <term>Dialogues of Dogs</term> <note>original: "κυνῶν διαλόγους" — likely a satirical or Cynic-influenced literary work</note>. Others, however, say that these were originally written by the Egyptians in their own language, and that he merely translated and published them for the Greeks. 

<term>Chrysippus of Cnidus</term>, the son of Erineos, studied under him regarding the gods, the cosmos, and <term>meteorological phenomena</term> <note>original: "μετεωρολογουμένων" — in antiquity, this included anything in the sky, from weather to stars</note>; however, he learned medical matters from <term>Philistion the Sicilian</term>. Eudoxus also left behind most excellent memoirs. His son was Aristagoras, whose own student was Chrysippus, the son of Aethlius; this Chrysippus is famous for his <term>ophthalmic treatments</term>, as many natural theories regarding the eyes occurred to his mind.

There have been three men named Eudoxus: first, this man himself; second, a man from Rhodes who wrote histories; third, a Sicilian, the son of Agathocles, who was a comic poet. This poet won three victories in the city festivals and five at the <term>Lenaea</term> <note>an Athenian festival featuring dramatic competitions</note>, according to <term>Apollodorus</term> in his *Chronology*. We also find another doctor from Cnidus, whom Eudoxus mentions in his *Circuit of the Earth*, stating that he was always advising constant...

> In Memphis, the story goes that Eudoxus once learned
> his own fate from Apis, the fair-horned bull.
> The bull said nothing. (How could he? For nature gave no 
> power of speech to cattle, nor a talking mouth to the calf Apis.) 
> But standing sideways by him, the bull clearly
> licked his cloak, showing that he would 
> cast off his life very soon.
> And indeed, his doom came swiftly upon him, 
> after he had looked upon the sun fifty times plus three.

For this reason, they called him "The Illustrious" <note>original: "Ἔνδοξον" (Endoxos)</note> instead of "Eudoxus" <note>original: "Εὐδόξου" (Eudoxos), meaning "well-reputed"</note> on account of the brilliance of his fame.

### HERACLITUS.

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'H' featuring elaborate foliate scrollwork inside a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

**HERACLITUS**, son of Blyson or, as some say, of Herakon, was a native of **Ephesus**. He flourished <note>original: "ἤκμαζε" — reached the peak of his career</note> during the 69th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>a four-year period used for dating; the 69th Olympiad corresponds to approximately 504–500 BCE</note>. He was more high-minded and arrogant than almost any other man, as is clear from his own treatise, in which he says: "*Much learning <note>original: "Πολυμαθίη" — polymathy, or the accumulation of many facts</note> does not teach understanding; for if it did, it would have taught Hesiod and Pythagoras, and again Xenophanes and Hecataeus.*" For he claimed that wisdom is one thing: to understand the thought <note>original: "γνώμην" — the intelligence or principle</note> which steers all things through all things. He used to say that **Homer** deserved to be expelled from the contests and beaten with a rod, and **Archilochus** <note>a famous Greek lyric poet known for his biting wit</note> likewise. 

He also used to say: "*Insolence <note>original: "Ὕβριν" (hubris)</note> should be extinguished more quickly than a wildfire,*" and "*The people must fight for the law as they would for the city wall.*" He also attacked the Ephesians for having exiled his companion **Hermodorus**; on this subject he says: "*The Ephesians would do well to hang themselves, every grown man of them, and leave the city to the boys; for they have cast out Hermodorus, the best man among them, saying: 'Let no one among us be the best; or if there be such a one, let him be so elsewhere and among others.'*" When he was asked by the citizens to establish laws for them, he refused, because the city was already gripped by a corrupt <term>constitution</term> <note>original: "πολιτείᾳ" — the political arrangement or form of government</note>. Having retreated to the Temple of Arte-

### HERACLITUS. Book 9

...[in the temple of Artem]is <note>original: "ιδος" — the ending of the name Artemis, referring to her famous temple in Ephesus</note>, he was playing at knucklebones with the children. When the Ephesians gathered around and stared at him, he said, "Why, you rascals, are you surprised? Is it not better to do this than to manage the government with you?" Eventually, becoming a misanthrope <note>original: "μισανθρωπήσας" — a hater of humanity</note> and withdrawing from the world, he lived in the mountains, feeding on grasses and herbs. 

However, because of this diet, he contracted dropsy <note>original: "ὕδερον" (hyderon) — an accumulation of fluid in the body, often associated with heart or kidney failure</note> and returned to the city. He asked the physicians in a riddle-like way if they were able to "produce a drought out of a rainstorm." When they did not understand his meaning, he buried himself in a cowshed, hoping that he would be dried out by the warmth of the dung. But achieving nothing even through this method, he died, having lived for sixty years. My own poem regarding him is as follows:

-> Often I have wondered at Heraclitus, how he eventually <-
-> drew out his life so wretchedly and then died. <-
-> For an evil disease, drenching his body with water, <-
-> extinguished the light from his eyes and brought on darkness. <-

Hermippus, however, says that he told the doctors to see if anyone could empty the bowels and draw out the fluid. When they said it was impossible, he placed himself in the sun and ordered the children to plaster him with dung. Thus stretched out, he died on the second day and was buried in the marketplace. 

But Neanthes of Cyzicus <note>a Greek historian from the 3rd century BCE</note> says that because he was unable to tear off the dried dung, he remained there, and having become unrecognizable due to the change, he was devoured by dogs. 

He was a marvelous person from childhood; even when he was young, he used to say he "knew nothing," but when he reached maturity, he claimed to have "known everything." He was a pupil of no one, but said he "searched himself" and learned everything from his own nature. Sotion, however, says that some report he had listened to **Xenophanes**. Ariston says in his work *On Heraclitus* that he was actually cured of the dropsy but died of another disease; Hippobotus <note>a biographer of philosophers</note> says the same. 

The book attributed to him is titled *On Nature* <note>original: "περὶ φύσεως" (Peri Physeos) — a standard title given by later scholars to many Pre-Socratic works</note>, based on its general content. It is divided into three discourses: one on the universe, one political, and one theological. He deposited the work as an offering in the temple of...

...the temple of Artemis. As some say, he chose to write in an obscure <note>original: "ἀσαφέστερον" — meaning "more unclearly," which earned him the nickname "The Obscure"</note> manner so that only those with the ability might approach his work, and so that it would not become an object of contempt by being too common. Timon also sketches his character, saying:

> Among them rose up Heraclitus, the mob-abusing cuckoo-caller,
> The teller of riddles <note>original: "Αἰνικτὴς" (ainiktes) — a person who speaks in enigmas</note>.

Theophrastus says that because of his melancholy <note>original: "µελαγχολίας" — in ancient medicine, an excess of "black bile" thought to cause both intense creativity and erratic behavior</note>, he left some parts of his work unfinished and other parts inconsistent. Antisthenes says in his *Successions* that his greatness of soul <note>original: "µεγαλοφροσύνης"</note> was proven by the fact that he yielded the title of king to his brother. His book gained such fame that it produced a school of followers who were called Heracliteans.

His general views were as follows: that all things are composed of fire and are resolved back into it; that all things happen according to fate <note>original: "εἱµαρµένην" (heimarmene) — a fixed destiny or natural law</note> and that existing things are harmonized through the "turning-back" of opposites <note>original: "ἐναντιοτροπῆς" (enantiotropia) — the principle that things turn into their opposites to create balance</note>. He also believed that all things are full of souls and spirits <note>original: "δαιµόνων" (daimonon) — intermediate divine beings</note>.

He also spoke about the conditions occurring in the universe, stating that the sun is exactly the size it appears to be. It is also recorded that he said: "Though you travel every path, you would not find the limits of the soul, so deep is its reason <note>original: "λόγον" (logos) — this word can mean 'word,' 'account,' 'reason,' or 'the underlying principle of the universe'</note>." He used to call self-conceit <note>original: "οἴησιν" — dogmatic pride</note> a "sacred disease" <note>original: "ἱερὰν νόσον" (hieran noson) — a term usually used for epilepsy; Heraclitus suggests that being full of one's own opinions is a kind of seizure of the mind</note>, and said that sight is deceptive.

Occasionally in his writing, he breaks out so brilliantly and clearly that even the dullest person can easily understand and receive an elevation of the soul. The brevity and weight of his expression are beyond comparison. His specific doctrines are as follows: Fire is the element <note>original: "στοιχεῖον" (stoicheion)</note>, and all things are an exchange for fire, coming into being through "rarefaction" and "condensation" (though he explains nothing clearly). All things happen by opposition, and the whole flows like a river. The universe is finite, and there is only one world. It is born from fire and again is consumed by fire <note>original: "ἐκπυροῦσθαι" — refers to the 'Ekpyrosis,' a periodic destruction of the world by fire</note> in certain cycles throughout all eternity. This happens according to fate. Of the opposites, that which leads to "becoming" is called war and strife <note>original: "πόλεµον καὶ ἔριν"</note>; while that which leads to...

<meta>This page continues the summary of Heraclitus's natural philosophy, specifically his cosmology and the "road up and down." The previous page introduced his core belief that the world is made of fire and governed by fate.</meta>

# HERACLITUS. Book 9. 345

...the periodic world-fire <note>original: "ἐκπύρωσιν" (ekpyrosis) — the Stoic and Heraclitean concept that the universe is periodically destroyed by fire and reborn</note>, harmony and peace, and the principle that "change is the road up and down"; he believed the world comes into being according to this process. For fire, as it condenses, becomes moist and, when compressed, turns into water; as water solidifies, it is turned into earth. This he calls the "road downward." Conversely, the earth is dissolved again, and from it water is produced; and from water, almost all other things are led back to the <term>exhalation</term> <note>original: "ἀναθυμίασιν" (anathymiasin) — a vapor or steam rising from water or earth, which Heraclitus believed fueled the stars</note> rising from the sea. This is the "road upward."

He taught that exhalations arise from both the earth and the sea: some are bright and pure, while others are dark. Fire is increased by the bright exhalations, while moisture is increased by the others. As for the nature of the "surrounding" <note>referring to the atmosphere or the heavens</note>, he does not make it clear. He does say, however, that within it are "bowls" <note>original: "σκάφας" (skaphas) — literally "troughs" or "skiffs"</note> with their hollow sides turned toward us. The bright <term>exhalations</term> collect within these bowls and produce flames, which are the stars.

The flame of the sun is the brightest and the hottest. The other stars are further away from the earth, and for this reason, they shine and warm us less. The moon, being closer to the earth, moves through a region that is not pure. The sun, however, resides in a transparent and unmixed region and maintains a balanced distance from us; therefore, it provides more heat and light. 

Eclipses of the sun and moon occur when these bowls are turned upward <note>i.e., when the hollow, flaming side is turned away from the Earth</note>. The monthly phases of the moon occur as its bowl gradually rotates. Day and night, months, the seasons of the year, years, rains, winds, and similar phenomena are all produced by the various <term>exhalations</term>. For the bright <term>exhalation</term>, catching fire within the circle of the sun, creates day; but when the opposite dark exhalation prevails, it produces night. From the bright exhalation, heat increases to produce summer; from the dark exhalation, moisture becomes more abundant and produces winter. He explains the causes of other things in a manner consistent with these principles. Regarding the earth, however, he declares nothing as to its specific nature...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS. Book 9. 346

...[what its distance] is, nor even any details about the "bowls." These were his own opinions. As for the stories concerning Socrates and the remarks he made upon encountering Heraclitus’s book—which had been brought to him by the playwright Euripides (according to Ariston)—we have already discussed these in our chapter on Socrates. However, Seleucus the Grammarian says that a certain Croton records in his work titled *The Diver* <note>original: "Κατακολυμβητῇ" (Katakolymbyte) — a lost work, possibly titled to mirror the "Delian diver" metaphor</note> that a man named Crates was the first to bring the book into Greece. Crates is said to have remarked that the work required a "Delian diver" <note>original: "Δηλίου τινὸς δεῖσθαι κολυμβητοῦ" — a proverbial expression referring to the famously skilled divers of Delos; here it implies the book is so deep and difficult that one might "drown" in its complexity</note> who would not drown within its depths.

People give the book various titles: some call it *The Muses*; others, *On Nature*; Diodotus calls it *A Precise Rudder for the Rule of Life*; still others, *A Guide to Character, an Orderly Arrangement of Conduct for the Whole Universe*. It is said that when Heraclitus was once asked why he remained silent, he replied: "So that you may chatter." Even King Darius <note>Darius I, the Great, King of the Persian Empire (r. 522–486 BCE)</note> desired to converse with him and wrote to him as follows:

->King Darius, son of Hystaspes, greets Heraclitus of<-
->Ephesus, a wise man, with joy.<-

You have composed a treatise *On Nature* that is difficult to understand and hard to interpret. In certain parts, when read according to your literal wording, it seems to contain a profound power of contemplation regarding the whole universe and all that occurs within it—things which are set in a most divine motion. Yet in most parts, the meaning is suspended <note>original: "ἐποχὴν ἔχοντα" (epochen echonta) — meaning the sense is withheld or requires a suspension of judgment</note>; so even those who have most extensively engaged with scholarly writings are at a loss as to the correct interpretation of your narrative.

Therefore, King Darius, son of Hystaspes, wishes to be a listener to your discourse and to partake in Greek education. Come, then, with haste to my presence and to my royal palace. For the Greeks, for the most part, fail to recognize their wise men, neglecting the beautiful things they demonstrate which deserve a serious hearing and study. With me, however, you shall have every place of honor, daily and earnest conversation, and a life made illustrious by your own counsels.

# HERACLITUS. Book 9. 347

Heraclitus of Ephesus to King Darius, son of Hystaspes, greetings.
All those who happen to dwell upon the earth are far removed from the truth and from just dealings; instead, they devote themselves to insatiable greed and vain-glory because of their wretched foolishness. But I, having attained a state of forgetfulness regarding all wickedness, and fleeing the excessive envy that attends every local custom, and because I dread all forms of arrogance, I could not come to the land of the Persians. I am content with a few things, according to my own judgment.

<note>This letter is widely considered by historians to be "pseudepigraphal"—a fictional letter written by a later author to illustrate Heraclitus’s famous disdain for society and royalty.</note>

Such was the man, even toward a king. Demetrius <note>Demetrius of Magnesia, a biographer and contemporary of Cicero</note> says in his work *Men of the Same Name* that Heraclitus also looked down upon the Athenians, even though he held a very high reputation among them. Although he was despised by the Ephesians, he preferred his own private life. Demetrius of Phalerum <note>A famous orator and statesman of Athens</note> also mentions him in his *Apology of Socrates*. There are a great many people who have written commentaries on his treatise. For indeed, Antisthenes and Heraclides of Pontus, as well as Cleanthes of Pontus <note>This may be a scribal error for Cleanthes of Assos, the famous Stoic, or refers to a lesser-known figure</note> and Sphaerus the Stoic have all done so. Furthermore, there are Pausanias (who was nicknamed "The Heraclitean"), Nicomedes, and Dionysius. Among the grammarians, Diodotus also wrote on him; he claims that the treatise is not actually about nature, but about politics, and that the parts concerning nature are merely used as examples. Hieronymus tells us that Scythinus, the iambic poet, even attempted to set Heraclitus’s prose work into verse. Many epigrams have been written about him, among which is this one:

->I am Heraclitus; why do you uncultured folk drag me down?<-
->I did not labor for you, but for those who understand me.<-
->One man to me is worth thirty thousand; but the countless are<-
->As nobody. This I declare even in the house of Persephone.<-
<note>Persephone is the Queen of the Underworld; the poem suggests Heraclitus’s elitism and his confidence that his work would endure even after death.</note>

->And another such as this:<-

->Do not roll the scroll of Heraclitus of Ephesus too quickly<-
->Toward its center; the path is truly hard to travel.<-
<note>The original uses the word "omphalon" (navel), which refers to the wooden cylinder around which a papyrus book was rolled. The poem warns that the book is too dense to be read in haste.</note>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

> Mist and darkness are without light; but if an initiate 
> leads you in, they become brighter than the sun's light.
<note>This couplet refers to the difficulty of Heraclitus's writing; though it seems "dark," it reveals great light to those who are properly initiated into his philosophy.</note>

There have been five men named Heraclitus: first, the philosopher himself; second, a lyric poet who wrote a hymn in praise of the twelve gods; third, an elegiac poet from Halicarnassus <note>A Greek city in modern-day Turkey</note>, about whom Callimachus <note>A famous scholar-poet of the Library of Alexandria</note> wrote the following:

> Someone told me, Heraclitus, of your death, and it 
> moved me to tears; I remembered how often we both 
> watched the sun set as we talked. But you, indeed, 
> my friend from Halicarnassus, have long been ashes; 
> yet your "nightingales" <note>original: ἀηδόνες (aēdones); here, a metaphor for his poems</note> live on, upon which Hades, 
> the snatcher of all things, shall not lay his hand.

The fourth was a man from Lesbos who wrote a history of Macedonia; the fifth was a writer of "serious-humor" <term>spoudogeloios: a literary style that blends serious philosophical themes with satirical or comic elements</term>, who transitioned to that style from being a singer to the lyre.

->XENOPHANES<-

Xenophanes, the son of Dexius or (as Apollodorus says) the son of Orthomenes, was from Colophon. He is praised by Timon <note>Timon of Phlius, a skeptical philosopher known for his satirical poems</note>, who says of him:

> And Xenophanes, somewhat arrogant, a mocker of Homer's deception.

This man, having been driven out of his homeland, lived in Zancle <note>Modern-day Messina</note> in Sicily, and also in Catania. According to some, he was no man's pupil; according to others, he studied under Boton of Athens, or some say under Archelaus. As Sotion says, he lived during the time of Anaximander. He wrote in epic verse, as well as elegies and iambics <note>different meters of Greek poetry</note>, attacking Hesiod and Homer and mocking what they said about the gods. He also used to recite his own poems in the manner of a rhapsode <note>A professional performer of epic poetry</note>. He is said to have held opinions contrary to Thales and Pythagoras, and he even attacked Epimenides <note>A semi-mythical Cretan seer and philosopher</note>. He lived to be very old, as he himself says somewhere:

> Already sixty and seven years have passed...

# XENOPHANES. Book 9, 349

> Tossing my restless thought throughout the land of Greece.
> From my birth until then, seventy years had passed,
> and twenty-five more in addition to those,
> if indeed I know how to speak the truth about these things.
<note>Xenophanes is here calculating his age as ninety-two years, describing a life spent traveling as a wandering poet and philosopher.</note>

<margin>φ</margin>He says that there are four elements of all things that exist, and that the worlds are infinite in number, though they do not change. He held that clouds are formed when the vapor from the sun is carried upward and gathered into the surrounding atmosphere. The essence of God is spherical, having nothing in common with man; He sees as a whole and hears as a whole, but does not breathe. He is entirely mind, wisdom, and eternal. Xenophanes was also the first to declare that everything that comes into being is perishable, and that the soul is breath <term>pneuma: literally "breath" or "spirit," which many early philosophers believed was the material substance of the soul</term>. He also said that the majority of things are inferior to the mind. He advised that one should encounter tyrants either as little as possible or as pleasantly as possible.

<margin>D</margin>When Empedocles <note>A later philosopher famous for the theory of the four elements</note> told him that a wise man is impossible to find, Xenophanes replied, "Naturally; for it takes a wise man to recognize a wise man." Sotion <note>A biographer who classified philosophers into "successions" or schools</note> claims that Xenophanes was the first to say that all things are incomprehensible, but in this he is mistaken. He also wrote a poem on the *Founding of Colophon* and another on the *Colonization of Elea in Italy*, totaling two thousand verses. He flourished <note>A term used by ancient biographers to mark the peak of a person's career, usually around age forty</note> during the sixtieth Olympiad <note>Approximately 540–537 BCE</note>.

<margin>χ</margin>Demetrius of Phalerum <note>An Athenian statesman and philosopher</note> says in his work *On Old Age*, and Panaetius the Stoic says in his work *On Cheerfulness*, that Xenophanes buried his own sons with his own hands, just as Anaxagoras did. He appears to have been sold into slavery by the Pythagoreans Parmeniscus and Orestades, according to Favorinus in the first book of his *Memorabilia*. There was also another Xenophanes, a poet of iambic verse from Lesbos. These, then, are the scattered accounts of him. Parmenides, the son of Pyres, from Elea, was a student of Xenophanes.

# PARMENIDES.

Theophrastus <note>The successor of Aristotle</note>, in his *Epitome*, says that Parmenides was a student of Anaximander. However, although he also studied under Xenophanes, he did not follow his system. He also associated with Ameinias...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS. Page 350

Parmenides was a student of Diochaetes the Pythagorean (as Sotion <note>A Roman-era biographer who organized philosophers into "successions" or schools</note> says), a man who was poor but noble and good, whom he followed closely. When Diochaetes died, Parmenides, who was of illustrious birth and quite wealthy, built a hero-shrine in his honor. Although he was a student of Xenophanes, it was actually Ameinias <note>Another Pythagorean philosopher</note> who led him to a life of "quietude" or contemplation. 

Parmenides was the first to declare that the earth is spherical and situated in the center of the universe. He held that there are two elements: fire and earth. He believed that fire plays the role of the creator or craftsman <term>demiurge: a divine artisan-like figure who shapes the world</term>, while the earth plays the role of matter. He also claimed that the first generation of human beings arose from the sun. He taught that the universe consists of the Hot and the Cold, from which all things are composed. According to him, the soul and the mind are the same thing, as Theophrastus <note>Aristotle's successor</note> also mentions in his *Physics* when he sets out the doctrines of almost all the early philosophers.

He said that philosophy is twofold: one part deals with truth <term>aletheia: reality as it truly is</term>, and the other with opinion <term>doxa: the common, often mistaken beliefs of people</term>. Therefore, he says somewhere in his poetry:

->— It is necessary for you to learn all things,<-
->Both the unshaken heart of persuasive truth,<-
->And the opinions of mortals, in which there is no true belief.<-
<note>original: "χρεὼ δέ σε πάντα πυθέσθαι / Ἤ μὲν ἀληθείης εὐπειθέος ἀτρεκὲς ἦτορ, / Ἠδὲ βροτῶν δόξας, ταῖς οὐκ ἔνι πίστις ἀληθής."</note>

Parmenides himself expressed his philosophy through poems, just as Hesiod, Xenophanes, and Empedocles did. He stated that reason <term>logos: the capacity for rational thought and argument</term> is the criterion for truth, and that the senses are not accurate. Indeed, he says:

> Let not a god <note>The text here says "god" (theos), though many manuscripts of Parmenides read "habit" (ethos). The philosopher warns against trusting the senses over logic.</note> force you along this path of much experience, 
> To use an aimless eye and echoing ear 
> and tongue, but judge by reason the much-contested proof.

Therefore, Timon <note>A skeptical poet known for his biting satires on philosophers</note> says of him:

->And the high-minded strength of Parmenides, the much-famed,<-
->Who raised his thought away from the deception of appearances.<-

It was for this man that Plato wrote his dialogue titled *Parmenides*, or *On Ideas*. Parmenides flourished during the 69th Olympiad <note>Approximately 504–500 BCE</note>. He also seems to have been the first to discover that the Evening Star <term>Hesperus</term> and the Morning Star <term>Phosphorus</term> are actually the same celestial body <note>The planet Venus</note>, as Favorinus says in the fifth book of his *Memorabilia*; though others...

<summary>This page introduces Parmenides of Elea, noting his Pythagorean influences, his scientific claim that the earth is a sphere, and his foundational philosophical distinction between rational Truth and sensory Opinion.</summary>

He was also the first to pose the "Achilles" argument <note>A famous paradox of motion, usually attributed to his student Zeno; Diogenes notes Favorinus's differing opinion here</note>, according to Favorinus in his *Miscellaneous History*. There was also another Parmenides, a rhetorician who wrote technical manuals.

### MELISSUS.

**M**elissus, son of Ithagenes, was a native of Samos. He was a student of Parmenides. He also engaged in discussions with Heraclitus <note>The philosopher of "flux" and change</note>, and even introduced him to the Ephesians when they failed to understand him, much like Hippocrates introduced Democritus to the people of Abdera. Melissus was also a statesman, held in high regard by his fellow citizens. Because of this, he was chosen as an admiral and was even more admired for his own personal excellence. 

His doctrine was that the Universe is infinite, unchanging, immovable, and a single thing that is uniform with itself and "full" <note>Meaning there is no empty space or "void" in reality</note>. He taught that motion does not actually exist, even though it appears to. Furthermore, he said that one should not make definitive pronouncements about the gods, for there is no real knowledge of them. Apollodorus <note>A prominent Athenian chronicler</note> says he reached his prime <term>acme: the height of a person's career, usually reckoned at age forty</term> during the eighty-fourth Olympiad <note>Approximately 444–441 BC</note>.

---

### ZENO OF ELEA.

**Z**eno of Elea. Apollodorus says in his *Chronicles* that he was the biological son of Teleutagoras, but the adopted son of Parmenides. Regarding him and Melissus, Timon <note>A skeptical philosopher and writer of satirical poems called "Silloi"</note> says the following:

> The great and unyielding strength of double-tongued Zeno,
> Who criticized even Plato, and of Melissus too,
> Who rose above many illusions, yet was defeated by few.
<note>original: "Ἀμφοτερογλώσσου τε μέγα σθένος οὐκ ἀλαπαδνόν· Ζήνωνος Πλατωνεπιλήπτορος ἠδὲ Μελίσσου..."</note>

Zeno was a student of Parmenides and was also his favorite <note>This term often suggested a close personal and educational relationship common in Greek philosophical circles</note>.

### ZENO OF ELEA

...and he was quite tall, as Plato says in his dialogue *Parmenides*. Plato also calls him the "Eleatic Palamedes" <note>Palamedes was a mythical Greek hero famed for his cleverness and for inventing the alphabet and logic; Plato uses this title to emphasize Zeno’s skill in argument</note> in the *Sophist*. Aristotle says that Zeno was the inventor of **dialectic** <note>The art of investigating the truth of opinions through logical discussion</note>, just as Empedocles was the inventor of rhetoric. He was a man of the most noble character, both in philosophy and in politics. Indeed, his books survive and are full of great intelligence.

When he wished to overthrow the tyrant <term>Nearchus</term> <note>Historical sources vary on the name; some claim the tyrant was Diomedon</note>, he was arrested, according to Heracleides in his summary of Satyrus. During his interrogation, when asked about his accomplices and about the weapons he was transporting to Lipara, he claimed that all of the tyrant’s own friends were his co-conspirators. He did this because he wanted to leave the tyrant isolated and without allies. 

Then, Zeno claimed he had something to say to the tyrant's ear. When the tyrant leaned in, Zeno bit down on him and would not let go until he was stabbed to death—meeting the same fate as the famous tyrant-slayer Aristogeiton <note>Aristogeiton was an Athenian hero who, along with Harmodius, attempted to kill the tyrant Hippias</note>. 

However, Demetrius says in his work *People of the Same Name* that Zeno bit off the tyrant’s nose. Antisthenes, in his *Successions of Philosophers*, says that after naming the tyrant’s own friends as his accomplices, Zeno was asked by the tyrant if there was anyone else. Zeno replied: "Yes, you—the scourge of the city!" Then, speaking to the bystanders, he said: "I marvel at your cowardice, that for fear of the things I am now enduring, you continue to be slaves to a tyrant." Finally, he bit off his own tongue and spat it at the tyrant. This so stirred the citizens that they immediately rose up and stoned the tyrant to death. This is the version told by most writers. 

Hermippus, however, says that Zeno was thrown into a large mortar <note>A heavy bowl used for crushing materials with a pestle</note> and pounded to death. Regarding this, I have written the following poem:

> You wished, O Zeno, a noble thing—to kill
> The tyrant and set Elea free from chains.
> But you were broken; for the tyrant took you
> And crushed you in a mortar. Why say "you"?
> He crushed your body, but he could not touch your soul.

In other respects, **Zeno** was a man of great excellence. However, he was also known to be disdainful of those in high power, much like Heraclitus. He preferred his home of Elea—which was a colony of the Phocaeans <note>Greek settlers from Phocaea in Asia Minor</note> and was formerly called Hyele—to the...

<meta>catchword: ...glory (presumably "dignity" or "majesty" of larger cities like Athens)</meta>

# ZENO OF ELEA. Book 8 <note>original: Βιβλ. η̅. Note that in modern editions of Diogenes Laertius, these biographies are found in Book 9</note>

He loved his own fatherland—though it was a city of little account and only skilled at producing good men—more than the arrogance of the Athenians. He did not often stay among them, but lived his life there in his home. This man was the first to propose the **"Achilles"** <note>This refers to the famous "Achilles and the Tortoise" paradox, which argues that a faster runner can never overtake a slower one because they must first reach the point where the slower one started</note> argument; however, Favorinus says it was Parmenides, as do many others. 

His philosophical views are as follows: there are multiple worlds; there is no such thing as a **void** <note>original: κενόν (kenon); the absence of matter</note>; the nature of all things arose from heat and cold, and from dry and moist, as these elements transform into one another. He believed that the human race arose from the earth, and that the soul is a mixture of the aforementioned elements, with none of them predominating.

It is said that when he was insulted, he became annoyed. When someone reproached him for this, he said: 

> "If I pretend not to care when I am insulted, I shall not feel any pleasure when I am praised." 

As we discussed in the section on Zeno of Citium, there have been eight men named Zeno. This Zeno flourished around the 70th <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used for dating in ancient Greece; the 70th Olympiad corresponds to approximately 500–497 BCE</note>.

---

### LEUCIPPUS.

Leucippus was a native of Elea; though some say he was from Abdera, and others from Melos. He was a student of Zeno. His doctrines were that the universe is infinite, and that all things change into one another. He held that the "All" consists of the **void** and the **full** (matter). He taught that worlds are formed when bodies fall into the void and become entangled with each other; and from their motion, according to their increase in size, the nature of the stars is produced. 

He claimed that the sun is carried in a larger circle around the moon. The earth is carried along, whirling about the center, and its shape is **drum-like** <note>original: τυμπανοειδὲς; shaped like a flat cylinder or tambourine</note>. He was the first to posit <term>atoms</term> <note>original: ἀτόμους; literally "uncuttable" or indivisible particles</note> as first principles.

These are his views in summary. In detail, they are as follows: he says the universe is infinite, as previously stated. Of this universe, one part is full and the other is void. He says these are the elements, and worlds are formed from them...

<meta>The previous page introduced Leucippus of Elea (or Abdera) as the founder of the Atomic school. It likely began the explanation of his primary principles: that the universe is infinite, composed of the "full" (atoms) and the "void," and that infinite worlds are formed from these.</meta>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...infinite), and that they are also dissolved back into these elements. The worlds come into being in this way: many bodies of all kinds of shapes move by being "cut off" from the infinite into a great **void** <note>original: κενόν (kenon); the empty space required for atoms to move</note>. These bodies, having been collected together, produce a single **vortex** <note>original: δίνη (dinē); a whirling motion central to early Greek scientific theories of the universe’s origin</note>, within which they collide and circle around in every possible way. In this process, like bodies are separated out and join with their like. 

When, because of their great number, they can no longer revolve in equilibrium, the light or fine bodies move toward the outer void, as if they were being sifted or tossed out. The rest remain together and, becoming entangled, run along with one another, forming a primary spherical system. This system stands apart like a **membrane** <note>original: ὑμήν (hymen); a surrounding "skin" or "film" that encloses the young universe</note>, containing within itself all sorts of bodies. As these bodies continue to whirl around due to the resistance of the center, the surrounding membrane becomes thin, as the continuous parts flow together through contact with the vortex. 

And thus the earth was formed, as those bodies carried toward the center stayed together. The surrounding membrane itself increases through the **accretion** <note>original: ἐπίκρισιν (epikrisin); the addition of matter from the outside</note> of bodies from the external infinite; as it is carried along in the vortex, it acquires whatever it touches. Some of these entangled bodies form a system: at first, they are damp and muddy, but as they are dried and whirled around with the vortex of the whole, they eventually ignite and produce the nature of the stars. 

The orbit of the sun is the outermost; that of the moon is the closest to the earth; and the orbits of the other stars lie between these. All the stars are ignited because of the speed of their motion, and the sun is also ignited by the stars <note>Leucippus believed the sun's heat came from the friction of its motion and the influence of the surrounding celestial bodies</note>. The moon, however, receives only a small portion of this fire. Eclipses of the sun and moon occur <note>The text here is somewhat condensed; Leucippus attributed celestial phenomena to the tilting of the earth</note> because the earth is tilted toward the south. The regions toward the north are always covered in snow, are very cold, and are frozen. 

The sun is eclipsed only rarely, but the moon is eclipsed frequently, because their orbits are unequal. Just as there are births of the world, so there are also its periods of growth, and...

## DEMOCRITUS

Democritus was the son of Hegesiratus, or according to others, Athenocritus; <margin>some say</margin> Damasippus. He was a citizen of **Abdera** <note>A wealthy city in Thrace known for producing great thinkers</note> or, as some claim, **Miletus**. He studied under certain **Magi** <note>Zoroastrian priests and scholars from Persia</note> and **Chaldeans** <note>Babylonian astronomers and mathematicians</note>, whom King **Xerxes** <note>The Persian Emperor who invaded Greece</note> left as tutors for his father when he was entertained by him (as Herodotus also records). From these men, he learned about **theology** <note>the nature of the gods</note> and **astrology** <note>the study of the stars</note> while he was still a boy. 

Later, he associated with **Leucippus** <note>The primary founder of the Atomic theory</note> and, according to some, with **Anaxagoras**, being forty years younger than the latter. **Favorinus** says in his *Miscellaneous History* that Democritus remarked of Anaxagoras that his views regarding the sun and the moon were not his own, but were ancient theories that he had stolen. Democritus is said to have mocked Anaxagoras' theories regarding the **arrangement of the cosmos** <note>original: διακόσμησις (diakosmēsis)</note> and the **Mind** <note>original: νοῦς (nous); Anaxagoras' principle of cosmic intelligence</note>, being hostile toward him because Anaxagoras did not welcome him as a student. If this is true, how then (as some claim) could he have been his pupil? 

**Demetrius** says in his *Work on People of the Same Name*, and **Antisthenes** in his *Successions*, that he traveled to **Egypt** to visit the priests in order to learn **geometry**, and to the **Chaldeans** in **Persia**, and that he traveled as far as the **Red Sea**. Some also say he associated with the **Gymnosophists** <note>literally "naked philosophers"; a term used for Indian ascetics</note> in **India**, and that he went to **Ethiopia**. 

Being the third of three brothers, he divided the family inheritance. Most say he chose the smaller portion, which consisted of money, because he needed it for his travels, while his brothers craftily chose the land. But Demetrius says his share was over a hundred **talents** <note>An enormous sum of money; one talent could pay a ship's crew for a month</note>, and that he spent it all. He was so incredibly hardworking that he walled off a small room in the garden and remained locked inside to study. Once, when his father brought an ox for a sacrifice and—

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS. Book IX

...having tied him up, he remained for a considerable time without noticing, until [his father] raised him up on the pretext of a sacrifice and explained the situation regarding the ox. <note>This anecdote illustrates Democritus' legendary powers of concentration; he would often become so lost in thought that he became oblivious to his physical surroundings.</note> It is thought, as some say, that he also went to **Athens** and did not strive to be recognized, for he looked down upon fame. While he knew **Socrates**, he was unknown to him. For he says, "I came to Athens, and no one knew me." <note>original: "ἦλθον γὰρ εἰς Ἀθήνας, καὶ οὔτις με ἔγνωκεν." This famous statement highlights Democritus' preference for a quiet, scholarly life over the public debates common in Athens.</note>

If the dialogue *The Lovers* <note>original: Ἀντερασταί (Anterastai); a dialogue traditionally attributed to Plato, though its authenticity has been debated since antiquity</note> is indeed by **Plato**, then (as **Thrasyllus** <note>A 1st-century scholar and astrologer who organized the works of Plato and Democritus into groups of four</note> says) Democritus would be the anonymous person who arrived there, the "other" mentioned alongside the followers of **Oenopides** and **Anaxagoras**. In the conversation with Socrates concerning philosophy, the philosopher says that this man resembles a **pentathlete** <note>original: πεντάθλῳ (pentathlō); an athlete who competes in five different disciplines—here used as a metaphor for a polymath or "all-around" scholar</note>. And he was truly a pentathlete in philosophy; for he possessed mastery over **physics**, **ethics**, and **mathematics**, as well as the **liberal arts** <note>original: ἐγκυκλίους λόγους (egkyklious logous); the "standard" or "rounded" curriculum of a Greek education</note>, and had complete experience in every technical art. To him is also attributed the saying: "**Speech is the shadow of action.**" <note>original: Λόγος ἔργου σκιά (Logos ergou skia)</note>

However, **Demetrius of Phalerum** <note>An Athenian statesman and philosopher of the Peripatetic school</note> says in his *Defense of Socrates* that Democritus never even went to Athens. This, if true, is even more remarkable: that he looked down on such a great city, not wishing to gain a reputation from a place, but choosing instead to confer reputation upon a place by his choice to stay away. It is clear from his writings what kind of man he was.

Thrasyllus says he appears to have been an admirer of the **Pythagoreans**. Indeed, he mentions **Pythagoras** himself, expressing admiration for him in the work titled after him. He seems to have taken all his ideas from him, and would have even been his student if the chronology had not made it impossible. Nevertheless, **Glaucus of Rhegium** <note>An early historian of music and literature</note>, who lived around the same time, says he studied under some of the Pythagoreans; and **Apollodorus of Cyzicus** says he associated with **Philolaus** <note>A major Pythagorean philosopher who was the first to commit the school's secret oral teachings to writing</note>.

**Antisthenes** <note>A pupil of Socrates and a foundational figure for the Cynic school</note> says that he practiced testing his **perceptions** <note>original: φαντασίας (phantasias); the mental images or impressions we receive from the world</note> in various ways, sometimes living in solitude and even spending his time among tombs. He says that when he returned from his travels, he lived in a very humble state, having spent his entire inheritance; because of his poverty, he was supported by his brother **Damasus**. However, after he predicted certain future events, he became highly...

<meta>catchword: ...esteemed [from the Greek εὐδοκίμησεν]</meta>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS. Book IX

### DEMOCRITUS

...consequently, he was deemed worthy of divine renown by the majority of people. There being a law that whoever had squandered their paternal inheritance should not be granted burial in their own country, **Antisthenes** says that Democritus—realizing this, and wishing not to be held accountable by certain envious and slanderous people—read to them his work, the *Great World-System* <note>original: Μέγαν Διάκοσμον (*Megas Diakosmos*); one of Democritus’ most influential works, though now lost, it detailed his atomic theory of the universe.</note>, which is the most prominent of all his writings. As a result, he was honored with five hundred talents. Not only that, but he was also honored with bronze statues; and when he died, he was buried at the public expense. He had lived for more than a hundred years. 

However, **Demetrius** says it was his relatives who read the *Great World-System*, and that it alone was valued at one hundred talents. **Hippobotus** also states this. **Aristoxenus**, in his *Historical Notes*, says that **Plato** wanted to burn all the writings of Democritus that he was able to collect, but that **Amyclas** and **Cleinias**, who were **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for their communal lifestyle and focus on mathematics and music.</note>, prevented him, saying it was no use, as the books were already in the hands of many people. 

This is indeed evident; for while Plato mentions almost all the ancient philosophers, he nowhere mentions Democritus—not even in places where he would have needed to argue against him. It is clear he knew he would be contending against the best of philosophers, whom **Timon** <note>A satirical poet and skeptic philosopher known for his "Silloi" (Lampoons).</note> praised in this fashion:

->Such a man was Democritus, the high-minded, shepherd of accounts,<-
->The versatile speaker, whom I have read among the foremost.<-

Regarding his dates (as he himself says in his work the *Small World-System* <note>original: Μικρῷ Διακόσμῳ (*Mikros Diakosmos*)</note>), he was a young man during the time **Anaxagoras** was old, being forty years younger than him. He says the *Small World-System* was composed seven hundred and thirty years after the capture of **Troy** <note>The traditional date of the Trojan War's end served as a chronological anchor for ancient historians.</note>. He would have been born (as **Apollodorus** says in his *Chronicles*) during the eightieth **Olympiad** <note>A four-year period between Olympic Games; the 80th Olympiad corresponds to 460–457 BCE.</note>. But **Thrasyllus**, in his work entitled *On the Reading of Democritus' Books*, says he was born in the third year of the seventy-seventh Olympiad, being (he says) one year older than...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS.

### Life of Democritus

...of Socrates. He would therefore have lived at the time of **Archelaus** <note>A philosopher of the 5th century BCE, a pupil of Anaxagoras and often cited as the teacher of Socrates.</note>, the pupil of **Anaxagoras**, and among the associates of **Oenopides** <note>A mathematician and astronomer from Chios.</note>; for he mentions the latter. He also mentions the opinion regarding "The One" held by the followers of **Parmenides** and **Zeno**, as they were the most celebrated figures of his time; and **Protagoras** of Abdera, who is agreed to have lived at the same time as Socrates.

**Athenodorus** says in the eighth book of his <term>Discussions</term> <note>original: περιπάτων (*peripatōn*); literally "walks," referring to philosophical strolls or treatises.</note> that when **Hippocrates** <note>The famous "Father of Medicine."</note> came to visit him, Democritus ordered milk to be brought. After inspecting the milk, he declared that it was from a black goat that had produced its first kid. Hippocrates marveled at the man's precision. Furthermore, when a young girl was accompanying Hippocrates, on the first day Democritus greeted her by saying, "Greetings, maiden." But on the following day, he said, "Greetings, woman." It turned out that the girl had indeed lost her virginity during the night.

**Hermippus** describes the death of Democritus in this manner: being already extremely old and nearing his end, his sister was grieving because he seemed likely to die during the festival of the **Thesmophoria** <note>An ancient Greek festival held in honor of Demeter and Persephone, celebrated exclusively by women.</note>, which would prevent her from performing her religious duties to the goddess. He told her to be of good cheer and ordered hot loaves of bread to be brought to him every day. By holding these to his nostrils, he kept himself alive throughout the festival. When the days of the festival had passed (there were three of them), he passed away quite painlessly, as **Hipparchus** says, having lived one hundred and nine years.

I myself have composed an epigram for him in my *Collection of All Meters* in this manner:

->And who was so wise, who performed such a feat,<-
->As the all-knowing Democritus achieved?<-
->Who held back death from his home for three days,<-
->And welcomed it with the scent of hot bread.<-

Such was the life of the man. His doctrines are as follows: the first principles of the universe are **atoms** and the **void**; everything else is merely thought to exist by convention. There are infinite worlds, which are subject to coming into being and passing away. Nothing comes into being from what does not exist, nor can anything be destroyed into what does not exist. Furthermore, the atoms are infinite in size... <note>The text cuts off here mid-sentence.</note>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS.

### DEMOCRITUS. Book 9.

...size and number; and that they are carried along in the whole universe, swirling in eddies. In this way, they produce all composite things: fire, water, air, and earth. For even these elements are systems composed of certain atoms; which are themselves impassive and unchangeable because of their hardness. He held that the sun and the moon are composed of such circular and spherical masses, and the soul likewise, which he considers to be the same as the mind. 

We see by the impact of "images" <note>original: εἰδώλων (*eidōlōn*); Democritus believed that objects constantly shed thin layers of atoms that travel through the air and enter our eyes.</note>. Furthermore, everything happens by necessity, the "eddy" <note>original: δίνης (*dinēs*); a cosmic whirlpool of atoms.</note> being the cause of the generation of all things, which he calls necessity. 

The ultimate goal of life <term>telos</term> <note>The supreme good or purpose toward which all actions are directed.</note> is cheerfulness <note>original: εὐθυμίαν (*euthymian*)</note>, which is not the same as pleasure—as some have misunderstood and interpreted—but a state in which the soul lives calmly and steadily, disturbed by no fear, superstition, or any other emotion. He also calls this state "well-being" <note>original: εὐεστώ (*euestō*)</note> and by many other names. He held that things perceived by the senses exist only by convention; in reality, there are only atoms and the void. These were his opinions.

**Thrasyllus** <note>A scholar and astrologer in the court of Emperor Tiberius who organized the works of both Plato and Democritus into groups of four.</note> has cataloged his books in order, just as he did with those of **Plato**, according to tetralogies.

* *Pythagoras*
* *On the Disposition of the Wise Man*
* *On Those in Hades*
* *Tritogeneia* <note>meaning "Thrice-born"; the text explains this refers to the three things—reasoning well, speaking well, and acting well—which hold human life together.</note>
* *On Courage*, or *On Virtue*
* *The Horn of Amaltheia* <note>A mythological reference to the "horn of plenty."</note>
* *On Cheerfulness*
* *Ethical Commentaries* (the work titled *Well-being* is not found).

These are the ethical works. 

The **Physical** works are as follows:
* *The Great World-System* (which the followers of **Theophrastus** say belongs to **Leucippus** <note>Democritus's teacher.</note>)
* *The Lesser World-System*
* *Cosmography*
* *On the Planets*
* *On Nature*, Book 1
* *On the Nature of Man*, or *On the Flesh*, Book 1
* *On the Mind*
* *On the Senses* (Some combine these and title them collectively *On the Soul*)
* *On Juices*
* *On Colors*
* *On Different Shapes* <note>original: ῥυσμῶν (*rhysmōn*); an Ionian word for "rhythms," which Democritus used to mean the shape or configuration of atoms.</note>
* *On Changes of Shape*
* *Confirmations* (a defense of the aforementioned works)
* *On Images*, or *On Foresight*
* *A Rule regarding Pestilences*, Books 1, 2, and 3
* *Secret Matters*

### DEMOCRITUS. Book 9. (Continued)

...the unclassified works are these: *Celestial Causes*, *Atmospheric Causes*, *Planar Causes*, *Causes Concerning Fire and Things in Fire*, *Causes Concerning Voices*, *Causes Concerning Seeds, Plants, and Fruits*, *Causes Concerning Animals* (in three books), *Mixed Causes*, and *On the Magnet* <note>original: Περὶ τῆς λίθου (*Peri tēs lithou*); literally "On the Stone," referring to the loadstone or magnet.</note>. These constitute the unclassified books.

The mathematical works are these: *On the Difference of Opinion, or On the Contact of the Circle and the Sphere*, *On Geometry*, *Geometric Treatise*, *Numbers*, *On Irrational Lines and Solids* <note>original: ναστῶν (*nastōn*); a term Democritus used for atoms or "full" bodies, here likely referring to solid geometry.</note> (in two books), *Projections* <note>original: Ἐκπετάσματα (*Ekpetasmata*); likely referring to mapping the celestial sphere onto a flat surface.</note>, *The Great Year, or Astronomy*, *The Calendar* <note>original: Παράπηγμα (*Parapēgma*); a stone tablet or almanac showing the risings and settings of stars.</note>, *The Contest of the Water-Clock*, *Description of the Heavens*, *Geography*, *Description of the Pole*, and *Description of Light-rays* <note>original: Ἀκτινογραφίη (*Aktinographiē*); a work on optics.</note>. These are the mathematical works.

The musical and literary works are these: *On Rhythm and Harmony*, *On Poetry*, *On the Beauty of Verses*, *On Euphonious and Harsh Letters*, *On Homer, or Correct Diction and Dialects*, *On Song*, *On Verbs*, and *A Vocabulary* <note>original: Ὀνομαστικόν (*Onomastikon*).</note>. These are the musical works.

The technical works are these: *Prognosis* <note>Medical forecasting.</note>, *On Diet, or Dietetics, or Medical Judgment*, *Causes Concerning Seasonable and Unseasonable Moments*, *On Agriculture, or Geometry*, *On Painting*, *Tactics*, and *Fighting in Armor*. So many are these works.

Furthermore, some writers list the following separately from his notebooks: *On the Sacred Letters in Babylon*, *On the Sacred Letters in Meroë* <note>Meroë was the capital of the Kingdom of Kush, in modern-day Sudan; Democritus was said to have traveled extensively in the East and Africa.</note>, *On History*, *Chaldean Treatise*, *Phrygian Treatise*, *On Fever and Those Who Cough from Disease*, *Legal Causes*, and *Handiwork, or Problems*. Regarding the other books that some attribute to him, some are reworked from his own writings, while others are admittedly the work of others. This concludes the account of his books.

There have been six men named Democritus: 
1. This man himself <note>Democritus of Abdera, the "Laughing Philosopher."</note>.
2. A musician of Chios, a contemporary of the first.
3. A sculptor, mentioned by Antigonus.
4. An author who wrote about the temple at Ephesus and the city of Samothrace.
5. An epigrammatic poet, whose style was clear and flowery.
6. A man from Pergamum, known for his rhetorical speeches.

# PROTAGORAS

### PROTAGORAS. Book 9.

**Protagoras**, the son of Artemon, or (as Apollodorus and Dion say in *The Persian History*) the son of Maeandrius, was a native of Abdera, according to Heraclides of Pontus in his work *On Laws* (who also claims that Protagoras wrote the laws for the colony of Thurii <note>original: Θουρίοις (*Thouriois*); a Greek colony in Italy founded in 443 BCE. Protagoras was famously commissioned by Pericles to draft its constitution.</note>). However, Eupolis in his play *The Flatterers* says he was from Teos; for he writes:

> "Inside there is Protagoras of Teos."

He and **Prodicus of Ceos** used to collect fees by reading their works aloud. Plato, in his dialogue *Protagoras*, mentions that Prodicus had a very deep, booming voice. Protagoras himself was a student of **Democritus**. He was nicknamed "Wisdom" <note>original: Σοφία (*Sophia*).</note>, as Favorinus mentions in his *Miscellaneous History*. He was the first to maintain that there are two sides to every question, opposing each other; he was also the first to employ the method of questioning to support these arguments. Furthermore, he began one of his works in this manner:

> "Man is the measure of all things: of those that are, that they are; and of those that are not, that they are not." <note>original: Πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον, ἄνθρωπος (*Pantōn chrēmatōn metron, anthrōpos*); perhaps the most famous sentence in the history of Sophistry, expressing the idea that truth is relative to the individual perceiver.</note>

He also used to say that the soul is nothing more than the senses (as Plato also notes in the *Theaetetus*) and that everything is true. In another work, he began with these words:

> "Concerning the gods, I have no way of knowing either that they exist or that they do not exist. For there are many obstacles to such knowledge, including the obscurity of the subject and the brevity of human life."

Because of this opening sentence in his book, he was expelled by the Athenians. They burned his books in the marketplace <note>original: ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ (*en tē agora*).</note>, having sent a public crier to collect them from everyone who owned a copy. He was the first to charge a fee of one hundred minas <note>original: μνᾶς ἑκατόν (*mnas hekaton*); an enormous sum of money, equivalent to 10,000 drachmae, emphasizing the high value placed on his "professional" education.</note>. He was also the first to distinguish the parts of time <note>likely referring to grammatical tenses</note>, to explain the power of the "right moment" <note>original: καιροῦ δύναμιν (*kairou dynamin*)</note>, to institute verbal contests, and to introduce sophistical tricks to those engaged in legal arguments. Ignoring the actual meaning of things, he focused his discourse on mere words, thereby giving birth to the now-superficial breed of "Eristics" <note>original: ἐριστικῶν (*eristikōn*); thinkers who argue for the sake of conflict or winning rather than reaching the truth.</note>. As Timon says of him:

> "And Protagoras, a man mixed with arguments, well-skilled in quarreling."

He was also the first to use the Socratic style of discourse, and the argument of **Antisthenes** which attempts to prove...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...that it is impossible to contradict oneself. He was the first to argue this point, as Plato says in the *Euthydemus*. He was also the first to demonstrate how to argue both sides of a specific thesis <note>original: θέσεις (*theseis*); established positions or propositions in a debate.</note>, according to Artemidorus the Dialectician in his work *Against Chrysippus*. Furthermore, he was the first to invent the so-called "porter’s pad" on which people carry their burdens, as Aristotle states in his book *On Education*. 

For Protagoras had been a porter <note>original: φορμοφόρος (*phormophoros*); a carrier of baskets.</note>, as Epicurus also mentions somewhere; it was in this capacity that he was brought to the attention of **Democritus**, having been seen skillfully binding a bundle of wood together. 

Protagoras was the first to divide speech into four parts: prayer, question, answer, and command. Others, however, divide it into seven parts: narrative, question, answer, command, announcement, prayer, and address; these he called the "foundations of speech" <note>original: πυθμένας λόγων (*pythmenas logōn*).</note>. But **Alcidamas** says there are four types of discourse: assertion, denial, question, and address.

The first of his works that he read in public was the one *On the Gods*, the opening of which we quoted previously. He read it at Athens in the house of Euripides, or as some say, in the house of Megaclides; others claim he read it in the Lyceum <note>A public gymnasium and park in Athens where philosophers often gathered.</note>, with his student Archagoras, son of Theodotus, lending him his voice to read aloud. He was accused of impiety by Pythodorus, son of Polyzelus, one of the "Four Hundred" <note>The Four Hundred was a short-lived oligarchy that overthrew the Athenian democracy in 411 BCE.</note>; however, Aristotle says his accuser was Euathlus.

The books of his that are still preserved are as follows:
*   *The Art of Eristics* <note>original: Τέχνη ἐριστικῶν (*Technē eristikōn*); "Eristic" refers to the art of debating solely to win an argument.</note>
*   *On Wrestling*
*   *On the Mathematical Sciences*
*   *On the State*
*   *On Ambition*
*   *On Virtues*
*   *On the Original State of Things*
*   *On Those in the Underworld*
*   *On the Misdeeds of Men*
*   *The Imperative*
*   *Lawsuit for a Fee*
*   *Two Books of Opposing Arguments*

These are his books. Plato also wrote a dialogue named after him. Philochorus relates that while Protagoras was sailing to Sicily, his ship sank, and he suggests that Euripides hinted at this event in his play *Ixion*. Some, however, say he died on a journey, having lived for nearly ninety years. Apollodorus states that he practiced as a Sophist <note>term: Sophist (σοφιστής); a paid teacher of rhetoric and philosophy in Ancient Greece, often criticized by Plato for prioritizing persuasion over truth.</note> for forty years and reached his prime during the 84th Olympiad <note>Approximately 444–441 BCE.</note>. # PROTAGORAS. Book 9. 363

And I heard the report of you, Protagoras, how departing
From Athens once, an old man, you died on the road.
For the city of Cecrops <note>A legendary king of Athens; here, the name refers to the city itself.</note> chose to exile you. But though you
Fled the city of Pallas <note>Athena, the patron goddess of Athens.</note>, you did not flee Pluto <note>The god of the Underworld; i.e., death.</note>.

It is said that once, when he demanded his fee from his student **Euathlus**, the latter replied, "But I have not yet won a case." Protagoras responded: "If I win the lawsuit against you, I must receive the money because I was the victor; but if you win, I must also receive it, because you have finally won a case <note>original: Ἀλλ' ἐγὼ μὲν ἂν νικήσω... ἐὰν δὲ σύ. This is a famous logical paradox: their contract stated the student would pay only after winning his first case. If Protagoras sues for the money and the student wins the trial, the student has "won a case" and must pay according to the contract, even though he won the right not to pay in court.</note>." 

There was also another **Protagoras**, an astronomer, for whom Euphorion wrote a funeral elegy; and a third, who was a Stoic philosopher.

## DIOGENES OF APOLLONIA.

**Diogenes**, son of Apollothemis, was a native of Apollonia <note>A city in ancient Thrace or perhaps Crete; he was a "natural philosopher" (physikos) who sought the physical origins of the world.</note>, a man of great reputation. According to Antisthenes, he was a student of **Anaximenes**. He lived during the time of **Anaxagoras**. Demetrius of Phalerum says in his *Apology of Socrates* that Diogenes came into great danger at Athens because of extreme envy.

His doctrines were as follows: that air is the primary element <note>original: στοιχεῖον (*stoicheion*)</note>, that there are infinite worlds, and an infinite void. He believed that air, by becoming denser or thinner, is the generative force behind the worlds. Nothing comes into being from nothing, nor is anything destroyed into nothingness. He held that the earth is spherical, supported in the center, and that it took its shape through the rotation of heat and its solidification by cold. 

The beginning of his treatise is as follows: "At the start of any discourse, it seems to me necessary to provide a starting point that is beyond dispute; the explanation should be simple and dignified."

->DIOGENES LAERTIUS<-
# 364

...this very thing: to know that he knows nothing <note>original: "αὐτὸ τοῦτο εἰδέναι ὅτι οὐδὲν οἶδε." Metrodorus of Chios began his book with this radical skeptical claim, echoing Socrates but taking it further.</note>. Metrodorus was a pupil of Nessus of Chios; though others say he was a student of **Democritus**.

**Anaxarchus**, then, was a companion of **Alexander** <note>Alexander the Great, whom Anaxarchus accompanied on his Asian campaigns.</note>, and he flourished during the 110th Olympiad <note>Approximately 340–337 BCE.</note>. He had a bitter enemy in **Nicocreon**, the tyrant of Cyprus. Once, at a banquet, when Alexander asked him what he thought of the feast, they say he replied: "Everything is magnificent, O King; but there should have been one more dish served—the head of a certain satrap," alluding mockingly to Nicocreon. 

The tyrant did not forget the slight. After the King’s death, when Anaxarchus was forced against his will to land in Cyprus during a voyage, Nicocreon seized him. He placed the philosopher in a large mortar <note>A stone bowl used for grinding grain or spices.</note> and ordered him to be pounded to death with iron pestles. But Anaxarchus, making light of the punishment, famously cried out:

> "Pound the pouch <note>original: θύλακον (thylakon). He refers to his physical body as a mere 'sack' or 'pouch' that contains his true self, which remains untouchable.</note> of Anaxarchus! You do not strike Anaxarchus himself."

When Nicocreon then ordered his tongue to be cut out, the story goes that Anaxarchus bit it off himself and spat it in the tyrant's face. We have written an epigram about him as follows:

> Pound on, harder and harder still; it is but a pouch.
> Pound away! Anaxarchus has long been in the house of Zeus.
> And to Persephone <note>Queen of the Underworld.</note>, after these clouded days, 
> You shall say these few words: "Be gone, you evil grinder of limbs."

Because of his <term>apatheia</term> <note>A state of being undisturbed by emotions or external suffering; "impassivity."</note> and the ease of his lifestyle, he was called "The Happy One." He was able to bring even Alexander to his senses with great ease. For instance, when he saw blood flowing from a wound the King had received, he pointed to him with his hand and said:

> "This is indeed blood, and not <term>ichor</term> <note>The ethereal fluid that flows in the veins of the gods instead of blood.</note>,
> —Such as flows in the veins of the blessed gods." <note>A parody of Homer's *Iliad* (5.340), reminding Alexander of his mortality despite his claims to divinity.</note>

**Plutarch**, however, says that Alexander himself said this to his friends. On another occasion, while Anaxarchus was drinking to the King's health, he pointed to the goblet and said:

> "A god shall be struck by a mortal's hand." <note>Anaxarchus often used irony to deflate Alexander's divine pretensions, suggesting that even a "god" is subject to physical needs or human violence.</note>

# 365
### PYRRHO. Book IX.

->PYRRHO.<-

**Pyrrho** of **Elis** was the son of Pleistarchus, as Diocles records. However, according to Apollodorus in his *Chronicles*, he was a painter before he became a philosopher. He was a student of Bryson <note>original: "Δρύσωνος" (Druso). Most scholars identify this with Bryson of Achaea.</note>, the son of Stilpo, as Alexander states in his *Successions*. Later, he followed **Anaxarchus** everywhere, even traveling as far as India to meet the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>Literally "naked wise men," referring to Indian ascetics and yogis.</note> and the Magi <note>The priestly class of ancient Persia.</note>. It was from this experience that he seems to have developed his most noble philosophy, introducing the concepts of <term>incomprehensibility</term> <note>original: "ἀκαταληψίας" (akatalepsia); the belief that the true nature of things is impossible to grasp.</note> and the <term>suspension of judgment</term> <note>original: "ἐποχῆς" (epoche); the practice of withholding assent to any belief or proposition.</note>, as Ascanius of Abdera says.

For he used to assert that nothing is truly honorable or shameful, just or unjust. He held the same for all things: that in reality, nothing exists in and of itself, but that human actions are governed entirely by law and custom. Each thing, he argued, was <term>no more this than that</term> <note>original: "οὐ γὰρ μᾶλλον τόδε ἢ τόδε" (ou mallon). This became a famous skeptical slogan used to balance opposing arguments.</note>. 

He remained consistent in his way of life as well. He would avoid nothing and took no precautions, facing everything as it came—be it wagons, precipices, dogs, or anything of the sort—never trusting his senses. However, he was kept safe (as the followers of Antigonus of Carystus say) by his friends who used to follow him around. Yet **Aenesidemus** claims that while Pyrrho’s philosophy was based on the suspension of judgment, he did not act without foresight in his daily life. He lived to be ninety years old.

Antigonus of Carystus, in his work *On Pyrrho*, says the following about him: that in the beginning he was obscure and poor, and worked as a painter; in fact, there are still preserved in the gymnasium at **Elis** some of his paintings of "torch-bearers" which are of respectable quality. He would often wander away from home to live in solitude, rarely appearing to those in his household. He reportedly began doing this after hearing an Indian rebuke Anaxarchus, telling him that "he could never teach another to be good while he himself frequented the courts of kings." 

Pyrrho was always in the same state of mind; so much so that if someone left in the middle of his speaking, he would finish the discourse to himself, even though he had been quite excitable in his youth. Often (Antigonus says) he would travel abroad without telling anyone, and would journey with whoever he happened to meet. And...
