### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

Once, when **Anaxarchus** <note>Pyrrho’s teacher and travel companion</note> fell into a marsh, **Pyrrho** passed by without offering any help. While others blamed him for this, Anaxarchus himself praised his <term>indifference</term> <note>original: "τὸ ἀδιάφορον" (to adiaphoron); a state of being unmoved by external circumstances</note> and his lack of emotional attachment. On another occasion, he was caught talking to himself, and when asked the reason, he said he was practicing how to be a good man. In philosophical inquiries, no one looked down on him because he spoke with great range and responded well to questions. It was this quality that "captured" **Nausiphanes** while he was still a young man. Nausiphanes certainly used to say that one should adopt **Pyrrho’s** disposition, but keep his own arguments. He also frequently mentioned that **Epicurus** <note>The famous founder of Epicureanism, who was a student of Nausiphanes</note>, admiring **Pyrrho's** way of life, would constantly ask questions about him.

**Pyrrho** was so highly honored by his native city <note>Elis, in the Peloponnese</note> that they appointed him a High Priest, and because of him, they voted to grant <term>tax immunity</term> <note>original: "ἀτέλειαν" (ateleian); an exemption from public burdens or taxes</note> to all philosophers. He also had many admirers of his "tranquility" or "inactivity" <note>original: "ἀπραγμοσύνης" (apragmosynes)</note>. This is why **Timon** <note>Timon of Phlius, Pyrrho's most famous student and a satirical poet</note> says the following about him in his work *Pytho*, and in his *Silli* (Lampoons):

> O old man, O **Pyrrho**, how or from where did you find escape
> From the slavery of opinions and the empty-mindedness of the sophists?
> How did you loose the chains of all deception and persuasion?
> You do not care to inquire what winds
> Possess Greece, or from where and toward what end each thing tends.

->And again in the *Images*:<-

> This my heart longs to hear, O **Pyrrho**, 
> How you still lead a man’s life most easily in tranquility, 
> Alone among men, guiding your way like a god.

The **Athenians** also honored him with citizenship, as **Diocles** says, on the occasion of his slaying **Kotys** the Thracian <note>This is likely a historical error by the source, as the assassination of the Thracian king Kotys I is usually attributed to students of Plato</note>. He lived a pious life with his sister, who was a midwife, as **Eratosthenes** records in his work *On Wealth and Poverty*. It is said that he would even take poultry or little pigs to the market to sell them himself; and he would clean the house with total <term>indifference</term>, making no distinction between tasks. It is even said that he once washed a pig himself due to this same indifference. Once, when he became angry about a—

### PYRRHO. Book 9

...[his] sister (she was called **Philista**), he said to the man who had seized her that the demonstration of <term>indifference</term> <note>original: "ἀδιαφορίας" (adiaphorias); the state of being unmoved or neutral toward external things</note> does not consist in the treatment of a woman. And once, when he was startled by a dog that rushed at him, he replied to someone who criticized him that it was difficult to entirely "strip off the human being." He said one must struggle as much as possible against circumstances, first through actions, but if not, then at least through reason. They also say that when septic medicines, surgery, and cautery <note>Applying extreme heat to a wound to stop bleeding or infection</note> were applied to an ulcer he had, he did not even knit his eyebrows.

**Timon** <note>Pyrrho’s student, known for his satirical poems</note> also clarifies his disposition in the works where he explains things to **Pytho**. Furthermore, **Philo of Athens**, who was an acquaintance of his, used to say that **Pyrrho** frequently mentioned **Democritus** <note>The "laughing philosopher" who proposed an atomic theory and a state of "cheerfulness" as the goal of life</note>, and after him **Homer**, whom he admired and would constantly quote, saying:

> "As is the generation of leaves, so is that of men." <note>A famous line from Homer's Iliad (6.146) highlighting the transience of human life.</note>

He also said that **Homer** compared men to flies and birds. He would also quote these lines:

> "But, friend, die also; why do you lament in this way? 
> Patroclus died too, who was much better than you." <note>From Iliad (21.106–107), spoken by Achilles to a pleading captive.</note>

He cited everything that points to the uncertainty, vanity, and childishness of human affairs. **Posidonius** <note>A Stoic philosopher and historian</note> also tells a story about him: once, when his fellow passengers on a ship were gloomy because of a storm, **Pyrrho** remained calm and encouraged their spirits by pointing to a little pig on the ship that was eating unbothered. He told them that the wise man should establish himself in just such a state of <term>ataraxia</term> <note>original: "ἀταραξίᾳ" (ataraxia); untroubledness or freedom from mental disturbance</note>. Only **Numenius** <note>A later philosopher who saw connections between Plato and Eastern thought</note> claims that he actually held positive doctrines. Among others, he had famous disciples, including **Eurylochus**, of whom the following shortcoming is recorded: they say he once became so provoked that he grabbed the spit with the meat still on it and chased the cook all the way into the marketplace. Once in **Elis**, when he was being overwhelmed by people questioning him in a debate, he threw off his cloak and swam across the river **Alpheus** <note>The main river of the Peloponnese, flowing through Elis</note>. He was, therefore, an extreme enemy of the <term>sophists</term> <note>original: "σοφισταῖς" (sophistais); professional teachers of rhetoric and argument who were often criticized for prioritizing winning over truth</note>, as **Timon** also says. **Philo** also used to discuss most things at length; which is why **Timon** says of him:

> "Or the man who is free from the bile of men, a self-wanderer," <note>original: "αὐτοπλανητήν" (autoplanētēn); suggesting one who wanders by his own choice or within his own mind</note>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...paying no heed to fame and relying on **Philo**. <note>This concludes a poetic fragment from Timon of Phlius describing Pyrrho's character.</note>
In addition to these, **Pyrrho** was heard by **Hecataeus of Abdera**, and **Timon of Phlius**, the author of the *Silli* <note>original: "σίλλους" (silloi); satirical poems or lampoons used to mock dogmatic philosophers</note>, whom we shall discuss later; also **Nausiphanes of Teos**, who some say was a teacher of **Epicurus**. All these were called **Pyrrhonists** after their master, but they were also called **Aporetics**, **Sceptics**, **Ephectics**, and **Zetetics**, based on the character of their teaching.

The philosophy is called **Zetetic** <note>original: "ζητητικὴ" (zetetike); from 'zetesis' meaning searching or inquiring</note> from its always "seeking" the truth; **Sceptic** <note>original: "σκεπτικὴ" (skeptike); from 'skepsis' meaning looking, considering, or examining</note> from its always "looking" and never finding; **Ephectic** <note>original: "ἐφεκτικὴ" (ephektike); from 'epoche' meaning suspension</note> from the state of mind that follows the inquiry—I mean the "suspension of judgment"; and **Aporetic** <note>original: "ἀπορητικὴ" (aporetike); from 'aporia' meaning a state of being at a loss or a dead end</note> from the fact that even the dogmatists <note>Philosophers who claim to have found the truth and lay down firm doctrines</note> themselves are "at a loss." They are called **Pyrrhonists** after **Pyrrho**.

However, **Theodosius** in his *Sceptic Chapters* says that Scepticism should not be called "Pyrrhonism." For if the movement of the mind in either direction is ungraspable, we will not know **Pyrrho's** actual disposition; and not knowing it, we could not be called **Pyrrhonists**. Furthermore, he argues that **Pyrrho** was not the first to discover Scepticism, nor did he have any formal doctrine. One might, however, be called a **Pyrrhonist** by having a similar way of life.

Some say that **Homer** was the founder of this school, since he expresses himself differently at different times regarding the same circumstances, and never lays down a universal doctrine in his pronouncements. They say the sayings of the **Seven Sages** <note>A group of 7th–6th century BCE Greek thinkers famous for their practical wisdom</note> are also Sceptical, such as "Nothing in excess" and "Give a pledge, and ruin is near" <note>original: "Ἐγγύα, πάρα δ' ἄτα" (Engua, para d' ata)</note>. This implies that ruin follows the person who has reached a firm and certain decision. Furthermore, they claim that **Archilochus** and **Euripides** were Sceptical in their outlook; among whom **Archilochus** says:

> Such is the mind of man, **Glaucus**, son of **Leptines**,
> As the day which **Zeus** brings upon mortals.

->**Euripides** says:<-

> Why then do they say that wretched mortals
> Have wisdom? For we depend on you <note>Addressing a god or fate; the spacing here reflects the original manuscript's layout</note>,
> and we do such things as you happen to will.

### PYRRHO. Book 9.

Furthermore, **Xenophanes**, **Zeno of Elea**, and **Democritus** are considered by the Skeptics to be among their number. Of these, **Xenophanes** says:
> And as for the clear truth, no man has seen it, nor will there be anyone
> who knows it. <note>original: "Καὶ τὸ μὲν οὖν σαφὲς οὔτις ἀνὴρ ἴδεν, οὐδέ τις ἔσται εἰδώς." This is a famous fragment expressing the limits of human knowledge.</note>

**Zeno** does away with motion, saying: "That which moves does so neither in the place where it is, nor in the place where it is not." <note>This is one of Zeno's paradoxes intended to show that our sensory perception of motion is logically contradictory.</note> **Democritus**, setting aside the reality of sensory qualities, says: "By convention cold, by convention hot; but in reality, atoms and the void." And again: "In reality we know nothing; for truth lies in the depths." **Plato**, too, leaves the absolute truth to the gods and the children of gods, while for humans he seeks only the "likely account." <note>original: "εἰκότα λόγον" (eikota logon); the idea that humans can only achieve probable stories or models of reality, not certain knowledge.</note> And **Euripides** says:
> Who knows if living is actually being dead,
> and being dead is what mortals consider living?

**Empedocles** likewise speaks this way: "These things are neither visible to men, nor audible, nor graspable by the mind." And earlier: "Each man is convinced only of that which he has personally encountered." Furthermore, **Heraclitus** says: "Let us not make random guesses about the most important matters." **Hippocrates**, too, is said to have expressed himself with hesitation and from a human perspective. And even before these, **Homer** said:
> The tongue of mortals is flexible, and many are the tales within it.

->and,<-

> -- the pasture of words is vast, extending here and there.

->and,<-

> Whatever kind of word you speak, such a word you will hear in return.

By this, he refers to the "equal weight" <term>isostheneia<gloss>the Skeptic principle that for every argument, there is an opposing argument of equal persuasive force</gloss></term> and the opposition of arguments. The **Skeptics** spent their time overturning all the doctrines of the various philosophical schools, while they themselves declared nothing dogmatically. Insofar as they brought forward the views of others and recounted them, they defined nothing—not even this very principle. Thus, they even did away with the idea of "not defining," saying, for example: "We define nothing" (for if they did, they would be making a definition). They say these statements are offered to reduce the risk of error, as if it were a medicine that might carry itself away along with the illness it treats. Because of this...

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
### Book 9.

"We define nothing" is a phrase that expresses a state of **non-inclination** <note>original: "ἀῤῥεψίας" (arrepsia). This refers to a state of perfect balance, like a scale that does not tip toward either side, representing a mind that does not lean toward any specific conclusion.</note>. Likewise with the phrases "No more [this than that]," and "To every argument an equal argument is opposed," and similar expressions. 

The phrase "No more" is used in a positive sense when things are similar—for instance, "A pirate is no more wicked than a liar." However, the **Skeptics** <note>The Skeptics, or Pyrrhonists, were a school of philosophers who believed that because arguments of equal weight can be made for any side of an issue, one should suspend judgment to achieve peace of mind.</note> do not use it positively, but rather to negate both options. It is like someone refuting a point by saying, "Scylla existed no more than the Chimera." <note>Scylla and the Chimera are mythical monsters; to say one existed "no more" than the other is to say that neither existed at all.</note> 

The word "more" itself is sometimes used to compare things, as when we say, "Honey is sweeter <note>literally "more sweet"</note> than a dried grape." At other times it is used to affirm one thing and deny another, as when we say, "Virtue is more beneficial than harmful," for here we mean that virtue is beneficial and not harmful. But the Skeptics even do away with the phrase "No more" itself. For just as they say "Providence exists no more than it does not," so too the phrase "No more" itself "is no more than it is not." 

Therefore, this phrase signifies (as **Timon** says in his *Python*) <note>Timon of Phlius was a famous Skeptic philosopher and poet; his work *Python* was a dialogue explaining Skeptical doctrines.</note> the defining of nothing, but rather an absence of commitment. The phrase "To every argument an equal argument is opposed" also brings about **suspension of judgment** <note>original: "ἐποχή" (epochē); the central Skeptical practice of withholding assent to any non-evident proposition.</note>. For when things are in conflict and arguments are of equal strength, ignorance of the truth follows. 

Even to this very argument, an argument is opposed; and after it has done away with the other arguments, it is itself overturned and perishes. It is much like a **purgative medicine**, which, after first expelling the waste matter from the body, is itself expelled and destroyed along with it. <note>This is a famous Skeptical analogy: their arguments are "self-refuting" tools that clear the mind of dogmatism and then disappear, leaving the mind in a state of quietude.</note> 

Against this, the **Dogmatists** <note>The "Dogmatists" was the Skeptics' term for philosophers like the Stoics or Aristotelians who claimed to have discovered the truth.</note> claim that the Skeptic does not actually remove the argument, but rather confirms it. The Skeptics, however, used arguments only as tools. For it was not possible to destroy an argument except by another argument, just as we are accustomed to say "there is no place," and yet we must necessarily use the word "place" to say it—though we use it not dogmatically, but for the sake of demonstration. 

Similarly, they might say "nothing happens by necessity," and yet they must use the word "necessity." They employed this manner of expression because things do not appear to be such-and-such by their inherent nature, but only *appear* so to the observer. They said they investigate not what they think...

<summary>This page explains key Skeptical slogans like "No more" and "We define nothing," detailing how Skeptics used these phrases to negate all dogmatic claims, including the slogans themselves, through the famous analogy of a purgative medicine.</summary>
<keywords>Skepticism, Pyrrhonism, suspension of judgment, Timon of Phlius, No More, non-inclination, Dogmatists, purgative analogy, epistemology</keywords>

# PYRRHO. Book 9.
->A. ii.<-

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing a thought from the previous page about how things are perceived.</note>

...is clearly understood) but from those things which they experience through the senses. The **Pyrrhonian** discourse, then, is a certain record of things as they appear or are thought of in any way, according to which everything is compared with everything else. When compared, these things are found to contain much inconsistency and confusion, as <term>Aenesidemus</term> <note>Aenesidemus was a major Skeptic philosopher (1st century BC) who revived the teachings of Pyrrho and formalized the "Ten Modes" of doubt.</note> says in his *Outline of <term>Pyrrhonism</term>*. 

In their inquiries into contradictions, they would first point out the ways in which things seem persuasive, and then by those very same means they would destroy one's confidence in them. For they say that some things persuade us because they agree with the senses, or because they never (or rarely) change, or because of custom, or because they are established by law, or because they give pleasure or cause wonder. They would then show that the opposite arguments have an equal degree of probability compared to those that were persuasive. 

The difficulties they raised regarding the agreement of things perceived or thought were classified into <term>ten modes</term> <note>original: "δέκα τρόποι" (deka tropoi). These are ten specific arguments used by Skeptics to prove that we cannot know the true nature of things, only how they appear to us.</note>, according to which the underlying objects appeared to vary. The first of these **ten modes** he sets down is the one based on the differences among animals regarding pleasure and pain, harm and benefit. From this it is concluded that the same impressions are not produced by the same objects, and that because of this conflict, the result is to <term>suspend judgment</term> <note>original: "ἐπέχειν" (epechein). This is the core goal of Skepticism: to stop oneself from making a definitive claim of "true" or "false" when faced with equal evidence on both sides.</note>.

For some animals are born without sexual union, such as those born from fire <note>original: "πυρίβια" (pyribia). Ancient naturalists believed certain insects could be generated within the intense heat of a furnace.</note>, the <term>Arabian phoenix</term>, and others; while some are born from union, such as humans and others. Some are composed in one way, some in another. Therefore they also differ in their senses, as hawks are most sharp-sighted, while dogs have the keenest sense of smell. It is reasonable, then, that different images should strike eyes that are constructed differently. 

For instance, to a goat, a young shoot is edible, but to a human it is bitter; hemlock is nourishing for a quail but deadly for a human; and dung is edible for a pig, but not for a horse. The second mode is based on the different natures of humans, according to their nations and bodily temperaments. <term>Demophon</term>, for example, the table-servant of <term>Alexander</term>, used to feel warm in the shade and shiver in the sun.

<summary>This page defines the Pyrrhonian method of comparing perceptions to reveal contradictions and introduces the first two of the 'Ten Modes' of doubt: the differences between species and the differences between individual humans.</summary>

# DIOG. LAERT.
### Page 372

Andron the Argive (as Aristotle says) traveled through the waterless desert of **Libya** <note>original: "Λιβύης" (Libuēs). In antiquity, "Libya" often referred to the entire continent of Africa or the region west of the Nile.</note> without ever needing a drink. Furthermore, one man desires iambic poetry, another farming, and another trade; and these very things harm some while benefiting others. For this reason, one must **suspend judgment** <note>original: "ἐφεκτέον" (ephekton). A core Skeptic term meaning to withhold one's opinion because the evidence is contradictory.</note>. 

The **third mode** is based on the differences between the various channels of the senses. For example, an apple appears pale to the sight, sweet to the taste, and fragrant to the sense of smell. Also, the very same shape is seen as different depending on the variations in the mirrors reflecting it. It follows, then, that the object appearing is *no more* <note>original: "μὴ μᾶλλον" (mē mallon). This was a famous Skeptical slogan: a thing is "no more" this than that.</note> of one character than another. 

The **fourth mode** is based on internal states and general variations; such as health, disease, sleep, waking, joy, grief, youth, old age, courage, fear, want, fullness, hatred, friendship, heat, and cold—and also according to how one breathes or whether the <term>pores</term> <note>Ancient thinkers believed the body had "pores" or passages through which sensory information flowed; their condition determined how we perceived the world.</note> are constricted. Thus, the things we encounter appear different depending on our specific internal states. For even those who are "mad" are not in a state contrary to nature—for why should they be considered more so than we? After all, even we see the sun as if it were standing still, though it is moving. **Theon of Tithorea** the Stoic used to walk in his sleep, and a slave of **Pericles** used to walk upon the very edge of the roof. 

The **fifth mode** is based on upbringings, laws, mythical beliefs, cultural customs, and dogmatic opinions. This mode covers ideas about what is beautiful or ugly, true or false, good or bad, and concerns the gods and the birth and destruction of all things we see. For the same action is considered just by some, but unjust by others; and good to some, but bad to others. 

For example, among the **Persians** it is not considered strange to have intercourse with a daughter, but to the **Greeks** it is unlawful. The **Massagetae** (as **Eudoxus** says in the first book of his *Circuit of the Earth*) hold their wives in common, but the Greeks do not. The **Cilicians** used to delight in robbery, but the Greeks do not. Regarding the gods, different people hold different views; some believe they exercise providence over us, while others say they do not. The **Egyptians** bury their dead by embalming them; the **Romans** by burning them; and the **Paionians** by throwing them into lakes. Hence, regarding the truth of these matters...

<summary>This page outlines several "modes" of Skeptical doubt, illustrating how differences in senses, physical states, and cultural laws make it impossible to determine the absolute nature of reality.</summary>

### PYRRHO. Book 9
### Page 373

<margin>Suspension of judgment</margin> <note>original: "ἐποχή" (epochē). This is the central goal of the Skeptic: a state where one neither denies nor affirms anything, leading to mental tranquility.</note> The **sixth mode** is based on mixtures and associations, according to which nothing appears purely by itself, but always in combination with air, light, moisture, solidity, heat, cold, motion, vapors, or other forces. For instance, purple dye shows a different color in sunlight, moonlight, and lamplight. Our own complexion, too, appears different at midday than at other times. A stone that is difficult to move in the air is easily shifted in water—either because it is heavy but lightened by the water, or because it is light but made to seem heavier by the air. We are therefore ignorant of a thing’s individual nature, just as we cannot distinguish the simple nature of oil when it is mixed in a perfume.

The **seventh mode** is based on quantities <note>original: "ὑποστάσεις" (hupostaseis). Here referring to the composition or scale of objects.</note>, and specific positions, places, and the things within those places. 

<margin>according to</margin> According to this mode, things that are actually large appear small; square things appear round; smooth things appear to have protrusions; straight things appear bent; and pale things appear to be of another color. For example, the sun appears small because of its distance. Mountains from afar look like misty clouds and smooth surfaces, but from close up they are rugged. Furthermore, the sun looks different when rising than it does at its zenith. The same body looks one way in a grove and another in an open field. An image <note>Likely referring to a painting or a statue.</note> changes according to its position, and the feathers on a **pigeon’s neck** change color as the bird turns. Since it is impossible to perceive these things outside of their places and positions, their true nature remains unknown.

The **eighth mode** is based on quantities—whether of heat or cold, speed or slowness, paleness or other variations. For instance, **wine** taken in moderation strengthens, but taken in excess, it unnerves the body; the same applies to food and similar things.

The **ninth mode** is based on whether a thing is constant, strange, or rare. For example, people do not marvel at earthquakes in places where they occur constantly; nor do they marvel at the sun, because it is seen every day. <note>The Skeptics argued that our "wonder" or "certainty" is often just a result of how often we see something, not the thing itself.</note> Favorinus calls this the eighth mode, while Sextus and Aenesidemus call it the tenth. Furthermore, Sextus calls the tenth the eighth, and Favorinus calls it the ninth.

The **tenth mode** is based on the comparison of things with one another; such as the light compared to the heavy, the...

<term>Pyrrhonists</term> <note>Followers of Pyrrho of Elis, who believed that because human perception is unreliable, one should live without fixed beliefs.</note>, <term>sixth mode</term>, <term>seventh mode</term>, <term>eighth mode</term>, <term>ninth mode</term>, <term>tenth mode</term>, <term>Favorinus</term> <note>A Roman-era philosopher and historian who wrote about the Skeptics.</note>, <term>Sextus</term> <note>Sextus Empiricus, whose writings are the primary source for our knowledge of ancient Skepticism.</note>, <term>Aenesidemus</term> <note>The philosopher who originally codified these "Ten Modes."</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the Skeptical "Ten Modes" of Aenesidemus, specifically the tenth mode regarding relativity. It then transitions into the "Five Modes" attributed to the later Skeptic Agrippa, and begins a broader critique of the possibility of logical proof.</meta>

### DIOG. LAERT.
### Page 374

...strong, compared to the weak; the greater, compared to the less; the **above**, compared to the **below**. For instance, the right side is not "right" by nature, but is understood according to its relationship <note>original: "σχέσιν" (schesin). This refers to the state of being related or disposed toward something else.</note> to another thing. If that other thing's position is changed, it will no longer be the right side. Similarly, "father" and "brother" are relative terms, as is "day" relative to the sun, and all things are relative to the mind. Therefore, things relative to something else are unknown as they are in themselves. These, then, are the **ten modes**.

But the followers of **Agrippa** <note>Agrippa was a Skeptic philosopher who lived likely in the 1st century AD. He distilled the earlier ten modes into five more abstract, logical challenges.</note> introduce five other modes:
1. The mode based on **disagreement** <note>original: "διαφωνίας" (diaphonias).</note>.
2. The mode that leads to **infinite regress** <note>original: "εἰς ἄπειρον" (eis apeiron).</note>.
3. The mode of **relativity** <note>original: "πρός τι" (pros ti).</note>.
4. The mode of **hypothesis** <note>original: "ἐξ ὑποθέσεως" (ex hupotheseos).</note>.
5. The mode of **reciprocity** <note>original: "δι' ἀλλήλων" (di’ allēlōn), often called the "circular" argument.</note>.

The mode of **disagreement** shows that whatever question is proposed, whether among philosophers or in common life, is full of the greatest conflict and confusion. The mode of **infinite regress** does not allow the matter under investigation to be established, because one proof takes its certainty from another, and that from another, and so on to infinity. The mode of **relativity** asserts that nothing is grasped by itself, but only in connection with something else; hence, things remain unknown. The mode of **hypothesis** occurs when certain people think they should take the primary principles of things as self-evident and trust them without proof—which is futile, for someone else could just as easily hypothesize the opposite. The mode of **reciprocity** occurs when that which ought to be the confirmation of the thing under investigation itself requires proof from the thing being investigated. For example, if someone were to prove that there are "pores" in the skin <note>A common ancient scientific theory to explain how substances move through the body.</note> because of "effluences" <note>Flows or discharges.</note>, but then used the existence of "effluences" to prove there are "pores."

Furthermore, they did away with all **proof**, **criteria**, **signs**, **causes**, **motion**, **learning**, **coming into being**, and the idea that anything is by nature **good** or **evil**. For every proof (they say) is composed either of things already proven or of things unproven. If it is from things already proven, those will in turn require some proof, and so on to infinity. If it is from unproven things—whether all of them, some of them, or even just one single disputed point—then the whole proof remains unproven. If you think (they say) that there are some things that require no proof...

<summary>This page concludes the "Ten Modes" of Skepticism and introduces the "Five Modes" of Agrippa, which focus on the logical impossibility of absolute proof through disagreement, infinite regress, and circular reasoning.</summary>
<keywords>Skepticism, Agrippa, Five Modes, infinite regress, relativity, circular reasoning, proof, Diogenes Laertius, Pyrrhonism</keywords>

# PYRRHO. Book 2
->379<-

...they are truly wonderful in their thinking, if they do not understand that for the very first thing they take as a foundation for belief <note>original: "πίστιν" (pistin). In this context, it refers to the grounds for conviction or the reliability of a statement.</note>, a **proof** is required. For one cannot confirm that there are four elements by arguing from the existence of those very same four elements. Furthermore, if individual proofs are untrustworthy, then the general concept of **proof** itself must also be untrustworthy.

In order for us to know that proof exists, we require a **criterion** <note>original: "κριτήριον" (kriterion). A standard, rule, or tool used to distinguish truth from falsehood.</note>; and to know what a criterion is, we require a **proof**. Thus, both are rendered incomprehensible, as each is constantly referred back to the other <note>This is the "Circular" or "Reciprocal" mode, where two things depend on each other for validation, resulting in neither being proven.</note>. How, then, could unclear things <note>original: "τὰ ἄδηλα" (ta adēla). In Skepticism, these are the hidden realities of nature as opposed to "phenomena" or appearances.</note> be grasped if the nature of proof remains unknown?

The inquiry is not whether things *appear* to be a certain way, but whether they are so in their actual **substance** <note>original: "ὑπόστασιν" (hupostasin). The underlying reality or essence of a thing.</note>. They showed that certain **dogmatists** <note>original: "δογματικούς" (dogmatikous). Philosophers who claim to have discovered the truth and assert definite "dogmas."</note> were acting strangely; for what is merely based on a hypothesis is not a matter of inquiry, but of simple assertion. Using such logic, one could even argue for impossible things. 

To those who believe we should not judge truth based on circumstances, nor establish laws based on nature, he <note>Referring to the Skeptic thinker, likely Pyrrho or Aenesidemus.</note> said that they were attempting to define the measures of all things without seeing that everything which appears, appears only in relation to a specific **disposition** or **counter-circumstance**. Therefore, one must either say everything is true, or everything is false.

If, however, only some things are true, by what means are we to distinguish them? It cannot be by **sensation** <note>original: "αἰσθήσει" (aisthēsei).</note>, because all sensations appear equal to the senses. Nor can it be by **thought** <note>original: "νοήσει" (noēsei).</note>, for the same reason. Aside from these, no other power for making a judgment is visible. 

Therefore, they say, whoever makes a firm assertion about something sensible or something thought must first settle the conflicting opinions regarding them. For some have abolished one set of things, and some another. It must be judged either through the sensible or the intelligible, yet both are disputed. It is not possible, then, to judge opinions about sensible or intelligible things. If the conflict within our thoughts requires us to demand a reason for everything, then the **measure** <note>original: "μέτρον" (metron). The standard or yardstick of truth.</note> by which we think we determine all things accurately will be abolished. Consequently, they will consider all things to be equal.

Furthermore, the person debating us says: "Is the appearance trustworthy or not?" If it is trustworthy, he will have nothing to say to the person who sees the exact opposite; for just as he is trustworthy in reporting his appearance, so is his opponent. But if it is untrustworthy...

<note>original: "ΠΥΡΡΩΝ, Sextus Empiricus, κριτήριον, ἀπόδειξις, ἄδηλα, αἴσθησις, νόησις, δογματικοί"</note>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
->876<-

...and he himself <note>The Skeptic philosopher.</note> will suspend belief, speaking only of **what appears** <note>original: "τὸ φαινόμενον" (to phainomenon). The Skeptics distinguished between how things seem to us (appearances) and how they are in reality.</note>. Furthermore, that which is **persuasive** <note>original: "πειθον" (peithon). Something that carries conviction or seems plausible.</note> must not be assumed to be true. For the same thing does not persuade everyone, nor does it consistently persuade the same people. **Persuasiveness** arises from external circumstances, or from the high reputation of the speaker, or from their mental acuity, or from their cleverness, or from habit, or even from being pleasing to the listener.

They also did away with the **criterion** <note>original: "κριτήριον" (kriterion). The standard or "ruler" used to distinguish truth from falsehood.</note> by the following argument: either the criterion itself has been judged [and validated], or it is **unjudged**. If it is unjudged, it is untrustworthy and fails to distinguish between truth and falsehood. But if it has been judged, it will fall into the category of things being judged part-by-part; thus, the same thing would be both the judge and the thing being judged, and the standard that judged the criterion would itself need to be judged by another, and that by another, and so on to **infinity** <note>This is the "Infinite Regress" argument: if every proof needs a proof, you can never reach a solid foundation.</note>.

Additionally, there is profound disagreement regarding the criterion. Some say **Man** is the criterion; others say the **senses**; others, **reason**; and some, the **apprehensive impression** <note>original: "καταληπτικὴν φαντασίαν" (kataleptiken phantasian). A technical term from Stoic philosophy referring to a "clear and distinct" perception that supposedly cannot be false.</note>. However, Man disagrees both with himself and with others, as is clear from the variety of different laws and customs. The senses are deceptive, and reason is full of conflict. As for the apprehensive impression, it is judged by the mind, yet the mind itself changes in a thousand ways. Therefore, the **criterion** is unknown, and consequently, the **truth** is also unknown.

They also argue that there is no such thing as a **sign** <note>original: "σημεῖον" (semeion). In Greek logic, a "sign" is an observed thing that reveals a hidden reality, like smoke signifying fire.</note>. For if a sign exists, they say, it is either **perceptible** <note>original: "αἰσθητόν" (aisthēton). Something known through the five senses.</note> or **intelligible** <note>original: "νοητόν" (noēton). Something known through the intellect or thought.</note>. It is not perceptible, because a perceptible thing is common to all, whereas a sign is specific to what it signifies. Furthermore, a perceptible thing is known by its own characteristics, while a sign is a **relative thing** <note>A relative thing (like "left" or "above") only exists in relation to something else.</note>.

Nor is the sign intelligible. For if it were something thought, it would have to be one of four things: 
1. An appearance of an appearance.
2. A hidden thing of a hidden thing. 
3. A hidden thing of an appearance. 
4. An appearance of a hidden thing.

But it is none of these; therefore, there is no sign. An **appearance** of an appearance cannot be a sign, because that which is already apparent does not need a sign to reveal it. A **hidden thing** cannot be a sign of another hidden thing, because that which is to be revealed must itself become apparent through something. A **hidden thing** cannot be a sign of an appearance, because that which provides the starting point for a discovery must be visible. Finally, an **appearance** is not a sign of a hidden thing, because the sign...

<summary>This page presents the Skeptical arguments against the possibility of having a "criterion of truth" (due to infinite regress) and the logical impossibility of "signs" that reveal hidden realities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Skeptical dismantling of philosophical certainty found in Diogenes Laertius's "Life of Pyrrho." The previous page concluded with the rejection of a "criterion" of truth; this page extends that doubt to signs, causality, motion, and the possibility of learning.</meta>

### PYRRHO. Book 3
->377<-

...being **relative** <note>original: "πρός τι" (pros ti). A category of things that exist only in relation to something else, such as 'left' being relative to 'right'.</note>, a **sign** ought to be perceived along with that of which it is a sign. But this is not the case. Therefore, none of the non-evident things could be understood; for it is said that non-evident things are understood through signs.

They also do away with **cause** <note>original: "αἴτιον" (aition). The Skeptics argue that we cannot prove one thing actually creates another, only that they appear together.</note>. For a cause is also among those things that are relative; it is relative to the **effect** it produces. But relative things are only conceived in the mind, they do not have real existence. Thus, the cause would also only be a mental concept. For if it is a cause, it must possess that which it is said to be the cause of; otherwise, it will not be a cause. Just as a **father**, if the person in relation to whom he is called "father" is not present, would not be a father, so it is with cause. But that in relation to which a cause is conceived (whether it be **generation**, **destruction**, or anything else) is not present <note>Because the cause must exist before the effect, they are never "present" at the exact same moment.</note>; therefore, cause does not exist.

Furthermore, if there is a cause, either a **body** <note>A physical object.</note> is the cause of a body, or an **incorporeal** <note>original: "ἀσώματον" (asomaton). Something without a physical body, like a soul or a mathematical point.</note> is the cause of an incorporeal. But it is none of these; therefore, there is no cause. A body could not be the cause of a body, since both have the same nature. And if one is called a cause insofar as it is a body, then the other, being a body, will also become a cause. And if both were causes, there would be nothing left to be the recipient of the action. Nor could an incorporeal be the cause of an incorporeal for the same reason. An incorporeal is not the cause of a body, because no incorporeal produces a body. Nor could a body be the cause of an incorporeal, because that which is produced must belong to the matter that receives the action; but since the incorporeal receives no action (being without a body), it cannot be produced by anything. Therefore, there is no cause.

From this it follows that the **principles of the universe** <note>original: "ἀρχάς" (archas). The fundamental starting points or elements of all things.</note> have no real substance. For there must be something that acts and does work [for there to be a principle].

Moreover, **motion** <note>original: "κίνησις" (kinesis).</note> does not exist. For whatever moves, moves either in the place where it is, or in the place where it is not. Now, it does not move in the place where it is <note>Because if it is in that place, it is stationary there.</note>; and it certainly does not move in the place where it is not <note>Because it is not there to do any moving.</note>. Therefore, there is no motion.

They also did away with **learning** <note>original: "μάθησιν" (mathesin).</note>. If anything is taught, they say, either **what is** is taught by virtue of its being, or **what is not** is taught by virtue of its not being. But "what is" is not taught by virtue of its being (for the nature of things that exist is apparent to everyone and is already known), nor is "what is not" taught by virtue of its not being (for nothing happens to that which does not exist). Thus, neither...

<summary>This page presents a series of Skeptical paradoxes designed to show that fundamental concepts like causality, physical motion, and the process of learning are logically contradictory and cannot be proven to exist in reality.</summary>
<keywords>Skepticism, Pyrrho, causality, motion, body and incorporeal, logic, paradox, Diogenes Laertius</keywords>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
->378<-

...[nor can anything] be taught. Nor indeed is there such a thing as **becoming** <note>original: "γένεσις" (genesis). The process of coming into being or starting to exist.</note>, as they say. For neither that which **exists** becomes (for it already exists), nor does that which **does not exist** become (for it has no foundation); and that which has no foundation and does not exist cannot even undergo the process of "becoming."

Furthermore, they say that nothing is **good** or **evil** by nature. For if anything were good or evil by nature, it ought to be good or evil for everyone, just as **snow** is cold to everyone. But there is nothing that is universally considered good or evil by all. Therefore, nothing is good or evil by nature. For either we must say that everything believed to be good by anyone is good, or not everything. We cannot say "everything," since the very same thing is believed to be good by one person—such as **pleasure** by **Epicurus**—and evil by another—as by **Antisthenes** <note>Antisthenes, the founder of the Cynic school, famously claimed he would "rather go mad than feel pleasure," while Epicurus held pleasure as the highest goal of life.</note>. It would follow, then, that the same thing is both good and evil.

If, on the other hand, we do not say that everything believed by someone is good, we will have to judge between these conflicting opinions. This, however, is not possible, due to the **equal weight of arguments** <note>original: "ἰσοσθένειαν τῶν λόγων" (isostheneian tōn logōn). A core Skeptical concept where for every argument, there is an equally convincing counter-argument, leading to a standstill of the mind.</note>. Therefore, that which is good by nature is **unknowable**.

One can also perceive the whole method of their collection of arguments from the treatises they have left behind. For **Pyrrho** himself left no writings, but his associates did—namely **Timon**, **Aenesidemus**, **Numenius**, **Nausiphanes**, and others. Against these men, the **Dogmatists** <note>original: "δογματικοί" (dogmatikoi). Philosophers who claim to have discovered the truth and hold definite beliefs, such as the Stoics or Epicureans.</note> argue, saying that the Skeptics themselves "grasp" certainties and hold dogmas; for in the very act of trying to refute others, they are "caught" making assertions. For in that very act, they are affirming and dogmatizing. For when they say that "nothing can be defined," and that "to every argument an equal argument is opposed," they are defining these very things and treating them as dogmas.

To this the Skeptics reply: "Regarding those things we experience as human beings, we agree. For we recognize that it is **day**, and that we are **alive**, and many other **phenomena** <note>original: "φαινομένων" (phainomenōn). Things as they appear to the senses, as opposed to how they truly are in their underlying nature.</note> of daily life. But regarding those things about which the Dogmatists make firm assertions through reason, claiming to have 'grasped' them, we **suspend judgment** <note>original: "ἐπέχομεν" (epechomen). The act of 'epoche,' or withholding assent when proof is lacking.</note> on the grounds that they are non-evident. We know only our own internal **impressions** <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē). The subjective experiences or 'feelings' produced by the external world.</note>. For we agree that we see, and we know that we are thinking this particular thought; but *how* we see, or *how* we think, we do not know. Similarly, we say that 'this thing appears **white**' merely as a report of our experience, not as a firm assertion..." <note>original: "διαβεβαι..." (diabebai). The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the word "asserting."</note>

<summary>This page outlines the Skeptical rejection of absolute moral truths and the process of "becoming," while defending the Skeptical stance as a report of appearances rather than a set of dogmatic beliefs.</summary>
<keywords>Pyrrho, Skepticism, Dogmatists, Epoche, isostheneia, Epicurus, Antisthenes, phenomena, ethics, becoming</keywords>

# PYRRHO. BOOK IX
->379<-

...suspicion as to whether it really exists. Regarding the phrase **"I define nothing"** <note>original: "Οὐδὲν ὁρίζω" (ouden horizō). This is a central Skeptical slogan used to avoid making dogmatic assertions about the nature of reality.</note> and similar expressions, we say they are not dogmatic. For they are not like saying "the universe is spherical"; that is a claim about something **unclear** <note>original: "ἄδηλον" (adēlon). A technical term for things that are not directly evident to the senses, such as the shape of the cosmos or the existence of atoms.</note>, whereas these phrases are simply confessions of one’s state of mind. Therefore, in saying that we define nothing, we do not even define this very statement as an absolute rule.

Again, the **Dogmatists** <note>Dogmatists (from 'dogma', meaning 'opinion' or 'tenet') were philosophers like the Stoics or Epicureans who claimed to have discovered the truth.</note> claim that the Skeptics abolish the very basis of life, since they reject everything that constitutes life. But the Skeptics say these critics are mistaken. For we do not abolish the act of **seeing**, but rather we admit to being ignorant of **how** we see. We accept the **appearance** <term>Phenomenon<note>From the Greek 'phainomenon', meaning 'that which appears.' The Skeptics argued we should live according to appearances—what we perceive—without claiming those perceptions represent the 'true' nature of things.</note></term>, but not as if the thing is actually and truly such as it appears. 

We feel that **fire** always burns; but as to whether it has a "burning nature" in itself, we **withhold judgment** <note>original: "ἐπέχομεν" (epechomen). The state of 'epochē' or suspension of judgment, which the Skeptics believed led to peace of mind.</note>. We see that someone moves and that someone dies; but how these things happen, we do not know. Therefore (they say), we only resist those **unclear** things that are hidden beneath the appearances. For even when we say a painting has "depth" <note>literally "projections" or "protuberances"</note>, we are describing the appearance; but if we were to say it has no depth, we would no longer be speaking of what appears, but of something else. 

This is why **Timon** <note>Timon of Phlius, a student of Pyrrho known for his satirical poems.</note> says in his *Python* that he has not strayed from common custom. And in his *Images*, he speaks thus:

> But the appearance prevails everywhere, wherever it may come.

And in his books *On the Senses*, he says: "I do not assert that a thing **is** sweet, but I confess that it **appears** so." **Aenesidemus** also says in the first book of his *Pyrrhonian Discourses* that Pyrrho defines nothing dogmatically because of the "contradiction in arguments," but rather follows appearances. He says the same in his work *On Wisdom* and *On Inquiry*. Furthermore, **Zeuxis** (the pupil of Aenesidemus) in his work *On Double Arguments*, **Antiochus of Laodicea**, and **Apellas** in his *Agrippa*, all put forward appearances alone.

According to the Skeptics, the **criterion** <note>The standard or "measuring stick" by which truth is judged.</note> is therefore the appearance, as Aenesidemus also says. **Epicurus** says the same. **Democritus**, however, said that appearances are nothing, and that they do not exist. Against this criterion of appearances, the Dogmatists argue that different **impressions** <note>original: "φαντασίαι" (phantasiai). The mental images produced by the senses.</note> strike us from the same objects—as when a **tower** appears round from a distance but square from nearby.

<summary>This page explains the Skeptical reliance on "appearances" (phenomena) as a guide for life while refusing to make dogmatic claims about the underlying nature of reality. It cites key figures like Timon and Aenesidemus to defend the school against the charge that they reject the evidence of the senses.</summary>

<keywords>Pyrrho, Skeptics, appearance, phenomenon, Aenesidemus, Timon, Epicurus, Democritus, criterion, Dogmatists, suspension of judgment</keywords>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS
->380<-

...the Skeptic, if he favors neither side, will remain inactive <note>original: "ἀπρακτήσει" (apraktēsei). This refers to the 'Inactivity Argument,' a common criticism that if one has no beliefs, one has no reason to act.</note>; but if he follows one side or the other, he will no longer grant **equal weight** <note>original: "τὸ ἰσοσθενὲς" (to isosthenes). The Skeptical principle that for every argument, there is an equally convincing counter-argument.</note> to the appearances. To these critics, the Skeptics reply that whenever different **appearances** <term>Phantasiai<note>From 'φαντασίαι,' referring to the way things "strike" the mind or senses before any judgment is made.</note></term> occur, each seems to exert its own pull. And because of this, they posit that things **appear** <note>original: "φαίνεται" (phainetai). The Skeptic avoids saying "it is," instead saying "it appears to be."</note> to be as they appear. The Skeptics say that the **end goal** of life is the **suspension of judgment** <term>Epoche<note>From 'ἐποχή' (epochē). By stopping the attempt to decide which appearances are 'true,' the Skeptic finds relief from the mental exhaustion of seeking certainty.</note></term>, which is followed by **unperturbedness** <term>Ataraxia<note>From 'ἀταραξία' (ataraxia), meaning a state of being 'untroubled' or 'serene.' The Skeptics claimed this peace follows suspension of judgment like a shadow follows a body.</note></term>, as stated by the followers of Timon and Aenesidemus. For we do not choose these things or flee those things among the matters that depend on our own judgment. But as for things that are not up to us, but happen by necessity—such as hunger, thirst, or pain—we are not able to avoid them, for it is not possible to remove these through reason. 

When the Dogmatists argue that a Skeptic would be able to live even if he did not avoid—if he were so ordered—slaughtering his own father <note>A classic "extreme case" used in ancient debates to show that a lack of firm belief would lead to immoral behavior.</note>, the Skeptics reply that they are able to live while abstaining from **philosophical inquiries**, but not from the **conduct of life** and the preservation of customs. Consequently, we do choose some things and avoid others according to habit, and we make use of the laws. Some say the end goal is **freedom from passion** <note>original: "ἀπάθειαν" (apatheian).</note>, while others say the Skeptics identify the end as **mildness of character**.

### TIMON

Timon was the son of Timarchus of Phlius. Apollonides of Nicaea, our contemporary, in the first book of his *Commentaries on the Lampoons* <note>original: "Σίλλους" (Silloi). These were satirical poems in which Timon mocked the dogmatic philosophers of his day.</note>, which he dedicated to Tiberius Caesar, says that Timon was a Phliasian by birth. Having been left alone as a youth, he first worked as a dancer in a chorus, but then, having developed a low opinion of that profession, he traveled abroad to Megara to study with **Stilpo** <note>Stilpo of Megara (c. 360–280 BCE) was a philosopher famous for his dialectical skill and influence on the Stoics.</note>. After spending time with him, he returned home and married. Then, he traveled with his wife to Elis to study with **Pyrrho**, and he remained there until he had children. He named the eldest of these Xanthus, whom he taught medicine and left as the successor to his way of life. This Xanthus became a man of great reputation, as Sotion also says in his eleventh book.

<summary>This page explains that Skeptics live according to appearances and custom rather than dogma, achieving peace of mind through the suspension of judgment. It also begins the biography of Timon of Phlius, noting his transition from a dancer to a student of Stilpo and Pyrrho.</summary>

...but finding a **scarcity of food**, he departed for the Hellespont and the Propontis. While teaching as a **sophist** <note>A professional teacher or intellectual who traveled to provide education for a fee.</note> in Chalcedon, he was held in even higher esteem. Having gained much wealth there, he moved to Athens and stayed there until his death, except for a brief trip to Thebes. He was also known to King **Antigonus** and **Ptolemy Philadelphus**, as he himself testifies in his iambic poems. 

Antigonus says he was also a **lover of drink** <note>original: "φιλοπότης" (philopotēs).</note> and took leisure from his philosophical studies. For he wrote poems, epics, tragedies, satyr plays, thirty comedies, sixty tragedies, and *Silloi* <term>Silloi<note>Lampoons or satirical poems. Timon is famous for using this genre to mock the "Dogmatists" (philosophers who claimed to know the absolute truth).</note></term> and obscene verses. There are also prose books of his totaling twenty thousand lines, which Antigonus of Carystus mentions, having himself written a biography of him. 

Of the *Silloi*, there are three books; in these, being a **Skeptic**, he mocks and lampoons all the **dogmatists** <note>Those who claim to possess certain knowledge or "dogmas."</note> in the form of a parody. The first book is a direct narrative; the second and third are in the form of a dialogue. He appears to be questioning **Xenophanes of Colophon** <note>An earlier philosopher (c. 570 – c. 475 BCE) who was also known for criticizing traditional religious views.</note> about everything, and Xenophanes answers him. In the second book he treats the older philosophers, and in the third, the later ones. For this reason, some have titled it "The Epilogue." The first book covers these matters, though the poetry is a monologue. It begins like this:

> Tell me now, all you meddlesome sophists!

He died at nearly ninety years old, as Antigonus and Sotion say in his eleventh book. I have also learned that he was **one-eyed**; indeed, he used to call himself a **Cyclops**. 

There was also another Timon, the famous "misanthrope" <note>Timon of Athens, the legendary hermit known for his hatred of mankind.</note>. But our philosopher was a great lover of gardens and a man of his own business, as Antigonus says. There is a story told by **Hieronymus the Peripatetic** <note>A member of the school founded by Aristotle, which met in the "Peripatos" or covered walkway of the Lyceum.</note> about him, that just as among the **Scythians** both those fleeing and those pursuing shoot arrows, so among the philosophers, some pursue...

### BOOK IX

...they hunt for students, while the students flee from them, just as they fled from **Timon**. He was sharp-witted and quick to mock <note>original: "διαμυκτηρίσαι" (diamuktērisai) – literally to "turn up the nose" at something, meaning to sneer or scoff.</note>, a lover of literature, and very capable of writing plots for poets and arranging dramas. He even shared his tragedies with **Alexander** and **Homer** <note>These are Alexander the Aetolian and Homer of Byzantium, two famous tragic poets of the time, not the legendary epic poet.</note>. Although he was often disturbed by the noise of maidservants and dogs, he did nothing about it, as he was eager to lead a quiet and tranquil life.

They say that **Aratus** <note>Aratus of Soli, the famous didactic poet known for the *Phaenomena*.</note> once asked him how he could obtain a reliable edition of **Homer’s** poetry. Timon replied: "By finding the ancient copies, and not those that have already been 'corrected' <note>original: "διωρθωμένοις" (diōrthōmenois) – Timon suggests that contemporary editors often ruined texts by trying to fix them.</note>." 

His own poems lay about in a mess, sometimes even half-eaten by mice. Consequently, when he was reading them to the orator **Zopyrus**, he would roll the scrolls up and simply go through whatever part came to hand. When he reached the middle of a scroll, he would only then find the passage he was looking for, having been unaware of where it was until that moment. Such was his **indifference** <note>original: "ἀδιάφορος" (adiaphoros) – a key Skeptic term for being unconcerned with external or trivial matters.</note>. He was so visible in public that he would not even allow his doors to be closed.

It is said that upon seeing **Arcesilaus** <note>Head of the Platonic Academy, who turned it toward Skepticism; Timon had a complex relationship with him.</note> passing through the **Cercopes** <note>A district in Athens named after mythical tricksters, often associated with shady characters or thieves.</note>, Timon said: "What are you doing here, where we free men spend our time?" 

He was also in the habit of constantly saying to those who accepted the evidence of the senses only when confirmed by the mind: "The **Francolin** and **Numenius** have come together" <note>original: "Συνῆλθεν Ἀτταγᾶς τε καὶ Νουμήνιος" – a proverbial expression used to mock two people of the same (often bad) character meeting together.</note>. 

He used to joke in this manner: to someone who marveled at everything, he said, "Why do you not marvel that we three have only **four eyes**?" For Timon himself was one-eyed, as was his student **Dioscurides**, while the man he was speaking to had both eyes healthy. 

Once, when asked by Arcesilaus why he had come back from **Thebes**, he replied: "So that I might laugh at you all with your mouths wide open <note>meaning: "gaping in gullible wonder."</note>." Nevertheless, despite attacking Arcesilaus in his *Silloi* <term>Silloi<note>Satirical poems or lampoons used to mock dogmatic philosophers.</note></term>, he praised him in the work titled *The Funeral Feast of Arcesilaus*.

According to **Menodotus**, Timon had no successor, and the Skeptical succession lapsed until **Ptolemy of Cyrene** restored it. However, **Hippobotus** and **Sotion** claim that his pupils included:
*   **Dioscurides** of Cyprus
*   **Nicolochus** of Rhodes
*   **Euphranor** of Seleucia
*   **Praylus** of the Troad

This Praylus became so steadfast in his character (as the historian **Phylarchus** records) that when he was unjustly...

...he chose to endure being punished as if for treason, without even deeming his fellow citizens worthy of an explanation <note>original: "λόγου" (logou) – here meaning a word of defense or a reasoned speech. Timon remained silent during a trial, showcasing his philosophical indifference.</note>. 

**Eubulus of Alexandria** was a student of **Euphranor**; his student was **Ptolemy**, and Ptolemy’s students were **Sarpedon** and **Heraclides**. **Heraclides'** student was **Aenesidemus of Knossos**, who composed the eight books of the *Pyrrhonian Discourses* <note>original: "Πυῤῥωνείων λόγων" (Pyrrhōneiōn logōn) – a foundational text for the revival of Skepticism, named after Pyrrho of Elis, the movement's founder.</note>.

**Menodotus's** student was **Herodotus of Tarsus**, son of Areus; and **Herodotus's** student was **Sextus the Empiricist** <note>Sextus Empiricus (c. 160–210 CE), the most important author of surviving Skeptic texts.</note>, who wrote the ten books on Skepticism <note>original: "σκεπτικῶν" (skeptikōn) – this likely refers to his major surviving works, such as the *Outlines of Pyrrhonism*.</note> and other excellent works. Finally, **Sextus's** student was **Saturninus of Cythenas**, who was also an empiricist.

## EPICURUS.

<image-desc>Decorative floriated initial 'E' with foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>EPICURUS, the son of Neocles and Chaerestrate, was an Athenian of the Gargettus deme <term>deme: a local district or subdivision of Athens, similar to a parish</term>, belonging to the family of the Philaidae, as Metrodorus says in his book *On Noble Birth*. Others, including Heraclides in his abridgment of Sotion <note>original: "ἐν τῇ Σωτίωνος ἐπιτομῇ" (en tē Sōtiōnos epitomē) – Sotion was a famous biographer whose work served as a primary source for Diogenes Laertius</note>, say that he was raised in Samos after the Athenians had sent colonists <term>colonists: "klērouchoi," Athenian citizens who were granted land in foreign territories</term> there. At the age of eighteen, he came to Athens, at a time when Xenocrates was teaching at the Academy and Aristotle was staying in Chalcis. After the death of Alexander the Great of Macedon, and when the Athenians were expelled [from Samos] by Perdiccas <note>Perdiccas (c. 355–321 BCE) was a general of Alexander the Great who became regent of the empire after Alexander's death.</note>, Epicurus went to Colophon to join his father. After staying there for some time and gathering disciples, he returned to Athens during the archonship of Anaxicrates <note>The "archon" was the chief magistrate of Athens; his name was used to date the year, in this case 307/306 BCE.</note>. For a time, he practiced philosophy in association with other thinkers, but later he established his own school <term>school: "hairesis," literally a "choice" or a "sect," referring to the Epicurean movement</term> which was named after him. He says himself that he took up philosophy when he was fourteen years old. However, Apollodorus the Epicurean, in the first book of his *Life of Epicurus*, says that he turned to philosophy because he held the sophists <term>sophists: professional teachers of rhetoric and debate</term> and schoolteachers in contempt, as they were unable to explain to him...

Hermippus <note>Hermippus of Smyrna (3rd century BCE) was a biographer known for his lives of famous philosophers and poets.</note> says that he became a schoolmaster <note>original: "γραμματοδιδάσκαλον" (grammatodidaskalon) — This was often meant as an insult, implying a low social status or a lack of advanced philosophical training.</note>; however, after coming across the books of Democritus, he rushed headlong into philosophy. His three brothers also joined him in his philosophical pursuits at his encouragement: Neocles, Chaeredemus, and Aristobulus, as Philodemus the Epicurean says in the tenth book of his *Arrangement of Philosophers*. He even had a slave named Mys, as Myronianus says in his *Historical Chapters*.

Diotimus the Stoic, being hostile toward him, slandered him most bitterly, producing fifty lewd letters and attributing them to Epicurus; he also compiled letters usually attributed to Chrysippus <note>Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BCE) was one of the most influential Stoic philosophers; the Stoics were the primary intellectual rivals of the Epicureans.</note> as if they were written by Epicurus. Furthermore, the followers of Posidonius the Stoic, as well as Nicolaus, and Sotion in the twelve books titled *Refutations of Diocles*, <margin>and those about his mot-</margin> and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, also attack him. They even say that one of his brothers acted as a pimp and that Epicurus lived with the courtesan <term>courtesan: "hetaira," a high-status companion and entertainer in ancient Greece</term> Leontion. <insert>And the</insert> ideas of Democritus regarding atoms and those of Aristippus regarding pleasure, they say he claimed as his own. They further claim he was not a genuine citizen, as Timocrates says, along with Herodotus in his book *On the Adolescence of Epicurus*.

They also accuse him of shamefully flattering Mithres, the steward of King Lysimachus, calling him "Healer" and "Lord" <note>original: "Παιᾶνα καὶ Ἄνακτα" (Paiana kai Anakta) — titles usually reserved for the god Apollo; here, it implies a god-like flattery of a political official.</note> in his letters. Furthermore, they say he praised and flattered Idomeneus, Herodotus, and Timocrates—men who had exposed his secrets—for that very reason. # EPICURUS, Book 10
387

And in his letters concerning Nausiphanes, he says these things: that [Epicurus] was driven to such a state of distraction that he would not stop reviling him, even while calling him his teacher. He used to call him a "lung," <note>original: "πλεύμονά" (pleumona) — likely an insult implying someone is soft, brainless, or perhaps "all wind."</note> illiterate, a cheat, and a profligate. He called the followers of Plato "flatterers of Dionysius," <note>Referring to Plato's controversial relationship with the tyrants of Syracuse.</note> and Plato himself "golden." <note>This was likely a sarcastic jab at Plato's high-flown style or his "Golden Age" theories.</note> Aristotle he called a spendthrift who, after squandering his inheritance, joined the army and sold drugs. <note>original: "φαρμακοπωλεῖν" (pharmakopōlein) — a disparaging claim that Aristotle was a traveling medicine-seller before becoming a philosopher.</note> He called Protagoras a "basket-carrier" and a mere scribe for Democritus who taught children their letters in villages. He called Heraclitus "the muddler," <note>original: "κυκητήν" (kykētēn) — a pun on the "stirred drink" (kykeon) and Heraclitus's reputation for obscure, "muddled" philosophy.</note> and Democritus he renamed "Lerocritus" <note>original: "Ληρόκριτον" — a pun meaning "Judge of Nonsense."</note>; Antidorus he called "Sainidorus" <note>original: "Σαινίδωρον" — a pun meaning "Fawning-gift."</note>; the people of Cyzicus he called "enemies of Greece"; and the dialecticians he called "consumed by envy." Pyrrho he described as ignorant and uneducated.

But these people are raving mad. Sufficient witnesses to the man's unsurpassed kindness <note>original: "ἀγνωμοσύνης" (agnōmosynēs) — Though the manuscript reads "ignorance" or "lack of feeling," most scholars agree this is a scribe's error for "εὐγνωμοσύνης" (kindness), as the following passage is a defense of his virtues.</note> toward everyone are his fatherland, which honored him with bronze statues; his friends, who were so many in number that they could not be measured even by entire cities; and all his disciples, who were held fast by the "Sirens" of his teachings. <note>A metaphor comparing his doctrines to the irresistible songs of the Sirens in Greek mythology.</note> The only exception was Metrodorus of Stratonicea, who went over to Carneades, perhaps because he was weighed down by Epicurus's unsurpassed goodness. 

There is also the evidence of the succession of his school which, while almost every other school has failed, continues forever, sending forth an unbroken line of leaders from among its members. We must also mention his gratitude toward his parents, his generosity toward his brothers, and his gentleness toward his servants—as is clear from the provisions of his will. Indeed, his servants even studied philosophy alongside him, the most famous of whom was the aforementioned Mys. <note>Mys was a slave of Epicurus who became a respected philosopher in his own right, illustrating the school's unusually inclusive nature.</note>

In general, his benevolence toward everyone was remarkable. As for his piety toward the gods and his love for his fatherland, his disposition was beyond words. Due to his extreme moderation, he did not even enter politics. And though very difficult times then held Greece, he lived out his life there, only crossing over two or three times to the regions of Ionia to visit his friends, who...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
588

From everywhere, people came to him and lived with him in the Garden, as Apollodorus also states; he adds that Epicurus purchased the Garden for eighty minae. <note>A mina was a unit of currency; eighty minae was a substantial sum, roughly equivalent to 8,000 days' wages for a laborer.</note> Diocles, in the third book of his *Survey*, says that they lived in an exceptionally simple and frugal manner. They were satisfied, at any rate, with a half-pint <note>original: "κοτύλῃ" (kotyle) — about a cup or 0.24 liters.</note> of thin wine, but for the most part, their drink was water.

He also notes that Epicurus did not think it right to require his followers to put their property into a common fund, as Pythagoras did—who famously said that "the things of friends are common." <note>referring to the Pythagorean practice of communal ownership.</note> Epicurus felt that such a practice implied a lack of trust; and if people were distrustful, they could not truly be friends. Epicurus himself says in his letters that he is satisfied with nothing more than water and simple bread. "Send me," he says, "some potted cheese, <note>original: "τυροῦ κυθριδίου" (tyrou kythridiou) — likely cheese preserved in a small earthen jar.</note> so that whenever I wish to have a feast, I may be able to do so." Such was the character of the man who dogmatized that pleasure is the goal of life. Athenaeus praises him in an epigram as follows:

> O men, why do you labor for worse things, and for the sake of 
> Insatiable gain start quarrels and wars?
> The wealth of nature has a narrow limit, 
> But empty opinions follow a path without end.
> The wise son of Neocles <note>Neocles was the father of Epicurus.</note> heard this either from the Muses,
> Or from the sacred tripods of the Pythian priestess.

We shall understand this even better as we proceed, both from his doctrines and from his own words. Diocles says that he especially admired the ancient Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who first brought philosophy to Athens.</note> (even if he disagreed with him on certain points) and Archelaus, the teacher of Socrates. He used to train his disciples, Diocles says, to commit his own writings to memory.

Apollodorus, in his *Chronicles*, says that Epicurus was a pupil of Nausiphanes and Praxiphanes; however, Epicurus himself denies this in his letter to Eurydicus, claiming instead to be self-taught. <note>original: "αὐτοδίδακτον" (autodidaktos) — Epicurus took great pride in claiming he was not beholden to previous schools of thought.</note> Furthermore, both he and Hermarchus maintain that a philosopher named Leucippus <note>The traditional founder of Atomism and teacher of Democritus.</note> never even existed—though some, including Apollodorus the Epicurean, say that Leucippus was indeed the teacher of Democritus. Demetrius of Magnesia says that Epicurus also attended the lectures of Xenocrates. <note>Xenocrates was the head of Plato's Academy at the time.</note> In his writing, he uses the plain and literal terms for things, which, because it is so straightforward...

### EPICURUS. Book 10.
389

...[his diction], <note>The text begins mid-sentence, referring to Epicurus's use of language.</note> which Aristophanes the grammarian <note>A famous scholar from Alexandria known for his work on Greek literature.</note> criticizes. He was so devoted to clarity, however, that in his work *On Rhetoric* he demands nothing but clarity. In his letters, instead of the standard "Greetings," <note>original: "Χαίρειν" (Chairein)</note> he used "Act well," <note>original: "Εὖ πράττειν" (Eu prattein)</note> and "To live earnestly is best."

Some say that he wrote the *Canon* <note>The *Canon* was Epicurus's foundational work on logic and the criteria of truth.</note> in his biography of Epicurus by drawing from the *Tripod* of Nausiphanes, whom he is said to have studied under. It is also said he studied under Pamphilus the Platonist in Samos. He began to study philosophy at the age of twelve and took charge of his own school at the age of thirty-two.

He was born (as Apollodorus says in his *Chronicles*) in the third year of the 109th Olympiad, <note>roughly 341 BCE</note> during the archonship of Sosigenes, <note>Archons were the chief magistrates of Athens, used to mark the calendar year.</note> on the seventh day of the month of Gamelion, seven years after the death of Plato. When he was thirty-two years old, he first established a school in Mitylene and Lampsacus, which he led for five years. After that, he moved to Athens. He died in the second year of the 127th Olympiad <note>roughly 270 BCE</note> during the archonship of Pytharatus, having lived seventy-two years. Hermarchus of Mitylene, the son of Agemarchus, succeeded him as the head of the school.

He died of a blockage of the urine caused by stones <note>This refers to kidney or bladder stones, a condition known as strangury.</note> (as Hermarchus also states in his letters), having been ill for fourteen days. Hermippus relates that at that time, Epicurus entered a bronze tub filled with warm water and asked for a cup of neat wine, <note>original: "ἄκρατον" (akraton) — wine undiluted by water, which was unusual for Greeks except in medicinal or ritual contexts.</note> which he drank. After exhorting his friends to remember his doctrines, he passed away. We have written an epigram for him as follows:

> "Farewell, and remember the doctrines." This was the 
> final word Epicurus spoke to his friends as he was dying. 
> For he entered a warm bath and drank neat wine, 
> then drew in the cold of death. <note>original: "ἀΐδην" (Haiden) — literally "Hades," used here as a metaphor for the coldness of the grave.</note>

Such was the life of the man, and such was his end. He made his will as follows: "In accordance with these terms, I give all my possessions to Amynomachus...

...because of his attachment to me and to philosophy since his youth, they shall take care of the children of Metrodorus. <note>Epicurus is here concluding the legal instructions found in his will, ensuring that his closest friend’s children are raised within his philosophical community.</note> And thus he made his will.

He had many disciples, and among them were very famous men: Metrodorus the Athenian, as well as Timocrates and Sandes of Lampsacus. The latter, from the moment he first knew the man <note>Referring to Epicurus.</note>, never left his side, except for a period of six months when he returned to his own home, after which he came back. He was a good man in every respect, as Epicurus also writes in his earlier works; Timocrates also testifies to this in his third book.

Being a man of such character, Metrodorus gave his sister, Batis, in marriage to Idomeneus, and he took Leontion, the Attic courtesan <note>original: "ἑταίραν" (hetairan) — high-status female companions in Athens who were often more educated than legal wives. They say that Metrodorus died seven years before Epicurus himself, in his fifty-third year. Indeed, Epicurus himself, in the aforementioned will—clearly because Metrodorus had died before him—gives instructions regarding the care of his children. He also had as a follower the previously mentioned Timocrates, who was Metrodorus’s own brother.

The books of Metrodorus are as follows:
*Against the Physicians*, three books; *On Sensations*, addressed to Timocrates; *On Greatness of Soul*; *On Epicurus’s Illness*; *Against the Dialecticians*; *Against the Sophists*, nine books; *On the Path to Wisdom*; *On Change*; *On Wealth*, addressed to Democritus; and *On Noble Birth*.

There was also Polyaenus of Lampsacus, son of Athenodorus, a fair and friendly man, as those in the circle of Philodemus <note>A later Epicurean philosopher whose library was famously discovered at Herculaneum.</note> say. 

And his successor was Hermarchus, son of Agemarchus, a man of Mitylene. He was the son of a poor father and initially applied himself to the study of rhetoric. The following excellent books by him are circulated: *Letters concerning Empedocles*, twenty-two books; *On the Disciples*; *Against Plato*; and *Against Aristotle*. He died of paralysis <note>likely a stroke or palsy</note>, having proved himself a man of great ability.

There was also Leonteus of Lampsacus, and likewise his wife Themista, to whom Epicurus also wrote. Furthermore...
