...and Colotes, and Idomeneus, who were also from Lampsacus. These were illustrious men, as was Polystratus, who succeeded Hermarchus <note>Hermarchus was the immediate successor to Epicurus as head of the school.</note>; he was succeeded by Dionysius, and Dionysius by Basilides. Apollodorus, known as the "Tyrant of the Garden," <note>original: "Κηποτύραννος" (Kepotyrannos). This nickname likely refers to his long or strict leadership of the Epicurean school, which met in a garden.</note> was also famous, having written over four hundred books. There were also two men named Ptolemy from Alexandria, distinguished as "the Black" and "the White"; Zeno of Sidon, a pupil of Apollodorus and a very prolific writer; Demetrius, surnamed the Laconian; Diogenes of Tarsus, who composed the *Selected Lectures*; and Orion, along with others whom the "genuine" Epicureans call "sophists" <note>Here used to imply they were perhaps more interested in rhetoric or public display than the core lived philosophy.</note>. There were also three other men named Epicurus: the son of Leonteus, another from Magnesia, and a fourth who was a fencing master.

Epicurus himself was a most prolific writer, surpassing everyone in the sheer number of his books. His scrolls <note>original: "κύλινδροι" (kylindroi) — the standard papyrus roll format for ancient books.</note> number around three hundred. In all these works, there is not a single citation from an outside authority; rather, they contain the words of Epicurus himself. Chrysippus <note>The famous Stoic philosopher, often seen as the intellectual rival of the Epicureans.</note> tried to rival him in productivity, as Carneades says, calling him a "parasite of Epicurus’s books." For whatever Epicurus wrote, Chrysippus felt a competitive need to write just as much. Because of this, he often wrote the same things multiple times, jotting down whatever came to mind and leaving it uncorrected in his haste. He also used so many citations that his books were filled with the words of others, a practice also found in the works of Zeno <note>Likely Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note> and Aristotle.

The writings of Epicurus are numerous and significant; the best among them are the following:

*   *On Nature*, in thirty-seven books <note>original: "Περὶ φύσεως" (Peri physeos). This was Epicurus's magnum opus.</note>

*   *Principal Doctrines* <note>original: "Κύριαι δόξαι" (Kyriai doxai) — a collection of forty short aphorisms summarizing Epicurean ethics.</note>
*   *On Sects*
*   *On Plants*
*   *On the End* <note>Referring to the "telos" or the ultimate goal of life (pleasure/absence of pain).</note>
*   *On the Criterion, or The Canon* <note>original: "Περὶ κριτηρίου, ἢ Κανὼν" (Peri kriterion, e Kanon) — his work on the theory of knowledge and how we judge truth.</note>

*   *On Lives*, in four books
*   *On Just Action*
*   *Neocles to Themista*
*   *Symposium*
*   *Eurylochus*
*   *To Metrodorus*
*   *On Seeing*
*   *On the Angle in the Atom*

*Opinions on the Passions, addressed to Timocrates*; *Prognostic*; *Exhortation*; *On Images*; *On Imagination*; *Aristobulus*; *On Music*; *On Justice and other Virtues*; *On Gifts and Gratitude*; *Polymedes*; *Timocrates* (3 books); *Metrodorus* (5 books); *Antidorus* (2 books); *Opinions on Sickness, addressed to Mithres*; *Callistolas*; *On Kingship*; *Anaximenes*; and the *Letters*.

I will attempt to set out one of these <note>Meaning one of the summaries or "short-hand" versions of his thought.</note>, if it seems right, presenting his three letters in which he summarized his entire philosophy. I will also include his *Principal Doctrines* <note>original: "κυρίας δόξας" (Kyriai Doxai) — a famous collection of 40 short aphorisms summarizing Epicurean ethics.</note>, and whatever else appeared worth selecting from his utterances, so that you may understand the man from every side and be able to judge him—if indeed I know how to judge.

Now, he wrote the first letter to Herodotus, concerning Physics; the second to Pythocles, which is about celestial phenomena <note>original: "μεταρσίων" (metarsion) — referring to things in the sky or "above," such as weather and stars.</note>; and the third to Menoeceus, which contains the material concerning ways of life <note>This is the famous ethical letter on the pursuit of happiness.</note>. We must begin then with the first letter, after saying a few words beforehand about the division of his philosophy.

It is divided into three parts: the **Canonical**, the **Physical**, and the **Ethical**.

*   The **Canonical** <note>original: "κανονικόν" (kanonikon) — from "kanon" meaning a measuring rod or ruler. This is the Epicurean version of logic or epistemology.</note> provides the methods for approaching the system and is contained in a single work entitled *The Canon*.
*   The **Physical** contains the entire theory of nature; it is found in the thirty-seven books *On Nature* and in the letters organized by elementary topics.
*   The **Ethical** concerns things to be chosen and things to be avoided. This is found in the books *On Ways of Life*, in his letters, and in his work *On the Goal*.

However, they <note>Referring to the Epicurean school at large.</note> usually combine the Canonical with the Physical. They call the former "On the Criterion and the First Principle" or "Fundamental Principles." The Physical they call "On Generation and Destruction" and "On Nature." The Ethical they call "On Things Chosen and Avoided," and "On Ways of Life and the Goal."

They reject Dialectic <note>The formal logic and verbal disputation favored by the Stoics and Platonists.</note> as redundant. For they hold that it is sufficient for natural philosophers to proceed according to the actual sounds of things <note>original: "φθόγγους" (phthongous) — this refers to Epicurus’s theory that words should be used in their primary, clear meanings based on immediate sensory experience.</note>. <meta>This page continues the discussion of Epicurean philosophy, moving from the general divisions of his system into the specific details of the "Canonical" (the rules of logic and knowledge). It focuses on the primary standards of truth that Epicurus established to distinguish fact from fiction.</meta>

# EPICURUS. Book X.

Epicurus states that the **criteria of truth** <note>original: "κριτήρια τῆς ἀληθείας" — the standards or "measuring sticks" used to judge what is real.</note> are the **sensations**, **preconceptions**, and the **feelings**. The later Epicureans also add the **mental apprehensions of images**. He says this both in his *Abridgment to Herodotus* and in his *Principal Doctrines*.

For, he says, every sensation is **irrational** <note>original: "ἄλογός" (alogos). This means sensations are raw data; they do not reason, argue, or remember. They simply report what is there without adding any interpretation.</note> and is incapable of memory. It is not moved by itself, nor can it add or subtract anything when moved by something else. There is nothing that can refute the sensations. A sensation of one type cannot refute another of the same type, because they have equal weight; nor can one type refute another of a different type, because they do not judge the same objects <note>For example, the sense of hearing cannot tell the eyes they are wrong about a color.</note>.

Nor can reason refute them, for all reason depends upon the sensations. Nor can one sensation refute another, for we pay attention to all of them alike. Furthermore, the fact that our external perceptions exist confirms the truth of the senses. Our seeing and hearing are just as much real facts as our feeling pain.

Therefore, we must use the **phenomena** <note>original: "φαινομένων" — things as they appear to us.</note> as signs to make inferences about things that are hidden from view. Indeed, all of our mental concepts have come from sensations through direct experience, analogy, resemblance, or by combining them, with reasoning also contributing its part.

The visions of the mad and the images seen in dreams are also **true**, because they produce a movement in the mind; and that which does not exist cannot produce movement.

By **preconception** <note>original: "πρόληψιν" (prolepsis). These are basic mental "blueprints" or universal concepts formed after seeing many examples of something.</note>, they mean a kind of apprehension, or right opinion, or a general concept stored in the mind—that is, a memory of what has frequently appeared to us from the outside. For example, the concept "This sort of thing is a man." As soon as the word "man" is spoken, the form of a man is immediately grasped by the mind through preconception, with the senses having led the way.

Thus, the primary meaning underlying every word is self-evident. We would not even look for what we are seeking if we did not already have a prior knowledge of it. For example, when we ask, "Is that thing standing far off a horse or an ox?" we must have previously known the form of a horse and an ox through preconception. We could not name anything at all if we had not first learned its form through a preconception. Therefore, preconceptions are self-evident. 

Moreover, matters of opinion depend on some prior self-evident fact...

<note>original vocabulary: Epicurus, criteria, sensations, preconceptions, feelings/passions, mental apprehensions, Herodotus, irrational, judgment, perceptions, concepts, apprehension</note>

<summary>This page outlines the Epicurean "Canon," or theory of knowledge, which asserts that sensations, basic mental concepts (preconceptions), and feelings are the only reliable foundations for truth. It argues that because sensations are "irrational" and direct, they provide the raw data from which all human reason and language must be derived.</summary>
<keywords>Epicurus, Epistemology, Criteria of Truth, Sensations, Preconceptions, Logic, Philosophy of Mind, Diogenes Laertius</keywords>

<page-num>396</page-num>
<header>DIOGENES LAERTIUS</header>

...depends on **clear evidence** <note>original: "ἐναργοῦς" (enargous) — referring to the self-evident clarity of a direct sensation.</note>. It is to this that we refer when we say, for example: "How do we know if this thing is a man?" They also use the terms **opinion** and **supposition**. These, they say, can be both true and false. If an opinion is confirmed by evidence, or not contradicted by it, it is true; however, if it is not confirmed or is contradicted, it turns out to be false. 

For this reason, the concept of **waiting** <term>original: "προσμονή" (prosmone) — the act of waiting for more information or a closer look before making a judgment.</term> was introduced. An example of this is waiting to get close to a tower to learn how it appears from nearby <note>A famous Epicurean example: a square tower looks round from a distance, so one must "wait" for a closer view to form a true opinion.</note>. They say there are two **feelings** <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe) — often translated as "affections" or "passions."</note>: **pleasure** and **pain**. These are present in every living creature. Pleasure is **congenial** <note>original: "οἰκεῖον" (oikeion) — natural or "at home" with our nature.</note>, while pain is **alien**. By these two feelings, our choices and avoidances are decided. 

Of philosophical inquiries, some concern actual things, while others concern mere words. This concludes our elementary account of the divisions of philosophy and the **criterion** <note>The standard or "measuring stick" of truth.</note>. We must now proceed to the letter.

## Epicurus to Herodotus, greetings.

For those, O Herodotus, who are unable to work out in detail every point of our writings on **nature** <note>original: "φύσεως" (physeos).</note>, or to study the larger books we have composed, I have prepared a **summary** <term>original: "ἐπιτομὴν" (epitomen) — a condensed version of a larger work.</term> of the entire system. This is so they may sufficiently retain a memory of the most general doctrines and be able to help themselves on every occasion regarding the most important matters, to the extent that they grasp the study of nature.

Even those who have made significant progress in the overview of the whole must remember the outline of the entire system as it has been laid down in its elements. For we frequently need a comprehensive grasp of the whole, but we do not need the detailed view as often. We must, therefore, proceed toward those details while constantly keeping in memory the primary points from which a general grasp of things is possible. Indeed, every specific detail will be discovered once the most general outlines are embraced and remembered. Even for the person who has reached perfection, the most important part of all accurate knowledge is the ability to make rapid use of such mental grasps and to refer them back to simple elements...

<summary>This page concludes the explanation of Epicurean epistemology (how we verify truth through 'waiting' for evidence) and begins the Letter to Herodotus, a summary of Epicurean physics designed for both beginners and advanced students.</summary>

<header>EPICURUS. BOOK 10</header>

...syllables and words gathered together. For it is not possible for the dense mass of the continuous cycle of the whole to be grasped if one cannot include within oneself, through brief phrases, everything that could be accurately understood in detail. Therefore, since such a method is useful to all who are dedicated to **natural science** <term>original: "φυσιολογία" (physiologia) — the study of the laws of nature, encompassing what we now call physics and biology.</term>, I recommend continuous activity in natural science—as this brings peace to one's life—and I have composed such an **epitome** <note>A condensed summary or handbook of a larger work.</note> and an elementary outline of the whole system of doctrines. 

First of all, then, Herodotus, we must grasp the underlying meanings behind our words, so that we may have a standard to which we can refer our opinions, inquiries, or problems for judgment. This prevents everything from remaining unjudged as we demonstrate to infinity, and ensures we do not have empty words. For it is necessary that the **primary concept** associated with each word be seen clearly and need no further proof, if we are to have a point of reference for our inquiries, problems, and opinions. 

Furthermore, we must keep everything in accordance with our **senses** <note>original: "αἰσθήσεις" (aistheseis)</note> and simply with the present apprehensions, whether of the mind or of any of the **criteria** <note>The standards or "measuring sticks" used to determine truth.</note>. Likewise, we must attend to the existing **feelings** <note>original: "πάθη" (pathe) — specifically the basic feelings of pleasure and pain that guide behavior.</note>, so that we may have signs by which to judge both what is waiting to be confirmed and what is **unapparent** <note>original: "ἄδηλον" (adelon) — referring to things that cannot be perceived directly by the senses, such as atoms.</note>.

Having distinguished these things, we must now look at what is unapparent. First, **nothing comes into being from what is not** <note>A fundamental law of ancient physics: matter cannot be created out of nothing.</note>. For if that were the case, everything would be created out of everything, having no need of seeds. And if that which disappears were destroyed into what is not, all things would have perished by now, since the things into which they were dissolved would not exist. 

Moreover, the universe always was such as it is now, and always will be such. For there is nothing into which it changes. For besides the universe, there is nothing that could enter into it and cause a change. Indeed, Epicurus says this both at the beginning of the *Large Epitome* and in the first book *On Nature*: the **universe consists of bodies** <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν ἐστι σῶμα" (to pan esti soma) — meaning the totality of existence is physical matter.</note>. That bodies exist, sensation itself bears witness to all; and it is by sensation that we must necessarily use reasoning to infer what is unapparent, as I said before...

<page-num>398</page-num>
<header>DIOG. LAERT.</header>

...if that which we call the **void** <term>original: "κενὸν" (kenon) — the empty space or "intangible nature" required for movement.</term>, space, and intangible nature did not exist, bodies would have no place to be, nor would they have anything through which to move, as they are clearly seen to be moving. Beyond these two—bodies and void—nothing can be conceived, neither by direct grasping of the mind nor by analogy with things already grasped, if we take these as whole and independent natures and not merely as **attributes** <note>original: "συμπτώματα" (symptomata)</note> or **accidents** <note>original: "συμβεβηκότα" (symbebekota)</note> of things. Furthermore, these points are discussed here and in the first book of *On Nature*, as well as in the fourteenth and fifteenth books and in the *Large Epitome*. 

Of bodies, some are **compounds** <term>original: "συγκρίσεις" (synkriseis) — clusters or aggregates of atoms that form the objects we see.</term>, while others are the elements from which these compounds are made. These latter elements are **atoms** <term>original: "ἄτομα" (atoma) — literally "indivisible" particles that cannot be cut or broken down further.</term> and are unchangeable; this must be so, unless everything is destined to be destroyed into non-existence. Instead, these elements remain strong and endure through the dissolution of compounds, being solid in nature, and possessing no way or means by which they could be dissolved. Therefore, it is necessary that the first principles be of an indivisible bodily nature.

Furthermore, the **universe** <note>original: "τὸ πᾶν" (to pan) — the totality of all that exists.</note> is infinite. For that which is finite has an edge, and an edge is perceived in relation to something else beside it. Since the universe has no edge, it has no limit; and because it has no limit, it must be infinite and not finite. Moreover, the universe is infinite both in the number of bodies it contains and in the magnitude of the void. 

For if the void were infinite but the bodies were limited in number, the bodies would not remain anywhere; instead, they would be carried along, scattered through the infinite void, because they would lack other bodies to support them and keep them in place by **collisions** <note>original: "ἀνακοπάς" (anakopas) — the rebounding of atoms as they strike one another.</note>. Conversely, if the void were limited, it would not have enough space to hold the infinite number of bodies. 

In addition to this, the atoms—those solid bodies from which compounds are formed and into which they are dissolved—possess an **inconceivable** <note>original: "ἀπερίληπτα" (aperilepta)</note> number of variations in their shapes. For it is not possible that such a vast variety of things could arise from the same limited set of shapes. While the number of atoms of each particular shape is strictly infinite, the number of different shapes themselves is not strictly infinite, but simply "inconceivably many." For Epicurus says elsewhere that we do not go on to infinity...

<summary>In this passage, Epicurus defines the two fundamental components of the universe: matter (atoms) and empty space (void). He argues that the universe must be infinite in extent and that atoms must be indivisible and varied in shape to account for the diversity of the physical world.</summary>

# EPICURUS. BOOK 10

### The Motion and Nature of Atoms

...to undergo division. And he says this because qualities change, whereas the atoms do not, unless one is prepared to allow the atoms themselves to be reduced to nothingness. Atoms move continuously throughout eternity. He says further on that they also move at **equal speed** through the void, for the void offers the same lack of resistance to the lightest and the heaviest alike. 

Some of these atoms bounce far away from one another; others maintain a **vibration** <note>original: "παλμὸν" (palmon) — a rapid, quivering motion</note> whenever they happen to be entangled <term>original: "περιπλοκὴν" (periploken) — the interlocking of atoms due to their irregular shapes</term> by their own branching shapes or are enclosed by other atoms that are prone to entangling. This occurs because the nature of the void, which separates each individual atom, brings this about by its inability to offer any resistance or "support." Meanwhile, the **solidity** which belongs to the atoms causes them to rebound <note>original: "ἀποπαλμὸν" (apopalmon)</note> upon collision, to whatever extent their entanglement allows them to recover from the impact. There is no beginning to these movements, for the atoms and the void have always been the causes.

### Qualities and Magnitude

He says further on that atoms possess no quality of the things we perceive except **shape, size, and weight**. Color, however, changes according to the arrangement and position of the atoms, as he explains in his work *The Twelve Basic Principles* <note>original: "δώδεκα στοιχειώσει" (Twelve Elements)</note>. Furthermore, not every size exists among atoms; at any rate, an individual atom has never been seen by the senses. This statement, when all these points are remembered, provides a sufficient outline for understanding the nature of existing things.

### The Infinity of Worlds

Furthermore, there are **infinite worlds** <term>original: "κόσμοι" (kosmoi) — separate universes or systems</term>, whether they are like our own or unlike it. For the atoms are infinite in number (as was just demonstrated) and are carried even to the furthest distances. Those atoms from which a world might be created, or by which one might be fashioned, have not been exhausted by the creation of a single world, nor by a finite number of them—neither those worlds that are like ours, nor those that are different. Thus, there is nothing to hinder the infinity of such worlds.

### The Theory of Images

Moreover, there exist "images" or **outlines** <note>original: "τύποι" (typoi) — often called 'idols' or 'films' in Epicurean physics</note> that are similar in shape to solid bodies <term>original: "στερεμνίοις" (steremniois)</term>, but far surpass visible things in their extreme thinness. For it is not impossible for such emanations to arise in the surrounding air, nor for there to be suitable conditions for the production of these hollow surfaces...

<summary>This page outlines the mechanics of Epicurean physics, explaining that atoms move at equal speeds in a vacuum and form solids through entanglement. It also introduces the radical concepts of an infinite number of worlds and the "images" (eidola) that emanate from objects to produce vision.</summary>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

### Book 10: The Philosophy of Epicurus

...and of such extreme fineness that they can be produced, nor do the **effluences** <note>original: "ἀπόῤῥοιαί" (aphorrhoiai) — streams of atoms flowing off the surface of objects</note> maintain the same relative position and foundation that they held when they were part of the solid bodies. These figures we call **images** <term>original: "εἴδωλα" (eidola) — thin films or "skins" of atoms that fly off objects and enter our eyes, allowing us to see</term>. 

Furthermore, motion through the void, when it encounters no resistance from colliding objects, completes every conceivable distance in an inconceivable amount of time. For the presence or absence of resistance takes on the appearance of slowness or speed. However, it is not true that a moving body reaches several places at once during a period of time discernible by reason. That is unthinkable. If a body arrives at a certain point within a perceptible timeframe from anywhere in the infinite, it will be departing from whatever place we first grasped its motion. For its motion will be like that of a body meeting resistance, even if we assume that up to that point its speed of travel was not hindered.

It is useful to hold onto this basic principle: that these swift images possess an **unsurpassable fineness**. Because of this, nothing in our observations contradicts the fact that they also possess unsurpassable speeds. They find every passage through the void to be proportional to their size, so that they meet either no resistance or very little resistance, whereas a great or infinite number of things would immediately encounter some resistance. 

In addition to this, the creation of these images happens as fast as a thought. For there is a continuous flow from the surface of bodies—though this is not detectable by our senses because of the constant replenishment of atoms—which preserves the position and order that the atoms had in the **solid body** <note>original: "στερεμνίου" (steremniou)</note> for a long time, although the image can sometimes become distorted. 

There are also rapid "compositions" that form in the surrounding air, because it is not necessary for the filling-in of the image to happen deep within the object. There are also several other ways in which such natures are generated. None of these facts contradicts our **sensory perceptions**, provided one looks at the way the senses operate to bring the "sympathies" <note>original: "συμπαθείας" (sympatheias) — here meaning the physical connection or "feeling across" from the object to the observer</note> from external objects to us. 

We must also believe that it is because something enters us from the outside that we are able to see shapes and think of them. For external objects would not be able to stamp their own nature of color and shape upon us through the air...

# EPICURUS. Book X.

...nor by the air between us and the objects, nor by rays <note>original: "ἀκτίνων" (aktinon) — referring to the rival theory that the eye shoots out beams to "touch" objects</note>, nor any other kind of stream flowing from us to them. Instead, perception occurs because certain **outlines** <note>original: "τύπων" (typon) — impressions or patterns of atoms</note> enter us from the objects themselves. These images share the same color and shape as the original, and they are sized appropriately to enter our sight or our mind, traveling with incredible speed.

Then, because of this process, the image provides us with a presentation of a single, continuous object. It preserves the "sympathy" <note>In this context, a physical correspondence or connection between the source and the image</note> from the underlying source, based on the rhythmic vibration of atoms deep within the **solid body** <term>original: "στερεμνίῳ" (stereomnio) — the dense, physical object from which the thin images shed</term>. Whatever impression we receive—whether by the mind's direct focus or by the sense organs—concerning either the shape or the essential properties of an object, that impression is the very shape of the solid body. It is created by the continuous succession of the image or by the remnants it leaves behind.

Now, **falsehood and error** always reside in the **added opinion** <note>original: "προσδοξαζομένῳ" (prosdoxazomeno) — the judgments we make about what we see</note> that a sensation will be confirmed by further evidence. We find ourselves in error if a sensation is not confirmed, or is even contradicted, according to the internal movement within us that is linked to the sensory impression, yet remains distinct from it. This distinction is the source of all error.

For the similarity of the images—such as those we perceive in a mirror, or those occurring in dreams, or other mental impressions and sensory judgments—would never exist and represent what we call "real and true" things unless there were actual objects to which we are directing our attention. On the other hand, error would not exist if we did not also experience a different kind of movement within ourselves, which is linked to the perception but possesses a "break" or a gap in continuity. 

Regarding this internal movement linked to the sensory impression: if it is not confirmed by evidence (or is contradicted by it), **falsehood** arises. But if it is confirmed (or not contradicted), then it is **truth**. 

We must hold onto this doctrine very firmly. We do this so that we do not destroy the "criteria" <note>The standards or rules by which we judge truth</note> that arise from our direct experiences, and so that we do not allow error to be established as equally certain as truth, which would throw

<meta>This page continues Epicurus's Letter to Herodotus. Having just finished the explanation of vision and how "images" (eidola) create mental and sensory perceptions, the text moves into the mechanics of hearing and smell before defining the fundamental, unchanging properties of atoms.</meta>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...is disturbed. Furthermore, hearing occurs when a certain current of **breath** <note>original: "πνεύματός" (pneumatos) — here meaning a physical stream of air-like particles</note> is carried from the person speaking, or from the thing making a sound or noise, or however it produces the sensation of hearing. This flow is scattered into **masses of similar parts** <term>original: "ὁμοιομερεῖς ὄγκους" (homoiomereis onkous) — particles that share the same nature as the whole sound</term>. At the same time, these particles preserve a "sympathy" with one another and a unique kind of unity that extends back to the source. It is this connection that usually creates the perception of the sound's origin; if not, it at least makes the external presence of the sound clear. For without some shared connection being carried from the source, such a perception could not occur.

We should not believe that the air itself is shaped by the voice being sent out (or by similar sounds). Indeed, the air would suffer great difficulty if it had to be molded in such a way by the voice. Rather, when we speak, the impact that occurs within us immediately produces a flow of certain **masses** that create a breath-like stream, and this produces the sensation of hearing in us.

In the same way, we must believe that **smell**, just like hearing, would never produce any sensation unless there were certain masses carried away from an object. These particles must be of the right size to stir the sense organ of smell. Some of these are "disturbed and alien" <note>referring to foul or pungent smells that irritate the nose</note>, while others are "calm and compatible" <note>referring to pleasant or sweet scents</note>.

Furthermore, we must believe that **atoms** possess none of the qualities of the things we perceive <note>such as color, heat, or smell</note> except for **shape, weight, and size**, and those properties that are necessarily part of a shape. For every quality changes, but atoms do not change at all. It is necessary that something solid and indissoluble remains during the dissolution of compound objects. This ensures that changes do not result in "nothingness," nor do things arise from nothing. Instead, changes occur through the **rearrangements** of atoms in many objects, and by the addition or removal of some atoms. 

Therefore, it is necessary that the things which are rearranged be imperishable, not possessing the nature of things that change, but having their own specific masses and shapes. For this is what must necessarily remain...

<meta>This page continues Epicurus’s Letter to Herodotus. Having previously discussed how the senses of hearing and smell operate through the physical flow of particles, Epicurus now transitions into a deep dive regarding the physical properties of atoms—specifically their shape, size, and why they cannot be infinitely divided.</meta>

### EPICURUS. Book 10.

For even in the objects around us that **change their shape** <note>original: "μετασχηματιζομένοις" (metaschēmatizomenois) — referring to how macroscopic objects can be reshaped</note> according to our choice, the shape is perceived as being present within them. However, qualities do not remain in the changing thing in the same way that the shape persists; instead, they are lost from the body as a whole. Therefore, these remaining properties are sufficient to create the differences between **compounds** <term>original: "συγκρίσεων" (synkriseōn) — the "clusters" or "mixtures" of atoms that form the visible world</term>, since it is necessary that something remains and is not destroyed into non-existence.

But one should not believe that every possible size exists among the atoms, so that the visible evidence of our world does not contradict us. Rather, we must believe there are some **variations in size**; for this is a better explanation. With this principle added, we can account for the things that occur according to our feelings and sensations.

However, having every possible size for atoms would not be useful for explaining the differences in qualities. Furthermore, if atoms could be any size, then **visible atoms** would surely have reached our sight; yet we never see this happening, nor is it possible to even imagine how an atom could become visible.

In addition to these points, one must not think that in a finite body there are infinite **masses** <term>original: "ὄγκους" (onkous) — bits of matter or "bulks"</term>, nor masses of any size whatsoever. Consequently, we must not only reject the idea of division into infinity into smaller and smaller parts—so that we do not make all things weak and find ourselves forced, in our attempt to grasp the whole, to exhaust existing things by crushing them into non-existence—but we must also not believe that in finite bodies there is an infinite transition to the smaller.

For it is impossible to conceive how, once someone says that there are infinite masses in a thing, or masses of any size, that the total magnitude could still be finite. For it is clear that these infinite masses must have some size; and no matter how small they might be, the total magnitude of the object would have to be infinite. Furthermore, even if these parts have a limit that makes them perceivable as distinct <note>The text here argues that if you can mentally "see" one part, you must be able to "see" the next</note>, it is impossible not to think of the part following it in the same way. And so, by proceeding from one part to the next in order, one arrives in the mind at an infinite size. Finally, one must consider the **minimum** <note>original: "ἐλάχιστον" (elachiston) — the smallest possible unit of matter or perception</note> found in sensation...

<meta>This page continues Epicurus’s Letter to Herodotus, preserved in Diogenes Laertius's "Lives of Eminent Philosophers." Here, Epicurus introduces the concept of "minimal parts" within the atom and discusses the nature of direction (up and down) in an infinite universe.</meta>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

<margin>60</margin>...one must understand that this [minimal part] is not of such a nature as to undergo **transitions** <note>original: "μεταβάσεις" (metabaseis) — the shifting of parts or internal movement</note>, nor is it entirely unlike those things that do. While it shares a certain commonality with things that can be divided, it possesses no distinct internal parts. However, when we imagine that we can distinguish parts of it based on this commonality—thinking one bit is "on this side" and another is "on that side"—the same result must occur: we reach a limit. 

We observe these [minima] in succession, beginning from the first, and they are not found in the same place, nor do their parts touch one another. Instead, they exist in their own **specific identity** <note>original: "ἰδιότητι" (idiotēti)</note>, measuring out the magnitudes of things—more units for larger objects and fewer for smaller ones. We must believe that the **minimum part** <term>original: "ἐλάχιστον" (elachiston) — the smallest possible unit of matter that cannot be further divided</term> within the atom functions by this same analogy. For it clearly differs in its smallness from the objects we see with our senses, yet it follows the same logical proportion. 

Indeed, we have already stated that the atom has magnitude based on this analogy; we have simply excluded the possibility of it being a large, visible size. Furthermore, these minimal and "unmixed" boundaries must be considered the basic **measuring units** <term>original: "καταμέτρημα" (katametrēma)</term> of lengths. They provide, from their own nature, the primary basis for our rational understanding of the "invisible" world, whether we are considering larger or smaller things. The commonality they share with unchanging things is sufficient to support this reasoning. However, it is impossible for a cluster of these parts to move independently.

Additionally, regarding the **infinite** <note>original: "τοῦ ἀπείρου" (tou apeirou) — the boundless universe or void</note>, we should not speak of "up" or "down" as if there were an absolute "highest" or "lowest" point. Nevertheless, the space above our heads—from whichever point a line might lead out to infinity—will never appear to us to be the same as the space below a certain point. To say that a single point is simultaneously "up" and "down" <margin>20</margin> relative to the same thing is impossible to imagine. 

Consequently, it is possible to grasp one motion as being "upward" toward infinity, and another as "downward," even if an object moving from us toward the feet of those above us reaches the very places that are "above" our heads, or if an object moving "downward" from us reaches the heads of those "below" us. For the **entirety of the motion** <note>original: "ἡ γὰρ ὅλη φορά" (hē gar holē phora)</note> in either direction is nonetheless understood to be opposite to the other and to extend into infinity. And indeed, it is necessary that [these motions] occur at an equal speed...

<summary>Epicurus explains that atoms contain "minimal parts" that serve as the fundamental units of measure for all matter and argues that while the universe is infinite, the directions of "up" and "down" remain logically distinct relative to an observer.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Letter to Herodotus" from Book X of Diogenes Laertius’s "Lives of Eminent Philosophers." The previous page discussed the minimal, indivisible parts of an atom. Here, Epicurus explains the uniform speed of atoms in a vacuum and begins his physical explanation of the soul.</meta>

# EPICURUS. Book X

<margin>61</margin> ...the **atoms must move at equal speed** <note>original: "ταχυτάτον" (tachytaton) — literally "fastest," referring here to the absolute speed of atoms in a vacuum</note> when they travel through the void and nothing collides with them. For heavy atoms will not move any faster than small and light ones, provided nothing stands in their way. Nor do the small atoms move faster than the large ones, as all find a path that fits them, so long as nothing pushes against them. This applies whether the motion is upward, sideways (due to collisions), or downward (due to their own weight). For as long as either type of motion prevails, the atom will move **as fast as a thought** <note>original: "ἅμα νοήματι" (hama noēmati) — a famous Epicurean expression for near-instantaneous speed</note> until something interrupts it—either from an external force or from its own weight—against the force of whatever struck it.

<margin>62</margin> Furthermore, when we consider atoms within **compounds** <term>original: "συγκρίσεις" (synkriseis) — clusters or aggregates of atoms that form the objects we see</term>, we cannot say that one atom is faster than another. All atoms move at an equal speed because they are all moving toward a single place in the aggregate. Even during the shortest continuous stretch of time, they move as one, unless they collide frequently during intervals that can only be grasped by reason <note>original: "λόγῳ θεωρητοὺς χρόνους" (logō theōrētous chronous) — time intervals too small for the human eye to see, but understood through logic</note>. This continues until the continuity of their motion becomes visible to our senses. For the common assumption about the invisible—that even these "theoretically graspable" times will show continuous motion—is not true in these cases. Only that which is actually observed, or grasped by the mind through **direct application** <note>original: "ἐπιβολὴν" (epibolēn) — the mind's focused attention on an object</note>, can be considered true.

<margin>63</margin> Next, one must look at the following, while referring back to our senses and feelings. In this way, you will have the firmest conviction that the **soul is a body** <note>Epicurus argues against the idea of an immaterial soul; for him, if it exists and acts, it must be made of matter</note> composed of fine parts, scattered throughout the entire frame of the person. It most closely resembles a **breath-like substance** <term>original: "πνεύματι" (pneumati) — a vaporous or airy material</term> that has a certain mixture of heat. In some ways it is like the breath, and in others like the heat. However, there is a part of the soul that is even more advanced in its fineness than these elements, and because of this, it is more "in sympathy" with the rest of the body. All of this is proven by the soul’s powers, its feelings, its ease of movement, its thoughts, and the fact that when it is lost, we die.

<margin>64</margin> Moreover, you must hold fast to the idea that the soul is the primary cause of **sensation** <term>original: "αἰσθήσεως" (aisthēseōs)</term>. Yet, it would not have gained this power if it were not "housed" in some way by the rest of the body. The rest of the body, having provided the soul with this...

->C. iii.<-

<summary>Epicurus explains that all atoms move at the same incredible speed in a vacuum regardless of weight, and defines the soul as a physical "subtle body" made of air-like and heat-like particles that enable sensation.</summary>
<keywords>atomic speed, vacuum, compounds, motion, soul as matter, pneuma, heat, sensation, Diogenes Laertius</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Letter to Herodotus" within Book X of Diogenes Laertius’s "Lives of Eminent Philosophers." On the previous page, Epicurus described the movement of atoms at equal speed. Here, he explains the physical nature of the soul, its relationship to the body, and the mechanism of sensation.</meta>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

The body has received this cause [of sensation] from the soul, and it shares in this same accident <note>original: "σύμπτωμα" (symptōma) — a property or "happening" that belongs to a thing</note> from the soul; yet the body does not possess all that the soul possesses. Therefore, when the soul departs, the body does not have sensation. For the body did not possess this power in itself, but rather provided the opportunity for sensation to that other thing [the soul] born along with it. The soul, through the power perfected within it during its management of the body, immediately creates a sensory accident for itself, and then transmits it to the body as well, due to their proximity and sympathy <note>original: "συμπάθειαν" (sympatheian) — the physical "feeling together" or connection between body and soul</note>, just as I have said. 

<margin>64</margin> Therefore, as long as the soul is present, it never lacks sensation, even if some part of the body is removed. Even if the soul is partially destroyed when its container [the body] is broken, whether as a whole or in part, as long as the soul remains, it will continue to have sensation. But the rest of the aggregate [the body], whether it remains whole or in part, does not have sensation once the soul has departed—however great the number of atoms that contribute to the nature of the soul may be. 

<margin>65</margin> Furthermore, when the whole aggregate is dissolved, the soul is scattered and no longer possesses the same powers, nor does it move; consequently, it no longer possesses sensation. For it is impossible to imagine the soul feeling sensation if it is not within this system [the body] and using these movements, when the containers and surroundings are no longer like those in which it now exists and performs these movements.

<margin>66</margin> Moreover, he [Epicurus] says elsewhere that the soul is composed of the smoothest and roundest atoms, far different from those of fire. He says one part of it is **irrational** <term>original: "ἄλογον" (alogon) — the part of the soul responsible for basic biological functions and reflexes</term>, which is scattered throughout the rest of the body; but the **rational** <term>original: "λογικόν" (logikon) — the mind or seat of reason</term> part is located in the chest, as is clear from our experiences of fear and joy. 

<margin>67</margin> Sleep occurs when the parts of the soul scattered throughout the whole structure are either held fast, or scattered, or driven apart; they then collide with the atoms that were already scattered. The seed <note>original: "σπέρμα" (sperma)</note> is also understood to be drawn from the whole body. We must also consider that he uses the term **incorporeal** <term>original: "ἀσώματον" (asōmaton)</term> according to the most common usage of the word, referring to what could be thought of as existing by itself; but it is not possible to conceive of the incorporeal as existing by itself...

<summary>Epicurus explains that the soul is a physical entity made of atoms that provides sensation to the body; once the soul is scattered upon death, sensation ceases. He further divides the soul into a rational part in the chest and an irrational part throughout the limbs.</summary>
<keywords>soul (psyche), sensation (aisthesis), atoms, death, rational part (logikon), irrational part (alogon), sleep, incorporeal</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Epicurus's "Letter to Herodotus" within Book X of Diogenes Laertius’s "Lives of Eminent Philosophers." On the previous page, Epicurus argued that the soul must be a physical entity within the body to facilitate sensation. Here, he expands on why the soul cannot be "incorporeal" (immaterial) and begins a technical discussion on the nature of physical properties—how we distinguish between a whole object and its qualities like shape, color, and weight.</meta>

# EPICURUS. Book X

-> [The soul is not] incorporeal, except for the void. And the void can neither act nor be acted upon, but only provides a space for motion through itself for bodies. Therefore, those who say the soul is incorporeal are talking nonsense. For the soul would not be able to do anything or suffer anything if it were such; but in fact, we clearly see both of these accidents <note>original: "συμπτώματα" (symptōma) — a property or something that 'happens' to an object</note> occurring in the soul. 

If one refers all these reasonings about the soul back to the feelings <note>original: "πάθη" (pathē) — internal states like pleasure and pain</note> and sensations, remembering what was said at the beginning, one will see that these points are sufficiently contained within these outlines, so that from them the details can be worked out with certainty.

Furthermore, we must consider that shapes, colors, sizes, weights, and all other things that are predicated of a body <note>meaning: qualities we attribute to an object</note>—belonging either to all bodies or to those which are visible and known through sensation—are not to be thought of as having independent existences <note>original: "καθ’ ἑαυτάς εἰσι φύσεις" — meaning they don't exist as separate "things" floating in space</note>. It is impossible to imagine such a thing. Nor should we think that they do not exist at all, or that they are some other kind of incorporeal things existing within the body, or that they are parts of it. Rather, we should think that the whole body, in its entirety, has its own eternal nature resulting from all of these things together. 

This is not like a larger heap being formed from smaller particles—whether from the primary atoms or from parts smaller than the whole—but simply, as I say, the body derives its own eternal nature from the sum of all these properties. All of these qualities have their own particular ways of being apprehended and distinguished <note>original: "ἐπιβολὰς... καὶ διαλήψεις" — how our minds focus on and categorize specific traits</note>; yet they follow the whole aggregate and are never separated from it, but instead they fall under the general category of "body."

Furthermore, it often happens that things "befall" <note>original: "συμπίπτει" (sympiptei) — from which we get 'accidents' or 'coincidences'</note> bodies which do not follow them eternally. These are not found among the invisible properties, nor are they incorporeal. Thus, using this name according to its most common usage, we make it clear that "accidents" <note>temporary qualities like being "warm" or "moving"</note> do not have the nature of the whole—which we call a body when we grasp it as a sum of its parts—nor do they have the nature of those eternal properties without which a body cannot be conceived. Each quality is perceived through its own focus...

<summary>Epicurus argues that the soul must be material because it interacts with the physical body, and he defines how we should understand physical properties (like color and weight) not as separate entities, but as the constituent qualities that make up a "body."</summary>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
# EPICURUS. Book X

<margin>Occurrences <note>original: "Συμπτώματα" (symptōmata) — often translated as "accidents" or "properties," these are qualities that can change or vary, unlike permanent properties like weight.</note></margin>
...as if they were following the whole, each property might be named. But when each of these occurring properties is observed, it should be seen as permanently accompanying the object. We must not cast this necessity out of existence—namely, that a property does not have the same nature as the whole "total" to which it belongs (which we call a body), nor does it have the nature of those permanent accompaniments. Yet, one should not think of these properties as having independent existence. For this must not be thought of, either for these or for the permanent properties. But, as it indeed appears, we must consider all "accidents" of bodies as things that do not accompany the body eternally, nor again as having their own independent rank of nature; rather, they are seen in the way that sensation itself creates their particular character.

<margin>On Time</margin>
And furthermore, this too must be understood very carefully. We must not investigate time as we do other things which we seek in a substrate <note>meaning: a physical object that "holds" qualities, like how a piece of fruit "holds" the color red.</note>, by referring it back to the preconceptions seen within ourselves. Instead, we must reason based on the actual clear experience <note>original: "enargēma" — a self-evident perception or clear mental grasp.</note> by which we speak of "a long time" or "a short time," treating it as something we grasp through a natural association. 

We should not exchange our language for what might seem "better" terms, but use those that already exist regarding it. Nor should we declare anything about time as if it had the same essence as that "peculiar character" of physical things (as some indeed do); rather, we should primarily reflect on how we link this "peculiar character" to time and measure it. For this does not require a formal proof, but a reflection: that we link time to days and nights, and their parts; and likewise to feelings and lack of feeling, and to motions and states of rest—conceiving of this very thing again as a certain "special occurrence" <note>original: "idion symptōma"</note> regarding these things, according to which we give it the name "time."

He also says in the second book of *On Nature*, and in the *Large Epitome*, that we must believe that worlds and every finite combination—which frequently possesses a form similar to those things we observe—have come into being from the infinite. These come from their own unique clusters of matter...

<summary>Epicurus explains that accidental properties (like being in motion) are not separate entities from the body, then defines time as a "property of properties" that we perceive through its association with days, nights, feelings, and motion.</summary>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
# EPICURUS. Book X

...having been separated off [from the infinite], both larger and smaller; and again, all things dissolve—some more quickly, others more slowly; some suffering this through one set of causes, and others through another. It is clear, then, that he says the worlds are [not] indestructible <note>The Greek text here says "indestructible" (aphthartous), but Epicurean philosophy famously holds that worlds are perishable. Scholars generally agree that a "not" was lost in the transcription of this passage.</note>, even as their parts undergo change. And in other writings, he says the earth is supported by the air. Furthermore, one must not believe that worlds necessarily have a single shape; rather, they are diverse. In the twelfth book of his work *On Form*, he says: some are spherical, some egg-shaped, and others are shield-shaped <note>original: "thyreoschēmonas" — shaped like an oblong, door-like shield used by ancient soldiers.</note>; however, they do not possess every possible shape. Nor are they living creatures that have been separated from the infinite.

For no one could prove that in a world of one kind, the "seeds" <note>original: "spermata" — the specific clusters or types of atoms required to produce life.</note> from which animals, plants, and all other things we see are formed could not be included, while in another kind of world, they could not have developed. We must assume the same regarding the growth of things on earth.

Moreover, we must suppose that human nature was taught and compelled by many various circumstances and things themselves. Reasoning <note>original: "logismos" — the human capacity for logic and calculation.</note> then further refined the things nature had handed over and made further discoveries—more quickly in some cases and more slowly in others, and in some periods and times [drawing] from the infinite, and in others in smaller increments.

Hence, names [for things] did not originally arise by deliberate convention. Instead, the very natures of men—undergoing unique experiences and receiving unique mental images <note>original: "phantasmata" — the impressions made on the mind by external objects.</note> according to their specific nation—expelled the air in a particular way, shaped by each of these experiences and images, just as there are differences [in speech] according to the regions of the nations. Later, within each nation, specific terms were established by common agreement to make meanings less ambiguous to one another and to express them more concisely. Some people, being aware of things not readily seen, introduced certain sounds that they were compelled to utter, while others chose terms through reasoning for the most part, and so...

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
# EPICURUS. Book X

...to explain. Furthermore, regarding the celestial phenomena <note>original: "meteōra" — in ancient Greek, this refers to everything in the sky, including stars, planets, and weather.</note>, we must not believe that their motions, turnings <note>original: "tropē" — referring to solstices or the points where planets appear to turn back.</note>, eclipses, risings, settings, and similar occurrences happen because there is some being who orchestrates them, or has ordained them, while simultaneously possessing perfect blessedness and immortality. For busywork, worries, anger, and favoritism are not consistent with blessedness; rather, these things arise from weakness, fear, and a dependence on one’s neighbors.

Nor should we believe that these celestial bodies, which are simply condensed masses of fire, possess blessedness and then take on these movements by their own will. We must preserve the full majesty <note>original: "semnōma" — the dignity or holy status appropriate to the gods.</note> of the divine in every name we apply to such concepts, provided that these names do not suggest anything contrary to that majesty. If we do otherwise, this very contradiction will produce the greatest turmoil in our souls. Therefore, we must hold the view that these cycles and necessities were set in motion from the very beginning, during the initial birth of the world.

Furthermore, we must believe that the task of natural philosophy <note>original: "physiologia" — the study of the nature of all things (physics).</note> is to precisely determine the cause of the most important matters. Our happiness depends upon this knowledge of celestial phenomena—understanding the nature of the things seen in the heavens and whatever else is necessary for such precision. 

Moreover, in such matters, we should not seek a single explanation, nor should we think things could only happen in one way. Rather, we must simply recognize that nothing in an incorruptible and blessed nature <note>i.e., the gods</note> admits of division or turmoil. The mind can grasp that this is an absolute truth.

However, the mere observation <note>original: "historia" — here meaning the gathering of data or facts without understanding the underlying theory.</note> of settings, risings, turnings, and eclipses contributes nothing to the happiness that comes from knowledge. In fact, those who have observed these facts, but remain ignorant of what the natures of these things are and what the primary causes are, feel just as much fear—perhaps even more—because the awe <note>original: "thambos" — a mix of wonder and terror.</note> arising from...

<summary>Epicurus argues that celestial events like eclipses occur through natural necessity rather than divine intervention, as gods are too blessed to be burdened with "managing" the universe. He asserts that the primary goal of science (physiologia) is to provide peace of mind by removing the fear of the gods.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Epicurus's "Letter to Herodotus" from the previous page. Having just argued that celestial phenomena are not the work of gods, Epicurus now explains his "method of multiple explanations"—the idea that for things we cannot observe closely (like the stars), many different scientific explanations are acceptable as long as they don't contradict our senses. This flexibility is what leads to tranquility (ataraxia).</meta>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS
# EPICURUS. Book X

...without a prior understanding of these principles, one cannot grasp the solution to these problems, nor the management of the most vital matters. Therefore, we find that there are multiple causes for solstices <note>original: "tropōn" — refers to the turning points of the sun's path.</note>, settings, risings, eclipses, and similar events, just as we see similar things happening in the specific events around us. We must not believe that our investigation into these matters has failed to achieve the level of precision necessary to contribute to our tranquility <term>ataraxia: a state of freedom from emotional disturbance and anxiety, which Epicurus considered the goal of life.</term> and happiness. 

We must observe how similar things happen in our own world and, by analogy, determine the causes for celestial phenomena and everything that is unobservable. We should hold in contempt those who do not recognize that a phenomenon can occur or exist in more than one way, and those who fail to consider that appearances change depending on distance. Such people are ignorant of the conditions under which it is impossible to maintain a peaceful mind. If we recognize that a thing can happen in this specific way, but also understand that it might happen in several other ways, we will remain as undisturbed as if we knew for certain that it happened in one particular way.

Above all, we must understand that the most fundamental disturbance <note>original: "tarachos" — the opposite of ataraxia; mental turmoil or anxiety.</note> in human souls arises because people believe that these celestial bodies are both blessed and immortal, yet they simultaneously attribute to them conflicting desires, actions, and purposes. Furthermore, people expect or suspect some eternal terror <note>original: "deinon" — something terrible or formidable, often referring here to punishment in the afterlife.</note> based on myths; they fear the lack of sensation in death as if it were something they would actually feel, and they suffer not because of settled convictions, but because of an irrational state of mind. Consequently, because they do not define what is truly fearful, they experience as much or even more turmoil than if they actually held these superstitious opinions. 

Tranquility consists in being released from all these fears and in maintaining a constant memory of the whole of our philosophy and its most fundamental principles. Therefore, we must pay attention to our present feelings and sensations—to common sensations for general things and to individual sensations for specific things—and to every clear evidence provided by each of the criteria of truth. For if we pay attention to these, we can correctly trace the source from which...

<summary>Epicurus explains that celestial events can have multiple natural causes and that the goal of studying them is to achieve tranquility (ataraxia) by removing the fear of gods and the afterlife.</summary>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...disturbance <note>original: "tarachos" — the mental agitation or anxiety that Epicurus sought to cure.</note> arises and fear is produced, if we explain these things correctly and resolve them, providing causes for celestial phenomena and the other things that constantly occur, as well as those things that terrify other people to the extreme. These points, Herodotus, are the most essential summaries of the nature of the universe. Consequently, if this reasoning is mastered with precision, I believe that—even if one does not proceed to every single detailed study—one will attain a depth <note>original: "hadrotēta" — referring to a robust or mature understanding of philosophy.</note> incomparable to other men. For one will also clarify many specific points for themselves through our complete work, and by keeping these principles in mind, they will be a constant aid. For these principles are such that even those who are already sufficiently advanced in detail, or those who are perfectly resolving their inquiries into such concepts, can perform most of their investigations into the whole of nature. As for those who have not yet reached such a complete state, they can use these primary principles to achieve a mental overview of the most important matters to serve as a bridle <note>original: "chalinismon" — a metaphor for restraining the mind from falling into mythical or fearful explanations.</note> against disturbance.

And this is his letter concerning Physics. The following one concerns celestial phenomena:

->Epicurus to Pythocles, greetings.<-

You noted that what we have written elsewhere is difficult to remember, even though (as you said) you keep those writings with you constantly. I gladly accepted your request and was filled with pleasant expectations. Having now written all the remaining points you requested, which will be useful to many others as well, I...

## EPICURUS. Book X

...these reasonings, especially for those who have recently tasted genuine natural science <note>original: "physiologia" — the study of the nature of things</note>, and for those who have become entangled in busier activities than the general course of education. Take these points up well, and keeping them in memory, traverse them quickly along with the rest, which we sent in the small summary <note>original: "epitomē" — referring to the "Letter to Herodotus"</note> addressed to Herodotus.

First of all, then, you must believe that there is no other goal from knowledge of celestial phenomena <note>original: "meteōrōn" — referring to everything in the sky, including stars, planets, and weather</note>, whether they are discussed in connection with other things or independently, than peace of mind <note>original: "ataraxia"</note> and firm conviction, just as with all other studies. Do not try to force the impossible, nor attempt to have a theory that is similar in all respects either to our discourses on ways of living <note>original: "peri biōn" — referring to ethics</note> or to the clarification of other physical problems. For example, the principle that the universe consists of body and intangible nature <note>original: "anaphēs physis" — referring to the void or vacuum</note>, or that the atoms are the fundamental elements, and all such things that have only one explanation consistent with the appearances.

This single-cause explanation does not apply to celestial phenomena. Instead, these events have multiple causes for their coming-to-be, and they have more than one description of their essence that is consistent with the senses. For we must not study nature according to empty axioms and laws, but as the appearances <note>original: "phainomena" — the things that are observed</note> themselves invite us. For our life does not have need of private theories and empty opinion, but of us living without disturbance <note>original: "athorubōs" — calmly or without turmoil</note>. All these celestial things happen unshakably in every respect and can be explained in multiple ways, in harmony with the appearances, provided that one properly allows for what is plausibly said about them. 

But when someone accepts one explanation and rejects another that is equally in harmony with the appearance, it is clear that they fall away from all natural science and collapse into myth. We should take certain signs of what is completed in the heavens by looking at phenomena that happen here among us, which are observed as they actually are, rather than focusing solely on the appearances in the heavens. For these celestial events may happen in multiple ways. However, one must observe the mental image <note>original: "phantasma"</note> of each phenomenon and distinguish those things connected to it which are not contradicted by the multiple ways things are completed among us. A world... <note>Epicurus here begins to define the nature of a "world" or "cosmos."</note>

<summary>Epicurus explains his methodology for studying the heavens, arguing that unlike fundamental physics, celestial phenomena often have multiple valid explanations, and choosing only one leads to superstitious "myth."</summary>
<keywords>Epicurus, Pythocles, natural science, ataraxia, celestial phenomena, plurality of causes, phainomena, methodology, myth vs science</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Epicurus's "Letter to Pythocles," as recorded by Diogenes Laertius. Having established that multiple explanations are acceptable for celestial phenomena, Epicurus now moves to define what a "world" is and how it forms.</meta>

->DIOG. LAERT.<-
614

<margin>88</margin>
A world <note>original: "kosmos"</note> is a certain encompassing of the heavens, containing the stars, the earth, and all visible things. It is a section cut off from the infinite <note>original: "apeiron" — the boundless universe of atoms and void</note>, and it ends in a boundary <note>original: "peras"</note> that is either rare or dense. When this boundary is dissolved, everything within it will be thrown into confusion. This boundary can be rounded, or triangular, or any shape whatsoever, for every shape is possible. This is because none of the visible evidence <note>the things we see in our own sky</note> contradicts the idea of a world in which a boundary cannot be perceived.

<margin>3</margin>
Furthermore, we can grasp that such worlds are infinite in number, and that such a world can come into being both within another world and in the space between worlds <note>original: "metakosmios" — the "intermundia" or the empty regions between different universes</note>, which is what we call the interval between worlds. This happens in a place with much void, and not in a large, pure, empty space as some say. It occurs when certain suitable seeds <note>original: "spermata" — here referring to atoms or clusters of atoms capable of forming matter</note> flow in from one world or an inter-world space, or from several. These seeds gradually cause additions, articulations, and movements to another place, should it happen so, and they provide irrigation <note>a metaphor for the flow of atoms</note> from sources that are suitable until the world reaches completion and stays stable, for as long as the underlying foundations can receive the additions.

For a world to form, it is not merely necessary for a collection of atoms to come together, nor a whirlwind <note>original: "dinos" — a vortex, a common theory in other Greek atomist systems like that of Democritus</note> in the void where a world must necessarily be born, according to common opinion. Nor does a world simply grow until it strikes another world, as one of the so-called "natural philosophers" <note>likely referring to Democritus</note> claims. For such a theory fights against the visible evidence.

The sun, the moon, and the rest of the stars did not begin as independent objects that were later swallowed up by the world; rather, they were formed immediately and began to grow along with it. This is also true of the earth and the sea. These were formed by the gathering and whirling of certain fine-grained natures <note>original: "physeis"</note>, which were either like breath <note>original: "pneumatikōn" — airy or gaseous</note>, or fire-like, or a mixture of both. For this is what our senses suggest to us.

As for the size of the sun and the other stars, in relation to us, it is **exactly as large as it appears**. <note>This is a famous and controversial Epicurean doctrine: because light reaches us from the sun without being distorted, they argued its size must be roughly what we see—about a foot wide.</note> This is also true in the...

<summary>Epicurus defines a "world" as a bounded system of stars and earth within an infinite universe and explains that worlds form from "seeds" (atoms) in the spaces between other worlds. He also introduces the counter-intuitive claim that the sun and stars are roughly the size they appear to be to the human eye.</summary>

...in his books *On Nature*. For he says: if the sun had lost its size because of its distance from us, it would have lost its color much more so. The rising and setting of the sun, the moon, and the other stars may happen by kindling <note>original: "anapsin"</note> and extinguishing <note>original: "sbesin"</note>, if the conditions of the environment at those specific places are such as to bring about what has been described. For none of the observed phenomena <note>original: "phainomenōn"</note> contradicts this. Or, the aforementioned rising and setting could be completed by the stars appearing above the earth and then again being obstructed <note>original: "epiprosthēsin" — passing behind the earth or some other barrier</note>; for again, nothing in the observed phenomena contradicts this.

As for their movements, it is not impossible that they occur according to the rotation of the whole heaven, or while the heaven stands still, the stars themselves rotate according to a necessity <note>original: "anagkēn"</note> that was generated at the beginning, during the birth of the world, at their rising. This might then be followed by heat, according to a certain spreading of the fire that always moves toward the next adjacent places.

The turnings <note>original: "tropas" — the solstices or the points where the sun and moon appear to "turn back" in their paths</note> of the sun and moon may occur because of a slanting of the heavens <note>the tilt of the earth's axis or the celestial sphere</note>, as necessitated by the seasons. Likewise, it could be due to the resistance of the air, or because the matter they require for fuel is always found in adjacent areas and catches fire; or it could be that from the beginning, a specific kind of rotation was impressed upon these stars so that they move in a spiral. For regarding all such things and those related to them, none of the clear evidence is in conflict, provided that one always holds fast to what is possible in these matters and can bring each of them into agreement with the phenomena, without fearing the slavish tricks of the astrologers <note>Epicurus viewed the deterministic, mathematical predictions of astronomers/astrologers as "slavish" because they ignored the freedom and plurality of nature</note>.

...and again, its fillings and the destruction of its body <note>original: "plērōseis... katastrophēn" — referring to the waxing and waning phases of the moon</note>. These things could happen through the configurations of the air in a similar way, or also by obstructions <note>original: "epiprosthēseis" — something blocking the light</note>, or in any of the ways by which the phenomena observed among us invite us to provide explanations of this kind—provided that one has not fallen so in love with the "single-cause" method <note>original: "monachē tropon" — the dogmatic insistence that only one scientific explanation can be true</note> that they vainly reject the others, failing to consider what is possible for a human to theorize and what is impossible, and thus desiring to observe the impossible. 

Furthermore, it is possible for the moon to possess light from itself, and it is also possible that it receives it from the sun. For among us, we see many things that have light of their own and many that have it from others. Nothing in the celestial phenomena <note>original: "meteōrois" — things in the air or sky</note> stands in the way of this, if one always keeps in mind the method of multiple causes and examines the hypotheses and causes consistent with them, without looking toward inconsistent theories or inflating them until one falls back, in one way or another, into the "single-cause" method. 

The appearance of the "face" in the moon <note>original: "emphasos tou prosōpou" — the visible markings on the lunar surface</note> can occur through the variation of its parts, or by obstruction, or in any other ways that might be observed to be in harmony with the phenomena. For in all celestial matters, one must not apply such a rigid approach. Indeed, if one fights against clear evidence <note>original: "enargēmasin" — the self-evident data of the senses</note>, they will never be able to genuinely partake in tranquility <note>original: "ataraxias" — the state of mental calm that is the goal of Epicurean life</note>. 

An eclipse of the sun or the moon can happen through "quenching" <note>original: "sbesin" — as if the fire of the star is temporarily put out</note>, just as this is seen to happen among us. It can also happen by the obstruction of other things—either the earth, or the heavens, or something else of that sort. In this way, we must examine the various methods that are related to one another, and consider that the simultaneous combination of certain causes is not impossible. 

In the twelfth book of *On Nature*, he <note>Epicurus</note> says these same things: that the sun eclipses when the moon overshadows it, and the moon eclipses when it enters the shadow of the earth—but also by its own withdrawal. This is also stated by Diogenes the Epicurean in the first book of his *Selected Doctrines*. Furthermore, the order of its period <note>its regular cycle</note> occurs just as some common things among us happen...

### EPICURUS. Book 10

...let it be understood, and let the divine nature never be brought into these matters in any way; rather, let it be preserved as free from any labor <note>original: "aleitourgētos" — meaning without public duty or tiresome work</note> and in a state of perfect bliss. For if this principle is not upheld, the entire study of causes for celestial phenomena <term>meteōrōn: things occurring in the sky or atmosphere</term> will be pointless. This has already happened to some who failed to grasp the method of what is possible; they fell into vanity by believing that things happen in only one way, and they rejected all other explanations that are equally possible. By doing so, they were carried away into the unthinkable and became unable to accept the visible signs that we see. 

One must bid farewell to the gods <note>original: "suntheō khairein" — a phrase often used to dismiss divine intervention in physical science</note> when considering the changing lengths of nights and days. These variations may occur because the sun's movements become fast and then slow over the earth, or because of the varying lengths of the regions it passes through, or because it crosses certain places more quickly or more slowly—just as some things are observed to happen among us on earth. We must speak in harmony with these earthly observations when explaining celestial things. 

Those who insist on a single cause <note>the "monachē tropon" mentioned on the previous page</note> conflict with the evidence of the senses and have failed to realize what is truly possible for a human to theorize. Furthermore, weather signs <note>original: "sēmasiai" — signals or omens</note> can occur by the coincidences of seasons, just as we see with the animals among us, and also through changes in the air. For neither of these explanations conflicts with the observed facts. 

Furthermore, it is impossible to see exactly which cause produces rain, but it is clear that it can be formed and consist either of a compression of the air through a wind-like <insert>pnevmat-ikēs</insert> squeezing, or by the interlocking of atoms that hold each other together and are suited for completing this process. Rain can also occur through a flowing <insert>revmat-ikēn</insert> collection of vapors from both the land and the waters; the formation of such things is not impossible to achieve in many other ways as well. 

Indeed, rain can be produced when clouds are squeezed, or when they undergo changes. Likewise, winds can occur through an outflow from suitable places, or by the air being moved through the forceful intrusion of certain collections of matter that are suited for such discharges. It is also possible for thunder to occur by the movement of wind <term>pneuma: breath, wind, or spirit</term> within the hollows of the clouds...
