...confinement <note>original: "aneilēsin" — a rolling up or compression</note> of wind, just as occurs in the vessels we use on earth, and also the rumbling within them from fire that has been infused with air <note>original: "pepneumatōmenou" — literally "wind-ified" or aerated</note>. It may also occur through the bursting and parting of clouds, and by the friction and collisions of clouds when they have taken on a crystal-like solidification. In general, one must say that this phenomenon—like many others—occurs in multiple ways, provided we call upon the evidence of what we can actually see. 

Lightning, likewise, is produced in several ways. For the friction and collision of clouds causes a certain atomic configuration <term>schēmatismos: the specific arrangement or "shape" of atoms that gives a substance its properties</term> capable of producing fire to slip out, thus generating lightning. It can also happen by the squeezing out of fire-producing currents from the clouds by winds <term>pneumatōn: translated here as winds or moving air; in Greek science, this term often refers to the active, moving element in nature</term> which prepare this bright flash. It may also occur through the pressure resulting from the clouds being squeezed, either by each other or by the winds. 

Another cause is the trapping of light scattered from the stars, which is then driven together by the motion of clouds and winds and eventually breaks out through the clouds. Or, it could be the filtering of the most refined light through the clouds, or the way fire collects in the clouds to produce thunder, followed by the motion of this fire. It could also result from the ignition of the wind caused by the intensity of its motion and its violent confinement. Furthermore, the bursting of clouds by winds might cause fire-producing atoms to fall out, creating the appearance <note>original: "phantasma" — the visual impression or image</note> of lightning. Many other ways will be easily seen if one holds fast to visible evidence and is able to contemplate what is similar to it. 

Lightning precedes thunder in such cloud conditions because the wind strikes and, at the same moment, pushes out the atomic configuration that produces the lightning; but afterward, as the wind rolls around within the cloud, it produces this rumbling sound. Also, even if both lightning and thunder occur at the same time, the lightning reaches us with a more intense speed, whereas the thunder lags behind. This is just like what is observed in some things viewed from a distance, where we see the blows being made...

...waves, thunderbolts <note>original: "keraunous" — specifically refers to lightning that strikes the earth</note> can occur through more numerous collections of winds, their confinement, and a powerful ignition, which leads to a bursting of a part of the cloud and a more forceful ejection of that fire onto the regions below. This breaking happens because the surrounding areas are denser due to the condensation of the clouds, and the fire has been caught up within them. Thunder can also occur in several ways when wind becomes more forceful and aerated, breaking the cloud because it cannot retreat into the adjacent areas due to their condensation; this happens mostly against a mountain or high ground, where thunderbolts fall most frequently against one another. 

Thunderbolts may be produced in many other ways as well, *provided only that myth be kept away* <note>original: "monon ho mythos apestō" — a famous Epicurean maxim. He argues that attributing weather to gods creates fear, while natural explanations bring peace of mind.</note>. And myth will be kept away if one, by following the evidence of visible phenomena, makes inferences about those things which are unseen. 

Whirlwinds <term>presteres: literally "burners" or "fire-spouts"; violent, often fiery windstorms or waterspouts</term> can occur through the settling of a cloud into the lower regions, pushed differently by a concentrated mass of wind and carried by a great current of air, while the external air simultaneously pushes the cloud toward its neighbor. They can also occur by a circular rotation of wind when air is compressed from above, and many bursts of wind occur that are unable to flow out sideways because of the condensation of the surrounding air. When the whirlwind descends as far as the ground, tornadoes <note>original: "strobiloi" — literally "spinning tops"</note> occur, as the birth of the storm follows the motion of the wind; if it descends as far as the sea, eddies and whirlpools are produced. 

Earthquakes can occur by the trapping of wind within the earth, or by its arrangement alongside small masses of earth <note>Epicurus often envisions the earth as having a porous, cavernous interior</note>, and its constant motion, which produces a trembling in the ground. This wind is either encompassed from the outside by falling into the soil, or it is driven into cave-like places of the earth from the winds that have been condensed...

Winds happen from time to time when some foreign matter <note>original: "allophylias" — refers to the intrusion of atoms or air masses of a different nature into the local atmosphere</note> is constantly and gradually introduced, and also by the collection of a vast amount of water. Other winds are produced even when a few [particles] fall into many hollow spaces, leading to a transmission of their motion. 

Hail is formed by a more intense freezing; it also occurs through the surrounding and division of certain windy <note>or "air-like"</note> particles, and by a more moderate freezing along with the simultaneous breaking of certain water-like parts. This causes them to be forced together <term>syōsin: a squeezing or compression of particles</term> and break apart so that they form into distinct pieces, freezing in a mass. The roundness [of hail] can easily happen by the edges being broken off from all sides as it falls, or because, during its formation, the parts are evenly arranged on all sides, whether they are made of water-like or air-like substances.

Snow can be formed by thin water pouring out from clouds in a symmetrical way, or by the pressure of suitable clouds, and by the trace of a "seed" <note>original: "sporas" — Epicurus suggests that specific types of atoms act as "seeds" or templates for weather phenomena</note> that takes on a frozen shape during its descent because of a powerful coldness in the regions below the clouds. Furthermore, such an emission from the clouds could occur through a uniform freezing in clouds that have a certain thinness, when water-like particles are pressed together and lie side-by-side; these, by being squeezed together, result in hail—this happens mostly in the air. Also, by the friction of clouds that have already taken on a frozen state, this collection of snow can break off and rebound. There are many other ways in which snow can be formed.

Dew is formed by the gathering together of particles from the air that are capable of producing such moisture...

A rainbow occurs when the sun shines against watery air, or because of a unique nature of light and air which produces the peculiarities of these colors, whether all of them together or a single type. This appearance of a circular shape occurs because the distance is perceived as equal from all sides by the sight, or because the particles in the air are compressed in such a way, or because atoms carried from the air toward the moon <note>The text here transitions from rainbows to halos, which can involve the moon</note> are diverted in a circular formation as they come together. 

A halo around the moon occurs when air is carried from all sides toward the moon, or when the flows <note>original: "rheumata" — the "effluences" or streams of atoms that Epicurus believed all objects constantly emitted</note> coming away from it are evenly held back to such an extent that a cloud-like circle forms and does not entirely dissipate; or perhaps because the moon holds back the surrounding air symmetrically on all sides, causing it to stand around it in a circular and thick-layered ring. This happens in certain parts, either because some flow has forced its way from the outside, or because heat has occupied suitable pores to bring this about.

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...**Comets** <note>original: "komētai asteres," literally "long-haired stars"</note> come into being either because fire is nourished in certain places at certain intervals of time in the **celestial regions** <term>meteōrois: things in the air or sky; the root of our word "meteorology"</term> whenever a particular state of the surroundings occurs; or because the heaven above us has a certain unique movement of its own at intervals, so that such stars appear; or because these stars themselves start to move at certain times due to some circumstance and come into the regions visible to us and become apparent. 

Their disappearance happens because of the causes opposite to these. Certain stars "turn back" <note>This refers to the retrograde motion of planets, where they appear to move backward in the sky</note>, which happens not only because this part of the cosmos stands still while the rest revolves around it—as some claim—but also because a circular vortex of air surrounds it, which acts as a barrier to their wandering in the same way the other stars do. It may also be because there is no suitable fuel for them in the adjacent space, whereas there is in the place where they are seen to reside. This can be explained in several other ways, if one is able to reason in harmony with what is observed.

That some stars **wander** <note>original: "planasthai," the root of the word "planet"</note> while others do not move, may be because they were originally compelled to move in circles in such a way that some are carried along the same uniform vortex, while others move in a vortex that has certain irregularities. It is also possible that in the regions through which they are carried, there are uniform expansions of air which push them forward in a continuous, uniform way, burning them steadily; or perhaps the air is irregular in such a way that the variations we observe are produced.

To assign a **single cause** to these things, when the phenomena suggest many different explanations, is the act of a madman <note>original: "manikon"</note> and is unbecoming of those who have devoted themselves to **vain astrology** <term>mataian astrologian: empty or useless star-prediction</term>. Such people assign causes to things in a vacuum, especially when they fail to release the **divine nature** <note>Epicurus argued that gods do not manage the weather or stars, as that would be beneath their perfect, peaceful state</note> from burdensome duties. 

Certain stars are observed to lag behind others; this happens both because of the slow...

### EPICURUS. Book 10

...secondly, they might be carried around by the same circular path as they revolve, or perhaps they move in the opposite direction and are met by the same **vortex** <term>dinē: a whirling movement of air or ether that Epicureans believed carried celestial bodies</term>. Or it could be that as they revolve, some cover a larger area and others a smaller one while circling the same vortex. To make a single, absolute declaration about these matters belongs to those who wish to perform wonders <note>original: "terateuesthai," to play the charlatan or use marvels to impress</note> for the masses.

So-called **shooting stars** <note>original: "asteres ekpiptein," literally "falling stars"</note> can be caused by the friction of the stars themselves, or by an expulsion of matter where a "breathing out" <note>original: "ekpneumatōsis"</note> occurs, just as we said regarding lightning. They can also occur through the meeting of fire-producing atoms when an affinity develops to produce this effect, and according to the direction of the initial impulse during that meeting. Another cause is the collection of wind in certain mist-like thickenings; these catch fire because they are hemmed in and then burst through their surroundings, traveling toward whatever place their impulse carries them. There are countless other ways this can be accomplished.

The **weather signs** <note>original: "episēmasiai," signs or omens often used in ancient meteorology</note> that are observed in certain animals happen by a coincidence of timing. For animals do not bring about any necessity for a storm to be completed, nor does any **divine nature** sit observing the movements of these animals and then bring these signs to fulfillment. For such foolishness would not occur even in a common animal, if it were slightly more refined, let alone in a being that possesses perfect happiness <note>Epicurus argues that gods are "blessed and incorruptible" and would not bother with the trivial task of using animals to signal weather to humans</note>.

Remember all these things, **Pythocles**; for you will escape far from **myth** <note>original: "mythou," referring to superstitious or supernatural explanations</note> and you will be able to understand things related to these. Most of all, give yourself over to the study of first principles, and of **infinity** <term>apeirias: the concept that the universe, space, and the number of atoms are boundless</term>, and of things related to them; and further, of the **criteria** <term>kritēriōn: the Epicurean standards of truth, including sensations, preconceptions, and feelings</term> and the **feelings** <term>pathōn: specifically the internal states of pleasure and pain</term>, and the purpose for which we reason through these things. For when these are contemplated together, they will make it easy to see the causes of specific details. But those who do not cherish these things above all, or...

<meta>This page continues the transition from Epicurus’s natural philosophy (the study of the heavens) to his ethical teachings on how a person should live. It specifically outlines the characteristics of the "Wise Man" (the Sage), reflecting the transition from the "Letter to Pythocles" into the general doxology of Epicurean ethics in Diogenes Laertius's Book 10.</meta>

### DIOGENES LAERTIUS

...have well contemplated these same things, nor have they attained the purpose for which one ought to study them. These are his views regarding **celestial phenomena** <term>meteōra: things in the air or sky, including stars, weather, and comets</term>.

But concerning the conduct of life, and how we ought to avoid certain things and choose others, he writes as follows. First, however, let us go through what he and his followers believe concerning the **wise man** <term>sophos: the ideal Epicurean person who has achieved perfect peace of mind</term>. Harm from other men arises from either hatred, envy, or contempt, all of which the wise man overcomes through reason. Moreover, once someone becomes wise, they never again take on the opposite disposition <note>original: "diathesin," a permanent state of character</note>, nor does he pretend to be so; he will be more susceptible to the passions, but this would not be an obstacle to his wisdom. Yet, a man cannot become wise from just any physical constitution, nor in every nation.

Even if the wise man is tortured on the rack, he is still happy <note>A famous Epicurean paradox: mental pleasure is so superior to physical pain that the Sage remains blessed even in agony</note>. The wise man alone will show gratitude, and will feel the same toward friends whether they are present or absent. Even when being tortured, he might let out a moan or a groan. The wise man will not have sexual relations with a woman where the laws forbid it, as Diogenes says in his *Epitome of Epicurus’s Ethical Doctrines*. Nor will he punish his servants, but will instead show them pity and grant pardon to any who are of good character.

It is not their view that the wise man will fall in love, nor will he worry about his burial. They do not believe that love is "sent by the gods," as Diogenes says in his twelfth book. Nor will he practice ornate rhetoric. **Sexual intercourse** <note>original: "synousia"</note>, they say, has never profited any man, and it is a lucky thing if it has not harmed him. Nevertheless, the wise man will marry and have children, as Epicurus says in the *Problems* and in the books *On Nature*. But depending on the circumstances of life, he will marry; at other times, he will be turned away from it.

Epicurus says in the *Symposium* that the wise man will not indulge in drunkenness; nor will he engage in politics, as stated in the first book *On Lives*; nor will he become a tyrant. He will not live like a **Cynic** <note>original: "kyniein," to act like a dog, referring to the Cynic philosophers who lived in poverty and rejected social norms</note>, as stated in the second book *On Lives*; nor will he live as a beggar. Even if he loses his sight, he will still participate in life, as he says in the same work. The wise man will also feel grief, as...

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the traits belonging to the Epicurean "Wise Man" (the Sage), contrasting Epicurean views with those of other schools like the Stoics. ### EPICURUS. BOOK 10.

Diogenes says in the fifth book of his *Selected Teachings* that the wise man will take legal action in court, and he will leave writings behind, but he will not participate in public festivals <note>original: "panēgyriein," referring to giving public speeches or seeking vanity at great gatherings</note>. He will provide for his property and for the future. He will love the countryside. He will set himself against Fortune <term>tychē: chance or luck, which the Epicureans believed should not control a person's life</term>, and he will not make just any person a friend <note>original: "philon te oudena ktēsesthai." This text is debated, as Epicureans valued friendship highly; it likely means he is highly selective or does not seek friends for vain reasons</note>. He will provide for his reputation only to the extent of not being despised. He will take more pleasure than others in public spectacles. 

He believes that errors <note>or "sins"</note> are not all equal <note>A direct rejection of the Stoic belief that all moral failings are equally bad</note>. He views health as a good for some, but for others as something indifferent. Courage does not come by nature, but by a calculation of what is beneficial. Friendship, too, exists because of its utility. There must be some initial benefit to start it (just as we sow the earth to get a crop), but it is sustained by a shared community of pleasure. 

Happiness is understood in two ways: the highest kind, such as belongs to God, which does not admit of any increase <note>meaning a state of perfect lack of pain and fear</note>; and the kind that involves the addition or removal of pleasures. He will dedicate statues of others if he has them, but he would be indifferent if he did not. Only the wise man can speak correctly about music and poetry, yet he would not actually compose poems himself. 

One wise man is not "wiser" than another. He will make money, but only from his wisdom and only when he is in need. He will serve a monarch when the timing is right. He will rejoice if someone corrects him, and he will establish a school, but not in a way that seeks to lead a mob. He will read his work in public, but not willingly. He will hold firm to his doctrines and will not be in doubt. He will be the same even in his sleep, and he will, at some point, even die for a friend. 

These are their views. But now we must move on to the Letter.

->Epicurus to Menoeceus, greetings.<-

Let no one delay in studying philosophy while he is young, nor let him grow weary of philosophy when he is old. For no one is either too young or too old for the health of the soul. To say that the time for philosophy has not yet come, or that the time has passed, is like saying that the time for happiness <term>eudaimonia: a state of flourishing and mental peace</term> is not yet here or is no longer present. Therefore, both the young and the old must philosophize: the old so that as he grows aged, he may stay young in good things...

->DIOGENES LAERTIUS<-

...to the good because of the gratitude for what has happened; but for the other <note>referring to the young man</note>, so that he may be both young and old at once because of his lack of fear regarding what is to come. We must, therefore, practice the things that produce happiness <term>eudaimonia: a state of flourishing or true well-being</term>, since if it is present, we have everything; but if it is absent, we do everything in our power to possess it.

The things I have constantly recommended to you, these things you must both practice and meditate upon, considering them to be the basic principles <note>literally "elements" or "first steps"</note> of living well. 

First, believing God to be an immortal and blessed being—just as the common notion of God has been outlined—do not attribute to him anything foreign to his immortality or inconsistent with his blessedness. Rather, believe everything about him that is capable of preserving that blessedness which accompanies immortality. 

For gods indeed exist; for our knowledge of them is clear. But they are not such as many people believe them to be; for they do not keep them as they believe them to be. The impious person is not the one who denies the gods of the many, but the one who attaches the opinions of the many to the gods. For the assertions of the many about the gods are not basic concepts <note>original: "prolepseis," meaning the innate ideas or preconceptions we have before being taught</note>, but false suppositions. From this, the greatest harms are brought upon the wicked from the gods, and also benefits <note>Epicurus argues that gods are indifferent to humans; "harms" and "benefits" are perceived by humans based on their own character</note>. For being always familiar with their own virtues, they welcome those like themselves, and regard everything that is not such as being foreign.

Accustom yourself to the belief that death is nothing to us. For all good and evil consist in sensation; but death is the deprivation of sensation. Therefore, a correct understanding that death is nothing to us makes the mortality of life enjoyable—not by adding an infinite amount of time, but by taking away the longing for immortality. 

For there is nothing terrifying in life for the person who has truly grasped that there is nothing terrifying in not living. Thus, the person who says he fears death is foolish—not because it will cause pain when it arrives, but because it causes pain in the expectation. For that which does not trouble us when it is present, is a hollow pain when it is merely anticipated...

### EPICURUS. Book X. ###

...[fearful] <note>The text begins with the end of the word "fearful." The full thought from the previous page is: "That which causes no trouble when it is present, causes only empty distress when it is anticipated."</note>, it grieves us in vain. Death, therefore, the most terrifying of evils, is nothing to us; because as long as we exist, death is not present; and when death is present, then we do not exist. It is, therefore, of no concern either to the living or to the dead; for as to the former, it is not, and as to the latter, they are no longer. 

But many people flee death at one time as the greatest of evils, and at another time seek it as a rest from the troubles of life. [The wise man] neither fears non-living, for living is not a burden to him, nor does he think non-living is an evil. And just as with food he does not simply choose the largest portion but the most pleasant, so with time he enjoys not the longest duration but the most pleasant. 

He who advises the young man to live well and the old man to end his life well is a fool, not only because of how much life is to be welcomed, but because the practice of living well and dying well is one and the same. But far worse is the one who says it is good not to be born,

->But once born, to pass through the gates of Hades as quickly as possible.<-
<note>This is a famous pessimistic quote attributed to the poet Theognis, often cited in antiquity to be refuted by Epicurus.</note>

For if he says this out of conviction, why does he not depart from life? For this is ready at hand for him, if he has truly decided upon it. But if he says it in jest, he is a fool in matters that do not admit such mockery. 

We must remember that the future is neither completely ours nor completely not ours, so that we may neither expect it as certain to happen, nor despair of it as certain not to happen. 

We must also consider that of desires, some are natural and others are empty <note>original: "kenai," meaning vain, groundless, or socially constructed rather than biologically rooted</note>. Of the natural desires, some are necessary and others are natural only. And of the necessary desires, some are necessary for happiness <term>eudaimonia: a state of flourishing or true well-being</term>, others for the body’s freedom from disturbance, and others for life itself. For a steady understanding of these things knows how to direct every choice and avoidance toward the health of the body and the tranquility of the soul <term>ataraxia: the state of mental peace and freedom from fear that is the goal of Epicurean ethics</term>. Since this is the goal of a blessed [life]...

# DIOG. LAERT. #

### Page 428 ###

...to live is the goal. <note>original: "ζῆν ἐστὶ τέλος"</note> For it is for the sake of this that we do everything: so that we may feel neither pain nor fear. And when once this state is achieved for us, every storm of the soul is dispelled, as the living creature has no need to stray as if toward something lacking, nor to seek anything else by which the good of the soul and the body might be fulfilled. For we have need of pleasure <note>original: "ἡδονή" (hedonē)</note> only when we feel pain because pleasure is absent; but when we do not feel pain, we no longer stand in need of pleasure. 

And for this reason, we say that pleasure is the beginning and the end of the blessed life. <note>original: "μακαρίως ζῆν"</note> For we recognize pleasure as the primary and innate good; it is the starting point for every <term>choice and avoidance</term> <note>original: "αἱρέσεως καὶ φυγῆς" – the fundamental Epicurean process of deciding what to pursue and what to shun</note>, and we return to it as we judge every good by using the feeling as our <term>standard</term>. <note>original: "κανόνι" (kanōn) – a ruler or measuring stick used to test truth</note> 

And since this is the primary and natural good, for this very reason we do not choose every pleasure. Instead, there are times when we pass over many pleasures when a greater discomfort follows from them; and we consider many pains to be better than pleasures, whenever a greater pleasure follows for us after we have endured those pains for a long time. 

Therefore, while every pleasure is a good because it has a nature akin to our own, not every pleasure is to be chosen; just as every pain is an evil, yet not every pain is always of a nature to be avoided. It is proper, however, to judge all these things by <term>comparative measurement</term> and by looking at the advantages and disadvantages. For there are times when we treat the good as an evil and, conversely, the evil as a good. 

We also consider **self-sufficiency** <note>original: "αὐτάρκεια" (autarkeia) – the state of needing very little from the outside world</note> to be a great good, not so that we may always use only a little, but so that if we do not have much, we may be content with the little we have. we are genuinely convinced that those who least need luxury enjoy it most pleasantly, and that everything natural is easy to procure, while that which is groundless <note>original: "κενόν" – literally "empty" or "vain," referring to artificial desires like fame or excessive wealth</note> is difficult to obtain. 

Plain flavors provide as much pleasure as a luxurious diet when all the pain of want is removed; indeed, bread and water provide the highest possible pleasure when someone in need partakes of them.

<summary>Epicurus defines the goal of life as "ataraxia" (tranquility) and "aponia" (absence of pain), arguing that pleasure is the standard for all choices, though some pleasures should be avoided if they lead to greater pain.</summary>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS #

### Page 429 ###

->EPICURUS. Book I.<-

Becoming accustomed, therefore, to simple and inexpensive diets is both productive of health and makes a person unshrinking in the face of the necessary requirements of life. And when we approach luxuries at intervals, it places us in a better condition and prepares us to be fearless towards <term>fortune</term> <note>original: "τύχην" (tychēn) – often personified as a goddess of luck or chance</note>. When, therefore, we say that pleasure is the goal <note>original: "τέλος" (telos)</note>, we do not mean the pleasures of the profligate and those that consist in sensual enjoyment—as some suppose who are ignorant and do not agree with us or who misunderstand our meaning—but rather the absence of pain in the body and of disturbance in the soul. 

For it is not continuous drinking bouts and revelry, nor the enjoyment of boys and women, nor of fish and the other delicacies that a luxurious table offers, which produces the pleasant life. Rather, it is <term>sober reasoning</term> <note>original: "νήφων λογισμὸς" (nēphōn logismos)</note>, which searches out the causes of every <term>choice and avoidance</term> and drives out the opinions from which the greatest turmoil takes hold of souls. 

Of all these things, the beginning and the greatest good is <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "φρόνησις" (phronēsis) – practical wisdom or the ability to make sound judgments</note>. For this reason, prudence is even more precious than philosophy, for from it all the other virtues spring; it teaches that it is not possible to live pleasantly without living prudently and honorably and justly, nor to live prudently, honorably, and justly without living pleasantly. For the virtues are naturally linked with living pleasantly, and living pleasantly is inseparable from these. 

For indeed, whom do you consider better than the one who holds pious opinions about the gods, and is always fearless regarding death, and has reasoned out the goal of nature? Such a person understands that the limit of good things is easy to fulfill and easy to obtain, while the limit of evils is either short in duration or short in intensity of suffering. He laughs at <term>Necessity</term> <note>original: "ἀνάγκην" (anankēn) – the idea that all events are predetermined</note>, which is introduced by some as the mistress of all things, and instead declares that some things happen by necessity, some by fortune, and some through our own agency. He sees that necessity is unaccountable and fortune is unstable, but what is <term>through us</term> <note>original: "παρ' ἡμᾶς" (par' hēmas) – the concept of free will or moral responsibility</note> is free from any master, and it is to this that praise and blame are naturally attached. 

For it would be better to follow the myths about the gods than to be a slave to the "Fate" <note>original: "εἱμαρμένῃ" (heimarmenē)</note> of the natural philosophers. For the myth offers a hope...

[The wise person] suggests the petitioning of the gods with honor; yet necessity possesses an unalterable compulsion. He does not regard <term>Fortune</term> <note>original: "τύχην" (tychēn)</note> as a goddess, as many people do—for nothing is done by a god in a disordered way—nor as an unstable cause. For he does not think that good or evil is given by her to humans to facilitate a blessed life, yet he believes the starting points for great goods or evils are provided by her. He considers it better to be <term>rationally unfortunate</term> <note>original: "εὐλογίστως ἀτυχεῖν" (eulogistōs atychein) – making the right choice even if it leads to a bad outcome</note> than to be irrationally fortunate. For it is better that what has been judged well in actions should be corrected through fortune. 

Therefore, meditate on these things and those related to them throughout the day and night, both by yourself and with someone like yourself, and you shall never be disturbed, whether awake or in a dream; rather, you shall live as a god among men. For a man who lives amidst immortal goods is in no way like a mortal animal. 

In other works, he rejects <term>divination</term> <note>original: "μαντικὴν" (mantikēn) – the practice of seeking knowledge of the future</note> entirely, as he also does in his *Brief Epitome*. He says: "Divination is non-existent; and even if it did exist, we should consider that what happens is nothing to us." So much he has discussed concerning the conduct of life, and even more elsewhere.

He differs from the <term>Cyrenaics</term> <note>A rival school of philosophy founded by Aristippus, which argued that intense, immediate physical pleasure was the only good.</note> concerning pleasure. For they do not approve of <term>static pleasure</term> <note>original: "καταστηματικὴν" (katastēmatikēn) – the pleasure of being in a state of equilibrium or lack of pain</note>, but only <term>pleasure in motion</term> <note>original: "ἐν κινήσει" (en kinēsei) – active, sensory enjoyment</note>. He, however, accepts both types, for both the soul and the body, as he says in his work *On Choice and Avoidance*, in his work *On the End*, in the first book of *On Lives*, and in his *Letter to friends in Mitylene*. Similarly, Diogenes in the sixteenth book of his *Selected Discourses* and Metrodorus in his *Timocrates* speak as follows: "Pleasure is understood as both that which is in motion and that which is static." And Epicurus in his work *On Choices* says: "For <term>tranquility</term> <note>original: "ἀταραξία" (ataraxia)</note> and <term>freedom from pain</term> <note>original: "ἀπονία" (aponia)</note> are static pleasures; but joy and gladness are seen as active pleasures in motion."

...[in the body] <note>original: "σώματι" (sōmati) – the first part of this word appeared on the previous page.</note> but he [Epicurus] argues for the pleasures of the soul. **I.** That which is blessed and immortal <note>i.e., the Divine or the Gods</note> has no troubles itself, nor does it cause them to another; so that it is constrained neither by anger nor by favor. For everything of this kind exists only in the weak.

**II.** Death is nothing to us; for that which has been dissolved lacks sensation; and that which lacks sensation is nothing to us.

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS #

### Page 432 ###

->DIOG. LAERT.<-

...in the flesh; but acute pain lasts only the shortest time. That which merely exceeds the pleasurable in the flesh <note>original: "τὸ δὲ μόνον ὑπερτεῖνον, τὸ ἡδόμενον κτ' σάρκα" — This refers to a state where the sensation is just barely more painful than pleasant.</note> does not persist for many days. Even long-term illnesses contain more that is pleasant in the flesh than that which is painful.

It is not possible to live pleasantly without living prudently, honorably, and justly, nor to live prudently, honorably, and justly without living pleasantly. <note>This is the famous fifth Principal Doctrine, arguing that virtue and pleasure are inseparable.</note> He for whom this is not the case does not live prudently and honorably; and he for whom justice is lacking cannot live pleasantly.

For the sake of feeling secure from other men, any means by which this can be provided is a natural good of power and kingship. Some have wished to become famous and conspicuous, thinking that in this way they would procure security from men. So, if the life of such men is secure, they have received the natural good; but if it is not secure, they do not possess that for the sake of which they originally reached out for it according to what is natural. <note>Epicurus argues that power and fame are only "goods" if they actually achieve the goal of safety; often, they do the opposite.</note>

No pleasure is a bad thing in itself; but the things which produce certain pleasures bring with them disturbances many times greater than the pleasures themselves.

If every pleasure were condensed in time and occurred throughout the whole organism or the most essential parts of our nature, pleasures would never differ from one another.

If the things that produce the pleasures of the <term>profligate</term> <note>original: "ἀσώτων" (asōtōn) — referring to those who live in excess or debauchery.</note> could dispel the fears of the mind—those concerning celestial phenomena and death and pain—and also teach the limits of desires, we would never have any reason to blame them, as they would be filled with pleasures from every side and have no pain or grief from any part, which is the essence of evil.

Furthermore, if we were not troubled by suspicions about celestial phenomena <note>original: "μετεώρων" (meteōrōn) — things in the sky, like thunder or eclipses, which ancients often feared as divine omens.</note> and about death (fearing that it might be something to us), and if we also understood the limits of pains and desires, we would have no need of <term>natural philosophy</term> <note>original: "φυσιολογίας" (physiologias) — the study of the laws of nature.</note>. It would not be possible to dispel fear about the most important matters if one did not know the nature of the whole universe but instead suspected something based on myths. Thus, without natural philosophy, it is not possible to receive unmixed pleasures.

# EPICURUS. Book 10. #

### Page 433 ###

->DIOG. LAERT.<-

...there would be no advantage in providing security against other men if things in the heavens above and things beneath the earth were still sources of dread, or in general, anything in the infinite universe. Security from other men is achieved to some extent, but the most unalloyed security <note>original: "εἰλικρινεστάτη... ἀσφάλεια" — meaning the purest or most refined form of safety</note> comes from the peace and withdrawal from the crowds.

The wealth required by nature is limited and easy to obtain, but the wealth desired by vain imaginings <note>original: "κενῶν δοξῶν" — referring to empty or false opinions about what one needs to be happy, such as fame or excessive luxury</note> extends to infinity. 

Chance has little impact on the wise man; for his greatest and most essential affairs are directed by reason, and are so directed throughout his whole life. 

The just man is the most free from trouble, but the unjust man is filled with the greatest confusion. 

Pleasure in the body does not increase once the pain of want <note>original: "τὸ κατ’ ἔνδειαν ἀλγοῦν" — specifically the physical suffering caused by hunger, thirst, or cold</note> is removed; it is only varied. The mind’s limit of pleasure is reached through reflection on these very things and those related to them, which used to provoke the greatest fears in the mind. 

Infinite time contains no more pleasure than finite time, if one measures the limits of pleasure by reason. The flesh perceives the limits of pleasure as infinite, and only infinite time could provide it. But the mind, having grasped the purpose and limit of the flesh and having dissolved fears about eternity <note>original: "τοὺς ὑπὲρ τοῦ αἰῶνος φόβους" — fears regarding the afterlife or the vastness of time</note>, has produced a perfect life and has no further need of infinite time. Yet the mind does not flee pleasure, nor does it feel it has missed out on the "unlimited life" when circumstances bring about its departure from living. 

He who understands the limits of life knows how easy it is to obtain that which removes the pain of want and makes the whole of life complete. Therefore, he has no need of things that involve competitive struggle. 

We must consider the ultimate goal we have set before us and all the clear evidence to which we refer our opinions; otherwise, everything will be full of uncertainty and confusion. 

If you fight against all your sensations, you will have no standard to which you can refer even those sensations you claim are false...

Ε. i.

<summary>This page lists several "Principal Doctrines" of Epicurus, emphasizing that true security comes from inner peace rather than power, and that pleasure is easily attained once the fear of the unknown and false desires are removed by reason.</summary>
<keywords>security, natural wealth, vain opinions, reason, justice, limits of pleasure, infinite time, sensations, Epicurean ethics</keywords>

# EPICURUS. Book 10. #

### Page 434 ###

->DIOG. LAERT.<-

...you judge the result. If you simply reject any single sense-perception <note>original: "αἴσθησιν" (aisthesis) — the basic information we receive through our eyes, ears, etc.</note>, and do not distinguish between what is a matter of opinion <note>original: "τὸ δοξαζόμενον" — beliefs we form that go beyond the raw data of the senses</note> based on what is expected to happen, and what is already present according to the senses, the feelings, and every mental apprehension <note>original: "φανταστικὴν ἐπιβολὴν τῆς διανοίας" — the way the mind focuses on an image or concept</note> of the intellect, you will throw even your remaining senses into confusion with your useless opinions, so that you will end up rejecting every standard of judgment <note>original: "κριτήριον" (kriterion) — the yardstick Epicurus used to determine truth</note> entirely. But if, in your ideas based on opinion, you treat as certain both that which awaits confirmation and that which does not, you will not escape error, for you will have preserved every cause for doubt in every judgment of what is correct or incorrect.

If you do not, on every occasion, refer each of your actions to the goal of nature <note>original: "τέλος τῆς φύσεως" — for Epicurus, this goal is the removal of pain and anxiety</note>, but instead turn aside to something else when you are pursuing or avoiding a thing, your actions will not be consistent with your principles.

Of the desires, those that do not lead to pain if they are not fulfilled are not necessary; instead, they involve a craving that is easily dispelled when the objects are difficult to obtain or seem likely to produce harm.

Of all the things which wisdom provides for the happiness of the whole of life, by far the greatest is the acquisition of friendship <note>original: "φιλίας κτῆσις" — Epicurus valued friendship as the highest earthly security</note>. The same conviction that gave us courage to believe that nothing terrible is eternal or even long-lasting, also saw that the security of friendship is most completely perfected within these very limited boundaries of life.

Of the desires, some are natural and necessary; others are natural but not necessary; and others are neither natural nor necessary, but arise instead from empty imagination <note>original: "κενὴν δόξαν" — false or groundless beliefs about what we need to be happy</note>. Epicurus considers those that release us from pain to be natural and necessary, such as drinking when we are thirsty. He considers natural but not necessary those which only vary the pleasure but do not remove the pain, such as expensive food <note>original: "πολυτελῆ σιτία" — literally "sumptuous meals"</note>. Finally, he considers those which are neither natural nor necessary to include things like crowns <note>original: "στεφάνους" — honorary wreaths given for public office or athletic victory</note> and the dedication of statues. In cases where natural desires do not lead to pain if unfulfilled, but are pursued with intense effort, such desires arise from empty imagination; they do not persist because of their own nature, but because of the person's vain conceit.

<summary>This page outlines Epicurus’s rules for clear thinking and his classification of desires, emphasizing that friendship and the fulfillment of basic natural needs are the keys to a happy life.</summary>

# EPICURUS. Book 10. #

### Page 435 ###

->EPICURUS<-

The justice of nature is a pledge <note>original: "σύμβολον" (symbolon) — a token, contract, or guarantee</note> of mutual advantage <note>original: "συμφέροντος" (sympherontos) — meaning utility or what is beneficial for the community</note>, to prevent people from harming one another or being harmed. For those animals that were unable to make covenants <note>original: "συνθήκας" (synthekas) — formal agreements or contracts</note> not to harm or be harmed, there is neither justice nor injustice. In the same way, for those nations that were either unable or unwilling to make covenants not to harm or be harmed, justice does not exist in an absolute sense. Instead, justice exists only in mutual associations, in whatever places and at whatever times a covenant is made not to harm or be harmed.

Injustice is not an evil in and of itself <note>Epicurus argues here that doing "wrong" isn't a mystical stain on the soul, but a practical social violation</note>, but rather consists in the fear born of the suspicion that one will not escape the notice of the punishers appointed over such matters. It is impossible for a person who secretly violates any of the agreements made with others (to not harm or be harmed) to be confident that he will remain undetected, even if he has escaped notice ten thousand times already. For until the very end of his life, it remains uncertain whether he will truly escape discovery.

In general terms, justice is the same for everyone, as it is a form of mutual advantage in social fellowship <note>original: "κοινωνίᾳ" (koinonia)</note>. However, when applied to specifics—such as particular locations or various other causes—it does not follow that the same thing is considered just for everyone.

Among those things held to be just by law, whatever is attested to be useful for the needs of mutual fellowship has the quality of justice, whether or not it turns out to be the same for everyone. But if someone establishes a law that does not result in mutual advantage for social fellowship, then it no longer possesses the nature of justice. Even if the utility regarding justice changes, but for a time it still fits the preconception <note>original: "πρόληψιν" (prolepsin) — the basic mental concept we have of what 'justice' should be</note> of it, it was nonetheless just during that time—at least for those who do not confuse themselves with empty words but look directly at the facts of the matter.

In cases where, although the circumstances have not changed, the established laws are shown in practice not to fit the preconception of justice, those laws were not actually just. On the other hand, in cases where circumstances have changed and the previously established laws are no longer...

<sig>E. ii.</sig>

# DIOGENES LAERTIUS: EPICURUS. Book 10. #

### Page 436 ###

->DIOG. LAERT. EPIC. Book 10<-

...justice in the actual practice of deeds, then those things were not just. But in cases where circumstances have changed and the established laws of justice no longer provide an advantage <note>original: "συνέφερε" (synephere) — meaning to be useful, profitable, or beneficial to the community</note>, then they were just only for as long as they contributed to the mutual association <note>original: "κοινωνίαν" (koinonian) — fellowship or communal living</note> of fellow citizens; later, they were no longer just when they ceased to bring that advantage.

The person who has best organized his sense of security against external threats has made those things that are possible akin <note>original: "ὁμόφυλα" (homophyla) — literally "of the same tribe"; here meaning he makes his surroundings friendly or compatible</note> to himself. As for those things where this was not possible, he at least ensured they were not treated as alien <note>original: "ἀλλόφυλα" (allophyla) — of a different tribe; here meaning hostile or "the other"</note>. Where even this was beyond his power, he avoided any interaction <note>original: "ἀνεπίμικτος" (anepikmiktos) — without mixing; staying unmingled or isolated for safety</note> and shut out everything that was beneficial to exclude.

Those who possessed the power to obtain the greatest security from their neighbors lived with one another in the most pleasant way, possessing the firmest pledge <note>original: "πίστωμα" (pistoma) — a guarantee, bond, or assurance of trust</note> of security. Having enjoyed the fullest intimacy, they did not lament the premature death <note>original: "προκαταστροφήν" (prokatastrophen) — a sudden overturning or early end to life</note> of a companion as if it were a cause for pity.

# FROM THE WORKS OF HIPPO-
->damus of Thurium, the Pythagorean, from<-
->his treatise On Happiness.<-

AMONG living beings, some are capable of achieving happiness <note>original: "εὐδαιμονίας" (eudaimonias) — often translated as "flourishing" or "well-being," referring to a life well-lived rather than a temporary emotion</note>, while others are incapable. Those capable of it are the beings who possess reason <note>original: "λόγον" (logon) — the capacity for rational thought, logic, and speech</note> (for happiness cannot exist apart from virtue; and virtue first arises in that which possesses reason). Those incapable of it are the beings that do not possess reason. For just as that which is deprived of sight cannot perform the work of sight or possess the excellence <note>original: "ἀρετάν" (aretan) — the "virtue" or specific "best-ness" of a thing</note> of sight, so that which lacks reason cannot perform the work of a rational being, nor possess the excellence of a rational being. Now, happiness and virtue belong to the rational being—the former as a finished deed <note>original: "ἔργον" (ergon) — the goal or functional outcome of a life</note>, and the latter as a kind of art <note>original: "τέχνα" (techna) — a systematic skill or craft</note>.

Among rational beings, some are self-sufficient <term>self-sufficient (autotelea): a being that is complete in itself and requires no external support to be perfect</term>, being perfect through themselves and needing nothing from the outside, neither for their existence nor for their well-being. Such a being would be God. Others are not self-sufficient, as they are not perfect through themselves, but require external causes. Such a being would be man. 

Among those who are not self-sufficient, some are complete <note>original: "τέλεα" (telea) — perfect or finished</note> and others are incomplete. Those who are complete are those who become so through both their own inner cause and through external causes. They achieve this through their own cause by contributing both a good nature and a deliberate choice <note>original: "προαίρεσιν" (proairesin) — a purposeful moral decision or "will"</note>; and through external causes, by [the absence of] lawlessness <note>original: "ἀνομίαν" (anomian) — the text breaks off here; it likely refers to being shaped by good laws or education</note>...

### FROM THE WRITINGS OF HIPPODAMUS OF THURIUM, THE PYTHAGOREAN

...and to receive good attendants. But those beings are not perfect <note>original: "τέλεα" (telea) — meaning complete, finished, or having reached an intended goal</note> who either share in neither of these, or in only one of them, or who are altogether base according to the rational principle of the soul. Such would be the condition of the other kind of man.

Of perfect men, however, there are two varieties: for some of them are perfect according to nature, while others are perfect according to their way of life. Those who are perfect according to nature are those who are solely "the good." These would be the ones possessing virtue <note>original: "ἀρετάν" (aretan) — excellence or moral virtue</note>. For virtue is the peak and the perfection of the nature of each thing. In the eye, virtue is the peak and perfection of the eye's nature. In a man, virtue is the peak and perfection of a man's nature.

Those who are perfect according to their way of life are those who are not only good, but also happy <note>original: "εὐδαίμονες" (eudaimones) — flourishing, or favored by a good spirit</note>. For happiness is the perfection of human life. Now, human life is a system of actions, and it is happiness that brings these actions to a successful conclusion. Two things bring actions to a conclusion: virtue and fortune <note>original: "τύχα" (tycha) — luck, chance, or divine providence</note>. Virtue does so through the proper use of things, while fortune does so through providing a successful outcome.

Now, God did not become good by learning virtue from someone else, nor did He become happy by fortune happening to Him. For He was good by nature, and happy by nature; He always was, and always shall be, and He will never cease to be so, being incorruptible and good by nature. 

Man, however, is not happy by nature, but stands in need of instruction and foresight. To become good, he needs virtue; to become happy, he needs fortune. Because of this, human happiness is summed up by two things: praise and congratulation. Praise is given for the merit arising from virtue, while congratulation <note>original: "μακαρισμῷ" (makarismō) — the recognition of one's outward prosperity or "blessed" state</note> is given for the success arising from fortune. 

A man possesses virtue through a divine portion, but he possesses fortune through a mortal one. Yet mortal things are dependent upon the gods, and things on earth are dependent upon heavenly things; the inferior things are ever dependent upon the superior. And for this reason, the man who follows the gods is good.

<summary>Hippodamus distinguishes between perfection of nature (virtue) and perfection of life (happiness), arguing that while God is inherently both, humans must acquire virtue through learning and happiness through a combination of merit and good fortune.</summary>
<keywords>Hippodamus of Thurium, Pythagorean ethics, virtue, happiness, nature vs. life, divine vs. mortal, fortune, eudaimonia, arete</keywords>

### IN THE TREATISE ON HAPPINESS

...is happy, but the one who follows mortal things is unhappy. For to the person who possesses wisdom <note>original: "φρόνασιν" (phronasin) — practical wisdom or prudence</note>, good fortune is a good and useful thing. It is good because of the knowledge of how to use it, and beneficial because it works together with one's actions. It is a beautiful thing, then, when good fortune is present alongside the mind; it is like a fair wind for one running toward virtue, keeping one's eyes on the goal while performing actions, just as a pilot <note>original: "κυβερνάταν" (kybernatan) — a ship's helmsman</note> looks toward the movements of the stars. For in this way, a person will not only follow God, but will also align human good with the divine.

Furthermore, this much is clear: that life becomes varied based on disposition and action. Necessarily, the disposition must be either excellent or base; while the action must be either happy or unhappy. The disposition is excellent if it partakes of virtue, and base if it partakes of vice. As for actions, they are happy when they occur in the midst of good fortune (for they are then brought to their intended conclusion according to reason), but they are unhappy in the midst of misfortune, for misfortune causes a failure to reach that conclusion.

Therefore, it is necessary not only to learn virtue, but also to possess it and to use it—whether for security, or for growth, or (what is greatest of all) for the restoration of households and cities. For one must not only possess noble things, but also have the enjoyment and benefit of them. All these things will be possible if a man happens to live in a city governed by good laws <note>original: "εὐνομουμένας" (eunomoumenas) — characterized by 'eunomia' or good order</note>.

Indeed, I claim that this state of affairs is what is called the Horn of Amalthea <note>The "Cornucopia" or horn of plenty, a symbol of inexhaustible abundance in Greek mythology</note>. For in good order all things exist; and without it, the greatest good of human nature can neither be born, nor, once born and grown, could it endure and remain. For good order encompasses virtue itself and the path toward virtue, because good natures are born under its influence; and under it, habits, practices, and the laws themselves are the best. Furthermore, it fosters right-thinking reasons, as well as piety and holiness toward the most honored things. So that for one who intends to be happy...

E.iiii.

**Vocabulary from this page:** happiness, virtue, good fortune, the Horn of Amalthea, good order, wisdom, action.

<summary>Hippodamus explains that happiness requires a "fair wind" of good fortune aligned with a virtuous mind, and argues that such human excellence can only truly flourish within a well-governed society (Eunomia).</summary>
<keywords>virtue, good fortune, wisdom, Eunomia, good laws, Horn of Amalthea, Pythagorean ethics, social order, divine alignment</keywords>

->### FROM THE WRITINGS OF HIPPODAMUS OF THURII THE PYTHAGOREAN<-

...and he will keep his own life "straight-sailing," <note>original: "ὀρθόπλοον" (orthoploon) — a nautical metaphor for a life that stays on a true course despite external storms.</note> even when lawlessness is present; he must pass through and go beyond it, leaving lawlessness behind. At the same time, this argument adds a sense of necessity to what was said previously. For a human being is a part of a community. By these means, a person becomes complete <note>original: "ὁλόκλαρος" (holoklaros) — entire, perfect in all parts, or whole.</note> according to the same principle: not just by participating in society, but by participating *well*.

For some things are natural to the many, but not to the individual; some are in the individual, but not in the many; and some are in both the many and the individual. Indeed, certain things are in the individual precisely because they are in the many.

For example, **harmony**, **symphony**, and **number** <note>These are core Pythagorean concepts where mathematical ratios create beauty and order.</note> are natural to the many. For no single part is self-sufficient enough to create the "whole" that these components produce. On the other hand, keenness of hearing, sharpness of sight, and swiftness of feet exist in the individual alone.

But **happiness** and **virtue of the soul** exist in the individual, in the many, in the whole, and in the universe. And for this reason, they exist in the individual because they also exist in the many; and they exist in the many because they exist in the whole and in the universe. For the organized arrangement <note>original: "διακόσμασις" (diakosmasis) — the act of ordering or the resulting world-order.</note> of each individual part is derived from the nature of the whole. Furthermore, the organized arrangement of each individual part completes the whole and the universe.

This follows because, by nature, the **whole** is prior to the **part**, rather than the part being prior to the whole. For if the <term>cosmos</term> <note>The Greek "kosmos" implies not just the world, but the world as a beautiful, ordered system.</note> did not exist, neither the sun, nor the moon, nor the wandering stars <note>The planets.</note>, nor the fixed stars would exist. But because the cosmos exists, each of these exists as well.

One can see this same principle at work in the nature of living animals. If the animal did not exist, there would be no eye, no mouth, and no hearing. But because the animal exists, each of these parts exists. Just as the whole relates to the part, so does the virtue of the whole relate to the virtue of the part. For if there were no divine **harmony** and <term>eunomia</term> <note>original: "εὐνομία" (eunomia) — "good order" or "well-ordered laws." It suggests a state where laws are both good and obeyed.</note> throughout the cosmos, the things arranged within it could no longer be maintained in a good state. Similarly, if "good order" did not exist within cities, no one could be good or happy...

<summary>Hippodamus argues that humans reach completion through community and that the "whole" (the cosmos or society) naturally precedes and defines the "part" (the individual). He concludes that individual virtue and happiness are impossible without the "good order" of the larger system.</summary>

# FROM THE WRITINGS OF
## EURYPHAMUS the Pythagorean, from the
## treatise "On Life."

A perfect human life falls short of the divine, in that it is not self-sufficient <note>original: "αὐτελὴς" (auteles) — meaning complete in itself or independent of external needs.</note>, but it surpasses the irrational animals because it has a share in **virtue** and **happiness**. For God is not in need of external causes; being good by nature and happy by nature, He is perfect within Himself. Nor are any of the irrational animals [in need of such things], for being without a share of reason <note>original: "λόγω" (logo) — here meaning the faculty of logic and speech.</note>, they are also without a share in the knowledge required for purposeful actions. 

But human nature is in need of some things from its own **free choice** <note>original: "προαιρέσιος" (proairesios) — the power of deliberate moral choice.</note>, and others from the assistance <note>original: "ἐπικουρήσιος" (epikouresios) — support or reinforcement, often implying divine grace or help from the gods.</note> that comes from the divine. For by reason, the human is capable of being molded and of perceiving both the beautiful and the shameful; and by being naturally inclined to stand upright away from the earth and look up toward heaven, the human is capable of perceiving the eternal gods. These faculties have obtained assistance from the gods...

<meta>This page continues the Pythagorean discourse of Euryphamus. <page-num>442</page-num>

<header>FROM THE WRITINGS OF EURYPHAMUS THE PYTHAGOREAN</header>

...[ability] to possess will and choice and to have within himself such a governing principle <note>original: "ἀρχὰν" (archan) — a starting point, origin, or ruling power.</note>, through which he is his own master. He is able to practice **virtue** or to pursue **vice**, and thus to be either brought near to the gods or separated from them. Man is capable of moving himself through these internal faculties. Because of this, he meets with praise or blame, honor or dishonor—some from the gods and some from men—depending on whether he has pursued virtue or vice.

For the whole argument stands thus: The Divine established man, the most precious of living creatures, within the **cosmos** <note>original: "κόσμον" (kosmon) — in Greek, this word implies both the 'universe' and 'orderly beauty.'</note> as a counterpart to His own nature, and as an "eye" to observe the arrangement of all that exists. For this reason, man gave names to things, acting as their interpreter <note>original: "χαρακτὴρ" (charaktēr) — one who marks or defines the character of a thing.</note>, and he discovered letters, providing a treasury for memory. 

He also imitated the arrangement of the universe, fitting together the fellowship of cities with justice and laws. For no work performed by men is so magnificent or worthy of the gods as the harmonization of a well-ordered city, and the arrangement of its laws and government. For each individual human being, existing only as himself, is nothing; he is not sufficient unto himself for life unless he is joined with others in the common consensus and harmonization of a political state, becoming well-adapted to the whole and perfect system of society. 

For human life is like the image of a **lyre** <note>The lyre was the primary instrument of the Pythagoreans, who believed music and mathematics revealed the secrets of the universe.</note> that has been perfectly tuned and completed in every detail. Every lyre requires three things to function: preparation, harmonization, and a certain musical touch. 

**Preparation** consists of the readiness of all the physical parts of the instrument—I mean the strings and the mechanical tools that contribute to the beauty of the sound and the striking of the notes. **Harmonization** <note>original: "συναρμογὰ" (sunarmoga) — a fitting together of disparate parts into a unified whole.</note> is the blending of the tones with one another. And the **musical touch** is the actual movement of these parts according to that harmony.

In the same way, the life of man also requires these three things. "Preparation" is the gathering of the various components of life. And these components of life include the goods of the body, wealth, reputation, and friends.

<summary>Euryphamus argues that humans are defined by their free will and their role as the "eye" of the cosmos, mirroring the divine order by creating cities and laws. He introduces a musical metaphor, comparing a successful human life to a well-tuned lyre that requires physical preparation, social harmony, and active practice.</summary>

<keywords>free will, virtue, vice, cosmos, naming, invention of writing, political harmony, lyre metaphor, Pythagoras, preparation, social order</keywords>

# ON THE CONDUCT OF LIFE

...[joined with others.] <note>Continuing from the previous page's discussion on the necessity of human society.</note> Social harmony is the organization of these elements according to **virtue** <term>aretā: often translated as excellence or moral virtue</term> and the laws. Musical resonance is the blending of these same elements according to virtue and the laws, as they are steered straight by the virtues and allow nothing from the outside to disrupt them. For **flourishing** <note>original: "εὐδαιμονῆν" (eudaimonēn) — often translated as happiness, but implying a state of living well or "blessedness."</note> does not consist merely in having noble intentions or voluntary goals, but in successfully achieving them. Nor does it consist in virtue being left without protection or service; rather, it is found in virtue being brought to fulfillment through its own inherent powers directed toward action.

For man is not self-sufficient but incomplete. His completion depends partly on himself and partly on external causes. There is a twofold completion: one according to nature and the other according to the way of life.

The completion according to nature occurs when a person becomes good. For the **virtue** of any thing is the summit and completion of its nature. For example, the nature of the eyes reaches its summit and completion in sight; the nature of the ears, in hearing. In the same way, virtue is the summit and completion of human nature.

The completion according to the way of life occurs when a person becomes happy. For **happiness** <note>original: "εὐδαιμονία" (eudaimonia)</note> is the perfection and fulfillment of all human goods. Thus, virtue and **good fortune** <term>eutychia: external success or luck, as opposed to internal character</term> become the components of this life: virtue acts as the soul, and good fortune as the body; together, they constitute life like a living creature.

One part involves the noble use of natural goods, while the other provides the opportunity for that use. Virtue provides the use, while good fortune provides the opportunity. And while the former provides deliberate choice and right reason, the latter provides the activities and the results. For wishing for what is noble and enduring what is terrible is the proper domain of virtue. However, steering those choices straight <note>original: "ὀρθοπλοῆσαι" (orthoploēsai) — literally "to sail a straight course."</note> and bringing actions to a successful conclusion is the domain of good fortune. For a general wins a victory through both virtue and good fortune; and the pilot <note>original: "κυ[βερνάτας]" (kybernātas) — the steersman or pilot of a ship.</note> sails...

<summary>Euryphamus argues that a fulfilled life requires both internal virtue (the soul of life) and external good fortune (the body of life), using metaphors of navigation and military victory to show how character and circumstance work together.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, happiness, good fortune, nature, Euryphamus, Pythagorean ethics, human flourishing, social harmony</keywords>

# FROM THE WRITINGS
## of Hipparchus the Pythagorean,
### from the work
#### On Tranquility of Mind. <term>euthymia: literally "good-spiritedness," a state of mental calm and cheerfulness.</term>

When considering the whole of eternity, human beings possess a very short span of life. Therefore, they should make the best of this life as if it were a kind of **brief stay in a foreign land** <note>original: "παρεπιδημίαν" (parepidēmian) — a temporary residence or pilgrimage, suggesting that life is a journey rather than a permanent home.</note>, not spending it in despair. This will be achieved most of all by those who accurately understand and recognize within themselves that they are mortal and made of flesh, possessing a body that is frail and corruptible, with the most difficult things hanging over them until their final breath.

And first, let us lament the things that happen to the body: **pleurisy**, **pneumonia**, **madness**, **gout**, **strangury** <term>difficulty or pain in urinating</term>, **dysentery**, **lethargy**, **epilepsy**, **putrefaction**, and a thousand other things. But regarding the soul, the troubles are much greater and more difficult. For all the lawless, evil, illegal, and impious things in life arise from the **passions** <note>original: "παθημάτων" (pathēmatōn) — the irrational emotions or sufferings that overwhelm reason.</note> of the soul. For because of those unnatural and immoderate...

[...of] **desires** <note>original: "ἐπιθυμίας" (epithymias) — the first half of the word was on the preceding page.</note>, many have run aground into uncontrollable impulses; they did not even abstain from the most unholy pleasures involving their own daughters or mothers. Some even succumbed to **child-murder** <term>paidoktonia: the act of killing one's own child</term>, and many slaughtered their own offspring. 

And what of the external things hanging over us? Consider heavy rains, droughts, excessive heat, and excessive cold. Often, from these irregularities in the atmosphere, **plague** <term>loimos</term> and **famine** <term>limos</term> arise, along with a variety of all sorts of misfortunes, causing entire cities to be made desolate.

Since many such things hang over us, let us not be prideful or obsessed with bodily health, which, by a blow from the gods <note>original: "σὺν θεῶν τύπῳ" — this suggests a sudden stroke of fate or divine intervention.</note>, quickly withers away if even a small fever comes on. Nor should we cling to these external things thought of as "good fortune." By their very nature, these things are often destroyed more quickly than they are created. 

For we have learned that all these things are unstable and insecure, existing within a state of many and varied **transformations** <term>metabolai: the constant shifting or changing of circumstances</term>. None of them are permanent, nor immovable, nor certain, nor indivisible. 

Therefore, having considered these things well—and realizing that if what we have now can endure for even the shortest time—we shall live in **tranquility** <term>euthymia: a state of cheerfulness or mental calm</term>, bearing nobly whatever befalls us. 

But as it stands, many people take everything provided to them by **nature** <term>physis</term> and **fortune** <term>tyche</term> and imagine them to be better than they truly are. They do not consider things as they really are, but as they might be if they reached the very height of success. Then, when they are suddenly deprived of these things, they weigh down their souls with many great, lawless, and foolish evils. 

And so it happens that they lead a most bitter and difficult life. This occurs when they lose money, or when friends or children die, or when they lose any of those other things we consider most precious. Then, weeping and wailing, they say:

<meta>This page continues the philosophical reflection from page 445, moving from the instability of external fortune to a psychological strategy for enduring hardship by comparing one's lot to others and seeking healing through philosophy.</meta>

<page-num>446</page-num>

<header>FROM THE WRITINGS OF HIPPARCHUS THE PYTHAGOREAN</header>

[...to think themselves] the only ones most unfortunate and ill-fated, not remembering that these same things have happened to many others, and are happening even now. They are unable to consider the lives of those presently living and those who have already departed—amidst how many disasters and **triple-waves** <note>original: "τρικυμίαις" (trikymaiais) — an ancient Greek idiom referring to an exceptionally large wave, symbolizing an overwhelming series of misfortunes.</note> of evils many people are now, and have been before. 

Therefore, having reasoned that many who lost their wealth were later saved by that very loss—perhaps because they would have otherwise fallen into the hands of bandits or a tyrant—and many who loved certain people with excessive folly, in later times came to hate them greatly. 

Having weighed all these things in the histories handed down to us, and having learned that many were destroyed even by their own children and most beloved friends; and by comparing their own life to the even more wretched lives of those who will come hereafter, and considering that these occurrences are merely human and do not happen to us alone, we shall lead a less despondent life. 

For it is not right for a human being to consider the painful accidents of others as unbearable, but rather to look at their own sorrows, seeing that many **fates** <term>keres: personified spirits of doom or the natural causes of death and destruction</term> are naturally present throughout all of life. 

Those who weep and lament—besides showing no benefit at all to the one who is perishing or the one who has departed—drive the soul into greater sufferings. Since the soul exists in the midst of many base "blasts" <note>The author uses a metaphor of the soul being tossed by gusts of passion or external pressures.</note>, it is necessary to sober up, to purify oneself, and to scrub away by every means the **hardened stains** <note>original: "ἐγκατεσκιῤῥωμένας κηλίδας" (enkateskirrhōmenas kēlidas) — a medical metaphor referring to stains that have become calloused or tumor-like (scirrhous).</note> through the reasoning found in philosophy. 

We shall do this by holding fast to **wisdom** <term>phronesis: practical wisdom or prudence</term> and **temperance** <term>sophrosyne: excellence of character and soundness of mind</term>, by being content with what is present, and by not grasping for many things. For while most people prepare many things as if it were not possible to live after the time of this life is over, let us instead make use of the good things at hand. Through the beautiful and solemn things of philosophy, we shall be liberated from base **insatiability** <term>aplestia: a greed or craving that can never be filled</term>.

<summary>Hipparchus argues that perspective and philosophy are the cures for grief, noting that personal misfortunes are universal and that the loss of wealth or love can often be a hidden blessing. He advocates for the use of reason to scrub away the emotional "stains" of life and find contentment in the present.</summary>

<keywords>Hipparchus, Pythagoreanism, grief, misfortune, philosophy as therapy, Phronesis, Sophrosyne, insatiability, perspective</keywords>

# FROM THE WRITINGS OF ARCHYTAS
## the Pythagorean, from the work *On the*
### *Good and Happy*
### *Man.*

First of all, one must know this: that while the good man is not necessarily happy by definition, the happy man is always a good man. For the happy man is someone who is both praised and called "blessed," while the good man is praised alone. Praise is given for **virtue** <term>arete: excellence of character or moral merit</term>, but the state of being "blessed" is given for **good fortune** <term>eutychia: external success, health, and prosperity</term>. A good man becomes such because of the goods within himself; but the happy man is one whose **happiness** <term>eudaimonia: a state of flourishing or "well-being," often seen as the ultimate goal of life</term> cannot be easily taken away. 

For the power of the virtues is not subject to the "audit" of external circumstances, while happiness is indeed "held to account" by them. Long illnesses of the body and the loss of the senses wither the blooming health of happiness. 

God differs from a good human in this way: God possesses virtue that is not only pure and filtered from every mortal passion, but he also possesses a power that is tireless and absolute, fitting for the majesty and magnificence of eternal works. A human, however, possesses a lesser degree of virtue, not only because of the mortal condition of their nature, but also because at times—through a lack of good influences, through the weight of strong habit, through a flawed nature, or many other causes—a person is unable to become **perfectly and truly good** <note>original: "παναλαθέως ἀγαθός" (panalatheōs agathos) — referring to an ideal of moral perfection rarely reached by mortals.</note>.

Now, since among "goods," some are chosen for their own sake and not for another, while others are chosen for the sake of something else and not for themselves...

<summary>Archytas defines the distinction between moral goodness (virtue) and happiness (blessedness), arguing that while virtue is internal and stable, true happiness also requires external health and fortune. He further contrasts the perfect, tireless virtue of God with the flawed and limited potential for goodness in human beings.</summary>

<keywords>Archytas of Tarentum, Pythagorean ethics, virtue vs. happiness, eudaimonia, arete, divine vs. human nature, moral philosophy, good fortune</keywords>
