<meta>This page continues the discourse by Archytas on the nature of "the Good," shifting from the distinction between the Good Man and the Happy Man to a formal classification of various types of "Goods." It echoes the Peripatetic and Pythagorean tradition of dividing goods into those of the soul, body, and external circumstances.</meta>

<page-num>448</page-num>

<header># FROM THE WRITINGS OF ARCHYTAS THE PYTHAGOREAN</header>

There is also a third species of good, which is desirable both for its own sake and for the sake of something else. Now, which of these goods are those that are naturally desirable to us for their own sake and not for the sake of another? It is clear that **happiness** <term>eudaimonia: a state of flourishing or "well-being," the ultimate goal of human life</term> is such a thing. For we choose all other things for the sake of happiness, but we choose happiness itself for the sake of nothing else.

And what, in turn, are the things we choose for the sake of another, but never for their own sake? Clearly, these are the **useful** things and those that involve the **choice of means** <note>original: "proairetika" - things chosen as tools or steps toward a goal</note> which become the causes of the things we truly desire. For example, bodily labor, exercise, and **massages** <note>original: "tripsies" - therapeutic rubbing or friction, common in ancient athletics</note> are for the sake of **fitness** <term>euexia: a state of physical "well-being" or a "good habit" of the body</term>; while reading, study, and disciplined practices are for the sake of noble things and **virtue** <term>arete: excellence of character or moral merit</term>.

And what things are chosen both for their own sake and for the sake of another? For instance, the virtues and the habits of mind that produce them, as well as our choices, our actions, and everything that partakes in the essence of the **Noble** <note>original: "tou kalou" - often translated as "the Beautiful" or "the Fine," referring to moral excellence</note>. Thus, that which is desirable for itself and not for another is a singular and unique good. 

But that which is chosen both for itself and for another is divided into three parts: for one part concerns the **soul**, another the **body**, and the third is **external**. 
* Regarding the soul, there are the virtues of the soul. 
* Regarding the body, there are the virtues of the body. 
* And external goods are friends, glory, honor, and wealth. 

Similarly, there are things chosen only for the sake of others: some produce goods for the soul, others for the body, and the external ones are the causes of wealth, glory, honor, and friendship.

That we happen to choose virtue itself for its own sake is clear from this: if we choose those things which are naturally inferior—I mean the goods of the body—for their own sake, and the soul is superior to the body, it is manifest that we must also love the goods of the soul for themselves, and not merely for the results that follow from them.

There are three conditions in human life: one in **prosperity** <term>eutychia: good fortune or success</term>, one in **adversity** <term>atychia: misfortune or "bad luck"</term>, and one that is between these. Since a good man is one who possesses virtue and uses it, he employs it throughout these three conditions: for he acts either in prosperity, or in adversity, <meta>catchword: or in the...</meta>

<summary>Archytas categorizes "goods" into those desired for themselves (happiness), those desired for other ends (exercise, study), and those desired for both (virtue). He argues that because the soul is superior to the body, the virtues of the soul must be loved for their own sake.</summary>

<page-num>449</page-num>

-> # IN THE TREATISE ON THE GOOD MAN AND THE HAPPY ONE <-

...or in the states between these. In misfortune, a person is wretched; in good fortune, they are happy; but in the middle state, they are not happy. It is clear, then, that **happiness** <term>eudaimonia: the state of flourishing or living well</term> is nothing other than the use of **virtue** <term>arete: moral or functional excellence</term> in a state of good fortune. Now, we are speaking of happiness as it pertains to a human being. But a human being is not the soul alone, but also the body. For the living being composed of both, and from such elements, is a human being. For even if the body is naturally the tool of the soul, it is also a part of the human being, just as the soul is.

Therefore, among "goods," some belong to the human being as a whole, while others belong to the parts. The good of the human being as a whole is happiness. Of the parts of the human: the goods of the **soul** <term>psyche: the animating principle or mind</term> are **practical wisdom** <term>phronesis: the ability to govern oneself by use of reason</term>, courage, justice, and moderation; while the goods of the body are beauty, health, fitness, and keen senses. 

External things, such as wealth, fame, honor, and noble birth, are naturally added to us, the human being, and follow upon the naturally preexisting goods. The lesser goods act as a **bodyguard** <note>original: "doruphoreitai" - literally to carry a spear as a guard for a king; implies that external goods protect and support the higher ones</note> to the greater ones. Friendship, fame, and wealth support the body and soul; health, strength, and sensation support the soul; while practical wisdom, courage, moderation, and justice support the **intellect** <term>noos: the highest part of the mind or spirit</term> of the soul; and the intellect supports **God**.

For God is the strongest and the leader; and for the sake of these, the other goods are always present. For a general leads an army, a pilot leads sailors, God leads the world, the intellect leads the soul, and practical wisdom leads the happiness found in life. For practical wisdom is nothing else than the **science** <term>episteme: organized, certain knowledge</term> of the happiness of life, or the science of those things that are naturally good for a human being.

And for God, happiness and the best life are inherent; but for a human, happiness comes through being completed by science, virtue, and thirdly, good fortune. By "science," I mean **wisdom** <note>original: "sophia"</note> concerning divine and spiritual matters, and "practical wisdom" <note>original: "phronesis"</note> concerning human affairs and the business of life. For by arguments and demonstrations...

<page-num>450</page-num>

-> ### FROM THE ANCIENT WRITINGS OF THE PYTHAGOREANS ### <-

...practicing virtues, it is necessary to call them **sciences** <note>original: "epistamas" - a Doric form of episteme, referring to organized, certain knowledge rather than mere opinion</note>. For **virtues** <term>aretai: moral excellences or strengths</term> are the ethical and best disposition of the irrational part of the soul, according to which we are said to be of a certain quality in our character—for instance, generous, just, and moderate. 

**Adversity** <note>original: "atychian" - literally "ill-fortune." While some versions of this text use "eutychia" (good fortune), this manuscript emphasizes the use of virtue during hardship</note>, on the other hand, is the presence of goods that occurs contrary to reason and not through one's own efforts. Since virtue and science are within our power, while adversity is not; and since happiness consists in the contemplations and actions of noble things—and while these contemplations and actions, being of such a kind, bring about service and necessity, they yet yield a way of life and happiness—and since these things occur in the midst of adversity, it is clear that happiness is nothing other than the **use of virtue in adversity**. 

For the good man is so disposed toward adversity just as one who is physically healthy and robust is toward his body. For such a man is able to endure both heat and cold, to lift a great weight, and to withstand many other difficult hardships.

Since, then, happiness is the use of virtue in adversity, let us speak about virtue and **good fortune** <term>eutychia: success or prosperity granted by luck</term>, and first about good fortune. For among goods, some do not admit of excess, such as virtue. For there is no such thing as an "excessive virtue," nor can one be "excessively good." For virtue has **the fitting** <note>original: "to deon" - the appropriate, the "must-be," or duty</note> as its standard, and it is a disposition of the fitting in practical affairs. 

But good fortune admits of both excess and deficiency. When it is excessive, it breeds certain vices and drives a human being out of their natural disposition, so that it often even opposes the very constitution of virtue. And it is not only good fortune that does this, but many other causes as well. For one should never be surprised if there are some boasters among us in the art of flute-playing, who, having abandoned the truth, always flow toward some false fantasy in an unartistic way. But concerning virtue, such a class of people does not exist. But...

<summary>This page defines virtue as the best state of the irrational soul and argues that true happiness is the exercise of this virtue even when facing ill-fortune. It distinguishes virtue, which is always balanced, from good fortune, which can be dangerous in excess.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Pythagorean ethics attributed to Archytas. While the previous page defined happiness as the "use of virtue in adversity," this section explores the difficulty of judging a person's true character and warns that prosperity can be more spiritually dangerous than hardship.</meta>

<page-num>451</page-num>

-> ### FROM THE TREATISE ON THE GOOD AND FORTUNATE MAN ### <-

For the more noble a subject is, the more numerous are the challenges that come against it. Many factors distort the outward appearances of the virtues. One is the class of those who plot against them <note>original: "epibouleuontōn" — those who actively scheme or harbor ill-will against virtuous people</note>, which falls upon them from the outside. Other distortions arise from natural passions that sometimes follow a person, creating an outward appearance <term>epiprepeian: a surface-level impression or decorum</term> that is the opposite of their true inner disposition. 

Some of these distortions are nurtured through habits formed over a long period; many others arise from the stages of life—both in youth and in old age—or from good fortune, or even from misfortune, and from countless other circumstances. Therefore, one should never be surprised if judgments are sometimes completely skewed, diverging from a person's true inner character.

Just as we might see the best carpenter making many mistakes in the tasks before him—and the same for a general, a pilot, a painter, and absolutely everyone else—we do not, for that reason, strip them of their established skill <note>original: "hexis" — a stable habit or state of being</note>. In the same way, we must not rank a man among the wicked just because he loses self-control in certain moments, nor because he does wrong or acts like a coward. Nor, indeed, should we rank those who happen to do something right among the truly good.

Rather, we must allow for the possibility of chance success in base men, and for the possibility of error in good men. To reach a true judgment, we must not look at a single moment, nor even at a substantial length of time, but at the whole of a life. 

For just as the body is harmed by both deficiency and excess, it is excess <note>original: "hyperbola" — overabundance or surplus</note> that is naturally inclined to produce greater diseases and what are called "superfluities" <term>peristomata: metabolic residues or waste products that the Greeks believed caused illness</term>. In the same way, the soul is harmed by both good and bad fortune when they arrive at the wrong time; yet, what is called "good fortune" by everyone is naturally inclined to cause greater diseases. Like wine, it intoxicates the mind of even good men.

Therefore, it is not harder to bear misfortune gracefully, but rather to bear good fortune. For everyone remains [steadfast] in misfortune...

<sig>F. ii.</sig>

<summary>This page argues that a person's character should be judged by their entire life rather than isolated actions, and warns that prosperity is more likely to corrupt the soul than hardship.</summary>
<keywords>Archytas, Pythagorean ethics, virtue, character judgment, prosperity vs. adversity, moral health, good fortune</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the variability of human character. The previous page ended by noting that just as we do not judge a professional by a single mistake, we should not judge a person's entire character based on a single act of weakness or a single stroke of luck.</meta>

<page-num>452</page-num>

-> ### FROM THE WORKS OF THEAGES THE PYTHAGOREAN ### <-

...for the most part, people follow a certain course and appear orderly in character to us; yet in times of success, they show themselves as brave, high-minded, and great-souled. For misfortune has the power to draw the soul together and set it in order, whereas success, by contrast, tends to puff it up and make it hollow <note>original: "kenōsai" — to empty out or make vain; here meaning that prosperity can make a person superficial</note>. Therefore, all those experiencing misfortune are persuasive and prudent in their manner, while those experiencing success are aggressive and bold in their ways. 

The boundary of good fortune <term>eutychia: literally 'good luck' or external prosperity</term> is when a good man takes it up as a partner to assist him in his own actions. It is like the size of a temple, or the size of a rudder, which a good pilot can use to guide a vessel while crossing great seas or setting out on a great voyage. However, an excess of good fortune is not naturally governed by the soul; rather, it governs the soul. Just as a brilliant light causes a blurring of vision in the eyes <note>original: "maraugian" — a dazzling or dimming of sight caused by excessive brightness</note>, so too does excessive good fortune dazzle the intellect of the soul. Let this be enough said regarding good fortune.

# THEAGES THE PY-
## thagorean, from the
## treatise on virtues.

The internal order of the soul is likewise structured. One part of it is reasoning <term>logismos: the rational or calculating faculty</term>, another is spiritedness <term>thymōsis: the seat of anger, courage, and impulse</term>, and the third is desire <term>epithymia: the appetitive part of the soul driven by physical needs</term>. Reasoning is that which governs knowledge; spirit is that which governs impulse; and desire is that which governs the appetitive part without restraint. When, therefore, these three come together into one...

<note>The text concludes with the famous "tripartite soul" model, which was central to both Pythagorean and Platonic philosophy, suggesting that virtue is the harmony of these three distinct parts of the human psyche.</note>

<page-num>453</page-num>
<header>IN THE TREATISE ON VIRTUES.</header>
<page-type>text</page-type>

...having received a single harmonious arrangement, then virtue and concord arise in the soul; but when the parts are in conflict and pulled away from each other, then vice and disharmony arise in the soul. Virtue must necessarily possess these three things: reason, power, and deliberate choice <term>proairesis: the moral intention or "will" behind an action</term>. In the **reasoning** part of the soul, the virtue is **prudence** <note>original: "phronēsis" — practical wisdom or the ability to discern the right course of action</note>. For it is a state of mind capable of judging and contemplating. In the **spirited** part, the virtue is **courage**; for it is a state that resists and withstands terrifying things. In the **appetitive** part, the virtue is **temperance** <note>original: "sōphrosynē" — self-control or moderation</note>. For it is a moderation and restraint of the pleasures that come through the body. And in the **soul as a whole**, the virtue is **justice**. For indeed, men become base either through vice, or through incontinence, or through ferocity. They do wrong to one another either for the sake of profit, or for pleasure, or for ambition. 

Now, vice is more properly associated with the **reasoning** part of the soul. For prudence is like a craft <note>original: "technē"</note>, while vice is like a "bad craft" <note>original: "kakotechnia" — a perversion of skill or cleverness used for harm</note>. It finds ways to do wrong through scheming. **Incontinence** is associated more with the **appetitive** part. For self-control <note>original: "egkrateia"</note> consists in mastering pleasure, while incontinence consists in failing to master it. **Ferocity** is associated with the **spirited** part. For whenever someone indulges the desire to do harm—not as a human would, but as a beast—such a thing is called "ferocious." 

The results of these dispositions follow from the motives for which they are practiced. Greed comes from vice, and vice from the reasoning part of the soul. Ambition <note>original: "philotimia" — literally "love of honor"</note> comes from the spirited part; but when it becomes excessive, it generates ferocity. Again, pleasure is found in the appetitive part, but when sought too vehemently, it generates incontinence. Thus, since wrongdoing occurs because of these causes, it is clear that acting justly occurs because of their opposites. For by its very nature, virtue is a doer of good and is beneficial, while vice is a doer of evil and is harmful.

# THEAGES THE PYTHAGOREAN
## ON VIRTUES

...moral matters <note>original: "pika," likely the end of "ethika" (ethics)</note>. Since of the parts of the soul, one is the **leader** and the other **follows**, and since virtues and vices are concerned with these, it is clear that among the virtues some are **leading**, some are **obedient**, and others are **composites** of these.

The **leading** virtue is **prudence**; the **obedient** ones are **courage** and **temperance** <note>original: "sōphrosynē" — the virtue of moderation and self-control</note>. The **composite** of these is **justice**. The passions <note>original: "pathea" — the emotions or "feelings" we undergo, which provide the raw material that virtue must shape</note> are the "matter" of virtue. For it is in relation to these that the virtues are formed. Of the passions, one is voluntary and the other involuntary; **pleasure** is voluntary, while **pain** is involuntary.

Political leaders tighten or loosen these same passions, harmonizing the other parts of the soul with the part that possesses **reason** <term>logos: the rational principle or the capacity for logical thought</term>. The standard for this harmony is that the **mind** <note>original: "noos" — the highest intellectual faculty of the soul</note> must not be prevented from performing its proper work by either a lack of emotion or an excess of it. For the lower is always ordered for the sake of the better.

Just as in the universe every passive part exists for the sake of those that are eternally in motion; and as in the union of living creatures, the female exists for the sake of the male (for the male sows the soul during procreation, while the female only provides the physical matter for the offspring <note>This reflects the biological theories common in antiquity, where the male was thought to provide the "form" or "soul" and the female the "matter"</note>); so, in the soul, the **irrational** part exists for the sake of the **rational**.

Indeed, **spirit** <note>original: "thymos" — the seat of anger, courage, and competitive drive</note> and **desire** are ordered toward the primary part of the soul: the one acts like a spear-bearer or a **bodyguard**, while the other acts like a **steward** and caretaker of the body's necessities. The **mind**, established at the very summit of the body and possessing a radiant and clear vision, searches for the wisdom of things that truly exist. This is its natural task: once it has sought and acquired this wisdom, it must follow what is superior and most honorable. For the origin, the cause, and the standard of human **happiness** <term>eudaimonia: a state of flourishing or "living well," rather than just a fleeting emotion</term> is the recognition of things that are divine and most honorable.

<summary>This page describes the soul as a hierarchy where the mind acts as a king, the spirit as a bodyguard, and desire as a steward, all harmonized to pursue divine wisdom.</summary>

# FROM THE WORKS OF METOPUS
## THE PYTHAGOREAN, FROM THE TREATISE
## ON VIRTUE.

**Virtue** <note>original: "Areta" — the Greek term "arete" implies excellence or fulfillment of purpose</note> in a human is the **perfection** of human nature. For each thing that exists becomes perfect and reaches its peak according to the nature proper to its virtues. For there is a virtue of a horse, which leads the horse’s nature to its peak. And the same logic applies to individual parts. For the virtue of the eyes is **keenness of sight** <term>oxydorkia: the sharpest possible vision</term>; and this is the peak of the nature of the eyes. And the virtue of the ears is **keenness of hearing** <term>oxyakoia: the highest state of auditory perception</term>; and this is the peak of the nature of the ears. And the virtue of the feet is **fleetness**; and this itself is the peak of the nature of the feet.

Every virtue must necessarily possess these three things: **reason**, **power**, and **deliberate choice** <note>original: "proairesis" — a technical term for a choice made with moral intention</note>. It requires **reason**, by which it judges and contemplates; **power**, by which it resists and prevails; and **deliberate choice**, by which it cherishes and loves. Now, the acts of judging and contemplating belong to the **intellectual part** of the soul. But resisting and prevailing are specific to the **irrational part** of the soul. For deliberate choice consists of both thought and desire. **Thought** comes from the logical part of the soul, while **desire** comes from the irrational part.

One might observe the multitude of all the virtues from these parts of the soul; likewise, one can see the origin and the composition of virtue. For regarding the parts of the soul, there are two primary ones: the **rational** and the **irrational**. Through the rational part, we judge and contemplate; through the irrational part, we are driven by impulse and desire. These two either harmonize with one another, or they disagree. The battle and disagreement occur... <note>The text breaks off mid-sentence; the final word "gí-" would likely have been "gínetai," meaning "becomes" or "happens."</note>

<summary>Metopus defines virtue as the "perfection of nature," comparing the soul's excellence to physical traits like keen sight. He argues that human virtue requires a harmony between the soul's rational capacity for judgment and its irrational capacity for desire.</summary>

### FROM THE WORKS OF METOPUS THE PYTHAGOREAN

### ON VIRTUE

[Vice] occurs in these parts through **excess** and **deficiency**. It is clear, then, that when the **rational part** of the soul holds power over the **irrational part**, **endurance** and **self-control** are produced. But when the rational part leads and the irrational part follows, and both harmonize with one another, then **virtue** is achieved.

Now, endurance and self-control arise through pain. **Endurance** <note>original: "karteria" — the ability to persist through physical or mental hardship</note> consists in holding out against toil, while **self-control** <term>enkrateia: the power of the will over one's own impulses</term> consists in holding out against pleasure. Conversely, **incontinence** <note>original: "akrasia" — literally 'lack of command' over oneself</note> and **softness** <note>original: "malakia" — a term for a lack of moral fiber or an inability to withstand discomfort</note> consist in failing to hold out or to maintain control. For this reason, it happens that men flee from good things because of pain, and cast them away because of pleasure. 

Yet praise and blame, and all noble things concerning human life, arise within these specific parts of the soul. In general, the composition of virtue is formed in this manner; now, let its forms and parts be examined once again.

Since there are two parts of the soul—the **rational** and the **irrational**—[the irrational is divided into two]: the **spirited part** and the **desiring part**. The rational part is that by which we judge and contemplate. The irrational part is that by which we are moved by impulse and feel desire. 

Of this irrational part, that which is defensive and acts as a champion against those nearby is named the **spirited part** <term>thymoeides: the seat of anger, courage, and social status</term>. But that which is appetitive and concerned with the sensations and needs of the body's own constitution is named the **desiring part** <term>epithymatikon: the seat of physical cravings such as hunger and lust</term>. It is clear, therefore, that the number of the virtues follows the logic of these parts of the soul, as do their differences and specific qualities.

<summary>Metopus explains that virtue is a harmony between the rational and irrational soul, distinguishing it from mere self-control which involves a painful struggle against impulse. He further divides the soul into three parts—rational, spirited, and desiring—which serve as the foundation for the various types of human excellence.</summary>

# FROM THE WRITINGS OF CLINIAS
## the Pythagorean.

All **virtue** <note>original: "aretā" — in this context, the moral excellence or functional perfection of a human being</note> is brought to completion, just as was defined at the beginning, through **reason**, **deliberate choice**, and **power**. Each of these factors, when considered on its own, is not a "part" of virtue, but rather a cause of virtue.

Those who possess the **intellectual** and **cognitive** part of it are called sharp-minded and sagacious; those, however, who possess the **ethical** and **volitional** <note>original: "proairetikon" — referring to "proairesis," the capacity for making a deliberate, moral choice</note> part are called useful and equitable. 

Whenever a person is incited by certain causes, it is human nature to do wrong. These causes happen to be three: **love of pleasure** <note>original: "philadonia"</note> in the enjoyments of the body; **greed** <term>pleonexia: the insatiable desire to have more than one's fair share or to "over-reach" others</term> in the pursuit of profit; and **love of glory** <note>original: "philodoxia"</note> in the desire to surpass those who are one's equals and peers.

Therefore, one must recognize that it is possible to set against these vices certain constraints: those which produce **fear** in men, those which produce **shame**, and those which produce **desire**. Specifically:
* **Fear** of the laws,
* **Shame** before the gods,
* **Desire** for rational arguments.

One must, therefore, teach the young from the very beginning to honor both the gods and the laws. For from these things it would be evident that every human work and every life will be most holy and, by participating in piety, will **sail a straight course** <note>original: "orthoploei" — a favorite Pythagorean nautical metaphor for a well-ordered life</note> at the same time.

<summary>Clinias the Pythagorean defines the components of virtue and identifies three primary drivers of vice—pleasure, greed, and ambition—which must be countered by law, piety, and reason.</summary>
<keywords>Clinias, Pythagoras, virtue, greed (pleonexia), love of glory, moral education, rule of law, piety, nautical metaphor</keywords>

# FROM THE WORKS OF THEAGES
## the Pythagorean, from his treatise
## On Virtues.

**T**he principles of all virtues are three: **knowledge**, **power**, and **deliberate choice**. 

**Knowledge** <note>original: "gnōsis"</note> is the faculty by which we contemplate and judge things. **Power** <note>original: "dynamis"</note> is like a kind of physical or mental strength of the frame <note>original: "skaneos" — literally a "tent" or "vessel," referring here to the bodily or human container</note>, by which we endure and persist in our affairs. **Deliberate choice** <note>original: "proaireis"</note> is like the "hands of the soul," by which we reach out and grasp hold of things.

The internal order of the soul is structured in this way: one part of it is **reason**, another is **spirit**, and the third is **desire**. 

*   **Reason** <note>original: "logismos"</note> is that which holds mastery over knowledge. 
*   **Spirit** <note>original: "thymōsis" — the seat of anger, courage, and drive</note> is that which holds mastery over vital force. 
*   **Desire** <note>original: "epithymia"</note> is that which holds mastery over the appetites. 

When these three components come together into one, accepting a single harmonious arrangement, then **virtue** and **agreement** <note>original: "homologia"</note> arise within the soul. But when they fall into conflict and pull away from one another, then **vice** and **discord** <term>anarmosia: literally "un-tuned," describing a soul that is out of harmony with itself like a poorly tuned instrument</term> arise in the soul. 

When reason dominates the irrational parts of the soul, then **endurance** and **self-control** are born. **Endurance** <note>original: "karteria"</note> is found in the holding out against pains; **self-control** <note>original: "enkrateia" — also translated as temperance</note> is found in the holding back from pleasures. 

On the other hand, when the irrational parts of the soul dominate reason, then **softness** and **lack of restraint** arise. **Softness** <note>original: "malakia" — a term for moral weakness or effeminacy in the classical sense</note> consists of fleeing from pains; **lack of restraint** consists of being defeated by pleasures. 

When the better part of the soul rules and the lesser part is ruled—when one leads and the other follows, and both are in mutual agreement and harmony with each other—then there arises virtue and...

<summary>Theages the Pythagorean outlines the tripartite soul (reason, spirit, desire) and explains that virtue is the harmonious "tuning" of these parts under the leadership of reason.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the fragment from Theages the Pythagorean, transitioning from the psychological components of the soul (reason, spirit, desire) to the specific virtues that arise when these parts are in harmony. ### FROM THE TREATISE ON VIRTUES.

**U**niversal goodness <note>original: "panagathia"</note> pertains to the whole of the soul. When the desiring part of the soul follows the reasoning part, **temperance** <note>original: "sōphrosynē"</note> is produced; when the spirited part follows it, **courage** <note>original: "andreiotēs"</note> arises; and when all the parts follow together, **justice** <note>original: "dikaiotās"</note> is achieved. For it is justice that distinguishes all the vices and virtues of the soul from one another. Indeed, justice is a kind of organized harmony of the parts of the soul—a perfect and most supreme virtue. For all things are contained within it. The other goods of the soul cannot exist without it.

For this reason, justice holds great power among both gods and men. The total virtue of the whole and the universe maintains the fellowship shared by both gods and humans. Among the celestial gods, it is called **Themis** <note>The personification of divine law and order</note>; among the gods of the underworld, it is called **Dike** <note>Justice or retribution</note>; and among men, it is called **Nomos** <note>Human law or custom</note>. These names are signs and symbols that justice is the most supreme virtue.

When virtue exists in the act of contemplating and judging, it is called **prudence** <note>original: "phronāsis"</note>. When it consists in the resisting of pleasures, it is called **temperance**. When it consists in abstaining from personal gain and from doing harm to one's neighbor, it is called **justice**. 

The arrangement of virtue according to right reason—and the transgression against right reason—is a hitting of the mark of **what is fitting** <term>to deon: literally "that which is binding" or "duty"; the appropriate action in a given circumstance</term>, and a falling away from what is fitting. Now, "the fitting" is that which ought to be; it requires neither subtraction nor addition, for it is exactly what it must be. 

Of "the unfitting," there are two types: **excess** <note>original: "hyperbola"</note> and **deficiency** <note>original: "elleipsis"</note>. Excess is more than what is fitting; deficiency is less. Virtue, however, is a certain stable habit <note>original: "hexis"</note> of the fitting. Therefore, virtues are both **extremities** and **means** at the same time. They are means because they fall between excesses and deficiencies; they are extremities <note>original: "akrotātes" — here meaning the "pinnacle" or "perfection"</note> because they require neither addition nor subtraction. For they are themselves these very things which they ought to be.

<summary>Theages defines justice as the supreme harmony of the soul and explains that virtue is a perfect "mean" that sits exactly between the vices of excess and deficiency.</summary>
<keywords>Theages, justice, temperance, courage, prudence, the fitting, mean, excess, deficiency, harmony of the soul, Themis, Dike, Law</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discourse by Theages the Pythagorean on the nature of virtue. Having previously defined the parts of the soul, he now argues that virtue is not the suppression of emotions, but their harmonious integration—a concept central to Pythagorean and later Aristotelian ethics. The text is written in a literary Doric dialect common to Pythagorean fragments.</meta>

->FROM THE WRITINGS OF THEAGES THE PYTHAGOREAN<-

**S**ince the virtues of character <note>original: "ētheos"</note> concern the passions, and among the passions, pleasures and pains are the primary elements, it is clear that these virtues do not arise from the total removal of the passions of the soul—namely, pleasure and pain—but from their harmonization. For even health, which is a certain tempering <note>original: "akrasia" - likely used here in the sense of a 'mixture' or 'blending' of qualities</note> of the body's powers, does not consist in the removal of the cold and the hot, or the wet and the dry, but in their proper blending. Indeed, health consists in a certain symmetry of these elements. 

In the same way, harmony <note>original: "symphōnon"</note> in music does not consist in the removal of the high-pitched <note>original: "oxy"</note> and the low-pitched <note>original: "bary"</note> notes, but in their specific tuning. Through the tuning of the high and the low, the consonant is achieved and the dissonant is cast out. When heat and cold, and the wet and the dry are harmonized, health is produced and disease is destroyed. Likewise, when the spirit <note>original: "thumos" - the seat of anger and courage</note> and the desire <note>original: "epithumia"</note> are harmonized, vices and passions are removed, while virtues and character take root.

The most characteristic feature of the virtues of character is the act of **choice** <note>original: "proairesis"</note> directed toward what is noble. For it is possible to use reason and power even without virtue, but this is not possible with choice; for choice indicates the true worth <note>original: "axiōma"</note> of one's character. 

Therefore, when reason overcomes spirit and desire through force, it produces **self-control** <note>original: "engkrateia"</note> and **endurance** <note>original: "karteria"</note>. But when reason is itself forced by the irrational parts, it produces **lack of control** <note>original: "akrasia"</note> and **softness** <note>original: "malakia"</note>. Such dispositions of the soul are "half-complete" virtues and "half-complete" vices. For in these cases, the reasoning part is healthy, but the irrational parts of the soul are diseased. 

Insofar as the spirit and the desire are ruled and led by the part of the soul that possesses reason, then self-control and endurance are counted as virtues. However, insofar as they do this by force and not willingly <note>original: "hekousiōs"</note>, they are counted as vices. For one must practice virtue not with pain <note>meaning with reluctance or internal struggle</note>, but with pleasure. Again, insofar as spirit and [desire] prevail...

<summary>Theages argues that virtue is the "musical" harmony of the soul's passions—reason, spirit, and desire—rather than their destruction, using analogies of bodily health and musical tuning.</summary>
<keywords>Theages, Pythagoras, virtue, ethics, harmony, passions, pleasure, pain, reason, choice, self-control</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the philosophical treatise by Theages, a pseudo-Pythagorean author. It picks up mid-sentence from the previous page, discussing how conflicting desires affect the soul and the role of "the fitting" (deon) in establishing virtue. This text is significant for its early articulation of the "Golden Mean," a concept later made famous by Aristotle.</meta>

### ON THE VIRTUES

...desire <note>original: "epithumia"</note> resists reason, bringing about a certain softness and lack of self-control? These conditions are indeed certain vices. However, insofar as people give in to their passions with a sense of regret, knowing they are erring because the "eye of the soul" <note>This refers to the intellectual capacity to perceive moral truth.</note> remains healthy, these are not complete or absolute vices. This very point makes it clear: virtue must perform what is fitting voluntarily. For an involuntary act is never without pain and fear, whereas a voluntary act is never without pleasure and a willing spirit. At the same time, the logic of this division should be applied, and let these things stand as they are.

For knowledge and the vision of things belong to the rational part of the soul, but power <note>original: "dunamis" - here meaning the raw capacity for action or impulse</note> belongs to the irrational part. The inability to endure hardships and the tendency to be overcome by pleasures are characteristics of the irrational part of the soul. However, **choice** <note>original: "proairesis" - a technical term for deliberate, moral intention</note> occurs in both parts: in the rational part of the soul and the irrational. For choice is composed of both thought and appetite. Of these, thought belongs to the rational part, while appetite belongs to the irrational. Therefore, every virtue arises from the harmonization <note>original: "sunarmoga"</note> of the parts of the soul; and both the voluntary and the act of choice are entirely contained within virtue.

In general, then, virtue is a certain harmony of the irrational parts of the soul with the rational part. This harmony occurs when both pleasure and pain accept the boundary of **what is fitting** <note>original: "to deon" - that which is right, proper, or necessary in a given situation</note>. For true virtue is nothing other than a habit of doing what is fitting. The "fitting" itself is simply how things ought to be; the "unfitting" is how they ought not to be. There are two forms of the unfitting: excess and deficiency.

Excess is that which is more than what is fitting; deficiency is that which is less than what is fitting. The fitting itself, being exactly what it ought to be, can be considered both an "extreme" and a "mean" <note>original: "akron" and "meson"</note>. It is an extreme because it requires neither subtraction nor addition; it is a mean because it stands exactly between excess and deficiency. The fitting and the unfitting relate to each other just as equality relates to inequality, or as the ordered relates to the disordered (both of which are expressions of the finite and the infinite).

<summary>Theages defines virtue as the harmony between the rational and irrational parts of the soul, achieved when choice (proairesis) aligns with "the fitting" (deon). He describes the fitting as a perfect mean between the vices of excess and deficiency.</summary>
<keywords>virtue, soul, rationality, choice, proairesis, the fitting, deon, mean, Pythagoras, Theages</keywords>

--- Page 476 ---
<meta>This page continues the philosophical treatise by Theages, a pseudo-Pythagorean author. It transitions from discussing the parts of the soul to applying the mathematical principle of the "mean" (the middle point) to human morality and biology.</meta>

### FROM THE WRITINGS OF THEAGES THE PYTHAGOREAN

...and for this reason, the parts of an unequal thing are defined in relation to the mean <note>original: "meson"</note>, but not in relation to one another. For an angle is called "obtuse" when it is greater than a right angle, and "acute" when it is less than a right angle. Similarly, a "greater" straight line is that which exceeds the radius <note>original: "ek tou kentrou" — literally "from the center." In this context, the radius serves as the fixed standard or "mean" for measuring other lines.</note>. A day is called "longer" when it exceeds the equinoctial day. Even the diseases of the body arise because the body becomes either too hot or too cold. For that which is "too hot" is an excess of the moderate, while that which is "too cold" is a deficiency of it.

The soul, and everything pertaining to it, possesses this same disposition and proportion. Thus, **rashness** is an excess of what is required in the face of dangers, while **cowardice** is a deficiency of the same. **Prodigality** <note>original: "asotia" — wasteful or reckless spending.</note> is an excess of what is required in the spending of money, while **illiberality** <note>original: "aneleutheria" — a lack of generosity or meanness.</note> is a deficiency. **Wrath** is an excess of what is required in the impulse of the spirit <note>original: "thumos" — the "spirited" or emotional part of the soul often associated with anger and courage.</note>, while **insensibility** is a deficiency of it. The same logic applies to all other opposing dispositions.

Virtue must be a stable habit <note>original: "hexis" — a settled state of character.</note> of the fitting, and a mean of the passions <note>original: "pathos" — emotions or "feelings" that act upon the soul.</note>, being neither "apathetic" nor "excessively passionate" within us. For **apathy** <note>original: "apatheia" — literally a "lack of feeling."</note> provides the soul with no impulse or inspiration toward "the Beautiful" <note>original: "to kalon" — in Greek thought, this refers to both physical beauty and moral goodness.</note>, while **excessive passion** leaves the soul agitated and incapable of reasoning.

Therefore, passion must be manifested in virtue just as shadow and line are manifested in a painting. For vitality, softness, and the imitation of truth—combined with the excellence of colors—are achieved primarily through these elements. The passions of the soul become "ensouled" or vital through the natural impulse and inspiration of virtue. For virtue is born from the passions, and once born, it is established again in company with them. This is just as a well-tuned harmony is composed of the sharp and the flat, a healthy temperament is composed of the hot and the cold, and a balance is composed of the heavy and the light.

One must not, therefore, remove the passions from the soul (for that is not even beneficial), but rather harmonize them <note>original: "sunarmosasthai" — to join together or tune, like a musical instrument.</note> according to reason, in accordance with what is fitting and moderate.

<summary>Theages explains that virtue is a "mean" between extremes of excess and deficiency, using analogies from geometry, medicine, and art to show that passions should be harmonized rather than suppressed.</summary>
<keywords>The Mean, Virtue, Passions, Ethics, Pythagorean Philosophy, Harmony, Geometry, Moral Balance</keywords>

# FROM THE WRITINGS OF ARCHYTAS
## the Pythagorean, from the work "On Moral Education."

I maintain that **virtue** is sufficient to prevent us from being miserable, and **vice** is sufficient to prevent us from being happy, if we judge these based on the internal dispositions themselves. For the bad man must necessarily always be miserable, whether he possesses resources or not; if he has them, he uses them badly. It is just like a blind man, who remains blind whether he is in brilliant light or in total darkness. 

However, the good man is not always happy <term>eudaimōn</term> <note>original: "εὐδαιμονεῖν" — a state of flourishing or "having a good spirit," often translated as happiness or prosperity</note>. For the mere possession of virtue is not happiness, but rather the **use** of it is. For example, a person who has the sense of sight does not see at all times; if they have no light, they will not see. Two paths are cut through life: one is the more gloomy path, along which the long-suffering **Odysseus** <note>The hero of the Odyssey, known for his many trials and "path" of suffering</note> traveled; the other is the more favorable path, which **Nestor** <note>The eldest of the Greek kings at Troy, often associated with a long, peaceful, and prosperous life</note> followed. I say, then, that virtue chooses the latter path, but is also capable of navigating the former. 

But true happiness is the fruit of a life that is stable and desirable to the soul, achieved because one's judgment has reached perfection. Thus, if a person does not meet with favorable circumstances, they may not be "happy" in the full sense, yet they are certainly not miserable. 

Therefore, let no one dare to say that the good man is free from labor or **insensible to pain** <term>analgeton</term>, nor should they boldly claim that he is free from sorrow. For just as we allow for certain pains in the body, we must also allow them in the soul. The sorrows of the foolish are irrational, but the sorrows of the wise occur only insofar as **reason** <term>logos</term> permits, as it weighs the reality of the situation. Furthermore, the boast of total **apathy** <term>apatheia</term> <note>original: "ἀπαθείας" — the Stoic ideal of being completely unmoved by emotion or suffering</note> actually weakens the nobility of virtue, especially when it faces various hardships or the threat of death...

<summary>Archytas argues that while virtue protects against misery, true happiness requires the active use of virtue in favorable conditions. He rejects the idea that a virtuous person should be "emotionless," suggesting instead that a wise person feels pain but regulates it through reason.</summary>

<keywords>Archytas, Pythagorean, Virtue, Happiness, Eudaimonia, Odysseus, Nestor, Apathy, Reason, Pain, Moral Education</keywords>

We say indeed that the **good man** is the one who makes noble use of great affairs and opportunities. If it is necessary to speak briefly and summarily: he is the one who, in all circumstances, competes well <note>The Greek "ἀγωνιζόμενος" (agonizomenos) evokes the image of an athlete or a soldier "struggling" or "contending" nobly against the challenges of life</note> according to what is possible. He not only conducts himself in this way, but also looks after those who have placed their trust in him and those who are struggling alongside him.

# FROM THE WORKS OF CRITO
## the Pythagorean, from the book "On
## Prudence and Good Luck."

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut headpiece featuring symmetrical scrolling foliage, floral motifs, and a central stylized urn or botanical element.</image-desc>

**P**rudence <term>phronasis</term> <note>original: "Φρόνασις" — often translated as "practical wisdom" or "intelligence," it is the ability to apply reason to life's circumstances</note> and misfortune <note>original: "ἀτυχία" — while the title mentions "Good Luck" (eutuchia), the text begins by contrasting wisdom with "misfortune" or "chance," representing the unpredictable element of life</note> stand in this relation to each other: Prudence is that which is expressible and possesses reason <term>logos</term> (for it is something ordered and defined); misfortune, however, is that which is inexpressible and irrational (for it is something disordered and indefinite). The former is primary in origin and power, while the latter is secondary in origin and power. For the one is by nature meant to govern and define, while the other is meant to be governed and defined. 

Nevertheless, both receive a **harmonious joining** <note>original: "συναρμογὰν" — a central Pythagorean concept where opposites are fitted together into a functional whole</note> when prudence and misfortune run together into the same result. For it is always necessary for the nature that is expressible and rational to have something which it will limit and arrange; likewise, the inexpressible and irrational must have something by which it will be limited and arranged. This principle <term>logos</term> holds true regarding all things: that of the **infinite nature** <note>original: "ἀπείρου φύσιος" — the "Unlimited," which in Pythagorean thought represents raw matter or chaos before order is applied</note> and that which provides the limit.

For those things which are infinite have a nature to be limited and arranged by those things possessing reason and prudence (for they hold the rank of matter and substance); but those things that provide the limit are, by their own nature, arranged and defined. For they hold the rank of arts and active causes.

The harmonious joinings of these natures, occurring in various ways, have created great and diverse differences among the things being joined. For in the encompassing of the whole, the joining of both natures—the ever-moving nature and the ever-passive—is the **Cosmos** <note>original: "κόσμος" — meaning "Order" or "Beauty"; Crito argues the universe itself is a harmony of active mind and passive matter</note>. For clearly it was not possible for the whole and the all to be preserved, unless there was a joining of the created to the divine, and the ever-passive to...

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence. The signature "G. i." at the bottom marks the beginning of a new gathering of pages in the printed book.</meta>

<summary>Crito the Pythagorean explains that Prudence (reason/order) and Fortune (the irrational/disordered) must work together, with Prudence acting as the "limit" that gives shape to the "infinite" or "unlimited" aspects of life and the universe.</summary>

<keywords>Crito, Pythagoreanism, Prudence, Phronasis, Fortune, Logos, Cosmos, Limit, Unlimited, Harmony, Ethics, Metaphysics</keywords>

<header>FROM THE WORKS OF CRITO THE PYTHAGOREAN</header>

## FROM THE WORKS OF CRITO THE PYTHAGOREAN

...the ever-moving <note>original: "τὸ ἀεικίνατον" — This completes the sentence from the previous page: the universe is a harmony of the "ever-passive" matter and the "ever-moving" divine or rational force</note>. In man, the **harmonious joining** <term>sunarmoga</term> <note>the Pythagorean concept of "fitting together" disparate parts into a unified whole</note> of the irrational part of the soul to the rational part is **virtue** <term>areta</term>. For it is not possible for virtue to be completed in these if there is a state of civil war existing between the two parts. 

And in a city, the joining of the governed to the governors produces power and concord. For to rule is the proper characteristic of the better part; to be ruled is easier for the inferior part; but to possess power and concord is common to both. 

The same reasoning <term>logos</term> applies to the harmonies of the whole universe and to those of the household; it composes them through "incantations" <note>original: "ἐπωδαῖς" — likely referring to the Pythagorean use of music and rhythmic instruction to soothe the soul</note> and education, which run together into the same result according to reason. This applies to pains and pleasures, as well as misfortunes and <gloss>good luck</gloss> <note>original: "εὐτυχίας" — added as a gloss to balance the mention of misfortune</note> successes. 

For life needs both relaxation and tension, both somberness and cheerfulness, and misfortune as well as good luck. For the former [misfortune] is able to hold together and collect the mind toward its own lack of resources and toward prudence; the latter [good luck], by providing rest and cheerfulness, prepares the mind to be more fresh and spirited for action. 

But if one of these should dominate throughout life, life becomes one-sided and leaning to one side—sometimes being carried down toward the somber and difficult, and other times toward the relaxed and light. 

The **harmonious joining** of all these things ought to happen according to **prudence** <term>phronasis</term>. For prudence itself is that which works upon both the infinite <term>apeiron</term> <note>the "Unlimited" or "Indefinite"</note> and the limiting <note>original: "περαῖνον"</note> in all our actions. Wherefore, prudence would be the leader and mother of all the virtues. For all the other virtues happen to be harmonized and arranged according to her reason and law. 

Indeed, the argument now seems true to me: for the irrational and the expressible <note>original: "ῥητὸν" — that which can be defined by logic or numbers</note> are in all things. One defines and limits; the other is defined and limited. And that which is composed of both of them is the harmony of the whole and of the all...

<summary>Crito argues that virtue, political stability, and a balanced life all stem from "harmonious joining," where Prudence (reason) acts as the limiting force upon the "unlimited" aspects of the soul and fortune.</summary>

<keywords>Crito, Pythagoreanism, Virtue, Areta, Soul, Politics, Harmony, Prudence, Phronasis, Luck, Education, Metaphysics</keywords>

# FROM THE WORKS OF ARCHY-
## tas the Pythagorean, from the treatise
### on the good and
### happy man.

**A PR**udent <term>phronimos</term> <note>the "phronimos" is the person who possesses practical wisdom, a key figure in ancient ethics</note> man would most likely become so in this way: by first obtaining a nature that is well-aimed <note>original: "εὐστόχω" — refers to a mind that can "hit the mark" or perceive truth quickly</note>, mindful, and industrious; and then, having from youth exercised the mind in calculations, mathematical sciences, and in theories aimed at exactness, having a share of right philosophy. After these, let him gain experience of the gods, the laws, and human lives. 

For there are two things from which the disposition of the prudent man arises: one is to acquire a mathematical and cognitive habit <note>a "habit" or "state" (hexin) refers to a permanent quality of the soul gained through training</note>; the other is to have encountered many theories and practical affairs—some by seeing them himself, and others by understanding them through some other means. 

For neither is the person who has exercised the mind from youth in calculations, mathematical sciences, and theories of exactness sufficient for **prudence** <term>phronasis</term>; nor is the person who lacks these but has spent time in many oral instructions <note>original: "ἀκροαμάτεσι" — refers to learning by hearing lectures or traditional stories</note> and practical affairs. 

Of these two, the one [the man of experience without math] becomes blind in his mind when it comes to judging particulars; while the other [the man of math without experience] is always looking toward the universal <note>original: "καθόλου" — the general or abstract principle</note>. For just as in calculations one calculates the whole by putting together the parts, so too in practical affairs: **reason** <term>logos</term> is able to outline the universal theory, but **experience** <term>empeiria</term> allows one to judge the particulars.

<summary>Archytas explains that becoming a "prudent man" requires a balance of two things: a youthful education in abstract mathematics and logic, and a later maturity gained through practical experience in human affairs and law.</summary>

# FROM THE WORKS OF THE SAME,
## in the treatise on mathematical 
### sciences.

One must become knowledgeable either by learning from another or by discovering for oneself the things of which one was ignorant. Now, learning from another is "foreign" <note>original: "ἀλλότριον" — meaning it comes from an external source or belongs to someone else</note>, while discovering for oneself through one's own efforts is "one's own" <note>original: "ἴδιον" — private or personal discovery</note>. Furthermore, discovering is easy and ready to hand for the one who seeks, but seeking is impossible for the one who does not know how to seek. 

**Calculation** <term>logismos</term> <note>in Pythagorean thought, "logismos" refers to both mathematical calculation and the faculty of reasoning</note>, when it is adopted, stops civil strife and increases concord. For when it exists, there is no **excessive greed** <term>pleonexia</term> <note>the desire to have more than one's fair share</note>, but there is **equality** <term>isotas</term>. For by this means we come to terms regarding our contracts with one another. Because of this, the poor receive from those who have power, and the rich give to those in need, both parties trusting that through this reasoning they will have what is fair. 

It is a rule and a restrainer of those who do wrong: it stops those who know how to calculate from doing wrong before they even begin, by persuading them that they will not be able to remain hidden when they come to the act; and for those who do not know how to calculate, it restrains them from wrongdoing by showing that they are acting unjustly in the very moment of the act.

<meta>This page continues the fragment from Polus the Pythagorean regarding justice. The previous page ended with justice being described as the harmony and peace of the soul. This page expands that definition, showing how justice acts as a unifying principle across every level of existence, from the stars to the household.</meta>

<page-num>469</page-num>
<header>IN THE TREATISE ON JUSTICE</header>

...orderly arrangement. Its power would become even more manifest if we were to examine the other dispositions of the soul. For they possess a **partial** benefit, directed toward a single thing; but justice is directed toward whole systems and is found in the multitude. 

In the **cosmos** <term>kosmos</term> <note>referring to the ordered universe</note>, therefore, justice is that which commands the whole principle as **providence** <term>pronoia</term>, **harmony** <term>harmonia</term>, and **justice** <term>dika</term> <note>original: "δίκα" — the Doric form of "dike"</note>, the gods having decreed it so. 

In the **city-state** <term>polis</term>, it is rightly called **peace** <term>eirana</term> and **good governance** <term>eunomia</term>. 

In the **household** <term>oikos</term>, it manifests as:
*   the **like-mindedness** <term>homophrosuna</term> of husband and wife toward one another; 
*   the **goodwill** <term>eunoia</term> of the servants toward their masters; 
*   and the **care** <term>kademonia</term> of the master toward his attendants. 

In the **body**, which is the primary and most beloved thing to all living creatures, it is **health** <term>hygieia</term> and **soundness** <term>artiotas</term> <note>the state of being complete or having all parts functioning correctly</note>. 

In the **soul**, it is **wisdom** <term>sophia</term>, which among men arises from knowledge and the practice of justice. 

Since justice thus guides and preserves both the whole and the parts, making them like-minded and in accord with one another, how could it not be called, by the voice of all, the **mother** and **nurse** of all virtues and of all things?

# BY A CERTAIN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR
Discourses in the **Doric dialect** <term>Dōrikē dialektos</term> <note>The dialect of Ancient Greek associated with Sparta and the Peloponnese, often used in Pythagorean and early philosophical texts</note>, Concerning the **Good** <term>agathon</term> and the **Evil** <term>kakon</term>, Concerning the **Beautiful** <term>kalon</term> and the **Ugly** <term>aischron</term>, Concerning the **Just** <term>dikaion</term> and the **Unjust** <term>adikon</term>, Concerning **Falsehood** <term>pseudos</term> and **Truth** <term>alētheia</term>, and Concerning **Wisdom** <term>sophia</term> and **Virtue** <term>aretē</term>, and whether it can be taught.

## CONCERNING THE GOOD AND THE EVIL.

<image-desc>Large historiated or decorative initial 'D' (Δ) at the start of the main text block.</image-desc>

**Two-fold arguments** <term>dissoi logoi</term> <note>A rhetorical technique of arguing both sides of a position to show that truth depends on perspective</note> are spoken in Greece by those who practice philosophy concerning the **good** and the **evil**. For some say that the good is one thing and the evil is another; but others say that they are the same thing, and that it might be good for some, but evil for others; and for the same man, at one time it is good, and at another time evil.

I myself also agree with these latter thinkers; and I shall examine it from the perspective of human life, which is concerned with eating, drinking, and sexual pleasures. For these things are **evil** for a man who is sick, but for one who is healthy and in need of them, they are **good**. Furthermore, the **excess** <term>akrasia</term> of these things is evil for the intemperate, but for the physicians, it is good <note>The physician profits or gains knowledge from the patient's lack of self-control</note>. 

The **death** of individuals is an evil for those who have died, but for the **undertakers** <term>entaphiopōlais</term> and the **tomb-makers** <term>tumbopoiois</term>, it is a good. When **farming** produces the crops well, it is a good for the farmers, but for the merchants <note>who benefit from scarcity and high prices</note>, it is an evil. That the merchant ships of some should be wrecked or shattered is an evil for the ship-owner, but for the **ship-builders** <term>naupēgois</term>, it is a good. Further, for **iron** to be broken, blunted, or crushed is an evil for everyone else, but for the **smith**—

<summary>This page introduces the 'Dissoi Logoi', an anonymous text arguing that good and evil are not absolute but relative to individual circumstances and professions.</summary>

<keywords>Dissoi Logoi, Relativity, Ethics, Good and Evil, Doric Dialect, Sophism, Greek Philosophy, Professional Interests</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Dissoi Logoi" (Two-Fold Arguments), specifically the section arguing that "good" and "evil" are relative concepts depending on the circumstances of different people. <page-num>471</page-num>

<header>CONCERNING THE GOOD AND THE EVIL.</header>

<meta>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the smith.</meta>

—is a **good**. And indeed, for **pottery** <term>keramon</term> to be broken is an evil for everyone else, but for the **potters** <term>kerameusin</term>, it is a good. That **shoes** <term>hypodēmata</term> should be worn out and torn is an evil for others, but for the **shoemaker** <term>skytei</term>, it is a good. 

Furthermore, in **athletic contests**, in **musical competitions**, and in **warfare**—for example, in a **footrace** <term>stadiodromōi</term> in the stadium, victory is a good for the winner, but for the losers, it is an evil. And this is likewise true for wrestlers and boxers, and all those who compete in the arts. For instance, in **singing to the lyre** <note>original: kitharōidia</note>, victory is a good for the winner, but for the losers, it is an evil. 

In **war**—and I shall speak of the most recent events first—the victory of the **Lacedaemonians** <note>The Spartans</note>, in which they defeated the **Athenians** and their allies, was a good for the Lacedaemonians, but for the Athenians and their allies, it was an evil. And the victory where the **Greeks** defeated the **Persians** was a good for the Greeks, but for the **barbarians** <note>To the Greeks, 'barbarian' simply meant anyone who did not speak Greek; here it refers to the Persian Empire</note>, it was an evil. The **capture of Ilium** <note>The city of Troy</note> was a good for the **Achaeans** <note>The Greeks</note>, but for the **Trojans**, it was an evil. And the same applies to the sufferings of the **Thebans** and the **Argives** <note>A reference to the mythological 'Seven Against Thebes'</note>. Also, the battle of the **Centaurs** and the **Lapiths** was a good for the Lapiths, but for the Centaurs, it was an evil. And indeed, the legendary battle and victory of the **gods** over the **Giants** was a good for the gods, but for the Giants, it was an evil.

But **another argument** is told: that the **good** <term>tagathon</term> is one thing, and the **evil** <term>to kakon</term> is another, and they are as different in reality as they are in name. And I myself also distinguish them in this way. For I think it would not be clear what sort of thing is good and what sort is evil if they were both the same and not distinct. Indeed, that would be a wonder. 

I think even a man who claims they are the same could not answer if someone asked him: "Tell me, have you ever done anything **good** for your **parents**?" He would likely say, "Yes, many great things." Then you owe your parents many **evils**, if indeed the good and the evil are the same thing. What about your **relatives**? Have you ever done them any good? Then your relatives—

I am not saying what "the good" is, but I am trying to teach this: that the evil and the good are not the same thing, but that each is distinct.

**Double arguments** are also spoken concerning the **just** <term>original: dikaion; meaning what is morally right or lawful</term> and the **unjust** <term>original: adikon</term>. Some say that the **just** is one thing and the **unjust** is another; but others say that the **just** and the **unjust** are the same. I will attempt to support this second view.

Therefore, it is already shown that it is **just** to **lie** to and **deceive** one's parents. 

Furthermore, it is **just** to **steal** the possessions of one's friends and to use **force** against those who are most dear. For instance, if a member of a household is grieving or distressed and intends to destroy himself—whether with a **sword**, a **rope**, or anything else—it is **just** to **steal** these things if one can; and if one is too late for that and finds him already holding them, it is **just** to take them away by **force**. 

And how is it not **just** to **enslave** one's enemies, if someone is able to capture and sell an entire city? ## ON FALSEHOOD AND
->the truth.<-

Twofold arguments <term>original: dissoi logoi; a rhetorical technique of arguing both sides of an issue</term> are also spoken concerning **falsehood** and **truth**. One of these claims that the **false statement** is one thing and the **true statement** is another; however, the opposing view claims that they are the **same**. 

I, for my part, argue the latter: first, because they are expressed using the same words; second, because when a statement is spoken, if the facts turn out as the statement says, then the statement is **true**; but if they do not turn out that way, the very same statement is **false**. For example, if you accuse someone of **temple-robbing** <term>original: hierosylia; a capital crime in ancient Greece involving the theft of sacred property</term>, if the deed actually took place, the statement is **true**; but if it did not take place, it is **false**. The same applies to the statement of the person making the defense. Even the **courts of law** <note>The dikasteria of ancient Athens and other Greek cities, where juries of citizens decided the truth of a case.</note> judge the very same statement to be both **false** and **true**. 

Consider this: if we were all sitting in a row and I were to say, "I am **Mimas**," <note>Mimas is likely a proper name used here for a logical puzzle; if several people say "I am Mimas," the sentence is identical, but its truth depends entirely on who says it.</note> we would all be saying the same words, but only I would be telling the **truth**, because I actually am he. It is clear, then, that the same statement is **false** when falsehood is present in it, and **true** when truth is present. It is just as a **human being** is the same entity whether he is a **child**, a **youth**, a **man**, or an **old man**. 

But it is also argued that the **false statement** is one thing and the **true** is another, differing in name as well. For if someone were to ask those who say the **false** and the **true** are the same statement: "Which of the two is the statement you yourself are speaking?" If they answer that it is **false**, then it is clear that there are two distinct types. But if they answer that it is **true**, then by their own logic, the same statement is also **false**. Furthermore, if a person has spoken or testified to many **true** things, would those same things also be **false**? And if one knows a man to be **truthful**, would he also know that same man to be a **liar**? In the course of the argument, they say these things because whenever... <meta>The text breaks off as the author prepares to refute the relativist position.</meta>

Therefore, if they were to perform the **same actions**, then the **wise** are mad and the **mad** are wise, and all things are thrown into total **confusion**.

And by saying this, they seem to add only a small thing—"when one should" and "when one should not"—so that the matter is no longer the same.

Since, therefore, the meaning is so different when nothing is actually **subtracted**, what would happen if someone were to either **add** or **subtract** something? I will show the nature of this: if someone were to take **one** away from **ten**, there would no longer be ten, nor would there be one. The same logic applies to all other things. As for the claim that the **same human being** both **is** and **is not**, I ask: is he then everything? It follows that if someone were to say he "is not," they are lying; for having said "all things," they acknowledge he is, in some way, all these things.

# ON WISDOM AND VIRTUE, whether they can be taught.

<note>This section begins the sixth chapter of the manuscript, addressing the "Arete" debate: whether human excellence is an innate gift or a skill that can be acquired through study.</note>

A certain argument is being made that is neither **true** nor **empty**: namely, that **wisdom** and **virtue** <term>original: arete; often translated as "excellence," referring to the fulfillment of one's purpose or moral character</term> can be neither **taught** nor **learned**. Those who make this claim use the following proofs: 

1. First, that it is impossible, if you were to **hand it over** to someone else, for you to still **possess** it yourself. 
2. Second, that if it were teachable, there would be **recognized teachers**, just as there are for **music**. 
3. Third, that the **wise men** who have lived in **Greece** did not teach these things to their own **children** or their **friends**. 
4. Fourth, that some people who have gone to **Sophists** <term>original: sophistai; professional teachers in ancient Greece who traveled between cities charging for instruction in rhetoric and virtue</term> received no **benefit**. 
5. Fifth, that many people who have never **associated** with Sophists have nonetheless become **noteworthy**.

I, however, consider this argument to be quite **foolish**. For I know that teachers teach **letters** <note>reading and writing</note> which they themselves also happen to **understand**, and **lyre-players** teach how to play the **lyre**. 

Regarding the second proof—that there are no **recognized teachers**—what else do the **Sophists** teach if not **wisdom** and **virtue**? And what else were the **Anaxagoreans** <note>followers of the philosopher Anaxagoras</note> and the **Pythagoreans** <note>followers of Pythagoras</note>? Regarding the third point, **Polykleitos** <note>one of the most famous sculptors of the classical era</note> taught his **son** how to make **statues**. And while—

<header>BY AN ANONYMOUS AUTHOR</header>

The fact that someone might not teach it is no sign that it cannot be taught; however, if there is even one person who can teach it, that is a **proof** <term>original: tekmerion; a piece of evidence or a sure sign</term> that it is possible to be taught. Fourthly, there is the argument that people do not become wise just by spending time with **wise Sophists**. To this I say: many have failed to learn their **letters** <note>the basic alphabet and reading</note> despite having had lessons. 

There is also such a thing as **natural talent**. Even if someone becomes capable without learning from the Sophists, it is because they were naturally gifted and able to quickly grasp the many details of a subject by learning only a few principles from the people from whom we also learn our **names** <note>the author argues that language and culture are "taught" by society at large, not just formal teachers</note>. Indeed, we learn these things—some more, some less—partly from a father and partly from a mother. 

If anyone does not believe that we learn names in this way, or that we gain knowledge through such constant association, let him consider this: if someone were to send a naturally gifted child away to the **Persians** <note>Greek: Persas; the traditional rivals of the Greeks, used here as the ultimate example of a foreign culture</note> and he were to grow up there, never hearing the **Greek language**, he would eventually speak Persian. Conversely, if someone from there were brought here, he would speak Greek. This is how we learn names—and we do not even know who our individual **teachers** were for them. My argument is now concluded; it has a beginning, a middle, and an end. I do not definitively state that virtue **can be taught**, only that these proofs are sufficient for my position.

# ON DEMOCRACY AND THE LOT

<note>This begins a new section of the manuscript critiquing sortition—the common Athenian practice of selecting government officials by random lottery rather than election or merit.</note>

Certain **public speakers** <term>original: demagoreonton; those who speak to the assembly, often used for "demagogues"</term> argue that government offices should be assigned **by lot** <term>original: klaro; the practice of "sortition" or drawing lots to ensure equality in selection</term>, but I do not believe this is the best practice. If someone were to ask a person who says such things: "Why don't you assign the chores of your **servants** by lot? Why not have it so that the **ox-driver**, if he draws the lot of the **cook**, must do the cooking, while the cook must drive the oxen?" 

The same applies to everything else. Why do we not gather the **blacksmiths**, the **shoemakers**, the **carpenters**, and the **goldsmiths**, and force each one to work at whatever trade they happen to draw by lot, rather than the one they actually **understand**? 

The same logic would apply to **musical competitions**: we would have the competitors draw lots and whatever each one drew, he would have to perform. A **flute-player** might happen to have to play the **lyre**, and a **lyre-player** would have to play the flute. And in **war**, the **archers** and the **heavy infantry** would serve as the **cavalry**, while the cavalryman would be forced to be an archer. The result would be that everyone would be doing things they neither understand nor are capable of. They claim this system is good and **democratic** <term>original: demotikon; pertaining to the common people or the democratic spirit</term>; but I consider it the least democratic of all. For in the **cities**... <note>the text cuts off here at the end of the page</note>

...in cities, there are men who hate the common people, and if the **lot** <term>original: kyamos; literally "the bean," the physical object drawn to select officials</term> happens to fall to them, they will destroy the **people** <note>original: dāmon; the common citizenry or the "demos"</note>.
