I believe it belongs to the same set of **skills** <term>original: techne; a craft, art, or specialized field of knowledge</term> for a man to be able to speak concisely, to know the truth of things, to know how to judge correctly, to be able to speak to the public, and to understand the **arts of discourse**. Furthermore, he should be able to teach concerning the **nature of all things**, explaining both how they are and how they came to be. 

First, will not he who knows the nature of all things also be able to act and speak correctly regarding all things? Moreover, he who knows the **arts of discourse** <term>original: technas ton logon; the rules of rhetoric and logic</term> will also know how to speak correctly about all matters. For anyone who intends to speak correctly must speak about those things which he understands. He will understand all things, for he understands the arts of all arguments, and all arguments are about all the things that exist. 

It is necessary for the man who intends to speak correctly to understand the subjects of which he speaks. * * * He must also know how to teach **good things** correctly and how to guide the **city** <note>the "polis" or city-state</note> to success, while knowing how to prevent **bad things**. Since he knows these things, he will also know their opposites, for he will understand all things. These matters are part of the whole. Such a man will achieve what is necessary toward that same end. 

If it were necessary, such a man should be able to play the **flute** <note>original: aulen; referring to the aulos, a double-reeded pipe</note>, even if he does not already know how, provided the situation requires it to be done. Furthermore, the man who knows how to judge must understand **justice** correctly; for justice is what those judgments are about. Knowing this, he will also know its opposite and everything else. 

He must also understand all the **laws**. If he does not understand the underlying facts of a matter, he will not understand the laws either. For who understands the **law in music** <note>original: nomon; a pun on the Greek word "nomos," which means both "statute law" and a "musical mode" or "rule"</note> except the one who understands music itself? He who does not understand music does not understand its laws. 

The argument holds that he who knows the **truth of things** will certainly understand everything. And even if his speech is brief, he must be able to answer any question put to him about any subject. Therefore, it is necessary for him to understand everything. And the most important thing is...

## BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

The most beautiful invention found for life is **memory** <term>original: mnama; the faculty of remembrance or a mental record</term>, and it is useful for everything, both for **philosophy** <note>literally "the love of wisdom"</note> and for **wisdom** itself. This is how it works: if you pay close attention, the thought passing through these steps will allow you to better perceive the whole of what you have learned.

The second step is **practice** <note>original: meletan; exercises or repetition</note> when you hear something. For hearing and speaking these things many times brings them into the memory.

The third step is, whenever you hear something, to place it upon what you already know. For example: if I must remember the name **Chrysippus** <note>A common Greek name meaning "Golden Horse"</note>, I must place it upon **gold** <note>original: chrysos</note> and **horse** <note>original: hippos</note>. Another example: for a **glow-worm** <note>original: pyrilampes</note>, place it upon **fire** <note>original: pyr</note> and **shining** <note>original: lampein</note>. 

These examples concern names. But for **actual things** <note>concepts or abstract ideas</note>, do it this way: 

*   For **courage**, place it upon **Ares** <note>the god of war</note> or **Achilles**. 
*   For **metalworking**, place it upon **Hephaestus** <note>the blacksmith of the gods</note>. 
*   For **cowardice**, place it upon **Epeius** <note>The builder of the Trojan Horse, who was often characterized in folklore as being fearful despite his craftsmanship</note>.

<vocab>Memory, Philosophy, Chrysippus, Ares, Achilles, Hephaestus, Epeius, Twofold Arguments, Mnemonics</vocab>

# THE LETTER OF LYSIS THE
## Pythagorean to Hipparchus.

**A**fter Pythagoras departed from among men, I never thought that the assembly of his followers would be scattered; I held this belief in my very soul. But since, contrary to my hopes—just as if from a great merchant ship wrecked in the desolate open sea—we have been driven and scattered, some to one place and some to another, I feel it is a sacred duty to remember his divine and solemn precepts. We must not share the treasures of wisdom <note>original: sophia</note> with those who have not even in their dreams had their souls purified. For it is not right to extend to every passerby things that were mastered with such great effort. Indeed, it is not permitted to describe the mysteries of the two Eleusinian goddesses <note>Demeter and Persephone, whose secret "Mysteries" were the most famous religious rites of ancient Greece</note> to the uninitiated. Those who do such things are equally unjust and impious.

It is good to reflect on how much time we spent measuring out our lives, scrubbing away the stains that were engraved in our hearts, until, after five years had passed <note>Pythagorean students famously underwent a five-year period of total silence and testing before being fully admitted to the inner circle</note>, we became receptive to his words. For just as dyers first clean and treat <note>original: estypsan; to use a "mordant" or fixative to help the fabric hold color</note> the garments to be dyed so that they may drink in the dye and never have it wash out or fade away, so did that divine man prepare those who fell in love with **philosophy**. He did this so that he would not be disappointed in any of his hopes for their eventual excellence. 

For he did not trade in counterfeit words, nor in the snares with which many of the **sophists** <term>original: sophistōn; professional teachers who were often criticized for prioritizing persuasive rhetoric over absolute truth</term> entangle the young, occupying them with nothing useful. Rather, he was a master of things both divine and human. But others, making a mere facade of his teaching, do many and...

<header>LYSIS'S PYTHAGOREAN LETTER</header>

...they do terrible things, netting the young in a disorderly and haphazard fashion. Because of this, they make their listeners both difficult and headstrong. For they mix noble theorems and discourses with characters that are disturbed and muddy. 

It is just as if someone were to pour clean, transparent water into a deep well full of mud; he merely stirs up the mud and causes the clean water to disappear. The same pattern holds for those who teach and are taught in such a manner. For dense and deep thickets have grown around the minds and hearts of those who have not been purely initiated <note>original: orgiasthentōn; referring to the "orgies" or sacred rites of the Pythagoreans which required moral purity</note>, overshadowing everything mild, gentle, and rational <note>original: logistikon; the reasoning part of the soul</note> that has tried to grow there. 

All kinds of vices have crept into this brushwood, grazing there, hindering and in no way allowing **Reason** <term>original: Logos; here referring to the divine spark of logic and order within the human mind</term> to peek out. I will name the "mothers" of these vices who have come upon them: **Incontinence** and **Greed**. Both are naturally very prolific. 

From Incontinence sprout lawless unions, drunkenness, corruption, unnatural pleasures, and certain violent impulses that drive people toward death and over precipices. For these desires have already forced some to spare neither mothers nor daughters. Indeed, they have pushed aside law, father, city, and ruler; having tied their victims' elbows behind them, these passions lead them by force like captives toward final destruction. 

From Greed, meanwhile, grow robberies, parricides, sacrileges, poisonings, and all things kindred to these. Therefore, one must first clear away the "woods" in which these passions dwell—using fire and iron <note>a surgical metaphor suggesting that purifying the soul requires drastic, even painful, intervention</note> and every possible means. Only when the reasoning faculty has been rescued and set free from such passions should one plant something useful within it. 

These are the things you learned, Hipparchus, with great diligence. But you did not keep them, O noble man, once you had tasted **Sicilian luxury** <note>Ancient Sicily, particularly Syracuse, was legendary for its opulence, fine dining, and excess, which Pythagoreans viewed as the ultimate distraction from a virtuous life</note>, which you ought never to have experienced a second time.

# TO HIPPARCHUS.

Many say that you even **philosophize in public** <note>original: damosia; the Pythagoreans were a secret society, and teaching their specific doctrines to the uninitiated public was considered a grave betrayal</note>, a practice which Pythagoras deemed unworthy. He, at least, entrusted his **commentaries** <term>original: hypomnamata; these were the personal notebooks or memoirs of teachings meant to be kept within the school</term> to his daughter **Damo**, charging her to hand them over to no one outside of the house. 

And she, though she was able to sell these discourses for a great deal of money, was unwilling to do so. She considered poverty and her father’s instructions more precious than gold. They say, too, that when Damo was dying, she passed on this same command to her own daughter, **Bistalia**. 

But we, though we are men, do not follow him with such integrity; instead, we have become violators of our agreements. If, then, you change your ways, I will hold you dear; but if you do not, **you are dead to me** <note>original: tethnākas moi; this likely refers to the Pythagorean practice of "ritual death," where a member who betrayed the order was shunned as if they were deceased, sometimes even having a tombstone erected in their "memory" while they still lived</note>.

# THE LETTERS OF THEANO, 
# who is called the daughter of 
# Pythagorean wisdom.

## On the Upbringing of Children.

### THEANO TO EUBULE, GREETINGS.

**I** hear that you are raising your children with too much luxury <note>original: trypherōs; this implies a pampered, soft upbringing which the Pythagoreans believed corrupted the character</note>. But the duty of a good mother is not to provide for the pleasure of her children, but to lead them toward **self-restraint** <term>original: sōphron; a core Pythagorean virtue involving temperance, moderation, and the mastery of one’s desires</term>. See to it, then, that you do not act the part of a flatterer rather than a mother who truly loves. For pleasure, when nurtured alongside children, makes them undisciplined. For what is more sweet to the young than habitual pleasure? 

Therefore, my friend, the upbringing of children must not involve a perversion of their character. This perversion of nature occurs when they become lovers of pleasure in their souls and seekers of comfort in their bodies—on the one hand, shunning work, and on the other, becoming too soft. 

But one must train those being raised to face fearsome things, even if they must suffer grief or toil; this is so they do not become slaves to these passions, nor greedy for pleasures and hesitant in the face of labor. Rather, let them honor what is noble above all else, abstaining from some things and persevering in others. 

Neither should you make them gluttonous in their food, extravagant in their pleasures, or unrestrained in their reckless play. Nor should you allow them to say or do whatever they please. Furthermore, you should not be frightened when the child cries, nor strive to make him laugh even if he strikes his nurse or [insults] you... <note>The Greek text cuts off mid-sentence at "κα-" (likely part of a word for insulting or mocking), continuing onto the next page.</note>

<summary>Theano writes to Eubule, criticizing a pampered upbringing and arguing that true maternal love requires training children in self-restraint and hardship rather than indulging their desires.</summary>

<keywords>Theano, Eubule, Pythagorean education, parenting, self-restraint, moderation, luxury, virtue, ancient Greek ethics, discipline</keywords>

<page-num>487</page-num>

->## ON THE UPBRINGING OF CHILDREN<-

...speak insultingly <note>original: kakōs; completing the sentence from the previous page: "even if he strikes his nurse or speaks insultingly to you..."</note>, they simply laugh. They provide their children with coolness in the summer and heat in the winter. They offer them much luxury—things which the children of the poor never experience. Yet those poor children are raised more easily, grow no less than yours, and are in a far better condition of body and mind. 

But you, as if you were raising the offspring of Sardanapalus <note>Sardanapalus was a legendary king of Nineveh, famous in the ancient world as the ultimate symbol of decadence, effeminacy, and extreme luxury</note>, weaken the natural character of your boys with pleasures. For what could anyone do with a child who cries if he is not fed immediately? Or who, when he does eat, demands the most delightful delicacies? If there is heat, he collapses; if there is cold, he shivers and wraps himself up. If someone rebukes him, he fights back; if his every whim is not served, he sulks; if he cannot have soft food, he becomes irritable. He spends his leisure wickedly in pursuit of pleasure and lives in an unfree, effeminate manner <term>original: batalizetai; a term suggesting a soft, "dandyish," or undisciplined lifestyle</term>. 

Be careful, then, my friend, knowing that children who live in luxury become nothing more than slaves <term>original: andrapoda; literally "man-footed creatures," a derogatory term for those who lack the inner freedom of a citizen</term> when they reach manhood; therefore, take away such pleasures. Make their upbringing austere, rather than so pampered, and allow them to endure both hunger and thirst, and even cold and heat. Let them also learn a sense of shame <term>original: aidōs; a core Greek virtue involving modesty, respect for elders, and the healthy fear of disgrace</term> before their peers or their teachers. For in this way, the disciplines that stretch and strengthen the soul will eventually become sweet to them. 

For labors, my friend, are like a preliminary dye for children toward the virtue that is to be perfected; once they are sufficiently steeped in these hardships, they will bear the permanent "dye" of virtue more naturally. Take care then, friend, lest—just as poorly tended vines fail to produce fruit—your children, through pampered luxury, give birth to the vice of insolence <term>original: hybris; reckless pride or outrage</term> and a legacy of total uselessness.

H.iiii.

# CONSOLATION TO THE JEALOUS WOMAN

## THEANO TO NICOSTRATE, GREETINGS.

**I** have heard of your husband’s folly <note>original: paranoia; literally "being out of one's mind." In this context, it refers to a lapse in judgment or moral madness caused by infatuation</note>—that he keeps a mistress—and that you are consumed by jealousy toward him. My friend, I have known many who suffer from this same "disease." For it seems men are "hunted" by these women, held captive, and lose their reason. You, however, are dejected night and day; you are distressed and even plot against him. Please, do not do this, my friend. For the virtue of a wife is not found in spying on her husband, but in her accommodation <term>original: symperiphora; a key Pythagorean and Stoic virtue meaning the ability to adapt oneself to another’s character to maintain harmony</term>. 

This accommodation consists in bearing with his lack of sense. After all, a mistress associates with a man for the sake of pleasure, but a wife does so for what is beneficial. And what is beneficial is not to mix evil with evil, nor to meet his madness with your own madness. Some faults, my friend, are provoked further when they are exposed, but they tend to cease when they are met with silence—just as they say a fire is extinguished by leaving it be <note>A common ancient proverb suggesting that some behaviors lose their power when they no longer receive an audience or a reaction</note>. If you rebuke him when he wishes to think he is being discreet, you strip away the mask of his passion, and he will only sin more openly. 

You must realize that your husband’s friendship with you is not currently guided by moral excellence <term>original: kalokagathia; the classic Greek ideal of a "gentlemanly" character that is both beautiful and good</term>. This is the grace of a shared life. Consider that he goes to the mistress for a brief period of idleness, but he remains present with you to share a life; he loves you by choice and rational judgment, but her only by impulse. The time for such a passion is short; it quickly leads to boredom, and it stops as fast as it began. For a man who is not entirely wicked, the time spent with a mistress is fleeting. What is more futile than the enjoyment of a desire that is unjust? Therefore, as he feels his life being diminished and his reputation <term>original: euschemon; his "proper form," dignity, or social standing</term> being tarnished, he will eventually come to his senses. No person of sound mind desires their own self-chosen harm. Called back by the justice of his duties to you, and seeing the losses in his own life, he will perceive...

<header>TO THE JEALOUS WOMAN. 485</header>

# TO THE JEALOUS WOMAN

...you <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "he will perceive you..."</note> one day, and being unable to bear the shame of your silent condemnation, he will quickly repent. But you, my friend, must live your life not by measuring yourself against mistresses. Distinguish yourself from him not by matching his disorderliness <note>original: ataxia; a lack of discipline or moral order</note>, but through your diligence toward the home, your grace in social dealings, and your maternal affection <term>original: philostorgia; specifically the natural, tender love between family members</term> toward your children. You must not, therefore, be jealous of that woman. For it is only noble to extend such emulation toward women of virtue; instead, you must make yourself ready for reconciliation.

For a beautiful character brings about goodwill even among enemies, my friend; and honor is the product of moral excellence <term>original: kalokagathia; the ideal of being both "beautiful and good" in character</term> alone. Through this excellence, it is possible for a wife to hold a kind of authority over her husband, and to be honored more than if she were merely catering to an enemy. 

When he is observed by you in this state of virtue, he will feel even more ashamed, and he will desire to be reconciled all the sooner. He will love you more gently, having recognized the injustice he did to you, observing your devotion to your shared life, and experiencing the proof of your affection for him. Just as the recovery from an ailment of the mouth makes the eventual rest sweet, so do the disagreements of friends lead to more intimate reconciliations. 

Consider also the opposing outcomes of these passions. While he is "ill" <note>Theano uses the metaphor of "sickness" to describe the husband's lapse into infidelity</note>, he invites you also to be ill with grief. While he fails in his dignity, he invites you to fail in your own conduct. While he damages his own life, he invites you to damage your own well-being. By doing so, you will seem to be arrayed against him, and in your attempt to punish him, you will only succeed in punishing yourself. 

For if you were to leave him and go elsewhere, you would only have to try another husband after being rid of the first; and if that one commits the same faults, you would seek yet another. For being "husbandless" is not easily borne by young women. Or will you remain alone without a husband, like an unyoked animal <term>original: azyx; literally "un-yoked," referring to a beast not paired for labor, here meaning a woman without a partner</term>? Or will you neglect the house and destroy the husband? If so, you will share in the harm of a painful life. 

But will you take revenge on the mistress? She will be on her guard, having anticipated you. And even if you do fight her, remember that she is a combative woman who does not blush with shame. Is it then good to fight every day...

<summary>Theano concludes her advice by arguing that a wife’s moral excellence and domestic diligence are more effective than jealousy. She warns that divorce or retaliation only leads to further personal hardship and loss of dignity.</summary>

<keywords>Theano, Nicostrate, marriage, jealousy, reconciliation, philostorgia, kalokagathia, Pythagorean ethics, household management, fidelity</keywords>

<page-num>490</page-num>
<header>LETTERS OF THEANO</header>

...with your husband? And what more will come of it? For fights and insults do not stop licentiousness, but rather increase disagreements by their very progression. What then? Will you plot something against him? Do not, my friend. Tragedy has taught us to master jealousy, having presented a dramatic composition in which Medea committed her crimes <note>Medea is the mythological figure who murdered her own children to take revenge on her husband, Jason, for his infidelity. Theano uses her as a "worst-case scenario" warning against unchecked jealousy.</note>. But just as one must keep one's hands away from an infection of the eyes, so also must you separate yourself from the pretense of this passion. For by enduring through it, you will quench the passion all the sooner.

### On the management of maidservants,
### An Advisory Letter.

->THEANO TO CALLISTO.<-

To you younger women, the law gives authority to rule over the household servants as soon as you are married; however, the lessons concerning domestic management <term>original: oikonomia; the art of managing a household and its resources</term> ought to be sought from your elders who are always offering counsel. For it is good to first learn what you do not know, and to consider the advice of your elders as most intimate. For a young soul must be nurtured in right patterns. 

The first authority of the home for women is the authority over the maidservants. And there is, my friend, nothing greater in servitude than goodwill. For this "possession" is not purchased along with their bodies, but wise masters generate it later through their own conduct. Just treatment is the cause of this, ensuring that they neither grow weary through excessive toil, nor become weak through deprivation. For they are human beings by nature <note>Theano highlights a key Pythagorean and later Stoic principle: that despite social status, slaves share a common human nature with their masters and should be treated accordingly.</note>. 

But some women consider the most profitless thing to be a "profit"—namely, the mistreatment of their maidservants; burdening them with tasks while withholding necessities. Then, while gaining profits of a few obols <note>An obol was a small silver coin of low value; Theano is suggesting these women are "penny-wise and pound-foolish."</note>, they are penalized with great calamities, such as the malicious thoughts and plots of those they mistreat. But for you, the measure of their labor will be ready at hand...

<summary>Theano concludes her advice on jealousy by citing the tragedy of Medea as a warning, then begins a new letter to Callisto advising that domestic authority over servants should be tempered with justice and humanity to foster goodwill.</summary>

<keywords>Theano, Callisto, Medea, household management, oikonomia, servants, slavery, ethics, Pythagoreanism, justice, domestic authority</keywords>

<page-num>491</page-num>
<header>ON THE CARE OF SERVANTS, CONTINUED. 491</header>

...[measured by the amount] of food in proportion to the quantity of their daily labors. Such is the rule regarding their diet <gloss>original: diaitan; the daily regimen or lifestyle</gloss>. But regarding their misbehavior <gloss>original: ataxias; disorder or lack of discipline</gloss>, you must provide what is fitting for your own character, not merely what serves their momentary whims. For one must honor maidservants <gloss>original: therapainas</gloss> according to their merit. Cruelty does not bring a sense of gratitude to the heart, but reason <gloss>original: logismos</gloss> is no less a judge of the hatred for wickedness. 

If the excess of the maidservants' vice is insurmountable, they should be banished through sale. For that which is useless to one's needs should also be alienated from one's ownership. Let your judgment <gloss>original: gnome</gloss> be the presiding guide, by which you will recognize the truth of the offense in relation to the justice of the verdict, and the magnitude of the errors in relation to the deserved punishment <gloss>original: kolaseos</gloss>. 

The authority of a mistress <gloss>original: despoines</gloss> is also a form of grace when it releases the offender from a penalty. In this way, you will preserve what is fitting within the household's pattern. For some women, my friend, out of cruelty, even use whips on the bodies of their maidservants; they become like wild beasts through jealousy or anger, effectively "writing a record" of their own excessive bitterness upon the flesh of others. 

As a result, some servants are consumed, being worn down over time; others seek safety through flight; and some have even ceased to live, departing by their own hand <note>Theano describes the tragic consequences of domestic abuse, including suicide, as a warning that a mistress's cruelty eventually destroys her own household.</note>. Then, the isolation of the mistress, as she laments her own thoughtlessness, brings only a lonely repentance <gloss>original: metanoian; a change of mind or regret</gloss>. 

But, my friend, know how to imitate musical instruments, which sound better when the strings are relaxed, but snap when they are overtightened. It is the same with maidservants: too much relaxation produces a discord in their obedience <gloss>original: peitharchias</gloss>, while the overstretching of necessity causes a destruction of their very nature. One must keep this pattern in mind: moderation is best in all things <note>The Greek phrase "metron ariston" (moderation is best) is a famous maxim of the Seven Sages, here applied to the social "harmony" of the home.</note>.

<summary>Theano advises Callisto on the balance of discipline and mercy, warning that cruelty leads to the loss of servants through flight or death, and advocating for a "musical" harmony in household management where moderation ensures obedience.</summary>

<keywords>Theano, Callisto, domestic ethics, slavery, punishment, moderation, metron ariston, household harmony, Greek ethics, Pythagoreanism</keywords>

# THE LETTER OF 
# MELISSA.

### MELISSA TO CLARETA, GREETINGS.

It seems to me that you possess a natural abundance of good qualities. For by your earnest desire to hear something regarding a woman’s lack of finery <gloss>original: akosmias; literally "disorder," here referring to a lack of elaborate ornamentation</gloss>, you give me great hope that you intend to grow old in virtue <gloss>original: aretan</gloss>. 

Therefore, a modest and free-born woman should approach her lawful husband adorned with quietness <gloss>original: hesychia</gloss>, rather than with extravagance. Let her clothing be white, clean, and simple, but not costly or excessive. For she must reject garments that are transparent or deep purple, as well as those interwoven with gold. 

Such things are useful to courtesans <gloss>original: hetairais; professional female companions or performers</gloss> for the purpose of hunting many men; but for a woman who seeks to please only her own husband, her "adornment" <gloss>original: kosmos</gloss> is her character, not her raiment. For it is a beautiful thing for a free woman to show reverence <gloss>original: aideesthai</gloss> toward her own husband, rather than toward her neighbors. 

Instead of rouge <gloss>original: phykeos; a seaweed-based cosmetic used to redden the cheeks</gloss>, you should wear upon your face the blush of modesty as a sign of your virtue. You should wear nobility, orderliness, and temperance <gloss>original: σωφροσύναν / sophrosyne</gloss> instead of gold and emeralds. For the woman who strives for modesty should not seek beauty in the costliness of her clothes, but in the management of the household <gloss>original: oikonomian</gloss>. She should please her husband by fulfilling his wishes. 

For a husband’s wishes ought to be an unwritten law <note>The "unwritten law" (nomos agraphos) is a classical Greek concept referring to natural or divine laws that supersede man-made statutes. Melissa suggests a wife should treat her husband's preferences with this level of sacred authority.</note> to a well-ordered woman, according to which she must live. Consider that you have brought with you the most beautiful and greatest dowry: good order. For one must trust in the beauty and wealth of the soul rather than that of the appearance or of money. For envy and disease take away the latter, but the former remains fixed until death.

<summary>Melissa writes to Clareta, advising that a virtuous woman should eschew expensive jewelry and transparent clothing in favor of modesty, household management, and a "dowry" of good character, which she describes as an unwritten law.</summary>

<keywords>Melissa, Clareta, Pythagorean women, modesty, sophrosyne, household management, oikonomia, unwritten law, cosmetics, domestic virtue</keywords>

# THE LETTER OF MYIA.

## MYIA TO PHYLLIS, GREETINGS.

**S**ince you have become a mother of children, I offer you the following advice. Choose a nurse <gloss>original: tithan; a wet-nurse who both breastfeeds and cares for the child</gloss> who is the most suitable and clean, and moreover, one who is modest <gloss>original: aidemona</gloss>, not prone to excessive sleep, and not given to talkativeness. For such a woman would be judged best for the purpose of rearing free-born children, provided she has nutritious milk and is not unable to resist the company of men. 

For the role of the woman who nurtures is a great portion of the child's life—the first and most fundamental part for the whole of their existence—in regard to being raised well. She will do everything beautifully at the appropriate time. She should offer the teat and the breast for nourishment not under pressure, but with a certain foresight. For in this way she will lead the infant toward health. She must not be overcome by sleep when she herself wishes to rest, but only when the newborn has a desire for repose. For this will provide no small remedy for the child. 

Let the nurse be neither prone to anger nor talkative, nor indifferent in her intake of food, but orderly and temperate <gloss>original: sophron; a key Pythagorean virtue involving self-control and moderation</gloss>. If possible, she should not be a barbarian <note>In the Greek world, "barbarian" (barbaros) referred to anyone who did not speak Greek. Myia suggests a Greek nurse to ensure the child is immersed in the proper language and cultural customs from birth.</note>, but a Greek. It is best if the newborn, having been properly filled with milk, then turns to sleep. For such a feeding is sweet and easy for the young to digest. 

If it is necessary to provide other food, let it be of the simplest kind. She must abstain from wine entirely because of its potent power, or if used, it should be given only rarely and diluted with water to a milky consistency. Do not give baths continuously; for the use of baths that are infrequent and undiluted <note>This likely refers to using pure water rather than mixing in oils or scents, or perhaps implies avoiding over-saturation of the skin.</note> is better. The air should also be suitable, possessing a balance of heat and cold. Furthermore, the dwelling should be neither too drafty nor too enclosed. Moreover, the water...

<summary>Myia provides Phyllis with a guide for selecting a wet-nurse, emphasizing that the nurse's character—being modest, sober, and Greek—is essential for the child's lifelong health and moral development.</summary>

# HENRI ESTIENNE
## sends greetings to the reader.

*When the previous edition of Diogenes Laertius which had been produced at Basel* <note>original: "Basileas." Basel was a major hub for European printing in the 16th century.</note> *had been compared with various ancient manuscripts, partly by me and partly by others; and when that <term>collation</term> <note>The process of comparing different versions of a text to identify changes or errors.</note> had given us a great number of <term>variant readings</term> <note>Differences in wording found between two or more manuscripts of the same work.</note>: of which most were better than those that the previous edition held, while some were of such a kind that one might doubt which of the two should be preferred, and others appeared to be of slight or even of no importance; amidst this variety of variant readings, I adopted this plan (which I trust you will approve of): that those which were clearly superior to what that edition had offered should be received into the main text itself in their place. Of the rest, some should be noted at the end of the book itself, and others should be passed over. As for those first ones, placed in the text—and likewise many passages where some words, and sometimes an entire sentence, were missing and have now been filled in—a comparison of the previous edition with this one will testify to you abundantly. The second kind, moreover, are those which I have now judged worthy of being noted; the third kind, on the contrary, I have judged should be passed over in total silence, because they are as I described <note>i.e., of no importance or merit.</note>. Furthermore, although I have used many manuscripts, I confess that passages are not lacking which still await some help from elsewhere; each of these I would have pointed out to you, if I had the leisure. But I could hardly steal even a tiny bit of leisure for this hurried writing, as I am occupied in finishing the edition of Herodotus <note>The famous Greek historian; Estienne's Greek edition of Herodotus (1570) is considered a landmark of scholarship.</note> (which I promised would be a companion to this one). Meanwhile, however, I hope you will take this labor, such as it is, in good part. Farewell.*

<summary>This preface by the printer-scholar Henri Estienne explains his editorial methodology for this 1570 edition of Diogenes Laertius, describing how he selected the best versions of the text from various ancient manuscripts while rushing to finish his work on Herodotus.</summary>

Page 10. In the line [ending in] "-mones"] <note>original: "μώνης"</note> <term>written as</term> "And Hieronymus and Rhodius say" <note>original Greek: "φησὶ δὲ Ἱερώνυμος καὶ Ῥόδιος"</note> instead of "And the Rhodian Hieronymus says." Regarding this reading, it is strange that the ancient manuscripts agree with one another, as if there were two authors, even though the verb is "he says" <note>singular</note> and not "they say" <note>plural</note>. Also, elsewhere a certain Hieronymus is surnamed "Rhodius." Some manuscripts have it with the article: "Hieronymus and the Rhodian."

In the line [ending in] "-mymos"] <note>original: "μύμος"</note> <term>written as</term> "that there would be a future crop of olives" <note>original Greek: "φορᾶς μελλούσης ἐλαιῶν ἔσεσθαι"</note>.

In the line "I will advance"] <note>original: "προπήσω"</note> <term>written as</term> "I will benefit" <note>original Greek: "ὀνηίσῳ"</note> instead of "I will advance." You have that word twice also from Heraclitus, further down on page 342. But there also, some manuscripts had corrupted the words "oneisos" and "oneison" into "isos" and "ison."

->### HENRI ESTIENNE ###<-

...for here the particle "evidently" <note>original Greek: "δηλονότι"</note> is placed, as if originating from a scholion <note>an ancient marginal commentary</note>, because the genitive "of Salamis" <note>original Greek: "Σαλαμῖνος"</note> had been omitted.

**Attic** [line starting with Ἀττικός]] In some manuscripts it is read as "releasing" <note>original Greek: "ἀφέντον"</note>, but the letter "n" <note>original Greek: "ν"</note> was mistakenly omitted for the sake of the meter: which can also stand as "of those releasing" <note>original Greek: "ἀφέντων"</note>, because a liquid consonant is joined to a mute. However, this reading—"having fled Salamis" <note>original Greek: "τὴν Σαλαμῖνα φυγὼν"</note>—was devised from the words of the translator. As if, indeed, these words—*He who fled Salamis*—were foreign to the meaning of the words we have. Add to this that "He flees" <note>original Latin: "Fugit"</note> ought to be in the present tense because of the meter.

Page 18. **In the line [starting with] "klēsian"** <note>original Greek: "κλῃσίαν"</note>] <gloss>it is written</gloss> <term>spear</term> <note>original Greek: "δόρατος"</note> instead of <term>breastplate</term> <note>original Greek: "θώρακος"</note>.

**In the line "of the"** <note>original Greek: "τῆς"</note>] The word <term>elegies</term> <note>original Greek: "ἐλεγῆα"</note> is inserted after <term>tyranny</term> <note>original Greek: "τυραννίδος"</note>. And thus the translator also has it.

**In the line "from the cloud"** <note>original Greek: "ἐκ νεφ."</note>] <gloss>it is written</gloss> <term>spirit</term> <note>original Greek: "μένος"</note> instead of <term>force</term> <note>original Greek: "βία"</note>.

**In the line "was poured out"** <note>original Greek: "χύετο"</note>] <gloss>it is written</gloss> <term>settled together</term> <note>original Greek: "συνῴκισεν"</note> instead of <term>settled</term> <note>original Greek: "ᾤκισεν"</note>.

Page 19. **In the line "themselves"** <note>original Greek: "αὐτοὶ"</note>] <gloss>it is written</gloss> <term>to these</term> <note>original Greek: "τούτοις"</note> instead of <term>these</term> <note>original Greek: "τούτους"</note>. However, "to these" must be joined with "giving" <note>original Greek: "δόντες"</note>.

**In the line "neither"** <note>original Greek: "οὔτε"</note>] <gloss>it is written</gloss> <term>neither is it fitting for me</term> <note>original Greek: "οὔτε οὐ προσῆκόν μοι"</note>, without the word "as" <note>original Greek: "ὡς"</note>, and more correctly. Page 21. **In the line "with"** <note>original Greek: "μετὰ"</note>] <gloss>it is written</gloss> <term>poralōn</term> <note>original Greek: "πωράλων," likely a misspelling of "paraliōn," the coastal dwellers of Attica</note> instead of <term>paraliōn</term> <note>original Greek: "παραλίων"</note>.

**In the last line**] <term>best</term> <note>original Greek: "ἄρειστα"</note> instead of <term>most beautiful</term> <note>original Greek: "κάλλιστα"</note>.

Page 22. **In the line "which for"** <note>original Greek: "αἳ γὰ"</note>] <gloss>it is written</gloss> <term>of diseases and a curse</term> <note>original Greek: "νόσων καὶ ἀρὴ"</note> without the word "and" <note>original Greek: "τε"</note>.

**In the line "and after"** <note>original Greek: "καὶ μεταπ."</note>] Instead of <term>noble</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀγαυάς"</note>, I do not doubt that another word ought to be restored: since neither can a suitable meaning be extracted from this reading, nor does the law of meter admit it.

**In the line "See"** <note>original Greek: "Ὅρα"</note>] Instead of <term>wound</term> <note>original Greek: "ἔλχος"</note> (which I left according to the consensus of all our old copies), "hatred" <note>original Greek: "ἔχθος"</note> was read by the translator, to which reading his interpretation corresponds, having "Hatred." ->### NOTES ON DIOGENES ###<-

...while in "heart" <note>original Greek: κραδίῃ</note>, (as I have changed it) it is most evident.

Page 23. **In the line "you announce"** <note>original Greek: ἐπαγγέλλεις</note>] <gloss>the variant reading is</gloss> "you report" <note>original Greek: ἀπαγγέλλεις</note>, which I prefer.

Page 25. **In the line "elegies"** <note>original Greek: ἐλεγεῖα</note>] I would prefer this over "elegy" <note>original Greek: ἐλεγείαν</note>; as seen below in the phrase "elegiac verses" <note>original Greek: ἐλεγεῖα ἔπη</note> in the section on Pittacus on page 29. Indeed, in other writers as well, you will find "elegies" used more often than "elegy."

**In the line "to him"** <note>original Greek: αὐτῷ</note>] <gloss>the variant reading is</gloss> "I know how to say, if those things lie there" <note>original Greek: ἐπίσταμαι, εἴπειν, αἲ δ᾽ ἐκεῖσθαι</note>. Otherwise, the meaning would have to be understood <note>implied by context rather than stated</note>.

**In the line "[ending in] -tyros"** <note>original Greek: τυρος</note>] <gloss>the variant reading is</gloss> "Herodotus in the first [book]" <note>original Greek: Ηρόδοτος ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ</note>.

Page 26. **In the line "to the..."** <note>original Greek: ταὶς ἀτ.</note>] <gloss>the variant reading is</gloss> "to be carried" <note>original Greek: φέρεσθαι</note> instead of "to travel" <note>original Greek: πορεύεσθαι</note>.

**In the line "to the"** <note>original Greek: τοῖς</note>] <gloss>the variant reading is</gloss> "of Cythera" <note>original Greek: Κυθήρων</note>, from the plural nominative <term>Cythera</term> <note>original Greek: Κύθηρα</note>, which is the more frequent form.

Page 27. **In the line "My"** <note>original Greek: Ἐμῆς</note>] Previously, "my" <note>original Greek: ἐμὴν</note> was read incorrectly instead of the <term>Doric</term> form "to me" <note>original Greek: ἐμὶν</note>, and "and" <note>original Greek: καὶ</note> instead of the dialectal "and" <note>original Greek: κα</note>: likewise "I" <note>original Greek: ἐγὼ</note> instead of "I" <note>original Greek: ἐγόν</note>.

Page 28. **In the line "as the"** <note>original Greek: ὡς τὸν</note>] Write "Tyrrhaean" <note>original Greek: Τυρρᾶῖον</note>.

Page 30. **In the line "The"** <note>original Greek: Τὴν</note>] In other authors, "he was brought into the house" <note>original Greek: εἰς οἶκον ἐπήγετο</note>.

Page 32. **In the line "In this way"** <note>original Greek: Τῇδε</note>] It is better to write, following other manuscripts, "it hides" <note>original Greek: κέκευθε</note>. Otherwise, if "it hides" is retained, "in this way" <note>original Greek: τῇδε</note> would have to be changed to "this [feminine]" <note>original Greek: ἥδε</note>.

**In the line "but, as..."** <note>original Greek: δέ, ἀς.</note>] Restore "it was pleasing" <note>original Greek: ἄρεσκε</note>.

Page 33. **In the line "Bronze"** <note>original Greek: Χαλκῆ</note>] Several writers quoting these verses read in the first line, "I sit upon a tomb" <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ σήματος ἧμαι</note>. In the fourth, "And the rivers overflow, and the sea washes around" <note>original Greek: Καὶ ποταμοὶ πλήθωσι, περικλύζῃ δὲ θάλασσα</note>. In the last line, "I shall signify" <note>original Greek: Σημανέω</note>.

Page 34. **In the line "of the sea"** <note>original Greek: σάλας</note>] This passage was greatly corrupted. For it used to read "praiseworthy-immense tomb" <note>original Greek: αἰνητέυμμος σήλας</note>, instead of "praise [was] the blame of the sea" <note>original Greek: αἰνηθέντα μῶμος σάλας</note>. But, to confess the truth, not even the old manuscripts were entirely free from error: since in them was "praise [was] the blame of the sea" <note>original Greek: αἰνηθέντα μῶμος σάλας</note>, with the letter "s" <note>original Greek: σ</note> evidently omitted at the beginning of the third word, because of the "s" that is found at the end of the preceding word <note>This is a common scribal error called haplography, where two similar letters next to each other are merged into one</note>. I have observed that this clashing of letters has also been the cause of other errors. As for the fact that someone previously restored "praiseworthy" <note>original Greek: αἰνητέμμον</note>, it cannot stand. However, it pleases me to translate this little piece of the Simonidean ode <note>Simonides of Ceos was a famous lyric poet who critiqued the epitaph of Midas mentioned here</note>, since the translator did not represent the poet's own words in his interpretation. I will render it almost word-for-word, and therefore more roughly. "Who (he says) relying on his mind [that is, having a sound mind] would praise Cleobulus, an inhabitant of Lindus, who..."

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s philological commentary on the lives of the Seven Sages in Diogenes Laertius. ->### HENRI ESTIENNE ###<-

...to perennial rivers, and spring flowers, and the flame of the sun, and the golden moon, and the waves of the sea, would he oppose <note>that is, compare</note> the strength of a column? For all things are inferior to the gods: but even mortal hands break a stone. This is the counsel of a foolish man. <gloss>or rather, this "opinion," so that it stands for "judgment"</gloss> <note>original Greek: γνώμη</note>

**Verse V. "And there was"** <note>original Greek: Εἷς δ’ ἦν</note>] <gloss>the variant reading is</gloss> "there were twelve children."

**Verse V. "but that which"** <note>original Greek: ἀλλ’ ὃ</note>] See whether we should read "the grace" <note>original Greek: ἡ χάρις</note>.

Page 35. **Verse "For many companions"** <note>original Greek: Πολλοὶ γὰρ ἑταιροι</note>] both here and a little later: which better suits the dialect in which this letter was written. But (what is of much greater importance) it must be seen what can be decided regarding these words, "ever-most-miserable" <note>original Greek: ποτ’ αἰνιοτάτων</note>. Previously, those were read as a single word, "ever-freshest" <note>original Greek: ποταινιωτάτων</note>: but that spelling was restored from an old manuscript. But what if we read "most-cleansing" <note>original Greek: ποταγνιωτάτων</note> from <term>potagnios</term> <note>original Greek: ποτάγνιος</note>, to which a new meaning might be attributed? However, the translator seems to have either had another reading or certainly restored one; since he renders it, "it would be most convenient for inhabiting." The same man seems to have read "many witnesses" <note>original Greek: πολλοὶ μάρτυι</note> since he interprets it as, "Indeed, very many are friends to you." But as for "fortune" <note>original Greek: τύχη</note> (which appears in some manuscripts), I do not see how it can be applied.

Page 36. **Verse "upon the"** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τῇ</note>] "the place" <note>original Greek: χώρᾳ</note> is wrongly restored instead of "the discovery of a theft" <note>original Greek: φωρᾷ</note>. For here we should rather agree with the copies that have the former reading [theft] than those that have the latter [place], as the immediately preceding words sufficiently show.

Page 37. **Verse "the..."** <note>original Greek: τὰ κερ.</note>] Previously it was "gaining" <note>original Greek: κερδαίντα</note>, a word corrupted only in its accent: therefore "gaining" <note>original Greek: κέρδοντα</note> is wrongly restored in place of "gaining" <note>original Greek: κερδαίντα</note>.

**Verse "cries out"** <note>original Greek: ἀϋτεῖ</note>] Instead of "there" <note>original Greek: αὐτεῖ</note>, I found "cries out" <note>original Greek: ἀϋτεῖ</note> in certain old manuscripts. This pleased me more, as the third person of the verb "to shout" <note>original Greek: ἀϋτῶ</note>, having "Apollo" <note>original Greek: Ἀπόλλων</note> as the subject (to be sought from the preceding lines): but it requires an interpretation a little different from what is commonly attributed to it. Furthermore, that "my letters" <note>original Greek: τὰς ἐμὰς ἐπιστολὰς</note> should be restored from the same sources instead of "to my letters" <note>original Greek: ταῖς ἐμαῖς ἐπιστολαις</note> can by no means be called into doubt.

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s line-by-line philological commentary on the text of Diogenes Laertius. ->### ANNOTATIONS ON DIOGENES ###<-

Page 38. **Verse "tau"** <note>original Greek: ταὺ</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "or I shall avenge such enemies." <note>original Greek: ἢ ἐχθρὸ τοῖα ἀμυνῶμαι</note> Likewise, instead of "having burned down" <note>original Greek: κατακαύσας</note>, some read "you might listen." <note>original Greek: κατακούσαις</note> This certainly cannot be sustained; but perhaps it contains traces of the true reading. In order to recover it, it seems that two other words should be formed from that term and the one immediately following. However, until this reading is brought to light, it can hardly be said whether we should read "the daughter" <note>original Greek: τήν τε θυγατέ'</note> (as in most <term>old manuscripts</term>) or "to the daughter" <note>original Greek: τῇ τε θυγατρί</note>.

Page 39. **Verse "pelet."** <note>original Greek: πελετ.</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "performing" <note>original Greek: ἐπιτελοῦντα</note>. This is more frequently read with this <term>accusative</term> case <note>the grammatical case used for the direct object of a sentence</note>.

**Verse "Paitas"** <note>original Greek: Παίτας</note>] More correctly "Grecian" <note>original Greek: Ἑλλαδικοῖς</note>, as you have it. For "Hellenic" <note>original Greek: Ἑλλανικοῖς</note> would have a long 'a' sound, as it stands in place of "Hellenic" <note>original Greek: Ἑλληνικοῖς</note> in the <term>Doric dialect</term>.

Page 40. **Verse "Ezr"** <note>original Greek: Ἐζρ</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "into the land of the Greeks." <note>original Greek: εἰς τὴν γῆν τῶν Ἑλλ.</note> But we are wrongly commanded to follow this reading, since the other is more elegant, leaving the noun to be understood <note>a grammatical device where a word like "land" is implied rather than spoken</note> according to the very common custom of the Greeks. Similarly, at the beginning of this page, "by power" <note>original Greek: κράτει</note> is undeservedly brought forward instead of "to rule" <note>original Greek: κρατεῖν</note>, as if it were necessary to replace the latter with the former; whereas we find such a use of <term>infinitives</term> in giving instructions throughout this very book.

Page 41. **Verse "having lived"** <note>original Greek: βιούς</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "seventy" <note>original Greek: ἑβδομήκοντα</note> instead of "ninety" <note>original Greek: ἐννενήκοντα</note>.

Page 42. **Verse "chyeto"** <note>original Greek: χύετο</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "finding everything moved/rearranged." <note>original Greek: μετεσκευασμένα πάντα καταλαβών</note> This reading should also have been received into the main text. The translator followed it as well, but did not interpret it well. For he translates it: *But when he saw the face of all things changed.* Whereas by the phrase "everything moved," he seems to have meant "all vessels moved elsewhere," or "all furniture moved elsewhere," although otherwise examples of this specific meaning may be lacking.

Page 49. **Verse "oisan"** <note>original Greek: οἶσαν</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "false-swelling" <note>original Greek: ψευδοιδῆ</note>. This was also in the previous edition, but "false-swelling" is more easily confirmed.

Page 50. **Verse "mlo"** <note>original Greek: μλω</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "having stepped out" <note>original Greek: ἐκβάς</note>.

**Verse "Euboul."** <note>original Greek: Εὔβουλ.</note>] It seems it should be read as "more ill-advised" <note>original Greek: ἀβουλότερος</note>.

Page 52. **Verse "of the Athenians"** <note>original Greek: Ἀθηναίων</note>] It is also read as a question: "Were you deprived of the Athenians?" <note>original Greek: ἐστερήθης Ἀθηναίων;</note>

Page 55. **Verse "But he"** <note>original Greek: Ἀλλ' ὁ</note>] Instead of "him" <note>original Greek: αὐτὸν</note>, I have restored "himself" <note>original Greek: αὑτὸν</note> with a <term>spiritus asper</term> <note>a "rough breathing" mark in Greek, looking like a reversed comma, which adds an 'h' sound and often makes a pronoun reflexive</note> in place of the longer form of "himself" <note>original Greek: ἑαυτόν</note>. Just as at the beginning of this page, you have "he led himself out" <note>original Greek: ἑαυτὸν ἐξήγαγεν</note>, whereas previously it was read as "he led him out," by the same error found here. Certainly the translator, although he seems to have read "him," did not at all grasp this manner of speaking. For he rendered it, *And he departed from there of his own accord*; whereas he ought to have rendered it, *And he brought death upon himself*. For one is said "to lead himself out" <note>original Greek: ἐξάγειν αὑτὸν or ἑαυτὸν</note>—understanding the <term>genitive</term> "from life"—when he leads himself out of life, to interpret it literally <note>Estienne is explaining that this Greek phrase is a common euphemism for suicide</note>. In the translation of the epigram, the precise meaning of these words was also not expressed; however, I think some injury was done to its author there. For he wrote that Pericles preserved a life unharmed for this man. But then the word "Destroyed," having nothing to refer to, is conveniently referred to that <term>accusative</term> <note>the direct object of the sentence</note>.

**Verse "with a gift"** <note>original Greek: δώρῳ</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "of Myson" <note>original Greek: Μύσωνος</note>.

**Verse "he says"** <note>original Greek: φησὶν</note>] You find this <term>genitive</term> case "of the peoples" <note>original Greek: δήμων</note> positioned this way in other places, as well as on pages 103 and 146. Instead of "to compose together" <note>original Greek: συμποιεῖν</note>, some read "to labor together" <note>original Greek: συμπονεῖν</note>. But I would gladly retain "to compose together," as it is well known that "to compose" <note>original Greek: ποιεῖν</note> is used in reference to poetic writing; and you find it so below, on page 146.

Page 56. **Verse "From the"** <note>original Greek: Ἐκ δ'</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "unacknowledged" <note>original Greek: ἀνομολόγης</note>.

Page 57. **Verse "having stood"** <note>original Greek: στύσαντα</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "the prizes of valor" <note>original Greek: τὰ ἀριστεῖα</note>. But I preferred to keep the other reading, because one says "they withdraw from this" <note>using the genitive case</note> rather than "they withdraw this" <note>using the accusative case</note>.

Page 58. **Verse "money"** <note>original Greek: χρήματα</note>] Instead of "hungry" <note>original Greek: προσέλιμος</note>, we are commanded to substitute "warlike" <note>original Greek: προσέλεμος</note>; as if indeed, just as "hungry" [is used], so also...

**Verse "rudder"** <note>original Greek: οἰακὸν</note>] We are commanded to substitute "marvels indeed" <note>original Greek: θαύματα μὲν</note> in place of "a marvel, the things..." <note>original Greek: θαῦμα, τὰ μὲν</note> etc. (a reading in which all our ancient <term>codices</term> <note>handwritten manuscript books</note> agreed). But this suggested reading would be more than "marvelous" <note>Estienne is likely being sarcastic about a poor suggestion from a rival editor</note>. However, whoever commands this follows the error of the translator, who rendered this passage as follows: *Moreover, he said it was easy for anyone to declare the wonderful things he possesses; but to name the friends he has is most difficult.* Whereas he ought to have rendered it: *Moreover, he said it was a wonder that every person can easily say whatever things he possesses, but cannot name how many friends he possesses.* <note>This refers to a famous saying attributed to Socrates on the scarcity of true friends compared to material goods</note>.

Page 60. **Verse "to make"** <note>original Greek: ποις</note>] Instead of "obscene speech" <note>original Greek: αἰσχρολογίαν</note>, one also reads "pedantic quibbling" <note>original Greek: γλισχρολογίαν</note>. This is more acceptable to me, since "pedantic quibbling" is aptly attributed to the "wrangling arguments" <note>original Greek: λόγοις ἐριστικοῖς</note> of the <term>Sophists</term> <note>intellectuals in ancient Greece who were often criticized for using clever but fallacious reasoning</note>.

**Verse "nay indeed"** <note>original Greek: ναι μὴ</note>] We are commanded to insert the particle "not" <note>original Greek: μὴ</note> between "the" <note>original Greek: τοῦ</note> and "knowing" <note>original Greek: εἰδέναι</note>, which however neither our ancient <term>codices</term> possessed, nor the passage allows. Otherwise, the sense would be that Socrates said he knew nothing, and did not even know this—namely, whether it were true that he knew nothing. Yet it can be known from other writers that he was accustomed to say, *This one thing I know: that I know nothing.*

Page 62. **Verse "the..."** <note>original Greek: τὰ ἀμ.</note>] Although the consensus of many <term>codices</term> confirms this reading, the other is more acceptable to me: "according to Meletus and Anytus" <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὸν Μέλιτον καὶ Ἄνυτον</note> <note>the primary accusers who brought Socrates to trial</note>.

Page 66. **Verse "twig"** <note>original Greek: κλώ</note>] The previous edition had: "they say that he, having met Socrates in a narrow alleyway..." <note>original Greek: τοῦτον ἐν στενωπῷ φασὶν ἀπαιτήσαντα Σωκράτην</note>. This reading can in no way be sustained. But since one or the other <term>accusative</term> <note>the grammatical case for a direct object</note> had to be changed into a <term>dative</term> <note>the case usually indicating the recipient of an action</note>, I preferred to change "this man" <note>original Greek: τοῦτον</note>—or rather, I was obliged to. For otherwise we would be ascribing to Xenophon that which was done by Socrates (as is also clear from what follows). I am not unaware, however, that in many ancient <term>codices</term> one reads "him" <note>original Greek: αὐτὸν</note> and "to Socrates" <note>original Greek: Σωκράτει</note>. <note>This describes the famous first meeting where Socrates blocked Xenophon's path with a staff to ask him where men are made good and virtuous</note>.

-># ANNOTATIONS ON DIOGENES #<-

...the consensus of the copies regarding this writing, and even that of the translator himself.

Line: "of those who returned" <note>original Greek: τῶν ἀναχ.</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "of their own" <note>original Greek: τῶν ἰδίων</note>.

Line: "loves" <note>original Greek: ἐρώτων</note>] In place of "he had" <note>original Greek: εἶχεν</note>, one also reads "he saw" <note>original Greek: εἶδεν</note>, but I prefer the former reading. It can hardly be determined from the translator's words which of the two he followed. However, the words that are added by him (to incidentally advise the reader on this matter)—"They say that he thus addressed someone concerning the Minerva of Phidias"—were poorly rendered. This was due to a failure to understand the usage that the verb "to ask" <note>original Greek: ἐρωτῆσαι</note> obtains here and elsewhere among those who deal with <term>dialectics</term> <note>the art of investigating the truth of opinions through logical discussion</note>. For it is just as if we were to say, "He proposed such an interrogation to him."

Line: "From where" <note>original Greek: Πόθεν</note>] In place of "garden" <note>original Greek: κῆπον</note>, we are instructed to restore "bosom" <note>original Greek: κόλπον</note>. Some of our <term>codices</term> <note>handwritten manuscript books</note> also contained this word, but the majority have "garden." My *Thesaurus of the Greek Language* <note>Estienne’s own comprehensive Greek-Latin dictionary, a landmark of Renaissance scholarship</note> will teach you abundantly that "garden" is the true reading.

Page 91. Line: "this" <note>original Greek: τόνδε</note>] Read rather (as in certain ancient <term>codices</term>) "this one, or that one" <note>original Greek: τόνδε, ἢ τόνδε</note>.

Page 94. Line: "and there" <note>original Greek: κάντ.</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "having become wealthy and being gathered into Elis" <note>original Greek: πλούσαντες καὶ συγχυόμενοι εἰς Ἥλιν</note>.

Page 95. Line: "for the" <note>original Greek: τῷ γὰρ</note>] <gloss>variant reading</gloss>: "mockery" <note>original Greek: ἐπισκώψεως</note>. The same diversity of reading is found below.

Line: "of fame" <note>original Greek: κλέους</note>] "Turning back with" <note>original Greek: συνανακάμπτοντος</note> is cited instead of "beating back with" <note>original Greek: συνανακόπτοντος</note>.

Page 96. Line: "lying" <note>original Greek: κειμένου</note>] The word "struggler" or "anxious one" <note>original Greek: ἀγωνιάτης</note> might be suspect to some, as no example of its use is cited from any other source. However, it is written this way in both places in all our ancient <term>codices</term>. Its origin from the verb "to be anxious" <note>original Greek: ἀγωνιᾷν</note> is manifest. Nevertheless, in the first instance the translator renders it as "fearing ignominy" <note>original Latin: Ignominiae metuens</note>, and in the second, "anxious and solicitous" <note>original Latin: Anxius atque solicitus</note>. But Budé <note>Guillaume Budé, a preeminent French humanist scholar</note> suggests "one who trembles" <note>original Latin: Trepidator</note> or "one who fears" <note>original Latin: Formidator</note>.

Page 97. Line: "herself" <note>original Greek: αὑτάς</note>] Unless we read "he was nourished" <note>original Greek: ἐτρέφετο</note> (as most ancient copies have it), it would be necessary to read "he was turned" <note>original Greek: ἐτρέπετο</note>. However, "he was nourished" is more suitable. From this, someone is also called "quick-turning" <note>original Greek: ἀγχίστροφος</note>; likewise, a certain poet spoke of a "versatile thought" <note>original Greek: πολύστροφον νόημα</note>. These descriptions suit that type of talent which the Latins call "versatile" <note>original Latin: versatile</note> by the same metaphor. Therefore, the translator should not have rendered it as "He was turning all things" <note>original Latin: Versabat omnia</note>. Likewise, "inventors of arguments" <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλόγοι</note> should rather be translated differently...

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s detailed linguistic analysis of terms found in Diogenes Laertius’s "Lives of the Eminent Philosophers." Having just mentioned the phrase "inventors of arguments" on the previous page, Estienne here provides a deep dive into the Greek root word "heuresilogos," distinguishing between simple talkativeness and the strategic invention of logical arguments in debate.</meta>

-># HENRI ESTIENNE #<-

...should have been interpreted. Concerning this word (since it occurs elsewhere as well), I will say a few things here in passing. But I will begin with the noun **inventor of arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλόγος</note>, from which another noun is formed, namely **invention of arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλογία</note>; then also that verb **to invent arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλογεῖν</note>. 

Therefore, an **inventor of arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλόγος, εὑρεσιλόγος, or εὑρεσιολόγος</note> (meaning, as it were, a "deviser or discoverer of words," or "one who continually devises new discourses") is not simply a "pourer-out of words." Rather, it is one who is never lacking an argument for pouring out words. However, do not understand this "pouring out of words" as occurring in just any manner, but as is customary in disputations—and specifically the more stubborn ones. 

The term was first used regarding philosophical or <term>sophistic</term> <note>referring to the Sophists, ancient Greek teachers who specialized in using tools of rhetoric and logic to persuade, sometimes through clever but misleading arguments</note> disputations, though later its use became broader. By Budé <note>Guillaume Budé, the great French humanist</note>, it is rendered as "Eloquent," "Articulate," or "Skilled in disputing." In the passage of this very author [Diogenes Laertius] regarding Arcesilaus: "He was capable and **most inventive in finding arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρεσιλογώτατος</note> to meet challenges aptly, to bring the cycle of discourse back to the matter at hand, and to adapt to every occasion." But these interpretations, especially the first two, are little approved by me. 

From this comes **argument-invention** <note>original Greek: εὑρεσιολογία, εὑρεσιολογία, or εὑρησιλογία</note>, that faculty of devising words. We read **argument-invention** <note>original Greek: εὑρεσιολογία</note> in Plutarch’s *Roman Questions* and in his book *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*. However, the form **argument-invention** <note>original Greek: εὑρεσιολογία</note> is found in Philo’s *On the World*, as well as in this author at the beginning of the *Life of Stilpo*; though in some copies, the reading **argument-invention** <note>original Greek: εὑρεσιλογία</note> is found there. 

That third variation, **invention of arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλογία</note>, appears in the same Plutarch, who writes: "if they consider philosophy not a game or a matter of **inventing arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλογία</note> for the sake of reputation, but a work worthy of serious study, as it truly is." 

But the verb **to invent arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλογεῖν</note>, just as it is used here, is also read in Athenaeus, Book 5, concerning Antiochus who was surnamed Epimanes <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, whose erratic behavior led critics to call him "Epimanes" or "The Madman"</note>: "he was found mostly at the silversmiths' and goldsmiths' shops, **inventing technical arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρησιλογῶν</note> and discussing craftsmanship with the engravers and other artisans." 

From these examples, let the reader judge whether an **inventor of arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρεσιλόγος or εὑρησιλόγος</note> is properly and simply a "pourer-out of words" or "wordy"; whether **argument-invention** <note>original Greek: εὑρεσιολογία or εὑρησιλογία</note> is a "pouring out of words" or "verbosity"; and whether **to invent arguments** <note>original Greek: εὑρεσιλογεῖν or εὑρησιλογεῖν</note> is "to pour out words" or "to be wordy."

<summary>Estienne analyzes the Greek term "heuresilogos," arguing that it describes a specific intellectual skill for generating logical arguments and technical vocabulary during debate, rather than mere talkativeness.</summary>
<keywords>Henri Estienne, Diogenes Laertius, philology, Greek etymology, Arcesilaus, Stilpo, Plutarch, Athenaeus, rhetoric, logical disputation, Sophistry</keywords>

-># NOTES ON DIOGENES LAERTIUS #<-

**Page 98. Verse...]** <gloss>It is written</gloss> **most active** <note>original Greek: πρακτικώτατος</note>. However, the alternative reading agrees better with what precedes it. For the author wishes to show that he who was quite **combative** <note>original Greek: μάχιμος, meaning pugnacious or fond of disputation</note> in his debates was altogether different in his actions: namely, **most gentle** <note>original Greek: πρᾳότατον, meaning most clement or mild-mannered</note>. 

Meanwhile, the translator must be corrected in his interpretation of the immediately preceding passage. He thought **under-the-eyes** <note>original Greek: ὑπώπια</note> referred to signs of a "fiery spirit" visible in the eyes; whereas that word actually signifies **bruises** <note>original Latin: sugillationes</note> on the face, specifically in the parts lying beneath the eyes <note>Estienne is correcting a poetic interpretation to a more literal, physical one: having a "black eye."</note>. From this is derived the verb **to be struck under the eye** <note>original Greek: ὑπωπιάζεσθαι</note>, which is used of one who is so bruised. Indeed, this very author uses it elsewhere, as in the *Life of Crates*: "Having provoked Nikodromos the cithara-player, he was **given a black eye** <note>original Greek: ὑπωπιάσθη</note>."

**Page 99. Verse...]** We must believe that the translator read nothing other than **salted fish** <note>original Greek: ταρίχον</note>, but wrote something other than "Satiusculum" <note>likely a Latin diminutive or corrupted term for salted meat/fish</note>, which was evidently derived from the word for salt.

**Page 100. Verse...]** The translator also read not "undisciplined" <note>original Greek: ἀκόλαστον</note> but **not a flatterer** <note>original Greek: ἀκόλακον</note>, and interpreted it correctly as "One alien to flattery."

**Verse...]** <gloss>It is written</gloss> **to free the fatherland from those [men].** <note>original Greek: ἐλευθερῶσαι τὴν πατρίδα ἀπὸ τῶν</note>

**Page 101. Verse...]** For **Such a man** <note>original Greek: Τοιοῦτος</note> one also reads **this man** <note>original Greek: οὗτος</note>, and indeed with a question mark added.

**Verse...]** <gloss>It is written</gloss> **eightieth** <note>original Greek: ὀγδοηκοστόν</note> instead of "tallest" or "longest" <note>original Greek: μηκοστὸν</note>.

**Page 102. Verse...]** <gloss>It is written</gloss> **Anaxiades** <note>original Greek: Ἀναξιάδης</note>.

**Page 103. Verse...]** Here, **the people** in the <term>accusative</term> <note>original Greek: τὸν δῆμον; the direct object of a verb</note> is wrongly put back in place of **to the people** in the <term>dative</term> <note>original Greek: τῷ δήμῳ; the indirect object</note>. This is an error, unless perhaps someone should argue that the singular accusative should be restored in every place where this plural <term>genitive</term> <note>showing possession</note> is found. These instances are not few. Indeed, this phrasing is found not only elsewhere, but also at the beginning of the *Life of Socrates* and the beginning of the *Life of Xenophon*. Furthermore (which is more surprising), at the start of the *Life of Speusippus*, several old manuscripts likewise had the dative form **to the people** <note>original Greek: τῷ δήμῳ</note> instead of the expected case.

**Page 104. Verse...]** It is suggested by conjecture that we read **to follow** <note>original Greek: ἀπολουθῆναι</note> instead of **to be released** <note>original Greek: ἀπολυθῆναι</note>. However, it seems that **to be released** can be sustained, if we understand it as being "released from the disease," since the text had previously mentioned "having fallen ill."

-># NOTES BY HENRI ESTIENNE #<-

**Page 106. Verse...]** For **to resemble** <note>original Greek: οἰκέναι, a variant of ἐοικέναι</note>: instead of "most similar" <note>original Greek: ὁμοιότατα</note> one also reads **likenesses** <note>original Greek: ὁμοιώματα</note>, and even **similarities** <note>original Greek: ὁμοιότητες</note>.

**Page 109. Verse...]** For **the things from** <note>original Greek: τὰν παρὰ</note>: One also reads **you would do** <note>original Greek: ποιοῖς</note>, which is more correct. The translator also followed this reading, for he translates: "**You would do well if you remember**" <note>original Latin: Rectè feceris si memineris</note>; and not, "**You do well because you remember**" <note>original Latin: Rectè facis quòd memineris</note>.

**Page 110. Verse...]** **He himself** <note>original Greek: αὐτός</note>. <gloss>Written as: **Theopompus**</gloss>. But he is called by that other name elsewhere, not this one.

**Page 111. Verse...]** **O Master** <note>original Greek: Ὦ δέσποτ’</note>. Previously it was read as **that of Plato** <note>original Greek: τὸ τοῦ Πλάτωνος</note>; and these words **pay attention now** <note>original Greek: πρόσεχε δή</note> were placed separately, as if the fourth verse began with them. But by retaining that article **the** <note>original Greek: τὸ</note>, the verse will be longer than allows for adding those two words, "pay attention now." Therefore, based on the consensus of some manuscripts, that article was rightly removed.

**Page 112. Verse...]** **O boy** <note>original Greek: Ὦ παῖ</note>. Instead of "O boy" one also reads **O pai** <note>a variant spelling in Greek: ὦ πᾶι</note>. But instead of **everyone turns around** <note>original Greek: πᾶς τις ἐπιστρέφεται</note>, in the *Epigrammatic Anthology* <note>a famous collection of Greek poems</note>, it is held as **he is gazed upon by all** <note>original Greek: πᾶσι περιβλέπεται</note>.

**Verse...]** **I begin** <note>original Greek: Ἀρχομαι</note>. You will find these written differently in the *Epigrammatic Anthology*, page 232 of my edition. In the second verse: **On whose wrinkles sweet love sat** <note>original Greek: Ἂς κ’ ἐπὶ ρυτίδων ὁ γλυκὺς ἕζετ’ ἔρως</note>. (In Athenaeus <note>a 2nd-century Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note>, however, it is written as **bitter love is upon them** <note>original Greek: πικρὸς ἔπεστιν ἔρως</note>). In the third: **Or the lovers, the first-shooters, having plucked her who had newly reached youth** <note>original Greek: Ἢ γ’ νέον ἡβήσασαν ἀποδρέψαντες ἐρασταὶ Πρωτοβόλοι</note>. But Athenaeus also recognizes that phrasing, not this one. And perhaps (as I have said elsewhere) that phrasing was changed by those for whose ears this use of the participle **having met** or **encountered** <note>original Greek: ἀπαντήσαντες</note> with the <term>genitive case</term> <note>a grammatical case usually showing possession or relation</note> was unfamiliar; even though elsewhere "to encounter" <note>original Greek: ἀντιᾶσθαι</note> appears in Herodotus with the genitive, meaning **to happen upon**; and the verb **to encounter** <note>original Greek: ἀντιάσαι</note> has this same use in Homer.

**Page 116. Verse...]** **Here** <note>original Greek: Ἐνθάδε</note>. In the *Epigrammatic Anthology*, page 191 of my edition, it is read as: **Here lies the divine man Aristocles** <note>original Greek: Ἐνθάδε κεῖται ἀνὴρ θεῖος Ἀριστοκλέης</note>.

**Verse...]** **This [one]** <note>original Greek: Τοῦτον, in the accusative case</note>. In the same place it is read, **This man holds the gates** <note>original Greek: οὗτος ἔχει πυλαώ, using the nominative case</note>, which <term>nominative case</term> <note>the grammatical case for the subject of a sentence</note> seems more suitable. However, the other reading can also be supported: so that a nominative is understood from the preceding words, and **this praise** <note>original Greek: τοῦτον τὸν ἔπαινον</note> is understood.

**Verse...]** **Image** <note>original Greek: Εἰκών</note>. <gloss>Written as: **but the body is earth**</gloss> <note>original Greek: σῶμα δέ γε γῆs</note>. In the epigram, however, it is **but the body [is] earth** <note>original Greek: σῶμα δ’ γῆ</note>.

**Page 118. Verse...]** [Greek term] <note>original Greek: τεῖα</note>. <gloss>Written as: **of beauty**</gloss> <note>original Greek: τοῦ κάλλους</note> instead of **of the beautiful** <note>original Greek: τοῦ καλοῦ</note>.

<margin>Verse... **Alcibiades** <note>original Greek: Ἀλκιβ.</note></margin>
