->### NOTES ON DIOGENES LAERTIUS ###<-

**Verse. Alcibiades]** <note>original Greek: Ἀλκιβ.</note> It appears that **Alcibiaden** <note>the accusative form: Ἀλκιβιάδην</note> should have been restored (as certain ancient manuscripts have it) instead of **Alcibiades** <note>the nominative form: Ἀλκιβιάδης</note>, as is also evident from what follows, where mention is made of **the second Alcibiades** and **the greater Alcibiades** <note>original Greek: Ἀλκιβιάδου δευτέρου, & Ἀλκιβιάδου τοῦ μείζονος</note>.

**Page 120. Verse. But the faithful...]** <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ πις.</note> Restore **the universal** <note>original Greek: τὸ καθόλου</note>, and **credible** <note>original Greek: πισεύσιμος</note> after the word **of the part** <note>original Greek: μέρους</note>.

**Page 121. Verse. ...cos]** <note>original Greek: κός.</note> Previously it was read as **or concerning the lover of gain** <note>original Greek: ἢ περὶ φιλοκερδοῦς</note>. But the other reading is confirmed even by the copies of Plato’s own works.

**Page 122. Verse. Natural...]** <note>original Greek: φυσικός.</note> Instead of **ethical** <note>original Greek: ἠθικός</note> one also reads **political** <note>original Greek: πολιτικός</note>. Likewise a little later, **or a nocturnal, political assembly** <note>original Greek: ἢ νυκτερινός, πολιτικός. σύλλογος</note>, etc.

**Verse. ...cos]** <gloss>It is written: **Seventh Swallow**</gloss> <note>original Greek: Χελιδὼν ἑβδόμη</note>.

**Page 123. Last Verse]** It is also read as **thunderbolt-like** <note>original Greek: κεραύνιον</note>.

**Page 124. Verse. ...symp]** <note>original Greek: συμφ.</note> Indeed, the previous edition has **obolos** <note>original Greek: ὀβολός, a small Greek coin</note> in this place, just as in the one immediately preceding; but there is no doubt that in both places **obelos** <note>original Greek: ὀβελὸς, a horizontal spit or the critical mark used by scholars to flag doubtful text</note> ought to be restored; although that other reading <note>obolos</note> is held in a certain ancient manuscript.

**Verse. ...gonos]** The word **having been published** <note>original Greek: ἐκδοθέντα</note> is a conflation of **to the one having been published** <note>original Greek: ἐκδοθέντι</note> and the particle **if** <note>original Greek: ἄ</note>. For this passage should be read: **in the [book] concerning Zeno recently published, if he says** <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ περὶ Ζήνωνος νεωστὶ ἐκδοθέντι. ἄ εἴπῃ</note> etc. The translator also recognizes this reading.

**Verse. ...moved]** <note>original Greek: κίνητον.</note> <gloss>It is written: **rational part**</gloss> <note>original Greek: λογιστικὸν μέρος</note>.

**Verse. ...to become]** <note>original Greek: γίνεσθαι</note> <gloss>It is written: **of those being set right**</gloss> <note>original Greek: ὀρθουμένων</note>.

**Page 125. Verse. ...but the]** <note>original Greek: δὲ τ'</note> <gloss>It is written: **unchangeable**</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀμετάβλητον</note>.

**Page 129. Verse. ...toward the sight]** <note>original Greek: πρὸς ὄψιν</note> <gloss>It is written: **placed** or **conventional**</gloss> <note>original Greek: θετόν</note>. But the translator follows the other reading, and seems to draw a suitable sense from it, rendering the passage thus:

> For when an act is completed, nothing remains that is subject to the eyes; rather, all the force is in the act itself.

**Page 131. Verse. ...and divided]** <note>original Greek: χὴ διαιρ.</note> <gloss>It is written: **rational** <note>original Greek: λογιστικὸν</note> instead of **logical**</gloss> <note>original Greek: λογικόν</note>; and likewise in the following places. Above, also, the same variety of reading was cited.

**Page 133. Verse. ...to err]** <note>original Greek: διαμαρτ.</note> <gloss>It is written: **will miss the mark** and **will not speak correctly**</gloss> <note>original Greek: διαμαρτήσεσθαι & οὐκ ὀρθῶς ἐρεῖν</note>.

**Page 134. Verse. ...of the address]** <note>original Greek: τῆς προσηγ.</note> I think **of unsociability** <note>original Greek: ἀπροσηγορίας</note> should be restored instead of **of sociability** <note>original Greek: προσηγορίας</note>. For we know that for humanity—that is, so that we may be considered human—it is especially required that we [not] be **unsociable** <note>original Greek: ἀπροσήγοροι; Estienne is likely discussing a Stoic or Cynic trait where the lack of a greeting/sociability is being debated as a vice or a specific character mark</note>.

->### HENRI ESTIENNE ###<-

**Page 137. Verse. and everything]** <gloss>Written as:</gloss> **and everything by chance, and such like** <note>original Greek: καὶ πᾶν τὸ τυχὸν, καὶ τὸ τοιοῦτον</note>. The translator, however, does not acknowledge that word **by chance** <note>original Greek: τυχὸν</note>, and indeed it does not seem to be necessary, although it is found in most copies. A little later, instead of **indivisible** <note>original Greek: ἀμερῆ</note>, <gloss>it is written:</gloss> **undivided** <note>original Greek: ἀμέριστα</note>.

**Page 139. Verse. to the Eurym...]** <gloss>Written as:</gloss> **of the demes** <note>original Greek: τῶν μὲν δήμων; a "deme" was a local subdivision or district of Athens</note>. I made mention of this reading above, in the notes on page 103. You also find this reading, **of the demes**, at the beginning of the *Life of Polemon*.

**Page 141. Verse. Xenocrates]** <gloss>Written as:</gloss> **the Chalcedonian** <note>original Greek: Χαλκηδόνιος</note>; a reading which the translator also followed.

<margin>2</margin> **Verse. by]** After the word **I anoint** <note>original Greek: ἀλείφω</note>, a question mark should not have been placed, since these words are pronounced as an exclamation.

**Page 144. Verse. Bronze]** <gloss>Written as:</gloss> **having struck against** <note>original Greek: προσκόψας</note> instead of **having stumbled** <note>original Greek: προσπταίσας</note>.

**Page 145. Verse. father]** It cannot be doubted that **the play of the nurse** <note>original Greek: δράμαν τροφοῦσαι</note> is the true reading; and the translator followed it. But that same man stumbled in the translation of the words immediately following. For he translates **to flee a lawsuit** <note>original Greek: φυγῆν δίκην</note> as "To have escaped judgment"; whereas we know that to the Latins, **to flee a lawsuit** <note>original Greek: φεύγειν δίκην</note> is nothing other than **to be called to court** or **to be accused**. <note>Estienne is correcting a common mistake: in Greek legal terminology, the one "fleeing" is the defendant, not someone who has already escaped.</note>

**Page 146. Verse. concerning Euripides]** Restore **sharpness** <note>original Greek: ὀξώτης</note>, just as in **swimmable** <note>original Greek: πλωτάς</note>; or certainly use the nominative forms, **sharpness** and **swimmer** <note>original Greek: ὀξώτης & πλωτής</note>.

**Verse. and a friend]** Instead of **of the comic poets** <note>original Greek: τῶν κωμικῶν</note>, although the translator seems to have read **according to the comic poets** <note>original Greek: τοὺς κωμικούς</note>, I think the truer reading is **according to the comic poet** <note>singular; original Greek: τὸν κωμικόν</note>. A little later, instead of **rejoicing** <note>original Greek: γαῦσις</note> it is read as **rejoicing** <note>original Greek: γαῦσις, a dialectal variant</note>, and likewise **sweetness** <note>original Greek: γλύξις</note>.

**Verse. Crates]** The translator reads, or certainly seems to have read, **the Athenian** <note>original Greek: Ἀθηναῖος</note> after **Crates**; for he renders it, "Crates the Athenian." It certainly seems right that this should be added, so that he may be distinguished from the Theban [Crates], of whom we shall speak later. As for the reading **the deme** <note>original Greek: τὸν δῆμον</note> being offered instead of **the demes** <note>original Greek: τῶν δήμων</note>, I have shown in the notes on pages 103 and 139 that many passages can be opposed to this reading.

**Page 149. Verse. Would give]** Without the agreement of the manuscripts, I did not dare to restore **in doubt** <note>original Greek: ἐν δοίη</note>. However, no one can deny to me that it ought to be restored; especially since we read these very words in Callimachus, in the *Hymn to Zeus*, and thus it may appear that this whole verse was an imitation of his verse. For he sang thus: **In doubt...** <note>original Greek: Ἐν δοίη</note>

->### ANNOTATIONS ON DIOGENES ###<-

**Page 19.**

...**greatly my soul. Since the voyage was around both sides** <note>original Greek: μάλα θυμός. ἐπεὶ πλόος ἀμφήεισον</note>. Since there had preceded: **How shall we sing of him, as Dictaean or Lycaean?** <note>original Greek: Πῶς καὶ νιν, Δικταῖον ἀείσομεν, ἠὲ Λυκαῖον; — a famous line from Callimachus' Hymn to Zeus, discussing the birthplace of Zeus</note>. It is read there as **in doubt** <note>original Greek: ἐν δοίη</note> as a single word; but it is more correctly written as **in doubt** <note>original Greek: ἐν δοίῃ</note> as two words. Eustathius also holds this reading in his commentary on Homer.

But instead of **he sat** <note>original Greek: ἧσε</note>, the reading **or you** <note>original Greek: ἤ σε</note> should have been substituted, as the following words clearly indicate. In the sixth verse, in the phrase **to you the portion** <note>original Greek: τοι αὖσα</note>, I followed those manuscripts (though fewer in number) in which it was **such as you** <note>original Greek: τοῖος σύ</note>, since no sense can be elicited from the other reading, nor can those words even cohere with what precedes or follows. On the other hand, these words conclude this passage most excellently, as if providing the reason for that hesitation as an **exclamation** <note>original Greek: ἐπιφωνηματικῶς; a rhetorical device where the author adds a concluding remark</note>. But since previously there was no punctuation between **of winds** <note>original Greek: ἀνέμων</note> and **to you the portion** <note>original Greek: τοι αὖσα</note>, a **full stop** <note>original Greek: τελεία στιγμή</note> ought conversely to be placed between **of winds** <note>original Greek: ἀνέμων</note> and **such as you** <note>original Greek: τοῖος σύ</note>. Since I have omitted it, it will now be your task to place it. Furthermore, because I see that these most beautiful verses have been most shamefully handled by the translator, who has indeed entirely perverted their meaning, I am pleased to favor those who do not understand Greek with my own interpretation. But first, I will present the verses of the translator:

> *Would that my mind were that with which I once, burning, sang*
> *The eternal offspring of the gods; then, Desire,*
> *I would begin to celebrate you first, and all the children whom dark*
> *Night and aged Erebus brought forth under the deep whirlpool of the wide*
> *Ocean, those born of Earth, and the boy of Venus;*
> *And I would sing the wandering courses of the winds, and human prayers,*
> *And your nature, and your twin body.*

See, I beseech you, reader, from how small a beginning of error someone can be carried into such great mistakes. First, he thought that **in doubt** <note>original Greek: ἐνδοίη</note> was some verb in the optative mood <note>a grammatical mood expressing a wish or possibility</note>; then from **he sat** <note>original Greek: ἧσε</note> (not noticing it stands for **or you** <note>original Greek: ἤ σε</note>), he thought he should make **I was** <note>original Greek: ἦσα</note>, which would be joined with **behind** <note>original Greek: ὅπι</note>, as if it had the same force as **that** <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note>. Finally, he took **I might say** <note>original Greek: εἴπω</note> for **I would say** <note>original Greek: εἴποιμι ἄν</note>, and **to him who** <note>original Greek: τῶ δ’ ὅστις</note> he translated as if it were **and also whoever** <note>original Greek/Latin: καὶ δ’ ὅστις</note>. Here he began to be carried away straying, and to follow paths plainly devious and unknown to me. Now see, on the contrary, how small a help from an emendation can lead someone back to the right path: and

Having just explained the errors of a previous translator, Estienne now offers his own improvised English (originally Latin) translation of the Greek poem. He then moves on to specific word-level corrections (scholia) for subsequent pages of the Greek text, focusing on metaphors of "unpolished" speech and various naming errors made by the printers.</meta>

->### HENRI ESTIENNE ###<-

Yet, you should remember that this interpretation of mine was written on the fly <note>original Latin: "ex tempore," meaning improvised or written quickly</note>.

> *In doubt is my mind (for it is told that your origin is uncertain)*
> *Whether I should place you, Desire, first among the number of the gods,*
> *Whom old Erebus <note>a personification of darkness</note> and Queen Night once bore beneath the deep waves*
> *Of the Ocean (as they recount)?*
> *Or should I say you were created from Venus, or the winds, or the earth.*
> *For, wandering, you bring so many evils to mortals*
> *And so many blessings. From this, nature gave you a two-fold body.*

**Verse: I am smooth** <note>original Greek: λῐῶ δὲ (liō de). Estienne is correcting a corruption in the text</note>] More correctly it should be **unpolished** <note>original Greek: ἀπελέκητον (apeleketon); literally "not hewn with an axe"</note>. Such a joke would be best understood if you said it in French as, *A voice poorly planed* <note>original French: "Une voix mal rabotée," referring to a rough or unrefined speaking voice</note>. However, I cannot guess from where the translator took that word **Broken** <note>original Latin: "Infractam"</note>. For we know that **unpolished** <note>apeleketon</note> sounds like "not planed or smoothed with an axe." But truly, whether it is more correctly written as **skiphes** <note>σκιφὴς</note> or **skiphes**, I have not yet discovered: for I find a definition for neither. If, however, we wish to believe **Suidas** <note>the author of a massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>, we shall follow that reading. For after **skiphe** (which he does not explain), he adds those very words which are read here: **and the philosopher Crantor said the verses of some poet were full of "skiphes."** Perhaps someone might say it should be read as **tow** <note>original Greek: στύφοις (styphois); meaning the coarse part of flax or hemp</note>, which is defined as **stupa** <note>term: Stupa; the coarse fibers of flax used for caulking or spinning</note>. But neither is this meaning of that word well-established, nor does it seem to be said aptly enough concerning verses.

**Verse: It came upon** <note>original Greek: ἐπεκλ. (epekl.)</note>] <gloss>Variant reading: the disease is most evil.</gloss>
**Verse: Let it stretch** <note>original Greek: τείτω (teitō)</note>] <gloss>Variant reading: of Pitane <note>a town in Aeolis</note>.</gloss>
**Page 150. Verse: Two**] <gloss>Variant reading: of those by the same father, Pylades is the elder; of those by the same mother, Moireas.</gloss> This is the reading which the translator followed.
**Verse: O maiden**] Restore **to me** <note>original Greek: μοι (moi)</note> instead of **not** <note>original Greek: μή (mē)</note>. This was a <term>mendum</term> <note>a printer's error or "blunder"</note> committed by the workshop. In the following verse, instead of **servant** <note>original Greek: δμῶτ’ (dmōt’)</note>, in some versions it is read as **female servant**.
**Page 151. Verse: For there**] <gloss>Variant reading: Menedemus <note>a Greek philosopher and founder of the Eretrian school</note>.</gloss>
**Page 152. Verse: Divine** <note>original Greek: δίας (dias)</note>] <gloss>Variant reading: of the cutting <note>original Greek: ἐπικόπης (epikopēs)</note>.</gloss> This was a diversity of reading mentioned above as well.
**Verse: Not**] <gloss>Variant reading: he will wash <note>original Greek: νίψεται (nipsetai)</note> instead of he will receive <note>original Greek: λήψεται (lēpsetai)</note>.</gloss>
**Verse: He said**] <gloss>Variant reading: neither again in this way.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s philological notes on the text of Diogenes Laertius. ->### ANNOTATIONS ON DIOGENES ###<-

**Page 153. Verse: Suspecting** <note>original Greek: ὑποπ. (hypop.)</note>] Previously it was read as **not depriving** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀποστεροῦντες (ouk aposterountes)</note>, which was incorrect. But the translator seems to have read **and being in need** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀποροῦντος (kai aporountos)</note> instead of **and depriving** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀποστεροῦντος (kai aposterountos)</note>. For he translated it as, *But when he was needy.*

**Page 154. Verse: Pos**] <gloss>Variant reading: Buselos, also Buselios, and Buseleos, and Busolos.</gloss> <note>These are variant spellings for a proper name that appeared corrupted in the text.</note>
**Verse: Fond of fame** <note>original Greek: φιλοδ. (philod.)</note>] <gloss>Variant reading: to him those around Hieronymus the Peripatetic <note>a philosopher and student of Aristotle known for his interest in literature</note>.</gloss>

**Page 155. Verse: And they him**] Previously it was read as **about those staying away** <note>original Greek: περὶ ἀπιζῶν (peri apizōn)</note>. **Hesychius** <note>an Alexandrian grammarian who compiled a famous dictionary of obscure Greek words</note> teaches that all birds are called **apizia** <note>original Greek: ἀπιζία</note>. From this, perhaps we might suspect the reading should be **the birds around the owl** <note>original Greek: γλαῦκα πέρι ἀπιζία (glauka peri apizia)</note>—that is, the birds surrounding the owl—if the word **apizia** could be joined with **they were being completed** <note>original Greek: περαινῶντο (perainōnto)</note> while preserving the meter of the verse.
**Verse: Foolish** <note>original Greek: Ἠλέμ. (Ēlem.)</note>] <gloss>Variant reading: crowd-pleasing <note>original Greek: ὀχλοαρέσκος (ochloareskos)</note>.</gloss> However, what a certain person notes—"you please the crowd"—does not fit.
**Verse: Being displeased**] <gloss>Variant reading: being pleased.</gloss>
**Verse: He said**] More correctly: **from men indeed** <note>original Greek: ἐκ μὲν γὰρ ἀνδρῶν</note>.

**Page 158. Verse: His own**] It is also read with a question mark after **I sell** <note>original Greek: πωλῶ (pōlō)</note>. In place of that, **I sell** <note>another Greek word: πιπράσκω (pipraskō)</note> is also found.
**Verse: To the wretched** <note>original Greek: Δυλοῖ (Dyloi)</note>] **Plutarch** <note>the famous Greek biographer and moralist</note>, when citing this verse, reads it as **bold-hearted** <note>original Greek: θρασύσπλαγχνος (thrasysplanchnos)</note>.

**Page 160. Verse: Bion**] These verses in the previous edition were not divided into certain spaces, but were written in the manner of prose. However, since we saw everywhere that an **Anacreontic** <note>a poetic meter named after the poet Anacreon, usually light and rhythmic</note> verse is followed by an **iambic dimeter** <note>a line consisting of two pairs of iambic feet</note>, we decided to distinguish them in the way you now see. But later, verses of this type coupled together appeared in the works of **Aristophanes** <note>the great Athenian comic playwright</note>, such as in *The Frogs*:

->*Then, from the very first lines, I left nothing idle.*<-
->*But the wife spoke for me, and the slave no less,*<-
->*And the master, and the maiden, and the old woman too. Aeschylus: "Then indeed,"*<-
->*"Should you not have died for daring such things?" Euripides: "By Apollo, no!"*<-

Where you should also notice that the Anacreontic meter sometimes admits other feet than it is accustomed to in the works of Anacreon, as in this fourth line you see there is a **tribrach** <note>term: Tribrach; a metrical foot consisting of three short syllables</note>. This will be more easily seen if it is separated in this manner:
->*Should you not have died for these things?*<-

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne’s (Henricus Stephanus) technical analysis of the poetic meter and textual accuracy in Diogenes Laertius' biographies. Here, he concludes a point about Aristophanes’ use of meter and applies those rules to the biography of Bion of Borysthenes, while also correcting a translator's misunderstanding regarding the epithet of the god Dionysus.</meta>

->### HENRI ESTIENNE ###<-

"For daring such things, by Apollo, no!" <note>original Greek: Τολμῶντα μὰ τὸν Ἀπόλλω; a quote from Aristophanes' The Frogs</note>.

Shortly before, however, he had also applied an **anapest** <note>term: Anapest; a metrical foot consisting of two short syllables followed by one long syllable</note> to a certain verse. Furthermore, you can find such verses in the same author and in other comedies. Now, therefore, it will be your task (if it seems right) to join these in the same way, writing them as follows:

->*Bion the Borysthenite, whom the Scythian land brought forth,*<-
->*We hear say that the gods truly are nothing.*<-
->*And if he had not remained holding this doctrine, it would have been likely, etc.*<-

And likewise in the rest. Notice, however, that in the first line, the **Anacreontic meter** <note>a light, rhythmic poetic style</note> accepts two anapests. But as for this verse:

->*Persuasion bound him,* <note>original Greek: Πεπεισμὸς ἔδησε (Pepeismos edēse)</note><-

I do not see how it can be sustained, since we know that a **pyrrhic foot** <note>term: Pyrrhic; a metrical foot consisting of two short syllables</note> has no place here. Perhaps, however, it could be restored by inserting the particle **ge** <note>a Greek emphasizing particle</note> in this way: *Persuasion indeed bound him* <note>original Greek: Πεπεισμός γ’ ἔδησε (Pepeismos g' edēse)</note>. Unless one should rather write *having been persuaded* <note>original Greek: πεπεισμώς (pepeismōs)</note> adverbially, which, however, might seem harsher in this context.

**Page 161. Verse: Flourished at the same time** <note>original Greek: συνακμ. (synakm.)</note>] After the word **two**, certain manuscripts add **in the Ionian dialect** <note>original Greek: ἰάδι (iadi)</note> (for which word there is erroneously **these things** <note>original Greek: ταδί (tadi)</note> in one copy). And after **having written** <note>original Greek: γεγραφώς (gegraphōs)</note>, it is written thus in those same copies: *in the Ionian dialect and year. Third is the aforementioned philosopher. Fourth, etc.*

**Page 162. Verse: Loosed** <note>original Greek: Λῦσε (Lyse)</note>] There is great consensus among the copies regarding the reading of this verse. Therefore, I think the translator did not read it differently but simply did not understand it. For instead of these words, **wherefore indeed was he not Lyaeus?** <note>original Greek: διὸ δὴ μήτι Λυαῖος ἔφυ (dio dē mēti Lyaios ephy)</note>, the translator has, *Therefore he was not born.* Yet it is manifest (or I am greatly mistaken) that these words are said as a question (and therefore I think a question mark should be added after **was**) and they refer to the **etymology** <note>the origin and meaning of a word</note> of the epithet **Lyaeus**. It is true (he says) that **Dionysus** <note>the Greek god of wine and theater</note>, when he has entered the body in abundance, is accustomed to loosen the limbs. Is he not, for this reason, called **Lyaeus**? <note>the name Lyaeus literally means "The Loosener" or "Deliverer," referring to how wine relaxes the mind and body</note>. But a certain person noted **metilyaios** as one word—neatly, to be sure, and very ridiculously composed.

**Verse: Sto.**] <gloss>Variant reading: most carefully the works of Chrysippus <note>a primary architect of Stoic philosophy</note>.</gloss>

**Page 163. Verse: Soloi**] <gloss>Variant reading: Alianus the Cappadocian.</gloss> But many historians protest against this reading.

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne's philological commentary on the biographies of philosophers by Diogenes Laertius. Here, Estienne critiques a previous translator's handling of an epigram about the philosopher Carneades, specifically focusing on a misunderstanding of Carneades' fear of death and a humorous anecdote regarding his final moments.</meta>

->### ANNOTATIONS ON DIOGENES ###<-

**Verse: Ignorant** <note>original Greek: Ἀμαθὴς (Amathēs)</note>] The translator of the verses which are read here and there in this book—whoever he may be, for he is someone other than the one who rendered the rest—has wandered far from the meaning of this epigram, especially in the second verse. For he thought that these words, *ignorant who...* etc., were said about **Carneades** <note>a Greek skeptic philosopher and head of the Academy</note>: as if they were placed there to mean *he who, being ignorant*... etc. And yet it would be foolish to follow this by adding, *he did not at all know how he feared death.* On the contrary, in the genuine interpretation we have a most fitting sense: that the word **is** should be understood (as is commonly done), just as if it were said: *That man is ignorant who does not at all know* etc.

But I will also add a Latin explanation, and indeed going a bit further. "Why," he says, "do you wish, O Muse, for Carneades to be rebuked by me? Whoever did not notice how greatly he feared death is possessed of a crude mind; for not even then, when he was suffering from **phthisis** <note>term: Phthisis; a wasting disease, usually referring to pulmonary tuberculosis</note>, a most foul disease, would he allow the **dissolution** <note>term: Lysin (λύσιν); the release or separation of the soul from the body</note> of the body from the soul."

But the translator rendered **dissolution** as *Care*: by which word I do not see what he could have understood in this place; unless perhaps he wished to signify a *cure* by which he might be freed from the disease. That use of the word would be very harsh, and certainly in no way would it correspond to the meaning of the Greek noun.

But I am pleased to proceed further in the interpretation of this epigram, since likewise the meaning of the following verses was plainly changed by him. When (he says) Carneades had heard that **Antipater** <note>Antipater of Tarsus, a Stoic philosopher</note> had been extinguished by drinking poison, he said, "Give it, therefore, to me as well, that I may drink." What then? What? (Which are the questions of those who stood around Carneades himself: wishing to know from him what he wanted to be offered to him to drink, since mention of poison had just been made. Just as if, to him saying, "Give it therefore to me too," they responded, "What? Do you thus ask for poison, by the drinking of which you may kill yourself?") "Give me **honey-wine**" <note>term: Mulsum; a popular Roman beverage made of wine sweetened with honey</note>. Here now he changes his mind; and though he had sought poison as if he were **magnanimous** <note>term: Megalopsychos; literally "great-souled," a person of high courage who does not fear death</note> and not at all a **lover of life** <note>term: Philozōos; someone overly attached to living, often implying cowardice in the face of death</note> (not adding the name "poison" indeed, but leaving it easily understood from those things which had been narrated about Antipater), on the contrary, as—

<summary>Estienne corrects a translation of an epigram about Carneades, arguing that the philosopher’s alleged bravery was a front and clarifying a joke where Carneades asks for wine instead of the poison he initially implied he would take.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Henri Estienne's critique of a translation of Diogenes Laertius. Estienne is specifically analyzing an epigram about the philosopher Carneades. He focuses on a joke where Carneades, after pretending he might commit suicide with poison like his contemporary Antipater, instead asks for honey-wine, revealing his fear of death.</meta>

->### ANNOTATIONS ON DIOGENES ###<-

<page-num>24</page-num>

->HENRY ESTIENNE<-

clearly **small-souled** <note>original Greek: μικρόψυχος (mikropsychos); meaning cowardly or lacking spirit</note>, he says it is not **poison** <note>original Greek: φάρμακον (pharmakon)</note>, but **honey-wine** <note>original Greek: οἰνόμελι (oinomeli)</note> that he wants to be given to him. But if we receive nothing else of value from the translator here, he at least gives us a better reading of the sixth verse than the one we have in our own manuscripts: namely, by omitting the particle **some/anything** <note>original Greek: τὶ (ti)</note> after **he said** <note>original Greek: ἔφησε (ephēse)</note>. (However, in the fact that he places punctuation between **to me too** <note>original Greek: κἀμοὶ (kamoi)</note> and **all/at all** <note>original Greek: πᾶν (pan)</note>, there is a manifest error). Unless we take the word **some** not to mean "something," but "a little bit": just as if he had said, "Give me therefore also a little bit of poison to drink." But **some** should not be written there at all. 

However, since I have brought the true interpretation of this epigram this far, it seemed right to bring it to a conclusion: especially since, in the work of the translator, the final parts correspond perfectly to the first (at least regarding the corrupted meaning). For in place of these words, **and he had these things very much at hand** <note>original Greek: σφόδρα τ’ εἶχε πρόχειρα ταυτὶ (sphodra t’ eiche procheira tauti)</note>, the translator has, *For this easy nature holds these things heavily.* Yet Diogenes actually says this: *And these things were very much at hand for him*—namely, the things which follow. This is as if to say: "These words were always in his mouth," or "He always had this response most ready" (doubtless to those who were rebuking him as **small-souled** and rather a **lover of life** <note>original Greek: φιλόψυχον (philopsychon)</note>): **"Nature which contains me, that very same will be that which also dissolves me"** <note>original Greek: Φύσις ἡ συνέχ. (Physis hē synech.)</note>. 

By these words, he signaled that the natural time of death must be awaited. Two verses remain, the latter of which the translator seems to have understood no better than the others. Their meaning is this: *And he indeed nonetheless (that is, although he was such a lover of life, and spared it so much) went beneath the earth. And yet he was allowed, having gained many evils (which he evidently suffered from that time on), to depart to the underworld.* That is to say: *From the time he changed his mind about drinking poison, he endured many evils; he would have "profited" <note>Meaning he would have avoided these extra sufferings</note> if he had persisted in his first intent, and having drunk the poison, had departed to the underworld.* 

As for this manner of speaking, **to have evils as gains** <note>original Greek: κέρδε’ ἔχειν τὰ κακά (kerde’ echein ta kaka)</note>, I think Diogenes wished to imitate one of the ancient comic poets, who however does not say "to have evils as gains," but "to profit..."

<sig>bb.iiii.</sig>

<summary>Estienne concludes his correction of the epigram about Carneades, explaining that the philosopher used a philosophical excuse about "Nature" to avoid suicide and arguing that his long life ended up being a "gain of evils" due to his prolonged suffering.</summary>

->HENRY ESTIENNE<-

<margin>evils <note>original Greek: κακά (kaka)</note>.</margin> You can find this passage in the little book I published of selected maxims from the Greek comic poets, along with my own interpretation.

**Page 164, Verse "Nothing"** — <gloss>Variant reading: "of analysis" <note>original Greek: ἀναλύσου (analysou)</note></gloss>. But I think "of analysis" is written more correctly here, so that he may say a foolish talkativeness exists within the **Academics** <note>The philosophers of the Academy founded by Plato, often criticized for their endless debates</note>.

**Page 167, Verse "But"** — <gloss>Variant reading: "of men and of the deceitful" <note>original Greek: ἀνδρῶν & δολίων (andrōn & doliōn)</note></gloss>. However, in the translator's version (whoever it was that translated the verses in Diogenes), we find "of a man and deceitfully." Just as we read in his translation: *He used the man's friendship insidiously.* But I suspect that he originally wrote "Of the insidious [man]": which was then corrupted into "insidiously," providing an occasion for the person who placed the Latin verses before the Greek ones to likewise change "deceitful" into "deceitfully." But it is much more ridiculous what someone else proposes: "of men and of the deceitful [singular]."

**Page 169, Verse [ending in] "-kanor"** — Most manuscripts have **Hipparchus** inserted between **Timarchus** and **Dioteles**, which the translator also acknowledges.

**Page 172, Verse "toward the"** — Someone has wrongly and ridiculously substituted **"lower"** <note>original Greek: κατωτέρω (katōterō)</note> for **"lowest"** <note>original Greek: κατωτάτω (katōtatō)</note>. Furthermore, regarding these words added a little later, **"for it is also related thus"** <note>original Greek: φέρεται γὰρ καὶ οὕτω (pheretai gar kai outō)</note>, I think they have a different meaning than the one given to them by the translator. For they signify that **Aristotle's** response is reported in this way as well, and not only as he reported it before: namely at the beginning of the preceding page. There is, however, a small difference between the two. For here he says that in giving alms to a wicked man, he had regard not for the man, but for **humanity**; whereas there, he says he pitied not the character, but the man.

**Verse [ending in] "-los"** — In most manuscripts it is also read **"in the ethics of the seventh [books]"**, which seems to be a strange <term>hypallage</term> <note>A figure of speech where the natural order of words is changed, often resulting in an adjective being applied to the "wrong" noun—e.g., "the ethics of the seventh" instead of "the seventh book of Ethics"</note>. Certainly, the reading of the previous edition would be more tolerable (if one wished to depart from the one we have received into the main text): **"in the seventh Ethics book."** Unless perhaps, due to the consensus of many manuscripts, one must think some secret meaning lies hidden beneath that first reading.

**Verse [ending in] "-kos"** — <gloss>Variant reading: **"of philosophy"** <note>original Greek: φιλοσοφίας (philosophias)</note></gloss> instead of **"of friendship."** And in the very next verse, **"of erotic matters"** <note>original Greek: ἐρωτικῶν (erōtikōn)</note> instead of **"of argumentative matters"** <note>original Greek: ἐριστικῶν (eristikōn); referring to a style of logical dispute common among the Greeks</note>.

**Verse "-os, and beautiful"** <note>original Greek: ος, καὶ κάλλ. (os, kai kall.)</note> — After **"of similar things"** <note>original Greek: παραπλησίων (paraplēsiōn)</note>, it is read in some manuscripts: **"it may be of a third kind, of those external"**, etc. <note>original Greek: ἐκ τρίτων ᾖ, τῶν ἐκτὸς (ek tritōn ē, tōn ektos)</note>.

**Page 176, Verse "and to the"** <note>original Greek: ταίς τε (tais te)</note> — It is also read **"to follow along"** <note>original Greek: αὐτακολουθεῖν (autakolouthein)</note>, which I prefer; for I remember reading this word elsewhere concerning these same subjects.

**Verse "pol-"** — It will be more correctly written **"will live with"** <note>original Greek: συμβιώσειν (symbiōsein)</note> than **"to have lived with"** <note>original Greek: συμβιῶσαι (symbiōsai)</note>, which the old manuscripts have instead of **"to live together"** <note>original Greek: συμβιῶναι (symbiōnai)</note>. A little after in the same manuscripts, **"he admitted"** <note>original Greek: ἐνέκρινεν (enekrinen)</note> for **"he preferred"** <note>original Greek: προέκρινεν (proekrinen)</note>. And soon after, **"he was released as the most defensive of all"** <note>original Greek: ἀπολογικώτατος παρὰ πάντας ἐχλύετο (apologikōtatos para pantas echlyeto)</note>, used with the same meaning.

**Verse "the motion"** <note>original Greek: τὴν κίν. (tēn kin.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"circular"** <note>original Greek: κυκλοφορητικήν (kyklophorētikēn)</note></gloss>.

**Page 177, Verse "-teron"** — <gloss>Variant reading: **"of Alcippus"** <note>original Greek: Ἀλκίππου (Alkippou)</note></gloss>.

**Page 178, Verse "Pamph-"** — Here also certain copies have **Pamphilus** <note>original Greek: Πάμφιλος</note> for **Pamphile** <note>original Greek: Παμφίλη</note>, as mentioned above. But in most places in this book, **Pamphile** is read with the consensus of all of them.

**Verse "chl-"** — For **"of the courtroom"** <note>original Greek: δικαστηρίου (dikastēriou)</note>, there is also read **"of the showroom"** <note>original Greek: δεικτηρίου (deiktēriou); a place where things are displayed or demonstrated</note>.

**Verse "pher-"** — The translator has: *In that letter he names the scholar.* <note>original Latin: "In ea epistola scholasticum nominat"</note> And in the margin, the word **"boasts"** <note>original Greek: καταλαζονεύεται (katalazoneuetai)</note> has been placed, as if the translator had rendered the word **"boasts"** as **"names."** In this matter, a great injustice is done to him. For it is not read otherwise here in all our manuscripts, nor even in the previous edition, than **"he named"** <note>original Greek: ὠνόμασε (ōnomasē)</note>. However, **"boasts"** <note>original Greek: καταλαζονεύεται</note> is found around the middle of the following page, as I will show shortly.

**Verse "newta"** <note>original Greek: νέωτα</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"of Phallion"** <note>original Greek: Φαλλίωνος (Phalliōnos)</note></gloss>.

->### ANNOTATIONS ON DIOGENES ###<-

<page-num>27</page-num>

**Page 179, Verse "life"** <note>original Greek: βίος (bios)</note> — Here finally we find that word **"boasts"** <note>original Greek: καταλαζονεύεται (katalazoneuetai)</note>, which I just mentioned <note>referring to the discussion on page 26 regarding a supposed translator's error</note>. The translator renders this passage as follows: *"Unless life tells lies under the pretext of many sweet glories."* <note>original Latin: "Niſi quòd multa dulcia gloriæ obtentu vita mentitur"</note> However, I believe that while he indeed read the word **"boasts"**, he did not understand its usage here at all. For while **"to boast"** <note>original Greek: καταλαζονεύεσθαι (katalazoneuesthai)</note> is indeed sometimes rendered as "to lie" (as boasters <note>original: alazones</note> are prone to do), it possesses that meaning only when used with a different grammatical construction. But when one says **"I boast of this"** <note>original Greek: καταλαζονεύομαι τοῦτο (katalazoneuomai touto)</note>, it means "I arrogantly commemorate," or "I brag," or "I proclaim."

**Page 180, Verse "first About"** <note>original Greek: ᾱ Περί (a Peri)</note> — There can be no doubt that **"libations"** <note>original Greek: χοάς (choas)</note> should be replaced by **"anecdotes"** or **"maxims"** <note>original Greek: χρείας (chreias)</note>, since I myself published this little book by Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus was Aristotle’s successor; "Chreiai" was a common title for collections of wise sayings</note> along with others that had never before been brought to light.

**Page 183, Verse "of the [wandering...]"** <note>original Greek: τῆς πλά. (tēs pla.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"of action"** <note>original Greek: πράξεως (praxeōs)</note></gloss>.

**Page 184, Verse "[they] saved"** <note>original Greek: σωσαν (sōsan)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **Craton** <note>original Greek: Κράτων</note> instead of **Strato** <note>original Greek: Στράτων</note></gloss>.

**Page 185, Verse "witnesses"** <note>original Greek: μάρτυres (martyres)</note> — I suspect the translator rendered the Greek name **"of Phidon"** <note>original Greek: Φίδωνος (Phidōnos)</note> as the Latin *Phidonis*, leaving the word "Son" to be understood by the reader—especially since it followed immediately after another name in the genitive case from which the relationship could be inferred. It seems that from this *Phidonis*, it was later corrupted into *Phidonus*, which is the reading currently found in his text.

**Page 190, Verse "he died"** <note>original Greek: κάτθανε (katthane)</note> — We are instructed by a certain individual to replace the phrase **"through waking"** <note>original Greek: δι’ ἐγρ’ (di’ egr’); likely short for "through vigilance"</note> with the word **"he might say"** <note>original Greek: λέγοι (legoi)</note>. But why he would wish for us to change our reading, **"I marvel at this most of all"** <note>original Greek: θαυμάζω τοῦτο μάλιστα (thaumazō touto malista)</note>—to use the very words of Diogenes himself. Furthermore, the particle **"if"** <note>original Greek: αἴ (ai)</note> should not be put in place of the particle **"would"** <note>original Greek: αν (an)</note> found in the third verse; otherwise, the grammatical structure would follow the rule for **"if"** <note>original Greek: εἰ (ei)</note>, and the entire arrangement of the speech would be thrown into confusion. For the particle belongs with **"he ran"** <note>original Greek: ἔδραμε (edrame)</note>. He says: "I marvel at this, namely **if** having walked with the feet of another [i.e., by being bitten by a snake], he **ran** such a long road to Hades, and that in a single night." <note>This refers to an epigram about the death of the philosopher Lyco, who died of gout or a snakebite</note>

**Page 191, Verse "pair"** <note>original Greek: ζεῦγος (zeugos)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"of small pomegranates"** <note>original Greek: ῥοΐσκων (rhoiskōn); likely referring to ornaments</note> instead of **"of pomegranate-trees"** <note>original Greek: ῥοΐακων (rhoiakōn)</note></gloss>. And a little after, **"a double-shaggy rug"** <note>original Greek: ἀμφίταπιν (amphitapin)</note>. By reading it as **"double-shaggy"** <note>original Greek: ἀμφίταπον (amphitapon)</note>, one might perhaps think it should be joined with the word **"coverlet"** <note>original Greek: περίστρωμα (peristrōma)</note>; however, you see a little later that these items are listed separately, with several words placed between them.

**Verse "month"** <note>original Greek: μὴν (mēn)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"being unmindful"** <note>original Greek: ἀμνημονοῦντες (amnēmoneuontes)</note>, which is the more widely accepted reading.</gloss>

->### HENRY ESTIENNE’S ANNOTATIONS ###<-

<page-num>18</page-num>

**Verse "read"** <note>original Greek: ἀνέγν. (anegn.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"unread"** <note>original Greek: ἀνάγνωστα (anagnōsta)</note> instead of **"unpublished"** <note>original Greek: ἀνέκδοτα (anekdota)</note>.</gloss>

**Verse "and"** <note>original Greek: καὶ (kai)</note> — There is also a reading, **"I leave to her,"** <note>original Greek: ἀφίημι αὐτῇ (aphiēmi autē)</note> which I prefer over the other option.

**Page 192, Verse "sixty"** <note>original Greek: ἑξήκ. (hexēk.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"five hundred."** <note>original Greek: πεντακοσίαις (pentakosiais)</note></gloss>

**Verse "la"** <note>original Greek: λὰ (la)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"to Lamis."** <note>original Greek: Λαμίδι (Lamidi)</note></gloss>

**Page 195, Verse "such"** <note>original Greek: σοῦτον (souton)</note> — Instead of **"speech"** or **"reason,"** <note>original Greek: λόγον (logon)</note> some read **"gift."** <note>original Greek: δῶρον (dōron)</note> However, this passage from Euripides’ *The Phoenician Women* <note>A tragedy by Euripides; the quote emphasizes the power of persuasion over force</note> supports the former reading:

->— For reason/speech accomplishes everything <-
-> that even the iron sword of enemies might achieve. <-
<note>original Greek: πᾶν γὰρ ἐξαιρεῖ λόγος / ὃ καὶ σίδηρος πολεμίων δράσειεν ἄν.</note>

Indeed, it seems that this philosopher, in his own saying, may have been alluding to those very words of Euripides.

**Page 197, Verse "the About"** <note>original Greek: τὸ Περί (to Peri)</note> — Perhaps it should be read as **"to him"** <note>original Greek: αὐτῷ (autō)</note> rather than **"it."** <note>original Greek: αὐτό (auto)</note>

**Verse "to all"** <note>original Greek: πασι (pasi)</note> — Instead of **"divided,"** <note>original Greek: διῃρημένος (diēirēmenos)</note> I would prefer to read **"finely adjusted"** or **"harmonized,"** <note>original Greek: διηρμοσμένος (diērmosmenos)</note> as it is written in certain copies. Hermogenes <note>A highly influential Greek rhetorician of the 2nd century AD</note> also uses this vocabulary in that particular sense.

**Page 198, Verse "and he said"** <note>original Greek: καὶ εἶπε (kai eipe)</note> — Previously the reading was, **"and he said everything [was] beautiful."** In our manuscripts, it is **"he held [himself] quite beautifully,"** and likewise **"all was well."** However, a certain person notes a reading—namely **"altogether beautiful"** <note>original Greek: παγκάλος (pagkalos)</note>—which simply cannot be tolerated <note>Estienne likely objects to this on the grounds of Greek grammar or accentuation</note>. The translator renders it: *"And so he conducted himself through all things."*

**Verse "and to"** <note>original Greek: καὶ πρὸς (kai pros)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"and regarding these things, Heraclides did not send letters, nor was he deemed worthy."**</gloss> But there was no need for the accusative word **"letters,"** <note>original Greek: γράμματα (grammata)</note> any more than there was earlier in the text when he used the word **"replied."**

**Page 200, Verse "ked."** <note>original Greek: κεδ. (ked.)</note> — The earlier edition had **"more from the city."** <note>original Latin: pléious ek tēs poleōs</note>

**Page 202, Verse "to the wicked"** <note>original Greek: πονηροῖς (ponērois)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"with the sick."** <note>original Greek: μετὰ τῶν νοσούντων (meta tōn nosountōn)</note></gloss> And a little later, **"wicked"** <note>original Greek: πονηροὺς (ponērous)</note> instead of **"envious."** <note>original Greek: φθονεροὺς (phthonerous)</note>

**Verse "lesson"** <note>original Greek: μάτιον (mation)</note> — In place of **"of lessons/learning,"** <note>original Greek: μαθημάτων (mathēmatōn)</note> it is also written as **"of disciples/students"** <note>original Greek: μαθητῶν (mathētōn)</note>—that is, of those things which are "learnable," if one may use that term for things that can be learned.

**Page 203, Verse "teaching"** <note>original Greek: διδαχ. (didach.)</note> — In place of **"teachable,"** <note>original Greek: διδακτὴν (didaktēn)</note> someone wrongly substitutes the word **"didactic."** <note>original Greek: διδακτικήν (didaktikēn)</note>

**Verse "kles"** <note>original Greek: κλῆς (klēs)</note> — The same person substitutes **"nor unworthy of love,"** <note>original Greek: οὐδ’ ἀπαξíεραστος (oud' apaxierastos)</note> which cannot be accepted at all; whereas the reading **"nor far from..."** <note>original Greek: οὐδ’ ἄπο (oud' apo)</note> might be tolerated.

**Page 209, Verse "to drink up"** <note>original Greek: ἐκπίνειν (ekpinein)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"with bent fingers."** <note>original Greek: συγκεκαμμένων δακτύλων (synkekammenōn daktylōn)</note></gloss> However, the previous edition had **"with interlaced fingers"** <note>original Greek: συγκεκραμμένοις τοῖς δακτύλοις (synkekrammenois tois daktylois)</note>, without these words: **"for his friends."** <note>original Greek: ἐπὶ τοῖς φίλοις (epi tois philois)</note>

**Page 210, Verse "pe tō"** <note>original Greek: πε τῳ (pe tō)</note> — Instead of **"himself"** <note>original Greek: αὐτὸς (autos)</note>, in some manuscripts **"it"** <note>original Greek: αὐτὸ (auto)</note> is read, and in one **"to him."** <note>original Greek: αὐῷ (autō)</note> But I agree more with those which have neither.

**Verse "in hunting"** <note>original Greek: κυνηγεσίᾳ (kynēgesia)</note> — It would be more correctly written as **"hunting festival."** <note>original Greek: κυνηγέσια (kynēgesia)</note>

**Verse "xandron"** <note>original Greek: ξανδρον (xandron)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"I would wish it had not happened."** <note>original Greek: μὴ γεγονέναι, ἐθελήσαιμ’ ἄν (mē gegonenai, ethelēsaim' an)</note></gloss>

**Page 215, Verse "having been written"** <note>original Greek: γεγραμμ. (gegramm.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"suffering a hangover from wine."** <note>original Greek: οἴνῳ κραιπαλῶσα (oinō kraipalōsa)</note></gloss> But this dative case <note>The grammatical form indicating 'by' or 'with' wine</note> seems to be superfluous. Likewise, instead of **"the owner,"** <note>original Greek: τὸν κεκτημένον (ton kektēmenon)</note> some have **"the master"** <note>original Greek: τὸν κύριον (ton kyrion)</note>—which perhaps crept in from a scholion <note>An ancient marginal note or explanatory comment preserved in the manuscript</note>.

**Page 217, Verse "according to the beast"** <note>original Greek: κατὰ τὸ θηρίον (kata to thērion)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"place"** <note>original Greek: χωρίον (chōrion)</note> instead of **"beast."** <note>original Greek: θηρίον (thērion)</note></gloss> But I have no doubt that this reading [place] is the one to be followed.

(p. erōt.)</note> — Instead of **"of a knuckle-blow,"** <note>original Greek: κονδύλου (kondylou)</note> it is also read as **"a knuckle-blow,"** <note>original Greek: κόνδυλον (kondylon)</note> and there is inserted **"or a helmet,"** <note>original Greek: ἢ περικεφαλαίαν (ē perikephalaian)</note> in this manner: **"Having been asked what he wanted, to receive a blow or a helmet, he said, 'a helmet'."** Truly, I do not see why anyone would have proposed such a question to him, nor what wit could underlie this response of his. One thing that one might wonder at in the other reading, which has the genitive case, is that no preposition is prefixed to it. But it might seem to have been omitted to leave a greater ambiguity. Having just discussed grammatical ambiguities in the previous page, Estienne now examines specific Greek idioms involving the verb "to receive" and continues his line-by-line correction of the text, citing authors like Andocides and the Emperor Julian to support his emendations.</meta>

<page-num>30</page-num>

->### HENRY ESTIENNE’S ANNOTATIONS ###<-

It is usually said **"I would not receive"** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἂν δεξαίμην (ouk an dexaimēn)</note> with a genitive case <note>A grammatical form often indicating "of" or "from"</note>: sometimes indeed with the preposition **"instead of"** <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ (anti)</note> prefixed, but sometimes it is omitted. Andocides <note>An Athenian orator of the 5th century BCE</note>, in the speech he titled *On His Own Return* <note>original Greek: περὶ τῆς ἑαυτοῦ καθόδου (peri tēs heautou kathodou)</note>, near the beginning, writes: **"for no amount of money"** <note>original Greek: οὐδενὸς ἂν χρήματος (oudenos an chrēmatos)</note> **"would they accept that you should experience some good from me."** Otherwise, we read it with the preposition **"instead of"** <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ (anti)</note> in this same orator, in the same speech: **"I would have accepted instead of all riches"** <note>original Greek: ἀντὶ πάντων χρημάτων (anti pantōn chrēmatōn)</note> **"if I could safely tell you what I reported to the Council in secret."**

**Page 220, Verse "fruit"** <note>original Greek: καρποῦ (karpou)</note> — In other manuscripts it is written much more correctly as **"he tastes,"** <note>original Greek: ἀπογεύεται (apogeuetai)</note> since **"they might eat"** <note>original Greek: ἐσθίοισι (esthioisi)</note> follows.

**Page 221, Verse "toward the..."** <note>original Greek: πρὸς τ. (pros t.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"philosophy."** <note>original Greek: φιλοσοφίαν (philosophian)</note></gloss>

**Page 223, Verse "of the race"** <note>original Greek: γένου (genou)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"serving."** <note>original Greek: θεραπεύων (therapeuōn)</note></gloss>

**Verse "pon to"** <note>original Greek: πον τὸ (pon to)</note> — In certain copies the particle **"then?"** <note>original Greek: ἆρα (ara)</note> is inserted between **"it is"** <note>original Greek: ἐστὶν (estin)</note> and **"absurd."** <note>original Greek: ἄτοπον (atopon)</note>

**Last Verse** — It is more correctly read as **"nothing indeed."** <note>original Greek: οὐδέν γε (ouden ge)</note>

**Page 224, Verse "according to nature."** <note>original Greek: κατὰ φύσιν (kata physin)</note> — Instead of **"concerning,"** <note>original Greek: περὶ (peri)</note> the preposition **"against"** <note>original Greek: παρὰ (para)</note> should rather be substituted <note>Changing the meaning from "according to nature" to "against nature"</note>.

**Verse "hedyp..."** <note>original Greek: ἡδυπ. (hēdyp.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"having been practiced."** <note>original Greek: μελετηθεῖσα (meletētheisa)</note></gloss>

**Verse "remain..."** <note>original Greek: λοιπ. (loip.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"The wise are friends to the gods; for all things are in common,"** etc. <note>original Greek: φίλοι δὲ τοῖς θεοῖς οἱ σοφοί. κοινὰ γὰρ (philoi de tois theois hoi sophoi. koina gar)</note></gloss>

**Verse "polit..."** <note>original Greek: πολιτ. (polit.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"of labors"** <note>original Greek: πόνων (ponōn)</note> instead of **"of the city."** <note>original Greek: πόλεως (poleōs)</note></gloss> Our reading <note>meaning "of the city"</note> should definitely be retained, but what follows is suspect.

**Verse "common"** <note>original Greek: κοινὰς (koinas)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"not even naming."** <note>original Greek: μηδὲ ὀνομάζων (mēde onomazōn)</note></gloss>

**Verse "but"** <note>original Greek: ἀλλὰ (alla)</note> — It seems it should rather be read as **"by the one having been persuaded."** <note>original Greek: τῇ πειθείσῃ (tē peitheisē)</note>

**Verse "it was necessary"** <note>original Greek: χρῆν (chrēn)</note> — In certain manuscripts it is **"meat"** <note>original Greek: κρέας (kreas)</note>; but likewise it should be read as **"bread"** <note>in the accusative case: ἄρτον (arton)</note>, not **"of bread"** <note>in the genitive case: ἄρτου (artou)</note>.

**Page 227, Verse "of poetic things"** <note>original Greek: ποιητικῶν (poiētikōn)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"of writings."** <note>original Greek: συγγραμμάτων (syngrammatōn)</note></gloss>

**Page 228, Verse "Monimus"** <note>A Cynic philosopher and student of Diogenes of Sinope</note> — The previous Greek edition had: **"There was a certain man, Monimus, a philosopher."** <note>original Greek: Μόνιμος τις ἦν ἄνθρωπος φιλόσοφος (Monimos tis ēn anthrōpos philosophos)</note> But in the Latin edition that immediately preceded mine, it is read as **"man, O philosopher,"** <note>original Greek: ἄνθρωπος, ὦ φιλόσοφος (anthrōpos, ō philosophe)</note> a reading that can in no way stand <note>Estienne is pointing out a "vocative" error where the translator mistook a description for a direct address</note>.

**Verse "inglorious"** <note>original Greek: ἀδόξ. (adox.)</note> — <gloss>Variant reading: **"most inglorious."** <note>original Greek: ἀδοξότατος (adoxotatos)</note></gloss>

**Page 229, Verse "sy paignia"** <note>original Greek: συ παίγνια (sy paignia)</note> — Here I can gratify the reader by providing some most elegant verses from this book of *Jests* <note>original Greek: παιγνίων (paigniōn)</note> by Crates <note>Crates of Thebes, a famous Cynic philosopher known for his cheerful disposition</note>, which I found in a certain pamphlet by the Emperor Julian <note>The 4th-century Roman Emperor Julian "the Apostate"</note>, which he wrote *Against the Uneducated Hounds* <note>original Greek: εἰς τοὺς ἀπαιδεύτους κύνας (eis tous apaideutous kynas); a critique of false Cynic philosophers</note>. The beginning of which is this: **"The rivers flow backward; so goes the proverb."** <note>original Greek: Ἄνω ποταμῶν, τοῦτο δὴ τὸ τῆς παροιμίας (Anō potamōn, touto dē to tēs paroimias)</note>

He also references the Emperor Julian’s writings to recover lost verses by the Cynic Crates.</summary>

->### ANNOTATIONS ON DIOGENES ###<-

**"A comic poet says Diogenes is vainglorious. And he does not wish to take cold baths, though being very strong in body,"** etc. <note>original Greek: ἀνὴρ κωμικὸς Διογένη φησὶ κενόδοξον. καὶ ψυχρολουτεῖν οὐ βούλεται, σφόδρα ἐρρωμένος τὸ σῶμα (anēr kōmikos Diogenē phēsi kenodoxon. kai psychroloutein ou bouletai, sphodra errōmenos to sōma)</note> *Near the end of this pamphlet [by the Emperor Julian], he writes:* **"and so that no one may suppose me to say these things in vain, I will transcribe for you a few things from the *Jests* of Crates."** <note>original Greek: ἵνα δὲ μή τις ὑπολάβῃ με ταῦτα ἄλλως λέγειν, ἐκ τῶν παιγνίων Κράτητος ὀλίγα σοι παραγράψω (hina de mē tis hypolabē me tauta allōs legein, ek tōn paigniōn Kratētos oliga soi paragraphō)</note> *But the reader will receive those verses from me at the front of this book.* <note>Estienne refers to his own printed edition of the text</note>

**Verse "lanta"** <note>original Greek: λάντα (lanta)</note> — *Instead of* **"ten"** <note>original Greek: δέκα (deka)</note> *one also reads* **"five"** <note>original Greek: πέντε (pente)</note>; *and* **"male prostitute"** <note>original Greek: πόρνῳ (pornō)</note> *instead of* **"female prostitute."** <note>original Greek: πόρνῃ (pornē)</note>

**Page 230, Verse "of the distinguished"** <note>original Greek: τῶν ἐπιφ. (tōn epiph.)</note> — *Written in certain copies,* **"of those in need."** <note>original Greek: τῶν ἀπόρων (tōn aporōn)</note>

**Verse "child"** <note>original Greek: παιδ. (paid.)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"this same father."** <note>original Greek: τοῦτον αὐτὸν πατρ. (touton auton patr.)</note>

**Page 232, Verse "bebr."** <note>original Greek: βεβρ. (bebr.)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"through saying nothing."** <note>original Greek: διὰ τοῦ λέγειν μηδέν (dia tou legein mēden)</note>

**Page 234, Verse "Who"** <note>original Greek: Τίς (Tis)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"To whom those beside..."** <note>original Greek: Τίνι τὰς παρ᾽ (Tini tas par)</note>

**Page 238, Verse "thickened"** <note>original Greek: παχύνη. (pachynē.)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"and firm."** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἀπαγής (kai apagēs)</note> *But while it seems this word* **"firm"** <note>original Greek: ἀπαγής (apagēs)</note> *fits well with the preceding word* **"thickened,"** <note>original Greek: παχύνητος (pachynētos)</note> *it fits poorly with the following word* **"weak."** <note>original Greek: ἀσθενής (asthenēs)</note>

**Page 239, Verse "then heard"** <note>original Greek: θεν ἤκουε (then ēkoue)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"vigorous."** <note>original Greek: εὔτονος (eutonos)</note>

**Verse "then o"** <note>original Greek: θεν ο (then o)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"him"** <note>original Greek: αὐτὸν (auton)</note> *instead of* **"of him."** <note>original Greek: αὐτοῦ (autou)</note>

**Verse "eia"** <note>original Greek: εία (eia)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"brings down."** <note>original Greek: κατάγεισι (katageisi)</note>

**Page 240, Verse "Ezr"** <note>original Greek: Ἐζρ (Ezr)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"of speech"** or **"of reason."** <note>original Greek: λόγου (logou)</note>

**Page 241, Verse "nō, in"** <note>original Greek: νω, ἐν (nō, en)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"toward Aristodemus."** <note>original Greek: πρὸς Ἀριστόδημον (pros Aristodēmon)</note>

**Verse "drōn"** <note>original Greek: δρων (drōn)</note> — *One also reads:* **"Hippocrates the fully participating."** <note>original Greek: Ἱπποκράτης ὁ τελέως ξυμπετέων (Hippokratēs ho teleōs sympeteōn)</note> *But I think the other writing, which contains proper names, should be followed entirely.*

**Page 246, Verse "the elegant things"** <note>original Greek: τὰ κεκομψ. (ta kekomps.)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"having been elegantly arranged"** <note>original Greek: κεκομψευμένα (kekompsyeumena)</note>, *which reading pleases me more.*

**Page 249, Verse "Atr."** <note>original Greek: Ἀτρ. (Atr.)</note> — *I think* **"pathway"** <note>original Greek: ἀτραπιόν (atrapion)</note> *ought to be restored.*

**Verse "Male"** <note>original Greek: Ἄρσενα (Arsena)</note> — *I would prefer* **"I shall make feminine"** <note>original Greek: ἐκθηλήσω (ekthēlēsō)</note>, *as it is written in certain manuscripts.*

**Page 251, Verse "eian"** <note>original Greek: είαν (eian)</note> — *After* **"having written"** <note>original Greek: γεγράφως (gegraphōs)</note> *I judge that* **"Phanias"** <note>original Greek: φανίαν (phanian)</note> *should be restored, as it is read in some manuscripts. I suspect this change happened because of the preceding accusative case word, which is likewise* **"history"** <note>original Greek: ἱστορίαν (historian)</note>. <note>Estienne suggests a scribe’s eye skipped between words with the same ending, a common error called homoioteleuton</note>

**Verse "pōnos"** <note>original Greek: πωνος (pōnos)</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"of Miltiades."** <note>original Greek: Μιλτιάδους (Miltiadous)</note>

<meta>This page continues Henry Estienne’s (Henricus Stephanus) philological notes on the lives of the philosophers by Diogenes Laertius. Transitioning from the previous discussion on Crates and the Cynics, Estienne now focuses on Book 7, specifically the life and logical terminology of Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism. He compares his current edition with his previous one and various ancient manuscripts.</meta>

<page-num>32</page-num>

->### HENRY ESTIENNE ###<-

**Page 253, Verse "dialekt."** <note>original Greek: διαλεκτ. (dialekt.), abbreviation for dialectic</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"the definitive"** <note>original Greek: τὸ ὁριστικὸν (to horistikon)</note> instead of **"the deictic"** <note>original Greek: τὸ δεικτόν (to deikton), meaning demonstrative</note>. And likewise a little later, where you also have **"discernment"** <note>original Greek: διάκρισιν (diakrisin)</note> instead of **"recognition."** <note>original Greek: ἐπίγνωσιν (epignōsin)</note>

**Verse "order"** <note>original Greek: τάξιν (taxin)</note> — Instead of **"delivery"** <note>original Greek: ὑπόκρισιν (hypokrisin), often referring to an actor's performance</note> one also reads **"response."** <note>original Greek: ἀπόκρισιν (apokrisin)</note>

**Last Verse** — In the previous edition, the word **"horned"** <note>original Greek: κερατίνας (keratinas), feminine plural</note> was read. But a second reading is confirmed by another passage in this very *Life of Zeno*, where it is written: **"and there are some puzzling arguments, veiled and hidden, such as 'the heaps,' 'the horns,' and 'the nobodies.'"** <note>original Greek: καὶ ἄποροι δέ τινες εἰσὶ λόγοι ἐγκεκαλυμμένοι καὶ διαλεληθότες καὶ σωρεῖται καὶ κερατίδες καὶ οὔτιδες (kai aporoi de tines eisi logoi enkekalymmenoi kai dialelēthotes kai sōreitai kai keratides kai outides). These refer to famous logical paradoxes used by the Stoics.</note> However, in the section on Diodorus in this same author, we also read **"horned argument,"** <note>original Greek: κεράτινον λόγον (keratinon logon), masculine</note> where certain copies had **"horned"** <note>original Greek: κερατίνην (keratinēn), feminine singular</note>.

**255, Verse "tai gar"** <note>original Greek: ται γὰρ (tai gar), a word fragment</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"accusatory."** <note>original Greek: ἐγκαλητική (enklētike)</note> Previously, however, it was read as **"invocatory."** <note>original Greek: ἐκκλητική (ekklētikē)</note>

**Page 256, Verse "sion"** <note>original Greek: σιῶν (siōn), a suffix fragment</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"impressions which as if..."** <note>original Greek: ἐμφάσεις αἱ ὡς ἂν (emphaseis hai hōs an)</note> etc. However, after the word **"becoming"** <note>original Greek: γινόμεναι (ginomenai)</note>, the punctuation mark that was placed after the word **"still"** <note>original Greek: ἔτι (eti)</note> ought to have been placed there instead.

**Verse "kat'"** <note>original Greek: κατ' (kat'), meaning "according to"</note> — After the word **"opposition"** <note>original Greek: ἐναντίωσιν (enantiōsin)</note>, these words were added in certain manuscripts: **"some naturally, others by privation."** <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν φυσικῶς, τὰ δὲ κατὰ στέρησιν (ta men physikōs, ta de kata sterēsin)</note> To which is joined, **"according to contrast, then,"** <note>original Greek: κατ' ἀντίπωσιν μὲν οὖν (kat' antipōsin men oun)</note> etc. But since no examples of these modes are brought forward afterward—as there were for the preceding ones—it seemed best to omit those words.

**Verse "nos"** <note>original Greek: νος (nos), a suffix fragment</note> — <term>Variant reading:</term> **"on the one hand as Tityus."** <note>original Greek: μὲν ὡς Τιτυός (men hōs Tityos)</note>

**Verse "itos. is conceived"** <note>original Greek: ιτος. νοεῖται (itos. noeitai)</note> — Instead of **"expressible things"** <note>original Greek: λεκτὰ (lekta), a technical Stoic term for things that can be said</note> the word **"expressive things"** <note>original Greek: λεκτικά (lektika)</note> is also found, not only here but in many other places. But that first reading [expressible] should be retained, as it rests on the authority of more manuscripts and other passages—not only of this writer, but of others as well, and especially of the philosopher Sextus <note>Sextus Empiricus, a skeptical philosopher and a major source for Stoic logic</note>. Furthermore, below, where the previous edition had **"expressive"** <note>original Greek: λεκτικὸν (lektikon)</note>, **"expressible"** <note>original Greek: λεκτόν (lekton)</note> was restored based on the consensus of the old manuscripts; specifically where it is written: **"they say the expressible is that which subsists according to a rational impression."** <note>original Greek: φασὶ δὲ τὸ λεκτὸν εἶναι τὸ κατὰ φαντασίαν λογικὴν ὑφιστάμενον (phasi de to lekton einai to kata phantasian logikēn hyphistamenon)</note> I confess, otherwise, that the word **"expressively"** <note>original Greek: λεκτικῶς (lektikōs)</note>, and not **"expressibly"** <note>original Greek: λεκτῶς (lektōs)</note>, is read in those same passages where ambiguity is defined as **"a speech signifying two or more things expressively and properly, and according to the same custom."** <note>original Greek: λέξις δύο ἢ καὶ πλείονα πράγματα σημαίνουσα λεκτικῶς καὶ κυρίως, καὶ κατὰ τὸ αὐτὸ ἔθος (lexis dyo ē kai pleiona pragmata sēmainousa lektikōs kai kyriōs, kai kata to auto ethos)</note> For the word **"habitually"** <note>original Greek: ἐκτικῶς (hektikōs)</note>, which is read in two copies instead of that **"expressively,"** can please me in no way.

<summary>Estienne refines the technical vocabulary of Stoic logic in the biography of Zeno, specifically adjudicating between terms like "lekton" (expressible) and "lektikon" (expressive) by citing the authority of Sextus Empiricus and other manuscript traditions.</summary>

-># NOTES ON DIOGENES #<-

**Page 257, Verse "men tēn"** <note>original Greek: μὲν τὴν (men tēn), a common phrase fragment</note> — After **"day"** <note>original Greek: ἡμέρη (hēmērē), the Ionic form</note> there is written in certain copies, **"and according to the Latin *mare* [sea]."** <note>original Greek: κτ' δὲ τὴν Λατίνην μάρε (kt' de tēn Latinēn mare)</note> These words were foolishly added by someone who thought that **"day"** <note>hēmērē</note> among the Ionians was the same as **"sea"** <note>original Greek: θάλαττα (thalatta)</note> among the Attics. For the dialectal difference is actually recorded as being that the Ionians say **"day"** <note>hēmērē</note> instead of **"day"** <note>original Greek: ἡμέρα (hēmera), the standard form</note>, while the Attics say **"sea"** <note>thalatta</note> instead of **"sea."** <note>original Greek: θάλασσα (thalassa). Estienne is mocking a scribe who confused a vowel change in one word for a completely different word in another language.</note>

**Page 258, Verse "tēs"** <note>original Greek: τῆς (tēs), "of the"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"of the word."** <note>original Greek: λέξεως (lexeōs)</note></gloss>

**Verse "emm."** <note>original Greek: ἔμμ. (emm.), a word fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"rhythmic"** <note>original Greek: ἔρρυθμος (errythmos)</note></gloss>; and likewise **"rhythmical,"** <note>original Greek: ἔρρυθμον (errythmon)</note> a little later.

**Page 259, Verse "ennoēma"** <note>original Greek: ἐννοημα (ennoēma), meaning a thought or notion</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"conception into a notion."** <note>original Greek: σύλληψις εἰς ἐννόημα (syllēpsis eis ennoēma)</note></gloss> But I think it should be restored as **"into one thought."** <note>original Greek: εἰς ἓν νόημα (eis hen noēma). Estienne suggests a subtle change in spacing/accents to clarify the meaning.</note>

**Verse "nos ouk echei"** <note>original Greek: νος οὐκ ἔχει (nos ouk echei), "it does not have"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"as the substance"** <note>original Greek: οἷον ἡ οὐσία (hoion hē ousia)</note> after the word **"has."**</gloss>

**Page 262, Verse "dial."** <note>original Greek: διαλ. (dial.), fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"of the connective conjunction."** <note>original Greek: συναπτικοῦ συνδέσμου (synaptikou syndesmou)</note></gloss>

**Page 264, Verse "phorai"** <note>original Greek: φοραὶ (phorai), "movements" or "tendencies"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"from truths to falsehoods."** <note>original Greek: ἐξ ἀληθῶν εἰς ψευδῆ (ex alēthōn eis pseudē)</note></gloss>

**Verse "phōs esti"** <note>original Greek: φῶς ἐστὶ (phōs esti), "it is light"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"minor premise: 'It is day.'"** <note>original Greek: πρόσλημμα, τὸ, Ἡ μέρα (proslēmma, to, Hē mera). The "proslēmma" is a technical term in Stoic logic for the second premise in a conditional syllogism.</note></gloss>

**Page 265, Verse "pk."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"it does not conflict."** <note>original Greek: οὐ μάχεται (ou machetai)</note></gloss>

**Page 266, Verse "hina"** <note>original Greek: ἵνα (hina), "in order that"</note> — After the word **"Stoics"** <note>original Greek: Στωϊκοὶ (Stōïkoi)</note> one reads in certain copies: **"those who especially maintain that only the wise man is a dialectician."** <note>original Greek: τὰ μάλισα κρατυόντες διαλεκτικὸν μόνον εἶναι τὸν σοφὸν (ta malista kratyontes dialektikon monon einai ton sophon)</note>

**Verse "tētos"** <note>suffix fragment</note> — After the word **"correctness"** <note>original Greek: ὀρθότητος (orthotētos)</note> there is written in some copies: **"and the rest: and how they arranged..."** <note>original Greek: καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν: ὅπως τε διέταξαν (kai tōn loipōn: hopōs te dietaxan)</note> etc. Furthermore, instead of **"to have"** <note>original Greek: ἔχειν (echein)</note> it seems it should be replaced with **"I might have."** <note>original Greek: ἔχοιμι (echoimi)</note>

**Page 267, Verse "ap' arch."** <note>original Greek: ἀπ' ἀρχ. (ap' arch.), "from the beginning"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"more securely."** <note>original Greek: ἀσφαλέστερον (asphalesteron)</note></gloss>

**Verse "ēsan"** <note>original Greek: ἦσαν (ēsan), "they were"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"was left behind."** <note>original Greek: ἀπελείπετο (apeleipeto)</note></gloss>

**Page 269, Verse "eiai"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"management"** <note>original Greek: οἰκοδομία (oikodomia), literally "house-building," but used for management/economy</note></gloss>, which the translator also follows; and here I agree with him.

**Verse "phasin"** <note>original Greek: φασὶν (phasin), "they say"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"by reason."** <note>original Greek: λόγῳ (logō)</note></gloss>

**Verse "kēn kai prakt."** <note>original Greek: κὴν καὶ πρακτ. (kēn kai prakt.), fragments of "theoretical and practical"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"theoretical and natural."** <note>original Greek: θεωρητικὴν καὶ φυσικήν (theōrētikēn kai physikēn)</note></gloss>

**Verse "tē de"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"an unyielding disposition of the..."** <note>original Greek: διάθεσιν ἀνυπέρητον τῶν (diathesin anyperēton tōn)</note></gloss> etc.

**Page 270, Verse "kobyl."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"of ignorance,"** <note>original Greek: ἀγνοίας (agnoias)</note></gloss> which I prefer, since **"knowledge"** <note>original Greek: ἐπιστήμαι (epistēmai)</note> follows.

**Verse "agath."** <note>fragment of "good"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"logical, or as logical."** <note>original Greek: λογικοῦ, ἢ ὡς λογικοῦ (logikou, ē hōs logikou)</note></gloss> One also reads **"logical"** <note>original Greek: λογικὸν (logikon)</note> in the latter place.

**Verse "tōn ag."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"to be concerning the soul,"** <note>original Greek: εἶναι περὶ ψυχὴν (einai peri psychēn)</note></gloss> and more correctly so.

**Page 272, Verse "ē leg."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"the perfectly good."** <note>original Greek: τὸ τελείως ἀγαθόν (to teleiōs agathon)</note></gloss>

**Verse "ison"** <note>original Greek: ἴσον (ison), "equal"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"that the Beautiful is equivalent to the Good."** <note>original Greek: ἰσοδυναμεῖν τὸ καλὸν τῷ ἀγαθῷ (isodynamein to kalon tō agathō)</note></gloss> One also reads...
