**"equivalent,"** <note>original Greek: ἰσοδυναμοῦν (isodynamoun)</note> likewise **"equivalent."** <note>original Greek: ἰσοδύναμον (isodynamon)</note>

**Verse "beauty"** <note>original Greek: κάλλος (kallos)</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"obscurity"** <note>original Greek: ἀδοξία (adoxia)</note> instead of **"glory."** <note>original Greek: δόξα (doxa)</note></gloss>

**Page 273, Verse "na dyn."** <note>fragment of "to be able"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"of those things being gathered together."** <note>original Greek: συλλαμβανομένων (syllambanomenōn)</note></gloss>

**Page 275, last Verse** — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"excluding."** <note>original Greek: ἀποκλείουσαν (apokleiousan)</note></gloss>

**Page 276, Verse "thois pr."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"but an uproar is a fear accompanied by a breakdown."** <note>original Greek: θόρυβος δὲ, φόβος μετὰ κατηπ. (thorybos de, phobos meta katēp.). "Katēp." is likely a fragment of *katēpeixeōs*, meaning "urgency" or "distress."</note></gloss>

**Verse "outh' otin"** <note>fragment</note> — There is no doubt that **"soothing"** <note>original Greek: κατακηλοῦσα (katakēlousa)</note> would be more suitable; however, in our manuscripts **"breaking down"** <note>original Greek: κατακλῶσα (kataklōsa)</note> was read, as you have it here.

**Page 277, Verse "pharm."** <note>fragment of "medicine"</note> — One also reads **"poisonous."** <note>original Greek: φαρμακοποιάν (pharmakopoian)</note>

**Verse "making"** <note>original Greek: ποιούσης (poiousēs)</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"the fiction"** or **"the formation."** <note>original Greek: τὸ πλάσμα (to plasma)</note></gloss>

**Page 278, Verse "sai g."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"of purifications and of the others"** <note>original Greek: καθαρμῶν τε καὶ τῶν ἄλλων (katharmōn te kai tōn allōn)</note> etc.</gloss>

**Verse "for if"** <note>original Greek: εἰ γὰρ (ei gar)</note> — Instead of **"concise"** <note>original Greek: σύντομον (syntomon)</note> one also reads **"absurd"** <note>original Greek: ἄτοπον (atopon)</note>; but that first reading is confirmed by the passage on page 236, at the end.

**Page 280, Verse "synē"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"and all things therefore."** <note>original Greek: πάντα τε οὖ (panta te ou)</note></gloss>

**Verse "aphe tōn"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"and practical regarding things to be done. But the..."** <note>original Greek: καὶ πρακτικὸν τῶν ποιητέων. τὰ δὲ (kai praktikon tōn poiēteōn. ta de)</note> etc. Likewise, **"to be bound under"** <note>original Greek: ὑποδητέα (hypodētea)</note> and **"to be tamed under,"** <note>original Greek: ὑποδμητέα (hypodmētea)</note> and in the same way a little later.</gloss>

**Verse "some indeed"** <note>original Greek: τὰ μὲν (ta men)</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"he does by choice."** <note>original Greek: αἱρετῶς ποιεῖ (hairetōs poiei)</note></gloss>

**Page 281, Verse "About"** <note>original Greek: Περὶ (Peri)</note> — One also finds **"sent with pleasure."** <note>original Greek: ἡδύπεμπτον (hēdypempton)</note>

**Page 283, Verse "math."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"mathematical."** <note>original Greek: μαθηματικῶν (mathēmatikōn)</note></gloss>

**Verse "destroys"** <note>original Greek: φθείρ.</note> — In certain copies it is written **"incorporeal things."** <note>original Greek: ἀσώματα (asōmata)</note>

**Page 284, Verse "sias"** <note>fragment of "substance"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"uniquely qualified."** <note>original Greek: ἰδίως ποιόν (idiōs poion). A Stoic technical term for individual identity.</note></gloss>

**Page 285, Verse "to ken."** <note>fragment of "the void"</note> — In certain copies: **"that which is capable of being occupied by bodies, but is not occupied."** <note>original Greek: τὸ οἷόν τε κατέχεσθαι ὑπὸ σωμάτων, οὐ κατεχόμενον (to hoion te katechesthai hypo sōmatōn, ou katechomenon)</note> <note>This is the classic Stoic definition of the Void.</note>

**Verse "nios"** <note>fragment</note> — It is written in several copies: **"similar to incorporeal things."** <note>original Greek: ἀσωμάτοις ὅμοια (asōmatois homoia)</note>

**Page 287, first Verse** — Instead of **"intelligent"** <note>original Greek: νοερὸν (noeron)</note> one also reads **"moist."** <note>original Greek: νοτερὸν (noteron)</note>

**Verse "chara"** <note>fragment</note> — In others **"going over"** <note>original Greek: ὑπερχομένη (yperchomenē)</note> or **"going away."** <note>original Greek: ἀπερχομένη (aperchomenē)</note>

**Verse "lēnēn"** <note>fragment of "moon"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"and that only full moons suffer eclipse."** <note>original Greek: καὶ τὰς πανσελήνους ἐκλείπειν μόνας (kai tas panselēnous ekleipein monas)</note></gloss>

**Page 288, Verse "Apoll."** <note>fragment of Apollodorus</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"and it is also passive"** <note>original Greek: καὶ παθητὴ δέ ἐστιν (kai pathētē de estin)</note></gloss>; and this reading ought to be restored. In the same place: **"the same man."** <note>original Greek: ὁ αὐτός (ho autos)</note>

**Page 290, Verse "ma katē."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"broken off from a cloud"** <note>original Greek: ἐρρωγὸς ἀπὸ νέφους (errōgos apo nephous)</note> and **"by a cloud."** <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ νέφους (hypo nephous)</note></gloss>

**Verse "chasm."** <note>fragment of "chasm" or "yawning"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"full of waves."** <note>original Greek: κυματίας (kymatias)</note></gloss>

**Verse "gontai"** <note>fragment of a verb</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"they do not compose."** <note>original Greek: οὐ συντιθέουσιν (ou syntitheousin)</note></gloss>

**Verse "lois"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"around the center."** <note>original Greek: περὶ τὸ κέντρον (peri to kentron)</note></gloss> For the zodiac...

<meta>This page continues Henry Estienne’s philological commentary on Diogenes Laertius. Estienne is currently working through the latter parts of Book 7 (on the Stoics), providing corrections based on different manuscript traditions and evaluating the choices made by previous translators.</meta>

-># NOTES ON DIOGENES #<-

->### HENRY ESTIENNE ###<-

**Page 292, Verse "rhēn"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"towards the things after."** <note>original Greek: πρὸς τὰ μετ. (pros ta met.)</note></gloss>

**Verse "pepoiēm."** <note>fragment of "made"</note> — In the previous edition these words were not included: **"and made for the crowd."** <note>original Greek: καὶ ὄχλῳ πεποιημένος (kai ochlō pepoiēmenos)</note> In some manuscripts, however, **"persuaded"** <note>original Greek: πεπεισμένος (pepeismenos)</note> is read instead of **"made."** But this participle can have no place here, in my judgment. Rather, that first term was used in the same way the Latins sometimes use the participle **"made"** <note>original Latin: *Factus*</note> when someone is said to be "made" <note>i.e., naturally suited</note> for a specific purpose. Nor does the translator seem to have poorly grasped the meaning, as he rendered it: **"And he especially accommodated himself to the common people."**

**Verse "kes."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"of the activity."** <note>original Greek: ἐνεργείας (energeias)</note></gloss>

**Page 293, first Verse** — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"daily"** <note>original Greek: καθ' ἡμέραν (kath' hēmeran)</note> instead of **"sitting."** <note>original Greek: καθήμερον (kathēmeron)</note></gloss>

**Page 296, Verse "ton"** — The translator reads **"more"** <note>original Greek: πλείων (pleiōn)</note> instead of **"near"** <note>original Greek: πλησίον (plēsion)</note>; for he translates it as: **"Preferring his own poverty to the wealth of the rich."**

**Page 298, Verse "anasch."** <note>fragment</note> — The translator joined these words, **"The same things to Zeno,"** <note>original Greek: Ταυτὰ Ζήνωνι (Tauta Zēnōni)</note> to what follows; however, they can also be joined to what precedes.

**Page 299, Verse "tois pl."** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"to the poor."** <note>original Greek: τοῖς πτωχοῖς (tois ptōchois)</note></gloss> Immediately after, it is more correctly **"of her."** <note>original Greek: αὐτής (autēs)</note>

**Page 301, Verse "maïkōn"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"in a state of discord"** or **"in a faction."** <note>original Greek: ἐν στάσει (en stasei)</note></gloss> And instead of **"in the Odeon"** <note>original Greek: ᾠδείῳ (ōdeiō); a public building for musical performances</note>, one also reads **"in the private house."** <note>original Greek: οἰκείῳ (oikeiō)</note>

**Page 307, Verse "of the base"** <note>original Greek: φαύλου (phaulou)</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"between the base,"** <note>original Greek: ἀνὰ μέσον τοῦ φαύλου (ana meson tou phaulou)</note> according to Metrodorus.</gloss>

**Verse "Concerning the"** <note>original Greek: Περὶ τῶν (Peri tōn)</note> — In some copies, **"of etymologies"** <note>original Greek: ἐτυμολογιῶν (etymologiōn)</note> appears in the first place.

**Verse "syntax"** <note>or "arrangement"</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"Timon"** <note>original Greek: Τίμωνα (Timōna)</note> instead of **"Timonax."** <note>original Greek: Τιμώνακτα (Timōnakta)</note></gloss>

**Verse "of ignorance"** <note>original Greek: ἀγνοίας (agnoias)</note> — Here too, in certain manuscripts, the word is **"of goodwill,"** <note>original Greek: εὐνοίας (eunoias); the text contains a typo 'aunoias'</note> and it was read this way in the previous edition. However, a similar error was noticed above. Likewise, instead of **"speaking for themselves,"** <note>original Greek: αὐτοδιαλεγομένων (autodialogomenōn)</note> certain old copies have **"speaking themselves,"** <note>original Greek: αὐτολεγομένων (autolegomenōn)</note> which is indeed more correct.

**Page 308, Verse "nēn"** <note>fragment</note> — After **"of things being said,"** <note>original Greek: λεγομένων (legomenōn)</note> there is added in certain old manuscripts **"by the,"** <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ τῆς (hypo tēs)</note> after which it is noted that the rest is missing.

**Page 309, Verse "sarchou"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"the Samian"** <note>original Greek: Σάμιος (Samios)</note> after **"Hermippus."** <note>original Greek: Ἕρμιππος (Hermippos)</note></gloss> As it see...

<meta>This page concludes Henry Estienne’s philological notes on the lives of the philosophers. He is wrapping up his corrections on the Stoic section, specifically debating the lineage of certain philosophers and the correct wording of ancient maxims regarding labor and burdens.</meta>

-># HENRY ESTIENNE’S ANNOTATIONS #<-

...namely these words, **"as Hermippus says,"** <note>original Greek: ὡς φησιν Ἕρμιππος (hōs phēsin Hermippos)</note> should be joined to what follows just as if it were written, **"Samian as Hermippus says, or Tyrrhenian as Aristoxenus says."** <note>original Greek: Σάμιος ὡς φησιν Ἕρμιππος, ἢ Τυῤῥινὸς, ὡς φησιν Ἀριστόξενος</note>

**Verse "Ēō"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"of Maimacus."** <note>original Greek: Μαιμάκου (Maimakou)</note></gloss> And likewise **"Maimacus,"** a little later.

**Page 311, Verse "Ion"** — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"in the Triagmi."** <note>original Greek: τοῖς τριαγμοῖς (tois triagmois); referring to a work by Ion of Chios titled "The Triads" or "The Threefold"</note></gloss>

**Verse "piadas"** <note>fragment</note> — Instead of **"Socrates,"** <note>original Greek: Σωκράτης (Sōkratēs)</note> I read **"Sosicrates"** <note>original Greek: Σωσικράτης (Sōsikratēs)</note> along with many manuscripts; a reading which other passages also confirm.

**Verse "phlias"** <note>fragment</note> — <gloss><term>Variant reading:</term> **"of the tyrant, to say something philosophical, to speak, the life,"** etc. <note>original Greek: τυράννου, λέξαι τί φιλόσοφον, εἰπεῖν, τὸν βίον</note></gloss>

**Page 312, Verse "kōs"** <note>fragment</note> — The previous edition had: **"not to be refuted by themselves."** <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐλέγχεσθαι ὑπ' ἑαυτῶν (ouk elengchesthai hyp' heautōn)</note> However, the translator also follows the other reading.

**Verse "nēn"** <note>fragment</note> — After **"spion"** <note>fragment</note>, some manuscripts have **"nor of sleeps."** <note>original Greek: μήτε τῶν ὕπνων (mēte tōn hypnōn)</note>

**Page 313, Verse "When"** <note>original Greek: Ἡνίκα (hēnika)</note> — The previous edition had **"he completed."** <note>original Greek: ἤνυκε (ēnyke)</note> This reading might perhaps be more suitable where this epigram is closed by these two verses, just as it is in the works of Athenaeus; yet in the *Anthology*, four verses are added.

**Page 314, Verse "to help pull down"** <note>original Greek: συγκαθαιρεῖν (synkathairein)</note> — Instead of **"to help place upon"** <note>original Greek: συνεπιτιθέναι (synepitithenai)</note>, some have read **"to help lay down."** <note>original Greek: συναποτιθέναι (synapotithenai)</note> We do not find this reading in our manuscripts, yet the translator is thought to have recognized it, since he renders it: **"A burden is to be lifted together, not to be laid down together."** <note>This refers to a famous Pythagorean maxim encouraging industry: help people with their work, but don't help them be idle.</note> It is thought that this can also be confirmed from Saint Jerome, who interprets it as: **"One must help the person lifting a burden, but not help the one who lays it down."** But in no way can **"to help pull down"** <note>original Greek: συγκαθαιρεῖν</note> mean "to lift together" or "raise up"; rather, it would better align with **"to help lay down."** <note>original Greek: συναποτιθέναι</note> Therefore, I would believe that Jerome and this translator, and others who rendered this symbol <note>i.e., this moral maxim</note> in that way, likewise read **"to help place upon,"** <note>original Greek: συνεπιτιθέναι</note> but that the negative particle occupied a different position in their texts, in this manner: **"Not to help pull down a burden, but to help place it upon."** <note>original Greek: φορτίον μὴ συγκαθαιρεῖν, συνεπιτιθέναι δέ</note> See my *Observations* on Erasmus's expositions of certain proverbs, added at the end of that work, where a passage of Plutarch is also found, writing: **"To take the weight off no one, but to help place it upon and help load it up."** <note>original Greek: μηδενὸς ἀφαιρεῖν βάρος, συνεπιτιθέναι δὲ καὶ συνεπιφορτίζειν</note>

-> There was no time to proceed further. <-

<meta>This page transitions from the annotations of Henry Estienne to those of Willem Canter (1542–1575), a Dutch classicist. Canter is providing a list of "animadversions" or critical observations on the text of Pythagorean fragments, which were often preserved in a corrupted or incomplete state in early manuscripts.</meta>

# WILLIAM CANTER

## Observations from Utrecht on certain passages of the fragments that remain from the writings of the Pythagoreans.

**Page 437, Verse** <term>becomes to the] but unacceptable</term> <note>original Greek: γίνεται τῷ] ἄδεκτα δέ</note>. We have restored the mutilated passage in this way, whereas previously it was read: **"but unacceptable, the work of late,"** etc. <note>original Greek: ἄδεκτα δέ, ὄψιος ἔργον</note>

**Verse** <term>unhappiness</term> <note>original Greek: ἀδαιμονία (adaimonia)</note> — We have corrected this passage in this way, which previously was read corruptly as: **"for the one having reason, the work is subject to fall; for the one as children."** <note>original Greek: τῷ λόγον ἔχοντι πτώσιμος ἔργον, τῷ δ᾽ ὡς τέκνα</note>

**Page 438, Verse 1,** <term>to take good overseers</term> <note>original Greek: ἐπισάτας ἀγαθώς λαβεῖν</note>. It seems that these words should be added: **"and such a person would be the noble and good man."** <note>original Greek: τοιοῦτος δέ κεν εἴη ὁ καλοκάγαθός ἄνθρωπος</note>

**Verse** <term>and let it be</term> <note>original Greek: τος δὲ καὶ εἴη</note>. Perhaps more correctly: **"it would be."** <note>original Greek: κεν εἴη (ken eiē)</note>

**Verse** <term>of this. For the</term> <note>original Greek: ταύ. αἱ γδ</note>. The word **"for each"** <note>original Greek: ἑκάστῳ (hekastō)</note> is missing. **"For the virtues for each..."** <note>original Greek: αἱ γδ ἑκάστῳ ἀρεταί</note>

**Verse** <term>...nor unhappy by nature</term> <note>original Greek: πος, οὔτε τᾷ φύσει ἀδαίμων</note>. The phrase **"nor good by nature"** <note>original Greek: οὔτε τᾷ φύσει ἀγαθός</note> is missing, which is absent just a little before.

**Page 440, Verse** <term>...and] those individually</term> <note>original Greek: σις, κ᾿] αἱ καθ᾿ ἕκαστον</note>. Previously read corruptly as **"those individually."**

**Verse** <term>...and this</term> <note>original Greek: ρωκε . τοῦτο δέ</note>. We have placed the conjunction **"but/and"** <note>original Greek: δέ (de)</note> instead of **"he shouts"** <note>original Greek: βοᾷ (boa)</note>.

**Page 441, Verse** <term>for there is...] but happiness</term> <note>original Greek: ἔςι γ’] ἀ δ᾽ εὐδαιμονία</note>. It should read **"lawlessness."** <note>original Greek: ἀνομία (anomia)</note>

**Page 443, Verse** <term>...of purpose</term> <note>original Greek: προθέσιος (prothesios)</note>, not **"of addition."** <note>original Greek: προσθέσιος (prosthesios)</note>

**Verse** <term>...the] summits and perfections</term> <note>original Greek: τας ταῖς] ἀκρότας καὶ τελειότας</note>. After the word **"of eyes"** <note>original Greek: ὀφθαλμῶν</note> I add **"of nature."** <note>original Greek: φύσιος (physios)</note>

**Verse** <term>of the body] for on the one hand</term> <note>original Greek: σώματος] τῷ μὲν γδ</note>. I prefer to read it this way rather than **"the one, the other."** <note>original Greek: τὸ μὲν, τὸ δέ</note>

**Page 444, Verse** <term>first indeed] let us be prudent</term> <note>original Greek: πρῶτόν γε] πνυτῶμεν</note>. In place of this, the word **"let us be venerable"** <note>original Greek: πρεσβυτῶμεν (presbytōmen)</note> would please me.

**Page 445, Verse** <term>...something] suspended</term> <note>original Greek: ξαν τί] ἐπηρτημένα</note>. I read **"evils"** <note>original Greek: κακά (kaka)</note> instead of **"according to."** <note>original Greek: κατά (kata)</note>

**Verse** <term>...being</term> <note>original Greek: βαια οὖσε</note>. Would **"it might be"** <note>original Greek: εἴη (eiē)</note> not be more correct?

**Verse** <term>having considered] thinking if the</term> <note>original Greek: μῦ ἐνθυμηθέντες] νομίζοντες εἰ τὰ</note>. Perhaps the particle **"but/and"** <note>original Greek: δὲ (de)</note> should be added: **"and thinking if the."** <note>original Greek: νομίζοντες δέ εἰ τὰ</note>

**Page 446, Verse** <term>...holding] and changing</term> <note>original Greek: τεχόμενοι] καὶ μεταποιούμενοι</note>. Or perhaps **"being satisfied"** <note>original Greek: καταρκούμενοι (katarkoumenoi)</note> should be read.

**Third line from the bottom,** <term>after the time of life</term> <note>original Greek: μετὰ τὸν τᾶς ζωᾶς χρόνον</note>. Something seems to be missing...

# ANNOTATIONS BY WILLEM CANTER

these things, "they do not reckon. Since therefore this is not permitted," etc. <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἀναλογίζονται. ἐπεὶ οὖν τοῦτο οὐκ ἔξεστι</note>

**Page 447, Verse** [ending in] "goods"] "nor did he care for good things." <note>original Greek: οὐ δ᾽ ἀγαθῶν ἐμετείει</note>. **A corrupt passage.** Perhaps "negligence" <note>original Greek: ἀμέλειαν (ameleian)</note>, or "lack of moderation" <note>original Greek: ἀμετρίαν (ametrian)</note>.

**Page 448, Verse** "indeed through"] I substitute "effective" <note>original Greek: ποιητικά (poiētika)</note> for "deliberate" <note>original Greek: προαιρετικά (proairetika)</note>.

**Verse** "and opinions"] "pleasant" <note>original Greek: ἡδύ (hēdy)</note>. Not "persuasion." <note>original Greek: πειθώ (peithō)</note>

**Page 449, Verse** "suffering"] "it always passed by." <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ παρῆλθεν</note>. Perhaps more correctly, "it must pass by." <note>original Greek: δεῖ παρῆλθεν</note>

**Page 450, Verse** "that the"] "that the good [man]." <note>original Greek: ὅτι ὁ ἀγαθός</note>. Read "from where the good [man]." <note>original Greek: ὅθεν ὁ ἀγαθός</note>

**Second to last verse,** "always flowing." <note>original Greek: ἀεὶ ῥέοντι</note>. Read "grieving" <note>original Greek: ἀχέοντι (acheonti)</note>, or "lifting up." <note>original Greek: αἰέροντι (aieronti)</note>

**Page 453, Verse** "and concord"] Otherwise "agreement." <note>original Greek: ὁμολογία (homologia)</note>

**Verse** "of reason"] "of the rational part." <note>original Greek: λογικῶ μέρεος</note>. Gessner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565) was a polymath and editor of early Greek texts whose versions Canter is critiquing.</note> also reads "of the reasoning [part]." <note>original Greek: λογιστικῶ (logistikō)</note>

**Verse** "arm's length"] "to be allowed." <note>original Greek: ἐξεῖν</note>. Otherwise "it might be allowed." <note>original Greek: ἐξείη (exeiē)</note>

**Same verse,** "for from where does he find the means?" <note>original Greek: μαχανάσιος γὰρ πόθεν εὑρίσκει</note>. I would prefer to read, "for having devised means, he finds them for the sake of injustice." <note>original Greek: μαχανάσας γδ εὑρίσκει ποτὶ τὸ ἄδικον</note>

**Verse** "and they shall do"] "they will do." <note>original Greek: πράσοντι</note>. Gessner also has "they will do."

**Page 454, Verse** "and temperance"] "justice." <note>original Greek: δικαιοσύνη</note>. Another manuscript of Gessner's has "righteousness." <note>original Greek: δικαιότας (dikaiotas)</note>

**Page 455, Verse** "of reason"] "part of the soul." <note>original Greek: μέρεος τᾶς ψυχᾶς</note>. We have **filled a gap** <term>lacuna | a missing portion of text in a manuscript</term> here: "but the act of affection and loving occurs in both of them, both in the irrational part and in the part of the soul that possesses reason." <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ στέργειν καὶ ἀγαπᾶν ἐν ἀμφοτέροις αὐτοῖς γίνεται, καὶ τῷ ἀλόγῳ καὶ τῷ λόγον ἔχοντι μέρει τᾶς ψυχᾶς</note>

**Page 456, Verse** [ending in] "rational"] "the spirited part." <note>original Greek: τὸ μὲν θυμοειδές</note>. Certain things are clearly missing here, to be filled in this way: "but the irrational part, on the one hand the spirited part," etc. <note>original Greek: τὸ δὲ ἄλογον, τὸ μὲν θυμοειδές</note>

**Page 457, Verse** [ending in] "part"] "they are named." <note>original Greek: ὀνομάζονται</note>. Previously it was read most corruptly as "they are not mad." <note>original Greek: οὐ μαίνονται</note>

**Following verse,** "and ethical." <note>original Greek: ἠθικόν τε</note>. I prefer to read "and related to horses." <note>original Greek: ἱπικόν τε (hippikon te)</note>

**Verse** [ending in] "unrestrained"] "having been fanned into flame, it is prone to do injustice." <note>original Greek: ἀναρριπισθεῖσα ἐῇ, ἀδικεῖν πέφυκεν</note>. Gessner has it differently: "to choose [certain things], through which it is prone to do injustice." <note>original Greek: αἰαιρεῖν, δι᾽ ἃς ἀδικεῖν πέφυκεν</note>

**Verse** "in forms"] "preparing." <note>original Greek: παρασκευάζοντα</note>. Gessner also reads "preparing within." <note>original Greek: ἐμπαρασκευάζοντα (emparaskeuazonta)</note>

**Verse** "fear"] "certainly by the laws." <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ δὴ τῶν νόμων</note>. Gessner reads it differently: "through the law, through God, through reason." <note>original Greek: διὰ τὸν νόμον, διὰ τὸν θεὸν, διὰ τὸν λόγον</note>

**Last verse,** "it sails straight." <note>original Greek: ἀμ᾽ ὀρθοπλοεῖ</note>. Better as "whenever it sails straight." <note>original Greek: αἰκ᾽ ὀρθοπλοῇ</note>

**Page 459, Verse** "it is rumored"] Another manuscript of Gessner's says "it is struck." <note>original Greek: φαπίζεται</note>

**Verse** [ending in] "it becomes"] "but when in the enduring of pleasant things." <note>original Greek: ὅκα δὲ ἐν τῷ ὑφίστασθαι τὰ ἡδέα</note>. Here too there is a **gap** <term>lacuna</term>, which we have restored in this way: "but when in the en-" <note>The text is interrupted at the end of the page.</note>

<meta>This page continues Willem Canter’s philological notes on fragments attributed to Pythagoras and his followers. # ON PYTHAGOREAN FRAGMENTS

"...enduring fears is courage; but when in the restraining of pleasant things, temperance, etc." <note>original Greek: φίσεσθαι τὰ δεινὰ, ἀνδρεία· ὅκα δ᾽ ἐν τῷ κατέχεν τὰ ἡδέα, σωφροσύνα. This completes the thought from the bottom of the previous page regarding the parts of the soul.</note>

**Verse: "middle states"** <note>original Greek: μεσότατας</note>] "for in this way also the middle states are..." <note>original Greek: οὕτω γὰρ καὶ μεσότατες αἱ</note>. It seems something is missing here: "for in this way both the duties and the middle states, etc." <note>original Greek: οὕτω μὲν γὰρ καὶ τὰ δέοντα καὶ αἱ μεσότατες</note>

**Following verse: "within,"** <note>original Greek: ἐντὸς</note> not **"without."** <note>original Greek: ἐκτὸς</note>

**Page 460, Verse [ending in] "-able"** <note>original Greek: λοῖς</note>] "possible." <note>original Greek: δυνατόν</note>. I prefer this to "it is possible." <note>original Greek: δύναται</note>

**Page 461, Verse: "the eye"** <note>original Greek: τὸ ὄμμα</note>] "this very thing is wandering." <note>original Greek: πλάνιον αὐτό γε τοῦτο</note>. Gessner reads "wandering" <note>original Greek: πλάνον</note> as an idle word. I consider the passage **corrupt** <term>corrupt | a portion of text that has been altered or damaged in transmission and no longer makes sense</term>, and thus I read: "this very thing is not a wandering." <note>original Greek: πλάν᾽ οὐκ αὐτό γε τοῦτο</note>

**Verse: "these things"** <note>original Greek: αὐτα</note>] "to the and these." <note>original Greek: τῷ καὶ ταῦ</note>. Previously it was read as "the and these." <note>original Greek: τὸν κᾀ ταῦ</note>

**Verse: "duty"** <note>original Greek: δέον</note>] "how." <note>original Greek: ὅπως</note>. Otherwise, "which." <note>original Greek: ὅπερ</note>

**Third to last verse: "into one another."** <note>original Greek: εἰς ἄλληλα</note>. Otherwise, "toward one another." <note>original Greek: πρὸς ἄλληλα</note>

**Page 462, Verse: "the disposition"** <note>original Greek: τὴν διάθεσιν</note>] "the [things] therefore." <note>original Greek: ἁ μὲν οὖν</note>. Otherwise, "for the [things]." <note>original Greek: αἱ μὲν γὰρ</note>

**Verse: "with them"** <note>original Greek: σὺν αὐτοῖς</note>] "it is composed." <note>original Greek: συνίσταται</note>. Gessner elsewhere has "it grows with these things." <note>original Greek: συναύξεται τούτοις</note>

**Second to last verse:** "the part possessing reason of the duty." <note>original Greek: τὸ λόγον ἔχον τῶ δέοντος</note>. There seems to be a **gap** <term>lacuna</term> here; perhaps "through" <note>original Greek: διά</note> or "with" <note>original Greek: μετά</note> is missing, in this manner: "the part possessing reason with the duty." <note>original Greek: τὸ λόγον ἔχον μετὰ τοῦ δέοντος</note>

**Page 463, Verse: "divine"** <note>original Greek: δαιμονίαν</note>] "it might proclaim." <note>original Greek: καρύσεια</note>. **Faultily** read as "it might proclaim" <note>original Greek: καρύσεια</note>, unless one might prefer "you might grant." <note>original Greek: χαρίσση α</note>

**Verse: "some present [plural]"** <note>original Greek: τις παρόντας</note>] "of one present [singular]." <note>original Greek: παρόντος</note>. I prefer to read it this way rather than "present [plural]."

**Following verse: "of those daring."** <note>original Greek: τολμώντων</note>. Not "to the one daring." <note>original Greek: τολμῶντι</note>

**Verse: "middle"** <note>original Greek: μεσοὶ</note>] "the reason." <note>original Greek: ὁ λόγος</note>. Read **erroneously** as "irrationally" <note>original Greek: ἀλόγως</note>, with Gessner providing the correction.

**Following verse: "defining."** <note>original Greek: ὁρίσδων</note>. Deformedly read as "mountain nymphs." <note>original Greek: ὁριάδων</note>

**Last verse: "indifferent."** <note>original Greek: ἀδιαφόροις</note>. Incorrectly read as "different." <note>original Greek: διαφόροις</note>

**Page 464, second to last verse: "neither."** <note>original Greek: μήτε</note>. Not "nor even." <note>original Greek: μηδὲ</note>

**Page 466, Verse: "toil"** <note>original Greek: μογᾶς</note>] "they might be silent." <note>original Greek: σωπήσησιν</note>. Otherwise, "he might be silent." <note>original Greek: σωπάσηται</note>

**In the same verse: "incantations."** <note>original Greek: ἐπῳδάς</note>. Perhaps "ignorance" <note>original Greek: ἀμαθίας</note>, unless some other mystery lies beneath the text.

**Verse: "pleasures"** <note>original Greek: ἠδονὰς</note>] "misfortunes." <note>original Greek: ἀτυχήματα</note>. Gessner also has "bad luck." <note>original Greek: ἀτυχίας</note>

**Verse: "it appears"** <note>original Greek: φαίνεται</note>] "it indeed appears." <note>original Greek: φαίνεται δή</note>. Otherwise "but." <note>original Greek: δέ</note>

<summary>Willem Canter continues his line-by-line textual criticism of Pythagorean fragments, focusing on refining grammar, identifying erroneous manuscript readings (such as "mountain nymphs" for "defining"), and proposing logical insertions where the text appears broken.</summary>
<keywords>textual criticism, emendation, Pythagorean fragments, Willem Canter, Conrad Gessner, lacuna, philology, Greek ethics</keywords>

# SEVERAL PASSAGES TO BE EMENDED <note>original Latin: Loci aliquot emendandi. This is a common heading in early modern scholarly texts for a list of corrections.</note>

**Page 150, Verse [starting] "O virgin"** <note>original Greek: Ὦ παρθ.</note>] replace with "there will be grace for me." <note>original Greek: ἔση μοι χάρις</note>

**Page 154, Verse: "polyp"** <note>original Greek: πούλυπον</note>] One should rather follow the examples in which the particle **"not"** <note>original Greek: μή</note> is not held, and **"Aeidelon"** <note>original Greek: Ἀείδηλον; likely referring to the "Unseen" or "Invisible" as a proper name or title</note> should be written with a capital letter.

**Page 236, Verse: "Whenever"** <note>original Greek: Ὅπι</note>] write **"in the halls."** <note>original Greek: μεγάροισι</note>

**Page 256, Verse [ending in] "-sion"** <note>original Greek: σιῶν</note>] Punctuate it thus: "becoming. Still of the [things] appearing." <note>original Greek: γινόμεναι. ἔτι τῶν φαιν.</note>

**In the verse whose beginning is "to go around,"** <note>original Greek: περινεῖν</note> write **"occurrence."** <note>original Greek: περιπτωσιν; also meaning chance or coincidence</note>

**Page 271, Verse: "unwise"** <note>original Greek: ἄφρ.</note>] read: **"freedom from pain and all."** <note>original Greek: ἀλυπίαν καὶ πᾶσαν</note>

**Page 298, Verse etc.**] replace with **"to agree."** <note>original Greek: συγκαταθεῖσθαι; a technical term in Stoic and Pythagorean ethics for mental assent</note>

**Page 377, Verse: "not yet, not"** <note>original Greek: πω, οὐ</note>] replace with **"in which not."** <note>original Greek: ἐν ᾧ δ’ οὐκ</note>

**Page 393, Verse: "of the books"** <note>original Greek: τῶν βιβλ.</note>] more correctly **"to write."** <note>original Greek: γράψαι</note>. And **"strives"** <note>original Greek: φιλονεικεῖ</note> can be joined with this **"to write."**

->**Decorative Marbled Endpaper**<-

This page features a full-page decorative **marbled paper** pattern, a traditional technique used to beautify and reinforce the **endpapers** <term>endpapers: the sheets of paper at the very beginning and end of a book; one half is typically pasted to the inside of the cover to help secure the book block to its binding</term> of high-quality volumes.

The design is a classic example of a **comb pattern**, specifically the **nonpareil** style <term>nonpareil: a pattern created by drawing a fine-toothed comb through pigments floating on a liquid surface, resulting in delicate, repeating arches</term>. The pattern is made up of:

*   Tightly packed, rhythmic rows of downward-pointing scalloped arches.
*   Vertical columns that create a dense, vibrating texture across the entire surface.
*   A rich color palette of vibrant **terracotta red**, **slate blue**, and a muted **cream** or tan background.

Such papers were highly prized for their aesthetic appeal and their ability to disguise the adhesives and structural elements of the book's binding.

<summary>A decorative marbled endpaper featuring a traditional terracotta and blue nonpareil comb pattern, used as a functional and aesthetic lining for the manuscript's cover.</summary>

-># **Decorative Marbled Endpaper**<-

This page features a full-page decorative **marbled paper** pattern, a traditional technique used to beautify and reinforce the **endpapers** <term>endpapers: the sheets of paper at the very beginning and end of a book; one half is typically pasted to the inside of the cover to help secure the book block to its binding</term> of high-quality volumes.

The design is a classic example of a **comb pattern**, specifically the **nonpareil** style <term>nonpareil: a pattern created by drawing a fine-toothed comb through pigments floating on a liquid surface, resulting in delicate, repeating arches</term>. The pattern is made up of:

*   Tightly packed, rhythmic rows of downward-pointing scalloped arches.
*   Vertical columns that create a dense, vibrating texture across the entire surface.
*   A rich color palette of vibrant **terracotta red** (orange-red), **slate blue** (dark teal-grey), and a muted **cream** or off-white background.

<note>This specific style of marbling was particularly popular in the 18th and 19th centuries, often used by bookbinders to provide a durable and visually striking finish that could hide the adhesives and structural materials used to attach the leather or cloth to the boards.</note>

The "feather-like" or "peacock" shapes visible in the design are achieved by a master craftsman moving a stylus or a specialized comb through floating pigments before transferring the image onto a sheet of paper.

<summary>A decorative marbled endpaper featuring a traditional terracotta and blue nonpareil comb pattern, used as a functional and aesthetic lining for the manuscript's cover.</summary>
<keywords>marbled paper, endpaper, nonpareil pattern, comb pattern, bookbinding, terracotta, slate blue, peacock pattern</keywords>

-># **Exterior Leather Binding**<-

The manuscript is bound in a dark brown leather cover, which serves as both its primary protection and a decorative statement. This binding shows significant evidence of its history through heavy wear and specific decorative techniques.

The cover features several artisanal details:
*   A border of three parallel lines of **gold tooling** <term>gold tooling: a decorative technique where gold leaf is pressed into the leather using heated brass stamps or wheels</term> runs along the left edge, near the spine.
*   The four corners are adorned with ornate **floral stamps** or **fleur-de-lis** ornaments <note>The fleur-de-lis is a stylized lily frequently used in heraldry and bookbinding to denote elegance or specific French influence.</note>, impressed into the leather in gold.

The physical condition of the leather tells a story of long-term use and environmental exposure:
*   The surface is heavily worn with deep cracking and scuffing.
*   There is significant loss of the top grain of the leather, particularly at the top and left edges, where the material has peeled away to reveal the fibrous structure beneath.

<note>While the binding is currently distressed, the presence of gold tooling suggests this was originally a high-quality production, intended for a library of some status.</note>

<summary>A distressed dark brown leather book binding featuring gold-tooled borders and floral corner ornaments, showing significant age-related wear and leather loss.</summary>
